en: Dharma is the foundation of the entire world;
[this is] the Prājña Pāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala Granthamālā Mīmāṃsā Koṣa.
Fifth Part: (Pa-Va) Editor:
Kevalānandasarasvatī
Mārgaśīrṣa Kṛṣṇa 10, Tuesday, Śaka 1882. This fifth volume was published by the hand of His Excellency the President of the Republic of India, Śrī Rājendra Prasad.
Mārgaśīrṣa Kṛṣṇa 10, Śaka 1882.

Table of Contents: Publisher’s Preface … … … … 1–8 The Essence of the Life of Śrī Kevalānandayati … … … … 9–14 Abridged Letters on the Text, etc., and Their Explanations … … … 2409–2995 Mīmāṃsākoṣa … … … … … 2409–2995 Publisher’s Preface
A long period of three years elapsed between the publication of the fourth volume of the *Mīmāṃsākoṣa* and the publication of the fifth volume.
The reason for this was that the manuscript prepared by the venerable teacher had to be revised once more.

Śrī Durgā Rāma Śāstrī, known by the surname Upādhye, undertook this task of revision; he corrected the draft of this volume—which had been written by the teacher—by following the method repeatedly demonstrated by Śrī Raṅganātha Śāstrī.
The proofreading and correction of this fifth volume were carried out with meticulous scrutiny by Śrī Raṅganātha Śāstrin, the editorial assistant of the Dharmakośa, according to the previous method.
His Holiness’s Guru also placed his trust in Śrī Raṅganātha Śāstrin’s capacity to perform such work;
indeed, the Guru engaged in repeated consultations with him to eliminate any deficiencies or excesses.

It has been our long-standing experience that Śrī Raṅganātha Śāstrin finds mental composure only upon the attainment of excellence in qualities; therefore, placing full trust in him, we have entrusted to him the work on the *Dharmakośa*.

The number of topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) is as follows: in this fifth volume, there are 99 *bhāṣya* topical sections, 43 *Saṃkarṣa* topical sections, 134 topical sections from the *Nandī-vṛtti* alone, 25 Tautātika topical sections, 127 *nyāyas*, and 4,484 minor conclusions (*laghusiddhāntas*).

Now, beginning from the first part, there are 698 *bhāṣya* sections, 227 *saṃkarṣa* sections, 590 sections from the *Nandīvṛtti* alone, 61 *tautātika* sections, 1,032 *nyāyas*, and 17,647 *laghusiddhāntas*.
Mārgaśīrṣa, dark fortnight, 10th day.
Lakṣmaṇa Śāstrī Jośī, Tarkatīrtha, Director of the Prājña Pāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala and Chief Editor of the Dharmakośa.

The essence of the life of the author of this treasury, the venerable Kevalānandayati, is as follows: he was one whose mind was tranquil due to the spiritual qualities born of yoga, who rescued the *Siddhitantra* from Jaimini.
I bow to that solitary, wise teacher, who is blessed, steadfast, the upholder of the fortune of liberation.
My guru, Śrī Kevalānandasvāmī, said: "Uttering the single-syllabled Brahman 'Om' and remembering Me, he who departs, casting off the body, attains the supreme goal."

Thus, following the established doctrine of the *Bhāgavata* as stated in *Bhagavad Gītā* 8.13, desiring non-return at the time of death, pronouncing the syllable "Oṃ"—the name of the Imperishable Brahman which is the gateway to liberation—while meditating upon the Lord who is its referent, he cast off his perishable body and attained the supreme state on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna in the Śaka year 1878.
Consequently, [this work] was composed in the *Mīmāṃsā-koṣa* immediately after his entry into the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

In accordance with the Jābāla Śruti, “One should renounce while still practicing the life of a religious student,” he completed his period of *brahmacarya* at the age of fifty-four and, having fulfilled the duties of his own established institution named “Prājña Pāṭhaśālā,” he entered the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

After embracing the life of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), and remaining devoted to the contemplation of its purpose until his final breath—intent upon the Dharma and Brahman—he, being a seeker of knowledge (*vividiṣu*), composed for the benefit of others the following works: (1) *Jaiminīyamīmāṃsāsūtrapāṭha* (printed), accompanied by a word-index, a sūtra-index, an inquiry into the designations of the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*), and a discussion of variant readings; (2) *Mīmāṃsākoṣa* (currently in the process of being printed); (3) *Kauṣītakibrāhmaṇāraṇyakaviṣayakoṣa* (printed); (4) *Aitareyabrāhmaṇāraṇyakaviṣayakoṣa* (printed); (5) *Taittirīyamantrasūcī* (unpublished); (6) *Taittirīyaśākhāviṣayasūcī* (unpublished); (7) *Satyāṣāḍhasūtraviṣayasūcī* (unpublished); (8) *Śāṅkarabhāṣyaparibhāṣākoṣa* (unpublished); (9) *Advaitasiddhi-marāṭhībhāṣāntara* (unpublished); and (10) *Navyavedāntaparamāṇumālikā*, a glossary of the technical statements of the established doctrines contained within the *Advaitasiddhi* (unpublished). These are the works he has produced.

By him, manuscripts of refined and unpublished works have been preserved and kept safely in the collection of the Prājña Pāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala Saṃsthā. We desire to undertake their printing and publication once the necessary funds are available.

This entire undertaking of composing the works was accomplished by him without any assistance in the form of money or other resources from others, considering the acceptance of wealth to be like a city of Vānta (vomit) according to the rules of the renunciant stage of life (*pravrajyāśrama*).
From his childhood until the time he took up the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), he sustained his life by means of alms sufficient merely to maintain the body, regarding them as nectar.

Since he had already renounced all worldly intentions even in his youth, his formal adoption of the ascetic life consisted merely of a change in external appearance; this indicates that his conduct was consistent with the stage of celibate studenthood (*brahmacarya*).
There is no fault of digression in recounting the essence of his life story here, so we shall relate it briefly.
From childhood until the end of my life, my mental disposition was inclined toward the gods;
however, upon merely hearing the exposition of the Upaniṣadic passages from one who belongs to the lineage of Nārāyaṇa, my intellect became absorbed in that [Brahman].
Thus, the grace of the true Guru alone has borne fruit, according to the saying: "The immediate realization arises from the word itself."
From Kāśī as far as Rāmeśvara, the fame of Mata Svāmī’s exposition of the Śārīraka Bhāṣya had spread.
Many scholars, having come to the city of Vārāṇasī, would return only after having beheld Mata Svāmī and heard his discourses.

At night, during moments of solitude, Mata Svāmī was devoted to the surrender to God (īśvarapraṇidhāna), either chanting the Sāmans or performing the congregational recitation of the Lord’s names, saying, “Viṭṭhala, Viṭṭhala! Victory, victory to Viṭṭhala!”
In the year 1826 Śaka, in the month of Āśvina, an outbreak of plague occurred in Vāīgrāma.
On the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) of that same month, due to the contagion of the plague, my master abandoned this body—which was afflicted by the three humors—and merged into the infinite Brahman.
Subsequently, beginning from the year 1887 Śaka, I commenced the exposition of the *Śāṅkara-gītā*, the *Upaniṣads*, and the *Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya*.

"I resolved that my life should be spent solely in self-study, teaching, and austerity; thus, at the age of twenty-three—though not yet old—I considered my physical, mental, and intellectual strength to be favorable [for such a path]. I also determined that I should not enter the householder's stage of life.

For I perceived that the householder's life cannot be undertaken without the acquisition of wealth, and that the acquisition of wealth generally cannot be accomplished without the faults of worldly activity, flattery, fawning, and a lack of self-respect."

I repeatedly reflected that dependence upon others is extremely difficult to endure and that self-elevation is impossible therein; thus, I resolved again and again that I would live in falsehood for as long as I lived.
From my twenty-third year until my sixty-third year, up until the moment I took up *saṃnyāsa*, I carried out my life considering teaching and austerity to be my primary duties.
Excluding bathing, counting [mantras], yoga practice, begging for alms, eating, and sleep during the third watch of the day and thereafter, all of my time was spent in study and teaching.
From time to time, in accordance with the circumstances, I also performed some work for social and political movements.
This portion has been extracted from the autobiography of my guru Kevalānanda, written in the Marathi language, and is presented here after being translated into Sanskrit.
In the year 1901 of the Christian era, my guru began his teaching, having obtained a residence in the house of Śambhu Bhaṭṭa, belonging to the Goḍabole family.

Three or four students, having first arrived for the purpose of studying Sanskrit, stayed with him for over two years. After that, Goḍabole left his home and established a Sanskrit school named Prājña Maṭha at his own guru’s residence, located near the Prastaraghaṭṭa on the banks of the Kṛṣṇā River at Gaṅgāpuṇya, for the sake of residing there.

In this school, approximately thirty students resided; they studied the five great epics (*pañcamahākāvya*), the *Viṣṇubhāgavata*, grammar, Vedānta, Nyāya, Dharmaśāstra, and other philosophical systems (*darśana*).
Those who had entered the highest class taught the students in the first class in order to lighten the burden of the teacher’s duties.
Devoted to both study and teaching, these students gradually became trained and acquired proficiency in the work of instruction.
Following this system of instruction, one teacher emerged from another like a lamp from a lamp;

the method of education was pursued in the Prājña Maṭha in accordance with ancient Indian tradition. However, the emphasis placed on the memorization of texts through oral recitation was maintained with as much rigor in that ancient tradition as possible.
"Oṃ tat sat— this is declared to be the threefold designation of Brahman" (Bhagavad Gītā 17.23). Our teacher did not adopt such a rigid insistence.
Therefore, the rote memorization of the lexicon has been abandoned.

In place of the recitation of the lexicon, other literary works have been introduced into the curriculum for the purpose of oral memorization. Furthermore, even the excellent erotic poetry found in the works of Kālidāsa and others has been refined according to the sequence of the syllabus.
Some modern subjects as well—such as history, geography, secular literature, and physical science—have been included in the curriculum.
Bearing in mind that knowledge of the modern Western cultures prevalent in worldly affairs is necessary, books on those topics have also been incorporated into the course of study.

Our teacher, Nārāyaṇa Śākhin, adopted such a system of instruction for his own institution so that a scholar and religious instructor might become conversant with the conditions of the present time and place.
Regarding *Prājñamaṭha*: it is now described as it was obtained on that occasion under the name of *Prājña Pāṭhaśālā*.

A national school, renowned by the name "Samartha Vidyalaya," was established in a forest near the village of *Talegaon Dabhade* in the Pune district by certain modern-educated individuals of their own country who desired to liberate their land from foreign subjection, honoring Viṣṇu, the son of Govinda, born of the Karakula lineage of Vijayapura.

In the year 1910 CE, the British authorities destroyed the Samarth Vidyalaya on the charge that, under the guise of national education, it was teaching opposition to and rebellion against British rule. Several mature students remained at Prājñamaṭha to re-establish the system of national education and for the purpose of studying Vedānta.

It was enjoined upon these students that they should undertake a fourfold program of action: the procurement of goods manufactured solely within one’s own country, the exclusion of goods produced in foreign lands, the exertion of effort for the sake of self-rule, and the promotion of national education.

Among them, Dinakara Śāstrī of the Kānaḍe family and Mahādeva Śāstrī of the Divekara family, keeping in mind that national education should be introduced at the Prājña Maṭha, rendered assistance to the Principal, Nārāyaṇa Śāstri.

In the year 1916 of the Christian era, in the month of September, corresponding to the month of Āśvina in the Śaka year 1838, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight (Vijayā-daśamī), the Prājña Maṭha was given the name "Prājña Pāṭhaśālā. For this school, a rule was established that the life of the students should consist of acquiring knowledge where they reside, rather than living in their individual homes and studying at a separate school.
In the residential quarters for students, a specific system for the various activities of the students was also prescribed, beginning from morning until bedtime at night.

It was as follows: at dawn, immediately upon waking, all students would assemble in one place to recite the Vedic hymns (*sūkta*) to be remembered in the morning, the praises of the deities, and songs imbued with patriotic devotion to the nation; they would perform acts of purification such as brushing their teeth, bathe in cold water, perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*), and engage in physical exercise such as sun-salutations (*sūryanamaskāra*). There would be collective prayers by teachers and students, and until the time for midday meals, they would engage in study in class groups according to the secondary and higher education curricula. All would eat together, followed by a rest after lunch at midday. Then, study would resume until the evening twilight. At the time of twilight, they would engage in physical exercise or games either in the playground or in the gymnasium. This included the evening twilight worship, dinner, private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), and retiring to bed; in this manner, [the routine continued] on non-holiday days.

I accepted the view of my venerable teacher that these [tasks] ought to be relinquished as being appropriate; thus, more than three years ago, I ceased all work related to that branch [of the Veda] by the consensus of all, while continuing until now the work on the *Dharmakośa*, the training in Sanskrit learning, and other activities.

Following that, my venerable teacher remained for a long time in the state of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), engaged in the contemplation of the Jaiminīya and Bādarāyaṇīya Mīmāṃsās regarding the sacred fires and their rituals, in the composition of treatises based on that study, and in the practice of meditation.

And when the time for departure arrived, having uttered aloud the recitation of the single-syllabled Brahman, the *praṇava*, which they had chanted for a long time, continuously and without interruption, they merged solely into Brahman.

It has been resolved by the Prājña Pathashala Mandal Samstha that the task of printing and publishing the works composed by them must be carried out as an offering (*umāpākaraṇa*) to the feet of the Guru.
With this, the brief presentation of the essence of the life of these venerable teachers is concluded.

Since this is a statement regarding the slaughter of those [females], the entire procedure—including the disemboweling and so forth—which is obtained through the force of the *codaka* (the archetypal injunction), is performed.
Therefore, there is no cutting [of the omentum] in those [animals].
By the masculine form in the phrase "they release the draft-oxen" (*pretarān utsṛjanti*), the draft-oxen (*anaḍvāhaḥ*) are referred to.

Regarding them, there is a doubt: do they, having entered into syntactic unity with the draft-oxen according to the procedure ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire), not take up the subsidiary parts by means of the *codaka* (general rule of transfer)—just as in the case of wild animals—or is there a prohibition of the ritual refinements (*saṃskāra*) at the time of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), as in the case of the *prājāpatya* offerings?

What, then, is the established position? This is a prohibition of the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*). At this time, the oxen to be sacrificed are not to undergo the preparatory rites, just as in the case of the *prājāpatya* offerings.
"One should sacrifice three-year-old [animals] on a single day"— this is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding the animal sacrifices during the *sutyā* days,

just as in the case of "one offers the *brahmāsamidh* fuel-sticks. However, if there were a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action, then the phrase "those various ones" would imply the assumption of a separate ritual action to be performed every year.
And regarding the phrase "three cows":
there, much unseen [result] would have to be postulated.
But if it is a prohibition of the consecration, then for those very [animals], in the second year, at the end of the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite, [the rule applies to] the ox.
[Objection: Only a preparatory act (*saṃskāra*) is enjoined, not a sacrifice (*yāga*).
[Reply: No, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction (*codanā*).
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): This is not so; it is not a prohibition of the preparatory act.
How then? It is a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action.
Why? Because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction.
"He prepares seventeen speckled butter-portions" is an injunction of a ritual action, because it designates a substance and a deity.
This [sentence], "seventeen spotted ones for the Uṣan," forms a single syntactical unit with that [preceding sentence].
How is this known? Because the sentence "seventeen spotted ones for the Uṣan" is incomplete by itself; it is completed by depending on that [preceding part], namely, "he obtains the Māktānas."
This being the case, it necessarily follows that there is a subsequent injunction (*anupajña*).
And thus, because of their equality, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Why, then, is it said that "there is unity of sentence with the injunction" (*codanaikavākyatvāt*)?
He said:
If that [word] is expected as a supplement to this, then it is not a subsequent addition (*anupajña*);
but if this [word] is [a supplement] to that, then there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*).
We consider this to be dependent upon that as its subordinate element (*śeṣa*). And this is logical here: that this [element] should be subordinate to that, but not that [element] to this.
If that were merely a matter of mutual expectation regarding the husband, then the other expectation would have to be experienced as well.
And it would be connected with the purpose;
thus, the meaning "he makes seventeen spotted animals anointed" and "seventeen spotted ones anointed" need not be stated,
for it is understood from the accumulation itself.
Therefore, by this single sentence, these twenty-four rites are enjoined.
Of those seventeen, the release is performed at the conclusion of the *paryagnikaraṇa*;
for the remaining seventeen, it is according to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
The same applies to the subsequent objections as well.
Furthermore, it is not logical for those [dharmas] that have been relinquished to be employed in another action,
because they no longer exist and because they have lost their potency.
Therefore, starting from that point, there is a prohibition against the remainder of the ritual action.
Furthermore, they are said to be "pure" (ukṣāṇaḥ) in various ways.
Due to the absence of the previous animal sacrifice (paśu), there is an abandonment of the original context (prakṛtahāna).
The expiation also applies to those [animals] after they have been consecrated (*upākṛta*) but before their release (*utsarga*).

Furthermore, the statement regarding "expectation" (*apekṣā*)—namely, that one should not expect others but rather those very ones, such as the speckled ones for the Maruts—would apply just as in the case of the injunction: "He cuts out a piece from that very sacrificial cake (*yajñāṃśa*) and spreads it out."
"These very same herbs, that very same partridge. [Dvaidhādhikaraṇa:
"He prepares seventeen speckled animals for the Maruts"—this is an injunction for a sacrifice because of the connection between the substance and the deity.
Since the statement "seventeen speckled [animals]" is dependent, it must be completed by supplying the missing elements of the action.
In that case, the requirement for syntactic expectancy is satisfied by the very fact that "he sacrifices to the Maruts" (*mārutīr ālabhate*) is revolving in the mind.
And here there are two possible courses:
either the phrase "he sacrifices to the Maruts" is supplied in connection with the oxen (*anaḍvāhaḥ*).
Alternatively, even in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice animals dedicated to Māruta," oxen are also led forward.
In that context, the oxen are dependent [on the same time];
for at the very moment the three-year-old heifers are connected [to the ritual], at that same moment the oxen are also connected.
In this way, there will be a mutual relationship and syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*).

Otherwise, one would have to assume a further expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for that which has already been rendered expectant-free in the preceding sentence; only then could there be a connection again. Therefore, "by a single sentence, twenty-four rites are enjoined" (this is the *Bhāṣya*, with a slight variation).

But surely the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) also accepts that there are twenty-four rites and that they form a single syntactical unit; he merely does not accept the prohibition of the remaining rites (but rather, like the *prājāpatya* sacrifice, he accepts the prohibition of the consecratory rite [saṃskāra] expressed in "they release them after they have been encircled by fire").
And he (the proponent of the prima facie view) is not refuted by this (explanation of the Commentator).

Therefore, how is this [sūtra] "Because of being a single sentence" (*ekavākyatvāt*) explained? It is said: In the case of the *prājāpatya* animals, the prohibition of consecratory rites (*saṃskāra-pratiṣedha*) exists by virtue of the force of the counter-exception (*pratiprasava-vākya*), namely, "He sacrifices the Brahmasāman.

While that [prohibition] exists, there is either a restatement (*anuvāda*) or a prohibition of the rites, as in "They release them after they have been carried around the fire" (*paryagnikṛtānutsṛjanti*).
But here [in the present case], it says: "One should sacrifice three on each day, and five on the final day."
Regarding the section on the Pañcaśāradīya sacrifice: it is not possible to perform the *pratisava* at the time of the *sutyā* based on the scriptural statement (*vākya*).

In this context, if one were to offer those five [animals] which are prescribed here, and those same ones on another day—since this would result in a prescription of two distinct meanings while treating them as subordinate qualities (*guṇa*)—there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
The same logic should be applied to the phrase "three animals" (*trīn paśūn*).

Therefore, this is a separate ritual action belonging to the time of the *sutyā* sacrifice (and since there is a prescription of something previously unknown at that time, there is syntactical unity); such is the meaning of the Sūtra.

He states another interpretation: Furthermore, for one [proponent] in whose view the consecration (*saṃskāra*) is prohibited, the ritual of carrying fire around the victim (*paryagnikaraṇa*) would not apply in the second year (because it has already been performed).

Therefore, that [consecration] must first be enjoined, and the abandonment (*utsarga*) must also be enjoined; since there is a difference in purpose (*arthabheda*) in those two cases, there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
And there would be a difference in the intended meaning (*vivakṣābheda*) [in the case of *paryagnikaraṇam*]:

in one instance (regarding the heifers), the *paryagnikaraṇa* is performed as established by the archetype; in the other instance (regarding the oxen), since the *paryagnikaraṇa* has already been performed previously, it does not apply again, and thus the *paryagnikaraṇa* is prescribed where it was not otherwise applicable.
It is improper for that which has been performed once to be performed again.
"And because of the observation of the ritual preparations (saṃskāra).

Commentary: Furthermore, he demonstrates the ritual preparations performed every year, stating: "They immolate those [animals] that have been encircled by fire and sprinkled; they yoke the draft animals for the deceased. But [one might object]: "Does not this statement refer to a specific occasion?"

No, because it would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*): "He performs the circumambulation with fire" (*paryagnikaraṇaṃ karoti*) and "They release the animals once they have been circumambulated with fire" (*paryagnikṛtāṃstrotsṛjanti*).
Furthermore, the circumambulation with fire for both the heifers (*vatsatarī*) and the bulls (*ukṣan*) is stated to occur simultaneously;
since that [circumambulation] is already established for the heifers by virtue of the archetype (*prakṛti*), it must apply elsewhere.
In the other cases, because [the quality] has not been previously established, it is enjoined; this is not tenable.
When the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) exist, both of these are inappropriate;
and [this applies to] the sacrifice as well.
Therefore, there is a sacrifice in both cases.
The connection with the example is as in the case of the *Soma-prājāpatya*.
As for the meaning of the Sūtra: even the animals of the Pañcaśāradīya sacrifice are elevated [to the status of being offered] like those of the Prājāpatya.
Vi—“Is the *ukṣotsarga* (the release of a bull) a case of excellence (*utkarṣa*) or of abandonment (*tyāga*)? Here, as before, it is the former;
the other two [options] involve the transposition (*utkrama*) of the two [terms] and the omission (*lopa*) of the word ‘five’ (*pañcatva*).”
Due to the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there would be an injunction for other specific actions;
therefore, let the abandonment of the forest-dwelling be accepted as the ritual disposal (*utsarga*).

Bhaṭṭa: The sacrifice called Pañcaśāradīya is a five-day *ahīna* sacrifice enjoined for a specific result: "He who desires, 'May I have many cattle,' he should sacrifice with this. In that context, on the new moon day of Vaiśākha, [the text says]: "Having consecrated seventeen *mārutī* animals with their necks turned away, [he offers] seventeen speckled and rough ones; having carried fire around them and sprinkled them, they immolate the others and release the remaining ones; then, after a year, they bring the *rājīva* ones; having approached them in the same manner and carried fire around them," and so forth, as before.

In the third and fourth years, because of the feminine gender used in the designation, the performance of the five [sacrifices] by women collectively is mentioned, as is the release of the bulls after they have been circumambulated with fire; then, in the fifth year, it is heard in the scripture: "The initiated one himself should sacrifice three bulls on the fifth day.

[They are] three-year-old heifers (*trivatsāḥ*), meaning three years old; *apra-vītāḥ*, meaning not yet having calved; *pṛśnīḥ*, meaning small-bodied; and *rājīvāḥ*, meaning having the color of a lotus (*rājīvam* means a lotus).
On this point, some maintain that even the females are indeed cows.

In this context, regarding the sentence "māstān" (do not touch them), which is the opposite of the [previous] "upākaroti" (dedicates), that too constitutes a separate sentence because of the difference in number.
And how there is a distinction of ritual acts (*karmabheda*) due to number in this sentence has been explained in the *Kaustubha*.

And regarding this, the Commentator [Bhāṣyakāra] maintains that because the single term "upākaroti" (he dedicates) is connected to both the cows and the men, this constitutes a single sentence that enjoins thirty-four rites.
However, we consider it more logical that these are indeed separate sentences.

In this regard, there arises a deliberation: Is it that those very bulls (*ukṣan*) who were consecrated by fire (*paryagnikṛta*) in the first year are themselves the ones for whom the rites beginning with the fire-consecration are performed in the second year and so on, such that in the fifth year their slaughter (*ālambha*) occurs during the four *sutyā* days—three each time—with the postponement (*utkarṣa*) of the slaughter occurring on the sixty-fourth day, just as in the case of the *prājāpatya* bulls? Or rather, is it that in each successive year other bulls are consecrated by fire according to the prescribed ritual procedure, and the rite is completed right then and there (with the *āraṇya-patnīvat* formula), while in the fifth year, different bulls altogether are slaughtered during those respective *sutyā* days? In this deliberation, due to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), the postponement of the slaughter applies to those same bulls, just as in the case of the *prājāpatya* bulls.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement, there is a repeated performance of the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) and other rites even for those animals already subjected to it; by the force of that word, it refers back specifically to those previously mentioned. As for the term "utsṛjati" (releases), it is merely restated as being already established by the displacement of the *ālambha* (seizing). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: since there is no displacement of the *ālambha*, and because the injunction "three black ones" would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if multiple qualities were enjoined simultaneously, these are enjoined as distinct rituals based on their specific qualities; there is no displacement of the *ālambha* here.
Likewise, in the case of the expression "pañcocame'hani" (on the fifth day from the last), there is also the prescription of multiple objects.

For this very reason, the view that—in the case of "pañcocame'hani"—since three [sacrifices] each are obtained for the remaining twelve days by the principle of "it should be equal, as nothing is heard to the contrary" (*samaṃ syādaśrutatvāt*) when five are prescribed for the last day, the phrase "trīn ahān" (three days) is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), is refuted.
This is because [the distribution] is already obtained even in the case of "pañcottame" (five on the last).

The section on the Pañcaśāradīya sacrifice: because there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda) if both the time and the number were prescribed by way of restatement (anuvāda) regarding the five-year periods.

Uttamāha says: because there is no evidence for this [sacrifice] being the locus [of the injunction] when five [days] are prescribed by the word *deśena* (by way of location), and because it would result in the non-attainment of a specific desired fruit;
therefore, since the capacity for both time and number is restricted to a distinct action (*karmāntara*), these seventeen [actions] are enjoined by two sentences.

Consequently, due to the absence of an injunction for transference (*utkarṣa*), these distinct actions—characterized by the subsidiaries ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa*—are enjoined to be performed with different deities in each successive year, beginning from the first.
Consequently, there is a fivefold division every year;
and in the fifth [year], there is a repetition of the rites ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa* and the branding.
And the word "that" (*tat*) [is used] because, despite the difference in individual instances, they belong to the same class.
The attainment of the quality of being "good" (san) through the act of touching is not contradictory;
as Maṇḍana states: "But the three sacrifices would occur for one who desires [them].
That which is enjoined by the word "three" is indeed something unprecedented (apūrva).

Śaṅkara says: "In the Pañcaśāradīya sacrifice, there would be a distinction of rites. The five *saṃcaras*—namely, the five oblations beginning with that for Agni which circulate through all five [sacrifices] during the Vaiśvadeva section of the Cāturmāsya—are called the 'five *saṃcaras*'."
(These first five—namely, "He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a pap to Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Pūṣan"—are thus enjoined.
Bhāṣya:
In the case of the five sacrifices, there is an extension of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) because of their proximity.

In the Vaiśvadeva section of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, five oblations known as the *pañcasaṃcaras* are prescribed along with their explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), as follows: "He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a pap to Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Pūṣan.

However, in the Varuṇapraghāsa sections, only the oblations are recited; the explanatory passage for the Vaiśvadeva is extended there by the statement: "These five oblations have the same explanatory passage, namely those of the others.
Here, "the others" refers to the Vaiśvadeva oblations.

In this regard, is there an extension (*atideśa*) of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) alone, or of the entire section (*kāṇḍa*), including both the explanatory passage and the injunction (*vidhi*)?
Regarding this, he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*):

among the five oblations beginning with the *Āgneya* in the five-day sacrifice (*pañca-saṃcara*), specifically in the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, there would be an extension of the explanatory passage of the Vaiśvadeva [section] alone.
Because of proximity;
that is, because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is proximate through forming a single syntactical unit.
They "move about" (saṃcaranti) and "stand near" (upatiṣṭhante) during all four seasonal festivals (parvan), and thus they are called "moving" (saṃcarāṇi); these are the five oblations (havīṃṣi).
Because of the identity of the word for the whole.

In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, by the statement, "These five oblations have this very Brāhmaṇa; those others have this Brāhmaṇa," there would be an extended application (atideśa) of the entire section belonging to the Vaiśvadeva parvan—including both the explanatory passages (arthavāda) and the injunctions—on account of the identity of the word, and not merely of the explanatory passages alone.
This is because of the identity of the word.
This single word "Brāhmaṇa" belongs equally to the injunctions (*vidhi*) and the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
Just as it includes the explanatory passages, so too does it include the injunctions.

Those for whom there is a single word [common to both] are the explanatory passages and their subject matter; they are called "single-worded," and the state of being such is "single-wordedness" (*ekaśabdyam*).
On account of the unity of the word, there should be an extension (atideśa) of the entire section;
the word "or" (vā) is for the purpose of setting aside the prima facie view;
because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga).

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) demonstrates the extension (*atideśa*) of the entire section—including both the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the injunctions (*vidhi*)—belonging to the *vaiśvadeva* sub-section within the five-fold *varuṇapraghāsa* sacrifices.

It shows thirty oblations in the *varuṇapraghāsa* sacrifices through the statement: "Thirty oblations should be offered; they sacrifice to the *vājina*s for the sake of the perfection of the oblations, because of their number being thirty."

Only when there exists a relationship as subsidiary elements to the injunctions for both the auxiliary and the principal rites does the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) become appropriate—namely, that in the subsequent sacrificial session (*uttara-vihāra*) there are two *ājyabhāga* offerings, eight oblations (*havīṃṣi*), nine *prayāja*s, nine *anuyāja*s, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, and the *vājinahoma*.
If the injunctions were not extended by analogy (*atideśa*), that would not be possible. Therefore, the injunctions themselves are also extended by analogy.
"If it is argued that [the procedure] is prescribed by the mention of various foods"—
thus the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) objects.
For even in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, certain ritual details (dharmas) belonging to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice are also prescribed.
For example, in the passage "They churn the fire; the *prasū* grasses are used," the meaning is that the sacrificial grasses (*barhis*) are lush and flourishing.
If there were an extension (*atideśa*) of the injunctions themselves, the restatement of those [grass-related details] already established by such an extension would be purposeless.
Therefore, there is no extension of the injunctions from what has been enjoined; rather, there is an extension of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) alone.
If this is argued, we say no, because it serves another purpose;
in that case, because it serves another purpose.

Injunctions such as "One churns the fire" and "The *prasuva* [libations] take place" pertain to the *āptvya* oblations to be performed in the southern sacrificial shed (*dakṣiṇavihāra*); therefore, this serves as an indicator that there is no extension (*atideśa*) of these injunctions.
Consequently, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is an extension of both the injunctions and the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices.
Who [holds this view]?

In the section on the five sacrifices (pañcasaṃcerāḥ), specifically regarding the fifth [sacrifice] among the Vāruṇapraghāsikas, there is an extended application (atideśa) of the section containing the injunctions and explanatory passages (arthavāda) pertaining to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
The touching of the oblation with the Pañcahotṛ formula takes place on the new moon day.
(And since the Pañcahotṛ mantra has been mentioned in the passage "Agnihotrā, Pañcahotrām," [the formula begins] "Agnihotrā | Aśvināvadhvaryū |")
"The mantra is: *laṣṭāram iṣṭe mitram upavaktāraṃ*.
The touching (*abhimarśana*) with the *pañcahotṛ* and *caturhotṛ* mantras is prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), not prompted by the aggregate [of the sacrifice].

Bhāṣya 9.1.11–19. Regarding the *pañcahotṛ* and *caturhotṛ* mantras, which serve as the instruments for the touching of the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) in the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between them in the *saurya* sacrifice.
[This is discussed] in the fifth chapter.
Now, the definition of the rule of sequence is stated here.
That [sequence] will be explained through the primacy of direct statement (*śruti*), purpose (*artha*), the order of recitation (*pāṭha*), and so forth,
as well as the relative strength and weakness of direct statement and the other criteria.
Bhāṣya 5.1.1:
"Or rather—the order of the Vedic text (*śruti*), the order of meaning (*artha*), and the order of recitation (*pāṭha*) pertain exclusively to the domain of direct instruction (*upadeśa*).

However, the order of performance (*pravṛtti*) and the order of the principal [action] (*mukhya-krama*) pertain even to the domain of extended application (*atideśa*), as they concern the constituent elements (*padārtha*) which are the primary factors."
The agent is subordinate;
for him who performs the performance according to each primary element, the sequence is already established. However, the rule regarding that sequence is now being considered.

Vi— "The specific distinctions of sequence [are established] by direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth in the context of the increase of rain; and the *liptā* [sequence] follows from direct statement and so forth. These are the sections of the fifth chapter.
In the first section (*pāda*) of the fifth chapter, the sequence based on direct statement, meaning, textual order, and ritual function (*dharma*) is defined.
In the second [section], there is a specific order, such as the similarity of individual characteristics among the animals belonging to the Vājapeya sacrifice.

In the third, there is increase, such as the eleven-fold nature resulting from the repetition of the five fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and so forth; and there is the absence of increase, such as the non-repetition of the *āgrayaṇa-graha* and the *citriṇī*. In the fourth, there is the relative strength and weakness of the factors that determine order, namely direct statement (*śruti*), purpose (*artha*), textual sequence (*pāṭha*), and so on.
Introductory Verse:
17. "In the Second Āditya, that which was proclaimed through the applications of the remaining *medas* is understood as the fifth stage, the sequence of performance to be carried out."
Bhaṭṭa: Thus, having established the range of purposes common to both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary rites (*pradhāna*), the order based on performance (*prayoga*) is now being examined.
For it will be stated that the subsidiaries and the primary rites are enjoined by one and the same injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*).

And therefore, since the performance of all [actions] together is intended by virtue of a single injunction, and because it is inevitable that there must be some order when multiple actions are performed simultaneously by a single agent, six means of proof (*pramāṇa*)—known as *śruti*, *artha*, *pāṭha*, *sthāna*, *mukhya*, and *pravṛtti*—will be examined as the determinants of that order.
In the fifth chapter, the mere sequence of those actions performed in separate ritual applications was incidentally discussed;
however, the actual subject matter of the chapter is sequence itself, applicable equally to both immediate and remote [connections].
And so forth.

Thus, the fifth verbal suffix (the optative) is used in its literal sense for prohibition, as in "He does not cut the grass" (*na saṃtṛṇatti*) and "He does not offer the *dīdhiti* oblation" (*dīdhito na juhoti*).
(Bālam Bhaṭṭī, p. 40). The fifth verbal suffix is used in its literal sense for injunction, as in "He performs the *samit* sacrifice" (*samidho yajati*).
The Smṛti [tradition] is as follows; Manu (2.29) says: "The birth-rite (jātakarma) is prescribed for the male before the cutting of the umbilical cord.
And (2.28): "By means of the great sacrifices (mahāyajña) and the [Vedic] sacrifices, the body is made fit for Brahman (brāhmī)."
But the fifth lakāra form is doubtful because it is expressed in the present tense. Vārttika 1.2.122, p. 136. The fifth [lakāra] (according to the *Bhāṭṭacintāmaṇi*).

The meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is "the state of being an *apādāna*," according to the rule *apādāne pañcamī* (Pāṇini 2.3.28). And the state of being an *apādāna* consists in being the locus of a separation produced by an action inherent in another [entity]. Its definition is: "being the locus of a separation while not being the locus of the action that causes that separation," according to the rule *dhruvam apāye ’pādānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.24).
*Apāya* (separation) is that which is denoted by terms such as "vibhāga" (division) and "viyoga" (disjunction).

When division, disjunction, or the like occurs in another thing—which serves as the locus of that division or disjunction—that which remains fixed (*dhruvam*) and stable (*sthiram*) as the locus of the division or disjunction, meaning it is the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of the division or disjunction, is the *apādāna*. This is the meaning of the rule. For example: "The leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ patati*).
The meaning of *pat* (to fall) is an action conducive to a conjunction with what is below;

or rather, an action that is the cause of a disjunction which itself brings about a conjunction with what is below. And thus, because the tree is the substratum of such an action and is the substratum of the disjunction produced by that action, it possesses the status of an *apādāna* (ablative).

And thus, the final conclusion is that [the object] possesses such an action as its fruit, because, while not being the locus of the action that produces the result of cutting the connection with those respective substrates, it is the determiner of the result produced by such an action.

And thus, in cases such as "he fears the thief or the tiger," "he protects from the thief," "he is defeated in study," "he keeps the cow away from the barley," "he hides from his mother," "he studies under the teacher," "the subjects are born from Brahmā," and "the Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat," regarding the causes of fear and so forth, and the taking [of objects] such as theft, the following *kāraka* designations apply according to Pāṇini’s rules: *apādānaṃ syād bhayādihetucoryādīnādāneṣu* (Pā. 1.4.25); *parājer asoḍhaḥ* (Pā. 1.4.26); *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ* (Pā. 1.4.27); *antardhau yenādarśanam icchati* (Pā. 1.4.28); *ākhyātopayoge* (Pā. 1.4.29); *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Pā. 1.4.30).
In the rule *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.31), the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative) is indeed primary (*mukhya*) as established by grammatical instruction.
Here, the meaning of the root *bibhī* (to fear) is an action conducive to removal (*apahava*),
and the momentary state conducive to that [removal] arises from the root *jan* (to be born).
The action that produces illness is defeated (*parājayate*).
The action conducive to traveling to a distant land is warded off (*vāryate*).
The action conducive to the absence of sight is hidden (*nīlīyate*).

The meaning is as follows: the activity conducive to the repeated utterance [of the Veda] from the presence of the Guru is the sense of the root *adhī-* (to study). The activity conducive to origination is the sense of the root *jan-* (to be born).
The activity of the mouth and other organs that produces manifestation is what descends upon the *apūrva* (unseen potency).

Grammarians and Mīmāṃsakas maintain that because [the forest] does not serve as the substratum for that [fear], yet it is the determiner of the action associated with it, the grammatical rules (anuśāsana) such as "the cause of fear is the *apādāna* of things to be investigated" (*mīmāṃsārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ*) indicate its status as an *apādāna*, rather than indicating that the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) is an "adjunct-case ending" (*upapadavibhakti*).
Since formless entities (*arūpyādi*) lack the quality of being a determiner, they do not possess the status of an *apādāna*.
For this very reason, the expression "he fears from the forest" (*araṇyād bibheti*) is not used.

If the usage "he fears from the forest" (*vanād bibheti*) occurs, then there is *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) of the word "forest" in the sense of a tiger or other predator residing in the forest.

In expressions such as "he cuts from the middle" (*madhyād avacati*), the status of *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) belongs to the lower portion, which is the locus of the separation and the factor that determines it, even though it is not the substratum of the action that causes the separation.

However, the Naiyāyikas, desiring that the status of *apādāna* consist solely in being the locus of separation, maintain that in cases like "he fears from the tiger" (*vyāghrād bibheti*), the usage is justified either through *lakṣaṇā* or by postulating a different action [namely, the tiger's causing fear].

Thus, in the expression "he falls from a running horse," although the horse is the locus (*āśraya*) of the action mentioned [in the sentence], its status as an *apādāna* (ablative point) is established because it lacks the nature of being the cause of the separation (*vibhāga*). Nor should it be argued: "In the case of 'the cloud moves away from the cloud,' how can the cloud have the status of an *apādāna*, since the separation produced by the actions of both is one and the same, and thus there is no locus of an action that produces that [specific] separation"? This objection is invalid because the actions producing the separation are distinct; therefore, the status of *apādāna* is established by taking into account one specific action [of the two].

In the expression "move away from each other" (*anyonyasmād apasarataḥ*), although the disjunction produced by the action of both is one and the same, the fact that each is the substratum of that [disjunction] is established by taking into account the respective action that produces it.

In the case of "the cloth falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣād vastraṃ patati*), this should be understood by taking into account the property of the action of falling. However, this is not the case for the expression "it vibrates from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt spandate*).
This is because [the usage] exists in such forms as "departed from the cave" (*guhāccalitaḥ*) or "departed from the kingdom" (*rājyāccalitaḥ*).
However, some say that the ablative case is ungrammatical here because the fifth case (*pañcamī*) conveys the status of being the source (*apādāna*) of an action produced.
In the example "lightning flashes from the cloud" (*balāhakād vidyud vidyotate*), the case of the adjunct (*upapada-vibhakti*) is justified by supplying the word "having emerged" (*niḥsṛtya*).

Thus, according to the rule *anyārāditarartedikśabdāñcūttarapadājāhiyukte* (Pāṇini 2.3.29), the words *anya*, *ārāt*, *itara*, and so forth are included by the term *anya*. Examples are: *kṛṣṇād anyaḥ tiṣṭhati* ("someone other than Kṛṣṇa stands"), *ārād vanāt* ("near the forest"), *kṛṣṇād itaraḥ* ("other than Kṛṣṇa"), and *ṛte kṛṣṇāt* ("except for Kṛṣṇa").
In connection with the mention of time (*kāla*) and place (*deśa*), as in "east of the village" (*grāmāt pūrvaḥ*) and "earlier than Caitra" (*caitrāt pūrvaḥ*);
when used in conjunction with a word whose final member is *ac*, such as *prākṛta* and so forth,
it is as in "to the east of the village" (*grāmāt prāk*).
In the case of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a word ending in the suffix *āc* [denoting direction] such as *dakṣiṇā*, we have "the south of the village" (*dakṣiṇā grāmāt*).
In the case of co-utterance with a word expressing distance such as *ādi*, we have "the south from the village" (*dakṣiṇāhe grāmāt*).
Here, the meaning of the ablative case is construed with the meaning of the *upapada*.
And this [example] is an illustration of words such as *prabhṛti* (starting from); for instance:
*bhavāt prabhṛti* (starting from existence), *ārabhya* (beginning with), or *grāmād bahiḥ* (outside the village).

Thus, in the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as *vinā* and *pṛthak*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is optionally prescribed alongside the second and third cases as a governing case (*upapadavibhakti*). Similarly, in the co-occurrence with words meaning "far" (*dūra*) or "near" (*antika*), the fifth case is optionally prescribed alongside the second and sixth cases as a governing case: e.g., *grāmasya* or *grāmāt* *dūreṇa* / *antikena*.
*Maṇi*, pp. 140–142. The fifth [case] (as found in the *Bhāṭṭarahasya*).
The fifth case also connects with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) itself;
and its meaning, according to the rule "the fifth case is used for the ablative" (*apādāne pañcamī*, Pāṇini 2.3.28), consists in the state of being an ablative (*apādānatva*).
And that [term] is defined by the sūtra: "That which is fixed (*dhruvam*) in separation (*apāye*) is the *apādāna*" (Pāṇini 1.4.24). To explain:
in the case of separation—that is, division—that which is fixed, meaning motionless and not the substratum of the action, shall be designated as the *apādāna*; such is the meaning of the sūtra.
Thus, the definition of the *apādāna* (ablative) is: being the locus of a separation produced by an action, while not being the locus of that action itself.

This definition applies to the tree in the sentence "The leaf falls from the tree," because the tree is not the locus of the action of falling, yet it is the locus of the separation produced by the action of falling.
In this context, both components of the definition are necessary to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to a neutral jar or to the leaf itself.
Furthermore, although the state of not being the substratum of an action does not, in general, consist in being the counter-correlative of a difference characterized by the interruption of an action—

because if one were to include the generality of counter-correlativity, then even in the case of falling (*patanatva*), there exists a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by duality (i.e., the difference from itself), which would lead to the undesirable consequence of the usage "it falls from itself" (*svasmāt patati*)— [the definition must be specified more precisely].

Furthermore, if the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) were introduced as being delimited by the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthāvacchedaka*), the expression "he falls from the substance" (*dravyāt patati*) would be untenable, because there is no absence of difference from "substancehood" (*dravyatva*) even within the state of falling (*patanatva*). Nevertheless, by introducing a counter-correlativity delimited by the individuality (*vyaktitva*) that establishes the substratum-hood of the delimitor of the meaning of the base, the counter-correlativity of the difference consisting in the interruption of the action must be defined.

Furthermore, since the state of having a counter-correlativity delimited by the individuality (*vyaktitva*) specified by the difference determined by the falling from that [tree] exists even in a neutral leaf, the inclusion of "being the substratum of a disjunction produced by an action" [as the definition of the ablative] is necessary; thus, in the cases "the leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt patati parṇam*) and "one leaf falls from [another] leaf" (*parṇāt parṇaṃ patati*),
the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is applied.

The ablative (*pañcamī*) has the sense of the accusative (*dvitīyārtha*), namely, "subsistence" (*vṛttitva*). The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an activity conducive to the absence of an activity conducive to destruction; the meaning of the suffix (the verb ending) is that which perishes. The meaning of the ablative is the connection with the limit of the destruction characterized by itself. The meaning of the accusative is the possession of the absence of the activity that serves as the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "There is an effort residing in Devadatta which is not conducive to an activity conducive to the absence of that activity—namely, eating and so forth—which is subsistent in the cow and is conducive to a destruction whose counter-positive is [Devadatta]."

And here, because the barley (*yava*) is in fact what is desired (*īpsita*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of the ablative also applying to the cow (*go*), for that [the cow] is established as the object (*karman*) by virtue of being the most desired (*īpsitatama*).

Indeed, it has been stated in the *Kaṇṭhastha* that the inclusion of the superlative suffix (*tamap*) in the rule "that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamam*, Pāṇini 1.4.49) is precisely for this purpose.

Since the destruction of the operation conducive to destruction—which serves as the delimitor of the root-meaning—resides only in the cow, the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs precisely there.

Similarly, in the expression "he restrains [the calf] from the well" (*kūpād andhaṃ vārayati*), the meaning of the ablative (*pañcamī*) is "residing" (*vṛtti*); the root-meaning is the operation conducive to the absence of the operation conducive to falling.

And thus, the final understanding is as follows: the action residing in Caitra is that which is conducive to the operation [of the blind man], which in turn is conducive to the absence of that operation [of the blind man] which is conducive to the falling—defined as an action suitable for conjunction delimited by the lower region—which constitutes the function of the well.

Similarly, in cases such as "he wards off the sunlight from the flowers" (*puṣpebhya ātapaṃ vārayati*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an operation conducive to the absence of an operation conducive to the state of becoming white (*śuklībhāva*).

Alternatively, the meaning is the absence of an operation—residing in the sunlight—that is conducive to the absence of the state of becoming white residing in the flowers; the understanding is as previously described, beginning with "conducive to that."

In expressions such as “he wards off the fire-boy” (*agnimāṇavakaṃ vārayati*), the meaning of the ablative case is *janyatva* (the state of being produced); the meaning of the verbal root is something like "conducive to burning.
Nor is there a lack of uniformity [in the application of this rule], because a lack of uniformity is not a defect when a definition is formulated by way of inference (*anumāna*).

One turns the cow away from the barley, thinking "otherwise it will eat [it]"; one turns away a blind man from a well, thinking "he will fall"; one turns away heat from the flowers, thinking "they will become white"; and one turns a young boy away from the fire, thinking "he will be burned. This is because the meaning is explained through the distinction of purpose (*prayojana*).

Others, however, who follow the traditional interpretation (*anugama*), hold that in all such cases, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is simply the activity conducive to that which resides in the object (*karmakāraka*)—namely, the absence of an activity that would produce contact.
And the state of residing (*vṛttitva*) is the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*).
So they say.

That is not correct, because in such instances as "he prevents the cow's contact with the barley" (*yavebhyo go-saṃyogaṃ vārayati*) or "he prevents [the cow] from the barley" (*yavebhyaḥ karmaṇi vārayati*), inference would be untenable.

Now, one might object that in the rule *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.27), there is no restriction that the status of the *apādāna* applies only when the action of preventing (*vārayati*) is connected with something desired (*īpsita*).

If it is argued that [the term *iṣṭa*] is seen even in cases where there is no desire for the result, such as in "he wards off from the snake" (*sarpāt vārayati*) or "he wards off from bathing in the Ganges" (*gaṅgāsnānāt vārayati*), this is not so;
for its meaning is that which is desired by the one who is restricted, in relation to the one who restricts.
For a snake and the like are indeed intended as the object to be warded off by the warder, precisely because they are present before him.

In expressions such as "he wards off the sun's heat from the flowers," the warder is mentioned because the object to be warded off is insentient. Alternatively, the connection of barley and the like—which are implicated as being related to the result (namely, destruction) that constitutes the essence of the action denoted by the verbal root—is with the warder, by virtue of their being the opposite of that [result]. This is because the result of the action, which consists in the absence of an activity conducive to destruction, is destruction itself; and since barley and the like would otherwise lead to such a result, their status as warders is established through their opposition to it.
Such is the meaning of that;
thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
In reality, however, all these sūtras have been rejected by the author of the Bhāṣya in many ways.
His intention is as follows:

in the sūtra *dhruvamapāye*, what is intended by "separation" (*vibhāga*) produced by action is not merely a physical reality, but rather a logical construct (*tārkika*). For if this action did not exist, there would be a connection between the object (*karmakāraka*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*); however, since that [connection] is prevented by the action, its absence is said to be produced. It is precisely with this underlying purpose that the word *apāya* (departure/separation) is employed.
And such an explanation is necessary for the sake of the meaning: "He fled from a thief who was not yet [actually] stealing.
Consequently, since the status of the ablative (*apādāna*) would be established for barley and the like by that very rule, other rules [dealing with this matter] would be rendered superfluous.
Nor does it follow that [the cow] and so forth would likewise incur the status of an *apādāna* (ablative) because such an absence is necessarily present there;

for the designation of *karman* (object), which involves being "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) and so on, being of higher priority, sublates the designation of *apādāna*. Furthermore, if one intends to express the opposite, the undesired consequence is accepted as the result.

Nor does the intention to express both lead to the simultaneous application of the *apādāna* designation to both, since the verb *vārayati* (he wards off) is transitive, necessitating that one or the other be intended as the *karman*.

Thus, by the rule *antardhau yenādarśanamicchati* (Pāṇini 1.4.28), which means that when there is concealment (*antardhi*), i.e., an obstruction, that [agent] whose own perception one desires to be absent shall be the *apādāna*, the fifth case is used in such instances as *mātuḥ nilīyate kṛṣṇaḥ* (“Kṛṣṇa hides from his mother”). And here, the meaning of the verbal root is an action opposed to perception, preceded by the desire for the absence of perception.
The meaning of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) is "being a state of occurrence" (*vṛttitvam*). This relates to "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), which is the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root.
"Opposition" (*virodhitvam*) consists in being conducive to the absence of the ordinary sense-contact (*laukika-sannikarṣa*) that produces that [perception].
The meaning of the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*) is volitional effort (*kṛti*).

Thus, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is as follows: "There is an effort residing in Kṛṣṇa, which is conducive to an activity that is itself conducive to the absence of a perceptual ordinary contact (*laukikasannikarṣa*), and which is preceded by a desire for the absence of a perception occurring in the mother with respect to its own object."
And through the fifth derivation [of the word "pratyakṣa"], the cognition of the fact that blackness is the object (*viṣaya*) in the case of perception is an incidental consequence (*pārthika*).

Thus, by the rule *ākhyātopayoge* (Pāṇini 1.4.29), which means that when knowledge is acquired through a formal restriction, the speaker is designated as the *apādāna* (ablative case), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is employed in the expression *upādhyāyād adhīte* ("he studies from the teacher").
Here, the meaning of the verbal root is the pronunciation [of the words] subsequent to [the teacher's] pronunciation, provided it is not yet mastered.
The meaning of the fifth case is the relation of occurrence (*vṛttitva*).
This sūtra as well has been rejected by the author of the Bhāṣya.

[He argues that] since the sounds produced by sounds—which are of the same class as those generated by the act of utterance—originate from the mouth of the teacher (*upādhyāya*), the teacher is the locus of the disjunction (*vibhāga*) produced by the action; therefore, the status of the *apādāna* is established by the very rule "dhruvam apāye" (A 1.4.24).
Nor should it be argued that because such a disjunction lacks the nature of a primary (*mukhya*) disjunction, the *apādāna* would not be of a single type.

This is because the intention [of the grammatical rule] is precisely that various types of such *apādāna*s have as their material cause (*upādāna*) the undivided adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) which constitutes the pervasive element (*vyāpaka*).
For this very reason, it can also be said that all such usages are indeed grammatically valid (*śakta*).
And the purpose of the rejection [of the rule] is precisely to make this known.

Considering that these *tattva-sūtras* are intended for the establishment of [ultimate] realization through the aforementioned form by means of conventional indication (*nirūḍha-lakṣaṇā*), we and others provide commentaries on these *tattva-sūtras*.

Thus, by the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.30), which signifies that the cause of that which is being born shall be designated as the *apādāna*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is employed in the phrase "creatures are born from Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ prajāḥ prajāyante*).
Here, the meaning of the fifth case is the state of being produced (*janyatva*).
And that [causality] connects with the substratumhood (āśrayatva), which is the meaning of the verbal suffix, by way of the relation of existence as occurring in its own locus.
Here, causality (hetutva) is intended in a sense common to both the ablative of separation (apādāna) and the instrumental cause (nimitta).
Therefore, the ablative case occurs in examples such as "joy arises from the son" (*putrāt pramodo jāyate*) and "a jar is produced from clay" (*mṛdo ghaṭo jāyate*).
However, because *brahman* possesses both natures [of being and becoming], the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used.

Similarly, by the rule *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.31), which means "that which is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the origin (*prabhava*) of that agent who is characterized by excellence (*prakarpa*) in the act of becoming (*bhavana*), shall be designated as the *apādāna*," the fifth case is employed in the expression *himavato gaṅgā prabhavati* ("the Gaṅgā originates from the Himālayas").
Here, "excellence" (*prakarpa*) consists in occurring in the moment immediately following the moment of the destruction of the conjunction [with the source].

And the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) here is a contact with the earth that is simultaneous with the destruction of the conjunction [of the body] with that [earth], which occurs at the time of the destruction of the production of that [contact].
The meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*).
And its connection with the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*) is mediated by the contact that constitutes the sense of excellence.

The meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*) is substratum-hood (*āśrayatva*). In the case of the conjunction of all [factors] that constitute the meanings of the verbal root and the prefix, the state of residing in the Ganges (*gaṅgāvṛttitva*) is what is obtained through linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Thus, the final resulting cognition is as follows: "That which resides in the Ganges is the substratum-hood of such a conjunction with the earth, which occurs in the moment immediately following the moment of the destruction of the conjunction of the Ganges with the Himavat (Himalaya), and which is simultaneous with the destruction of the conjunction of the Ganges with the mountain where that rain occurred."

In this context, since the first such contact with the earth occurs immediately after the destruction of the contact with Vaikuṇṭha, there would be the undesirable consequence that the expression "the Gaṅgā originates from Vaikuṇṭha on the earth" would not be used; therefore, the word *avyaya* [is included]. Furthermore, since some of those aforementioned contacts with the earth occur at a moment immediately following the destruction of the contact with Kāśī, there would be the undesirable consequence that the expression "the Gaṅgā originates from Kāśī on the earth" would not be used; hence, [the condition] "simultaneous with the destruction of such a contact" [is required].
And thus, *ā*...

It should not be argued that the use of the ablative case would result even in instances such as "The cloth is not a pot" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo na*), "the mutual absence of the pot" (*ghaṭasyānyonyābhāvaḥ*), "the absence of conjunction in the pot" (*ghaṭasya saṃyogābhāvaḥ*), or "the absence of identity in the pot" (*ghaṭasya tādātmyābhāvaḥ*); for the use of the ablative would be unavoidable even when denoting a mere property, as in "separation from the pot" (*ghaṭād vibhāgaḥ*) or "the difference of the cloth from the pot" (*ghaṭād bhedo paṭasya*). Furthermore, even when intending to express a property, the occurrence of the ablative would be difficult to avoid in cases such as "possessing the mutual absence of the pot" (*ghaṭasyānyonyābhāvavān*). Thus, one must state this.

For, in our own view (*asman-mate*), the meaning of the fifth case (*pañcamy-artha*) is counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*), which is conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-tānīya*) through a relation consisting of a difference whose relatum is itself (*sva-nirūpaka-bheda-ādi-ghaṭita-saṃsargeṇa*).
In that context, words such as *anya* serve to indicate the intention regarding that relation.
However, in the view of others (*para-mate*), the connection occurs precisely with the difference and so forth presented by those [words]; this is the distinction.

Therefore, in this context, since [the property of] difference (*bheda*) and so forth is presented specifically as "difference-ness" (*bhedatva*) and so on within words such as *anya*, the use of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in connection with them is appropriate.

However, in the case of words such as *anyonyābhāva* (mutual absence), because there is a cognition [of the object] as the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*) which is denotable by the word *anyonya*, the fifth case is not used in connection with them. Furthermore, the negative particle (*nañ*) also denotes [an absence] simply as "absence-ness" (*abhāvatva*) for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), and not as "difference-ness" (*bhedatva*) and so on, because that would entail the fault of postulating multiple powers (*anekaśaktikalpanā*).
For this very reason,

when the nature and basis of the wife [as the agent] are already established and perceived, there can never be the possibility of postulating the superimposition of non-existent invalidity for the sake of resolving doubt.
Or: *paṇaḥ* means ghee.
"He stakes for a hundred. (Maṇi, p. 126). "For a wise man does not buy what can be obtained for one *paṇa* with ten *paṇas*. (Vārttika 1.2.13, p. 180).
Such is the maxim.

Medhātithi (on Manu Smṛti 2.79). The maxim of the moth: just as a particular insect called a moth, having fallen under the sway of affection, does not abandon its flight toward a lamp—even though it knows that its own body will be consumed by it—so too is the conduct of a true friend.
Sāhassī. 326. Patañjali is equal in authority to Manu and others.
Vi.
The maxim: "He has gone," even though one is running after him as he falls.

Just as children might chase after a bird that has somehow fallen, or one that is flying even though it is worthy of praise, or one that has escaped even though it was bound, so it is in the present case as well.

Furthermore, according to the logic of the present context, if one did not accept the status of Brahmanhood for Hari, Hara, and others, there would be no disparagement of them in their respective Purāṇas and other texts which extol their greatness; yet such disparagement is indeed observed. Thus, because the facts cannot otherwise be accounted for, the opponent’s doubt arises: "Even equality is difficult to attain; what then can be said of the status of being a sacred field (*kṣetra*)?"
A thousandfold. 135. The maxim: "Even a bound bird escapes from one who runs after it as it falls. Summary. The maxim: "All elevations end in a fall."

In short, the application of the present maxim to this subject is as follows: just as for those who ascend to a high position, a fall is inevitable, so too [is it for those who rise to high status]. (Sāhassī 926) A woman may have many husbands, but one man does not have many wives.

Durga [explains]: If the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) "patnī" is the predominant factor and is stronger, then since the word "patnī" exists in applications involving one, two, or many wives, the case ending (*vibhakti*) would also, by virtue of that component, be in the singular even for all three, intending the number of the class (*ākṛti*).

If, on the other hand, the case ending is the predominant factor, then the meaning of the nominal stem culminates only where that [ending] finds its own specific meaning; thus, there would be no mantra at all in the case of two or many wives.

Regarding which of these two positions is logical, this has been explained in the *Pāśādhikaraṇa*: that the expression follows the form of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, the meaning of the Bhāṣya passage, "Even if unity were somehow intended to be expressed," is as follows: the singular number is uttered for the sake of the [nominal] base itself, not for the purpose of denoting an inherent number, because duality and plurality are not being denoted.
And where there is the cognition of a denotation elsewhere, there the principle of the *pāśa* applies.

We do not say that there is an intention to express duality.

As for the meaning of the sūtra: in the original model sacrifice (prakṛti), the term "the wife" (patnīm) has its scope of application (adhikāra); this is understood because there is no extension (atideśa) due to the lack of transfer (apradeśa) through the commonality of the ritual rule (sāmānavidhyena).
Vi—Regarding the word "wife" (*patnīm*), in cases where there are two wives and so forth, the substitution [of the dual] does not occur because it is excluded by the actual meaning;
nor does the non-application of the extended rule (*atideśa*) follow from the generality of the original instruction (*upadeśa*).

"Therefore, there is no modification (ūha) here. Bhaṭṭa: For this very reason, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mantra ending with 'the wife has been girded' must be employed without any change, whether in a ritual involving one wife or even in a ritual involving two or many wives."
Nor is it correct to argue that the mantra is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) only in the performance involving a single wife, while it is excluded from performances involving two or many wives;
for there is no evidence for a relationship of *prakṛti* (archetype) and *vikṛti* (modification) between these two performances,
and because, according to the method to be explained, the indicative power (*liṅga*) applies universally to all.

For *ūha* (modification) occurs only where the means of proof known as direct instruction (*upadeśa*) has a single specific object as its domain, while elsewhere the application is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) by way of the ritual action; it does not occur, however, when the means of proof is universally applicable.

And in this case, because the gender of the nominal stem is established as being universally applicable according to the logic of the *pāśa* [mantra], and because there is no reason to restrict it, this means of proof does not have as its domain merely the performance involving a single wife.

Nor should it be argued that, just as in the *kṛtvā-cintā* regarding the common procedure (*samānavidhānatva*) of the seasonal animal sacrifices (*ṛtupaśu*), where the word "to him" (*prāsmai*) is restricted to exclude the ewe in accordance with its masculine gender, so too here the mantra may be restricted by the singular number; for while there is justification for such restriction there because the masculine gender would otherwise require a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) without a specific cause, there is no such evidence for restriction in the present case. Indeed, in the performance involving two or more wives, the singular number does not involve figurative indication, as its application is justified by the intention that it refers to each individual [wife] separately.

For just as in expressions such as "white pots" (*śuklā ghaṭāḥ*), the quality of being white is construed as residing in each individual [pot], so too here, there is no defect whatsoever in construing even a single [entity] that is not accompanied by a plural suffix as residing in each individual. Nor does this result in the loss of the restrictive nature of grammatical rules such as "the plural is used for many," because such a rule is justified when there is an intention to convey plurality in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Furthermore, this does not lead to the undesirable consequence that one might take two animals in a case such as "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), since, in the absence of a reason to bypass the first [singular number], the singular ending would be restricted to its own specific scope by choice.

And the completion occurs on the final day.
Therefore, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the non-completion and the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja*.
And there is no completion prior to the final day;

Or rather, it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), just as [the rule for] the night-deposit applies to the initiation (*dīkṣā*).

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) states again that in a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*) lasting twelve days, the rule of ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings applies to all the days.

The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the established conclusion (*siddhāntapakṣa*). As for the indicative mark (*liṅga*) cited—namely, "the days conclude with the *patnīsaṃyājas*; he does not throw [the grass-bundle] outside, for at that time the sacrifice is as yet uncompleted"—that is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to support the fact that the days end with the *patnīsaṃyājas*.
While the days are indeed still standing [uncompleted], the statement regarding them as "not yet established" is for the purpose of praising the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Just as the *dīkṣā* initiation pertains to the subject of initiation: "He who is initiated is bound by the two nooses of Varuṇa;
day and night are indeed the two nooses of Varuṇa."
Alternatively, if one were to count [the days] until liberation from the two Varuṇa-nooses, he would remain bound by them.

"He is to be concluded at night; thus indeed he is released from the Varuṇa-noose, for 'one who is near the end is not to be harmed'"—this statement regarding the release from initiation is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for concluding the rite at night.
Thus, having considered that the conclusion would take a long time, there is the statement that it is "not to be concluded" [at that point].

Therefore, the conclusion that [the ritual] ends with the *patnīsaṃyāja* applies only to those [sacrifices] prior to the last one; however, it should rather apply to all of them because of the injunction made outside of a specific context (*anārabhyavidhāna*), whereas for others there is a contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*). The word "or" (*vā*) is used to refute what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).
It may well be that the conclusion at the Patnīsaṃyājas occurs prior to the last day;
