Śabarabhāṣya 3.1.7.14, p. 716.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the ritual properties pertaining to the substances to be offered—such as boiling and so forth—are not to be performed in the case of milk and other substances used in the dwellings of the Maitrāvaruṇa and others. (Mīko., p. 184;
see under "jyotiṣṭome maitrāvaruṇādi0"). In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, there are milk-offerings and spirituous liquor-offerings.
In the subsequent [passages]: "He offers the cups of milk in the north, and the cups of *surā* liquor in the south" (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 3.5.13–14).
The fact that milk is the substance [of the offering] is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice as its archetype (*prakṛti*).
Bāla, p. 119.
The extension (atideśa) of the characteristics of the *payas* (milk) offerings belonging to the *Sāṃnāyya* [to the *āmiṣā*] in the *Vaiśvadeva* section:
see Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 222, under the entry “atideśaḥ vaiśvadevyāḥ...”.
The extension of the properties of milk applies to *āmiṣā*.
*Āmiṣā* is a derivative of milk.
The animal dedicated to Agni and Soma is a modification of milk, not a modification of curd.
The milk-vow (payovrata) need not be observed on the fourth day of the lunar fortnight and similar occasions if indigestion is likely; otherwise, it must be observed.
VI. 6|8|8: The milk-vow (*payovrata*) must be observed by the initiated Brāhmaṇa at the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
4|3|4: "The milk-vow for the Brāhmaṇa, rice-gruel (*yavāgū*) for the Rājanya, and meat (*āmiṣa*) for the Vaiśya.
This is a rule based on the agent, established by explicit scriptural injunction.

Bāla, p. 18: The milk-vow (*payovrata*), the gruel-vow (*yavāgūvrata*), and so forth, must be performed even when other foods are available; furthermore, nothing else should be eaten because [the vow] serves a transcendental purpose (*apūrvārtha*).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the milk-vow and similar observances are not mandatory during the latter part of the night.
6|8|9. See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1785, under the entry ‘jyotiṣṭome apara0’.
The milk-vow (*payovrata*) and other such observances are mandatory (*nitya*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Bhāṣya 6|8|8|28. See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1843, under the entry ‘jyotiṣṭomādi payo0’.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, through the *payovrata* (milk-vow) and other such rites belonging to the Soma ritual, the requirement for the *dārśika araṇyānasa* (forest-food of the New Moon sacrifice) is established by *prasaṅga* (incidental application).

Bhāṣya 12.1.24.30. Furthermore, the extension (*atideśa*) of the *payovrata* and other such rules does not constitute a sublation because they are dharmas taught separately under distinct headings; rather, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of them.
The obligation to perform the milk-vow (*payovrata*) and other such observances is to be understood from the section titled “The Topic of Vows” (*vratādhikaraṇa*) at 4.3.4.
[Regarding] milk, barley-meal, parched grains, and so forth, [the rule applies] by means of milk (2441).

In the case of milk, parched barley flour, grains, and so forth, the ritual rules pertaining to the offering (*pradāna-dharma*) are not to be performed in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, as in the injunction: "He mixes [the Soma] for Mitrāvaruṇa with milk" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.4.9). This is the principle of the milk-oblation (*payo-homa-nyāya*). Bhāṣya 9.4.12.45–50. The Principle of the Milk Oblation.

Bhāṣya 10.8.47: This is precisely the *jatilayavāgūnyāya*. See under the entry ‘*jatilayavāgūnyāyaḥ*’ on page 1449 of the Mīmāṃsākośa. In the Gavāmayana sacrifice, according to the *payohomanyāya*, the time for initiation (*dīkṣā*) is indeed the month of Caitra; for in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) concerning the Paurṇamāsī [offering] therein, the Caitra full moon is praised: “One should undergo initiation at the Citrā-Pūrṇamāsa; this Citrā-Pūrṇamāsa is indeed the mouth of the year,” and so forth. Thus, the Caitra month alone is the time for initiation.
Such is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
Bhāṭṭa 6.5.10:
Just as this injunction for the milk-oblation (*payohoma*) is like the statement regarding the offering of groats of *jatilā* millet.
Bhāṣya 10.8.47:
*Payasyā* refers to curdled milk products (*āmiṣā*) produced from milk.
Taisaṃ. 2.3.13.2: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, one places the *payasyā* in the cup belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa.
This connection with a single portion pertains only to that which exists in the *savanīya* [oblation], and not from anything else.

In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, a single portion of the *payasyā* already established in the *savanīya* is to be placed in the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa; however, the *payasyā* is not produced beforehand solely for the purpose of being deposited.
VI. 3|8|12. There is an absence of the *praṇītā* waters in the case of the *payasyā* (curd-mixture).
“Just as there is an absence of the *praṇītā* waters when there is no *puroḍāśa* (cake), so it is in the case of the *payasyā*.
Bhāṣya 4|2|5|15.
However, [the word "vavara"] is merely due to a commonality of sound;

by this principle, one accepts that the word *vavara* is an imitation of a sound, and that the word *prāvāhaṇa*—derived from the analysis "one who carries excellently" (*prakṛṣṭeṇa vahati*)—refers to the eternal wind (the cosmic air). (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.2.18, p. 38)
One becomes initiated (*dīkṣita*) through the announcement made by another, because of the connection with all the elements of initiation.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is said, "He initiates with a staff" (*daṇḍena dīkṣayati*); thus, by the statement that he effects the initiation with a staff, the staff is declared to be for the purpose of initiation.
The offering to Agni and Viṣṇu (*āgnāvaiṣṇava*) is also for the purpose of initiation.
In this regard, when considering whether one becomes initiated by all [the rites] or whether one is indeed considered initiated [by some], the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated:
because of the instruction by the other, the *adhvaryu*, that "this Brāhmaṇa is uninitiated," the sacrificer should become initiated thereafter.
This is because initiation is connected with all [the following]: the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* cake, the staff, the girdle, the black antelope skin, and so forth.
And from that, following the formal announcement (*āvedana*), the status of being initiated (*dīkṣitatva*) arises.
Once the status of being initiated is established, one should undertake the vows of the initiated, such as: "The initiated does not give, does not offer oblations, and does not cook," and so forth.

Regarding this, the *Tantraratna* states: "An effort must be made to establish the ablative case in 'from the announcement' (*āvedanāt*), because it was employed by the venerable Great Sage, who is a treasury of knowledge regarding the true nature of all words."
Therefore, it must be stated that in the rule "enapā dvitīyā," the ablative case is also observed;
according to this view, the construction is "after the announcement" (āvedanāt pareṇa),
meaning "subsequent to the announcement."
The word *pareṇa* is an indeclinable expressing this very opinion;
or rather, those meanings are intended because of their connection with the specific purpose of the oblation.
Having set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) reached through the Sūtra by means of the word *vā*, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
It is desired that one should be consecrated;
for it is because that sacrifice is for the sake of consecration,
and by means of that consecration, one becomes consecrated.
As for the statement, "He initiates with a staff," and so forth, this is because of its connection with an object that lacks specific distinction.
Since it is connected with an object such as a staff—a substance devoid of any specific action—it does not produce initiation by itself, because it lacks the nature of an action.
Therefore, the state of being initiated is indeed desired [to be produced by another means].
And from that point on, the vows of the initiated [apply];
even in the *Kutūhala* reading, "because of the connection with the teacher without distinction," the very same meaning has been stated. And the designation is likewise similar to that.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the state of being initiated (*dīkṣitatva*) arises through the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice itself, and not by means of the staff, deerskin, girdle, and so forth; this subsequent sūtra provides another reason for this.
The *dīkṣaṇīyā* is for the purpose of initiation, and it is desired that the state of being initiated and the duties of the initiated (*dīkṣitavrata*) should proceed from it.
Because of the designation—that is, the name "initiation-offering" (*dīkṣaṇīyā*)—it is accepted as establishing the state of being initiated, just like the reasons stated in the preceding sūtra.

The term *dīkṣaṇīyā* is an etymological designation meaning "that which is fit for making one initiated (*dīkṣayitum*), that is, for making one endowed with initiation. And this designation is appropriate only when initiation is possible through the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, and not otherwise.
Therefore, the designation *dīkṣaṇīyā* also serves as a proof for the fact that the state of being initiated is intended [by this sacrifice].
Therefore, it is accepted that one should be consecrated (*dīkṣita*).
Who?
After the announcement (*āvedana*); [one should be consecrated] because of the connection with all the elements of consecration.

In the section (5|1|1|19) of the *Tantraratna*, it is stated: "The *āgnāvaiṣṇava* [offering], through its syntactical connection with the word 'being initiated' (*dīkṣyamāṇa*), is for the purpose of initiation.
(*Bālakrīḍā*, p. 74). By means of the subsequent [text], [the author] [discusses] the ancient account of others... 2442. [End of fragment].

In a conflict between what precedes and what follows, the former is sublated because it has not yet attained its application. (Vārttika 31.7.42, p. 860) § There would be a prohibition of subsequent [elements].
It is stated: "In the case of the *soma* sacrifice, the threshing-floor post (*akhalevālī*) serves as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

In that context, because it is a threshing-floor post, there would be a prohibition—that is, a sublation—of other sacrificial post characteristics belonging to [ordinary] posts, such as selection (*joṣaṇa*), carving (*takṣaṇa*), and raising (*uccayana*).
These [rites] should not be performed.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Because of contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*),
he states another reason for that very point.
If those [other] ritual acts were performed, it would result in a contradiction regarding the *khalevālī*.
A *khalevālī* is that wooden post which is set up when oxen are engaged in threshing grain;
it must be prepared in exactly that manner.

If carving were performed, it would be destroyed; but to leave it as it is would mean missing the proper opportunity. Furthermore, since the threshing-fence post (*khalevālī*) has already been set in the ground, re-carving it would be useless.
Thus [is] the accumulation.
Therefore, rites such as carving and so forth are not to be performed upon the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*).
For others, the term "not the word" (*apraśabda*) should apply as before to those beginning with that [post].

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard for the sake of specific desires: "One who is ill should draw the cups beginning with the Āśvina," "One who is practicing sorcery should draw those beginning with the Śukra," and "One who is being practiced against should draw those beginning with the Manthin. Among these cups that follow the Aindravāyava, the word *agra* ("beginning")—as in the previous case—is indicative of its own immediate successor. Thus, the word *agra* would apply to those [cups] starting from that point.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: since the precedence of each cup (*graha*) is already established by the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), that very precedence is merely restated (*anūdya*) while its status as yielding sevenfold results is enjoined; however, the precedence itself is not being enjoined.
Therefore, the sevenfold nature would apply only to the cups beginning with the Āśvina, which remain in their own respective positions. [The Siddhāntin replies:
"Or rather, there is a displacement (*pratikarṣa*), because the name [of the sacrifice] is for the sake of the obligatory [rite], and it has no connection with that [precedence]."
The word "vā" (or) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The precedence of the Āśvina cup, the precedence of the Śukra cup, and the precedence of the Manthin cup are heard [in the scripture] for the sake of specific desires (*kāma*).

In that regard, it is not the case that the Āśvina and other cups serve the purpose of those desires while remaining in their own original positions; rather, they must be drawn forward (*pratikarṣa*) from before the Aindravāyava cup.
For the sake of the result:

because it is for the purpose of the permanent, the priority of the *āśvina* and other cups—which is established by the text as being for the purpose of the permanent—is not connected with that; that is, because of the absence of connection with the result characterized by the cause of illness and so forth.
Consequently, whatever priority exists by virtue of remaining in its own place is for the purpose of the permanent.

Furthermore, that priority which pertains to the fruit of the *abhicāra* (malevolent rite) and so forth will be established through a displacement prior to the cup for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*).
Therefore, for the sake of the specific fruit, there is a displacement of the cups for the Aśvins and others prior to the cup for Indra and Vāyu.
This is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
In this case, it should be understood that the rule for the sequence of cups (*grahavidhi*) is not as in the preceding instance; rather, it is a rule concerning the *āgrayanāgratā* itself.
Furthermore, it indicates a displacement (*pratikarṣa*).

In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, for the sake of specific desires, the precedence of the cup for the Aśvins (*āśvināgratā*), the precedence of the Śukra cup (*śukrāgratā*), and the precedence of the Manthin cup (*manthyagratā*) are prescribed in the scriptures.
In this regard, it is stated in the Siddhānta that there is a displacement (*pratikarṣa*) of the cups beginning with the Āśvina, prior to the Aindravāyava cup.
Regarding this, he states the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The indicative mark, found in the *dhārāgraha* (stream-cups), shows the displacement of the Āśvina and subsequent cups from the very beginning.

"One should hold that [cup] for which one might take it for a specific desire; having taken the Aindravāyava, one should set it down, and then one should set down that [other cup] for which one might take it for a specific desire.
This indicative mark (liṅga) shows that when a cup taken for a specific desire is being held, the taking of the Aindravāyava occurs.
Therefore, there is a displacement (pratikarṣa) of the cups taken for specific desires prior to the Aindravāyava.
This is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
What then? The *prakṛti* is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), as it was said by Vaṭkurvāṇṇi: "Cook the *māghāna* for me.
(Bālakrīḍā, p. 50).
*Prakṛti*: A narrative concerning a single agent; for example, "Thus indeed said Vaṭkurvāṇṇi: 'Cook the māghas for me,'" and so forth. *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* 6.1.11.
The mantra is the primordial nature: "Truly wonderful is the King; indeed, they call him King, he who is over Sarasvatī.
Like Parjanya, he has extended himself with boldness; a thousand gifts have been bestowed."

(Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.21.18) | Here, O kings— O rulers— the king named Citra, indeed (*iti*) as a certainty, along the Sarasvatī in that region, gave, yes, he gave a thousand cows and tens of thousands (*ayutāni*) in whatever other place whatsoever.
Like Parjanya, spreading [his rain] with rain;
*hi* is used in the sense of well-known fact (*prasiddhau*).
(Bāla. pṛ. 61–62)
The ancient account regarding the nature of human conduct may indeed be recited as a chapter [of instruction].

Thus said Vaṭkurvāṇi: "Cook for me the Māghas; for they do not take the sacrificial oblation (havis) from these. In this original narrative concerning a single agent, it is stated that on the day of the fast (upavasatha), there is no eating of the Māghas.
"Formerly, seven [sages] arrived with firebrands; the Asuras and Rakṣasas struck them down.
In this formulation of a past event involving many agents, the *purākalpa* (ancient narrative) is presented together with the firebrands;
thus, there are *prakṛtipurākalpas*.
It has been stated that going is undesirable.
"Nature and the ancient accounts" (*prakṛtipurākalpa*) is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) consisting of nature (*prakṛti*) and the ancient accounts (*purākalpa*).
The collection of dharmas taught therein is expressed by that term.

And thus, the duty (*dharma*) of the *prakṛti-purākalpa*—such as the abstention from meat-eating (*māṃsa-bhakṣaṇa*) and so forth—would be a duty for humans; that is, it would be a duty for the human who performs the sacrifice.
For the mention or recitation of the duty is indeed for the sake of a purpose or a specific objective.

Therefore, the abstention from meat-eating during the *upavasatha* and other such occasions must be performed by Barkurvaṇi and other humans as well; thus, this is an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding the abstention from meat, not a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). This is the first prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
"And because of the prohibition when that [human nature] is associated.

This sūtra provides another reason for the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position, which holds that in the case of the fast-day (upavasatha), regarding practices such as not eating, since there is a prohibition—such as "one should not do it in that way"—of those very acts prescribed as human duties, the injunction itself must be a rule of human duty (manuṣyadharma). Furthermore, the purpose here is to provide an additional supporting reason.
In the *Kutūhala*, however, this sūtra is read as the twenty-ninth, following the sūtra "vidhau tu vedasaṃyogāt.
The commentary explains it as follows: In the section on the Vājapeya sacrifice, two types of animal ritual (*paśukalpa*) are heard in the Vājasaneyi recension.

At the time of the animal sacrifice, having consecrated three animals—those dedicated to Agni, Indra-Agni, and Indra—one consecrates a barren cow (*vaśā*) for the Maruts and a ewe for Sarasvatī; then, having consecrated a ram for Sarasvatī, one consecrates the animals for Prajāpati together with the *sasandaśa* (the "biting" [animal]).
At the conclusion of the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite, they immolate the animals beginning with those dedicated to Sarasvatī; they keep those beginning with the Sarasvatī animals for later.

In the middle of the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), during the *ukthaparyāya*, once the *brahmasāman* has been introduced, they immolate the animals following the one dedicated to Sarasvatī. They proceed with these [animals] using verses that have not been previously employed.
Having proceeded with the omentum of the Sarasvata animal and having taken portions from all [the animals], he proceeds with the omenta of the Prajapatya animals.
Having proceeded with the Hāriyojana cup, he proceeds with the heart and other organs of the animals beginning with the Sarasvata.
Thus, the Anuyāja offerings become the most excellent; while the two spoons remain fixed, they proceed with the oblations of these [animals].
"One should not do it in that way.
For the sacrifice falters (moves away) when they act thus.

Therefore, at whatever place they should proceed with the omenta of the first [group], there they should proceed with the omenta of the others; at whatever place they should proceed with the sacrificial portions (*havir*) of the first, there indeed they should proceed with their sacrificial portions."
In this case, there is a prohibition of the "animal-like" [offering] (*paśukalpa*) which is heard in a sentence containing the word *yat*;
and that [prohibition] applies only to what is already applicable.
Therefore, for this reason as well, such an injunction must indeed be a positive rule (*vidhi*).
The rule regarding the desire to speak (*uktukṛtūhaloka*) is seen in *kriyāścitte śatapaye* (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 5.1.3.14), but not in every instance.
However, the sequence of the syllables of the sentence is for the most part seen here in its entirety.
Or rather, by virtue of the specific instruction, it should possess that quality, just like the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvatta*).

The first position—that the duty of fasting and so forth on the day of preparation (*upavasatha*), as declared in the *prakṛti* (archetype) and the ancient narratives (*purākalpa*), is a duty for all humanity within the Vṛṣṇi clan—is reached by means of two sūtras; however, by using the word "or" (*vā*), that [first] position is refuted, and another prima facie view is stated. Because of the designation by the word "Vāṇi," that duty belongs only to those born in the Vṛṣṇi clan. That which is both "that" and "duty" is "that-duty": the duty consisting of the non-eating of meat (*mābhakṣaṇa*) would be the duty, but not for those born in the Vṛṣṇi clan [in general]. It is like the case of the five-fold portion (*pañcāvatta*).

Regarding the statement, "The five-fold cutting belongs to the Jamadagnis," this means that the five-fold cutting applies only to those of the Jamadagni lineage and not to others; for that is the case.

Alternatively, because of the specific mention—namely, the mention of the Vṛṣṇi lineage—the rule would apply as a duty specifically to those Vṛṣṇis born of the Vṛṣṇi lineage; such is the meaning of the words.
However, in the case of an injunction, there should be an instruction based on its connection with the Veda.

From such [passages] as "Mābhānaiva mahaṃ pacata" (Do not cook for me), because of the connection with the Vedic injunction (*vāṇisa-yoga*), there would be an instruction for all human beings born in the *Vṛṣṇi* lineage regarding that which is enjoined and that which is inferred to be enjoined; thus, there would be an instruction for the *Mābhāpākṣa*.
In the first sūtra, "prakṛtipurākalpam," only the position of the injunction (*vidhi-pakṣa*) was stated; however, it was not specified therein for which human beings [the injunction applies].
Thus, there is no tautology. Or rather, it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) because it is supplementary to an injunction; therefore, it must be a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*).

Regarding the cases of *prakṛti* and *purākalpa*: the phrase "Thus said Vaṭku Vārṣṇi: 'Cook for me [the meat] with the breast [of the animal]' etc. is an injunction concerning the cooking of the *mābha* [animal]; the word "or" (*vā*) is intended to refute three prior positions—namely, that this injunction applies only to those of the Vṛṣṇi lineage, or that it applies to all human beings. The passage beginning with "Thus said" is a supplement to the injunction "One should resort only to wild [meat]."
Because it is supplementary to an injunction, it must be an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

For the injunction, "The householder should offer [the oblation] with fire produced by friction on the *avāñci* grasses," this statement—"They previously came together with firebrands; the Asuras and Rākṣasas struck them down"—is a supplement. Therefore, that too is an explanatory passage. Consequently, because it is an explanatory passage, it would be a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*), not an injunction.
This is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Some say that *prakṛti* and *purākalpa* are types of *arthavāda*.
(In this regard, they state that a narrative with a single agent is a *prakṛti*,
while a narrative with multiple agents is a *purākalpa*).
Bhāṣya 6.1.2.26–30: Section on Primordial Matter and Ancient Cosmologies (Prakṛti-purākalpa-adhikaraṇa). The Atom (Paramāṇu) as the Section on Primordial Matter and Ancient Cosmologies.

The section concerning the cooking of beans (*māṣapākādhikaraṇa*). Descriptions of origins and ancient events are *arthavādas*. And a description of an origin or an ancient event would constitute a duty for humans, because it is mentioned as something to be performed.
Commentary: Here, the compositions of others and ancient accounts (*purākalpa*) serve as examples.
For instance: "Thus indeed said Baṭu Kurvāṇiṣma: 'Cook for Pānna; they do not accept the oblation from these [others]'";
and the ancient account: "With firebrands, the Asuras and Rakṣasas used to strike down the assembly of our ancestors," and so forth.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: are these injunctions of human duty (*manuṣyadharma*) concerning the objects [of the ritual], or are they for those who perform that specific rite? Or rather, are they merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)? What, then, is the initial position? That these are injunctions of human duty.
Why? Because this recitation is for the sake of, that is, for the purpose of, [establishing] meaning.
By reciting the connection with what is praiseworthy, the action becomes praiseworthy;
and it is the praiseworthy that is to be established.
This very injunction is of this nature;
therefore, it is understood that it must also be performed by other men.
And because there are prohibitions associated with it.
Commentary: There is a prohibition of an injunction of this kind, namely, "one should not do it in that way.
And a prohibition is logical only with respect to what has been occasioned [as a possibility]. Therefore, for this reason as well, it is an injunction.
Or rather, by virtue of the specific mention, it should be a duty of those [particular groups], just like the five-fold cutting.
The Commentary states: This injunction of such a kind is understood to be a duty of human beings in general;
however, because there is a specific mention of particular lineages (*gotra*) therein, it is understood that this duty belongs to them alone.

For it is understood that the praise must indeed be performed; and that [praise] is heard [in the scripture] as belonging to specific lineages (gotra). Therefore, it must be performed by those of those very lineages alone.
It is like the case of the *pañcāvatta*. Just as the rule "the *pañcāvatta* belongs to the Jamadagnis" applies only to those belonging to that specific lineage (*gotra*), so it is here as well.
However, in the case of an injunction, there would be an instruction based on the connection with the Veda.
Commentary: By the word "but" (tu), this position is also set aside. Their instruction would occur in the context of an injunction;
for in an injunction, the Veda provides a statement of praise.
It does not apply to a person who is the locus of an injunction.
The mention of "person" is for the purpose of praising the injunction.
By "injunction," one refers to action.
Because the state of this action is performed by this person, he is therefore "good" (*sādhu*).
However, here the person is not indicated by way of a connection with the action, but rather by way of being worthy of praise. Why is this so? Because this is a word of praise.

Moreover, when there is an indication of an action, the injunction is established by direct audition (*śruti*); but when there is an indication of the relationship between the action and a person, it is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*).
And that [syntactical connection] is weaker.
Therefore, it follows that the injunction applies to any person whatsoever, not specifically to those belonging to the *gotra*s of those [particular families].
Or it is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), because it is supplementary to an injunction; thus, it would be a restatement (*anuvāda*) in that manner.
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): This position is also excluded by the word "or" (*vā*) and so forth.
This is not an injunction for those [specific] nights, nor is it an injunction for human beings in general, nor is it an injunction at all.
But it is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). Why? Because of its specific nature; for they hand down a different injunction.
In the case of an example of a *parakṛti* (an action performed by another), there is the statement: "Therefore, one should eat only forest-grown [food].
In the case of an example of a *purākalpa* (a past event), there is the statement: "One should offer [the oblation] by churning the fire in the very fires of the householder.
And there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyabhāva*) between these two types of injunctions.

For when the two—the statement concerning the primordial past (*purākalpa*) and the statement of the injunction (*vidhi*)—are connected according to the rule, the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*) is one way;
but it is another when they function for the purpose of praise (*stuti*). And both cannot occur simultaneously.
"Regarding that, it is an *arthavāda*.
Śā—Having considered [the possibility] of *kṛtvācintā*, the subject matter (*adhikāra*) is now considered.
Or, by taking it as an *arthavāda*, the *kṛtvācintā* is set aside.
Soma: Just as in the case of the word *aparimita* (unlimited), there is no lack of distinction here either; thus, because of this counter-argument, there is a connection [to the previous topic].

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: both "the archetype" (*prakṛti*) and "ancient practice" (*purākalpa*) would constitute human duties (*manuṣyadharma*), and as such, they should be understood as injunctions.
This being the case, their mention serves a specific purpose.
Vi— "In the case of the statement, 'Cook the beans for me,' [the injunction] applies either to Vārṣṇa alone or to all [beans].
These two alternatives have been stated; having set them aside as a matter of deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*), it is treated as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Bhāṭṭa—Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, Baṭukurvāṇiṣma said: "It is heard in the scripture: 'Cook the beans for Pānna.'"
And this [passage] is an *prakṛti* (archetype) because it is devoted to a narrative (*upākhyāna*) having a single agent;
and this injunction regarding the forest-dwelling (*araṇyāyani-vidhi*) is its *śeṣa* (supplement).

Furthermore, a sentence devoted to a narrative having young students as its agents is a *purākalpa*, as in the Sūtra: "In former times they gathered together with firebrands; the Asuras, the Rākṣasas, struck them down."

And this [passage], "The householder himself, having churned [the fire] in the fires, should offer," is equal to the application of the *nirmanthya* (fire produced by friction) because it is connected with the *ulmuka* (brand); it is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to that injunction, and not an independent injunction, as is determined in the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*. However, in the example of *parakṛti* (an action performed by another), when the injunction is already established, it is deliberated upon through a hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvā-cintā*).

The injunction regarding the cooking of beans (*māṣapāka*) is either for the sake of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices by specifying the Vṛṣṇi lineage, or for the sake of purifying the performer of those sacrifices; thus, the entitlement to cook beans belongs only to one who possesses that [Vṛṣṇi] lineage, just as the entitlement to [certain rites] is restricted by the accompaniment of being a Vaiśya, or just as the entitlement to [certain rites] is restricted by the rising of the lunar mansion Nakṣatra. Since it is difficult to establish "being of the Vṛṣṇi lineage" as a restrictive condition—whereby the injunction for that ritual alternative would have a general scope—this being the position reached: because there is no evidence for assuming that the mention of the Vṛṣṇi lineage, which was introduced merely as a means of praise, serves as a qualifying attribute for the enjoined cooker of beans, the injunction of the mere cooking of beans grants entitlement to all.
Maṇḍana: "The praise [of the Māṣapāka] is like the words of one who has finished cooking the beans.
Śaṅkara: "In the Māṣapāka, there is the completion of the injunction.
But for all men, that [injunction] resides in the ritual rule (vidhi).
"This is another alternative view," according to the *Ṭippaṇī* (Vāla., p.
12). [An *upākhyāna*] is a narrative having a single agent, distinct from the primary subject matter (*prakṛti*).
Vāla-pṛ. 12:

A narrative (*upākhyāna*) concerning the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is not an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), nor is it an injunction (*vidhi*). For example: "With these two, he offered this cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni at the full moon.
This is a narrative concerning Indra.
Bāla, p. 12:

These [sacrificial acts]—namely, the sacrificial rites pertaining to the *iṣṭi* which have the offering of medicinal herbs as their quality and depend upon the *havirdhāna* shed—are entitled to subsist upon the dependent [shed] exactly as it exists. Just as the *paśupuroḍāśa* (the cake-offering for the animal sacrifice) subsists upon the *prayāja* offerings belonging to the animal sacrifice even though they occur at a different time, such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Bhāṣya.

The extrinsic nature (*paratastva*) of invalidity consists in its being established by a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), a cognition of a defect in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣajñāna*), or a cognition of non-correspondence (*visaṃvādajñāna*). (Bālapriya, p. 6) The extrinsic nature of invalidity is its dependence upon a subverting cognition, a cognition of a defect in the cause, and a cognition of non-correspondence; and this extrinsic nature applies to invalidity in the form of non-conformity with reality (*ayāthārthya*).
"An assault on another's wife is improper conduct.

The performance of a penance based on a subsequent cause (*paranimittaprāyaścittānuṣṭhānam*—meaning the performance of that penance for which the cause exists later) is for the sake of avoiding the fault of "cutting off" (*apaccheda*).
Bhāṣya 6.1.15.14. It is simply not tenable that one should incur equality with the opponent's position (*parapakṣasāmyāpatti*).
And because both you and he are subject to the same objection from another [source].
Vārttika 2.1.15, p. 404:
In the context of one matter, it is illogical to enjoin the property of something else.
The use of sentences by speakers is for the purpose of communicating with others. (Vākyapadīya 2.1.14.46, p. 444). Or: [the sentence is] for the purpose of making another understand.
(Vākyapadīya 3.1.8.16, p. 864).

The principle of the superiority of the later [in conflict with the earlier] (*paraprābalyanyāya*); the principle of the inferiority of the earlier (*pūrvadaurbalyanyāya*); the principle of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparyanyāya*); the principle of the greater strength of the later over the earlier (*paurvāparyabalīyastvanyāya*); and likewise, the principle of the simultaneous suspension [of conflicting rules] (*apacchedanyāya*).
See Bhāṣya 6.5.1.154; Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 495, under the entry "apacchedanyāya."

According to the principle that "the highest state is accepted as being without foundation," here too, the five well-known fluctuations of the mind (*manas*) from the Yogaśāstra are adopted: namely, "right cognition (*pramāṇa*), error (*viparyaya*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), sleep (*nidrā*), and memory (*smṛti*).
It has been stated that when the word "highest" (*para*) is applied elsewhere, it enters into the attributes of that [object]. (Śāṃbhā. 2.4.12; Brahma Sūtra).
Bhāṣya 7.4.2.8: The word *para* does not denote even that which is praised as being "beyond.
Vārttika 1.4.12.1–1, p.
355: When the word *para* functions with reference to what is beyond, its specific property is understood.
Where it is already known, it is restated (anūdyate), as in "Devadatta is a lion.
Where it is not known, it is enjoined (vidhīyate), as in "Let these lumps of clay be made into lions. Bhāṣya 7.3.1.1.

That which is prescribed in another branch of the Veda is set aside by that which is prescribed in one's own branch; this is "sublation by non-proximity" (*atrāsabādha*), as for example, the offering after sunrise (*uditahoma*) and so forth being set aside by the offering before sunrise (*anuditahoma*) and so forth.

Furthermore, because there is no contradiction in the principle that "one should be informed by means of exclusion" (*parisaṃkhyā*), it was stated that [the fivefold mental activity] established in the Yogaśāstra is not firmly established.
Nyāya-sūtras 2.4.15–12:

Su. pṛ. 928:
The atom (paramāṇu). This is the objection that [the atom] is not perceived.

That very thing which we perceive as a triad (*tryaṇuka*)—which you consider to be such—is precisely what we regard as an atom (*paramāṇu*), because its parts are not perceived and because the grounds for postulating it [as a composite] are established. Furthermore, that which is grosser and possesses parts is [in fact] an atom by those very same [parts], namely the triads; thus, the atom is established.

Because [the cause] arises from an initial commencement (*ārambha*), and because even a non-massive quality (*guṇa*) is not visible due to its smallness, the possession of magnitude (*mahiman*) cannot be the cause of that visibility.
Alternatively, if the inherence (*samavāya*) in a single substance were the cause of that, it would follow that a triad (*tryaṇuka*) could not be perceived.
Or, if both [magnitude and inherence] were mutually the causes for each other, then both the triad and the quality—which each possess only one of those causes—would fail to be visible.
If, however, the causes were mutually independent, it would be difficult to rule out the possibility of a third category as well.

Or, even if one were to grant that a specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) alone is the cause for being visible (*cākṣuṣatva*), there would still be no justification for a restriction based on dimension (*parimāṇa*). (Kaṇikā, p. 119; *paramāṇuḥ*).
"By means of a single act of investigation, atoms must necessarily be manifested;
for if one imagines the falsity of that which is perceived by a small amount [of cognition], it would follow in this manner."
He who asserts that an atom is composed of atoms that possess magnitude and are perceived by the senses would be telling the hare that it has horns, even while hearing others say that it lacks horns.
Since it has been established that [the object] consists of an aggregate, its existence is proven without further cause;
even if the existence of atoms were somehow understood once again.
In the *Anumānapariccheda*, verses 183–186, the logicians (*tārkika*) maintain that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is admitted to be pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*) in atoms.

They argue that since there is the possibility of [the atom] being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) for that specific location, there is no logical inconsistency even in [conjunction] being non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*).
(Maṇi, p. 46).
The Proof of the Atom. Now, the existence of the atom is being established. The gradation of smallness in dimension must have a limit somewhere, just like the gradation of largeness in dimension.

It must be endowed with an eternal dimension (*nitya-parimāṇa*), because if it were non-eternal, it would follow that even this [dimension] would lack a limit due to having a cause. That which is this limit is the atom (*paramāṇu*).
Likewise, a triad (*tryaṇuka*) possesses a dimension other than its own perceptible form and other dimensions, because it is a product-substance (*kārya-dravya*), like a jar and so forth.
For instance: "The dyad (dvyaṇuka) has parts, because it is composed of parts, like a jar and so forth.
[Objection: But then the dyad would also be an effect-substance, because it is an effect-substance, like a jar and so forth; therefore, there is no proof of eternal atoms. [Reply:
Not so, because a large effect-substance is an effect-substance [only in relation to something larger].

In that case, since that very substance is seen to possess a cause, the status of being a cause cannot be established even for the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). Nevertheless, if the status of being a cause were inferred solely from the fact of being an effect, then the status of being an effect-substance (*kāryadravyatva*) could likewise be inferred from the same fact; what reason is there for such partiality? It is not so, for if the dyad were also an effect-substance, it would follow that it too must have an effect-substance as its cause, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, the status of being an effect-substance were not admitted in some instance, then what would be the rule for the first one? Thus, that [first instance] is indeed the atom (*paramāṇu*).

If it is asked, "What is the fault even in the case of infinite regress?"—this itself is the fault: because for all composite wholes, the series of their own parts would never reach a final term anywhere, it would follow that there are no partless entities at all.

If you say this, then it would follow that even a mustard seed and a mountain would have equal dimensions. For everywhere, the smallness or greatness of the dimension of composite wholes depends upon the smallness or largeness of their constituent parts; and if there were an infinity of parts, then even a mustard seed would have infinite parts, and a mountain likewise—thus, their equality of dimension would be unavoidable. Therefore, due to the consequence of the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), it is impossible to establish even that the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*).
Now, one might object: "The inference of a causal substance from its effect is also not tenable, as it too would lead to the consequence of infinite regress."

This is not so; for if the abandonment of one of the two pervasions were to follow, it is the pervasion of being an effect-substance (*kāryadravyatva*) alone that must be abandoned, and not the mere pervasion of having a cause (*kāraṇavattvamātra*), since the latter is necessarily present. To explain: having accepted the general pervasion that "an effect has a cause," its cause is then established by a second inference as being itself of the nature of an effect. Therefore, in the event of a conflict with the general inference, you would have to abandon the specific inference that depends upon it, but not abandon both of them.

Let it be granted that neither the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) nor the atom (*paramāṇu*) be relied upon; let the very first perception itself serve as the limit for the quality of magnitude (*mahiman*), and let the inference proving the atom also be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). This is not so, because it cannot withstand critical analysis (*vikalpa*). Is that first perception possessed of parts (*sāvayava*) and non-eternal, or is it partless (*niravayava*) and eternal? If it is possessed of parts and non-eternal, then by virtue of its being a composite and a cause, another substance would have to be inferred, and thus the atom is established.
If one were to rely upon [the doctrine that] the eternal is partless (*niravayava*), then there could be no causality for subsequent composite eternal effect-substances.

For whatever is the cause of an effect-substance such as a jar—namely the lump of clay and so forth—is observed to be both composite and non-eternal; furthermore, it is not observed that space (*ākāśa*) and the like, which are partless, possess the capacity to originate substances. Therefore, the production of successive effects by means of a partless, eternal, and initially imperceptible [cause] is not established.

Now, even if such a perception exists, if one were to postulate that the first perceptible cause is eternal on the strength of observing successive effects, then it would be an equal argument to say that the atom (*paramāṇu*) must also be eternal and partless as the cause, and that the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) must likewise be an effect of an eternal substance.

Now, even if one assumes that our eternal partless [atoms] are not the cause of the substratum for the effect-substance—which would contradict their being subject to disintegration—only a mere property (*dharmamātra*) needs to be postulated regarding the initial perception, which is admitted by both parties. However, having postulated the properties consisting of dyads and atoms, it is not equally reasonable to then postulate the property of being partless and eternal in relation to them. True; the establishment of atoms is based on the nature of what is perceived, whereas the Supreme Self is [established] otherwise.
In the case of the initial perception, it is not appropriate to postulate contradictory properties, as that would entail the fallacy of abandoning what has already been established (*klṛptahāni*).

It is only atoms and the like whose nature is unperceived that are postulated; therefore, to avoid abandoning what is established, it is more logical to postulate only what is not yet established (*aklṛptakalpanā*). Otherwise, if one were to postulate something additional as the cause of mountain smoke, there would be simplicity (*lāghava*), which would lead to the undesirable consequence of the destruction of all other forms of inference.

If it is argued that there is the consequence of abandoning what has been established (*klṛptahāni*) because another [entity] belonging to the class of smoke is understood to be dependent [on something else], then even in this case, since substance is established as having the nature of being composed of parts and impermanent, the abandonment of that would be equally a case of abandoning what has been established.
In this way, there could be no inference based on parsimony (*lāghava*) regarding the power of action, the sense organs, and so forth.
For this very reason it was said: "Those things which are to be postulated by the force of valid cognition are friends."

Therefore, the inference is simply this: "An effect-substance possesses an inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇavat*); it is not that "a large effect-substance possesses a cause," nor that "it has the property of being the locus of motion and origination.

Furthermore, the statement "an effect-substance possesses a cause" depends upon a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) and serves to negate [the specific claims] such as "a large effect-substance possesses a cause" and "the cause must also be an effect-substance itself. This being the case, since there is no absence of concomitance (*vyatireka*) with respect to largeness (*mahattva*), its status as a logical reason (*prayojakatva*) is untenable.

For instance, even when other causal complexes are present, that factor whose absence is observed to prevent the production of the effect is alone the efficient cause (*prayojaka*). In this case, however, although the status of being an effect is present, the absence of the property of magnitude (*mahattva*) results in the absence of the status of being a cause.
Since this [absence] has never been observed anywhere else, it is precisely this [magnitude] that is the efficient cause.

Furthermore, the pervasion that "an effect-substance is characterized by the properties of an effect-substance" is inconclusive for both disputants; for you, there is an inconclusiveness regarding the first perception which initiates a subsequent effect, whereas for me, the dyad (dvyaṇuka) is established from the triad (tryaṇuka), which is an effect of the supremely great, and the atom (paramāṇu) is established from the dyad, which is its effect.

Is it not the case that since the nature of the atom itself is the cause of production, why should there be an intervening dyad (dvyaṇuka) as the cause? It is not so; for it is observed that a large effect-substance is produced from another effect-substance of smaller dimension, and according to this principle, the dyad must be inferred to be an effect-substance itself serving as the cause. Since the specific character [of being an effect] cannot be abandoned, and because atoms are eternal, there is no production of a triad (tryaṇuka) directly from atoms.

[Objection: Surely atoms are impermanent because they possess form, like a jar and so forth; likewise, atoms must have parts because they face all directions, like a jar and so forth. How, then, can atoms established by such [arguments] be proven? [Response: They are indeed proven by those very same reasons. For there is no reason that lacks the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva). Since these [reasons] reside in the subject, the atoms themselves are established by the very means of valid cognition that prove them; otherwise, these would not even qualify as reasons. This is the sense.

To explain: in this case, are the atoms (paramāṇu) which have been made the subject (pakṣa) established or unestablished? If they are established, then because they are apprehended by the very means of valid cognition that establishes the locus (dharmin), the reasons (hetu) have their objects sublated.

If, on the other hand, they are unestablished, then for that very reason—namely, the non-establishment of the locus—they cannot prove the probandum (sādhya). Now, if it is argued that the reasons establish the probandum provided they are free from sublation by perception, even so, if there is a reductio (prasaṅga) based on the locus consisting of atoms as the subject, there is still sublation by the very cognition that apprehends the locus.

If it is argued that [the fault does not apply] because of non-acceptance [of the subject], even then the previously mentioned "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) remains in its original state. Furthermore, this bringing about of an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is not a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized as inference; rather, it is merely a specific mode of application of inference itself. Since these [modes] are also characterized by proof and refutation, the bringing about of a consequence is not a separate category [of argumentation]. Thus, everything is logically consistent. Moreover, this doctrine of an eternal cause is identical whether one holds the position that Brahman is the cause or that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is the cause.
Therefore, it is accepted that all the defects found in the doctrine of atoms as the cause are equally applicable to all [other theories].
(Pracīna, pp. 43–46).

The Supreme Self (paramātman) is worshipped with water being poured by means of the Gāyatrī mantra—"tatsaviturvareṇyam"—which, by its reference to the sun as the locus of the Supreme Self, designates the Supreme Self as Brahman.

The principle "those [rites] intended for another purpose should be performed once" does not apply here.

Because that rule pertains to actions performed for the sake of another. *Vaijayantī* 1.7.18: "Actions for the sake of another may be performed by anyone. If the wife is not present, all [the priests] should remain on the ground.
(Satyāśrautasūtra 1.7.102).
The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of excluding the notion of a single performance (*pratipatti*) or repetition (*āvṛtti*).
This is so that the principle—"those [acts] intended for another may be performed by one"—does not apply to a single consecration (*saṃskāra*) intended for another.

Nevertheless, even when it occurs for its own sake (*svārtha*) and likewise in the case of an external object that is difficult to obtain (*evaṃkaṣa*), the act is accomplished by means of a single wife alone. As the *Vaijayantī* will state, beginning with "But in the case of another's purpose, there is a commonality of purpose" (9.2.14.43) and continuing with "or they may be performed," [it shows that] even without being for that specific purpose, because one merely observes the assistance rendered by the curd and milk offered at sunrise, the properties of the *praṇītā* water are indeed obtained.
Or [it may be argued]: "But in the case of another purpose, there is no commonality of purpose for the consecration, because it is intended for that [other] purpose. [The text continues:
"Verily, he deprives him of offspring and cattle, and increases his rival, for whom the moon rises while the sacrificial offering has already been set out.

He should divide the rice grains into three parts: those which are of medium size, he should offer as a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dāta; those which are the smallest, he should offer as a pap of curdled milk to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa; and those which are the largest, he should offer as a pap of boiled milk to Indra Pradātṛ. Thus, after Prajāpati had spoken, these [rites] were prescribed for one for whom the moon has risen.

In this regard, concerning the deliberation as to whether the ritual duties (*praṇītā-dharma*) should be performed for the boiled milk and the curd or not, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The word "therein" (*tatra*) indicates the absence of the necessity for performance.
For the sake of another—namely, for the purpose of offering together with the *caru*—the ritual duties of the *praṇītā* water should not be performed for the boiled milk and the curd.
The praises of the curd share a common purpose with the *praṇītā* waters because they possess a commonality of meaning;
this is because the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*)—such as the pouring out—is for that purpose, namely, for the purpose of cooking.
Thus, the properties of the *praṇītā* waters are for the purpose of cooking.

However, since the curd and the milk are for the purpose of offering (*pradāna*) and not for the purpose of cooking (*śrapaṇa*), the duties of the *praṇītā* water do not arise for them; this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

Regarding this, some read the sūtra as "parārthena tv artha" with the instrumental ending, while others read it as "parārthe na tv arthe" with the locative, as in the sūtra text of the Ānandāśrama edition.

In the Ānandāśrama edition, however, the printed text of the *vārttika* on Sūtra 1.7.14 reads: "He will state [later]: 'But in the case of another's purpose, there is no commonality of meaning. Since the word *tu* (but/however) exists in the sūtra, there is no need for a separate *na* (not), as it is not required at all.
Alternatively, the reading *arthāsāmānyam* must be accepted as the correct one according to Sudhāsāgara.
Accordingly, that term is explained in the Bhāṣya: "For there is no commonality of purpose whatsoever between the *praṇītā* water and the curd."
Thus, this reading from the *Sudhā*, which follows the *Bhāṣya*, has been accepted by the venerable teacher.
However, the reading accepted in our own Mīmāṃsā system must be modified:
"Or they should be performed, because the purpose is accomplished."

The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The ritual duties (*dharma*) pertaining to the *praṇītā* water should be performed—that is, they must be carried out—upon the production of the curd, because the purpose has been accomplished; that is, because the purpose, namely the cooking of the *caru*, has been fulfilled, since the completion of the cooking has occurred.
Having stated, "The *caru* in boiled milk, the *caru* in curd," it is understood that the cooking of the *caru* takes place both in the boiled milk and in the curd;
and there is also the purchase [of the materials].
