Sūtra 8.1.17: 32. The qualified object (*viśeṣya*) present in the mind is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for both [the agent and the object]. Thus, the Hotṛ should perform [the ritual] with the mantra "parivīrasi. Now, who would perform this separation (*vigraha*)? "The other among them, from whom the distinction arises. It would be another than the Hotṛ, namely the Upaga, whose [function] is not occupied, or one who possesses a specific predominance (*prādhānya-viśeṣa*).

Or rather—there arises a doubt: since the two mantras, "parivīr asi" and "yuvā suvāsāḥ," which respectively describe the instrument and the action being performed, are employed simultaneously by the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ in the archetype sacrifice, yet in the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana they are observed to have a single performer due to the combination of the Hotṛ and Adhvaryu functions, one of the two must necessarily be omitted. Which one, then, should be accepted? In this regard, the prima facie view is that there is no fixed rule;
for when the mantra belongs to the Hotṛ, whose established nature is already defined, its application as an Adhvaryu function occurs without abandoning its own inherent character.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
in this case of conflict, the instrumental case should be employed.
Why? Because of a specific relationship of inherence.
Some say that the specific nature of inherence (*samavāya-viśeṣa*) is proximity to the primary factor (*pradhāna-pratyāsatti*).
For an external [auxiliary], being of the nature of a remote helper (*ārādupakāraka*), is a restatement of what is being performed (*kriyamāṇānuvādī*); however, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is internal.
That is not the reason.

For if, by way of the principal [act], a restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*) were being made regarding the subsidiaries, then this [phrase] "suvāsāḥ" would also be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *hautra* [function].

And both of these [mantras]—by virtue of the injunction "Recite for the one being girt around the sacrificial post" (yūpāya parivīyamāṇānubrūhi) and because of their subsequent recitation—are to be recited while the two ropes are being girt around the post. Since this occurs at the same time as the efficient force (bhāvanā) of the exclusion (parisaṃkhyā) of the first [rope], there is no contradiction with their status as *kriyamāṇānuvādins* (recitations accompanying an action in progress).
And in the modification of the oblation, namely the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, they are obtained in exactly the same way.
And in that context, it is heard in scripture: "He who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu.

Since this is a *satra* sacrifice, and because in a *satra* there is an absence of the Hotṛ-hood and Adhvaryu-hood produced by the appointment (*ānamana*) [of priests] due to the lack of such necessity, the sentence "he who is the Hotṛ" enjoins the identity of the agent for both functions through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of those functions by the two words "Hotṛ" and "Adhvaryu," even though there are two distinct tasks.

Consequently, by the force of this directly stated (*aupadeśika*) identity of agent and the original (*prākṛta*) unity of time, the *karana-mantra* (the mantra for the cutting) and so forth are performed first, followed by the animal sacrifice and the rest.

Since it has been established that the status of being a *hotṛ* and so forth is caused solely by the mere act of officiating (*avyavasāya-mātra-nimittakatva*), there is no evidence for a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of "action" (*karman*) in both terms through that connection even in the *satra*. Therefore, only the term *adhvaryu*, being the subordinate one, is accepted as having figurative indication; thus, there is an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the non-performance of the duties of the *adhvaryu* in the *satra*. This is because the sūtra on exclusion (2.4.6) does not specify particular distinctions.

For if this definition [of syntactic unity, such as "that which has a single purpose (*arthatva*) constitutes one sentence," etc. were stated in general terms—applying even to cases where there is the instruction of isolated words—then, by way of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), it would be understood merely that this [definition] does not apply to Vedic [passages] (this being the prima facie view). Vārttika 2.1.2–4.46, p. 444: "Or rather, exclusion is not intended through the process of elimination (*vyāvṛtti*). Vārttika 13.8.27, p. 282: "The apprehension of a general application arises from the mere connection of the sentences."
From what is heard, attainment arises; and when there is a distinction, it is an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā) based upon that.
For its faultlessness is obtained when it is enjoined there;
indeed, as something to be assumed, it is considered superior to a result that is already established.

Since the inclusion of the term *sarva* (all) serves to preclude the knowledge of the path—which depends for its very existence upon the rejection of the application of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) situated prior to the words of the same sentence—the threefold defect (*tridoṣatva*) of this restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) is unavoidable. (PMS 3.1.14, p.

710). Because the heart and other organs are heard in scripture as being connected specifically with the act of cutting out (*avadāna*), they are excluded from being the sacrificial oblation (*havis*); consequently, the assumption of a result [for the injunction] applies to their placement in the *ātithya* and other such rites.

Because there is no evidence for a connection with that [Aditya] either, and because it is possible to supply a connection within the context (*prakaraṇa*) according to the rule [Jaimini Sūtra] 1.2.24, and because it follows from the previously established specific position, the conclusion is that this is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise).
This establishes the distinction between a praise whose subject is correctly heard as being like Aditya and one whose subject is something else.
("Correctly heard" means as it is heard; "like Aditya" refers to the subject matter of the restatement; such is the praise whose subject matter is correctly heard as being like Aditya.)
That which has for its object (*viṣaya*) something other than what was stated without error is "having another as its object" (*anyavi�ṣayā*).

This is a *karmadhāraya* compound with two members in apposition (*viśeṣobhayapada*), consisting of that which has as its object the sun exactly as it is heard from the correct scriptures (*samyakśrutayathādityaviṣayaḥ*) and that which has another as its object (*anyaviṣayā*).
That [is] praise, and it is this; "attainment through discrimination" (*vivekasiddhi*) means that the attainment of discrimination results from such praise— this is the analysis of the compound.

In this context, "properly heard" (*samyakśruta*) refers to being heard through a connection (*saṃbandha*), as in the example: "Just as the north (*udīcī*) is appropriate for humans, so the east (*prācī*) is for the gods. And "discrimination" (*viveka*) is as follows: "In the example concerning the *nīvī*, if there is praise by way of appropriateness (*aucitya*)."
Even from that, by way of propriety;

how could the status of being made of *parṇa* wood become an auxiliary element (*kratvaṅga*) of the sacrifice according to the logic of the *parṇamayī* [passage]? It would be so by the logic of the *parṇamayī*.
It is an ornament.

Furthermore, there is no non-application of those desiring a specific quality (*guṇakāma*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). This is because the *vaṣaṭkāra* is enjoined directly for the sake of a specific purpose by the statement, "This indeed is the seventeenfold Prajāpati; that which is dependent [on him]," and thus, due to the absence of the logic of the *parṇatā* (palāśa-wood) rule, it is taught as common to both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*), making it logical that such a desire for a quality applies even in the modification.
(Bhāṭṭa 10.1.10)

In the sentence concerning the "being made of parṇa wood," having accepted that the injunction indicates the sacrifice (kratu) through an unerring indicative mark (*liṅga*), one must also accept that the remainder of the sentence indicates its excellence (*prāśastya*). [This is stated in] *Parimala* on *Brahma-sūtra* 3.2.142: "If it were extended by the quality of being made of parṇa wood, then from the sentence regarding the parṇa wood, the quality of being made of parṇa would enter into the entire sacrifice, [and thus] half of the *juhū* ladle [would be so]."
And that *juhū* ladle, being prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself, is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to all the modified rites (*vikṛti*). [Example:
"The *juhū* is made of *parṇa* wood" (*parṇamayī juhūḥ*; *parṇamayī* means produced from the wood of the *palāśa* tree).
Bhāṣya 3:
Regarding "hearing evil verses," it is not stated by this word that the act is performed with the *juhū* ladle, or that the *juhū* itself is exhausted by it.
But surely this is understood through inference:
that it is certainly performed with a ladle made of *pālāśa* wood, because when that [ladle] exists, that [result] occurs.
To this, it is replied:
Inference regarding the relationship of cause and effect does not function in this manner.

That which is called the "relationship of cause and effect" exists when, given the presence of X, Y occurs; and when X is absent, Y is absent—only in such a case is there a relationship of cause and effect.
In the present instance, however, while the presence [of the cause] upon the presence [of the effect] is known, the absence [of the cause] upon the absence [of the effect] is not.
There is no such statement as, "For one who does not have [spoons] made of *pālāśa* wood, there is no hearing of ill-repute";
therefore, it is not understood through a mandatory injunction that "this is done by him.
Rather, this is understood as a characteristic of the person.
And from that, there is inference.
Furthermore, even for one whose *juhū* ladle is made of *pālāśa* wood, there occurs the hearing of evil verses.
How is this known? Through direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*).
But if this is so, then the fruit is not accomplished here by mere verbal expression;
for a fruit is not seen [to arise] by the mere utterance of words.
This is not a fault.
For it is not stated there that the result is achieved by that alone;
here, however,
[the rule is] "having performed the circumambulation with fire" (*paryagnikṛta*), [there is] the discarding of those [animals] for whom the circumambulation has been performed.

In the passage, “He releases the Pālīvata animal after it has been encircled by fire,” there is an injunction regarding the subsidiary detail (guṇa) of the rite ending with the encircling by fire (paryagnikaraṇa). [Vi.
214|8] Regarding the release of those animals that have been encircled by fire, its purpose is for that specific end, just like the placing of bricks (upadhāna).

In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, having introduced the rule, “One should sacrifice a wild ass (parasvat) to Īśāna,” it is heard in the scripture: “They release the others after they have been encircled by fire.”

Regarding the inquiry as to whether these wild animals (āraṇya) are to be released immediately upon being seized, or whether they are to be released after being consecrated by the ritual refinements ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa*—which would constitute a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action—the proponent states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

When the release of the wild animals that have undergone the *paryagnikaraṇa* is heard in the scripture, the purpose of the seizing must be understood as being for that [release]; likewise, the carrying of fire is for that purpose, just as in the case of the *upadhāna*.

Just as in the *abhicayana* sacrifice, where it is said, "This indeed is direct food: this very *caru* which they place [on the altar]," the *caru* is taken up solely for the purpose of being placed there;
so too here, the seizing (*ālambha*) must be performed solely for the purpose of the offering (*utsarga*).
Or rather, there is a prohibition of the remainder because of the absence of purpose, as in the case of the *idā*. 52.
This is a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action.
The word "or" (vā) serves to set aside the prima facie view that the act of touching is enjoined for the purpose of disposal.
It is a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action because there is no further purpose [for it].

If the purpose were merely relinquishment (*utsarga*), there would be an absence of the act of touching (*ālambha*); the statement regarding touching would be rendered purposeless. The sentence, "One should touch the *parasvat* for Īśāna," would become meaningless.
Therefore, by the mention of touching, it is actually the act of giving (*dāna*) that is enjoined.
The statement "paryagnikṛtān" (having been carried around with fire) is for the purpose of prohibiting other subsidiary rites;
it is like the case of the *idā* [offering].
Just as in the rule "here the Ātithyā ceremony concludes," there is a prohibition of the subsidiary rites subsequent to the *iḍā*, so it is here.
Therefore, the statement regarding Īśāna is an injunction for the sacrifice, while the statement of "releasing" (utsarga) is for the purpose of prohibiting the remaining rites.
Furthermore, as before, the word "atha" (then) and the expression "he concludes" (saṃsthāpayati) would not be appropriate if the action had already commenced.

Just as in the Aśvamedha, having introduced the rule "one should sacrifice a wild ass to Īśāna," it is heard: "they release the others after they have been encircled by fire"; so too, in the context of the Ekādaśinī, having introduced the rule "one sacrifices [the animal] belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ and Patnīvat," it is heard: "he releases the Patnīvat animal after it has been encircled by fire; he concludes the remainder with clarified butter."
These two statements are consistent.
In that context, the cake-offering (puroḍāśa) with clarified butter as its substance is equal to the Patnīvata animal sacrifice, due to the identity of the deity.

In that case, regarding the phrase "he completes the remainder" (*śeṣaṃ saṃsthāpayati*) when the sacrifice has not yet commenced or is not under discussion, the words "completes" (*saṃsthāpayati*) and "remainder" (*śeṣam*) would be inappropriate.

Because of the word’s status as before, and because it is preceded by an initiation—just as it is preceded by the initiation of the sacrifice—if the statement regarding Īśāna in the present context were an injunction for a sacrifice, and if the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) were to prohibit the subsequent subsidiary rites, then, due to the equality of the scriptural expression (*tulyaśrutitvāt*), the statement regarding the Pālīvata would likewise prohibit the subsequent *paryagnikaraṇa*. Furthermore, since the subsequent subsidiaries of the Pālīvata statement follow the *paryagnikaraṇa*, the injunction of a separate rite in the form “He completes the remainder with clarified butter” becomes logically consistent.

Thus it is established that the statement of Īśāna, the injunction for the sacrifice, and the statement regarding the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite are all intended to prohibit the remainder of the ritual action.

Since engagement [in action] is caused by knowledge, in the case of a prohibition, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) would not be performed because they are brought about by that [action]; just as when the *prayāja* offerings are prohibited, there is no taking up of the clarified butter (*ājya*).

The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) states the flaw in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) which holds that the touching (*ālambha*) is solely for the purpose of releasing [the animal].

If only the relinquishment (*utsarga*) of the animal substance were enjoined, then there would be no performance of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as those involving the sacrificial implements and so forth; for the engagement in purificatory rites is known to be caused by the engagement in the sacrifice.

If the sacrifice is prohibited, in the absence of the sacrifice, why would the purificatory rites be performed? Since they are brought about by that [sacrifice]—that is, brought about by the sacrifice—and because the engagement in purificatory rites is known to be caused by the prohibition [of the sacrifice], there would be no performance of the purificatory rites.

Just as in the case of the *upasads*, where the statement "they are without *prayājas* and without *anuyājas*" prohibits the *prayājas*, and consequently the drawing of the clarified butter (*ājya*) intended for the *prayājas* is not performed, so too, in the absence of a sacrifice, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) intended for the sacrifice would likewise not be performed.
But this is not tenable.
Therefore, in the passage concerning Īśāna, one must accept that it is indeed an injunction for a sacrifice, and the purificatory rites must also be performed.
The prohibition of the remaining rites, however, follows from the injunction of their release (*utsarga*).
Alternatively, [if the animal were not released], there would be no performance of the rite; otherwise, there would be a total abandonment.

In the passage, “They release the others after they have been circumambulated by fire,” if there were a non-performance of the sacrifice, then there would be a total abandonment—that is, the abandonment of all ritual actions such as the consecrations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth.
It is stated thus:

therefore, because of the delimitation—that is, because of the exclusion of everything subsequent to the *paryagnikaraṇa*—there would be the performance of the ritual action (*anuṣṭhāna*) consisting of the sacrifice, which takes the form of the renunciation of the substance (*dravya*) for the sake of the enjoined deity, as well as the section of purificatory rites (*saṃskārakāṇḍa*) ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa*.
Consequently, there is an injunction for the sacrifice by means of the *īśāna* passage, and [an injunction] by means of the *utsarga* passage.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the "release" (*utsarga*) of those animals around which fire has been carried (*paryagnikṛta*) constitutes a "prohibition" (*paryudāsa*), meaning a prohibition against performing the remaining ritual acts.
The proponent of the opposing view (*vādī*) states another position:

In the passage, "The abandonment of those for whom the fire has been carried around" (9.4.13–15), it will be considered whether the injunction for abandonment is made by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to those for whom the fire has been carried around, or whether the injunction for carrying the fire around is made by way of reference to the abandonment.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 913).

Regarding the release of the animals consecrated by fire (*paryagnikṛta*), there is a release of the ritual action itself in the case of the *prājāpatya* animals, because of the commonality of the scriptural statement, as in the case of the forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*). Therefore, there should be a distinct injunction regarding the *brahmasāman*.
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, with reference to the *prājāpatya* animals, it is heard in scripture: “They release them after they have been consecrated by fire; they immolate them at the *brahmasāman*.

Here, when the release of the *prājāpatya* animals—those dedicated to Prajāpati—is being enjoined after they have been consecrated by fire, it must be understood that there is a release of the ritual action itself (*karmotsarga*).

Because of the similarity of the scriptural statement (*śrutisāmānya*), as in the case of the *āraṇya* [animals], just as in the *Aśvamedha* there is the scriptural statement, "They release the others after they have been encircled by fire," therefore the scriptural statement regarding the *vājapeya* does not apply to the original context.
Thus, due to the similarity of the scriptural statement, there is the abandonment of the ritual for the *prājāpatya* animals as well, just like the *āraṇya* ones.
Since there is first the abandonment of the ritual, therefore, at the time of the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* chant during the *brahmasāman*, there should be a separate injunction for another distinct ritual.
Seventeen animals are to be released first; and at the time of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s Sāman, another seventeen animals are to be sacrificed.
This is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa).
Alternatively, there is a prohibition of the preparatory rites, because the sentence is a single unit due to the commonality of the sacrifice.

The proponent says: This is not a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action (*karmaśeṣa*), but rather a prohibition of the consecrations (*saṃskāra*). It is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) at that time of those consecrations whose opportunity had arrived; this is the principle of exclusion (*paryudāsanyāya*).

Indifferent: *Bāla.*, p. 99. Exclusion (*paryudāsa*): In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, because the acts of giving, cooking, and offering oblations for the sake of the person are performed by the consecrated (*dīkṣita*), [the sacrificer is excluded]. *Bhāṣya* 10.8.7.12–15. Exclusion: It serves the purpose of restricting [the application] to that which is other than that.
Sūtra 1.2.2, p. 8: Prohibition of giving, offering oblations, and cooking for one who has been initiated (dīkṣita).

Bhāṣya 10.8.7.12–15: An exclusion (paryudāsa), such as "not in the after-sacrifices" (nānuyājeṣu) and so forth. If it were a prohibition (pratiṣedha), an error on the part of the scripture would have to be assumed, due to the contingency of an option (vikalpa).

Furthermore, there would be a twofold conceptualization: that some benefit arises from non-performance due to the prohibition, and [another] from performance due to the injunction. Therefore, it is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
In that case, there is only indication (*lakṣaṇā*), not external conceptualization (*bāhyakalpanā*).

And indication is superior to the postulation of the unperceived (*adṛṣṭakalpanā*). (Ṭup-ṭīkā 10.8.14). Exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is [seen] in such cases as "not in the *anuyāja* offerings," and so forth.

According to the rule "A grammatical operation concerning words applies to those that are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), a compound occurs between two things that possess semantic connection (*sāmarthya*). And this semantic connection would exist if the word *rājan* did not depend on [the gender, number, and so forth of] the word *puruṣa*; therefore, it is compounded with *puruṣa*.
Therefore, even when heard within a compound, the meaning of the constituent parts is understood as being devoid of gender and number, because the cognition [of the meanings] is equal.
This being the case, there is a single meaning;
consequently, both [the individual and the compound meanings] must be followed.
And in both cases, where there is no mention of a name, the *paryudāsa* (exclusion) is established.
[Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 10.8.14]. Regarding the *paryudāsa*: "He does not choose a non-Arṣeya" in the Mahāpitṛyajña.
Bhāṣya 10.8.1.1–4. Regarding the *paryudāsa*: "He does not choose a Hotṛ" in the Mahāpitṛyajña.
10|8|1|12–4. *Paryudāsa*: capable; mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
*Paryudāsa* is the state of being similar to that [thing] while being different from it.
There are various types of *paryudāsa*, which have been analyzed with subtlety in the *Mīmāṃsābhāṣyaprakāśa*.

And all of this should be seen in the *Bindu* under the heading "Exclusion-Positive-Injunction" (*paryudāsavidhi*). What is exclusion? It is the exclusion of the status of being performed by one who has undergone initiation (*dīkṣita*) in the case of the gift, the cooking, and the oblation intended for human ends. (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2303; see the section titled "The Topic Concerning One Not Initiated").
Paryudāsa (exclusion) occurs when the negative particle (*na*) is connected with something other than the verbal root, as in the case of "One should not look at the rising sun" (Bhāṭṭa 4.1.3).

However, in the case of "One does not eat *kalañja*," I maintain that this is indeed a *paryudāsa*. By means of the direct denotation (*śruti*) characterized by proximity (*upaśleṣa*), it enjoins the performance of the act of eating for those [other things] [excluding the *kalañja*].
And because the negative particle (*nakāra*) is intervened by the object (*karman*), it does not connect with the expression denoting "the state of being something to be done" (*kartavyatā*).
Therefore, when connected with this [object], it becomes an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
In that case, this [negative particle] does not connect with the *kalañja*.
What is the reason? Because it is not a compound (*asamasta*).
When two words ending in case-terminations (*subanta*) form a compound, there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*); this does not occur when they are not in compound.
Therefore, that which is excluded is connected with the verbal root (*dhātu*).

In that case, because there is an absence of word-final inflection (*subanta*), no compound (*samāsa*) exists. Therefore, the non-eating of *kalañja* and other such things, qualified [by the prohibition], must be performed by one who desires the result.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 6.1.5.19: "One does not give to a maned horse (*kesarin*)"—this is not a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), but rather an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
The reason for this will be demonstrated in the tenth book (10.8.1) through the example of the mantra "yemajāmahe.

Therefore, by that same principle (*nyāya*) of exclusion, since the horse is excluded, the injunction that "all one's property except the horse is to be given" is obtained as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the prohibition; thus, there is not even an occasional (*pākṣika*) giving of the horse.

VI. 6|1|3: When, in a sentence, there is an indication (lakṣaṇā) of a meaning contrary to its own [direct] sense for a verbal root mentioned together with the negative particle *na*, that is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
By means of exclusion, the archetypal rule (*prākṛta*) is set aside.

*Bāla.*, p. 131: In the case of a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), there is a restriction to that which is merely other than [the negated object]. In the *Mīmāṃsā* section on *paryudāsa* (10.8.1), it is stated that the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*). *Vākyārtha.*, p. 20: If a specific detail found in one scriptural passage (*śruti*) is not adopted in another scriptural passage, then an option (*vikalpa*) would have to apply everywhere; this is not the case.

In that case, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) alone is accepted as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Even though the application (*prāpti*) is weak, it is equal in strength to the prohibition because it possesses the nature of being understood through that [prohibition].
[Objection: In that case, since the recitation would otherwise be purposeless, the acceptance of the mantra is appropriate;
however, here, because there is the possibility of scope for both general injunctions even in a different domain, there is no purposelessness.
Therefore, he says: "The Vedic verses are not accepted there on the grounds of being useless.
Why? For uselessness is a reason for rejection, not for acceptance.
Therefore, an option (*vikalpa*) is appropriate.
If it is argued that [the distinction] is due to the difference in meaning, the Bhāṣya states: "If this is understood, there would be an option (vikalpa);
but that is not so."
Because it is already established by the sense of the matter.

Thus, in common worldly usage, when there is a prohibition regarding something that would otherwise be obtained by its own nature—such as "Poison must not be eaten," "A finger must not be given to a serpent," or "A thorn must not be stepped upon with the foot"—the result is simply the non-performance of that action, not an option. Therefore, we consider that between an injunction and a prohibition, the prohibition is stronger;
for a prohibition occurs only when an injunction has been reached.
That which is indeed appropriate when something has been obtained becomes its sublater.
Therefore, in the *anuyāja* offerings, there is simply no performance of the *yejyā-maha*, and in the *mahāpitṛyajña*, there is no choosing of the *hotṛ* priest for him.
It is not a case of the definition of the word being based on a common cause.
Commentary: This is not so.
For the reason here is the same for both the application and the prohibition;
both are characterized by the word—both the application and the prohibition.
Prescription occurs when there is a possibility of prohibition, and prohibition occurs when there is a possibility of prescription.
Furthermore, in common worldly experience, both are perceived through direct observation as being characterized by either merit or defect.
In that regard, between these two—prescription and prohibition—that which possesses merit is performed.
However, it is not possible to discern the merits and defects within the definition of the word itself.
Therefore, whatever is obtained through the sentence, both of those must be determined;
and thus, both the acquisition and the prohibition are obtained.
Therefore, there is no option here.

Rather, it should be a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), because an option is improper; it should be a part of the injunctions. The Commentary: The word "api tu" (but rather) serves to set aside the previous position.

The prohibition would be a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) of both the specific injunctions (*pradeśa*) and the general injunctions (*anārabhyavidhāna*). This is not so; the meaning is not that "in the *anuyājas*, the *yajyā* mantra should not be recited.
How then? The word "not" (*na*) is connected with the word "*anuyāja*," not with the verb "to do" (*karoti*). Thus, it means "not in the *anuyājas*."
What follows from this? This sentence—"not at the after-sacrifices" (*nānuyājeṣu*)—is incomplete by itself; therefore, it will be connected with the portion of the preceding sentence.
That which was stated as "he performs the sacrifice" (*yajati*) applies [only] to those [sacrifices] that are not the after-sacrifices.

It would amount to saying that he performs the sacrifice in those sacrifices excluding the *anuyāja*s. Therefore, since the *anuyāja*s are excluded by the injunction itself, there is no prohibition; thus, there will be no option.
Furthermore, regarding the *Mahāpitṛyajña*, because of the statement "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*), it follows that the selection of the *hotṛ* priest must be performed here as well.

This is stated: "The selection should be performed as in the archetype (prakṛti), excluding the choosing. Here, the negative particle (*na*) is connected with the meaning of the root *vṛ* (to choose).
It is a restatement of the sense of the object [of the rule].
"In that case where it is to be performed according to the archetype, one should exclude the *varaṇa*.
But for what reason is the negative particle (*na*) connected with both "in the *anuyājas*" and "by means of the *jyāmahatva*"? It is said: because an option would otherwise be improper.
For conceptual construction (vikalpa) is indeed unjustified.
How so? In this context, regarding sacrifices, it is said: "I perform the sacrifice" (yajati).
If it is understood in this way, then that sacrifice cannot be accomplished without the performance of the sacrificial act (yejyāmāha).
In that case, the statement of prohibition would be purposeless;
and even when the prohibition is understood, the statement of injunction would be purposeless.
Therefore, an option is illogical.
"Surely, because it would result in the pointlessness of one of the two injunctions, [the latter] must be accepted as the basis.
It is replied:
Where one of the two results in pointlessness, an option (*vikalpa*) may indeed be assumed; however, where no meaningful purpose whatsoever is possible, [an option cannot be assumed].
And here, it is for the purpose of excluding the connection with the *anuyāja* offerings; therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*). He says:
But surely, if there were a connection with *anuyāja*, the word *na* would have to form a compound;
for the venerable Vārttikakāra Kātyāyana held that this word *na* is necessarily compounded when connected with a *subanta* (inflected word), as he stated:
"The option [to compound] is redundant because it is established by its very nature."
"No," says the Blessed One Pāṇini.
For he, having introduced the rule "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*), stated this compound.
Since it belongs to the *saddharmādi* group, the statement of Pāṇini is authoritative.
Because Kātyāyana is a proponent of non-existence;
for one who propounds non-existence would speak thus without perceiving that which actually exists.
Therefore, this is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusionary negation).
When there is a negation (*pratiṣedha*), a misconception (*bhrānti*) regarding the scripture must be postulated,
for it is that which is being conceptualized;
and thus, there is a double conceptualization.
In the case of a prohibition, there is some benefit in the non-performance [of the action], whereas in a positive injunction, it lies in the performance.
Therefore, this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
In that case, the definition is simply [the absence of] external conceptualization (*kalpanā*).
Furthermore, indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is superior to the postulation of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭakalpanā*).

Now, one might object that the principle "because of the unity of purpose" (*arthakatvāt*, 2.1.14.46) applies here, whereby there would be a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*). To this it is replied:
This logic is not sound;
however, as in the case of "He offers with curd," the oblation already established by a preceding sentence is set aside.

In that case, curd is enjoined, and there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) [with the rest of the sentence]. Likewise here as well, when the *yajeta* (he should sacrifice) is being reconsidered, the negative particle (*an-*) is enjoined for the purpose of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
Since in the case of exclusion a separate verb is heard, even though word-syntactic unity (*padaikavākyatva*) is possible, sentence-syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatva*) is certainly possible as well.

And likewise, even in the case of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), that [prohibition] would apply as it does to the archetype; one should not sacrifice in that manner, just as in the case of the exclusion [of the *anuyāja*s].

Alternatively, the "sacrificial day" (*yejyāmaha*), being obtained through its general application, is further specified by the sentence regarding the *anuyāja*s (meaning: "one performs the sacrificial day excluding the *anuyāja*s").
On this point, the text says: "But surely, if there is a connection with the *anuyāja*s, a compound of the negative particle (*nañ*) would result."
And there is no compound here (which would allow for a paryudāsa). Therefore, only a simple negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha) is accepted. It is said:
By the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*), there occurs either a compound (*samāsa*) or a sentence (*vākya*).
If one were to rely solely on the definition of a compound, the expression "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) would not be used.
Therefore, both "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣa*) and "king-man" (*rājapuruṣa*) are correct, because both are experienced [in usage].

Where there is no grammatical derivation (*anugama*), there is an incorrect usage (*asādhu-prayoga*), as in the word *gāvī*. Therefore, even in a compound (*samāsa*), that same meaning exists; thus, there is no fault in the absence of a compound.
"For in this case, when there is a connection with a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*), the compound is indeed eternal.
What is the intended meaning? It is that the sentence and the compound possess distinct meanings.
By means of the sentence, a person qualified by the masculine gender and singular number is perceived.
In a compound, however, it is not known whether [the meaning] belongs to two males, or to many, or to a female, or to a neuter.
Therefore, the sentence and the compound do not have the same meaning;
in the word *go*, however, a single meaning is perceived.
In this regard, that [usage] which conforms [to the rule] is correct; others are not praiseworthy.
For example, the word *goṇī* is correct when it means "a granary," but not when it means "an ox.
Here, in the case of the phrase *rājapuruṣaḥ*, which is devoid of gender and number, the compound alone is always correct.
When that [suffix] is attached, it is simply the sentence "the king's man.
Therefore, he says: "And the statement of the option (vā) is purposeless because it is established by its own nature.
Consequently, there is no exclusion (paryudāsa), due to the absence of a compound.

To this it is replied: "The rule regarding words [forming a compound] applies when they are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*); thus, a compound occurs between two things that possess semantic connection.
And if, in that semantic connection, one did not depend on gender, number, and so forth, then [the compound] would apply even to that which possesses the word *rājan*.

Thereafter, it is compounded with a noun (*puruṣa*). Therefore, in a compound, the meaning of the constituent members is understood as being free from gender and number (even when they are not explicitly heard), because the cognition [of the members] is identical.
Thus is the meaning "with a companion" (*salleka*).
Therefore, the application of both [the general rule and the specific exception] must be carried out.

Through the application of both, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is established in the sentence. As the Śāstra says: "In that case, for the sake of obtaining the literal meaning, there is a prohibition; otherwise, however—"
"For both terms would indeed involve figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) because they would be directed toward something else"—
this being the position reached, we reply:
"Precisely because this dilemma arises in the case of a prohibition..."
Therefore, to avoid that [fault], it is better to rely on *paryudāsa* (exclusion).

Soma: Thus, after the examination of the two types of sublation—namely, that based on the loss of purpose (*arthalopa*) and that based on substitution (*pratyāmnāna*), which are not clearly defined—the primary examination in this section (*pāda*) concerns that which is based on prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), which is very clear; hence there is a difference between sections and immediate succession.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: when there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the Ārbhava-śastra by the *codaka* (general rule) to a specific location (*pradeśa*), and when there is an independent injunction (*anārabhyavidhāna*) regarding the *yajñāyajñīya*, the negative particle (*nañ*) in "not the Ārbhava" (*nārbheyam*) and "not in the *anuyāja*s" (*nānuyājeṣu*) has the sense of prohibition.

And therefore, because it is intended to be performed, there is an option (*vikalpa*). As stated in the *Cintāmaṇi*: "In the case of the passage, 'Neither on the *nārmedha*, nor for the *hotṛ*, nor in the *anuyāja*s,' there would be either an option or an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), due to the two-fold nature of the statement."
Because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is illogical, that voice of negation (*niṣedhagīḥ*) results in its total destruction;
therefore, in the case of the sentence concerning the *anuyāja* offerings, it is set aside from that purpose.

*Bhāṭṭa*: Thus, sublation (*bādha*) has been defined through the principle of "smearing of the purpose" (*arthalepa*) and through "substitution" (*pratyāmnāna*); now, negation (*pratiṣedha*) and the other [grounds of sublation] are being defined.
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, the prohibition of the selection of the Hotṛ priest, which is obtained by extended application (atideśa), is heard in the text: "He does not choose a Hotṛ.

Similarly, regarding the formula *yejyāmahaṃ*, which is prescribed for all sacrifices by a general rule (*anārabhyādhīta*)—namely, "The call *āśrāvaya* has four syllables, *astu śrauṣaṭ* has four syllables, *yaja* has two syllables, *yejyāmahaṃ* has five syllables, and the *vaṣaṭ* call has two syllables; this indeed constitutes the seventeen-fold Prajāpati-sacrifice"—the prohibition "He does not perform the *yejyāmahaṃ* in the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s)" is heard.

Then, when considering whether this [negation] consists in the permanent exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the nature of the selection of the *hotṛ* priest and so forth, or whether it is a simple negation (*niṣedha*), it cannot first be a *paryudāsa* of the form: "And at the sacrifices, I must perform the sacrifice excluding the selection of the *hotṛ*. This is because there is no logical justification for it; for since the primary productive energy (*bhāvanā*) cannot be connected with anything else, and since there is no authority for accepting a subordinate status by resorting to mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), the negative particle (*nañ*) would then require a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward another word-meaning such as "that which is other than it" (*tadanya*). Therefore, this is indeed a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*).

And because that [prohibition] depends upon a prior application (*prāpti*), and because in this context such application is based on scripture, there arises an option (*vikalpa*)—like the choice between taking and not taking [the soma]—regarding what has been established by scripture, since its absolute sublation is impossible.

Now, what is the reason for a prohibition depending upon a prior application? It cannot be simply because the cognition of a non-existence (*abhāva*) is dependent upon the cognition of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
Because there is no production of cognition itself.
And that "attainment" has come from somewhere; it is for the sake of attaining the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), such as the *yeyajāmaha* and so forth.
In some cases, this occurs through scripture (*śāstra*).
"‘One should not eat kalañja’— even though [kalañja] is well-known in the context of the *anuyāja* offerings and so forth, it is because it is well-known in other sacrifices,
and so on.
Another [example] pertains to the subject at hand."

And since that [non-existence] is indeed of the nature of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is logical that the establishment of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) with respect to a vanished yogi is the cause for the cognition of non-existence, as in the case of "there is no yogi in the lake.
This is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For such a possibility does not arise by taking a [counter-positive] established through an erroneous cognition (*bhrama*).
Even when the existence of fire is well-known, the cognition that "fire exists" is not a delusion, because it is based on experience;
for as long as one has not considered the prohibitory scriptures, it remains merely a general rule.
For this very reason, the requirement of a prior attainment [of the object] is solely for the purpose of establishing what is to be enjoined.

Even if there were a possibility [of conflict], the claim that a prohibition is a "special rule" (viśeṣa) upon initial consideration is refuted; for since the counter-positive is presented within the context of the prohibition, no error can arise from the general rule, as it is in fact intended to apply to the occurrence of the counter-positive.
Nor is it the case that, even so, [the general rule] would be applicable...

Because such a counter-positive is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), there can be no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the absence of its being the intended object; furthermore, since the purpose [of the injunction] resides in the activity of the person, the negation would apply only where something is actually applicable (*prasakta*).

Nor should it be argued that, because the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) would result in futility (*vaiyarthyāpatti*) upon mere observation, one must assume the existence of an occasion for application (*prāpti-pakṣa*) in order to avoid that futility.

Because of the knowledge that the *yeyajāmaha* and other [mantras] have a basis in error regarding their being means [to the sacrifice], they are [already] established in the *anuyāja* offerings by the general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*), just as the *āhavanīya* fire is [established] by its specific rule.
This is because, through the well-known fact of being performed by that person (the sacrificer), the *āhavanīya* fire is present in the *yeyajāmaha* recitation within the *anuyāja* offerings;

and since it exists as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) by virtue of being performed by him, there arises the logical necessity of understanding the non-existence of that [fire] in those [specific instances].
And therefore, it must be stated that just as the rule for *pada* (P. 6.1.85) [is an exception] to the general rule, so too this [rule P.

2.4.71], by acting as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) regarding the absence of the application of the *tatpuruṣa* rule within its own domain, postulates for that [general rule] a scope beyond that [specific domain].

Because it is established by its own nature, an injunction regarding that aspect would be purposeless; likewise, even a prohibitory scripture [is meaningful] only if the general scripture has a scope beyond that [prohibition], since it would otherwise be impossible for the prohibition to have the purpose of preventing this person from performing an action that is already absent. Its meaningfulness arises precisely from its function as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Nor is there an absence of general rules; for even when considering the prohibition inferred from the removal [of an operation], the rule concerning words (*padaśāstra*)— just as it prescribes words—
is the constituent of the causal complex for the cognition that serves as the counter-positive of the non-existence [of the application].
The capacity to generate the understanding of a word arises through the state of being attached [to it], just like the understanding derived from grammatical rules (*padaśāstra*).

Nor can there be an understanding delimited by a property that is not a counter-correlate to the cognition of a powerful undesirable consequence resulting from the causal complex of another's action; for such a non-existence is not established here, as it would entail the status of being a means to the undesirable for another.
Because of this, since a prohibition is applicable even to that which has attained [the status of] an error, it does not follow from [prior] attainment.
And therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*) based on the scriptural nature of these qualities residing in this self, as performed by those whose minds are fixed upon this very self.
If this is argued, we say no;
for [the injunction] must be understood as being connected to a state that is associated with all the factors of action (*kāraka*), and thus it is what is to be turned away from.

And that cultivation of the negation (*niṣedha-bhāvanā*) would indeed have the form of a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*); thus, because it is associated with that [negation], it would not be of the nature of an error (*bhrama*), as it possesses the perception of a specific feature (*viśeṣa-darśana*) at the initial observation, unlike other generalizations (*utsarga*). [This applies to] the *anuyāja* context, which is favorable to the *ye-yajāmahe* formula.
It is possible;
however, an effort produced by that [effort] which would serve as the counter-positive is simply unestablished.
This is because [the word] generates verbal cognition even without such an effort serving as its counter-positive.

Therefore, even upon the initial consideration of a prohibitory scripture (*niṣedha-śāstra*), it necessarily depends on that [general rule], because this [prohibition] is dependent upon the prior attainment of that [action].

For a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) cannot possibly exist merely through effort; rather, for the sake of establishing the counter-positive, one must first consider the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) regarding the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) and so forth.
And therefore, since the reality [of the injunction] necessarily consists in being qualified by the factors of action (*kāraka*),

it is precisely those volitions (*kṛti*) delimited by being conducive to the *kāraṇakya*, *yajāmahe*, and so forth that constitute it, as there is no general rule of parsimony (*sāmānyavinigamanā*) [to favor one over another].
For this very reason:

By means of the authority of the scripture (*śāstrapramitayā*), one must accept that the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) is [the *yajñāyajñīya*], and thus the determination of the meaning of the prohibitive scripture (*niṣedhaśāstra*) as referring solely to the *yājyānuvākyā* mantra is not our primary position; rather, it must be accepted that the counter-correlate is the principal element. Therefore, since it is impossible for the object established by the general scripture (*sāmānyaśāstra*) to be set aside, the other [element] which is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) must be connected.
For this very reason...

Since that [prohibition] is also absolutely incapable of being sublated, a conceptual distinction (vikalpa) is indeed appropriate. For instance, in cases such as "there is no fire in the lake" or "not in the atmosphere,
nor in heaven," there is a sublation of the *yeyajāmaha* by the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) through the abundance of results in the *anuyāja* offerings.

In that case, having accepted that fire and so forth are the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) by virtue of their arrival there, there is an inference based on the principle of producing excellence; and through negation, there is the prescription of being the correlate (*anuyogin*) with respect to the abundance of the fruit, because it is intended for that purpose, provided there is no sublation (*bādha*).
Where, however, there is no sublation, [the rule holds].

Even in the absence of the *yeyajāmaha* formula when the [sacrifice] exists, because the other parts produce excellence (*sādguṇya*), there is no contradiction— just as in the cases of grasping both or grasping neither— since the non-existence is inferred solely with reference to that [formula] as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) by those very authors of the *Nirukta*,
and thus it is a rule (*vidhi*) obtained through natural inclination (*rāga*).
For this very reason, while [the understanding of] an "etcetera" (*ādi*) depends upon the well-known existence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*),

in the case of a prohibition— such as that of eating *kalañja* and the like— the [prohibition] also requires the attainment [of the act] through passion, by way of apprehending it as a means to a desired end; for the prohibition, being distinct from that [desire], negates only that which has been prompted by the verbal [text], namely, the volitional effort (*kṛti*) conducive to the eating of *kalañja*.

The principle of *paryudāsa* (2479): The rule of exclusion (*paryudāsavidhi*) functions as a restriction because it does not arrive at the object of prohibition [itself], but rather through the sense of its subject matter—the eating of *kalañja*—and by means of a limitation to that alone. Because it restricts what is other than that, there is always the occurrence of an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*) regarding its definition, even in terms of being a means to an undesirable end.
"This is a distinction regarding the servant," says the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*.
Nor is there a disparity [between this case and others], because even in the case of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), cessation from that [action] occurs due to aversion toward what is undesirable.

Therefore, since the *hotṛ* priest also depends upon the attainment of what is to be excluded (*paryudāsanīya*), there arises the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*); consequently, there is no permanent sublation (*bādha*) of the *varaṇa*, *ye yajāmahe*, and so forth, in the *Mahāpitṛyajña* and other rites.
This is because [the rule] can be explained even by resorting to the misconception of a logician (*tārkika*), as in the case of the word-initial [consonant].
When it is argued that "it does not go there," since the alternative of a prohibition (pratiṣedha) is vitiated by the eight defects of optionality (vikalpa),
and because— unlike a prohibitive injunction— a verbal cognition does not arise from a restrictive injunction (paryudāsa) independently [of its positive correlate],
for this very reason there is the employment of a restrictive exclusion (paryudāsīkaraṇa).

And the nature of *paryudāsa* (exclusion) [is established] for the sake of beauty, because that is possible through the well-known path of the *hotṛ*-selection, the *anyāja*, and so forth, which serve as the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) to the difference in meaning;
it is the status of being a sentence that conveys an absence whose counter-correlate is something distinct, and not a property of the negative particle (*nañ*) itself.

Furthermore, although the interpretation of *nañ* as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is possible in the case of "he does not choose the Hotṛ," the status of this as a permanent compound (*nityasamāsa*) does not follow simply because it is distinct from a finite verb (*ākhyāta*).

In the case of "not in the *anuyāja*s," since the meaning of *nañ*—namely, the state of being other than the choosing of the Hotṛ—is connected with a nominal stem (*subanta*), there would necessarily result in a permanent compound in the form *ananuyājeṣu*. Thus, the status of the *nañ* in "not in the *anuyāja*s" [would be that of a compound].
Because there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with that which ends in a case-suffix;
and because even in that instance, as in "he does not choose the *hotṛ* priest," the sentence remains logically consistent,
and there is no evidence for a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*).

Even when the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)— namely, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*)— is construed as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the act of choosing a *hotṛ*, according to the grammatical view that a compound possesses a unitary power (*śakti*) toward a qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭārtha*), whereas in a sentence the negative particle has a distinct meaning consisting of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the absence [of the action] within the scope of each individual word as a qualifier or a qualificand; even so, since the choice of a different person is not something achievable through volitional effort (*kṛtisādhya*), its connection with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) would be untenable.

Therefore, since the grammatical correctness of the sentence cannot be prevented even without a rule for compound formation due to its being a *karmadhāraya*, it does not possess the status of a qualifier either; thus,
there is no obstacle whatsoever to the connection of the meaning of the verbal root with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the sentence "not in the *anuyājas*."
For this very reason, and because of the derivation [of the word],
the negative particle (*nañ*) also denotes that which is delimited by the absence of another.

Since the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) of the compound and the sentence— whether involving conceptualization or non-conceptualization— is established for the purpose of rejecting the seven [types of] options, one must accept that its primary referent is precisely that [absence].
In that case as well,

by the rule of Kātyāyana— "The mention of the option (*vā*) is purposeless because it is established by its own nature"— since there is the cognition of the entire class of objects other than the act of choosing (*varaṇa*), the statement regarding the reality (*tattva*) is also consistent.
Because it is established by its own nature (*svabhāva*), there is a concomitance (*anvaya*) with the manifestation of the single object of the self;
and although [the object] is "other than that," "contrary to that," or "absent of that," the meaning is that this is established by the logic of its own form (*svarūpa*).

In reality, however, the word *nañ* is well-known to possess denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to both [the absence of identity and mutual exclusion], even though it is established as signifying mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*). Nevertheless,

since the qualified meaning and the unity of meaning are equal in both the compound and the sentence, and because the connection of the verbal root's meaning with that [negation] is not conventionally established within a compound, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is necessarily required.

And that [objection] is as follows: if the rule were to result in the ungrammaticality of the sentence, then the provision of an option (*vikalpa*) by means of the term *vibhāṣā* would not be faulty, because it depends upon what is to be optionally excluded.
This is likewise the case regarding the expression "not in the *nājya* sacrifices."

The statement of Kātyāyana—that Pāṇini’s Sūtra is meaningful—is itself the logical principle (*nyāya*). In that regard, although the negative particle (*nañ*) and the words *ye-yajāmahe* do not contradict the meaning of the *ye-yajāmahe* [formula], it is nonetheless an authority.

For this very reason, the ancient masters, having accepted the definition of the optional rule (*vibhāṣā-sūtra*) as being known from the context, enjoin that [formula] with reference to the *anuyāja* offerings.
In compounds such as *kumbhakārānu* and *papadānu*, there is no optionality.
Therefore, even an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) that is not concordant [with the preceding term] is not possible.
Nevertheless, [this applies] to that which is distinct from the *yeyajāmaha*.
Since the sentence "in the *yāja*s" (*yājeṣu*) is also grammatically correct, an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is appropriate there as well.
When the word "but" (*tu*) requires a correlate, the correlates are those beginning with ignorance (*ajñāna*) up to the *ārṣeya*.
Maṇḍana states: "In the case of the *ārṣeya*, there would be no option."
Because it is not present [in the context], that [prohibition] is not accepted; rather, there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the case of non-Arṣeya [lineage].
Śaṅkara says: "In the case of non-Arṣeya, there is an exclusion."
By means of the two words *na* and *yajati*, one indicates that which is other than the *anuyāja*s; thus, there is a connection with that [indicated object].

Since the principle of exclusion (*paryudāsanyāya*)—which is synonymous with the principle of the *ye-yajāmaha*—is accepted as the objective (the *uddeśya*), the injunction for the *ye-yajāmaha* is formulated with that objective as its referent. Thus it is.

Regarding its own nature (*svarūpa*): "Even though the injunction is weak, it possesses a self-dependence upon that [prohibition] because it is not separated from it; for when there is equality between the general injunction and the specific prohibition regarding another sacrifice, it occurs [as such]. (Bālakrīḍā, p. 98). This is because it is presented by the general rule.

The *paryudāsavidhi* (prescriptive exclusion) is of sixteen kinds: 1. Exclusion of that which brings about the primary purpose (*rādāpakāri*) pertaining to the archetype (*prakṛti*). 2. Exclusion of the taught (*upadiṣṭa*) *rādāpakāri* pertaining to the modification (*vikṛti*). 3. Exclusion of the extended (*atidiṣṭa*) *rādāpakāri* pertaining to the modification. 4. Exclusion of the *rādāpakāri* pertaining to an entirely new ritual action (*apūrvakarman*). 5. Exclusion of the direct application (*saṃnipāta*) pertaining to the archetype. 6. Exclusion of the direct application for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) pertaining to the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the archetype. 7. Exclusion of the direct application for a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) pertaining to the disposal of the archetype. 8. Exclusion of the direct application for both a seen and unseen purpose pertaining to the archetype. 9. Exclusion of the direct application for a seen purpose, distinct from the disposal, pertaining to an entirely new ritual action. 10. Exclusion of the direct application for both a seen and unseen purpose pertaining to an entirely new ritual action. 11. Exclusion of the direct application for a seen purpose pertaining to the taught [substance] in the modification. 12. Exclusion of the direct application distinct from the disposal for a seen purpose pertaining to the taught in the modification. 13. Exclusion of the direct application for both a seen and unseen purpose pertaining to the disposal of the taught in the modification. 14. Exclusion of the direct application for a seen purpose pertaining to the extended in the modification. 15. Exclusion of the direct application distinct from the disposal for a seen purpose pertaining to the extended in the modification. 16. Exclusion of the direct application for both a seen and unseen purpose pertaining to the disposal of the extended in the modification.
Examples, however, must be sought elsewhere.

The animal victim has the status of a single oblation because it is enjoined as a whole.

By the sūtra, "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," the suffix (taddhita) indicates that the entire animal—just like the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) and other offerings—is to be understood as the oblation (*havis*) characterized by being intended for the deity; thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established that the entire animal is to be cut up. However, by the sūtra, "Or rather, it is direct [cutting], like the drawing [of Soma], because the portions are conceived separately," the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) will be established: since the very form of the animal is destroyed by the act of dismemberment, it is impossible for the whole to be the object of offering. Therefore, because the rule for cutting (*avadāna*) is prescribed specifically for the separately conceived parts such as the heart and so forth, and because the connection with the deity expressed by the suffix cannot apply directly to the whole, one must understand—out of necessity—that its scope refers to the indirect [parts]. Thus, the cutting is established as being performed upon the [specific] oblations that are directly perceived.

Mīmāṃsākośa 312: There is no deficiency; likewise, when the sacrifice of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is performed by another deity, because there is no inclusion of the deity of the animal sacrifice (paśuyāga), there is the occurrence of the loss of that inclusion.

The sense is that in the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice dedicated to the animal deity (*paśudevatā*), which is of the nature of a consecratory rite (*saṃskāra*), if it were performed otherwise—that is, as a sacrifice for a [separate] divinity—there would be a loss of the consecration consisting of remembrance; thus, the statement of the elders becomes justified.

And so, in the *Sautrāmaṇī*, the statement of the elders serves as an indicative mark (*liṅgadarśana*) showing that in another context, namely the animal sacrifice and the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice, there is not just one single deity; therefore, it is established that the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice is indeed a consecratory rite for the deity of the animal sacrifice.
Furthermore, regarding the cups (*graha*), that statement [of the elders] applies when there is a commonality [of deities], because it is for that purpose.

In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, regarding the cups (grahas) that have deities in common with those [of the animal sacrifices], there is that statement concerning the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas): "There are no sacrificial cakes for these animals; these animals have the cups as their sacrificial cakes.

In reality, however, it is not that the sacrificial cakes do not exist; rather, this is said considering the absence of the preparatory rites (saṃskāra) for those [animals] whose deities are different—namely, that "the cups are their sacrificial cakes," because the cups, like the sacrificial cakes, serve that purpose, being intended for the preparation of the deity.
From this it is known that where there are actual *puroḍāśas* in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and where the animal sacrifice is for many deities,
and where there is an animal sacrifice on both sides as well as on one side in the case of sacrifices (*iṣṭi*), [the same rule applies].
Saṃkarṣa 3.2.12:
And because of the observation of indicative marks in the animal sacrifice.
In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice as well, the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) should be that of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, just as it is in the case of the iṣṭis.

The indicative marks are: "He performs eleven *prayāja* offerings" and "eleven *anuyāja* offerings," as well as "Having poured the *sruva*-ladle full of clarified butter, he anoints the animal with the *juhū*.
Furthermore, in the *darśa* sacrifice there is "the milk for Indra," and in the animal sacrifice there is "the animal for Agni-Soma"; thus, the substance and deity [are established].
Moreover, in the animal sacrifice, it should have a common ritual procedure (*samānatantra*) together with the cake offering (*puroḍāśa*).

In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, there is both the animal and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). Regarding the release of speech at the time of placing the oblation-holder (haviṣkṛt), the established conclusion is that it occurs only at the time of placing the oblation-holder for the cake-offering, and not for the animal-offering. Thus he says: "In the case of the animal accompanied by the cake (sapuroḍāśe)—that is, when the animal is together with the cake—the ritual procedure (tantra) would be common; that is, there would be one and the same ritual procedure."
The rope is a limb of the animal. The section concerning the singularity of the animal. The section concerning the singularity of the animal.

The section concerning the oneness of the animal: It is heard in scripture, "Having encircled [the post], he dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni. In the inquiry as to whether this rope belongs to the animal or is an auxiliary of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The rope (raśanā) should be an accessory of the animal. Why? Because when the animal is brought—that is, when the context of the animal is established—the rope is enjoined.
In the original injunction, the connection of the rope with the animal is heard directly.
Therefore, the rope is either an accessory of the animal or an accessory of the sacrificial post, because it serves as a consecration for it;
thus he establishes the final conclusion.
The rope (*raśanā*) is not a subsidiary part of the animal, but rather a subsidiary part of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
This is because it serves as a consecration for that [post], since the rope functions as a means of refining the sacrificial post.
Indeed, the rope produces a measure of firmness in the sacrificial post to the full extent of its length.
Therefore, the rope is an accessory to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). And the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is meaningful for that purpose.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the aphorism is intended to establish the true nature of the mantra’s meaning and other supporting reasons.
The word *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The neuter gender in the phrase *tad arthavat* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*) resulting from a transposition [of the genders].

Since the girdle (*raśanā*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), [the mantra] reads: “The youth, well-attired and girt, has come; he becomes even more excellent as he is being born.”
"The wise poets, seeking the divine with their minds and desiring the gods, bring him forth.
Thus, that explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) in the form of a mantra would become meaningful, purposeful, and fulfilled in its aim.
As for the meaning of the mantra: being "youthful" and "encircled"—that is, enveloped by a girdle—he has come, as if "well-clothed" and wearing beautiful garments, and now stands there.
He, being thus born, becomes superior.

The wise ones—the steadfast, the intelligent, the well-versed (svādhyas), those whose thoughts are beautiful and directed toward him on all sides—being seekers of the gods, regarding him as the Āditya, the sages, the learned, and the officiating priests, raise him up and elevate him with their minds.
This is the praise of the sacrificial post (yūpa).
Ke. Paśvaṅgaṃ svada. Bhā.

4.1.10.25–28. Since the benefit for the animal cake (paśupuroḍāśa) is already accomplished by the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and other rites performed for the sake of the animal sacrifice itself, separate performance of those subsidiary rites for its sake need not be undertaken. This should be examined under the section titled “The Section on the Animal Cake” (Paśupuroḍāśādhikaraṇa).

The form of the animal (*paśvākṛti*) is not an auxiliary of the sacrifice, for the sacrificial portions (*avadāna*) are the oblations that serve as the auxiliaries of the sacrifice, not the form of the animal.

For that [form], by qualifying the two types of material from which the portions are cut, has assisted the primary act in its status as the archetype; thus, even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), by qualifying the material from which the portions are cut, it will likewise assist the primary act.

Bhāṣya 2.2.7.29: In the case of animal sacrifices and the like, there is the performance of the archetypal procedure (*itikartavyatā*), such as the *sāmidhenī* verses. Vi. 10.3.1: The fruit [of the sacrifice], such as cattle, is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the use of implements like the *godohana* vessel, not the ritual itself.

Ke. (Bhāṭṭa 4.1.2): In a modified form (*vikṛti*) of the animal sacrifice and the like, the eleven *prayāja* offerings and other such elements specifically enjoined do not exclude the other archetypal auxiliary elements.
Bhāṣya 10.3.1.19–22: The animal (paśu) is produced for the sake of the sacrifice; and being performed for that very purpose, it also assists in the acts of [shedding] blood and the *śakṛt* (dung).

Bhāṣya 11.1.1.1, p. 2096: The disposal of the blood of the animal is not the motive (*prayojaka*) for its slaughter, but rather it is a *pratipatti* (concluding ritual act) in the case of the *āmīṣomīya* animal sacrifice.
Bhaṭṭa 4.1.12: Since the *godohana* (milk-pail) is enjoined with reference to the animal, the *godohana* is indeed prompted by the animal.
And that [act] must be performed only when there is an independent desire for it.
Bhāṭṭa 4.1.2, Section 3. *The Topic on the Singularity of the Animal* (Paśvekatvādhikaraṇa).
*The Principle of its Inclusion* (Tadāgamanyāya).
In the phrase "the animal for Agni and Soma," the singular number is intended to be significant.
In that regard, there is unity because that which resides as a constituent part of the sacrifice is subordinate.
The Commentary states: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, according to the text, "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.
Likewise, [for the purpose of the cart on which the purchased Soma is placed], it says, "He yokes two oxen."
Likewise, in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, there is the injunction: "One offers the Kapiñjala birds to the Spring.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the singular, dual, and plural number intended to be significant, or is it not intended?
In this context, the meaning is that the singularity is a subordinate element of the sacrifice and is therefore not intended to be significant.
Because the purpose (artha) is subordinate;
neither the number nor the binding is subordinate to that which is to be sacrificed.
To what, then? To the animal, the two oxen, and the kapiñjala birds.
Why should the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) express the meaning of number residing in the nominal stem,
while the syntactical connection (*vākya*) would express it as a subordinate element of the sacrifice?
For the direct Vedic statement is more authoritative than the syntactical connection.
And therefore, it is intended as a constituent part of the sacrifice.
He says: "Let it not be a constituent part of the sacrifice; nevertheless, food for animals and so forth is intended.
It is replied: there is no purpose whatsoever served by mentioning or not mentioning food for animals and so forth.

For there is a purpose served by the injunction of the sacrifice when it is not defective; for even if it is defective, provided that the animal and so forth are not disclosed, the ritual remains valid. And from the sacrifice comes the fruit, not from the animal and such.
Therefore, since there is no purpose served by the quality of the animal and so forth— whether it be unknown or known— that quality is not intended to be expressed.
If something possesses a purpose, then it is said to be intended for expression.
[The answer is] "No," because in that case, the single [recitation] is subordinate as a subsidiary element of the sacrifice.
The quality of redness (*aruṇa*), because it is conveyed by another word (*aruṇāpada-upāttatvāt*), serves the purpose of the action.
Singularity, however, because it is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārthatvāt*) as indicated by the case-ending (*vibhaktiśrutyā*), does not serve the purpose of the action.

(According to the Ānandāśrama edition, the phrase "it would [serve] the purpose of the action through syntactical connection" [*kriyārthā vākyena syāt*] appears here; this is not found in the *Ratna*.).

The intention of the *Bhāṣya*—“Even though the food of cattle and so forth is intended”—is that the meaning is conveyed by what is expressed only once (*sakṛduccaritatva*). It raises an objection: [the meaning is that] because the single animal (whose singularity is internally implied) is connected to the action, the sacrifice qualified by the animal qualified by singularity is performed once; thus, by means of the injunction, it effects that which is qualified by what is to be obtained only once.

That which is an auxiliary (*upakāraka*) to the substance-less [animal] (i.e., the animal ignorant of the sacrifice)—namely, its singularity—is also an auxiliary, even if indirectly (*praṇāḍyā*), to the action as well (once it has been brought about).

What is the intended meaning of the *Parihārabhāṣya* passage: "There is no purpose whatsoever in stating the word 'animal' (*paśu*) or the word 'food' (*anna*)"? [The answer is: "While this relationship between the animal and the number is being presented, there is no relationship between the action and the animal" (this is the reading in the Ānandāśrama edition; the reading in the *Ratna* is: "When the relationship between number and case-role exists simultaneously as qualifiers of the nominal stem-meaning within a single moment, there is no relationship between the action and the animal").

In the case of a connection between the action and the animal, where there is a connection between the time and the number of animals, the animal alone [is connected] (not one qualified by a number); consequently, since the sacrifice would possess its required quality through the mere animal, no regard would be paid to the number.

In the case of a *tantra* (simultaneous) connection, because the word "animal" is uttered only once (i.e., simultaneously), the word would have to refer to its own primary meaning [for each instance].
(This is an illustration of the presence of two sets of three contradictory factors.)

In that regard, as for the objection raised—that even if the number [of recitations] is omitted from the sacrifice, there would be no deficiency and thus the number might be disregarded—that defect remains exactly the same even in the case of a connection with a *tantra* (the common performance). (The reading found in the written and printed versions—"the defect of the direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth remains exactly the same"—is indeed incorrect.
Therefore, the *saṃsthā* is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the ritual action.
For this very reason, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, intending this, said: "For there is a purpose in using a non-defective word that is an auxiliary of the sacrifice."

Even when the animal victim and so forth have perished, the sacrifice remains entirely unimpaired; this is because there is a single scriptural injunction [regarding the procedure]. (This is the reading of the *Ratna* following the *Bhāṣya*.)

Commentary: There are certain cases where something else is intended, by which it is made known that [the specific form] is not what is intended to be expressed. For example: "If they should steal the Soma, one should give a single cow as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
For if this were intended to be expressed, he would not have said "one" (*ekām*); because the singular number in the word "cow" (*gām*) is intended to be expressed.

Likewise, in the cases of "two ewes" (*avī dve*) and "two milch-cows" (*dhenū dve*), the expression "two" (*dve*) serves as an indicator that the dual number in "ewes" (*avī*) is not intended to be significant. Similarly, in the case of "three with white spots on their foreheads" (*trīn lalāmān*), the expression "three" (*trīn*) is the indicative mark that the plural number in "with white spots" (*lalāmān*) is not intended to be significant.
If it is argued that it is perceived:
Commentary: If you view it thus—that the number is not intended to be expressed—then [we reply]:
for the number is indeed perceived as subordinate to the verbal expression.

Just as when it is said, "Bring the paśu," only one is brought; when "paśū" (dual), two are brought; and when "paśūn" (plural), many are brought—whatever is thus understood is the meaning of the word. Therefore, it is understood from the word that number is an auxiliary constituent (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice.
And that which is understood from the word does not become unintended in the absence of a reason;
like destruction, because it possesses that same means of valid cognition, as in the previous case.
Commentary: This is not so. It is true that it is perceived, but this is not the meaning of the word. It is perceived only through delusion.
Whence is this? For that which is perceived as possessing sound is seen upon the arrival of that [sound], and its cognition occurs just as it does for others.
Commentary: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.

This is not so; it is not that number is not heard by means of the word in the case of the sacrifice. Rather, it is perceived in the meaning expressed by the verb. In common usage, when one says "bring a beast," because the singular number is present, one brings that which is qualified by a single beast.
In the expression "two animals are to be brought," what is understood is the qualification by duality.
For in that case, singularity departs and duality arises;
and it is understood that whatever arises upon the arrival of something else is the meaning of that thing.
His cognition is like that of other words:
