when "Bring the horse" is said, one understands something other than a horse; when "Bring the cow" is said, there is the bringing of a cow.
In that case, the horse departs and the cow arises.
From this it is known that the meaning of the word "horse" is a horse, and the meaning of the word "cow" is a cow.
As for what was said— that "the meaning of the sentence is sublated by the direct Vedic statement"— it is replied:
The scripture does not state that there is no sentence-meaning;
rather, it merely expresses the number residing in the nominal stem.
Such a number is enjoined for the sacrifice by means of the sentence.
For the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha), as well as the meaning of the case-ending (vibhaktyartha), is connected with that which is expressed by the verb.
Thus, the act of offering (ālambha) is understood as qualified by those specific attributes.
In that case, because they share a single purpose, it is appropriate for them to constitute a single sentence (ekavākya).

For if the number were being enjoined with respect to the animal (*paśu*), a single verbal form (*ākhyāta-śabda*) would be unable to enjoin both the meaning of the verb and the connection with the number.
Therefore, the number must be intended as pertaining to the sacrifice.

[The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: "For the case-ending (*vibhakti*) declares, by direct audition (*śruti*) itself, that all three—the gender, the number, and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—are for the sake of the action."

Action is that which is to be accomplished, and it requires its means as well as the gender, number, and other attributes that delimit it (and all the factors of action [kārakas] require the action as well). Therefore, it is precisely the action, qualified by all these qualifiers, that is enjoined.

In this regard, the suffix denoting the injunction first operates upon the qualifier; otherwise, it would be logically untenable. (He states how it is untenable: "For there can be no cognition of a qualified object if the qualifiers have not been apprehended."

Granted that the sentence may indeed have the purpose of enjoining an action (*kriyārthatva*), even so there is no fault, because there is no contradiction between the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the syntactical connection (*vākya*). As he says: through the *upaśleṣa-lakṣaṇā* (characterized by proximity) [or *upapada-lakṣaṇā*] of the direct statement regarding the animal and its singularity, only the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) is understood, not subordination to that purpose (*tādarthya*). Therefore, since there is no occurrence of both [the *śruti* and the *vākya*] with respect to a single object, there is no contradiction.
Consequently, the Commentator says: "The direct statement does not lack the meaning of the sentence."
That is the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

The Commentary asks: "What [is the mark]? (What is the indicative mark? "[The animals] with slit ears are for Yama; those with curved ears are for Rudra; those with bent forms are for Parjanya; of these, the one with ten [fingers/teeth] is for Indra-Agni" (slit ears means cut ears;
"for Yama" means having Yama as their deity).
The *avalitāḥ* are the most arrogant, having Rudra as their deity;
the *namo-rūpāḥ* are blue-colored, having Parjanya as their deity—this is the meaning of the words.
If a triad is intended, then the tenth [cup] belongs to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*).

Likewise, having introduced the subject with "The black ones are terrestrial, the smoky ones are atmospheric, the great ones are celestial, the variegated ones are lightning, and the perfected ones are the stars," he says: "This is the form of the half-months, namely, those consisting of fifteen.
From this also, we see that the number is intended to be significant.
As for what was said—that the phrase "one cow" indicates a figurative usage—this is now addressed.
This is stated in order to prescribe the connection with the number of cows; for otherwise, the connection between the cow and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) would be understood as already prescribed.
Therefore, even though it is intended [to be significant], this must be explicitly stated.
The statements "two barren cows," "two milch-cows," and "three with white marks on their foreheads" are restatements (anuvādas).
This is the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). This is stated in order to enjoin the connection between the cow and the number.

(Quoting the *parihāra-bhāṣya*: "Otherwise, the connection with the cow as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is understood," he explains: First, the text would simply state, "One should give a cow as the sacrificial fee. (In that case,) there would be an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the horse and so forth. (The opponent objects: "If you say that the number itself is being enjoined, and not the cow—[we reply: in that case, since the number is being enjoined, the relationship between the cow and the number must be enjoined. And in enjoining that, [the cow] would not enter into the action; thus, there would be an extreme syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) (meaning: there is not even a trace of direct scriptural statement [*śruti*] here)."

Therefore, the statement "whatever one should give as the sacrificial fee, that is a cow" is intended to favor the direct Vedic text (*śruti*) by avoiding a displacement of the syntactical connection (*vacanavyatikarṣa*). In the other case, however, it is understood as an injunction regarding the number with reference to the cow.
(The opponent says: This [solution] also is [not tenable] whenever [it is proposed] (meaning: it is not appropriate).
Why? Because number is not enjoined with respect to the action itself, such that a connection between the cow and the number would have to be enjoined. [The proponent of a partial view] replies:
It is said that number, when being enjoined, becomes the means (*sādhana*) for the action by way of the object to be numbered.
In that regard, there are many numbers, and it is not known which one serves as the delimiting factor.
(The objector says: Since the number "one" is already present in the production of horses and so forth (when the term *dakṣiṇā* is mentioned), it is not applied there because it would be redundant;
[it applies] to cows.
But [it] does not exist.

(The proponent of a partial view says: "Even for cows, there are twelve hundred [to be given] (therefore, it is introduced there to contradict that). The opponent says: If by the *codaka* (if the acquisition of twelve hundred cows occurs through the *codaka*, and because a contingent [rule] is subject to constant consideration, it is replaced by the directly taught [number] 'one'—this is the meaning).

The proponent of a partial view (*ekadeśin*) says: "Even otherwise, the singularity of the horses and so forth is obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) itself. Since the *codaka* manifests the intention of the owner, and since those [horses and so forth] are already obtained as being joined with singularity from the *codaka* alone, the singular number taught in the direct injunction (*aupadeśikī ekatvasaṃkhyā*) would be purposeless. To this, the proponent of the partial view states his own intention: It is replied.
(The number [of cows] based on direct instruction) is obtained quickly because it is directly perceived, even when another [number] has not yet been reached; thus, it is not purposeless.

However, that which is based on extended application (*atideśika*) is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). (Since this solution offered by the "Partialist" [Ekadeśin] is not very convincing, he explains otherwise: Or rather, if only the cow itself were obtained [as the sacrificial fee], then the injunction regarding the cow would be improper, as it would be purposeless.
This is not the case, for other substances as well—such as horses and the like—are obtained.
Therefore, it is not true that "the quality is enjoined, while only the number is enjoined.
Consequently, by virtue of this restrictive rule (*niyama*), there must necessarily be an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*).
To exclude others [such as horses], he says "one cow.
And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) [to this effect].
The Commentary states: "And by doing so, the gender (*liṅga*) which shares the same phonetic form [as the word for 'cow'] will be intended."

In this regard, the following view is established: "In the spring, at dawn, one should sacrifice a black-necked [cow] dedicated to Agni; in the summer, at midday, a brindled [cow] dedicated to Indra; in the autumn, in the afternoon, a white [cow] dedicated to Bṛhaspati.
Regarding this, it is heard in the scripture: "They are pregnant. Pregnancy is a quality of females.

Therefore, it will be said that "he shows women. Likewise, regarding [the texts] "The horse, the bull, the ram, the goat, the man" and "These belong to Prajāpati," it is heard therein: "They are bright, for the sake of possessing virility."
Whiteness is a quality of males;
by that [quality], he indicates [the presence of] males.

Śā—The doubt is as follows: is the number—such as being accompanied by a case-ending denoting a substance that is to be adopted—a subordinate factor of the action and thus unintended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*), or is it intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*) according to its grammatical role?

In that regard, by direct statement (*śruti*), there is the singularity of the animal; because that [singularity] possesses a uniform form, its status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) is understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*) with what resides in another word. And since syntactical connection is weaker than direct statement, the singularity is not for the sake of the sacrifice.
And because there would be a deficiency in the sacrifice if that were not intended,
it is said:
"It has been made one's own by the factor of action residing in the same suffix."

Number is led toward the action, not toward the substance; indeed, it follows from the word itself. And it has been said: "Just as in the case of *pañca-paśūn* (five animals), oneness is understood [in each animal], so too the status of being the object of the action is understood through the stronger force of the identical verbal suffix (*samāna-pratyaya-śruti*)."
Thus [it is said].

Soma: Just as by such scriptural passages as "They dig with a spade," the purpose of digging and so forth is not for the sake of the sacrifice because of the statement regarding the weapon, so too here, since there is an objection that the singularity—which has the animal as its referent according to the rule of the animal—does not have the sacrifice as its purpose, there is a connection [to the discussion]. Vi: "In the case of the unity [of the animal] in the passage 'The animal is to be sacrificed,' [the singularity] follows from the act of sacrificing."

Whether it exists or not, since the singularity of the animal is understood through direct audition (*śruti*) within its own word, its connection first occurs with the proximate factor brought about by its own cognition; subsequently, it connects with the sacrifice and the animal. Thus, in this sequence, its status as an auxiliary to the sacrifice is appropriate.

Bhaṭṭa: In passages such as "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), where the number residing in the animal—the object to be employed—is expressed by the case-ending, there arises the inquiry: is that number intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*) or not? In this deliberation, based on the traditional rule (*smṛti*) "substantives have the substance as their primary meaning," and because the case-ending expresses a specific number, the animal is understood through its designation as a qualifier of the nominal stem's meaning; furthermore, by the mark (*liṅga*) of fitness—namely, that the animal is capable of being a qualifier for the nominal stem's meaning—the connection of the animal with the action expressed by the sentence is untenable [if the number were also significant]. Since the action remains unimpaired even in the absence of that [number], the number is not intended to be significant.

Nor can it be argued that, even though oneness and so forth are qualifiers of the animal, they may still be intended as specifications of the animal because of the animal’s connection with the action through its relation to the *kāraka*—as in the case of "one wearing a red turban"—since number and the *kāraka* are presented simultaneously by the case-ending. For if one were to first express the number’s connection with the animal and subsequently express the qualified animal’s connection with the *kāraka*, this would result in the fallacy of a "cessation-and-resumption" (*viramyavyāpāra*) of the verbal operation.

Nor should it be argued that, since you also accept that number is apprehended through direct word-hearing (*padaśruti*) and so forth, and because a simultaneous cognition of two distinct things is contradictory, you too would fall into the error of "cessation and renewed operation" (*viramyavyāpāra*)— first accepting the connection of the pure animal with the verbal action (*kāraka*), and only subsequently accepting the connection of the number with the animal. For even so, in cases where there is no disagreement regarding the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified among the *kārakas* conjoined with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of the number is justified due to the absence of any other established linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) for the productive urge in such instances.

Otherwise, since the redness (*āruṇya*) could also be logically established as a qualifier of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) itself— by way of its characteristic of being an instructional attribute— it would follow that one must first accept its connection with the action (as per Mīmāṃsākośa 313).

This would lead to accepting the conclusion of the section on the singularity of the animal (*paśvekatvādhikaraṇa*) [which states that the number qualifies the substance], rather than the final established position (*siddhānta*) regarding its connection with the one-year-old cow.

And here, although *lauhitya* (redness) and so forth are qualifiers of the specific *kāraka* conjoined with the *bhāvanā*, there is no defect because they reside within a compound word (*samastapada*). Furthermore, since the connection with the *bhāvanā* expressed by the verbal suffix (*kvāśabda*) occurs precisely in the case of the *vāravantīya* being the object (*dāsya*), there is no defect whatsoever.
For this very reason, even in the case of *somapra* and so forth, there is no primary connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
Moreover, it has been stated in various places that [the number] follows from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) alone.

Furthermore, the singularity denoted by the suffix does not function as a qualifier (*prakāratā*) of the animal, which is the meaning of the stem, because that would result in the loss of the predominance of the meaning of the suffix.
Rather, just as [singularity] qualifies the animal, it also functions as a qualifier of the agent (*pratīc*), who is the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Therefore, because oneness is the instrument (*karaṇa*), it cannot be a qualifier (*prakāra*) of the enjoined efficient force (*vidheyabhāvanā*); thus, it is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣā*).

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: the connection [of the animal] is only with the instrument-hood of the animal, and not even with oneness, due to the absence of any means of proof (*pramāṇa*).

Consequently, while the animal connects to the efficient force through that [instrument-hood], the number [oneness] also—by virtue of its stronger status as being expressed by the same word (*samānābhidhānaśruti*)—is first accepted as having the nature of a factor of action (*kārakatva*) either as a substrate (*ādheyatva*) or through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); and subsequently, it is connected to the animal through the relation of being a substrate, characterized by "animal-ness" (*paśutva*) and so forth.

Regarding the *paśukāmeṣṭi*: "One who desires cattle should have a herd of animals; having performed the New Moon sacrifice, he should drive away the calves... those that are the middle ones, for his giver, he should prepare a cake on eight potsherds; those that are the smallest, for Indra Pradātṛ, a pap of rice; those that are the largest, for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa, a pap of boiled milk.

In this new rite (*apūrva karma*), only the properties of the *praṇītā* water are to be applied to the curd and milk, but not the properties of the materials to be offered (*pradeyadharmāḥ*), such as the driving away of the calves.
In the *Paśukāmeṣṭi* (the sacrifice for one desiring cattle), the ritual properties (*pradeyadharma*) pertaining to curd and milk are not to be performed.
See *Mīmāṃsā-nyāya-prakāśa* 2008: "Regarding curd and milk in the *Paśukāmeṣṭi*.
[This concerns] groups of animals (*paśugaṇa*).
"In spring, one should sacrifice a beautiful bull.
Likewise: "One should sacrifice a white animal to Mitra and a black one to Varuṇa, as a composite offering to the waters and the plants.
Thus [it is said].
In this case, the model (vidhyanta) is that of the set of eleven animals (aikādaśina), not that of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (agnīṣomīya).
Bhāṣya 8.1.8.15:
The set of eleven animals is the archetype for a group of animals; the archetype for the set of eleven animals is the Savanīya animal; [the archetype] for the Savanīya...
The section concerning animal characteristics in the injunction for an animal sacrifice:
the animal characteristics pertain to the Agniṣomīya animal.
The sacrificial procedure for the animal is equal for all, because there is no distinction in the context.

Commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is the Agnīṣomīya animal sacrifice, as stated in the text: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the Agnīṣomīya animal. Likewise, there are the Savanīya and the Anūbandhya animals.

And there are the animal-ritual practices: the preparatory service, the leading forward, the binding with a cord, the tying to the sacrificial post, the leading [to the altar], the quieting, the immolation, and so forth.

Do these apply to all—the Agniṣomīya, the Savanīya, and the Anubandhya—or to the Agniṣomīya and the Savanīya, or to the Agniṣomīya alone? What is the prima facie view? Because there is no distinction, they apply to all.
How is there no distinction? All animals are mentioned within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Because they fall within that same context, all the ritual requirements for animals apply to them.
And there is no distinction made here between one animal and another.

This being the case, we reply: these ritual details should belong to the Savanīya [animal sacrifice]. The procedure for the animal sacrifice would be the same for all, if there were no distinction within the context.
In the case of one who is capable of grasping [the meaning], there is no occasion for the "law of cattle" (paśudharma); the absence of such an occasion has indeed already been stated.
Therefore, they are not for the sake of the *savanīya*.

If it is argued that this is a prescription of time for [the offering] that has been displaced, the Bhāṣya states: This is not so; by virtue of the sequence, they are indeed for the sake of the *agnīṣomīya*.
By virtue of the context, they are for the sake of the *savanīya* [animal sacrifice].
Their mention together with the preceding ones is for the purpose of injunction.
The mention of the *āśvina-graha* is for the purpose of enjoining the time and its quality.

How so? By that performance of the omentum-offering (*vapā-pracāra*), this time is prescribed for what has been postponed. Since the performance of the omentum-offering is enjoined at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the subsequent bath (*avabhṛtha*) would also follow there.
When an uncertainty regarding the time arises in that regard, the injunction "having taken the *āśvina* cup" prescribes the time alone.
The statement, "Having encircled the sacrificial post with the threefold rope, he performs the preparatory rite," is a restatement (anuvāda).
Otherwise, both the time for the encircling and the preparatory rite would be enjoined;
in that case, because multiple qualities would be enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda).
Therefore, the characteristics of the animal sacrifice belong to the *savanīya* [offering].
Or rather—now, the establishment of this section depends upon the thorough knowledge of which sentence is the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) for the *savanīya* offerings.
Regarding that, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) says: "If you think there is an absence of a context (*prakaraṇa*) for the *savanīya*, that is incorrect."

Why? Because: "Having deferred the omentum (vapā) of the Savanīya animals from the morning pressing by virtue of the scriptural statement, and since another [time] would otherwise be obtained there as well, its specific detail is enjoined.

By this very statement, "They proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing," once the primary act has been deferred and the subsidiary elements have also been deferred because they share the location of the primary act, and when a restriction of time is required, the specific rule regarding the Āśvina cup is enjoined.
Therefore, let that very same [sentence] be understood as an injunction regarding the time for the *śravaṇa* offering;
otherwise, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*),
because it would involve enjoining both the time for the encircling (*parivyāṇa*) and its accessories, as well as enjoining a sacrifice associated with a specific substance and deity.

But is it not the case that the *parivyāṇa* (encircling) is already obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), and thus, being enjoined at that very time, it would be a mere reiteration (*anuvāda*)? True, it is indeed obtained through extended application; however, it is not performed at that time.

This is because the benefit is already accomplished simply by virtue of its belonging to the time of the *āgnīṣomīya* sacrifice, due to the commonality of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). As stated in the rule: "But they belong to that time" (11.3.14).
If that is so, then since it is already obtained by virtue of its commonality, it would merely be restated as something existing.
However, it is not possible to restate it, because there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of it.
That which is restated from another source is indeed that which, having been obtained in such a manner, is recognized.
Nor is there a reference to what was performed on the previous day by way of restatement, because [the act] exists as something present at the time subsequent to the drawing of the Āśvina cup;
for it does not persist until then.
Furthermore, there is no such reference to what was performed on the previous day by means of such a word, as is the case with acts like the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire).
Because it is not delimited by actions belonging to either the preceding or the succeeding time.
If that is so, then let it be restated as obtained from this very sentence: "Having taken the Āśvina cup and gone out, he encircles the sacrificial post.
That too is not possible, precisely because there is no recognition [of the action as being the same].

Since this non-standard (*aprākṛta*) encircling of the *savanīya* animal is heard as being pure [in its injunction], and since the original (*prākṛta*) encircling is the basis for the composition [of the rule], if the act were performed with any material whatsoever—such as cloth and so forth—the restatement of the "threefoldness" (*trivṛttva*) would not be applicable.
In that case, because multiple matters would be enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). And then, the text of the Bhāṣya is as follows:
"Otherwise, the time for the encircling (parivyāṇa) would be enjoined. This means that the substance *trivṛt*, which is presented as being enjoined in all cases, would instead be enjoined as a time;
and by the phrase "and of the accessory," it follows that the time for the accessory and the ritual action qualified by the substance and deity would both be enjoined.
Therefore, because this [text] serves the purpose of enjoining a quality, there exists the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *savanīya* offerings on the previous day.
"Not so, because they occupy different locations.
The Commentary states: "This is not the case;
for, according to the sequence, they are intended solely for the sake of the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice]."
The mention of the time of the Āśvina cup is indeed for the purpose of an injunction;

it would constitute a syntactical split if it were for the purpose of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), not for the purpose of an injunction. For an injunction regarding the time of that which has been displaced by the offering of the omentum (*vapā-pracāra*) is not possible.
For the omentum (*vapā*) is but one part [of the animal].
Therefore, one should postpone the preparatory rites (*saṃnipātinaḥ saṃskārāḥ*) pertaining to the omentum, but not the auxiliary implements (*upakaraṇam*).
Or rather—(here it is said)—when on the previous day the *savanīya* offerings together with their subsidiaries have been prepared, then at that very time...
In that case, since the cognition of that [object] is easily obtained through that [means], this is the principle of the injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhānanyāya*).

However, where an action qualified by its own qualifiers is enjoined, and the qualifier belongs to another action already established by a different sentence, there the injunctive suffix refers to the state [of the action].
For when a sacrifice qualified by a deity is being enjoined, it is capable of implying only its own qualifiers, not the qualifiers of the *pariṣyāṇa* (enclosing) which are not being enjoined.

Therefore, this same distinction must be applied even to the rules for unprecedented rites (*apūrva-karma-vidhi*): which [term] is a qualification of that [specific rite], and which is a qualification of another?
Consequently, because both terms apply to both sides, neither one should be raised as an objection.
In that case, the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) must necessarily state the resolution: that the two cords (*raśanā*) are common to both [the Agniṣomīya and the Savanīya].
For he will say: "And the girdle, because of the observation of an indicative mark" (16.1.13).
Whatever constitutes the girdling of this sacrificial post, each of those is understood through this sentence.
Thus, since it is obtained [as a single unit], there is no split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Alternatively, since it was previously established by the earlier [passages] that "having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted rope, he dedicates the animal," this [latter passage] merely restates that act of encircling as a subordinate element (*upakāraṇa*) and prescribes its immediate sequence following the drawing of the Āśvina cup.
And it is better to accept three instances of supplying ellipses (*vyavahita-kalpanā*) than to incur a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).
Therefore, it is explained in this manner.
Necessarily, there must be the origination of the Savanīya offerings by one [text], and the prescription of a quality by the other.
In that regard, first of all, there is no reason for the text on the previous day to be considered the originative statement.
But surely, there is no reason for the other one either?

Even though this is so, nevertheless, because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is possible, a distinction is stated regarding the basis for one or the other by means of some specific qualification.

This very point has been established previously: "A quality (*guṇa*) that is to be adopted (*upādeya*) can be enjoined by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to a hidden action, but not one that is not to be adopted.
For that [latter] necessarily brings about the status of a distinct ritual action (*karmāntaratva*), as in the case of the *homa* in the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana*.
That is the section concerning the practice of animals;
that is the section concerning the practice of animals.
The consistency and inconsistency of the *sthāna* with what precedes it are now considered.
By means of the first [sūtra], the equality or inequality of the ritual injunctions for the archetypes (*prakṛti*) and their modifications (*vikṛti*) was examined;
here too, that same principle continues to apply.

In this regard, it is now deliberated: are these ritual elements (dharmas) enjoined for all animals equally, including the black ones; or only for the *savanīya* animal; or for both the *agnīṣomīya* and the *savanīya*; or indeed only for the *agnīṣomīya*?

For that purpose, one must consider whether the position of the *agnīṣomīya* is contradicted by the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, or by the intermediate context (*antaraprakaraṇa*) of the *savanīya*, or not. And to establish that, it must be considered whether there is a context for the *savanīya* animals on the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*).
Even from that, this must be discerned: does the origin of the *savanīya* [animal] occur on the day of the fast (*aupavasathya*), or on the day of the Soma-pressing (*saumya*)?

Now, it might be argued: "But since position (*sthāna*) is weaker than context (*prakaraṇa*), how can it [the *savanīya*] belong to the *agnīṣomīya* in this way through its properties? To this, it is said:

What was stated regarding their being subsidiary to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice is indeed true; however, we maintain that they serve the purpose of the Savanīya, for what reason? Because there is no *prakaraṇa* (contextual setting) for the Savanīya within its own ritual details.
Indeed, the *savanīya* [offering] is not prescribed on the day of the fast (*upavasathya*),
because the context (*prakaraṇa*) of that [day] belongs to the *savanīya*.
However, it is prescribed as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) for the purpose of diversifying the performance.
It is proclaimed that the *savanīya* [animal] belongs here; however, this rule is prescribed in the context of the Soma sacrifice.

This is the procedure for the ritual action, and therein the context (*prakaraṇa*) would apply. But where there is a mention for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), the [primary] context does not exist there.
Therefore, the procedure does not belong to the *savanīya* because of the proximity of the subordinate qualities (*guṇa*).
These [qualities] do not belong to all [the offerings], nor to the *savanīya*, nor to both;
rather, the ritual duties (*dharma*) are established by the injunction solely for the *agnīṣomīya*.
In other cases, however, they proceed by way of extended application (*atideśa*), not by way of direct injunction (*vidhāna*).
In the Sūtra stating "Let there be the injunction of the *daikṣa* [animal sacrifice] itself," an injunction is cited.
Regarding the Soma sacrifice—the purpose in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the *savanīya* and *anubandhya* [animals] do not apply; consequently, the *daitya-puroḍāśa* does not occur.

In the Siddhānta, however, because the Agniṣomīya is the archetype (*prakṛti*), and because therein the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is a direct constituent (*saṃnipātin*) according to the rule of the tenth book, and because in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛtis*) the application occurs through modification (*ūha*) by virtue of that direct constituent relationship, there is the application of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) dedicated to the same deity as the Savanīya and others. Likewise, even in the case of the *Anubandhyā* sacrifice, there is the application of the *adhigu-praiṣa* through modification (*ūha*).
Thus it is said.

Vi—The animal sacrifices dedicated to Agni-Soma, the Savanīya, and the Anubandhya possess certain ritual duties (*dharma*). Are the primary duties, beginning with the *upākaraṇa*, common to them, or not?
Since they are recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, these duties are common to all.
Because they do not adopt the characteristics of sacrificial animals,
those [animals] in the Soma sacrifice would be devoid of [the status of] sacrificial victims;
their status as having the nature of the Agniṣomīya animal is established by virtue of their position.
"Those two [details] are obtained for the other two animals by means of the *codaka* (extended injunction).

[Bhāṭṭa: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the Agnīṣomīya animal is prescribed in proximity to the purchase [of Soma]; however, according to the statement, "This Savanīya [animal] is on the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*"), it is performed on the fourth day.
And in that very same context, the ritual acts pertaining to animals are prescribed, including the offering of the animal victim;

furthermore, the *savanīya* animal is prescribed for the Soma-pressing day: "Having drawn the *āśvina* cup and having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-strand rope, he dedicates the *savanīya* animal to Agni.
And the *anubandhya* animal is prescribed at the conclusion.

Now, here the inquiry is as follows: do these animal-related rites apply to all three animals, or only to the *savanīya*, or to both the *savanīya* and the *agnīṣomīya*, or indeed only to the *agnīṣomīya*? Because of the context of the great sacrifice (*mahāprakaraṇa*), the rites belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma are connected directly as animal rites; yet, by the principle of "uselessness elsewhere" (*ānarthakyatadanyanyāya*) (3.1.9), their application extends to the animal sacrifices in general. Furthermore, since there is no specific evidence—such as a stronger authority—that would override the context for any one among them, they apply to all without distinction. This is the prima facie view (*pakṣa*).

The second [view], however, maintains that although the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma exists, because the characteristics of the animal sacrifice (*paśudharma*) are not grasped by it, they are instead governed by the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the Savanīya. For its origin occurs on the very day of the fast (*aupavasathya*):

"An animal dedicated to Agni is to be sacrificed at the *Āgniṣṭoma*; a second one dedicated to Indra-Agni at the *Ukthya*; a third, a ram dedicated to Indra, at the *Ṣoḍaśin*; and a fourth, a ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī, at the *Atirātra*"—by these scriptural injunctions.
This is because the *pṛṣṭhas* of the sacrifice are prescribed [therein].

Even though there is a connection with the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiary elements whose assistance has been determined, there is no possibility of a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) for the animal-rites (*paśudharma*), because those required rites are already proximate and connected to the archetypal subsidiaries. As for the injunctions regarding the *aindrāgna* and other offerings, there is no suspicion that they would take up the animal-rites, precisely because—according to the principle of the section on the *saṃsthās* (3.6.16)—they do not share the same ritual procedure (*samānavidhāna*). Or, even if they were to take up the rites due to having a subordinate context, this does not imply that they apply to all [the sacrifices].

That injunction does not apply on the day of the *sava*, because it merely prescribes that the time for the wrapping of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-parivyāṇa*) occurs at the moment of drawing the *āśvina* cup, with reference to the *savanīya* offering. This is because the wrapping of the post is already established—either by the general rule, "He wraps the post with a triple-stranded cord" (*trivṛtā yūpaṃ parivyayati*), or by the specific rule for wrapping, "Having drawn the *āśvina* cup and gone out, he wraps the post. Furthermore, the property of being triple-stranded (*trivṛttva*) will be applied to another instance of wrapping in the very section concerning the common substrate of the cords (*raśanā-sādhāraṇādhikaraṇa*, 3.6.10).
And yet, it is not the case that this is a matter concerning the nature of animals; it is indeed a matter concerning the nature of animals.

A prescription regarding time can be established by means of a reference (*anuvāda*) to that which is situated at a distance; for even though the animal sacrifices (*paśus*) are prescribed on the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*), they are subject to a rule of postponement (*utkarṣa*) by the statement, "They proceed with the omentum (*vapā*) at the morning pressing, with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) at the midday pressing, and with the limbs (*aṅgas*) at the third pressing. Consequently, since these sacrifices are performed on the day of the Soma purchase (*saulya*), they become present [in the mind].

Therefore, just as in the final view (*siddhānta*), the Agniṣomīya sacrifice—which is recited in proximity to the purchase—is established as a recipient of the ritual details (*dharma-grāhaka*) precisely because it is performed on the day of preparation, so too is it here; thus, there is no fault.

Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (vinigamanāviraha) regarding which [set of rules] constitutes the injunction for the *savanīya* even in this case, because the abundance of specific characteristics (*dharma*) serves as the regulator.
Therefore, by virtue of the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), these [rules] are for the sake of the *savanīya*.
Thus it is said.
The third [view], however, is that they truly belong to the *savanīya* sacrifice; yet, by virtue of their position (*sthāna*), they also belong to the *agnīṣomīya*.

For that [animal sacrifice] has its requirements satisfied by the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries whose assistance is already established through the injunctive scripture in proximity to the purchase (*kraya*); thus, when it is displaced to the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*), its presence is merely due to its position.
Since there is no syntactical connection (*vākya*) as there is with the *savanīya*, the suspicion of context (*prakaraṇa*) is untenable.
For this very reason, there is proximity between two sentences that are unfit for a relationship of *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance).

This is the definition of position (*sthāna*). Although, in this case, because the characteristics of the animal sacrifice (*paśudharma*) have already been enjoined by direct statement (*śruti*) and other means, there is no possibility of context (*prakaraṇa*) or position (*sthāna*) acting as the enjoiner, nevertheless, it should be understood that the designation "enjoiner" is used figuratively only insofar as they serve to grasp the intended meaning of the qualification as a means to the *apūrva*.

Even so, there is no occurrence of the sublation of position (*sthāna*) by context (*prakaraṇa*), because the assumption of extended application (*atideśa*) occurs only when the animal sacrifice for Agni-Soma has a requirement for the ritual details of the animal; it is more appropriate to assume that the directly taught position itself is the factor of application (*viniyojaka*). Otherwise, since the ritual details would belong to the archetype (*prakṛti*) due to the stronger authority of the direct scriptural injunction, it would be impossible for them to serve any purpose in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

The distinction is that, since Indra and others can be remembered through other means as well, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth do not necessitate the assumption of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Thus, the prima facie view is that it serves both purposes.

However, this is not the case; there is no intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) for the *savanīya* offering, because its origin occurs on the day of the Soma extraction (*saumya ahan*). Otherwise, it would be impossible to enjoin a non-subordinate accessory in the form of time by referring back to a distant sequence (*krama*).

Nor is there a presentation [of the *savanīya*] based solely on its being displaced to the morning extraction (*prātaḥsavana*), for although practical proximity (*ānuṣṭhānika-upasthiti*) may serve as a grasper of subsidiaries (*aṅgagrāhaka*), we have never observed it acting as a substitute for a distinct context (*prakaraṇāntara*).

Or let that be granted; nevertheless, even if the mere *vapa* (omentum) is postponed to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), there is no evidence for the postponement of the *upākaraṇa* (dedication), because its presence [at that time] would be untenable.

And although the sacrifice itself is indicated by the term *upākaroti*, nevertheless, since the primary meaning—the act of dedication—is not established as occurring after the drawing of the *āśvina* cup, its restatement (*anuvāda*) is impossible.

Although it might be possible for the items occurring after the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) to be postponed according to the principle of postponement based on that [omentum] (5.1.12), nevertheless there is no authority for the postponement of those preceding it, such as the dedication (*upākaraṇa*).
In fact, however, by the Vedic principle of the *vaidhāna* [or *vaidhānika*] rite, because they are unprecedented (*apūrva*), there is no postponement even for those occurring after it.

In reality, however, since we observe *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in cases such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) even though the literal meaning (*śakyārtha*) is capable of being construed with the hamlet, and because the indication of proximity is established by the verb *upākaroti* even in the absence of the temporal sequence between those two [actions],—for instance, in the case of the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) which is useful for the commencement of the animal sacrifice, the second foot of every [animal] is tied to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and thus the time following the drawing of the *āśvina* cup is determined precisely for that; consequently, the time following the drawing of the *āśvina* cup is established for the subsequent *praṇayana* (leading forward) as well.
It is precisely out of fear of this [latter] becoming redundant that the origin of this [subsequent action] is marked by repetition (*abhyāsa*).

In that case as well, since everything else—the girding with the second sacrificial post and so forth—is already established by other sentences, it is the action itself—either qualified by time or simply pure—that is enjoined as qualified by the material and deity.

Consequently, since the Āgneya Savanīya is enjoined by this very sentence, and the Aindra and others of the same class by other sentences, their re-mention on the day of fasting (aupavasathya) is merely a restatement (anuvāda).

Nevertheless, just as [the text] says, "Just as a fish shakes off the mountain," so too these [animals], not being pacified, shake off the people; this constitutes a censure based on the continuous performance [of the slaughter]. To provide the means for removing the animal [from this state] required by this word of censure, and for the purpose of avoiding the fault [already mentioned], there is the injunction of the time—such as the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*)—with reference to the offering of the omentum (*vapā*), as in the passage: "They proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing.

For if the performance were carried out in separate parts at different times, there would be an opportunity for the recollection [of the prohibition] in the interim, and thus the fault would be avoided.

And although here too it is impossible to enjoin a time by way of a restatement of a sequence that is spatially remote, nevertheless there is no fault, because that [sequence] is possible as a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

As for the resolution stated in the *Mūla*—that there is no fault because the quality of "remoteness of the *pravara*" exists as something to be enjoined—that has been disregarded, since such remoteness is not verbal and thus cannot be an object of injunction.
Therefore, there is no intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) for the *savanīya*.
The animal-related rites belong to the *sthāna* [position] of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.

Nor is there a sublation of *sthāna* within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, because the animal-related rites—having been enjoined by direct statement (*śruti*) and other means as sanctifications of the animal—are unsuitable for inclusion in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Therefore, the principle of "uselessness elsewhere" (*ānarthakyatadanyanyāya*) applies only where a connection is explicitly heard, such as in "of the Vājapeya" (3.1.9) and so forth, but not here.

Even this being the case, if for that animal sacrifice also there were no specific other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish it as the locus for the animal-dharma that accomplishes the *apūrva*— namely, the section concerning the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*)— then, by the principle of "uselessness [of the main act] leading to its being for its parts" (3.1.9), these [animal-dharmas] would apply to all [sacrifices]. But this is not so, because by virtue of their position (*sthāna*), they pertain specifically to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.
Therefore, it is established that there is direct instruction (*upadeśa*) regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*), whereas in other cases there is extension (*atideśa*).

The purpose of having a common injunction (*sāmānavidhya*) is clear from the tenth book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] onwards. Maṇḍana [states]: "But the ritual properties [are taken] from the vicinity of the goat of Dakṣa."

"From proximity" means from nearness. Śaṅkara says: "Abiding in the common state of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*). In the section concerning the properties of the animal (*paśudharmādhikaraṇa*, 3.6.18–27), while it will be explained that the sequence—by avoiding contradiction with the context—serves the purpose of the animal-initiation (*daikṣa*), the sequence characterized by the place of performance (*anuṣṭhānadeśa*) will also be easily understood as a cause for application (*viniyoga*).
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the animal-dharma pertaining to the sacrificial post (yūpa) consisting of twenty-one spokes is [extended] by way of the sacrificial post;
the tethering of the animal to the enclosing-stick (paridhi) is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi).
This is the resolution of the question; the purpose is visible.

A large enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) must be made for the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices dedicated to Soma. Bhāṣya 10.3.18–22: The ritual duty of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), namely the tethering of the animal, must be performed upon the enclosing-stick in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices that involve animals.
"One should tie the animal to the enclosing-stick" (Vi. 9.2.12).
This enclosing-stick is the middle one, which is thick.
In this case, neither carving nor raising [the sacrificial post] should be performed;
however, the anointing and other rites should be performed.
Furthermore, in the ritual injunction, one should say "for the sacrificial post being anointed," and not "for the enclosing stick being anointed."
9|2|13. The Rule of the Animal Sacrifice (Paśunyāya). The Section on the Singleness of the Animal.
The animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) adopts the ritual procedure from the cake-offering to Agni and Soma belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Dvādaśādhyāya 1.1.1.1:
The animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) serves both purposes—the refinement of the deity and the production of the unseen potency (apūrva).
See Mīmāṃsākośa, page 1095, under the entry "āśrayiṇyāyaḥ."
It has been stated in the sūtra, "Or rather, because it is a subordinate element" (10.1.9.23), that the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is for the purpose of consecrating the deity.
(Consecration consists in being made the object of remembrance;
by this, even though [the substance] is not eaten...)
Bhāṣya 12.1.2.19: The animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), having arisen within the ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice (paśutantra), adopts that animal procedure.
12.1.5.14: The animal-cake subsists upon the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) pertaining to the animal, even though they occur at a different time.

12.1.7.15: By virtue of scriptural extension (śāstrātideśa) and because of the commonality of the ritual rules (sāmānavidhya), the animal-cake—which serves the purpose of consecrating Agni and Soma—is not included within the animal-ritual properties (paśudharma) in the context of the deity-ritual (devatantre).

Or [it may be argued]: Vārttika 3.8.16.131 states that the *paśupuroḍāśa* (animal-cake offering) must also be performed at the *savanīya-paśu* (animal sacrifice of the Soma-pressing), because its purpose is the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the deity.
This is to be understood from the discussion under the sūtra "At the *savanīya-paśu*" (12.1.2.8–10).
The *paśupuroḍāśa* belongs to whichever deity the animal belongs.

Bhāṣya 10.1.9.20: In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, for the animal victims dedicated to the deities Aśvin, Sarasvatī, and Sutrāman, there are animal-cake offerings (paśupuroḍāśa) dedicated to Indra-Vāruṇa and Savitṛ.
10.1.9.22: The cooking of the animal-cake offering, which is connected with the Amīṣomīya and other rites, must be performed on the Śālāmukhīya fire, and not on the Śāmitra fire.
12.1.5.12: In the animal-cake offering, the butter-portions (ājyabhāga) and other elements that provide assistance from elsewhere must be performed.
"But the prohibition 'he does not perform those two in the animal sacrifice' applies to the animal sacrifice itself, not to the animal-cake offering (paśupuroḍāśa). (12.1.2.7).
This is to be understood under the principle of "the portions of cake and clarified butter" (*paurauḍāśājyābhāganyāya*).
In the case of the animal-cake offerings, the requirements for the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) are fulfilled by extension (*prasaṅga*) through the after-offerings belonging to the animal sacrifice.

VI. 5.1.1.15. In the case of the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) sacrifice, the offerings of the flour-smear (piṣṭalepa) and the husks (phalīkaraṇa) occur only after the consumption of the iḍā portion; they are not postponed together with the after-offerings (anuyāja). 5.1.1.18. Even though there is a difference in time regarding the performance of the animal-cake sacrifice and the primary rites, there is no repetition of the auxiliary elements (aṅga).
See Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 779. In the animal-cake sacrifice and the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, as well as in the ritual formulas of renunciation (tyāga) and recitation (nigama), only the fire Sviṣṭakṛt is mentioned.
Bhāṣya 10.4.18.36–37. See Mīmāṃsākosa, p. 102, under the entry "amīṣomīyapaśupuroḍāśasviṣṭakṛt. This is the section concerning the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa).
For the animal-cake of the Amīṣomīya sacrifice, the ritual procedure (tantra) pertaining to the animal sacrifice itself is extended [to apply].

In the case of a collection of Tantras, there is unity of the single Tantra for those that are common due to the injunction; however, among those that are dissimilar, there is a distinction because of the sequence of the injunctions and their respective purposes, since that purpose is indicated by the direct Vedic statement and the timing. Commentary: Regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (Agnīṣomīya), there is a cake offering: "Having performed the offering of the omentum of the Agni-Soma animal, one should offer the eleven-potherd cake of the Agni-Soma animal. Should its subsidiary rites be performed separately, or do those which have been performed for the animal sacrifice also benefit it? Therefore, the discussion begins with the Sūtra itself.
"Because of the indication of time in the *tantrasamavāya*.
*Tantra* refers to the common set of ritual elements (*dharmagrāma*).
For example, the *ājyabhāga* offerings and so forth in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
The first [portion] begins with the *sviṣṭakṛt* and so forth;
those primary rites for which these apply are "shared" (*tantrīṇi*) primary rites.

When there is a combination of these—meaning they share the same place, time, and performers—there is "single performance" (*ekatantratva*) for those that are identical because of the injunction, being enjoined by a single sentence.
As in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, and as in the case of the Citrā sacrifice;
however, there would be a distinction in the case of unequal [rites].
But for those which are not equal by virtue of their injunctions—that is, those enjoined by various distinct sentences—there would be a distinction of the *tantra* (the common ritual procedure).
As in this very context: "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma," and "One should offer the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) for Agni and Soma on eleven potsherds.
What is the reason? Because of the commencement of the injunction being for that purpose.
"Injunction" (vidhi) means the prescription; its "commencement" (prakrama) is the performance of its constituent parts; it is the engagement [of the agent] directed toward that end.

The sequence of the injunction is understood to have that [animal] as its purpose; thus, the sequence of the injunction is for the sake of the animal, not for the sake of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). But how is the sequence of the injunction for the sake of the animal? Because its purpose is established by the scriptural indication of the time.
In that regard, the time is specified by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
The time for the animal sacrifice is immediately after the *iṣṭi* of Agni and Soma;
for its injunction occurs therein.

The time for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is after the offering of the omentum (vapā). Since the ritual procedure that follows the animal sacrifice is understood to pertain solely to the animal— because the sacrificial cake has not yet been introduced—
a separate set of ritual requirements (tantra) must be performed for it.
And the indicative mark (*liṅga*) shows that it serves the purpose of the animal sacrifice:
"In that he performs eleven fore-offerings (*prayāja*), he thereby offers to the animal; in that he performs eleven after-offerings (*anuyāja*), he thereby offers after the animal.
From the use of the particle *eva* (only/just), a restriction is understood: [it serves] the animal alone, not the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
ḌuP—[The suffix] ḌuP [is applied] in the sense of "assemblage" (samavāya), because it is so taught.

(Regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma: "Having performed the offering of the omentum of the animal to Agni and Soma, one should offer the animal-cake for Agni and Soma on eleven potsherds"—so it is heard in the scripture.

In this regard, there arises a doubt: should separate ritual acts (*jñāni*) be performed for that [cake] apart from the limbs of the animal, or do those very limbs which were prepared for the sake of the animal also benefit that [cake] by way of *prasaṅga* (incidental application)?
Consequently, for the purpose of resolving this doubt, it is deliberated whether *prasaṅga* exists or not.
(Regarding this, the prima facie view is: "There is no contingency.

Why? (He applies the sūtra as the answer: "In the case of a common performance (*tantrisamavāya*), there is a single performance (*aikatantrya*) for those injunctions that are identical, when their principal rites—such as the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*āgneya-paśu*) and the cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*)—are combined in terms of place, time, and performer."
Those things that are enjoined by a single injunction (enjoined together with a single primary injunction) possess the quality of having a common ritual procedure (*samānatantra*).
This is as in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and as in the case of the various curd offerings (*dadhi* etc. in the Citrā sacrifice.
However, where the elements are unequal, there would be a distinction.
Furthermore, those [rites] which differ from the primary injunction (*codanā*)—such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice and others—possess that very difference.
Therefore, because rituals have two modes of time, there is no third mode.
(Thus, having established this through general principles, he applies it to the case at hand.)

The animal sacrifice (*paśu*) takes its ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) from the *āmīṣomīya* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dāśapūrṇamāsika*), while the animal itself [takes its details] from the *sānnāyya* offering. Such is the scope of the extended application (*atideśa*). In that regard, because those two—the animal and the sacrificial cake—are enjoined separately, there is no commonality of performance (*tantra*).

In the world, however, such an objection is appropriate because the benefit (*upakāra*) is perceivable through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Here, an objection is raised: "This is not an example [of a single act], because there is no single sacrifice consisting of many [substances] (due to the absence of a *tantra*).

How so? [In the passage]: "Curd, honey, ghee, parched grain, water, and rice—these, when mixed together, constitute the offering to Prajāpati," the pronoun *tat* ending in the singular number is connected with the word *saṃsṛṣṭa* (mixed), which likewise ends in the singular.

If it were to be connected with curd and the other substances, there would have to be either a plural ending (*tāni*) or a distributive repetition (*tattat*); however, neither a distributive sense nor a plural number is heard in the text.

Therefore, the connection is only with the word *saṃsṛṣṭa*. Furthermore, that which is indicated by the pronoun *tat*—namely, the *saṃsṛṣṭa*—is connected with Prajāpati (i.e., connected with the word *Prajāpati*).
And the object is a single composite entity.
Therefore, because of the unity of the substance and the deity, there is only one sacrifice; why, then, [should it not be] a *tantra*?
To this, it is replied:

The pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is connected with *dadhi* and the others individually (and not with them as a composite). For a pronoun is a substitute for that which has been specifically mentioned (*nirdiṣṭa*), and here *dadhi* and the others are specifically mentioned by means of their case-endings (*vibhakti*) in the first instance. Therefore, it is those very words, as they are presented by the linguistic expression and remain expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), that are referred back by the pronoun as it revolves through its various forms; however, no connection with *dadhi* and the others has been mentioned by any word such that it could be referred back by the pronoun. (Therefore, it is a reference to those very items.)

Now, if one were to consider that at the end [of the compound], there would result either a plural number or a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) due to the connection with *dadhi* and so forth, it is said in response:

for a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) which is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*), its capacity lies in being a substitute for what has been previously specified; however, the function of number (*vacana*) is to convey a single referent.
Therefore, there is a conflict between these two.

In that case, because [the nominal stem] presents itself first, and because gender and number are for the sake of that [stem]—that is, they are the meaning of the nominal stem—we accept the nominal stem exactly as it is heard.
Furthermore, since gender and number occur at a later time, their conflict [is logical].
This very same principle— that "it is [included] under the quality because it is a portion [of it] as determined by that logic" (Pādukānyāya 1.1.16)—
applies here as well.
Mīmāṃsākośa 3.15: Section on the Animal-Cake Offering (Paśupuroḍāśa).
It is appropriate that there be a repetition of the primary rite.
Furthermore, the primary act does not depend on the subordinate details.
Granted, there may be an expiation for the reversal of the sequence, but there is no repetition [of the entire rite].
Should an expiation then be performed? It is indeed performed; one offers the "all-expiation" oblation with the mantra, "O Agni, the unassailable... (ayāścāgne).
In the incidental discussion (*prāsaṅgika-vāda*), there is an absence of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction. [Durga: Now, as for what was said—that it does not apply because of the difference in substance, number, and time—that is being addressed.
All [auxiliaries] require assistance in their "how-to" mode (*kathambhāva*); the *codaka* (the extended injunction) produces and brings about that assistance through similarity.
Once produced and brought about, the *prayogavacana* (the injunctive statement of performance) incorporates them.

Since those [assisting elements] cannot exist without another scriptural authority, it effects the production and attainment of those scriptures (the mention of "scriptures" is an elliptical indication for the ritual items themselves).
And there is inclusion by means of the original injunction (*prayogavacana*).
Therefore, in this case, both the *codaka* and the *prayogavacana* pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) perform all these [actions].
However, the *codaka* pertaining to the cake-offering (*paurauḍāśika*) merely effects the attainment of what has been prescribed above.

However, because the injunction for the performance (*prayoga-vacana*) is subsumed by the injunction for the performance of the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka-prayoga-vacana*), it does not subsume the auxiliary services (*upakārān*).

If it does not subsume them, then those constituent elements (*padārthāḥ*) do not exist here [in the case of the *puroḍāśa*] (meaning they are not to be performed). Much less, therefore, can there be qualities (*guṇāḥ*) of those constituent elements.
And from that [difference], there would be a deficiency in the performance due to non-repetition.
Furthermore, no new transcendental result (*apūrva*) arises merely through a difference in number or a difference in substance.
What then? The original number (consisting of five) and the original substance (pure clarified butter) are simply set aside.
But that very assistance remains [present].

Thus, even a difference in time is not a defect; so he says: those assistances of the *prayāja* offerings which arise at the beginning persist until the completion of the fruit—that is, until the production of the animal-apūrva which constitutes the fruit. And if they persist, there is no defect whatsoever in the difference of time.
(Therefore, there is the consequence.
And because it is impossible for some [petitioners].
The Bhāṣya states: "And because it is impossible for some petitioners, the action is performed separately."
As in the case of the non-removal of the altar (vedi) and the undertaking of the vow (vratopāyana):
the altar, once prepared, remains unremoved; it cannot be made [again].
For an object that has already been accomplished cannot be made [to be accomplished] again.
If it is argued that he will perform another [act],
that would be mere boasting.
And it may be horizontal;
in that case, the orientation toward the cardinal directions is established by the mouth.
The distinctness of the monastery is indeed established by the authoritative scripture.

In this regard, the established principle is that "the eleven [limbs] are characterized by their temporal sequence. This would be overturned; thus, the kindling of the fire is for the purpose of accomplishing the Āhavanīya fire.
And this [destruction] is accomplished by a single extraction;

yet that which has been accomplished cannot be accomplished again, just as what has already been done cannot be done over again. If it is argued that another [extraction] will bring it about, [we reply: no.
When that [Gārhapatya] has been extinguished, there is no second fire to be enkindled there. For what reason? Because both the Gārhapatya and the Āhavanīya must be visible.
Even when the Āhavanīya has been carried forward, the Gārhapatya remains as a remnant.
Just as from the clarified butter common to all, one takes a portion for the sake of the *upāṃśuyāja*, and what remains is for the sake of other deities;
and as before, a separation of the ritual performance (*vihāra*) occurs.
In that case, the same faults as previously mentioned apply.
Likewise, that vow which has been undertaken cannot be taken again once it has been greedily grasped;
and at that time, it is well-performed because of the primary liberation.
This is the vision of the single pressing.

The Commentary states: A single [fire] indicates both the animal sacrifice and the cake offering, as it says: "In the middle of the fire, one offers the oblations of the animal sacrifice, the oblations of the cake, and the oblations of the animal.
There is no distinction regarding the taking out of the fire.
Therefore, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) pertaining to the animal sacrifice is extended to the cake offering.

Śā—Even if a subsidiary (*aṅga*) is performed only once, because many primary rites (*pradhāna*) share the same place, time, and agent, it is unable to provide assistance [to all of them]. Relying on this definition of *tantra* (the principle of common performance), the following is considered: does this occur simply because there is no distinction in the object of the action, or rather, even when a distinction is perceived such that "this performance is for this [rite] and not for that," yet a subsidiary performed for one purpose can still assist others when there is no difference in place and so forth, and thus need not be performed again for their sake? This concludes the discussion of the causes of *tantra* and *prasaṅga*.
In this regard: "The subsidiaries are for the sake of the animal and the time is for the sake of the animal; of this there is no doubt.
For when the time for the *puroḍāśa* has not yet arrived, they cannot have that [the *puroḍāśa*] as their purpose.
Furthermore, a subsidiary performed for one purpose does not assist another."
Furthermore, because its nature is observed to be such, it is indeed performed by that [agent];
moreover, "the rite being enjoined at a specific time and so forth is enjoined as complete with all its constituent parts (sāṅga).
Therefore, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) must be prepared at its own proper time, conjoined with all its auxiliary elements."
Furthermore, a deficiency caused by the quality or the time [of the performer] has been mentioned in the Bhāṣya;
even because of that, there is no occasion [for the objection], since it is stated with reference to what has already been established:
when the extensive *pāśuka* ritual procedure has reached its conclusion.
Falling into the midst [of the ritual], the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) subsists upon the primary procedure (tantra).
When that sacrificial cake, which has been established by the extended injunction (codaka),
is seen as spread out like a snare belonging to the iṣṭi-sacrifice;
At that time, the injunction for the *puroḍāśa* itself, being satisfied by that very [act],
does not include the constituent elements (*padārtha*) belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*). Therefore, there is the principle of *prasaṅga* (extended application).

The meaning of the *Soma-sūtra* is as follows: When there is a conjunction of principal rites that share a common set of subsidiary elements (*aṅga*), provided they possess the same location, time, and performers, those rites—such as the *Āgneya* and others—which are enjoined by a single injunction, should indeed have a single performance (*eka-tantra*). However, in the case of rites enjoined by separate injunctions, such as the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) and the cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*), there must be a difference in the performance (*tantra-bheda*) for the sake of the cake-offering. This is because the performance of the subsidiaries for the animal sacrifice is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), and the timing is indicated through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*) as occurring immediately after the carrying forward of the fire (*agnīṣomīya-praṇayana*) for the purpose of the animal sacrifice; therefore, for the sake of the cake-offering, there must be a distinct performance. Vṛtti: "Is there assistance rendered to the cake-offering when it is performed for the sake of the animal sacrifice? Or is there not? Because there is no such injunction, it should be as in the world."

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the scriptural injunction, "He offers the cake for Agni-Soma," which pertains to the animal-cake sacrifice (*paśupuroḍāśa*) that is a subsidiary of the Agni-Soma animal sacrifice (*agnīṣomīyapaśuyāga*), there arises the question: do the subsidiaries such as the *prayāja* offerings from the animal sacrifice apply by extension (*prasajyante*), or are they to be performed separately? In considering this, it cannot be accepted that the extension (*prasaṅga*) applies solely on the grounds of admitting both the extended application (*codaka*) and the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*) for the cake-offering, even while including the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries.

Because of the performance of the omentum offering according to the injunction for the ritual procedure, and because of the subsequent specific subsidiary elements of the cake-offering (puroḍāśa-yāga) procedure, it would be impossible for the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and other rites previously performed to provide assistance, as they would have been performed at the wrong time.

If, however, this is not an injunction regarding time, but rather—due to the proximity of the performance of the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) being performed multiple times, or because its status as an auxiliary to the animal sacrifice is established by the sentence itself—it is argued that the performance is accomplished through its connection therein and thus this is indeed an injunction of sequence (*krama*), even so, the occurrence of deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) resulting from the non-performance here of the archetypal auxiliaries—which have already been prompted for the sake of the cake by the primary injunction itself—would be unavoidable.

For where there is no difference between the animal-offering components (*paśvaṅga*) and the cake-offerings (*puroḍāśa*), even though there is an absence of deficiency when performed once, the consequence would be that they constitute a *tantra* (a common performance), and thus the application of *prasaṅga* (incidental benefit) does not arise. Where, however, there is a difference—as in the case of the animal-offering, where there are eleven *prayāja*s and the *anūyāja*s are performed while the animal stands with *pṛṣadājya* butter, and eleven modified *yājyā* verses are used; whereas for the cake-offering, there are five *prayāja*s performed after the placing of the oblation, and three *anūyāja*s with pure *ājya* butter, and so forth—[the distinction holds].

In that case, since the number three and so forth is obtained as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), and its performance is brought about by the *prayogavidhi* (the injunction of performance), how can there be no occurrence of deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) when the complete [number] is performed?
Therefore, the proponent of *prasaṅga* must necessarily admit that the operation of the scripture itself applies to that specific instance.
Let it be then that even if the *codaka* applies to that instance, there is still a lapse of the *prayogavidhi*.

If that were the case, since the human effort directed toward the location of the *puroḍāśa* would not possess the status of a *kāraka* (instrumental factor) for the *prayāja* and other rites due to their lack of conformity [to that location], the *puroḍāśa* itself would not be obtained, rendering the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) purposeless.
Furthermore, because the performance of the *prayāja* and other rites is intended for the animal (*paśu*), it lacks the intentionality directed toward the *puroḍāśa*.

Now, if it is argued that the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries belong to the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice as its procedure (*itikartavyatā*) precisely because they are conducive to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) favorable to that sacrifice—and thus have no other [application]—even so, in the absence of actual performance, if there were a presence of the place and other factors dictated by the injunctions for the subsidiaries, then the application of the rule of *avaghāta* (threshing) to the *karaṇas* (instruments) would follow, resulting in the undesirable consequence of entering the Prābhākara position.

Alternatively, since the transfer (*atideśa*) of ritual items occurs through the mediation of the benefit (*upakāra*), even if the benefit is obtained from another source, there is no transfer of the ritual items when the benefit itself is lost.

This is because, once the benefit is established, there is no further requirement for its producer; therefore, there is no evidence for postulating a transfer of the place and other factors when the benefit is already accomplished.

For this very reason, by the extended application (*atideśa*) of the *puroḍāśa* [sacrifice], it is only the distinct auxiliary benefit (*vijātīyopakāra*) produced by the *prayāja* and other rites that is extended, and not the *prayāja* and other rites themselves which produce that benefit.

Consequently, since such a distinct auxiliary benefit is already obtained through the *prayāja* and other rites performed for the sake of the *padya*, the capacity to generate [the required fitness] is established by those very rites even in the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice; thus, there is no contradiction with the principle of incidental performance (*prasaṅga*).
For this same reason, there is no deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) caused by the absence of [specific] time, number, and so forth.

If it is argued that because the *prayāja* and other such subsidiaries are not extended [to the animal sacrifice], and because they exist as its own subsidiaries (*tadṛṣṭhabhāvena*), they are all the more not extended [to the cake-offering], even so,

since the subsidiaries like the *prayāja* performed for the sake of the animal sacrifice contribute their fruit only toward the benefit of the animal, it is impossible for them to be contributive to the cake-offering.

Otherwise, the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices, when performed for the sake of heaven, would result in the undesirable consequence of having to be performed again even at the time of the original production [of the result].

Therefore, since it is untenable for the auxiliary rites such as the *prayāja*s performed for the sake of the animal sacrifice to assist the *puroḍāśa* cake, those *prayāja*s and other auxiliaries must be performed separately for its sake. Nor can it be argued that, because the injunction "he performs eleven *prayāja*s" and so forth prescribes the number eleven and so on with reference to the *prayāja*s common to both the auxiliary and the primary sacrifices, the assistance to both is accomplished through a single performance by way of *tantra*.

"One performs eleven *prayāja* offerings; thereby one sacrifices for the animal itself. "One performs eleven *anūyāja* offerings; thereby one sacrifices after the animal itself. By such statements, since the number eleven and so forth are understood to serve the purpose of the *prayāja* offerings—which are themselves means for achieving the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the animal sacrifice—they possess a specific character that precludes the possibility of their being performed once for all (*tantratva*). This being the position reached, there follows the section concerning the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) of the animal sacrifice.
The *paśupuroḍāśa* principle applies here because there is no obstacle to the production of even a capacity when the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is present;

for there is no restrictive rule that a single cause produces only one effect, whether simultaneously or sequentially, since we observe that a single jar can produce color, taste, conjunction, and so forth, either simultaneously or in succession.

Furthermore, it is logical that the destruction of sin belonging to the obligatory performance (*nityaprayoga*) also arises from the *apūrva* (unseen potency) produced by the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices performed with the desire for [specific] objects (*kāmoddeśena*).
This is because the difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrībheda*) is the same in the present case as well;
for from a single cause, there can be a single nature (*ekarūpatva*) characterized by the delimitors of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) that are simultaneously [produced].
Otherwise, the simultaneous production of two jars would also follow as a consequence.

For this very reason, in cases such as "The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices [are for] all," since it has been established that the delimitor of the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) is precisely the state of not being the object of the motivating means of knowledge (*pravartakapramāṇa*) that operates in accordance with the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), only that which is delimited by such a delimitor is produced simultaneously,
and not multiple things.
In that case, there is no possibility of its arising sequentially, because when a previously arisen effect is destroyed by a new one, there is no cause for the subsequent production [of the first].
Nor does the logic of the animal-sacrifice cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) apply here, as in the case of the initial series of cakes (*puroḍāśa*).

For the principle of the *paśupuroḍāśa* applies here: in the view that it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), the statement of exclusion is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); likewise, in the other view, it will be an explanatory passage.
It is not [a prohibition] because there is no removal, as in the case of the potsherds (*kapāla*).
Commentary: This is not so.
In your position, nothing at all is deficient.

Just as when one potsherd is employed as a point of comparison, nothing is taken away from the other potsherds, so too, when the animal-cake sacrifice (paśu-puroḍāśa-yāga) is being performed for another deity, nothing is deficient for the deity of the animal sacrifice.
In that case, there is indeed a contradiction in the statement. In my view, however, the manifestation of the deity—which is a subsidiary element—is lost.
As for the claim that even what is contradictory becomes successful, that is something else entirely.
But when the word *vyudva* is uttered in the context of the *ahīna* sacrifice, the literal meaning of the word is not grasped;
rather, that statement refers to the drawing of the cups (*graha*), because its purpose is for that end.
The Commentary states: "In this way, it is a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*)."
In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, regarding the cups (grahas) dedicated to deities who are currently receiving [the offering], there is that statement concerning the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa):
"There are no sacrificial cakes for these animals; for these animals have the soma as their cake.
Yet, such cakes do not exist.
