This is stated with reference to the absence of consecratory preparation (*saṃskāra*) for those deities that are associated with different ritual procedures.
[The text says: "The *puroḍāśas* are their cups; for these are indeed cup-*puroḍāśas*.
Is it their commonality that these are intended for the consecratory preparation of the deities? Yes.

If the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are also for the purpose of consecrating the deities, then this [interpretation] is consistent. Therefore, the view that they are consecratory acts (*saṃskāra*) alone is superior.
And there is a scriptural statement to that effect regarding their greatness.

The Commentary (Bhāṣya) states: It is heard thus: "They do not take the draught-cup (graha) for this animal; the animal is [offered] at the time of the cake-offering (puroḍāśa). This scriptural statement regarding the absence of the cup, which is based on the presence of the animal-cake offering, demonstrates that the cup and the cake serve a single purpose.
In that context, it is known that the cup serves to consecrate the deity;
if the cake also serves to consecrate the deity, then this [scriptural statement] becomes consistent.
And since the status of the deity as a cause is well-established, he demonstrates this [in the following] commentary:
"For this reason also we see that it is a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*).

For it is thus recorded in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): 'Animals are sacrificed for the fires and for desires; the fires are indeed desires; there are cakes (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Agni, for animals are dedicated to Agni.'"
By hearing that the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are caused by animal deities, [the text] shows that the cakes serve the purpose of consecrating those deities.
The logical justification is not contradictory because of the attainment of the purpose; it would be a subordinate modification, just like the boiled milk (*śṛta*).
Commentary: Now, as for what was said—that the property belonging to two subordinate elements would become the property of these two principal elements—[this is addressed].
It is said:
This reasoning is not contradictory even for those two primary objects of desire.
Why? Because of the attainment of the goal.
Even though it is a natural (prākṛta) effect, when it brings about the accomplishment of the sacrifice, it is accepted as being a door for the two properties, just like boiled milk (*śṛta*).

For example, in the cases "the sacrificial pap (*caru*) [is cooked] in boiled milk" and "curd-boiled milk (*dadhiśruta*)," since the curd and the boiled milk perform the function of the *praṇītā* water for the purpose of the offering, they are accepted as being the locus for the two properties;
and no fault arises.
That [reasoning] would be futile because both are established by direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*); in the event of a conflict, the modification (*vikāratva*) follows from that very purpose.

Commentary: Now, as for what was stated—that because the *aindra-vāruṇa-sāvitra* sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) constitute the *sautrāmaṇī* ritual, their displacement (*utkarṣa*) would follow—this is now addressed.
That sacrifice at the two [junctions] is for the purpose of consecrating the deity and for the purpose of closing the gaps,
because both purposes are established by direct scriptural statement (śruti).

Therefore, in the case of those [rites] having deities contrary [to the norm], there will be no displacement from the context for the purpose of closing a defect; thus, this modification will remain within that very ritual procedure. Even in that case, its displacement would be purposeless.
Commentary: That which was stated [previously] is now being explained:
in the case of a conflict among them, there would be no modification of their position.
Commentary: If that is so, then by this method, there is no displacement from the context.
To begin with, the refinement of the deities cannot be set aside by the displacement [of the ritual] due to the context.
In that regard, in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) are obtained through the extended application (codaka) as having deities common to both [the animal and cake offerings].
In that case, words such as "Indra" and so forth denote only the deities of the animal sacrifice.

How so? For it is understood that these parts of them are uttered together with other phonemes; indeed, the parts are capable of signifying the whole and thereby causing the meaning of the whole to be understood.
Just as in the case of *gānya* and other such terms;

and just as in the *nigada* addressed to Sarasvatī— "O Sarasvatī, carry away the revilers of the gods, the progeny of every deceitful *bṛsa*" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 6.61.3)— the word *bṛsa* conveys the meaning of the word *bṛhat*.

Why, then, is it imagined in this way? Because if other deities were to be invoked in sacrifices intended for the consecration of animal deities, they would be rendered purposeless. Therefore, the words denoting the deities of the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are themselves the modifications of the animal deities.
The principle of the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa). According to the principle of the animal-cake,
there is either a repetition, as in the case of the fore-offerings (prayāja), or one part belongs to another deity.
Commentary: In the case of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone, the word "or" (*vā*) excludes the logical argument, not the position itself.
Nor is there a modification of the name;
for when the case of the latent impression is otherwise untenable, modifications of the name occur.

Even in the case of an unexpressed modification (*anākhyā-vikāra*), the position of the *saṃskāra* (preparatory rite) is indeed tenable. How so? It will be a repetition of the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice itself.
For in that case, both the animal deity and the *puroḍāśa* are obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
A different substance, namely the cup (*graha*), is prescribed for the animal deity;
the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) has a different deity;
yet the sacrifice itself remains entirely unchanged.
It must be connected both with the animal deity and with the cup (graha).
Since it is not possible to perform both of these [connections] simultaneously in a single sacrifice, the sacrifice itself is performed repeatedly by implication.
One part of that [repeated sacrifice] is dedicated to another deity, just like the *prayāja* offerings.

For example, when the five *prayāja* offerings are obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*), the number eleven is prescribed. Since that number cannot be achieved without repetition, the *prayāja* offerings are repeated.
Among those being repeated, other deities are assigned to one portion [of them].
[The examples] beginning with "Upāsānaktā" [are cited].
Thus, here too, there is a repetition of the cake-offering (puroḍāśa-yāga).
Therefore, there is a displacement [of the mantra], even according to the view that it is a purificatory act (saṃskāra).

Ṭup—In this [Sautrāmaṇī], by virtue of the *codaka* (extended application), the deity of the animal sacrifice (*paśudevatā*) and the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) are obtained [from the archetype].
Therein, a different substance (*graha*) is prescribed for the animal deity, and a different deity (such as Indra) is prescribed for the animal-cake offering.
However, the sacrifice itself remains unchanged (*avikṛta*), just as in the *abhyuditeṣṭi*.
That [sacrifice] is practiced just like the Soma sacrifice.
These two [statements], the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya, are incorrect.

In this Sautrāmaṇī, animal sacrifices are prescribed as the primary elements; and by means of the consecration of the deities, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are obtained for them through the rule of extension (*codaka*).
In this case, this procedure for the deity is expressly stated by the scriptural injunction.
Therefore, the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) sacrifices—which perform the functions of the archetypal (prakṛta) rites—occur by virtue of the power of that specific statement.
That which is connected to a deity [in the archetype] is not connected to the animal-cake sacrifice [unless so specified].

How so? Because there is no displacement [of the original elements]. How is there no displacement? Because they are not enjoined [here]. How is there no injunction? (The answer: Here, in this modification (*vikṛti*), the auxiliary benefits (*upakāra*) are extended by analogy (*atideśa*), but not the constituent items (*padārtha*). However, where there is a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) for those [items], there is displacement.
And that [context] belongs only to the archetype (*prakṛti*). Granting it for the sake of argument, we say:

even if there were context (*prakaraṇa*) and recurrence (*viparivṛtti*) here for the cake-offering (*puroḍāśayāga*), nevertheless, it is not connected [to the cup-deity relationship], because there is no evidence; this is not equal to the Soma-sacrifice.

In that context, by the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), a sacrifice qualified by Soma is prescribed. Furthermore, the various "drawings" (*grahaṇa*)—such as those for Indra and others—are the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the substance of the Soma-sacrifice. All these drawings are included within the ritual context (*prakaraṇa*);
that is to say, there is a repetition of the sacrifice (*yāgābhyāsa*) therein.
In this case, however, no refinement (*saṃskāra*) is performed for either the animal-cake (*paśu-puroḍāśa*) or the deity of the cup (*graha-devatā*).
Therefore, this is a distinct sacrifice (*yāgāntara*).
[Objection: But will it not be like the *abhyuditeṣṭi*?
This is not equal to the *abhyuditeṣṭi*.

In that case, when the occasion (*nimitta*)—the rising of the moon—has occurred, the division [of the sacrificial materials] among the deities is enjoined, and the sacrifice itself is likewise enjoined. But here there is no such mention of a division, whereby it would be equal to the *abhyuditeṣṭi*.
Is it not the case that the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice is directly perceived (meaning it is already established),
whereas the sacrifice involving the connection between the cup (*graha*) and the deity is only inferential (meaning it must be postulated)?
Therefore, rather than abandoning what is already established, another sacrifice [involving the *graha*] should be postulated.
This is not so.
If there were an inclusion [of the accessory] in that very sacrifice by some manner, then another sacrifice would not be postulated (though such inclusion is not possible).

Furthermore, if an inferred [sacrifice] were not obtained while a directly perceived sacrifice exists, then the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites would be devoid of their specific ritual properties (*adharmaka*).

And if there were only one sacrifice in the Sautrāmaṇī, then only one [set of auxiliaries] would be enjoined [or prescribed]: "Two [cups] for the two [deities]"—this being the meaning—then even though there is a difference of sacrifices, because they share the same ritual framework (*samānatantratvāt*), the *prayāja* offerings and so forth should be performed only once; however, there would be a repetition only of the preparations of the substances. And since those [preparations] must indeed be repeated in a single sacrifice due to the difference of the substances, what undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*) is there here? It is replied: [The text continues: "If there were only one sacrifice in the Sautrāmaṇī, then only one [set of auxiliaries] would be enjoined: 'Two [cups] for the two [deities]'—this being the meaning—then even though there is a difference of sacrifices, because they share the same ritual framework, the *prayāja* offerings and so forth should be performed only once; however, there would be a repetition only of the preparations of the substances. And since those [preparations] must indeed be repeated in a single sacrifice due to the difference of the substances, what undesirable consequence is there here? It is replied:
In that case, the consecration would apply to only one substance, while for the second substance, even the *codaka* (extended injunction) would not apply.

Furthermore, there would be an offering of only one; the second, however, would result in an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), like sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth. Moreover, if the deity were to reside in only one [substance], it would have to be by way of option (*vikalpa*).

(As for the claim that, like the *prayāja* offerings, that very same sacrifice is repeated and joined with different deities—that too is not comparable; thus he says: The number is enjoined by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *prayājas*; therefore, in that case, there is no separate sacrifice at all.
(But here,) there is a separate sacrifice—this is the difference.
[The reading of Ānandāśrama’s *ṭīkā*, however, is not accepted as it is not consistent with the *tantra* principle.]

The *paśupuroḍāśanyāya*: According to the *Śābarabhāṣya*, regarding the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-paśu*), there arises the doubt whether the *paśupuroḍāśa* (the sacrificial cake for the animal) is an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) to the animal sacrifice, or rather a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the deity of the animal. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is an indirect auxiliary.
It is not so; for when a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) based on what has been seen exists, there is no postulation of an unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*).
Furthermore, because of its connection with the characteristics of animals, its status as such is well-established.
Soma: The connection [of this section] is stated by saying that, as in the previous case, here too there is an absence of a purificatory rite (*asaṃskārakatva*) due to the difference in the deity.
Vi— "The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) mentioned in the context of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) is a benefactor because it is a consecration (*saṃskṛti*);
by the expression of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), there is a distinction between the two deities, and thus it serves as a benefit.
Since its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is established through the principle of *sandamśa* (enclosure), its visible purpose is the consecration (*smṛti-saṃskṛti*) [of the deity]."
If there is a different deity in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), then the status of being dedicated to Agni and Soma (*āgnīṣomīyatva*) [does not apply].

According to the Bhaṭṭa school, regarding the statement in the *Daikṣa* ritual, "Having performed the offering with the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, he offers the *paśupuroḍāśa* cake belonging to the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma," even though it pertains to the *paśupuroḍāśa*, it is not a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the deity of the animal by way of being the object of reference (*uddeśa*). This is because, since there is no distinction in the designation using the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in both cases, both are equally remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*).
Thus, [the cake belongs to] the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*).

In the animal sacrifices (*paśusavanīya*), the animal sacrifice consists of the offering of the omentum (*vapā*), the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and the performance of the subsidiary rites (*aṅgapracāra*).
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 60). In these animal sacrifices, the *manotā* mantra is addressed solely to the deity Agni; there is no modification (*ūha*) therein for the deity of the animal.
The *manotā* principle:

Even in animal sacrifices (*paśuyāga*) and the like, the *agnihotra* oblation is performed on the southern altar (*sāyana*), not on the northern altar (*auttaravedika*). However, if by chance the animal ritual is postponed (*utkarṣa*), then it is indeed performed on the northern altar.
This is discussed under the section on "Resolution" (*saṃkalpa*) at Mīmāṃsākośa, page 86, entry "agnihotrahoma. One should consult that source for further details.

In the section concerning the commencement of animal sacrifices (*paśuyajñaprakramādhikaraṇa*; *paśusomādhikaraṇa* 2.2.6.17–20), the Commentator himself has described the superiority of a statement supported by reasoning over a statement contrary to reasoning. [This principle is applied in] Sūtra 2.2.9: "Like the animal sacrifice."

Just as in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), even though the times are different, because they share a single location—as in the rule, "They perform the omentum (*vapā*) at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina*), and the limbs (*aṅga*) at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*)"—there is no separate fetching of the materials;

likewise, when the *sāsadasya* [offering] is heard of in connection with the animal sacrifice, the application of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dāśapaurṇamāsika*) is not prohibited there, because the *sāsadasya* is based on a direct scriptural injunction (*vācanikatvāt*).

Regarding animal-offerings (*paśuvikṛti*), in the injunctions "one should sacrifice a cow (*dhenu*) to Heaven and Earth," "a calf (*vatsa*) to the Maruts," and "a bull (*ṛṣabha*) to Indra," these animals possess the genus *go* (cow), and not the genus *aja* (goat).

(A *dhenu* is one that has recently calved. By the words *dhenu*, *vatsa*, and *ṛṣabha*, the mother, the son, and the father—respectively the relata and correlates of the action of multiple births—are to be understood.)
And it has already been stated that these possess the universal of cowness (*gotvajāti*).
Who [uses the word]? People employ the word "animal" (*paśu*) as a designation for a specific substance characterized by a particular form, possessing horns, a tail, hair, and four feet.
In the Bhārata Rāmāyaṇa (6.17), because the word *paśu* has a fixed gender, the action is also used in the masculine gender.
See Sūkti-pṛṣṭha (Su. pṛ. 1.44.

Regarding the placement of animal heads: that which is offered therein is for the benefit of man; bricks are not to be fashioned [from them], but rather they are to be filled with parched grain (*saktubhiḥ*).
This is the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
(2.1.4) The immolation of the animal must be performed by the Adhvaryu priest alone.
*Saṃkalpa*: 1.1.15. See Mīko., p. 360, under the entry "abhyaryugaṇastyanaiva.
By the principle that "the state of being seventeen animals cannot be established without a sacrifice," the determination of what was doubtful is established.

Regarding the statement, "There would be an option (*vikalpa*) in the case of the animal sacrifices of the *savana* offerings" (*vā.* 3.1.12, p. 650), it is stated in the twelfth [book]: "In the *savanīya* animal sacrifice, because of the *sūktavāka-praiṣa* performed by the Maitrāvaruṇa—which is not extended (*anatidiṣṭa*) from the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice [but is rather] extended (*atidiṣṭa*)—there is a specific grasping of the distinction regarding the agency through the mantra, since the determination of that [agency] occurs when the *savanīya* oblations are known to be performed by the *pravṛttijīpa* (the one who has entered upon the performance) even in the absence of the Maitrāvaruṇa.
(*Bālakrīḍā*, p. 188).
There should be an option regarding the modified [rites] among the animal sacrifices and the *savanīya* offerings, because both are equally based on scriptural injunction.

Among the animal sacrifices and the *savanīya* offerings—that is, in the case of the animal sacrifice at the *savana*, the *savanīya* animal, and the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes—there should be an option by way of extension (*prasaṅga*).
The sense is that either five *prayāja* offerings or eleven *prayāja* offerings should be performed.
The animal sacrifice has modified mantras; the cake offering has modified mantras.
In that case, it is thus.
But in reality, there is no doubt that all of them are indeed modified.

Why are all [the details] modified? Because both the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) and the cake offering (*puroḍāśa*) have not been directly heard in the primary injunction; since the subsidiaries are not explicitly stated (*aśruteḥ*), they are not heard.
Because the subsidiaries are obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), both are merely restated (*anuvāditārau*).

Therefore, regarding the question of which of the two—the animal sacrifice or the *savanīya* cake offering—is the occasioning factor (*prasaṅgin*) and which is the occasioned factor (*prasakta*), there is an option (*vikalpa*). This is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Or rather, it belongs to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*), because of its specific connection to that; thus, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding its purpose.
The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) of an option.
The ritual procedure (*tantra*) pertaining to the animal sacrifice applies to the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), not as an option.
For that animal sacrifice, a specific rule is traditionally taught: the *sūktavāka* and the *praisha*.
If there were an optionality [regarding these], then those specific rules would be rendered meaningless.
By virtue of the force of their traditional teaching (*āmnāna*), they are mandatory.

Therefore, the conclusion is that the ritual procedure (*tantra*) pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) applies to the cake offerings (*puroḍāśa*). Furthermore, there is a temporal separation (*viprakarṣa*) in the case of the animal sacrifice because it is prescribed within the middle of the ritual sequence.
For this reason as well, he states that the *pāśuka* ritual procedure applies to the cake offerings.

The separation of the animal sacrifice from the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is heard in scripture: "They proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing, with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) at the midday pressing, and with the limbs at the third pressing.
Because the *savanīya* cakes are prescribed in the midst of that ritual procedure, there is a commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) with the animal sacrifice.

The section concerning the animal and Soma sacrifices establishes the conclusion that the ritual procedure (*tantra*) pertaining to the animal sacrifice undoubtedly applies to the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and there is no optionality (*vikalpa*). Who [holds this view]?
The properties of the rope are common to both the animal sacrifice (the Agniṣomīya and Savanīya) and the Soma sacrifice.
The animal and the Soma function as the means of accomplishment by virtue of being the material cause of what is to be offered.
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 797.
The section concerning the Animal and Soma sacrifices:
In the injunctions "One should immolate the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma" and "One should sacrifice with Soma," the acts of immolation and sacrifice are enjoined as novel (apūrva) rites.

The connection with a substance [in the context] of the animal and Soma sacrifices is for the purpose of enjoining [the act], because in the context [of the Jyotiṣṭoma], the connection with a substance would otherwise be meaningless, as it is not for the sake of a subordinate quality (guṇa).
Bhāṣya: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma," and therein this is enjoined:
"First he cuts from the heart, then from the tongue, then from the chest."

Likewise, there are such injunctions as "One should sacrifice with Soma," and "He draws the portion for Indra-Vāyu," "He draws the portion for Mitra-Varuṇa," "He draws the portion for the Aśvins," and so forth.

In this regard, a doubt arises: are the two [injunctions] "He immolates" and "He sacrifices" merely restatements (anuvādau) of the rites already enjoined by the verbs "he draws" (*gṛhṇāti*) and so on—which pertain to the constituent parts of the whole—or are they the original enjoiners (*vidhitārau*) of two entirely new rites?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That they refer to the whole.

Why? Because these two actions, which are enjoined by the words "he seizes" (*ālabhati*) and "he sacrifices" (*yajati*), are considered to have already been understood through the terms "seizing" (*gṛhṇāti*) and "extracting" (*avadyati*).
Furthermore, it is not the case that an object already understood is being enjoined.
Rather, [the text] refers back (*anuvadati*) to the heart and other organs by means of the word "animal" (*paśu*), and to the juice by means of the word "Soma."
Therefore, in the statement "one should sacrifice with Soma," the verb *yajati* is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
In the statement "one desiring heaven should sacrifice every spring," the verb *yajeta* is for the purpose of enjoining the accessory (*guṇa*).
And in the statement "one should immolate an animal," the verb *ālabheta* is for the purpose of establishing the connection with Agni-Soma.
Moreover, there is the sequence: "The Adhvaryu priest draws ten cups at the morning pressing; the third is offered.

If two unprecedented sacrifices were being enjoined, then the deities would have to be enjoined by means of the Aindravāyava and other vessels, and being co-equal in purpose, they would have to be treated as options, just as in the cases: "He binds with Khadira wood," "He binds with Palāśa wood," and "He binds with Rohitaka wood. In that case, the observation of both sequential order and combination would not be possible.
Furthermore, in this statement regarding the aggregate, this is properly established for one who sacrifices;
therefore, these two are restatements of the aggregate.
This being the case, we reply:
in the injunctions for the previously unknown rites of the animal sacrifice and the Soma sacrifice, [the terms refer to the substances].
Why? Because the word "Soma" is well-known to denote the milky creeper, not the juice.
For the word *soma* denotes a class (*ākṛti*), not an individual (*vyakti*).
Likewise, they employ the word *paśu* (animal) as denoting a class with respect to a specific substance that has horns, a tail, hair, and four feet.
Nor are there any sacrifices under discussion here that have such substances as their material, for which these two [words] could serve as restatements of a collective whole.
But is it not the case that the heart and other parts are modifications of the animal, since the word "animal" (paśu) is used for the purpose of the connection with Agni and Soma?
This is not so;
it is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma that is offered, and this [heart and so forth] is not the animal as it was originally constituted.
In that case, if there were a reference to a worldly animal, then the word "animal" (paśu) would be used in its primary sense;
if, however, it referred to the heart and other organs, then it would be used in a secondary sense through its connection with a modification (*vikāra*).
By that same logic, the word "Soma" (*soma*) would also be a restatement (*anuvāda*) through its connection with a modification.
Therefore, two previously unknown actions should be enjoined, not mere restatements.
Alternatively, it might be argued that the creeper is enjoined with respect to the sacrifices already established in the context of the Aindravāyava and other offerings.
To this, it is replied:
That [cup] dedicated to Indra and Vāyu cannot be understood through the syntactical connection (*vākya*);
for by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the juice itself belongs to Indra and Vāyu.

Therefore, if it were unable to enjoin or refer to the existence [of the cup] even within the context of the original sacrifices, the statement regarding the connection with the substance would be purposeless.

Therefore, two new actions (*apūrva-karman*) should be enjoined, rather than being mere restatements (*anuvāda*) of those already established. Alternatively, because the nature of the fault has been demonstrated, the prior statement [is justified]. Furthermore, two words are here suspected of being restatements of their constituent parts: the word "animal" (*paśu*) and the sacrifice (*yaji*), which is inferred from its connection with Agni and Soma.
For this sentence, "One should sacrifice with the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma," is based on a portion that is both heard and inferred.

In this regard, a doubt arises: is the word "animal" a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the heart and other organs [inferred from other texts], and the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) a restatement of the sacrifices [inferred] for those possessing those parts; or rather, is a new (*apūrva*) animal and sacrifice enjoined, while the others are injunctions of subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*)?

Likewise, by means of the sentences concerning the Aindravāyava and other offerings, sacrifices are established on the basis of the relationship between the substance and the deity. In this context, the question arises: is the Soma juice merely restated (anūdya) by the roots *yaji* (to sacrifice) and *grah* (to take), or is an action associated with a substance being enjoined? Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "Is it [the case] here that those [actions] enjoined by the roots *yaji* and *grah*... This is intended to demonstrate that these two [roots] are synonyms for sacrifice (*yajña*), and that because they are inferred from the connection [with the deity], they are either expressed by the verbal suffixes of those [verbs] or are enjoined by them.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of indicating the animal inferred by that [act].
Alternatively, it is not a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the sacrifice through its constituent parts.
How then? It is a restatement of the touching (*saṃsparśana*) implied by that [sacrifice], by means of the word "ālabhati."
The section concerning the Animal and Soma sacrifices.
And the imparting of the cognition occurs precisely through the door of the connection with the deity, and [it applies] to that many sacrifices.

How can there be an injunction for sacrifice by means of the *tina* (grass), or how can there be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the heart and other parts, or rather, is it that a single sacrifice connected with the animal is inferred? It must be said: "by means of the taking up" (*grahaṇena*). This is what is stated: [The opponent asks: How can there be an injunction for sacrifice by means of the *tina* grass, or how can there be a restatement of the heart and other parts as being the animal, or is it that a single sacrifice connected with the animal is inferred? [The author] says: It must be said: "by means of the taking up. This is what is stated:

"Just as it is in the case of the generic animal sacrifice, so too in the case of the Soma sacrifice, this very same sacrifice [is intended], provided that by means of this specific location the material is taken up; for through the mantra, a goat is understood, and likewise, 'this is mine' refers to the heart and other organs."
That being the case, the presentation of the doubt occurs precisely according to the literal wording of the Bhāṣya:
"The *prakṛti* (archetype) serves as the basis;

since the materials such as the heart (*hṛdaya*) and so forth are required as the constituent substances, there is, just as in the case of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), a restatement of the aggregate."
For instance:
when a goat is obtained from the wording of the mantra, the state of being an animal (*paśutva*) contained therein is first restated (*anūdya*).
In that regard, it is as with the sentences concerning the *Āgneya* and other offerings, which do not [originate] the sacrifices prior [to their restatement].
Granted that once the deity has been established, the sacrifice may indeed be enjoined;

or rather, let it be understood that [the injunction] culminates in its own purpose even in the case of the *soma*. By this very principle—that "the *sānnāyya* [is primary] because it possesses both [deity and substance]"—this is not so, for in the case of the *aindravāyava* and other [cups], there is no [independent] substance or deity.
The section concerning the animal and Soma sacrifices:
"And because they are not injunctions, the preparatory rites [do not apply]."

Commentary: Thus far, it has been stated that even though the primary acts (prakṛta) exist, there can be no two restatements (anuvāda). Now, it is argued that the primary sacrifices themselves do not exist at all.
Why? Because the preparatory rites (saṃskāra) are not injunctive of the sacrifice (acodaka).
Furthermore, sacrifices are not enjoined by means of the [cups] dedicated to Indra-Vāyu and others;
therefore, the act of drawing [the soma] being prepared serves a visible purpose,
whereas the mention of the deity during that preparation serves an invisible (transcendental) purpose.
Therefore, by the statement "He takes [the cup] for Indra and Vāyu," what is meant is simply that he forms a mental resolve (saṃkalpa) with respect to Indra and Vāyu.
In this context, since it is not logical to form such a resolve without a sacrifice, a sacrifice must be inferred.
That very sacrifice which is already traditionally handed down (āmnāta) is the one in whose existence the resolve becomes possible.
And therefore, sacrifices are enjoined by such [injunctions] as "He draws the cup for Indra and Vāyu";
since there is no sacrifice previously mentioned [to which they could refer], the word *yajati* is not a term denoting a collective. The same applies to the word *ālabhati*.

Or rather—these two are not restatements (*anuvāda*) of a collective whole, precisely for the reason stated in [Sūtra] 2.4.10: "Or rather, it is an injunction (*codanā*), because the subject matter is not previously established.
How is it that they cannot be previously established? Because the acts of cutting (*avadyati*) and taking (*gṛhṇāti*) do not pertain to the sacrifices themselves.
What then? They are injunctions of mere preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*), since they terminate in that alone.
Since the sentence culminates in that alone (the act of taking), it is not possible to assume an unmentioned sacrifice;
for such a sacrifice could only be assumed on the grounds that "the substance taken for the sake of a deity does not fulfill its purpose until it is connected with a sacrifice.
Only when one begins to assume a sacrifice because of this apparent inconsistency (*anyathānupapatti*) is the directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) root *yaj* (to sacrifice) already present at hand.

Since there is no distinction, the means of proof for postulating another sacrifice—which would have to be established in order to account for all the connections between substances and deities—is now examined.
That being the case, of what will this be a restatement of the collection?
As it has been said: "Like the Āgneya and other [sacrifices], a sacrifice cannot be expected from another sentence unless it has already been conceptualized."
To this we reply:
"In all cases, a sentence is completed by the application of merit and demerit;
when that [application] is not obtained, there is incompleteness, but when it is obtained, there is the completion of the sentence."
In the case of the statement, “There is an eight-potherd [oblation] for Agni,” no meritorious activity other than the sacrifice is perceived;
therefore, prior to that inference, the sentence remains incomplete.
Here, however, in the case of “He draws the cup for Indra-Vāyu,” the person is enjoined toward the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) of drawing the cup.
In this regard, even prior to the inference of the sacrifice (*yajya*), there exists the statement "it exists by means of the things to be enjoined" (*vidheya*) for the sake of completion.
But this is something else: that something further is expected beyond that.
For every sentence, while reaching its conclusion in its own primary meaning, does not abandon its dependence on another meaning; yet, it does not thereby become incomplete.
Since that requirement is understood to be fulfilled by another sentence, it does not tolerate a connection with yet another sentence.
Therefore, at the time of inferring the sacrifice, the presence of the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" for each individual sentence is not contradicted.

However, in the case of the injunction “An eight-potherd [cake] for Agni,” because the root *bhavati* (to be) does not consist of human activity, nothing is enjoined and nothing is prohibited prior to the verb *yajati* (to sacrifice). Thus, while the sentence remains incomplete and no other sentence is required, the sacrifice (*yajati*) being inferred is not connected with anything contained in another sentence; this constitutes the difference.

Now, as for what was said—that since the animal and the Soma are prescribed by the originative injunctions (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), it is not proper for a modification (*vikāra*) to occur through another sentence—in that regard we reply:
“The relative strength [of two rules] must be considered together with the fact that one substance is distinct from the other.”
The state of being a sacrificial substance (ājya) similar to the heart and other organs belongs to both the animal and the soma.

Furthermore, if some entirely different substance were prescribed after setting aside both the animal and the Soma, then there would be a contradiction. But here, the sacrifice is accomplished by means of the animal itself through its heart and other parts, and by means of the Soma through its juice.
And there is no contradiction whatsoever regarding the connection with the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*).

For the animal and the soma, being enjoined as the means of sacrifice, require a procedure (*itikartavyatā*). In that regard, the requirement of "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*) is fulfilled by means of the *rasahṛdaya* and so forth through that [procedure].
Therefore, because they are supportive, there is no logical inconsistency in postulating them.
In that case, since [the requirement for] purchase and so forth is already established by the general rules (*prakaraṇika*), the connection with a substance here would be purposeless.
To this also, the reply is simply: "And because the preparatory rites are not injunctions" (*acodakācca saṃskārāḥ*).
For those [rules regarding substances] are not injunctions that enjoin the *soma* or the animal sacrifice.
What then? It is the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for those two [the goat and the ram] themselves.

Since it might follow that any substance whatsoever, when impelled by that [impulse], could serve as the means for the sacrifice through some manner of procurement, it is enjoined that [the sacrifice] is to be accomplished by means of [the substance] procured through purchase and so forth, and prepared by means of pressing and so forth.

Furthermore, the wording of the mantra lacks the capacity to bring about a goat not already enjoined elsewhere; however, even if there were doubt regarding what is enjoined by the injunction for the animal (*paśu*), it serves merely to restrict [the choice] to another [specific type].

Furthermore, the act of cutting (*avadyati*) does not invariably imply a sacrifice (*yāga*), for it is established both in common worldly usage and in the Veda that this act occurs even without a sacrifice, as in the mere cutting of a piece of sugar-candy.

Moreover, the connection between the substance and the deity is not established in any way through a sacrifice or similar rite; thus, there is a disparity with the inference [proposed by the opponent].

Nor is the cutting of the *sānnāyya* (curdled milk offering) enjoined in the archetype (*prakṛti*); therefore, because it remains exactly as it was, the transfer of its specific properties (*taddharmaprāpti*) would also not occur.
Furthermore, its status as a sacrificial substance is not a *itikartavyatā* (procedural detail), such that it could be extended [by analogy] to the other sacrifice.
Nor does an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) apply here.

The injunction of identity [of the *pūtīka* plant with the *soma*] is established through both direct statement (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), resulting in a lack of similarity [to cases where extension applies].
In the section concerning the Soma-sentence as well, there is the section on the qualified animal and Soma; that is,
the section on the animal and Soma.
In the section concerning the animal and Soma sacrifices, [the materials] are applied by their respective individual sentences.
But is it not the case that the sentence "He takes the Aindravāyava cup" itself is observed to be the applicatory injunction?
And therefore, the capacity of the expression "maitrāvaruṇam" to enjoin a deity is understood as being independent of what precedes it.
True, they are enjoined with mutual independence regarding the act of drawing [the cup];
however, there is no such unity of purpose, because their purpose is transcendental (adṛṣṭa).
If it is asked, "In what sense is it for a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha)? it is replied:

"If a mantra connected with the primary sacrifice is heard in relation to a preparatory act (saṃskāra), then that [hearing] is for a visible purpose; otherwise, it would not be established. For if the deities already connected with the sacrifice were to be mentioned again during the acts of drawing [the soma], such as the *nirvāpa* and *āvāhana*, just as they are in other rites—or if the drawing itself could not be accomplished without them—then their mention there would be for a visible purpose, and could be assumed to serve as a reminder of what was previously known.
However, [the cups] dedicated to Indra and others are not heard of as being primary in the Jyotiṣṭoma;
nor is their extraction established merely by the absence of those [deities].
This being the case, even though it is heard that "the extraction must be performed joined with a deity," there is no purpose served therein by an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*).
The section concerning the animal and Soma sacrifices; the section concerning the animal and Soma sacrifices.

Because there is an absence of manifestation characterized by a specific state (*bhāva*), the principle "but in the case of unmanifest [sacrifices], it is that of Soma" does not apply, as in the case of the *Viśvajit* and other such rites;
however, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), that principle does apply.

In the example of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because there is a difference in sacrifices, it would follow that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the sacrifice applies only once in the modified rites (*vikṛti*); yet, in that case, the sacrifice would be performed with only one part, such as the heart. In the final conclusion, however, the sacrifice is performed with all parts.

When, in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), regarding the injunctions such as "a ram for Sarasvatī" and "a bull for Indra," one does not perform the slaughter and other rites, the sacrifice must be performed with unmodified substances of the same class, such as those mentioned in the scripture.

Because acts such as slaughter (*viśasana*) are not prescribed in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), and because the creeper—already established by the original injunctions (*utpattiśiṣṭa*) through the rules for pressing and so forth—cannot be turned into juice, the text [of the *Tantravārttika*] concludes that if there were an indirect hearing (*paraṃparā-āśravaṇa*) [of the injunction], it would result in a contradiction with the direct Vedic text (*śrutivirodha*). By that same logic, since there would be the contingency of contradicting the direct Vedic statement regarding the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) in the case of rams, bulls, and so forth, it is impossible for slaughter and other such acts to be obtained through the extended application (*codaka*). In the final position (*siddhānta*), however, just as in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), even though there is an indirect hearing in the modified sacrifice, there is no contradiction with the substance directly stated in the Veda; therefore, in accordance with the extended application (*codaka*), the heart and other organs [are used] subsequently.

The term *pākya* [refers to] that which is known later being sublated by what was previously established. For example, in the *Adhvarakalpa*, because the twelve-kapāla offering for Indra and Agni pertains to the *āmāvāsya* (new moon) rite, the *paurṇamāsa* (full moon) ritual procedure—which had been obtained for Sarasvatī’s *ājyabhāga* offering—was sublated by the *āmāvāsya* ritual procedure.

In expressions such as "Look, the deer runs," because the word "look" (*paśya*) generates a verbal cognition with respect to its object without requiring another [object], it is appropriate that the running (*dhāvana-bhāvanā*) functions as its object; thus, there is no other [object] in that case.
(Rahasya, p. 24).
Even though the *pākayajña* (cooked sacrifice) takes the place of the *anvāhārya* (subsidiary fee), it is not to be performed in the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice.

The cooked offering (*pāka*) is not to be performed on a cloth placed upon the *anvāhārya* [fire] during the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice. The cooked offering should be prepared in black vessels, having the nature of heat (*auṣmyarūpa*). This should be seen under Mīko., p. 1475, regarding the statement: "Because cooking in black vessels is impossible."

In the *kṛṣṇala-caru* sacrifice, the act of cooking (*pāka*) must be performed even though it serves no visible purpose, because it is directly enjoined by the text: "He cooks [it] in clarified butter.
This so-called cooking refers to the softening of the rice grains (*taṇḍula*), as established by the recitation of the mantra at the time of the offering.
What is established? The preceding mantra brings the subsequent one to mind through its very recitation (just as perception does).
For example, the mantra "He sacrifices the fuel-sticks" (samidho yajati), upon being completed, brings the [mantra for] Tanūnapāt to mind.
Therefore, since both are directly present in the recited text of the Samhitā, there is no fixed rule [regarding their order].
This being the case, we reply:
the recitation of the mantra is more authoritative. Why? Because the recitation of the Brāhmaṇa is remote [from the ritual action].
For instance, by the injunction "He offers the *samidh* oblations," a ritual act (*padārtha*) is prescribed.
At the time of performance, that act causes one to remember the specific sentence by which it was originally enjoined.

Once that sentence has been recalled, the ritual act—being thus remembered at the time of performance—is carried out; and once performed, it does not immediately cause the second ritual act to be recalled (because meanings do not depend on a physical text, and therefore their sequence cannot be fixed).
What then? After the performance has been completed, one reflects upon that ritual act which has been performed;
and while being reflected upon, it causes one to remember the specific portion of the Brāhmaṇa by which it was enjoined (namely, "He sacrifices with the *samidh*").
And that [remembered injunction] in turn causes one to remember the subsequent portion of the Brāhmaṇa (namely, the section beginning with "He sacrifices to *tanūnapāt*").
Furthermore, that Brāhmaṇa prescribes the meaning of the words (the *punaḥ* word has the sense of "but").
At the time of performance, that (Brāhmaṇa) must be required as a reminder.
This is the remoteness (of the Brāhmaṇa passage from the mantra recitation).
Furthermore, a mantra being employed in the internal ritual action, as it reaches its conclusion, brings the subsequent mantra to mind.
And that subsequent mantra, while being brought to mind, remains present precisely by bringing the subsequent ritual act to mind.
Therefore, because there is no requirement for [further] reflection (*ālocanā*) in that case, there is no remoteness (*viprakarṣa*).

The meaning of the portion of the Sūtra, "That [is] the place of origin," is as follows: the sequence of existing items—namely, that "the first item has been enjoined" and "the subsequent item has been enjoined"—is what makes the order of the Brāhmaṇa recitation meaningful, not the order of performance.
(Therefore, the order of the Mantras is stronger. Śābarabhāṣya: "The order of injunction is stronger because it is determined at the time of origination."
When the [mantras] have arisen and been assigned [to their respective functions], there would be a sequence of mantras;
it is not thus that a sequence of performance arises merely from memory here.
Even for memories, a sequence is desired on account of the sequence of the reminders.
Since the mantras do not have the function of an injunction (*nāmnāya-kāryatva*), their purpose lies in recollection (*smṛti*).
Furthermore, because they fulfill their role through the injunction alone, they are necessarily considered to be reminders (*smāraka*).

Therefore, the performance must follow the sequence of the mantras; however, in their absence, the injunction itself serves as the reminder. Thus, it is precisely there that the authority for that sequence resides.

Soma [says]: Because it is first understood, just as the priority of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) was established in the previous case, so too should it be here; thus there is a connection [to the previous discussion]. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: when there is a conflict between the order of the Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa, the order of the Mantra’s recitation should be the order of the ritual acts (*padārthakrama*), because of the efficacy of the Mantra—namely, its capacity to remind one of the act to be performed at the time of performance. The Brāhmaṇa’s order, however, is merely the locus of origin (*utpattideśa*) and is not useful for recollection at the time of performance. Vi [tithi] says: "Is the *Amīṣomīya* sacrifice before or after the *Āgneya*? Let it be before."

"It is not so, because of the strength of the order of the mantras; the performance follows the order of the *brāhmaṇa* because the mantras serve as reminders. The *brāhmaṇa* possesses authority even by means of its injunction (*vidhi*), for it accomplishes its purpose through that."

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the two orders—the order of the Mantra-text and the order of the Brāhmaṇa-text—the order of the Mantra-text is stronger, not the order of the Brāhmaṇa-text. This is because the Brāhmaṇa-text, being associated with the originative and applicatory injunctions (*utpatti-viniyoga-vidhi*), is already present [in the mind] through its own power; yet it is stated that the order of its textual recitation determines sequence only as a rule of memory (*smāraka-krama-vidhi*). Furthermore, when a Mantra exists, it is that very Mantra which serves as the reminder; and since an injunction that is either employed for the purpose of enjoining or is incapable [of reminding] lacks the capacity to remind, the order of the Mantra-text alone is stronger.

Therefore, according to the order of recitation of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras and so forth, the performance of the offering to Agni (*āgneya*) comes first, and subsequently, after the *upāṃśuyāja*, that of the offering to Agni and Soma (*āgnīṣomīya*). It is not the case, however, that the offering to Agni and Soma comes first according to the order of the Brāhmaṇa text, followed by the offering to Agni after the *upāṃśuyāja*. For this very reason, the order of recitation there is also utilized for the purpose of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*).

Maṇḍana: "In that case, the sequence of the mantra is more powerful," [meaning] when there is a conflict between the recitation of the Brāhmaṇa and the recitation of the mantra. Śaṅkara: "The recitation of the mantra [takes precedence] over the recitation of the injunction."
Balī:
11. In this recitation, an inferred injunction is set aside by a directly perceived injunction.
Bhāṣya 8.4.5–6. In the section on recitation (pāṭhādhikaraṇa), it will be stated that the Brāhmaṇa serves both purposes: being a reminder and being an injunction.
Su. Pṛ. 666: The ordering function of the sequence of recitation and so forth exists only in cases where multiple [elements] are encompassed by a single performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*).

Bhaṭṭa 5.3.22: When a sequence is presented by the order of recitation, there is no need to postulate a further applicatory statement (*viniyojakavākya*); rather, its application is enjoined directly by the performance injunction once it has been understood.
Bhaṭṭa 5.1.4.

The order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) also determines the sequence of the ritual items (*padārtha*) conveyed by the sentences. And the capacity to convey ritual items is, in some cases, the capacity to convey the items to be performed, and in other cases, the capacity to convey the substances, deities, and so forth associated with them.
By both of these types [of sentences], the sequence of the items to be performed is determined.

Bhāṭṭa 5.1.4: The order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is set aside by the order of meaning (*arthakrama*), as in "He offers the Agnihotra oblation; he cooks the gruel," and so forth. The order of recitation is derivative (*ātideśika*) and is weaker than the primary order of instruction (*aupadeśikamukhyakrama*). The order of recitation pertains exclusively to matters of direct instruction (*upadeśaviṣaya*).

*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 5.1.21, p. 1287: The order of recitation is not a restrictive rule for the performance of optional rites (*kāmya`nuṣṭhāna`); rather, the performance may be carried out according to one's desire.

The order of recitation (pāṭhakrama) is stronger because it does not depend on an injunction, whereas the order of principal action (mukhyapravṛttikrama) is weaker because it depends on the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*).

(Ṭupṭīkā 5.1.20.18). The order of recitation is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), while the order of principal action is inferential (*ānumānika*); therefore, the order of recitation is more powerful than the order of principal action.

Consequently, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the pouring out of the clarified butter (*ājyanirvāpa*) should not be performed first; rather, the pouring out of the *agnīṣomīya* offering must be performed before the clarified butter.

The order of recitation (pāṭhakrama) is stronger than the order of principal elements (mukhyakrama). However, in the archetypal rite (prakṛti), [the order] is understood according to the sequence because it is based on its own words. The Commentary states: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, first the properties of the vegetable offerings (auṣadha) are prescribed, and then those of the clarified butter (ājya).

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the ritual details (dharmas) of the clarified butter (*ājya*) be performed first according to the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), or according to the order of the textual recitation (*yathāpāṭha*)?
When it is argued that the performance should follow the order of the principal acts and thus the details of the *ājya* come first, we reply:
In the archetype (prakṛti), the order is understood according to the recitation;
for their own verbal expression is the sequence of recitation.
If that were performed otherwise, it would be sublated.

Furthermore, the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*) which summarizes the simultaneous performance will not be contradicted when the constituent elements (*padārtha*) are brought into proximity according to their own sequence.
Moreover, in the case of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), there is the word "one's own" (*sva*) in the injunction "One's own Veda is to be studied.
In the case of the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), however, the syntactic unity with the injunctive statement is subtle.
Ṭup— (In this section, first, in order to state the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by way of a preliminary inquiry, the relative strength of the primary and the textual order is considered.
The offering of clarified butter (*ājya-nirvāpa*) is the example here.
Since it would follow from the previous principle that the performance should be according to the primary order (*mukhya-krama*), an exception (*apavāda*) is now commenced.

Performance according to the order of recitation is direct (*pratyakṣa*), because it is understood through the study of the text (*svādhyāya*) without depending on anything else. (Mīmāṃsākośa 318: "The primary [order] is inferential;

and conceptualization is delayed," thus he says—) among the ritual elements (*padārtha*), this property called "simultaneity" (*sahatva*) is required, in the sense that "the ritual elements must be performed together."

In that context, simultaneity is understood through the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*). And while making this simultaneity known, it—on the grounds of its otherwise being inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*)—infers a sequence for the sake of establishing the existence of the primary acts (*pradhāna*).
In that regard, whatever inference of an unexpressed sequence occurs among the fires is sublated by the directly perceived sequence of the recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).
Then follows the arrangement according to the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*).

(He explains the *bhāṣya*:—) In the case of the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), there is a subtle syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunction of performance; the meaning is that an unexpressed order is inferred.
The *Śāstra* says: "In that case, by virtue of the order of the principal acts, the offering of the clarified butter (*ājyanirvāpa*) is performed first."
In terms of the recitation of the medicine, the primary mantra is therefore used.
Due to the grace of the principal *sattva* mentioned in the preceding section, the order based on the principal [element] (*mukhyakrama*) is appropriate.
For this very reason, there is a logical connection (*saṃgati*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: In the *prakṛti* (archetype), the order of performance is understood according to the order of the recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), because the order of recitation is established by its own words; since it is a property of the verbal expression that conveys the subsidiaries, it is perceived directly and immediately. As Viśvarūpa states: "Regarding the *upāṃśuyāja*, should the priority belong to the *āgneya* or the *agnīṣomīya*? Let it be the former, because of the sequence of the principal [offerings]."
It is logical that the properties of the medicinal substances (*auṣadha*) take precedence due to their prior mention;
because there is no delay in the order of recitation, the properties of the clarified butter (*ājya*), however, come later.
Bhaṭṭa: Thus, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been defined according to the Bhaṭṭa school.
Furthermore, their relative weakness should be understood according to the sequence stated in the section on conflict (adhikaraṇa), and not according to the sequence of the Sūtras.
In that regard, when there is a contradiction with Śruti, weakness arises because the meaning itself must be interpreted otherwise.
When there is a contradiction with the meaning, the weakness of the textual recitation (pāṭha) will be explained.

Thus, when there is a conflict with the modified (vaikṛta) recitation, the meaning of the position in the original (prākṛta) rite also [prevails]. Even in this case of non-conflict regarding the original nature, it will be stated that the primary order (mukhyakrama), which depends on the injunction for the performance of the principal act, is weaker.
Similarly, when there is a conflict with the primary order, the order of procedure (pravṛttikrama) is likewise weaker.
Thus, here the relative strength of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) and the order of principal acts (*mukhyakrama*) is considered.

In the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, according to the order of the principal acts—namely, the sequence of the *Āgneya*, *Upāṃśuyāja*, and *Āgnīṣomīya* offerings—the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) of the clarified butter for the *Upāṃśuyāja* occurs first, followed by that of the substance for the *Āgnīṣomīya*.
However, according to the order of recitation, the sequence is the reverse.

In this regard, the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) possesses greater strength because it is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), existing as a statement that causes the sequence to be remembered, and because it is more swiftly established.

On the other hand, the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*) is weaker because it is delayed; for the order of the principals is first understood through some means of knowledge, and only thereafter is the order of their accompaniment inferred in relation to that.
Maṇḍana states: "The order of recitation is stronger than the order of the principal acts."
10. Śaṃkara: "The order of recitation (pāṭha) is stronger than the primary [order]. 11. For the order of recitation is occasional (naimittika); it enters by setting aside this order of recitation.
[Duhkha 4.3.16.139] Since a preceding ritual act, upon being completed, imposes itself upon the intellect as the subsequent one, thus the order of recitation is set aside.

5|1|6|13: Where the constituent parts of a ritual act are enjoined in a sequential order, that is the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). For example: "Having first cut out the heart, then the tongue, then the chest."

5|1|129, p. 1289: The *ṛc* verses must be brought in according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) to complete the required number through addition—in the twenty-one-fold, the twenty-seven-fold, and the twenty-three-fold *atirātra* sacrifices.
Bhāṣya 5|1|6|13: The order of position (*sthānakrama*) is set aside by the order of recitation.

For example, after prescribing the preceding ritual acts such as the *sāvitra-homa* and the *ukhā-sambharaṇa*, the archetypal (*prākṛta*) rites beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* are heard of as being accompanied by their specific qualities.

In that regard, since the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are already present through the word "prācīna" in the archetypal (*prakṛta*) injunction, they would be performed first by virtue of their position; thus, the section concerning the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) applies to what precedes that.

However, in the case of the *pātnīvata*, there is an inclusion by the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*), as is the case with those optional (*kāmya*) rites; therefore, the order of recitation is not the restrictive factor there.
In this context, however, it should be understood that [the order] is employed specifically for the purpose of establishing the status of the *svādhyāya* (recitation).
Maṇḍana states: "The sequence in the case of the *samidh* and other [oblations] is due to the order of recitation.
Śaṅkara states: "And the sequence shall be according to the order of recitation."
6. The Principle of the Order of Textual Recitation (Pāṭhakramanyāya).

According to the principle of the order of textual recitation, due to the sequence of the motivating factors, the principal elements, and the original forms, the first remnant of the oblation is remembered first.
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1542). Similarity of textual recitation is of two kinds: recitation according to numerical correspondence (yathāsaṃkhyapāṭha) and recitation by proximity (saṃnidhipāṭha).
The *aindrāgnī* and other such optional *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses possess the nature of being addressed to Agni (*āgneyatva*), due to their recitation in sequential order (*yathāsaṃkhyapāṭha*).
The status of modified (*vaikṛta*) auxiliary elements as belonging to the modification (*vikṛti*) arises from their recitation in proximity (*saṃnidhipāṭha*).

Pāṇini did not compose an instruction on the seers (*ārṣa-anuśāsana*); rather, he composed a grammatical instruction (*śabda-śāsana*) regarding the existence of words exactly as they are established in writing.
Vārttika 6.1.6.22, page 1374: Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali are expounders [of grammar] equal to Manu and others.
Vi. 1319: The followers of Patañjali (Pātañjalas) consider Īśvara to be the cause of the world.
(This is to be considered.)

The statement "they release the Pālīvata" does not constitute a separate ritual act; rather, by means of the verb *utsṛjati* ("releases"), a specific portion of the preceding [rite] is enjoined. This is simply the sequential order of the animal sacrifice (*paśukrama*).

2|3|8|19. One takes the *pālīvata* cup with the *upāṃśu* vessel from the *āgrayaṇa*. Bhāṣya 3|2|1|33. For the *pālīvata* animal sacrifice, the ritual procedure extends up to the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire), as indicated by the text: "They release the *pālīvata* after it has been circumambulated with fire. Vi. 2|3|8. But in the case of the *pālīvata*, there is a restriction due to its prior occurrence.

Having performed the *pālīvata* sacrifice by means of abandonment—according to the injunction, "He releases the *pālīvata* after it has been encircled by fire"—there arises a doubt: is the release of the *tvāṣṭra* animal, which has already been encircled by fire, what is being enjoined here, or is this a separate sacrifice for that [animal]?
This statement is refuted as a counter-example to the immolation of the self (*ātma-lambhana*) and other such cases; likewise, in the present example under discussion, this statement is also refuted.

In this regard, the intention of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) is as follows: although, after enjoining a sacrifice with the words "One should offer the *pālīvata* animal," it is heard in reference to that very sacrifice that "one releases the *pālīvata* after it has been encircled by fire" (*paryagnikṛta*), nevertheless, because a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is enjoined previously, this must be an injunction for a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

To explain: first of all, the word *pālīvata* cannot be enjoined as an alternative to the deity of the previous sacrifice, because the deity prescribed at the time of the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) already occupies that place.
Nor is there the act of carrying fire around [the animal] (*paryagnikaraṇa*), because that is already obtained through extension (*atideśa*).
Nor is there the act of release (*utsarga*), because it is perceived by the original injunctive statement (*utpattivākya*).

Therefore, this injunction—having transferred its purpose to the connection between the substance and the deity denoted by the word *patnīvata* (like the *dhavākyavat* case)—prescribes a distinct sacrifice characterized by a specific substance and deity. This sacrifice has the *paryagni* sacrifice as its archetype (*prakṛti*) due to the commonality of the deity's attribute, or rather, it has the *āmīṣomīya* sacrifice as its archetype, for the sake of fulfilling the intended purpose of the imagined *yajñaiṣṭha*.
This being the case, it is replied:
this would indeed be so if the injunction of the qualities related to the archetype were not possible.

In that regard, even though other qualities are not enjoined here, nevertheless, only those subsidiary elements ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa* (the act of carrying fire around the victim) will be enjoined here.

For instance, one who desires the optional result (*kāmya*) and is enjoined to abandon the performance (*tyājya-yoga*), while requiring the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) whose assistance is established in the archetype (*prakṛti*), takes up only those instructional (*aupadeśika*) auxiliaries ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa*—as brought forward by the word *paryagnikṛta*—and having thus fulfilled its purpose, does not require other auxiliaries obtainable through extension (*atideśa*).
Now, an objection may be raised: "In such cases as 'The *ātithyā* sacrifice concludes with the *idā*,' there is no word here that indicates an end at the *paryagnikaraṇa*;
therefore, how can there be an injunction to conclude with that? It is replied: [This is so].

For the word *paryagnikṛta* (having had the fire carried around) denotes a substance qualified by a *paryagnikaraṇa* (the rite of carrying fire around) that has been performed in its established manner.

And that *paryagnikaraṇa* was already accomplished in the archetype (*prakṛti*) with respect to the previously mentioned Viṣṇu-sacrifices; therefore, the word *paryagni* here brings forward precisely the entire set of subsidiary elements (*aṅgakalāpa*) established by the injunction of the archetype.
That very [set] is here enjoined by the verbal root *utsṛj* (to release/abandon), which functions as a rule for the performance of the abandonment (*utsarga*), and not as the abandonment itself.
The author of the Bhāṣya has stated, "An original injunction (utsarga) is prescribed," due to the specific proximity of the injunctive suffix (vidhi-pratyaya).
Nor should it be argued that "since [the rite] is already obtained through extension (atideśa), what is the use of an injunction?
For the answer is that the injunction is purposeful because its result is delimitation (avaccheda).
This being the case, it is not a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*), because the injunction is already established prior to the extension of the rule (*atideśa*).

Nor should it be argued that "since the sentence would be complete with merely the words 'that which he abandons is the one for which the fire-circumambulation has been performed,' the addition of the qualifier 'pātnīvata' would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the restatement of a qualified object";

for the qualifiers such as the word 'pātnīvata' do not qualify the subject (*uddeśya*), since even without such a qualifier, the injunction for the fire-circumambulation can apply to the sacrifice for Tvaṣṭṛ by virtue of the context itself.
Furthermore, this is a reiterative statement (*nityānuvāda*).

Although there may be no other purpose for that which is reiterated, nevertheless, when two deities denoted by dual-ended words are combined (*samuccaya*), it is possible to denote them even with a single word ending in that [dual] suffix; however, it is not possible to denote the two deities Agni and Soma—who are combined and denoted by words ending in the singular and dual suffixes respectively—with either one of those words. This is as in the case of the Pātnīvata sacrifice: "To Pātnīvata, the animal... (Pālīvate tu paśau).
The purpose is solely for the sake of making known the present context and for the recognition of the ritual procedure (*pratyaya*).

Therefore, it is established that in this very sacrifice recognized through the context, there is an injunction of the form [of the rite] ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa* (the act of carrying fire around).
As it has been said: "Because of the recognition of the present context, another performance is understood."
After the rite of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), the rule for the movement [of the animal] is prescribed therein.

Thus (Vākyapadīya 607). Now, if this is the case, what is the distinction between this [view] and that of the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice? It is said in reply: by refuting the designation of a deity here and establishing it as an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi), that very same principle is being firmly established; therefore, nothing is inconsistent. The practical application (prayojana): according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there would be the performance of a separate sacrifice having only the wives as its deities.
In the Siddhānta, it is not so.

As for the Sūtra: in the case of the *pātnīvata* [offering], because the status of possessing archetypal (*prākṛta*) characteristics is possible through direct instruction (*upadeśa*) as in the previous case, the meaning is that the result of the injunction is the exclusion of the *paryagnikaraṇa*, the *jñāptikārī*, and the *jñāna*.
(Tautā.)

In the case of the *pālīvata*, however, there is a delimitation by priority (*pūrvatva*). Having prescribed the offering to Tvaṣṭṛ as the *pālīvata*, it is stated: "They release the *pālīvata* after it has been carried around with fire. Here, in the deliberation as to whether this release (*utsarga*) of the Tvaṣṭṛ-offering that has been carried around with fire is being enjoined, or whether this is a different sacrifice from that [original one], and whether the term *utsṛti* (release) is a synonym for *yajati* (sacrifices), or whether the verb *utsṛjati* (releases) is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), or whether it is a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*)—the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) against the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it is a different sacrifice.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In the sentence "the *pālīvata* [is] the *pālīvata* for which the fire-circumambulation has been performed," there is no injunction of a separate ritual action (*karmāntaravidhi*).

Rather, because it refers back to what precedes it—due to the recognition of the same context—it constitutes an injunction of the entire set of auxiliary elements ending with the fire-circumambulation (*paryagnikaraṇa*), thereby excluding the subsequent auxiliaries.
Cessation has been stated.
Therefore, the conclusion is that the delimitation of the preceding rite—the completion of its constituent complex ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa*—is expressed by the sentence "utsṛja" (release).
Who [says this]? Ke. (Kevalānanda Sarasvatī).
Regarding the *pālīvata* cup, it is as before.
In the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) of the Agniṣṭoma, there are two double-portioned cups (*dvivedayā grahāḥ*), namely the Aindravāyava and the Maitrāvaruṇa.
When these have been offered, their remnants (*śeṣāḥ*) are poured into the Āditya vessel.
Furthermore, there is the Āditya-graha at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*),
and it is offered with its residue remaining.
Moreover, there is the rule for the drawing of the Āgrayaṇa-graha at the third pressing.
"One draws the Āgrayaṇa from four streams; one makes the second stream for the Āgrayaṇa, the third for the Āditya, and the fourth after the drawing of the Āditya.
This refers to the drawing of the Pālīvata cup from the Āgrayaṇa, based solely on the statement: "One draws the Pālīvata from the Āgrayaṇa."

Now, regarding the discussion as to how the mention of the deities should be made in the *bhakṣa-mantra* while consuming the remnant of that *pālīvata* offering which has been sacrificed: the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated.

According to the conclusion established in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), in the case of the Soma-consumption for the *pālīvata*, a reference to all the deities must be made; thus one should recite: "O you who belong to Indra, Vāyu, Mitra, Varuṇa, Āditya, the Patnīs, and Pāvaka. Or rather, [the previous rule] should be set aside because of the specific act of taking [the portion].
The word "vā" (or) indicates a difference from the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the preceding section.

Furthermore, because of the re-consecration (*punarabhyujjītanā*) of this very [offering] through the act of pouring out (*unnayana*), and because the remnants of the offering to Indra are not connected with another deity such as Mitra-Varuṇa, it is logical that the previous deity is not to be removed.
Thus it is proper.

Regarding the injunction, "One takes the *pālīvata* from the *āgrayaṇa*," since the *pālīvata* consists of the remnants of the two-deity offerings and others, that which is taken from the *āgrayaṇa* is grasped in a mixed form; because the deity *Pālīvat* intervenes, the previous remnant would be removed from its connection with the previous deity.
Therefore, in the mantra for consuming the *pālīvata* remnant, the modification (*ūha*) should be simply "O husband of the wives.
(Ke.)
Regarding *pālīvata*, [the suffix] *taddhita* is elided by Vārttika 3.1.5.26.

In the passage, "They release the *pālīvata* which has been circumambulated with fire" (*paryagnikṛtaṃ pālīvatam utsṛjanti*), because the word *patnīvat* serves as a secondary indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) for the animal (*paśu*), there is disregard for its etymological meaning. This was stated in the sūtra: "In the case of *pālīvata*, there is no restriction because of the sequence [of the ritual]" (2.3.8.19).
In the case of the animal sacrifice to Pāvīraka, the injunction "he completes the remainder with clarified butter" constitutes the prescription of a separate ritual act.

There should be a substitute for the clarified butter (*ājya*) because of the relinquishment of the substance. The Commentary states: With reference to the rule, "He relinquishes the *pālīvata* [victim] after it has been circumambulated by fire," it is heard [in scripture]: "He completes the remainder with clarified butter.

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the clarified butter a substitute for the previous [substance], or is a different ritual action (*karmāntara*) consisting of clarified butter as its material enjoined in place of the previous one?
What is established? That there is a substitute.
Why? Because the substance "pālīvata" is mentioned, and in that very context, the act of relinquishing (*utsarga*) is heard [in the text].
The word "remainder" (śeṣa) here implies that which exists and is understood [to remain].
Thus, by the statement "he completes it with clarified butter," clarified butter is prescribed as the substitute for the animal sacrifice.
But was it not already stated that the preceding ritual action has been completed?
To this it is replied:

since the statement regarding the relinquishment of the substance (*dravyotsarga*) is directly perceived, and since the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) would otherwise be indeterminate, the preceding rite must be completed again up to its conclusion.
Therefore, we maintain that clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth are substituted.
Furthermore, the statement "he establishes" is not applicable to something previously non-existent, because it refers to completion.
The Commentary says: "In this regard, we raise an objection."

This statement regarding completion is "he brings it to a conclusion" (*saṃsthāpayati*). By this we understand that what was previously commenced with an animal sacrifice is concluded with clarified butter (*ājya*) when the animal is released.
In this case, the very commencement of the undertaking of this new ritual action must be stated.

Since, however, the completion is mentioned without first stating the commencement, we conclude that it is the completion of the very same previous rite, and that no new action is being enjoined. Or rather, there is an injunction [of a new act], because it would be indistinguishable from the end of the abandonment of the ritual action. The Commentary states: "Or rather, it is an injunction of a different ritual action."
Why? Because the preceding rite has reached its completion.

Now, it might be argued that if the disposal of the substance (*dravyotsarga*) or the mention of the remnant (*śeṣavacana*) is not performed, the non-completion of the preceding rite would be suspected. To this it is replied:
This substance is also set aside;
it is connected with the word *pālīvata* from the context, which means "he sets aside the *pālīvata*.
Thus, the meaning there is: "He sets aside the *pālīvata*."
This very sacrifice is enjoined;
and the verb *saṃsthāpayati* (he completes) is employed in its full form. Indeed, some verbal root preceded by the prefix *sam-* must necessarily be used to express the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).
