In that case, when the non-contradictory meditation (*bhāvanā*) is being inferred, the verb *saṃsthāpayati* (to conclude) is employed as it is implied by the sense, and the verb *ālambhati* (to seize) is employed because of its similarity to the remaining words.
Furthermore, the relinquishment of the substance (*dravyotsarga*) is indeed not contradictory when the sacrifice is being described.

Therefore, just as other verbs such as *nirvapati* (to offer) occur in the injunction of a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*), so too the verb *saṃsthāpayati* ought to be understood as such, since it is not distinguished from them.
And he shows that the sacrifice to Vanaspati is well-known.
The Commentary states: He shows that the sacrifice to Vanaspati is indeed well-known for this very reason.
How so? "When you cause Tvaṣṭṛ and Vanaspati to be invoked, then you shall sacrifice to these two; the ninth fore-offering is dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ, and the tenth is dedicated to Vanaspati."
By stating, "One should know these two right here," he expresses a favor through the word *addhā* (certainly), thereby demonstrating the absence of the *vanaspati* sacrifice.

When the remaining portion [of the rite] is completed, the *vanaspati* sacrifice is performed according to the injunction, "He offers the *vanaspati*. Now, if the preceding ritual action were already finished, then [the *vanaspati* sacrifice] would indeed be absent; in that case, the observation of its absence would be logical.
Therefore, the previous rite is completed;
this too is another rite.
It would constitute a formal conclusion because it possesses the same deity.
Commentary: Now, as for what was stated—that "the expression 'he establishes' is not applicable to an apūrva"—that must be refuted. To this it is replied:
this statement regarding "establishment" refers to establishment in the sense of non-establishment [i.e., completion].
That [rite] is also called "Pālīvata" because it shares the same deity; thus, its association with completion is known.
There, that Pālīvata rite was commenced, and here it reaches completion. Therefore, on account of this association, the expression "he completes it" is appropriate.
Regarding Soma: in the preceding section, the statement "He completes the remainder with clarified butter (*ājya*)" was raised by way of observing an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

In that context, its status as an indicative mark is only tenable if it prescribes a different sacrifice; thus, there is a connection because the purpose is to establish that this [statement] prescribes a different sacrifice.

As for the meaning of the sūtra: in the passage "He completes the remainder with clarified butter," clarified butter should serve as a substitute (*pratinidhi*) for the animal substance, because the substance is prescribed for the rite that has been abandoned.
If it is stated, "The remainder [is offered] with clarified butter," there would be a substitute material (dravya-pratinidhi) for the rite;
this is because of the expressions regarding the completion of the ritual, the relinquishment of the remainder, and the formal conclusion (saṃsthāpana).
Because it is similar according to the ritual procedure (*aṅgarīti*), because it follows from the mention of the deity,
and because of its similarity [to other sacrifices], the remaining [act] is established as a sacrifice (*yāga*), just like the touching (*ālambhana*) and so forth.
Bhaṭṭa: There is a further objection regarding the Pālīvata passage.
For there, after stating, "He offers the Pālīvata [oblation] when it has been sprinkled with ghee," it is heard: "He completes the remainder with clarified butter.
Indeed, if this were a new (apūrva) rite, the completion of the remainder would be untenable.

In the sentence concerning the *paryagnikaraṇa* (the act of carrying fire around the victim), the performance of the primary sacrifice (*pradhānayāga*) is enjoined as being deferred immediately after the *paryagnikaraṇa*. And since there is no authority for the non-omission of other constituent parts when that [primary sacrifice] is performed—even though elements such as the slaughter (*viśasana*) are omitted—it is enjoined that "whatever remains, such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *pra-sthāpita*, one should complete with clarified butter (*ājya*).

Although clarified butter is already established for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, nevertheless, the injunction regarding clarified butter for the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *pra-sthāpita* offerings is not contradicted.

Nor can it be argued that the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of clarified butter (*ājya*) is obtained by the rule "for whom all the oblations... precisely because of the possibility of its manifestation even in the absence of the slaughter (*visasana*), since it would not be obtained due to the absence of the specific occasion such as destruction;

furthermore, because the slaughter applies equally to both the subsidiary and the primary rites, its manifestation is logically possible even there, and thus the injunction for clarified butter is also applicable in cases such as the *vanaspati* sacrifice.

For there is no evidence whatsoever for any other action here; on the contrary, the remaining ritual procedures (*śeṣasaṃsthā*) would become untenable. When it is established that the vessels are for the Pārṇīvata animal sacrifice, [the text] asks: "When you invoke Tvaṣṭṛ and Vanaspati, will you then sacrifice to these two? In response, it is said: "The ninth fore-offering (*prayāja*) is dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ, the tenth is dedicated to Vanaspati; one should know that these two are indeed present right here."

Thus, since it is understood from another scriptural injunction (*ajñāntara*) that there is no mention of the Vanaspati sacrifice being included [in the *anuyāja*s], and since that [mention] would be inexplicable without its being a novel injunction (*apūrva*), the injunction here does not merely prescribe the primary agent as in the preceding sentence;
rather, like the injunction for the *iṣṭi* ending with that [Vanaspati sacrifice], it results in a novel injunction (*apūrvatva*).

And although the invocation of the deity (*devatā-āvāhana*) is not even obtained for the Vanaspati sacrifice when it is not being performed, nevertheless, because of the mention as if it were already established, the assumption of an injunction for the invocation follows precisely from the fact that otherwise it would be inexplicable.

Since Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the principal deity, there is no contradiction regarding his invocation; furthermore, the mention of "favor" for the ninth [offering] is intended with reference to the absence of an oblation-material (prakṣepa).

Consequently, because there is no remnant (śeṣa) from the preceding rite, the prescription of clarified butter (ājya) as the material would otherwise be untenable; therefore, this is a distinct ritual act characterized by the material of clarified butter, having the Anuṣaktṛ as its deity, and modeled after the Upāṃśuyāja.

However, in the case of the conclusion of the remnant (śeṣasaṃsthā) and so forth, since the preceding rite is not yet essentially completed, it may somehow be considered a supplementary statement (anuvāka).

Siddhiviniścaya: "In this case, one sacrifices separately with the clarified butter for the *saṃsthā*. Maṇḍana: "Even in the statement regarding the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājyaśeṣa*). Śaṅkara: "Even in the statement regarding the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājyaśeṣa*)."

The principle of the vessel (*pātranyāya*): At the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, the vessel for holding the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) intended for the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) was broken.
In the modified sacrifice (*vikāra*), there should be a separate vessel for the after-offerings because of the difference in purpose.
Commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.
Regarding that, it is heard in the scripture: "He performs the after-offerings (anuyājas) with speckled butter (pṛṣadājya).

In this regard, there is a doubt: is there a single vessel for holding both the clarified butter (ājya) and the speckled butter for the fore-offerings (prayājas) and after-offerings, or are they distinct?
What is obtained? That there is one.
Why? Because in the archetype there is one;
here too, in accordance with the archetype, there must be one.
This being the case, we reply:
there should be a distinction of vessels. Why? Because of the difference in purpose.
The *prayāja* offerings are for the sake of the pure [milk], and the *anuyāja* offerings are for the speckled [milk].

If the speckled milk is taken, there is a deficiency in the *prayājas*; if the pure milk is taken, there is a deficiency in the *anuyājas*. Furthermore, it is not possible to separate these two within a single vessel.
Even if a boundary were established, what is being offered would become mixed;
moreover, due to the difference in shape, the *upabhṛt* ladle would be impaired,
for it has a handle the size of a hand and possesses only a single bowl.
Now, it might be argued that even *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter) is indeed just *ājya*, and thus its being mixed is not a defect.
This is not so;
for in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the purpose of the stirring and inspection is precisely this: that the *ājya* is not in contact with any other substance.
If this were so, it would be untenable that the *prayāja* offerings should be performed with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).
Moreover, such being the case, a certain portion of the oblation (*havis*) would necessarily be set aside;
and once the purpose of the *prayāja* has been completed, it is not possible to take [that same portion] for the purpose of the *anuyāja*.
In the archetype, the taking up occurs at one time;
here too, it must be performed at one time alone.
Therefore, there is a distinction of vessels.

Ṭup—(He states the prima facie view: Since the singularity of the *upabhṛt* vessel in the archetype is intended (on account of its occurrence in such passages as "he takes eight [spoonfuls] in the *upabhṛt*"), the taking of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) would logically take place at that very same time. Just as, even though the subsidiaries share the same time as the primary rite, no separate agent is appointed due to the excellence of the performer's role and not because of the fault of temporal separation, so too, despite the difference between the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the speckled butter, no other vessel need be employed.
(But for the sake of favoring their unity, one must indeed accept the separation. This being the position reached, we reply:
Just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), a single vessel is intended, so too is a single time;
however, here—where, due to the difference in substances, it is possible to favor both—a single time is intended (not a single vessel).

What is the reason? Because the *ājya* being taken for the *prayāja* offerings, by virtue of the sequence of the recitation of the mantras and the *brāhmaṇa*, brings to mind the taking of the *ājya* for the *anuyāja* offerings.
(Thus, it has been established as the final conclusion that even the intended singleness of the vessel is here set aside.)

He states another view: Or rather, by the sentence "He takes eight [spoonfuls] in the *upabhṛt*," the purpose of the substance taken in four spoonfuls—which was produced without a specific number being mentioned—is established as being for the sake of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings through another sentence ("That which is in the *upabhṛt*, from that [he offers] to the *prayājas* and *anuyājas*"). However, the *upabhṛt* itself is not enjoined as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings (much less its singularity). It is obtained through the force of the context (since when a vessel must be used for taking [the offering], the *juhū* and *dhruvā* are already occupied with holding other clarified butter, the *upabhṛt* is mentioned because it is otherwise unoccupied).
Nor is it said that what is obtained through implication is intended [to be expressed].
Therefore, because the two substances are distinct, there is a distinction of vessels by implication. (How has this inquiry come to be included in the section on the definition of sequence?)
Therefore, he says: there is an occurrence [of the action] due to a difference in the sequence of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final (*siddhānta*) positions.
(In the *pūrvapakṣa*, the taking of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) occurs after the *prayāja* oblations; in the *siddhānta*, however, it occurs in its original place.

Śā—It is considered whether both—the *prayāja* clarified butter and the *anuyāja* speckled butter—should be taken in that same *upabhṛt* ladle at different times, or at the same time using different vessels.
In this regard, "Because it is a substance and because it is explicitly stated, the singleness of the vessel is included;
however, because it is a subordinate quality and because its recitation is [already] established, only the sequence is set aside.
Therefore, having first taken the *prayāja* clarified butter in a single vessel, one should subsequently take the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) after the *prayāja* offerings have been made.
This being the case, it is replied:
"Because both the taking [of the portions] and the single vessel are subsidiary elements,
and because the sequence is established in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) through inference, the support of the fourfold [set] is equal."
And thus, at the very time of taking the clarified butter (ājya), another vessel should be taken and the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) should be taken.

7. Mīmāṃsākośa 319: The connection [of this case] as a counter-argument is that whereas in the previous instance there was a unity of the *ulūkhala* (mortar), here there is a unity of the *upabhṛt* (offering-ladle).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: In the case of a modified animal sacrifice (*vikāra-paśu*), there should be a distinction of vessels due to the distinction of purposes and the distinction of substances for the after-offerings (*anuyāja*). [Objection]: "Is there unity of the vessel for the sake of accomplishing the fore-offerings (*prayāja*) and after-offerings (*anuyāja*), or is there distinctness? Just as there is one *upabhṛt* vessel for both here, so it should be [here] as well."
In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), let there be a separation of vessels for the pure clarified butter (*śuddhājya*) and the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).
In the case of the cups and so forth, where the substance is one, there is unity of vessel in the archetype (*prakṛti*) for both;
therefore, [in this instance] there must be separate vessels.

In the land of the Bhaṭṭas, regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter) is prescribed for the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) by the text: "He performs the after-offerings with *pṛṣadājya*.
For the fore-offerings (*prayāja*), however, pure clarified butter (*ājya*) alone is obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*).
And in the archetype, the clarified butter for the fore-offerings was taken four times in a single vessel, namely the *upabhṛt*.

In this case as well, if it were taken in that same manner, there would be the undesirable consequence of the *prayāja* butter being divided into eight parts due to its contact with the curd and honey; furthermore, this would result in it performing a function not prescribed in the archetype (*aprākṛta-kārya*), and it would lead to a deficiency in the *prayāja* butter at the time of the *samānayana* (the pouring back).

Therefore, when considering whether the sequence should be set aside in favor of the unity of the vessel, or whether the sequence itself should be reversed, the sequence alone must be sublated. This is because the unity of the vessel is directly stated in scripture (*śruta*) and constitutes a constituent element of the ritual act (*padārtha*), making its sublation untenable; whereas the sequence is weaker, being merely inferred from the order of the mantra recitation and being a mere property (*dravya*). Thus, according to the principle of the section on "Non-conflict with the Learned" (*Śiṣṭākopa*, Jaiminisūtra 1.3.15–16), the sequence is sublated. Likewise, there is also a sublation of the simultaneity—which is indicated by the phrase "eight [spoonfuls] in the *upabhṛt*"—which serves as a mark for the coexistence of the insignificant substances understood from that sentence.

Nor can it be argued that because those two [the *nāmadheya* and the *guṇavidhi*] possess the status of being "established" (*klṛpta*) and "assumed" (*kalpya*) respectively in the archetype (*prakṛti*), they lack relative strength even when transferred to the ectype (*vikṛti*) by extension (*atideśa*), since both are equal in that regard.

This is because, although the specific forms of strength such as being "established" or "assumed" may not exist in the ectype, the strength derived from factors such as being a primary substance (*padārtha*) or a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) can still function as a regulator in the ectype.

When another name exists in the ectype, the relative strength of the archetypal elements is indeed applicable through the force of the words; for instance, in the case of the four-fold number, the handfuls, the oblation, and the sacrifice, the latter's predominance serves as the regulator.

Therefore, since it is argued that the *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter) should be taken in that very same vessel at the time of performing the *anuyāja* offerings—this being the prima facie view—it is replied: although the identity of the vessel is a property of the ritual act (*padārtha*), the mere transgression of the sequence of the acts to be performed does not constitute a violation of its specific characteristics (*dharma*). On the contrary, by the principle of "conflict between the primary and the subordinate" (*aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*), the identity of the vessels used for the taking (*grahaṇa*) is weaker than the sequence and other details belonging to the constituent parts of the taking itself. Consequently, one should prepare two separate *upabhṛt* vessels and take two portions of four ladles each—one pure and one prepared with curds.
Maṇḍana: "The vessel for the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) should be distinct [from the other vessels] in the animal sacrifice.
Śaṅkara: "There is a distinction of vessels regarding the speckled butter;
it is a bowl (pātrī)."

If it is argued that [the term] applies even in the absence of that [original substance], the Commentary states: This is not so—that which was said regarding the non-application [of the term] to modified (vaikṛta) rites.

Even in its absence, although this [term] denotes a collection (*samudāya*), and such a collection does not exist in the modified rites either, nevertheless, the two *parvan* oblations (*parvaṇahomau*) must indeed take place.
Why? Because there will be other deities of this kind;
or rather, the aggregate [of deities], even if not present, will be invoked for the sake of assisting the *saurya* sacrifice and others.
Just as in the case of "Bring Agni hither," one invokes either the present or the absent [deity] by means of the name of the oblation (*āhuti*).
"The same applies here as well. [Objection: No, because it pertains to a specific office (adhikāra). The Commentary states: "This is not so."
This statement is indeed *ādhikārika*, meaning it pertains to the qualification (*adhikāra*); it prescribes a quality for that which possesses the qualification.
And the qualification belongs to the [sacrifices] beginning with the Āgneya;
furthermore, these [deities] are the divinities in this context.
The oblation for them is for the sake of the deity.
Thus, where that deity is absent, the oblation intended for her shall not be performed.
Therefore, there is an exclusion of the *parvan-homa* from the modified (*vaikṛta*) rites.

The six sūtras from 50 to 55 have been explained by the author of the Bhāṣya as constituting a single topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), whereas the two subsequent sūtras (56–57) were explained by him as forming a separate section.
However, the author of the Vārttika, having criticized that view, explained those two sūtras as being intended solely to demonstrate the purpose of the topical section under discussion.

Thus, we find ourselves in a dilemma: whether these Vārttika passages should be inserted here into this very section, or whether they should be inserted into the subsequent section belonging to the author of the Bhāṣya.

However, we have already established this in the subsequent section [of the *Tantravārttika*] beginning with "But in the case of the *parvan*-oblations, it belongs to that very [sacrifice]," so it should be consulted there.

Śa: Regarding the statement, "One offers the two *parvan* oblations with the *sruva* ladle," there arises a doubt: are these two oblations, which have the *parvan* as their deity according to the *taddhita* suffix, extended (*atidiśyete*) to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), or not?

For that purpose, one must consider whether these oblations are merely auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) or whether they serve as a preparatory rite (*saṃskārārtha*). And for that purpose, one must reflect on whether the word *parvan* denotes time, or whether it refers to the collection of offerings such as the *Āgneya* and others.

In that context, because the word "time" (*kāla*) is primary, it is understood as referring to the sacrifice performed at the proper time (*kālābhījya*). (He states the established conclusion: Because it is the object of the act of "sacrificing at the proper time," and because the word is primary even with respect to the ritual action, the term "parvan" refers to the ritual action of sacrificing at the proper time.

And that [term] is primary when applied to time through the derivation based on the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), meaning "that in which it is given"; it is also primary when applied to the object (*karman*) through the derivation based on the abstract state (*bhāva*).

The principle of the *parvaṇahoma* (2549): regarding the two *parvaṇahoma* offerings, there is no application in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), because the word *parvan* refers to the entire collection of rites. This is the meaning of the sūtra.
Therefore, it is dedicated to that [deity].

Vi— "In the *saurya* sacrifice and others, do the two *pārvaṇa* oblations exist or not? Because of the time [of the full moon] and the deity [Sūrya], there is a doubt; however, because this [sacrifice] is a modification (*vikṛti*), those two do not exist there."
(“We worship Ṛṣabha, the vigorous, the slayer, the Full Moon”—this and similar passages are the *parva-homa* mantras belonging to the Full Moon sacrifice.
“The New Moon is fortunate and very gracious, swelling again like a cow”—this and similar passages are the *parva-homa* mantras belonging to the New Moon sacrifice.
Bhāṭṭa: Regarding the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is revealed in scripture: "One performs the two *parva-homas* with the *sruva* ladle."
In that context, two offerings accompanied by the *saṃyājyā* verses are enjoined as distinguished by specific deities.

Nor is this [the word *saṃyājyā*] a *taddhita* suffix denoting a deity simply because of its co-occurrence with the oblation (*havis*); rather, it is appropriate for it to refer to the deity precisely because it denotes a general relationship. Thus, when considering whether these two offerings are extended (*atidiśyate*) to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) or not, the possibility of extension exists, just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings.

Nor can there be an extension (*atideśa*) based on the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the collection of rites denoted by the word *parvan* itself—which has become the deity—for that [collection] is absent in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). This is because there is no evidence for accepting the word *parvan* as primarily referring to time and secondarily indicating the rite (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, since time alone is the deity here, and since that [time] cannot be refined, the extension of these two [rites], which provide remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*), is indeed appropriate.

If, however, because time also serves as an auxiliary to the ritual (*karmāṅga*), it is intended that time possesses the character of a preparatory rite (*saṃskāraka*)—so that, by the force of the Smṛti, even though it was previously remembered as being "all-encompassing" (*sarvādī*), one may avoid misplaced confidence based on the possibility of its being non-temporal (*ākālika*) once again, and thus its remembrance is justified as being like that of the deities of the ritual (*karmadeva*) for the sake of attaining the status of being an integral part of the sacrifice (*sāmavāyikatva*)—even so, there is no obstacle to its extension (*atideśa*) when the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) occurs at that same time.

Furthermore, even when it occurs at another time, there is no deficiency whatsoever, since the extension of the object of reference (*uddeśa*) is possible, as in the case of the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and others.

Or, even if the word *parvan*—because it denotes a meritorious time (*puṇyatādin*)—could, like the word for "time," be derived as a locative to signify a period, or like the interpretation in the Bhāṣya, be derived to signify an action (*karman*), and thus, by virtue of the context, refer specifically to the action; nevertheless, since the collection [of offerings] denoted by the word *parvan*, such as the Āgneya and others, possesses the status of a deity even when modified, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the extension (*atideśa*) of these two [subsidiaries], which provide assistance from afar (*ārādupakāraka*).

If, however, the intention is that it serves as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the deity for the sake of attaining the status of being an auxiliary by immediate contact (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), even so, since the state of being a "portion" (*parvatva*)—which is synonymous with being an object of giving (*dānatva*)—resides in each individual [offering] such as the *Āgneya* and does not reside in the aggregate, the deitieship of the *Āgneya* and others is established individually by virtue of their being means to the *apūrva*. Consequently, just like the mantra for the inspection of the oblations (*havir-nirīkṣaṇa-mantra*), the extension (*atideśa*) to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is logically justified. It cannot be argued that in that case, because the deity is understood from the word itself to be the one to whom the oblation is offered, and because the requirement for the simultaneity of the objects of offering (*uddeśya-sāhitya*) is absent, the extension is appropriate. [This is not the case, as the logic remains consistent.]
In the present case, however, because these [deities] are presented as deities by means of a *taddhita* suffix, their conjunction is logically established.

Even though, according to the principle of deficiency (*vaiguṇya*), one might assume other words denoting the objects to be addressed so that each of the *āgneya* and others could be an object of address individually, nevertheless, since their conjunction is intended at the stage when they are presented as materials for the rite, it is understood that the *āgneya* and others themselves—possessing that intended conjunction—are the deities. Consequently, since those [deities] are not applicable in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) and thus cannot be the objects of a purificatory act (*saṃskārya*), it must be stated that there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the two *parvan-homas*, which serve to purify the deity.

Because the deific status (*devatātva*) of the *Āgneya* and other offerings is understood by virtue of their capacity as the intended objects (*uddeśya-sāmarthya*), in the form of being the means to the *apūrva*, their extension (*atideśa*) to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is logically established.

Otherwise, even in cases such as the *svāhākāra* or the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), there would be the undesirable consequence of deific status arising through [the formula] "to Agni-Soma" and so forth, which would result in the non-extension of those [deities] to the *Saurya* or the *Savanīya* offerings.
And all of this has been stated on the assumption that the *taddhita* suffix functions as an injunction of the deity (*devatāvidhāyaka*).

In reality, however, because a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) would entail unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) cannot be determined as a *taddhita* suffix due to the absence of a co-utterance with the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), the formation of the *taddhita* suffix is possible even in the sense that "they exist during the *parvan*" and "they are the purifiers of the *parvan*"; since such a derivation is possible, it is inappropriate to restrict [the meaning] in that way, and thus this is not a *devatā-taddhita*.

Rather, since the attainment of the deity is established through the mantra-text itself—given that its status as an auxiliary is understood from the sequence—the name "this is for the *parvan*" (*parvaṇam*) is indeed appropriate.

For this very reason, among the ritualists (*yājñika*), at the time of the formal dedication (*tyāga*), it is precisely the words *pūrṇamāsa* and *amāvāsyā* found in the mantras—"We worship the full moon as the bull, the vigorous; the new moon, the fortunate and auspicious"—that constitute the designation, and not the word *parvan*. Thus, since those words *pūrṇamāsa* and *amāvāsyā* are not used to denote the [specific] times, an examination of the meaning of the mantras reveals that they refer to the rituals themselves. Consequently, although each [mantra] consecrates a triad of rites beginning with the *āgneya*, there is no obstacle to its extension (*atideśa*) to the *saurya* sacrifice and others by the aforementioned method, just like the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and similar offerings.

Since the intended deity depends upon the intended portion [of the sacrifice], it is possible for the nature of the Āgneya and other offerings to exist in their own form within the act of abandonment (*tyāga*). Therefore, it is logical that the status of being a deity with respect to the portion of abandonment occurs in that very same form by which there is the state of being an object of refinement (*saṃskāryatā*) toward the intended portion as a specific means to the *apūrva* (unseen result). Consequently, just as in the case of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and so forth, the extension (*atideśa*) of the rules applies even to the *parvan-homa*.

Thus, even in the case of a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*), by that very form in which the Full Moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāsa*) is the objective because it is a specific means for the *apūrva*, it possesses the status of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) at the subsequent time, since this serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*). It does not, however, possess the status of being the objective in its entirety as a composite whole (*samuditatva*), because the inclusion of the collective totality within the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the objective is not intended to be expressed. Therefore, the extension (*atideśa*) of even a deficient rite into a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is indeed appropriate.

Or rather, let there be a desire for inclusion [of the conjunction] in the case of the *saura* sacrifice and others, because even if the conjunction is not intended within the scope of the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the objective (*uddeśyatā*), it is nevertheless included as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the subsequent time, just as in the expression "having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Consequently, since there would be the contingency of the *saumya* being subsequent to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), and since there is no state of being subsequent to the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) in the *saura* and other such sacrifices, there is no contingency of its extension (*atideśa*). However, in the case of the *anyārambhaṇīyā*, there is a desire for inclusion of the conjunction, because the status of being a Darśapūrṇamāsa is not included within the scope of the delimiting factor of the objective; thus, such an extension is logical.

In the present case, however, since the *parvan-homas* are dependent rites (*āśrayika-karma*), they subsist upon deities employed by another [the primary sacrifice]. Consequently, it is not possible for the *Āgneya* and other offerings to function as deities in their own essential form; therefore, the extension (*atideśa*) [of the deity] is indeed appropriate. As for the argument that because the *parvan-homas* are prompted by the collective *parvan*, they do not exist in modifications (*vikṛti*) such as the *Saurya* sacrifice—and thus there is no extension due to their absence—that is not correct. For even so, since those [deities] would exist in the *Vaiśvadeva* and other *parvans*, the undesired consequence of extension would still follow.

Furthermore, because the *prayāja* and other such rites would also be connected to their respective [specific] contexts, it would follow that they could not be extended (*atideśa*) to the *saurya* sacrifice and others;
for the *prayāja* and other rites in the archetype are not prompted by the *parvan* as a *pūrva* (an intermediate result), since that would entail the fallacy of performing them twice.
Rather, they are prompted solely by the *parvan* as a collective whole.

Now, if it is argued that his status as the instigator (*prayojakatā*) does not depend on the *parvan* being a collective whole, but rather on its being a preceding *parvan* (i.e., the first day of the lunar fortnight), then there would be an extension (*atideśa*) of those [rites] to the *Saurya* sacrifice and others; consequently, the same would apply to the *parvaṇa-homas*.

This being the position reached, we reply: It is true that this is so; nevertheless, because some ritualists do not perform the *parvaṇa-homas* in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it is precisely the practice (*ācāra*) that indicates an intention to include the conjunction (*sāhitya*) within the defining scope of the deity-status of the *Āgneya* and other offerings in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*). However, since that [conjunction] is absent in the modified sacrifice, there is no extension of the *parvaṇa-homas* and the like.

For this very reason, there is no extended application (*atideśa*); nor can the scriptural text be otherwise interpreted even by means of the instruction regarding the respective secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), as that would result in excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

Without providing [an independent] commentary on the sūtras, they should be explained there according to the stated method as being intent upon other reasons for the collective meaning of the two *pārvaṇa-homas*.
The two mantras for the Pārvaṇa-homa: "O Purifier, [lead us] to the thousandfold [wealth];
to Prāṇa, the bestower of divine power."
"Oblation to the Full Moon!
(Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.10.5.13)—thus at the Full Moon sacrifice.
"The New Moon is fortunate and most gracious."
Like a cow, swelling again and again,
may she milk for us excellent heroism and thousandfold abundance of wealth.
To Apāna, the possessor of abundant wealth;
to the New Moon, svāhā!
Thus [is the offering] on the night of the new moon.

In this context, having formed the first half-verse (*ardharca*) from the first sentence and the second half-verse from the three subsequent sentences, these two mantras should be employed at the time of the oblation (*homa*).
For each mantra, a single sentence ending in *svāhā* has been joined with the Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of the oblation;
however, the two mantras themselves consist of metrical feet (*padyapāda*) in the *paṅkti* meter.

**Collateral Cognition (Pārśvikabodha):** When a certain expression is uttered in proximity to a particular upapada (secondary word), whatever other [meaning] is understood from those two meanings— namely, that very relation between their respective meanings— is the object of collateral cognition.
For this very reason, in the case of *aṇaikahāyana*, the relation of qualifier and qualified (*paricchedya-paricchedaka-bhāva*) alone is the object of collateral cognition.
Bhāṭṭa 10.4.2. The Section on the Rope (Pāśādhikaraṇa) concerning the qualified ritual act.
The section concerning the nooses (*pāśādhikaraṇa*):

In the case of conflicting injunctions, there should be an option (*vikalpa*), because they are equal; for [the injunction regarding] the accessory (*guṇa*) is established by that same principle as being a part [of the whole].

Commentary (*bhāṣya*): There exists a second animal sacrifice (*dvitīyemīya*) belonging to one who has been initiated, as stated in the text: "When one who is initiated eats, he should immolate the *abhīya* animal."

In this regard, two mantras are recorded: one expressing the singularity of the noose, "May Aditi release this noose" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.1.1.19), and another expressing the plurality of nooses, "May Aditi release these nooses" (Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā 1.2.1.8; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā 3.45). Regarding these two, does the one expressing singularity belong within the context while the one expressing plurality is displaced from it, or do both belong within the context? What is the prima facie view? That the one expressing plurality is displaced.
Why? Because he is the releaser from many bonds (*pāśa*). And there are not many bonds in this context! Therefore, since it finds no support in the context, it is led to where there are many bonds.
Just as [it is said]: "One should use the *pratipad* verse, 'For you two are possessed of heaven,' for two sacrificers."
The section concerning the noose;
the maxim of the noose; the maxim of the snare.

The principle of the *pāśukājyabhāga* (the clarified butter portions for the animal sacrifice): Maṇḍana states, "Indeed, the two *pāśa*-mantras are modified (*ūha*) in the *vikṛti* [subsidiary] sacrifices"; Śaṅkara states, "The two *pāśa*-mantras are modified like [the *ājyabhāga*]."
"Where there is a disagreement regarding different designations, there the *pāśa* principle applies;
but where there is only a single mantra, there the *patnī* principle applies, as in the case of [the mantra] 'You two are purifiers' (*pavitre sthaḥ*). (Ṭupṭīkā 1.2.16.20)

In the passage "abhigraṃthe meghapataye meghapatibhyām," the word *pati* refers exclusively to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and not to the deity. Nor is there an inconsistency regarding the dual number because of its singularity, for that is justified by the logic of the *pāśa* (rope) rule. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the Siddhāntin replies]: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mantra "patnī saṃnahya" ending in the singular must be employed without modification even in ritual performances involving two wives. This is because, according to the *pāśa* logic, the gender of the nominal stem is applicable to all instances, and thus there is no justification for restricting it in order to avoid conflict with the singular suffix.

In the case of the injunction "patnī saṃnahya" (having girded the wife), since the instruction is general and applies to all ritual performances, both the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the accusative case ending (*karmakāraka-vibhakti*) in the word *patnī* are subject to the principle of the rope (*pāśanyāya*), as well as the principle of the animal and the butter-portions (*pāśukājyabhāganyāya*). Regarding the section on the *pika* and the *nemi* (the crow and the wheel-rim):
in the statement "pikam ālabheta" (one should sacrifice the *pika*), the *pika* is the cuckoo (*kokila*), according to the usage of non-Aryans.
The section concerning the *pikanemi* [bird];
the section concerning the Aryans and Mlecchas.

Is there any authority for that which is well-known among the Mlecchas? It is argued that it is indeed recognized as authoritative because it is not contradicted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The Commentary states: "Now, those words which the Āryas do not employ in any sense, but which the Mlecchas do employ in a particular sense—such as the words *pika*, *nema*, *sata*, *tāmarasa*, and so forth."

Regarding these, there is a doubt: should the meaning be inferred from the verbal root by means of the Nigamas, Nirukta, and Vyākaraṇa, or is that which the Mlecchas practice the meaning of the word? It has been stated that the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭas) is authoritative, not the tradition of the unlearned. Therefore, the determination of meaning is based on the Nigamas and so forth.
In this way, the meaningfulness of the *nigama*s and so forth will be established;
furthermore, there will be a lack of application regarding the meanings of words among the unrefined, while there will be application among others.
Therefore, the meaning must be inferred from the verbal root (*dhātu*).
This being the case, we reply:
even though it is enjoined for one who has not yet reached the stage of a householder, it is prescribed for those who are disciplined.

"It should be understood by its own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As for the claim that this [object] is not apprehended because the scripture (*śāstra*) is more authoritative, that is not so.

In the absence of contradiction, even that which is weak must be accepted because it is primary; however, whatever appears as a mere semblance of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*), like the cognition of a mirage, must always be rejected. On the other hand, that which becomes a means of valid cognition only in dependence upon a stronger contradiction must be determined to be indeed a valid cognition when no such contradiction exists. But no such [contradiction] exists here, because there is no established contrary meaning. For this very reason, with the intention of asserting the superior strength of the initial non-establishment regarding the mere objects denoted by words within the scope of the meaning of Vedic sentences, [the author] says:
"When there is established common usage, its superior authority is accepted; but when such usage is absent, claiming superior authority is like the power of the son of a barren woman.

For in the case of the Aṣṭakā and other rites whose purposes are unseen (transcendental), which are rooted in tradition and accepted by all people—including even the Mlecchas—there truly exists among the Āryas knowledge of the actual forms of words such as 'cow' and their respective meanings, as well as proficiency in them."

But in the case of words such as *pika* and others, which denote only a nature already understood through the [Persian] Āryas alone, they become functionless among the Āryas because they lack knowledge of the specific denoted object— just like a word [unfamiliar to them].
The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is for the sake of a visible purpose.

The Piṇḍapitṛyajña (6.8.18): The Piṇḍapitṛyajña must also be performed at the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and in the modifications of the Darśa; however, there is no extended application (atideśa) of it [to other sacrifices].
Bhāṭṭa 4.4.8.
Oṃ: The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is performed at its own proper time even on the day of the new moon (darśa).

The New Moon sacrifice (darśeṣṭi) must be explained as occurring precisely after the Piṇḍapitṛyajña on the new moon day. First, let it be established that in the Soma sacrifice, such a sequence—where the New Moon sacrifice follows the Pitṛyajña—is indeed impossible;
for it is understood from the fact that [the injunction] is intended to grant the attainment of the ancestors.
This is also because of the Vedic text: "In that he performs the Pitṛyajña.

For this very reason, even the *praṇayana* (the ritual carrying forward of the fire) enjoined by the rule, "Having offered the morning Agnihotra, he carries forward the Āhavanīya fire," is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the Pitṛyajña. Otherwise, since the fuel-substance would be exhausted at the end [of the preceding rite] and the ritual would have concluded on the following day, the Pitṛyajña would necessarily fail to take place due to the removal of that [fire].
Furthermore, the fire-bringing (*praṇayana*) at night cannot serve as an auxiliary to the *darśa* sacrifice, because the *pitṛyajña* is an independent rite (*apūrva*).
Nor can it serve as an auxiliary to the fire-bringing of the Soma sacrifice, like those of the *iṣṭi* sacrifices, because that [Soma sacrifice] is not part of the *darśa*.

If the fire-bringing were indeed an auxiliary to the *pitṛyajña*, then upon its conclusion, there would be a connection with the fire-bringing again for the sake of the *darśa*. Moreover, since the suffix *-tvā* in the word "having offered" (*hutvā*) merely indicates a prior time, it is appropriate to bring the fire in the afternoon itself; or else, there is a displacement [of the time] due to a direct scriptural injunction.
Therefore, the anvādhāna must indeed follow immediately after completing the pitṛyajña.

This being the case, since it is impossible for the *anvādhāna* and the *pitṛyajña*—which are prescribed for the forenoon and afternoon respectively—to exceed their proper times, and because the statement "having offered the morning *agnihotra*" would become purposeless if the carrying forward of the fire (*praṇayana*) were omitted; and because even upon the conclusion of the *pitṛyajña*, the benefit is accomplished through the incidental application (*prasaṅga*) of the *darśa*-related *praṇayana*; and because the sequence established by the observation of the injunctions for various *darśa* ritual elements immediately following the injunction for *praṇayana* leaves no room for doubt—the *pitṛyajña* must indeed take place at its own time only after the commencement of the *darśa* ritual framework (*tantra*).
Because the expression "on the previous day" is intended for the purpose of requesting a boon, and because this [request] generally applies to that which pertains to the primary rite (Saṃkarṣa.
the Piṇḍapitṛyajña does not constitute a separate injunction.
The followers of the *Mūla* [the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] maintain that this [the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*] is for the sake of attaining heaven (*svarga*).
In reality, however, it is indeed obligatory (*nitya*).

(Bhāṭṭadīpikā 4.4.8) Regarding the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*: if it is performed on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), then it must be performed on the immediately following new moon day (*amāvāsyā*); however, in the context of the *Kuṇḍapāyināmayana*, as in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* for a month," it is not to be performed there.
Bhāṣya 4.4.8.29: The Piṇḍapitṛyajña has a fruit.
4.3.5.10–12: The Piṇḍapitṛyajña has a single fruit; it is not for all purposes. 4.3.16.13–14: The Piṇḍapitṛyajña has heaven as its fruit.
Oṃ, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña should be performed on the following day when there is a conjunction of Sinīvālī and Kuhū.

When both Sinīvālī and Kuhū arrive in succession, even then, although the Pitṛyajña would—by the principle of the preceding section—fall on the first lunar day (the full moon), it is stated that it should be performed on the latter [lunar day]. This is because, through syntactic unity with the injunctions "On the very day it is seen in the east, one should give," "One gives on the previous day for the ancestors," and "One gives in the afternoon," the specific time of the new moon (Amāvāsyā)—characterized by the non-appearance of the moon and the afternoon—is obtained precisely there.

In the single sentence, "On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), when the moon is visible, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña in the afternoon," the injunction is for a specific time characterized by both attributes; this is established in the Bhāṣya because the two qualifiers are intended to be significant, as they are not merely for the sake of expectancy (*pratīkṣā*) but are themselves to be adopted (*upādeyatva*).

Nor should it be argued that, since the moon is not visible on the preceding day, the new moon day itself cannot exist in the afternoon of the following day, and thus, given the necessity of abandoning one or the other, it is more appropriate to discard the visibility of the moon in accordance with the statement "that which [occurs] on the previous day. [The reason for this is that] the presence of the moon on the previous day does not preclude the existence of the *amāvāsyā* on the following day, as the term refers to the conjunction of the sun and moon, and the visibility of the moon is merely a secondary characteristic. Furthermore, the ritual injunctions take precedence over astronomical observations. Thus, even if the moon is visible, the performance of the rite remains valid if the conjunction occurs within the prescribed timeframe.]

Because the *Smṛti* states, "The day upon which the sun arrives [at conjunction] is [the new moon]," it is declared that the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is complete on the following day. Furthermore, [it is said]: "In the afternoon, due to the close proximity of the sun and the moon. Now, one might object: another *Smṛti* states, "The *Piṇḍānvāhāryaka* Śrāddha is recommended when the moon has waned," thus explaining the phrase "when the moon is visible" as an indicator of the moon's waning; and regarding the moon's waning, it is said: "On the eighth and the fourteenth days, the moon becomes waned."

Furthermore, because of the Smṛti text, "And again, [the rite] should indeed take place on the eighth part of the new moon," it is observed that the Pitṛyajña occurs only on the *sinīvālī* (the new moon joined with the fourteenth day). For this very reason, by the same logic applied to the injunctions such as, "One should perform the new moon sacrifice on that day when the moon is not seen at all," where the visibility of the moon serves as a qualification for the time of the *anvādhāna*, it would follow that [the Pitṛyajña] is a subsidiary part of that [new moon sacrifice] on the following day. Thus: "Having completed the rites up to the end of the fortnight and the Vaiśvadeva, the one who maintains the sacred fires should then perform the Piṇḍayajña;
thereafter, the wise man should perform the *Anvāhāryaka*."

If you argue that—because [the texts] beginning with "Thus... do not prescribe the performance of the *anvādhāna*, the *pitṛyajña*, and the *śrāddha* as a single act, the phrase "non-appearance of the moon" in the *anvādhāna* injunction must be understood merely as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) of the waning of the moon, as stated in the *Karmapradīpa*—we say: no. For it is said: "If the second lunar day is seen even before sunset, one should not perform the sacrifice there; the gods turn their faces away."

By this statement, since both [the subsidiary and the primary] require the sight of the moon on the first day (pratipad) characterized by the evening moonrise for the sake of the primary rite, if the moon is not visible when the subsidiary and primary rites are performed at an improper time, then according to the principle of "conflict between a subsidiary and its quality" (*aṅgaguṇavirodha-nyāya*), the Piṇḍapitṛyajña takes place even during the *anvādhāna* (preparatory rite).
This is the basis for the eligibility for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
Thus, because such a sublation is logical, for this very reason the Śruti states, "Having seen it at that very time, they fast," and Gobhila says, "even when it is visible, sometimes.

However, regarding the Pitṛyajña, because another Śruti—namely, "on the day it is seen both before and after"—prescribes a specific rule for the *kuhū* (new moon) alone, it is not appropriate here to explain [the term] through Smṛti as indicating a moon that has waned; rather, it is proper to accept that the word *amāvāsyā* itself refers to the conjunction of the sun and the moon, as established in the section of the fifteenth chapter and stated in the Sūtra.

Nor should it be argued that the Smṛti rule prohibiting sacrifice on the day the moon is visible—based on such Śruti texts as "On the day when the moon rises in the west, one conquers these worlds"—is sublated [by the injunction for the *parvan* sacrifice].

This is because, although the day the moon is visible is praiseworthy, it is indeed inferior to the day when it is not visible; thus, this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) can be justified even as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to the injunction for sacrificing on the day the moon is visible, just like the praise of *jatilā* and *gavedhukā* grasses in relation to the injunction for using milk.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction between the Śruti and the Smṛti because the moon exists from the eighth part of the new moon (amāvāsyā) onwards, since it is seen by people as soon as it has risen,
then what follows?
Therefore, the anvādhāna (preparatory rite) takes place on the Sinīvālī day, and the Pitṛyajña (ancestral sacrifice) occurs after the yāga on the Kuha day.
Because of the statements regarding the granting of boons and so forth, [the time] is established as the conjunction of the full moon day and the first day of the lunar fortnight.
Saṃkarṣa. 1.2.10.
Regarding the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, which is prescribed to be performed on the *atipraṇītāgni* (the fire brought forward prematurely), it is stated that the *āhavanīya* fire is its locus.
Su. Pṛ. 780.
Oṃ. In the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, the fire that has been carried forward (atipraṇīta) or the aupāsana fire should be attended by one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni).

The worship (*upasthāna*) of the *gārhapatya* fire is prescribed in the *pitṛyajña* by means of the mantra: "Whatever [we have harmed] in the intermediate space, on the earth, in the immortal heaven, or whatever we have injured our mother or father.

Since this worship, which belongs to the archetype (*prakṛti*) performed by one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), is extended by analogy to the case performed by one who has not maintained them (*anāhitāgni*), the *gārhapatya* must be established for that purpose;
for in the archetype, the fire upon which oblations are offered is distinct from the fire to be worshipped.

This being the prima facie view, [the conclusion is as follows]: Since the status of being the *gārhapatya* fire belongs only to that which is distinguished by specific consecrations (*saṃskāra*), and since the performance of such [a consecration] would result in the failure of one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the original injunction (*codaka*) does not extend the distinction of purpose from the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*). Therefore, even though there is only the physical location, because there is no difference between the *gārhapatya* and *dakṣiṇāgni* fires in their mere site, and because of the scriptural statement, "One should worship that very fire into which the offering is given," the worship of the *atipraṇītāgni* is indeed the worship of the *aupāsana* fire.
(Saṃkarṣa 1.2.14).
Oṃ. In the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, there is also the entitlement for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).

In rites to be accomplished by means of fire, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and others, as well as in the Pitṛyajña, one who has not established the sacred fires (anāhitāgni) has no entitlement. As for that which is heard in scripture: "Even by one who has not established the fires, this must indeed be performed; 'This has been done by me, this I have understood, this I have been able to accomplish; may the ancestors acknowledge this of me,'" this is explained even as being for the purpose of showing that this [Pitṛyajña] must be performed even by one who has not established the fires, let alone by one who has.

This being the prima facie view, [the conclusion is as follows]: because the word "also" (*api*) has the sense of restriction, and because the explicit injunction "it must indeed be performed" establishes that even one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) possesses the entitlement, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the other part [of the rite] is for his sake.
Saṃkarṣa. 1.2.12.
Oṃ. In the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, there is the omission of the word "Gārhapatya" in the mantra of worship [when the performer is an *āhitāgni*].

In that very mantra, "Agni, the Gārhapatya fire, [is] my protector from that [danger]," since the word *gārhapatya* is impossible [in the case of a non-fire], even though the principle of the *mantrānugrāhaka-adhikaraṇa* (the section on the favoring of mantras) would suggest its use in the ritual application, and since it is to be consecrated as the locus of the oblation (*homa*), there arises the question of whether the word *gārhapatya* should be removed and a necessary substitute word inserted—resulting in an *ūha* (modification). In this case, however, only the word *gārhapatya* is elided, because that word alone does not denote anything other than fire.

Because the mantra is obtained as the instrument for the act of "he should attend" (*upatiṣṭheta*) and so forth, and because that archetypal mantra—devoid of the word *gārhapatya*—possesses a meaning directly connected to the rite; and because there is no substitute for fire, which consists of an invisible mass of merit, through any other fire such that a requirement for another word would even be possible; therefore, the principle stated in the Bhāṣya, "There is no deity, fire, word, or action [to be modified]," is consistent.

The view of some ritualists (*yājñika*) that there is an omission (*lopa*) of a mantra composed of such words is indeed to be considered merely speculative. This is because, in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, those specific details are not established from elsewhere; and since it is impossible for there to be a "disruption" (*viccheda*) in the absence of those details, one must assume the existence of mantras denoting those specific features (those specific features being the application, eligibility, and performance). *Saṃkarṣa.* 1.2.15. Regarding the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, since the specific qualifications are not established from another source, and because a "break" cannot logically occur in their absence, there is the assumption of mantras expressing those particulars (those particulars being the application, entitlement, and performance).

Kaṇikā, p. 380: Regarding the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, it is stated that "the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has its roots," thus establishing the presence of roots for those [blades] seen [in the ritual]. And given that this is the case, there is the explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*): "That which is cut at the joint belongs to the gods; that which is between [the joints] belongs to humans.
This is the section concerning what is cut at the joint (*paruṣiditādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. The section concerning the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
The principle of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña:
the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is for the sake of the human goal (puruṣārtha) and is not an auxiliary part of the Darśa sacrifice.
The Pitṛyajña should occur at its own time.
Commentary: In the New Moon (Āmāvāsya) rite, there is the Pitṛyajña, as it is said, "On the new moon day, in the afternoon, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the Piṇḍapitṛyajña an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the New Moon rite, or is it not an auxiliary?
What is established? That it is an auxiliary (aṅga), because of its proximity to that which possesses a fruit and because of the statement regarding its ransom.
He says: But surely, when something without a fruit is in proximity to something with a fruit, it becomes an auxiliary to that;
otherwise, one would have to assume a fruit for it.
It is said: True;
because of its syntactical unity with the new moon sacrifice (amāvāsyā), it is possible to postulate heaven [as the result].
He says: "And because it expresses time, its syntactical unity with the action is possible. It is replied:

Even in the case of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), syntactic unity with the action is possible. If heaven were to be assumed [as the result], there would be neither figurative indication nor direct statement (*śruti*).
And thus they recite: "When he performs [the rite] for the ancestors on the previous day, having thereby redeemed the sacrifice from the ancestors, the sacrificer extends it toward the gods."
Having purchased [the Soma] on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one extends that [purchase] further;
therefore, those [subsequent acts] are subsidiary to it.
This being the position reached, we reply:
The Pitṛyajña should take place at its own time;
the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is not an auxiliary part [of the Soma sacrifice].
Why? Because it has its own specific time.

Its connection is with time denoted by its own word, not with an action indicated [by another]. For example: "One should sacrifice with the Soma after the Darśapūrṇamāsa," and "They perform the Soma before the Upasad."

In this context, this word is primarily denotative of time and not of action; its application to action is figurative (lakṣaṇā). And direct denotation (śruti) is more powerful than figurative indication.

As for what was said—that there will be syntactical unity with the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*)—that is not so. Why? Because a secondary function is appropriate in a restatement (*anuvāda*), not in an injunction (*vidhi*).
This is a scriptural injunction.
Therefore, there is no connection with the New Moon (Amāvāsyā) rite;
rather, two rites at the same time are mutually unconnected.
[The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: "The Pitṛyajña should be performed at its own specific time."

(The author states the established conclusion: “The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [of the terms] ‘on the new moon day’ (*amāvāsyāyām*) and ‘in the afternoon’ (*aparāhṇe*) is understood.
And that is possible only if [the word *amāvāsyā*] denotes time.
Otherwise, by the word ‘new moon day,’ the offerings to Agni and the others would be denoted.”
The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is prescribed as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to them;

by means of the statement "the afternoon is its time," there could be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) whatsoever [between the two]. Furthermore, this construction—[attempting to establish] coreferentiality through the mediation of non-coreferentiality—is strained and impossible.
Therefore, because it denotes time, the action is enjoined for the sake of a result with the term *amāvāsyā* as the temporal occasion.
(Consequently, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is distinct from the fruit [of the sacrifice] and is not connected to the seasonal sacrifices).
And because it is praised in an equal manner.
Commentary: And it is praised as being equal to other principal sacrifices.
"There are indeed four great sacrifices: the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Jyotiṣṭoma, and the Piṇḍapitṛyajña"—thus it is praised as being on the same footing as the great sacrifices.
What else could constitute its status as a great sacrifice, were it not for its possession of fruit?
Therefore, it is a limb [of yoga]. And because it is seen even when [other limbs] are prohibited.
Commentary: This refers to the knowledge of the Self.
For when the New Moon sacrifice (āmāvāsya) is prohibited, it indicates the performance of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña:

"One who has rivals should sacrifice only at the Full Moon, not at the New Moon; having struck down his rival, he should sacrifice at the New Moon; by means of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, he gratifies the New Moon.
Thus, it indicates the Piṇḍapitṛyajña even in the absence of the New Moon sacrifice.
Therefore, its being a non-auxiliary is established;
for this reason as well, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is not an auxiliary. What is the purpose of this investigation?
If the installation (ādhāna) takes place on the full moon day, then it is not performed on the immediately following new moon day, as in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
Rather, it must be performed according to the established conclusion (siddhānta).
This is another purpose [of the discussion].
In the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana*, it is said: "One should offer the *Agnihotra* for a month," and "One should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* for a month.
As in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* should be performed;
as in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it should not be performed.
They cite this verse: "If the establishment of the fires (ādhāna) takes place on the full moon day, and the new moon sacrifice (darśa) is to be performed after [the full moon] has passed,
then the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) is not a constituent part [of that darśa], and it shall not be performed here."
Śā—(He states the established conclusion: “Even though it is common to both, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it must denote time; and the action depends upon that.

Although the word *amāvāsyā* is common to both [the action and the time] in that context, nevertheless, because of the desire for coreferentiality with the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), it is determined to denote time.

Regarding *soma*: in the previous case (*ṣaṭcitriṇī*), since the result was introduced by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), let it be considered occasional (*naimittika*). However, in the present case, it is improper to assume a result that is entirely unestablished; thus, the connection [of this discussion] arises from an objection based on this disparity. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: because the word *amāvāsyā* denotes time, the *pitṛyajña* is connected with a time expressed by its own specific term.
Topic 2569: The Piṇḍapitṛyajña Homa is not a subsidiary part [of the Darśa sacrifice].

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), it applies by extension to the modifications (vikāra) of the Darśa; however, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), it does not apply.

Vi—“Is the Piṇḍapitṛyajña an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, or not? For it occurs within the sacrifice because it is mentioned in connection with the New Moon (*amāvāsyā*). It is not so; its status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) follows from its being mentioned as having that specific time.
Bhaṭṭa—It is heard in an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*): “On the afternoon of the New Moon, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.”

In this context, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is [included] within the Darśa sacrifice; for it is understood from the sentence through the term *amāvāsyā*, which denotes the ritual action—just as in the expression "one should offer oblations there.
Although this term is primarily denotative of time, nevertheless, just as in the case of assuming a result (*phala*), it is more appropriate to regard it as referring to the ritual action itself.

In reality, however, although it is primarily denotative of time by way of a threefold figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) due to its connection with the ritual action, in the present instance it refers specifically to time because of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "the afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*); nevertheless, the Pitṛyajña is performed on the preceding day.

Thus, since the *darśa* sacrifice is present by virtue of the *vaimṛdha*-principle within this sentence, it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) [of the *darśa*]. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: the claim that the word *amāvāsyā* denotes the ritual action itself has indeed been refuted. Furthermore, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is dismissed from afar both because there is no evidence for it and because it would contradict its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with time.

Even the statement regarding the previous day (*pūrvedyus*) does not refer to a time associated with that sacrifice, because the sacrifice has not yet been introduced; rather, it merely refers to the deity, reiterating the time established by the lunar date (*tithi*) in the passage: "That day on which the sun sets, the ancestors worship.
Some, however, explain "the previous day" as being the day before the moon is visible, and thus they perform the *pitṛyajña* on the following day during a *khaṇḍaparvan*.
In any case, the *pitṛyajña* is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*).

And thus, even in the *Daśagrāma*, the mention of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is consistent with such statements as: "One who has enemies should sacrifice only at the full moon, not at the new moon; having struck down the enemy, one should sacrifice at the new moon; one gratifies the ancestors with the Piṇḍapitṛyajña at the new moon.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the fact that the sacrifice is present even in the explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, such as: "Having ransomed the sacrifice from the ancestors, the sacrificer extends it. As for the statement:
"For one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the Śrāddha does not arise in his mind without the [observance of] the new moon [sacrifice]," [this is also explained].

Regarding this statement of Manu (Manu Smṛti 3.122): "That śrāddha [performed] in the dark fortnight occurs for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) except on the new moon day (*darśa*)," it should be explained as meaning "except on the new moon day," just as it is for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).

It does not mean that without the new moon day—the new moon being the specific time—the *pitṛyajña* (ancestral sacrifice) does not take place; for there is no evidence for such a figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*) of the term "new moon" (*darśa*).
Therefore, according to the followers of the root text, this [śrāddha] is for the sake of attaining heaven.

In reality, however, this [sacrifice] is indeed obligatory (*nitya*), because Āpastamba and others record the *Saptahotṛ* sacrifice as a penance for its non-performance, and because it is mentioned as being equal to the performance of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other such rites.
Its purpose is that it must be performed even when the *Darśa* sacrifice is absent, and there is no extension (*atideśa*) of its details to other sacrificial contexts.

As for what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—that when the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires) is performed on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), there is no performance of the *darśa* (new moon sacrifice) on the following new moon day because the time has passed—this should be understood to apply when the full moon occurs on the day after the *pavamāneṣṭis* within the twelve nights following the *ādhāna*. However, when the full moon occurs on the very day following the *ādhāna*, then one performs the *ādhāna* together with the *iṣṭi* and the *sānnāyya* on that full moon day itself; in this case, there is no contradiction whatsoever in performing the *pitṛyajña* immediately after the *agnidarśaiṣṭi* on that same full moon day.
Maṇḍana: "The Pitṛyajña is a subsidiary (guṇa) of the Darśa.
Śaṃkara: "The Pitṛyajña is not a subsidiary of the Darśa.
This is the principle of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.

Regarding the statement, “On the new moon day, in the afternoon, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña,” a doubt arises as to whether the Piṇḍapitṛyajña mentioned in this independent (anārabhyādhīta) injunction is for the sake of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because of its co-occurrence with the word *amāvāsyā* (new moon), which denotes a ritual action, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is a subsidiary part of that [sacrifice]. Although this term is common to both [the time and the action], nevertheless, in order to avoid the necessity of postulating a separate result, it must denote the ritual action itself; therefore, it is for the sake of the sacrifice. This being the position reached, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Although the term *amāvāsyā* is common to both time and action, it refers exclusively to time when construed with the term *aparāhṇa*. Nor is there any ambiguity, because the word is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of time, whereas its application to action is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) by virtue of its connection to that time.
Therefore, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña has heaven as its fruit.
*Kalpataru*, p.

1114; see also p. 112. [Bhāṣya]: "The ritual procedures (*vidhi*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* do not apply to the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* and the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. (Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya 3.1.12–14). The *piṇḍapitṛyajña* oblation is offered in the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire), not in the *āhavanīya* (offering fire).

In the *pitṛyajña*, even though the oblation (*havis*) is cooked on the *dakṣiṇāgni*, it is offered in the *āhavanīya* alone; for we observe the same procedure even when [the oblation] is cooked on the *gārhapatya*. There is no evidence to override the statement, “Whatever he offers in the *āhavanīya*...”; furthermore, since there exists another scriptural injunction—“He draws out a flame from the *dakṣiṇāgni*”—the *atipraṇītāgni* also exists. And since that fire serves a visible purpose, just like the *atipraṇītāgni*, the offering may take place right there.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached by the very statement: “One offers in that in which one cooks. However, because the *praṇītā* water has been moved from its original location and so forth, it is distinct from that [cooking vessel].
For this very reason, its purpose as the first [offering] is not impaired, as in the case of those forms intended for the ancestral invocation in the *pitṛyajña*.

This is because the mantra "praṃtisujhamānāḥ" is heard to have the purpose of warding off demons (rakṣas). This is the maxim of the one who, having gone for the sake of begging for oil-cake (piṇyāka), agreed to give a *khārikā* measure of oil;
this maxim appears in the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha* under the section on Pūrṇaprajña.
It is rash [to claim otherwise]. 709. § "The father or the grandfather shall not drink Soma" (Bhāṣya).

This statement—that the father's or grandfather's lack of Soma-drinking is not a cause for [the son] being permanently excluded from cattle—is established by the principle of concomitance (*sāhitya*).
Vārttika 3.6.12, p. 696. Or rather, the father subsists on the son during the rainy season.
And likewise, there is the Smṛti: "Manu has declared that aged parents, a virtuous wife, and an infant son must be maintained even by performing a hundred improper acts."

"‘He recognizes the father by means of the father’—this is the *śruti* of application (*viniyoga-śruti*) consisting of a third-case kāraka-vibhakti. (Bālakrīḍā, p. 44). **The Maxim of the Breast-nourished Child:** Just as a father attends to a breast-nourished child, so too should the ignorant person be attended to by the wise.

Summary: The father and others are not objects to be given away in the Viśvajit sacrifice when there is a gift of one's entire property (*sarvasva*). For it is not possible to relinquish one's own ownership over the father and others.
Nor is it reasonable that the father and others should be in a state of service;
for in the world, an equal division of the father’s property among the sons is observed. (Bhāṣya 6.7.1)
VI.
The Principle of Father and Son (pitāputranyāya).
For example, the very same person is a father with respect to one [person], and a son with respect to another.
The same should be understood regarding the present case as well; this is clear from the commentary on the sūtra *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.66).

[Sāhasī 607] Just as ancestors and maternal relatives are satisfied by words that denote specific relationships to them, they are not so satisfied by the mention of their own names; on the contrary, they actually become angry. [Vi.
10.4.14] § The Pitṛyajña should take place at its own time, because it has its own specific occasion.
It is heard in the Śruti: "On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), in the afternoon, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.

In the inquiry as to whether this Piṇḍapitṛyajña is an auxiliary (aṅga) of the new moon sacrifice or not, the author establishes the final conclusion (siddhānta) against the prima facie view (utsūtra):
"The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is [the name] of the Pitṛyajña; it is not an auxiliary of the new moon sacrifice; it should not be an auxiliary."
Because it has its own time (*svakālatvāt*).
That which has its own (*sva*) time is "having its own time" (*svakāla*); because of having its own time.
The new moon night (*amāvāsyā*) alone is its own time.
In this regard, the following has been established:

although the time for the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā-yāga*) is indeed that same lunar day (*tithi*), nevertheless, these two rites at one and the same time are mutually unconnected. Therefore, [the latter] is not an auxiliary part (*anaṅga*) of the former.
"And because of the enumeration as equal.
This sūtra provides another reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is indeed independent and not a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*).

For the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is enumerated—that is, counted—as if it were equal to the other "Great Sacrifices" (*mahāyajña*): "There are indeed four great sacrifices: the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Jyotiṣṭoma, and the Piṇḍapitṛyajña."
And because it possesses a fruit, it has its own primary status;
therefore, it is not a subsidiary (aṅga).
Furthermore, it is seen [to be so] even when [the primary act] is prohibited.

The *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is indeed independent and not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *āmāvāsya* sacrifice; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). To demonstrate the third reason for this, there is the following sūtra:
"Even when the *āmāvāsya* rite is prohibited, because the performance of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is observed, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is not a subordinate part of the *āmāvāsya*.
