Having offered from their cups with four mantras at the *hotṛ*'s *vaṣaṭ* call and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ* call, and having offered once each from the cups of the *hotṛkā*s at the *vaṣaṭ* call itself, the *soma* is poured over again into those very vessels while they still contain remnants.
For thus does the *adhvaryu* give the direction there: "O cup-bearers of the *madhyataḥkārin*s, offer at the *vaṣaṭ* call and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ* call!"
The *camasādhvaryus* of the *hotṛkas*, having drawn the *śukra* cup once, [say]: "Return! Therein, the *hotṛkas* sacrifice to various deities:

the *maitrāvaruṇa* sacrifices to Mitra and Varuṇa with "We invoke Mitra... (*mitraṃ vayaṃ havāmahe*); the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* to Indra with "O Indra, we [invoke] you, the bull... (*indra tvā vṛṣabhaṃ vayam*); the *potṛ* to the Maruts with "In whose dwelling, O Maruts... (*maruto yasya hi kṣaye*); the *neṣṭṛ* to Tvaṣṭṛ and the wives [of the gods] with "O Agni, bring the wives here... (*agne patnīrihā-vaha*); and the *āgnīdhra* to Agni with "For the bull... and for the barren cow... (*ukṣāṇāya vaśāñcāya*).
There, with those mantras, at the first *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, Indra was worshipped here.
Having again poured out [the soma], the deities beginning with Mitra and Varuṇa were sacrificed to.
(The remnants therein belong to Indra and to Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others—and also to the deity of the *prasthita* offering, namely Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others.)
Is it a characteristic mark, or rather that Indra is not to be characterized?
What, then, is the prima facie view? There should be a characterization of all [deities] when they are poured out again.
Why? Because of their being remnants.
In each and every cup (*camasa*), there remains a remnant of two;
in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it was stated that the remnant belongs to whichever [deity] it was offered to, and that one drinks it as such.
Here too, it must be declared in exactly the same way.
Therefore, in every cup (*camasa*), there is the indication of two [deities].
Or rather—having thus established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in this very section, he considers the subject of modification (*ūha*).
When the cups have been offered while still containing remnants, the Soma that is poured in again is called "re-poured" (*punarabhyunnīta*).
He demonstrates, by way of analysis, how they are to be brought forward again and how they fall within the scope of modification (*ūha*).
There are ten *camasa* cups.
Of these, the four belonging to those who act from the middle—the Brahman, Hotṛ, Udgātṛ, and Yajamāna—are each offered twice at the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls of the Hotṛ.
By the cups of the *hotṛkāḥ*—namely the Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, Acchāvāka, and Āgnīdhra—the offering is made only at the single *vaṣaṭ*-utterance.
In all of these, Indra is the deity.
Then, while the Soma still remains in the cups, more is poured in and offered.
How is this understood? The Commentator demonstrates all of that through the *preṣa* (direction).
In that context, during the second *homa*, the *hotṛkās* sacrifice to various deities;
he shows this very point through such sentences as "We invoke Mitra and Varuṇa" (*mitraṃ vayaṃ havāmahe*).

In that context, when these cups have been offered and are brought forward for consumption, two [deities] are seen: Indra in the previous offerings, and Mitra, Varuṇa, and others in the subsequent ones.

When the mention [of the deity] is being performed, a doubt arises: should Indra—who, though his turn has passed—be mentioned along with the subsequent deities such as Mitra and Varuṇa (in the formula "drunk by Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa"), or should only Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others be mentioned (here again, the word "Indra" is printed in the Ānandāśrama edition and elsewhere, and it is indeed stated)?
Whence arises the doubt? Is the possibility of the previous deity removed by the transition to another deity, or not?
If it is removed, then there is only the indicative reference (*upalakṣaṇa*) to Mitra and Varuṇa; if it is not removed, then Indra must also be indicated.
What, then, is the prima facie view? [The answer follows] according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Regarding the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*), [it is said]:
"One who has established the fire and then suffers misfortune or loses his wealth should perform the *punarādheya*.
(Bhāṣya 10.3.15.30). Regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the re-establishment: "A garment that has been mended is the fee; for one who has mended it again, an ox."

10|3|130. In the occasional *punaḥsādhana* (re-performance), there is a sublation of the general rule for eleven sacrificial fees (*ekādaśadakṣiṇā*) by the specific fee prescribed in the scriptural injunction.
10|3|15–13. In the *punaḥsādhana*, "a chariot that has been cast off again is the sacrificial fee" (Vi.
The re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) is like the *odana* offering.

Regarding the Agnihotra, it is heard in scripture: "For one whose two fires have both gone out before sunset, or for one whose [fire] has been extinguished by dawn, the re-establishment of the fires is his expiation.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this expiation, the re-establishment of the fires, should be performed like the *pañcaśarāva* offering even upon the extinction of either one of the two fires, and not only when both have gone out.

The meaning of the scriptural passage is as follows: for that *āhitāgni* whose two fires— the *gārhapatya* and the *āhavanīya*— have both gone out and become extinguished (the meaning being "while they are extinguished"),
if the sun should set (*nimlocet*),
or if the sun should rise (*udiyāt*) while his two fires remain extinguished, for him the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādhāna*).
The production of the substance [is required] from both.

Rejecting the position reached in the *pūrvapakṣa* sūtra by means of the word "or" (*vā*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): From both; that is, the production of the two substances—the *gārhapatya* and the *āhavanīya*—constitutes the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
And thus, only when there is a transgression of both [rules] does the expiation for the production of those two occur through the non-establishment [of the fire];
it does not occur upon the transgression of each one individually.
Here, the word "of both" (*ubhayoḥ*) is construed with the word "substance" (*dravya*), which is a member of the compound.

In this context, the production of the substance—that is, the fire—occurs only upon the extinction of both the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires; the production of the substance, the fire, occurs through its formal installation (*ādhāna*), which constitutes the expiation.
However, if only one of the two is destroyed after the installation has been performed, the production of another [fire] for the pair is interrupted because one remains.
Therefore, the occasional rite of re-installation (*punarādheya*) applies only when there is the extinction of the entire collection, and not upon the extinction of either one individually.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "What is the *punarādheya*? It is like the *odanavat*," it has been stated that in the passage—"For one whose two fires have both gone out and [the sun] has set, the *punarādheya* is the expiation for him"—the intended meaning of the conjunction (*sāhitya*) as a qualification of the occasion (*nimitta*) is obtained through the force of what is to be enjoined (*vidheya-sāmarthyāt*).
(Bālakrīḍā, p. 122).

According to the principle of *punarādheya* (re-establishment of the sacred fires) [Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 94, entry on "agnihotre ubhayāgnināśe"], there is a restriction of the subject (*uddeśya*) in accordance with the capacity of the predicate (*vidheya*). Murāri, p. 1180: they do not accept what is redundant (*punarukta*) for fear of making the text overly cumbersome.
Bhāṣya 4.2:
Repetition is not a great fault;
even by speaking much, that which is beneficial ought to be said.

Out of fear of making the text overly voluminous, they do not desire repetition; however, those who fail to grasp the meaning are indeed highly appreciative of what is stated repeatedly. Bhāṣya 4.2.4143.
Tautology:
This is the restatement of what has already been said.
It is so stated.
The word of a trustworthy person remains strictly logical even if repeated many times, whereas that of an untrustworthy person is illogical even once.
He says: "If it has been stated once, there is no purpose in stating it a hundred times.
It is replied: [True].
There is also a purpose for [the existence of] non-refuge.
Bhāṣya 5.1.1.1, Section 1.
Since it is impossible to enjoy heaven in this very body, the attainment of another body—though not explicitly heard in scripture—is inferred through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Furthermore, the chariot that was cast away is the sacrificial fee for the *apunarādheya* (the rite of re-establishing the fires).
Having been broken, it was again restored and then cast away once more.
VI. 10|3|15. Regarding the *punaḥpadā*:
"This *bṛhatī* which has repeated feet is indeed the foundation."

In the *pragātha* which serves as the basis for the two [verses] consisting of the *bṛhatī* and the *sato-bṛhatī*, the first [verse] is "ami tvā śūra" (O Hero, these [men] toward you...); its fourth quarter is "īśānam indra tavyasam" (O Indra, the ruling one, the most powerful...). Having taken that [quarter] again, it is chanted together with the first half of the subsequent *ṛc*.
By this means, it becomes known by the name "punar-padā" (the repeated-quarter).
Furthermore, a repeated scriptural mention serves to exclude other things that have not been heard [in the context].
Bhāṣya 10.7.2.4.

The purposes of a repeated scriptural mention are: an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), the status of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*, i.e., praise), or the injunction of something else.
Furthermore,
[there are] the two *sāmans* named "Rathavidhi" for the *punaḥstoma* sacrifice, and the "Apacitivat" *ṛcs* for the *punaḥstoma* sacrifice.
"Furthermore, the midday pressing of the *punastoma* is recorded as having twelve *stomas*;
on both sides of it, the two pressings have nineteen *stomas* [namely,
the morning pressing has nine *stomas*, and the third pressing has ten]."
The meaning is that the Indra-stoma sequence is at the beginning, while the middle consists of the twelve-fold stoma (dvādaśastomaka). —
Bhāṣya.

"The man Devadatta" means that Devadatta possesses a gender non-different from masculinity; such is the understanding according to the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas). Maṇi, p. 124: "Masculine, feminine, neuter"—these are indeed specific types of substances (dravya).
Bhāṣya 3.1.12, p. 681: The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that males possess the requisite substance (*dravyavant*), whereas females do not;
the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that even those who perform the ritual action possess the requisite substance.
6.1.3.15–16: Only a male has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for the single kindling of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), along with his wife.
6|2|15|22-23. Only a man who possesses a wife has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other such sacrifices.
6|2|13-13. See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 293, under the entry "Entitlement to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices.
Only a man has the entitlement to perform the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) and so forth, not a woman.

The Keśavaśrama-nyāya: 6.1.16. "Women are more numerous than men; therefore, one man finds many wives, but one woman does not find many husbands," as stated in the *Yūpaikādaśinī* [section], Vārttika 1.3.4.9, p. 221.
In the case of a pair of males: Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.2.12 states, "The term *mithuna* denotes the collective aggregate of a female and a male."
In this collective compound, it is restricted that the modification (*ūha*) must be performed in the masculine gender alone;
this is the *Nārāyaṇavṛtti*.
Even in a masculine statement, [the original form] is stated otherwise only so long as another [form] is not perceived.
In that case, one must not adopt anything other than what has been heard [in the scripture], nor should there be an acceptance of alteration. (Vākyapadīya 3.1.7.13, p.
699). This is the principle regarding the object [of knowledge] as a person (*pūṃviṣayanyāya*).

(Just as the male person (*pumān*) and the object (*viṣaya*), such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), are distinct, so too are the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*); this is the principle [applied] here]. This is an instance of boldness (*sāhasī*). It is an intended expression of gender and so forth, as seen in such cases as "one sacrifices a black-necked animal" (*kṛṣṇagrīvām ālabhate*) and "the horse, the bull, the ram" (*aśva ṛṣabho vṛṣiḥ*).

The statement "the *puro'vayī* distributes the speech" is indeed a reference to place (*deśavāda*). Having prescribed the distribution of speech in the form of directions (*praipa*)—namely, "O Hotṛ, recite the offering prayer! O Potṛ, recite! O Neṣṭṛ, recite! O Brahman, recite! O Acchāvāka, recite!"—it is heard in the scripture: "The *maitrāvaruṇa*, as the *puro'vayī*, distributes that [speech] in front.
In this context, the words "in front" (*puraḥ*) and "behind" (*paścāt*) refer either to place or to time, for they are applicable in both cases.

Since it might be argued that there is an option— namely, that one should stand in the very same place and distribute the *praipa* (directions) to the *adhvaryu* and *maitrāvaruṇa* according to their earlier or later times, or else stand in different directions at the same time— the following is stated: this is indeed a statement regarding location, because this is taught in connection with the passage beginning, "He goes to the *āhavanīya* fire."
In such cases as "he goes to Pāṭaliputra," because that locus (the place) is presented [in the cognition], [the rule applies];
therefore, it is said: "The Adhvaryu [stands] on the Uttaravedi; the Maitrāvaruṇa shall give the directions in the Sadas" (Saṃkarṣa).
"Puronuvākyā" is a technical designation. It is called "puro'nuvākyā" because it is recited first (pūrvam anūcyate).
The word "first" (pūrva) is relative, being used in relation to the *yājyā*.

Bhāṣya 12.4.2.4: The *puro'nuvākyā* (‘O Agni, lead us by a good path,’ etc. and the *manotā* are repeated for the two black-necked animals because of the difference in time; this is explained by the *saumya* [offering]. 11.4.12.57–59: The *anuvacanāni* consist of the *puro'nuvākyās* ending with the *praiṣas*;
they are not mere *anuvākyās* alone.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the animal offerings and so forth: Vārttika 3.3.2.143, p. 1107; "He first employs the *puro’nuvākyā*," thus [it is] the property of the *yājyā*.
Sūtra 3.2.15, p. 760: "Sitting, he recites the *puro’nuvākyā*."
Purauṣṇik is a type of Uṣṇik;
the syllables in its quarters are 12, 8, and 8.
For example: "They yoke the two bay horses" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.98.9).
Why? Because the place for the first cup dedicated to Indra and Vāyu has already been established.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the displacement of the cups dedicated to the Aśvins and others—which are prescribed for the sake of specific results—has been stated.
That displacement occurs before the cup dedicated to Indra and Vāyu, and not before all [the cups], nor from some arbitrary point;
because the position of the first [cup] has already been established.
From what is the location known to belong to that [cup]? Because it is of such a nature:

"This is the location of the first [cup], since they take up [the cups] from the two ends, with the Aindravāyava being in front. Therefore, the final conclusion (siddhānta) is that there is a displacement (pratikarṣa) prior to the Aindravāyava.
And this is because of their having equal characteristics.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the cups dedicated to the Aśvins and others, which are heard [in the scripture] for the sake of specific results, [are to be treated as such] because they possess the same characteristics as the cup dedicated to Indra and Vāyu.
Those whose characteristics (*dharma*) are equal are "possessors of equal characteristics" (*tulyadharman*).
The state of being such is "possession of equal characteristics" (*tulyadharmatva*); [the reason is] because of that.
In that context, it is observed in connection with the continuous stream (*dhārā*); therefore, this precedence is prescribed specifically with reference to the stream.
And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) to this effect:

in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, for the sake of a specific result, the precedence of the cup for the Aśvins (*āśvinagraha*) is prescribed; and that precedence of the Aśvin cup occurs prior to the drawing of the cup for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyavya*).

Because it is preceded by the principle that the human goal is the sole purpose (*puruṣārthaika*), because the human goal is closely proximate, and because the accomplishment of the human goal is the singular result, there would be an entitlement for that [individual] according to the rule *tasyatvādhikāraḥ syāt* (6.2.12). Thus, through the application of these five grounds for entitlement, the performers of the sacrificial session (*sattriṇaḥ*) each obtain the entire fruit individually.
Su. Pṛ. 544:
Oṃ. Because the accomplishment of the human goal (puruṣārtha) depends solely on that [the sacrifice], there must be eligibility for it.
Among those [seventeen priests], the agency consisting of seventeen by seventeen, which effects the execution of a single performance, would exist as a distributed function (vyāsajyavṛtti).

If that were the case, the entirety would belong to all [the parts] combined as one single whole, and not to each individually; thus, in response to this objection which deviates from the established doctrine (*sūtra*), he states the final position (*siddhānta*):

"Therefore, for each [part], there is an independent entitlement (*adhikāra*), and the equality of the fruit of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-phala*) occurs in its totality; it is not the case that the fruit belongs to all [parts] collectively as a distributed property (*vyāsajyavṛtti*).
This is because the entitlement results solely in the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*)."

The accomplishment of a single human goal is "the accomplishment of one human goal" (puruṣārthaikasiddhi). This refers to the qualification (adhikāra). The accomplishment of the qualification is "the accomplishment of the qualification for the single human goal" (ekapuruṣārthasiddhādhikārasiddhi).
Moreover, the state of being an agent is not a collective property (vyāsajyavṛtti) residing in each [agent] in dependence on the other; rather, it resides in each individually.
Furthermore, the fruit is also complete in each individual [agent] and is not a collective property.
Moreover, because of the connection with origination, just as there would be a perception of all [agents], so too would the existence [of the action] be undivided.
In the *satra* sacrifice, each of the seventeen sacrificers possesses the status of a priest and performs the act of sacrificing individually, though in dependence upon the others.

However, the complete fruit must be obtained by one alone. Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the fact that a single ritual action is performed by many, because of its connection with the original injunction (*utpatti-saṃyoga*).

In the originative injunction, "Those desiring supernatural power (ṛddhi) should perform the Sattra," the use of the plural number expresses the connection of many individuals with the Sattra rite as its performers.
Precisely because this is taught in the originative injunction, there is no contradiction even in the case of a single rite having multiple performers,
just as it occurs in the case of seventeen [priests] participating without division.

Just as in the world, even though the action consisting of driving a chariot or a plow is undivided and unitary, there is the perception of many living beings—such as horses, oxen, and so forth—as its agents; likewise, there would be the existence [of agents] in the case of an undivided action.

Thus, just as in the case of living beings, even though the sacrificial action (*sattra*) is undivided and unitary, there would be the existence—the presence—of many agents; there is no contradiction whatsoever.
This second *siddhānta-sūtra* is intended to dispel the suspicion of such a contradiction.
Furthermore, "api ca" (moreover) is used as a conjunction of reasons (*hetu-samuccaye*).
However, in the *Sudhā* commentary, the reading is: "api cotpatti... tathā bhāvavibhāge syāt."

And this is the explanation (pp. 962–963): "Those desiring prosperity (*ṛddhi*) should perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*). Since the plural number inherent in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) expresses a plurality of those desiring prosperity, it is understood that each individual possesses the desire for prosperity; thus, because there is entitlement (*adhikāra*) for each individually, and since the plural number inherent in the verbal suffix expresses a plurality of agents (*kartṛ*), it is understood that each individual is an agent—therefore, there is entitlement for each individually. When it is stated by the rule, "Because of the connection with agency in the action, even when the existence of an agent is not determined at the time of origin," that there is entitlement for each individual, one might object: "If there is agency for each individually, then other actions would be rendered purposeless. To address this, it is shown that just as the simultaneous perception of a substance such as a cow by many people does not result in the purposelessness of either [the perceiver or the object], so too, even though the action (*bhāva*) is divided among separate agents, there is no purposelessness of other actions.
Thus [it is asked]:
"What is the logical option between two human goals? [It is] among optional sacrifices (kāmyeṣṭi) that have a single purpose."
"Being for the sake of man (*puruṣārthatva*) means being the object of an action that generates a cognition residing in the person.
*Bhāṭṭa.*, 3.4.8: "That the fruit is for the sake of man is understood precisely from the employment of the word 'desire' (*kāma*)."
"Or [it is] *puruṣārthatva* (being for the sake of the person), which is the state of being a performance of that which is to be accomplished as desired by oneself," according to the *Tantraratna*.

And that [is defined] in the *Śāstradīpikā* as: "The state of being for the sake of the person consists in being a means (*karaṇa*) and a fruit (*phala*), [and] being connected as a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) with what is to be done (*kartavyatva*), and being determined as such."

That too is not [the case]. Rather, it is the state of having a predicate-property as determined by being an object sought for its own sake (*svayaṃprārthita*). And "being sought for its own sake" means, in the view that heaven (*svarga*) is a particular place, the state of not being an object of a cognition produced by a knowledge of the means [to it] that is independent of scripture; or, in the view that it is a particular pleasure (*sukha*), the state of not being an object of a cognition produced by a knowledge of the means [to it] that is dependent on scripture.
Bhāṭṭa 4.1.2:
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an exclusion of the giving, cooking, and offering of oblations for the sake of human ends when performed by the consecrated sacrificer;
[this constitutes] a prohibition against those other than the officiating priests.
If one transgresses the prohibitions regarding human goals (*puruṣārtha*), there is for the person a transgression (*pratyavāya*) characterized by falling into hell. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 1395).
Furthermore, in the Veda, which consists of injunctions (*vidhi*), that which pertains to human goals is desired for the sake of facilitating the engagement of persons.
"Because it is closer to the human goal, the optional (kāmya) [rite] sets aside the obligatory (nitya);
and especially because the specific sets aside the general, since it operates when the former has already been established."
"Since all effort is indeed for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*), that effort is more powerful than the [mere] object.
Vārttika 2.1.12.22, p.

352. *Sudhā*: This is precisely the primary principle regarding the sublation of the obligatory (*nitya*) by the optional (*kāmya*); it is what will be stated in the third section (*adhikaraṇa*) under the rule "But in the case of the occasional (*naimittika*) in the archetype... (2.6.3.10).

p. 488. Because it is proximate to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), [it is] "like a person" (*puruṣakalpena*). According to the maxim, "That which is desired (*kāmya*) sublates that which is obligatory (*nitya*)" (Vārttika 1.4.11.22), the quality (*guṇa*) is one that is desired.
Even by one who has risen [from a previous state], it can be performed.

Or rather, in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there should be a restriction regarding the performer based on human capacity; because the sacrifice possesses that quality, this injunction applies specifically to him, excluding others.

In the preceding section, it was stated that regarding the sacrificial session (*sattra*) enjoined with reference to a collective group of seventeen performers, the qualification (*adhikāra*) belongs exclusively to Brāhmaṇas.
Here, however, the word "or" (*vā*) is used to indicate a distinction from that case; the meaning is:
where the injunction is based on the individual person rather than the collective group—that is, the injunction for the ritual act which refers to each individual person.

Thus, when a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is enjoined as being performed by a "man-like man"—that is, by a specific type of person—as in the case of the *adhvarakalpa* or the *āgrayaṇa-paśu* and so forth, there would be a restriction regarding the performer; specifically, only a Vaiśya is restricted as the performer.
This is because the sacrifice, such as the *adhvarakalpa*, possesses that quality [of being performed by a Vaiśya], namely the quality of having seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.
Furthermore, this is because such a similarity to the *sāmidhenīs* does not exist for those other than Vaiśyas, and because it is absent for Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas who are distinct from the Vaiśya.
For seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses have not been prescribed for them; rather,
this injunction regarding the similarity to the *sāmidhenīs* is possible only in the case of the Vaiśya, as it is the Vaiśya alone who is capable of performing this rite in its entirety.

Therefore, the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that in those sacrifices such as the *adhvarakalpa* and others where seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses are prescribed, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) belongs only to the Vaiśya, and not to the Brāhmaṇa or the Rājanya. This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), just as in the case of the *ājyeya* [sacrifice]. He states another reason for the prima facie position: that in those sacrifices where seventeen *sāmidhenīs* are mentioned, the entitlement belongs only to the Vaiśya and no one else.
Because of the statement, "The Vaiśya is indeed seventeenfold," the Vaiśya has the entitlement to perform sacrifices that have seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses;
the word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the reasons.
This is similar to the case of specific types of sacrifice.

The entitlement does not belong to the Vaiśya alone; rather, the entitlement belongs to all three social classes (varṇas) in rites such as the Adhvarakalpa and others, because of the distinctness of the connections.

The sentence "seventeen for the Vaiśya" prescribes seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses for the Vaiśya as a specific occasion (*nimitta*) within the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

However, the other sentence, "he should recite seventeen," prescribes the number seventeen for the Sāman based on its being obtained through the extended application (*codaka*) to the modified forms (*vikṛti*) of the sacrifice, such as the *adhvarakalpa*, which apply to all social classes (*varṇa*). Since this quality of being seventeen is subordinate to the primary act of sacrifice (*ijyā*), it does not have the agent (*kartṛ*) as its primary referent.

For this reason: since the injunction regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) is not connected with the Vaiśya—meaning that the injunction for the *sāman* chant is connected with the sacrifice (*ijyā*), not with a person such as a Vaiśya—it follows that in those sacrifices which possess similarity to the *sāmidhenī* verses, all three castes have the right to perform them, and not the Vaiśya alone; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Because it is a subordinate element of the sacrifice, it would be restricted by way of specification.

By the phrase "like a specific sacrifice," the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) has presented the Vaiśyastoma as an illustration for the position that only a Vaiśya is entitled to perform sacrifices such as the Adhvarakalpā and Āgrayaṇa, which require seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

Bhāṣya 6.4.5.17: "But the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) [are used] when there is no specific designation, because the deity is connected with that. It has been stated in the Brāhmaṇa that for a Brāhmaṇa, there is an option regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna): either preceded by the Soma sacrifice or preceded by the Iṣṭi sacrifice.

Furthermore, it was stated in the preceding sūtra that by the passage, "Whatever full-moon oblation (paurṇamāsa-havis) is today, that indeed follows immediately," only one oblation is displaced after the Soma sacrifice.
Now, he provides the answer to the question, "What is that single oblation?
That single oblation should be the *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Agni and Soma; by the word "but" (*tu*), other oblations are excluded.

Since there was no prior mention of Agni alone or Soma alone, when they are mentioned together in connection with Soma, because of the presence of the deity—given that the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) exists as a distributed property (*vyāsajyavṛtti*)—the conclusion is that the cake for Agni-Soma (*agnīṣomīyapuroḍāśa*) itself is that single oblation (*havis*), which is deferred after the Soma sacrifice.
We have explained this *sūtra* in such a manner, considering it appropriate and possible to explain it as a supplement to the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*).
However, in the *Bhāṣya* and other works, it has everywhere been explained as a *sūtra* belonging to the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*).
In this regard, the meaning intended by the author of the Sūtra remains the same; however, the introduction (avataraṇa) is different. It is as follows:
It was stated previously that there is a displacement of only one oblation belonging to the Full Moon sacrifice after the Soma sacrifice;
such is this doubt:
"Let it be that there is a displacement of only one oblation."
But that [deferral] should apply to the offering to Agni alone.

Since it was previously stated that "the Brāhmaṇa indeed has Agni as his deity," and because the word *adaḥ* (that) in the phrase "whatever offering belongs to the full moon today" can include the offering to Agni as well,
let there be a deferral from Soma only for the offering to Agni.
To this he replies: Although Agni was mentioned previously, Soma too has indeed been mentioned;
moreover, it is stated that "having sacrificed with Soma, one becomes associated with Agni and Soma."

Likewise, since Agni alone has not been specified, and because the status of being a deity has already been stated for Soma when it is joined with him due to the absence of [Agni] as a deity [in that context], the *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Agni-Soma (*agnīṣomīya*) alone is postponed after the Soma sacrifice. (This is the sūtra of the established conclusion.
The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of excluding Agni alone.

however, that clarified butter (*ājya*) should also be present, not the *puroḍāśa* alone.

It is not possible to displace the clarified butter of the Upāṃśuyāja.
This is because it has mixed deities;
for that [animal] belongs either to Agni and Soma, or to Prajāpati, or to Viṣṇu.

Therefore, although the *ājya* (clarified butter) belonging to Agni and Soma is postponed after the Soma sacrifice due to its *agnīṣomīya* nature, there is no postponement of the *upāṃśuyāja* *ājya*, because it can also occur before the Soma sacrifice by virtue of its *prājāpatya* or *vaiṣṇava* nature; rather, only the *puroḍāśa* (cake) is postponed.
This is like the case of the offering to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*).
Just as in the injunction "He makes the fourth [offering] for Agni," the term "for Agni" (*āgneya*) does not include the *aindrāgna* cake, because that belongs to mixed deities.
Thus, it arises directly;
likewise, the clarified butter (ājya) does as well.
Therefore, the Upāṃśuyāja should not be displaced from the Soma sacrifice.
The sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) are of two kinds: primary and secondary.
Among these, those dedicated to Agni and others are primary.
And the second is the *paśupuroḍāśa*, which consists of the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the deity of the animal sacrifice.
According to Ke. (Vi. 10.1.9), the *puroḍāśa* is not employed for the purpose of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, but rather it is employed for the purpose of the *āgneya* sacrifice.
In the *traidhātavī* sacrifice, the middle *puroḍāśa* is made of barley alone.
Bhāṣya 10.7.16.51–57. The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is prescribed for the sacrifice, not for the oblation (homa).

The instruction regarding "the two *puroḍāśas*" applies to those who are already qualified by the context of the *puroḍāśa* offerings, because it is based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), just as in the case of the *vaiśyastoma*.

Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One should cause a non-Soma-sacrificer to sacrifice with the two *puroḍāśas* alone—namely, the one for Agni and the one for Indra-Agni; but one should cause a Soma-sacrificer to sacrifice with the *sānnāyya*."
From the sentence "with the two *puroḍāśa* cakes," it is understood that there is an instruction regarding the two *puroḍāśas* for those who are qualified but have not performed the *soma* sacrifice;
the meaning is that the instruction is understood as granting eligibility for the two *puroḍāśas* to one who has not performed the *soma* sacrifice.
This is because of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), for it is heard [in scripture]: "One should cause him who has not performed the *soma* sacrifice to sacrifice."
It is like the Vaiśyastoma; just as by the injunction "A Vaiśya should sacrifice with the Vaiśyastoma," a Vaiśya has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for the Vaiśyastoma, so too here.

Therefore, the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" has the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*): "One should cause a non-Soma-sacrificer to sacrifice with the two *puroḍāśa* cakes. That is to say: a non-Soma-sacrificer desiring heaven should sacrifice with the two *puroḍāśas*.
Thus ends the first prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
However, there is no independent application for the non-eternal; rather, because the injunction is connected with the eternal, it constitutes a supplementary part of the statement (*vākyaśeṣatva*).
Having refuted the position that it is a supplementary part of the statement, he states another position.
The section concerning the non-permanent does not apply here;
for the state of being a non-Soma-sacrificer is non-permanent, since after performing the Soma sacrifice one becomes a Soma-sacrificer. The New and Full Moon sacrifices, however, are permanent.
And likewise, for one who is impermanent and has not performed the Soma sacrifice, eligibility for the obligatory Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is not possible.
The injunction "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" is connected exclusively with what is obligatory.

Therefore, for this reason, that which was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin)—namely, that it functions as a supplementary part of the sentence (vākyaśeṣatva)—is not tenable.

However, for one who desires heaven but has not performed the Soma sacrifice (*asomayājin*), the *āgneya* and *aindrāgna* offerings— being distinct rites— are prescribed as additional elements possessing the original (*prākṛta*) characteristics of the *āgneya*. And since [the agent] is not a primary factor by virtue of a single part,

the position that the statement "with two *puroḍāśa* cakes [he should sacrifice] for the non-Soma-sacrificer" is a supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the injunction "one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" is seen through another method.

And if it were a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), then a connection would have to be stated between the non-Soma-sacrificer and the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) which constitute parts of the Darśapūrṇamāsa; yet that is not tenable.

Alternatively, even if it were a supplementary part of the sentence, a connection between the non-Soma-sacrificing agent and the two sacrificial cakes would be tenable, because the agent is primary and is designated as the primary factor.

Therefore, it is not a supplementary part of a sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), but rather an injunction for a distinct ritual action (*karmāntaravidhi*). Furthermore, because [the *stoma*] is complete, it is likewise in the case of the *stoma*.
This refutes the example of the *vaiśyastoma* stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).
In the case of the Vaidya-stoma, it is logical that it serves as a supplementary element (śeṣa) to the injunction regarding its specific application (adhikāra),
because the Vaidya-stoma is a complete whole;
for it is not a mere part of anything else, owing to its independence.
And because [the sacrifice] possesses fruitfulness,
whereas the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are merely constituent parts and not themselves the means of accomplishing the fruit;
therefore, they do not constitute a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to the qualification (*adhikāra*).
But it is an injunction for another action.
If it is argued that it must belong to the agent [of the original action], we reply:
no, it is not an injunction for another action.

However, this injunction—"One should cause a non-Soma-sacrificer to sacrifice with two *puroḍāśa* cakes"—might pertain to the agent (*kartṛ*), the subsidiary agent (*aṅgakartṛ*), or the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). And that [injunction] will be based on the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*). This is the third position.
If this is argued,
we say no, because it is for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), and once [the act] is already established, there is no purpose in an instruction.
There is no instruction regarding the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) who is the performer of the subsidiary acts (*aṅga*).

Because it serves as a subordinate purpose—that is, because the performance of the subsidiary member (*aṅga*) exists for the sake of the quality (*guṇa*)—the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is merely subordinate to the principal agent, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
Furthermore, he has no fruit of his own.
And since the act of officiating is already established by implication, its restatement (*anuvāda*) does not serve the purpose of an original injunction (*upadeśa*).
Therefore, it is an instruction for the officiating priest.
Consequently, it is an injunction for two distinct rites.

Since that is the logical principle within the context of the two rites, there would be a teaching regarding the time [of performance] by means of an indicative mark (liṅga) for the subordinate elements (guṇas).

Furthermore, regarding the *saṃpāta* and *āgrayaṇa* cups which occupy the same location, it can be said that "whoever departs from the one [the *saṃpāta*] departs from the *āgrayaṇa* as well.
And that much constitutes the occasion [for the rite].
That which is excluded even from the mixed *anāgrayaṇa* is not utilized either for the prohibition or for the injunction;
for there is no statement that "what is excluded from the *anāgrayaṇa* is not *pālīvata*.
Or, if this were the meaning, then even that which is excluded from the *āgrayaṇa* would, by virtue of being excluded from both the *āgrayaṇa* and the *anāgrayaṇa*, result in being *apālīvata*.

Therefore, because the statement "he has departed from the Āgrayaṇa" is a verb and lacks an independent basis for its own authority, one must necessarily understand it as "having departed from the Āgrayaṇa [cup] for the time being.
And since this applies equally to the *saṃpāta* (the mixture), its connection with the deity is established.
Furthermore, it is not possible to perform the subsequent mixing while discarding the status of the previous deity; thus, its non-recognition is justified, just like the eating of the *pūrṇaka*.

"But surely this is merely a part of that very same substance which was previously intended for another deity"—this statement from the *Bhāṣya* intends to refer to the state of having previously been so.
However, the Teacher, thinking "I myself accept this," offers a rebuttal: "For no part of what has been offered is seen.
The intention is that nothing other than what was offered remains for that deity, because it has already been removed.
But the opponent, intending to show that [the deity] has not arisen, says: "Is it not the case even in the case of the primordial matter (prakṛti)?
The answer is: "At the time of its conceptualization (saṃkalpa), there is the designation of a deity therein.
The other says: "In this case too, it was exactly so."
The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntavādī) says: "This alone is the defining characteristic of the original state (prakṛti).
Furthermore, no indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) of the Agnīdhra has been made there;
however, in this case, the fact of being removed is clearly stated.
Therefore, it is established that the term "burning" (*palīvāna*) is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Soma: The connection [of this section] is due to the counter-argument (*pratyavasthāna*) as before.
At the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), there are the cups for Indra and Vāyu, Mitra and Varuṇa, and the Aśvins; these are the cups for two deities (*dvidevatya*).
After their oblation, their remnants reach the Āditya vessel; at the third pressing, they pass from the Āditya vessel into the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
As it is stated in the Viṣṇu-śruti: "The two-deity [cups] proceed from the Āditya vessel to the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
Then, after the morning pressing, when the Pātnīvata cup is being drawn..."
At the time of the carving, are those two deities [to be offered] together with Pālīvata?
Are they to be indicated or not? According to the previous principle, let there be an indication;
however, in the case of Pālīvata, this does not apply beyond the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
Regarding the desire for the former deities, only one who possesses a wife (*patnīvān*) is eligible.
*Bhāṭṭa*: The remnants of the dual-deity offerings, such as those dedicated to Indra-Agni and others, having come into the *āditya* vessel, then proceed to the *āgrayaṇa* vessel.
This is the section concerning the indication of the former deities (sūtra 2597): "Those which possess the former..."
The Pālīvata cup is drawn from the Āgrayaṇa vessel.

When that [Āgrayaṇa] is being consumed, the Dvidevatya cups should also be indicated [as part of the same act], just as before, because of the connection of the Āgrayaṇa itself with the deities of the Pālīvata.

This being the prima facie view, [the correct conclusion is: since the scriptural statement "he draws the Pālīvata from the Āgrayaṇa" expresses the Āgrayaṇa as the source (apādāna), the status of being Pālīvata belongs to what has departed from that [source], and not to the Āgrayaṇa itself.

And just like the *āgrayaṇa* cup, even that which is not an *āgrayaṇa* is excluded because of its contact; therefore, even a cup for two deities (*dvidevatya*) excludes [the previous deity] due to its connection with another deity. Furthermore, because they were not indicated in the archetype (*prakṛti*) by way of their former state, [deities such as] Indra-Vāyu and others are not to be indicated.
Maṇḍana says: "But in the case of the *pālīvata*, [one excludes] the previous [deity] by means of the offering.
Śaṅkara says: "The same applies to the *pālīvata* cup."
[Devatānoddhā]: This is the principle of the "preceding deities" (*pūrvadevalvanyāya*).
For it is accepted that a collection of words situated within a single sentence constitutes a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) when they produce a cognition that is mutually interdependent.

Because they produce cognitions that are mutually dependent, there is no possibility here of the principle of the "destruction of the earlier by the later" (*pūrvadaivalyanyāya*). This is because it is illogical for a cognition produced by a subsequent word—which contradicts the cognition generated by the preceding word—to constitute a sublation (*bādhaka*) of that former cognition. (Su. p. 1172).
[This refers to] the principle of the "destruction of the earlier by the later."
6|5|159. Mīko., p. 499: For the word "subsequent" (uttara) is conditioned by what precedes it, and the word "prior" (pūrva) is conditioned by what follows it.
Bhāṣya 10|3|4|127: The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin) must refute the position of the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntavādin), not just anything at random.
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3.1.36, page 663:

"The very sequence of the meanings of the constituent parts (*pūrvapadārtha*)—supported by the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) understood from the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*)—is the authority for the restriction of the sequence of the produced meanings (*utpannārtha*).
Here, "prior" (*pūrva*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), since the same applies to the subsequent as well.
This is the principle of the sequence of means of proof (*pramāṇa*).
Among the means of proof beginning with direct statement (*śruti*) and ending with indicative mark (*liṅga*), each preceding one possesses greater force than the subsequent ones.
That which precedes becomes an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*).
(That which has a preceding [element] for this subsequent one is "possessing a predecessor" [pūrvavān].
"Possessing a predecessor" is for the purpose of non-injunction; its capacity [is established] in the traditional collection [of texts].
"The Vaiśvānara [offering] on twelve potsherds should be offered when a son is born"—thus the Jāteṣṭi is heard in scripture.

In that regard: "Insofar as it is on twelve potsherds, the Gāyatrī purifies him with spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa); insofar as it is on nine potsherds, the Triṣṭubh bestows splendor upon him; insofar as it is on ten potsherds, the Triṣṭubh bestows food-eating power upon him; insofar as it is on twelve potsherds, the Jagatī bestows cattle upon him."

Regarding the passage, "Upon the birth of which [son] one performs this sacrifice, he becomes purified, radiant, an eater of food, possessed of sensory power, and rich in cattle," various options for the number of potsherds—from eight up to eleven—are heard in the scripture.

In the inquiry as to whether these numbers, such as eight and so forth, are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The accessories, such as the fire-altar and others, are "possessed of prior authority" (*pūrvavantaḥ*); that is, they have authoritative scriptures for their application, being obtained through mantras and other means.

Therefore, in those cases, words such as *agnihotra* do not have the purpose of enjoining; they do not function as injunctions. However, in the present context, within the collection of terms such as *aṣṭakapāla*, there would be that capacity—the capacity to enjoin a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhāna*). Consequently, these are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), but they are indeed injunctions of qualities.

On this point, the *Sudhā* states: Those words such as "vaiśvadeva" and the like, which possess a prior [context], refer to a ritual action already produced by another sentence as qualified by a specific accessory (*guṇa*); yet when they denote a subsequent accessory that is contradictory to that [prior one], they do not function as injunctions because they lack the capacity to denote a subsequent contradictory accessory in a ritual action that has already become self-sufficient through the accessory mentioned in its own [original] sentence.

However, because words such as *aṣṭākapāla* are part of the traditional recitation (*samāmnāya*), are uttered together, and occur within a single sentence, their capacity for application is understood through the restrictive force of the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*). Thus, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the word *vaiśvadeva* possesses that same capacity [to restrict the sacrifice]. The meaning of the Sūtra is this: while there is a slight sublation (*bādha*) of what is enjoined after the originative injunction by what is enjoined at the time of the originative injunction, such a sublation does not exist here. The author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) while refuting the prima facie view with the word "but" (*tu*): "But if the purpose were the injunction of a quality (*guṇa*), those [words] would be devoid of that quality in the performance; they would be meaningless, for they have no purposeful application toward that [quality]. The meaning is: if the purpose of these words were merely to enjoin a quality (such as the eight potsherds), then in the actual performance of the rite, those words would lack that specific quality; they would become redundant, as they would have no functional significance regarding that quality. By using the word "but," he sets aside the prima facie position and asserts the final view.

If a sentence were accepted for the purpose of enjoining qualities such as "eightfold" and so forth, then those qualities—namely the eightfold nature and the rest—would not be qualities of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice;
therefore, they would be useless in its performance, that is, in the ritual execution of the Vaiśvānara.
For there is no meaningful application of them either toward that sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) or toward the sacrifice itself.
If, however, it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), then the praise of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice arises.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the eight-pot-sherd offerings and so forth are explanatory passages;
thus, their rejection is not tenable.

To this, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says: "If it is argued that because those [qualities] such as 'eightfoldness' and so forth are not prescribed, the *śeṣa*—that is, the supplementary explanatory passage (*stāvaka vākyaśeṣa*)—is inappropriate; [we reply:
they are appropriate for the purpose of praise, since there is no distinction [between what is prescribed and what is praised]."

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) states that the sentences concerning the eight potsherds (*aṣṭakapāla*) and so forth are supplementary to the sentence concerning the twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*). [He explains:

"In the sense of an injunction" (*vidhānārthe*), it is enjoined; here *vidhāna* is derived from the root *dhā* with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*), meaning the injunction is being enjoined upon the twelve potsherds for the purpose of praise.
By means of the purpose consisting of praise, the statements regarding the eight potsherds and so forth become logically consistent.
Because there is no division—that is, because of the absence of division—due to the identity [of the number] with twelve, eight, and so forth;
therefore, the establishment of the numbers eight and so on as subsisting within the twelve-potsherd offering is justified as being for the purpose of praise (*stuti*).

However, in the *Sudhā* commentary, following the *Vārttika*, it is stated: "And because of proximity, the words 'eight' and so on are capable of producing the cognition of that which is a part of it," thus explaining [the term *avibhāga*] as "because of non-division" and [the term *sāmīpya*] as "because of proximity."
If it be argued that there must be a cause,
to this the opponent replies again:
"The number eight and so forth may be the cause of the fruit, such as spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa)."
The fruit is stated by the passage beginning with "He indeed becomes purified and radiant.
The injunction regarding each individual [recitation] follows the praise beginning with "By the Gāyatrī alone.

Through the *sārvavācika* (all-encompassing) statements such as "That which consists of eight potsherds," the connection with the fruits—beginning with "he becomes purified"—is established for each of the rites enjoined individually, according to their respective order.
If it is argued that "therefore, [the injunction] has an object," [we reply:
the reason is its lack of purpose; for the causes belong to the agent, and the injunction is indeed for the sake of a subordinate element (guṇa).

In this context, the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) argues using the sūtra "It would be the cause" (*kāraṇaṃ syāt*), asserting that the sacrifices involving eight potsherds (*aṣṭakapāla*) and so forth should be the subject matter as having results such as spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and not that the twelve-potsherd sacrifice (*dvādaśakapāla*) is being praised by means of [the others]. To this, the proponent (siddhāntin) replies:
The passage beginning with "vaiśvānaram" and ending with "paśumān bhavati" constitutes a single sentence.
It concludes with the result stated in the sentences concerning the eight-potsherd and other offerings, namely, "When [a son] is born, one performs this *iṣṭi*," and so forth.
Therefore, having eight sons and so forth cannot be the cause for the fruits such as having a son or possessing Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*), nor can they be enjoined as such a cause;

for that would result in meaninglessness, which entails the consequence of fruitlessness. Why? Because those [qualities] are the causes for the father—the agent—of the results consisting of having a son or not having a son.

Therefore, the word *aṣṭākapāla* and so forth is neither a name (*nāmadheya*), nor an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the ritual action, nor an injunction of an accessory regarding the results; rather, it has the purpose of praising through its accessory qualities—that is, its aim is praise by means of those qualities—and thus the Vaiśvānara sacrifice itself is what is being enjoined.

Consequently, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the state of having eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapālatva*) and so on is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already known, serving as an *arthavāda*.
[Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 6.1]: "Those preceded by the former are not for the purpose of injunction; their capacity is [found] in the traditional recitation."

"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born. In that there is a cake on eight potsherds, he purifies him with the Gāyatrī and with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). In that there is one on nine potsherds, he bestows vigor through the Triṣṭubh. In that there is one on ten potsherds, he bestows food-eating through the Virāj. In that there is one on eleven potsherds, he bestows sensory power through the Triṣṭubh. In that there is one on twelve potsherds, he bestows cattle through the Jagatī."

Regarding the passage: "He for whom, upon birth, one performs this sacrifice—he indeed becomes pure, radiant, possessed of vigor, endowed with sensory power, and rich in cattle"—various options concerning the number of potsherds (*kapāla*) are heard.
In this regard, there is a doubt: are the numbers such as eight injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*), or are they merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*)?

In this regard, Prabhākara, out of a desire for systematic coherence (*saṃgati*), has described the topic as follows: Since [the words] such as "that which is on eight potsherds" (*yadaṣṭakapāle bhavati*) do not serve as reminders of what has already been enjoined, they cannot be non-connected as *mantras*. They are not names (*nāmadheya*) merely because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verbal root-meaning; nor are they injunctions of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), because there is no proximity of a verbal action capable of being connected with qualities such as "eightness" (*aṣṭatva*).
Nor is there an injunction of a quality in the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, because it is impossible to enjoin another number while the number twelve is already delimited.
Because the numbers eight and so forth have an equal connection with the injunctional state (*vidhyadaśā*), they are not merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*).
Thus, since there is no injunctional character whatsoever, there is a lack of authoritative validity for such passages as "when it consists of eight potsherds" (*yadaṣṭākapālo bhavati*).
This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is precisely as stated in the *Bhāṣya*, namely that it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

As it has been said: "Because, according to the logic of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) to be stated later, its connection is possible as a prescription of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
Thus, the section (*adhikaraṇa*) is introduced exactly in the order [of the text].

Having defined *nāmadheyatva* (the status of being a name) as that which has *guṇavidhitva* (the status of being an injunction of an accessory quality) as its counter-correlate, the status of being an *arthavāda* (an explanatory or commendatory statement) is now defined by extension as that which has *guṇavidhitva* as its counter-correlate.
Herein lies the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*):

in the passage, "Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara," since an action qualified by both a substance and a deity is enjoined, the injunction of the twelve potsherds is indeed established.
Nor is there any other way for the [offerings] heard immediately following that— from the eight potsherds up to the eleven potsherds— to be understood.
For they cannot be understood by name, because in the ritual involving twelve potsherds, the name "eight potsherds" lacks a basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
Nor can it be an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), because it is impossible to praise the twelve-potsherd offering by means of the eight-potsherd [offering].
Now, one might argue: "Since the eight-potsherd is indeed included within the twelve-potsherd, it must therefore be either a name (*nāmadheya*) or an explanatory eulogy.
This is not so.
In a "great number" (*mahāsaṃkhyā*), there is no intermediate number beyond unity.
For number is produced by relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).
Indeed, one does not designate the number eight with respect to the same set of objects with respect to which the number twelve is designated.
(Why? Because when another number arises, there is no other cognition that serves as the cause for the arising of that other number, due to the inherent nature of numbers.
A number does not define its object merely by its own existence; rather, it does so by excluding other numbers. Thus, the number eight and others are not included within the number twelve.
However, there are no other distinct types [of numbers] capable of giving rise to different numbers.

Furthermore, the terms "eight potsherds" (*aṣṭakapāla*) and so forth do not denote the physical substrates themselves, such that they could somehow constitute either a name (*nāmadheya*) or a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). This will be explained later when the matter of the final offering is discussed. Or, even if the intermediate number is contained within the larger number, nevertheless, this is a *saṃskṛta-taddhita* (a secondary derivative meaning "prepared upon") in the sense that "the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) prepared on eight potsherds is called 'eight-potsherded'."

Furthermore, in the sentence concerning the twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*), it is not understood that the number eight—which fulfills the number twelve—is an independent qualification of the specific potsherds for the purpose of preparing the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); rather, it is [an attribute] only in relation to the number four.

As for the claim that even when there are eight potsherds, the attainment of the number eight is intended only in relation to the number four, that is not possible, because since it is dependent, the production of the entire substance would be impossible.

Now, if it is argued that the number eight—which is independent of the group of four and included within the twelve potsherds—serves as a qualification for the specific potsherds intended for the preparation of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), then, in the statement concerning the "twelve-potsherd" offering, such an eight would neither function as a name nor as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). What then? It must be a prescriptive injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).

As it has been said: "Even though [the number eight] exists in reality as part of the larger number [twelve], because it does not serve as a defining delimiter, it cannot be a qualifier of the ritual action."
(Vārttika, p. 349).
Likewise: "By expressing a meaning already known, the name sublates the meaning [of the generic term];
otherwise, these [characteristics] such as non-attainment would exist here in the case of an option with the Vaiśvadeva."
(Vārttika, p. 349).

Nor should it be argued that since the Vaiśvānara sacrifice under discussion has twelve substances prescribed by its originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), how can qualities such as "eight" and so forth be enjoined therein?
For this single sentence is not one [injunction], but rather multiple, each enjoining the Vaiśvānara sacrifice with distinct qualifications.

Therefore, since all [of these] are prescribed as originating together (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), there is no distinction whatsoever regarding their relative strength or weakness. Even though they are enjoined within a single sentence, the option (*vikalpa*) arises precisely from the inherent nature of the numbers.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to enjoin again that very twelve-pot-sherd cake (*dvādaśa-kapāla*) which has already been prescribed, its mention at the end serves solely for the purpose of restatement (*anuvāda*).

Therefore, those [sentences] which express a matter already previously enjoined are not for the purpose of injunction; thus, in the enumeration of "eightfoldness" and so forth, their capacity is indeed only the capacity for injunction. This being the prima facie view, it is replied: "But when the purpose is the injunction of a quality, its subordinate qualities would be useless in the performance; for there is no meaningfulness with respect to that [injunction]."
This is the intended meaning:

this would indeed be so if, in the Vaiśvānara sacrifice which is already restricted by the number twelve enjoined in the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), the [qualities] could be enjoined by means of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Nor should it be argued that, because of their being part of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), all of them are equally enjoined in the originative injunction and thus there is no restriction by the number twelve.
Because when there is an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), there is no unity of sentence (*ekavākyatva*) at all.

Indeed, the definition of a single sentence is: "Now, [two or more words] constitute a single sentence because of their unity, provided that if they were separated, they would be expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*)" (Mīmāṃsāsūtra 2.1.46).
And such unity does not exist here, because it is impossible for mutually contradictory numbers to be connected to a single efficient force (*bhāvanā*).
Nor can there be mutual expectancy through a process of differentiation, precisely because of their mutual contradiction;

thus, there is no possibility of prescribing a quality (*guṇavidhi*) for the twelve-potsherd Vaiśvānara sacrifice. Nor can there be the prescription of another distinct sacrifice qualified by a quality—such as "the eight-potsherd Vaiśvānara [cake] comes into being"—with the word *vaiśvānara* understood in its reverse sense, due to the very fault of such a reversal in what is to be performed.
For indeed, a modified rite is performed only when there is no other alternative;
and it must be stated that in this case, there is an alternative by way of being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
As it has been said: "The term *vaiśvānara* here is not intended for the performance of a sacrifice."
And because it is connected with a different case-ending, this [suffix] is not meaningless.
(Vārttika, p. 350).

[Objection: "In that case, then, let the qualities such as being eightfold and so forth be enjoined with respect to the results, such as purity and the like, in their respective order by depending upon the Vaiśvānara sacrifice under discussion; thus, the statement 'By the Gāyatrī alone he purifies him with spiritual luster' and so forth will function as an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise).
[Reply: Not so.

Beginning with "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*) to Vaiśvānara when a son is born," and concluding with "Because it is on twelve potsherds; on the birth of whom one offers this sacrifice," this single sentence is understood to be intended for the injunction of the twelve potsherds, since the twelve potsherds are mentioned both in the opening and the conclusion. Even so, if—as in the case of "For one desiring cattle, [one should use] a milk-pail"—the connection with a result were more clearly perceived as being through the desire for a specific outcome (such as cattle) regarding the eight potsherds and so forth, then let a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) be admitted, provided that [the result] is already established by a prior [text].
"The Vedas are the source of expression through distinctness" (4.4.19).

However, as for the nature of the principle of non-difference, it is stated: "The words *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* follow the duality of that [composite], and thus they are intended to be so" (Vārttika 2.2.3).

It is stated that the terms *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* possess the status of denoting a composite whole (*samudāyitva*), following the duality of the two groups expressed by the words *sudhā-paurṇamāsa* and *māvāsyā*.
"The Vedas have their origin in distinct declarations.

Since specific sacrifices possess fruits, and since possessing a fruit is the primary characteristic—another term for which is "predominance"—and because that which is proximate and connected to a fruit possesses the status of being a cause for subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*), and because postulating a fruit through unspoken logic would result in excessive complexity (*gaurava*), it is proper that the Āghāra offerings and other such elements are merely subsidiaries; this is the meaning of the Sūtra.
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 723).

For there are indeed designations based on distinctness, such as: "The *nigadas* are not to be recited as sacrificial formulas; one sacrifices with the *ṛc*s alone" (Bhāṣya 2.1.13). [Sūtra: Because they reside in distinct entities, number should cause a difference in ritual acts.

There is the Vājapeya sacrifice; "By means of the Vājapeya, one attains self-sovereignty (svārājya)"; [the ritual procedure] for the earth-altar, the Pṛṣṭha-chandas, and the earth-altar [is as follows].

Just as on earth, herbs do not grow by way of being the substratum because their conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) supersedes their etymological derivation (*yoga*), so too in the present case; this is indeed the *Sāhasrī* [view], namely *Saṃkarṣa* 3.3.17: "This other substance composed of clay called the 'earth-globe,' which is taught as independent (*anārabhyādhīta*) from the *pṛṣadājya*, *prāṇa*, and *graha* offerings—this very great earth is not to be given away in the *viśvajit* sacrifice where one's entire property is donated."

In the *Bhāṣya* (on Jaimini Sūtra 6.1.23), it is stated that at the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), [the deities] are seen as the lords of territories on the introductory day (*prāyaṇīya*), the concluding day (*udayanīya*), and the tenth day, but not as a settlement (*niveśa*).

Of the entire terrestrial globe. 6.12.3. Whether by means of the rotation of the terrestrial globe and the three worlds as described in the Purāṇas, or because—as in the case of the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter) and the *praṇagraha* (libations)—those [offerings] mentioned without a specific context are seen to be actually earth through some figurative description of its qualities, it would follow that they should be placed within the *prakṛti* (archetype). However, due to the statement: "At the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* [sacrifices], on the tenth day, just as we see the gods above, so too are [the libations] taken from above the lower region," this constitutes the *pṛṣadājya-adhikaraṇa*.
The *pṛṣṭha* [laud].
For the purpose of the *pṛṣṭha*, the *pṛṣṭha* [laud] in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is accomplished by means of a single *sāman*.
It is established that [the *bṛhat*] should be used in the *bṛhat-pakṣa*.

Thus, in the Jyotiṣṭoma and likewise in its modification (namely, the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* of the Gavāmayana), it must be accomplished by means of one or the other for the sake of conforming to the injunction (*codanā*).

Bhāṣya 10.6.15: Regarding the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* as the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras], because the context (*prakaraṇa*) is the same, they possess identical characteristics (*samānadharmī*), as indicated by the mention of "the first" and so forth.

The term *pṛṣṭhāni* is the name of the ritual action prescribed by the injunction "they praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*"; it is established through the well-known meaning of its parts (*avayavaprasiddhi*), as all [the hymns] are called *pṛṣṭhas*. Bhāṣya 1.4.13 states:

"Because Vāyu moved upon their backs (*pṛṣṭhe vyakrāmat*)," since the *Rathantara* and other [sāmans] were produced when the waters were touched upon their backs, therefore they are understood to be *pṛṣṭhas*.
And because they have that as their nature, the term *pṛṣṭha* is well-established in the case of the Vāmadevya and others.
(Vārttika, Pṛṣṭha section, pp. 331–332).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are only four *pṛṣṭhas*, such as the Māhendra-stotra and so forth, not all six.

Bhāṣya 7.3.16: "In the Viśvajit sacrifice, the *pavamāna* [laud] has the *rathaṃtara*; the *ārbhava* has the *bṛhat*; the *vairūpa* belongs to the Hotṛ; the *vairāja* belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa; the *raivata* belongs to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; the *śākvara* belongs to the Acchāvāka. 7.3.18: It is heard in the context of the *cayana* (fire-altar construction) that "one worships with the *pṛṣṭhas*.

In that case, the properties of the *pṛṣṭhas*—such as meditation on the earth, the ocean, and so forth, or the *hikāra* and other such elements—are not to be performed; rather, the worship is to be performed with those [specific *sāmans*] alone.
Therefore, the word *pṛṣṭha* here refers to something else related to it.
In the expression "he worships with the *pṛṣṭhas*" (*pṛṣṭhair upatiṣṭhate*), the word *pṛṣṭha* denotes those substances.

As stated in the Bhīko (Bhāṣyakaumudī), p. 38: "In the case of 'in the fire-piling (*agnicayana*) he worships with the *pṛṣṭhas*', the verbal root prescribes the act of worship itself, which has the piling as its substrate through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); in that very context, the *pṛṣṭhas* function as the instrument (*karaṇatva*)."
What was stated by the *Kaustubha* itself—namely, "it is indeed denotation (*abhidhāna*) through indication (*lakṣaṇā*)" and so forth—has been set forth in another way by another [author].
However, because this is a different example, there is merely a difference in the manner of description;
thus, the mind need not be troubled regarding the view of the *Kaustubha*.
(Bhāṣya on PMS 7.3.12): Having begun with "They praise with the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]," six verses (*ṛc*) are recited.
‘*Ami tvā śūra nonumaḥ*’ is the first [verse]; there the *Rathantara* Sāman [is sung]. ‘*Tvāmiddhi havāmahe*’ is the second; there the *Bṛhat* [is sung].
‘*Kayā naścitra ābhuvat*’ is the third; there the *Vāmadevya* [is sung].
The fourth [day] is with the hymn "taṃ vo dasmamṛtīṣaham"; therein is the Naudhasa.
The fifth is with "abhi pra vaḥ surādhasam"; therein is the Dyeta.
The sixth is with "tarorbhirvo viduṣṭamam"; therein is the Kāleya.

In that regard, there is an option between the Bṛhat and the Rathantara; likewise, there is also an option between the Naudhasa and the Śyaita. And that [latter pair] is the Naudhasa in the case of the Rathantara.
In the case of the *bṛhat* [sāman], it is established that "it should be chanted.
Thus, in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, there are four fixed *pṛṣṭha-stotras*:

"the *pṛṣṭhas* are seventeenfold" (in the archetype); "the *hotṛ*'s *pṛṣṭha* is twenty-onefold," "the *maitrāvaruṇa*'s is twenty-threefold," "the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*'s is seventeenfold," and "the *acchāvāka*'s is fifteenfold" (in the modified sacrifice).
"They praise with the *pṛṣṭha* [hymns]"—this *stotra* is a primary act (*pradhānakarman*), not a subsidiary act (*guṇakarman*).
Mā. 2.1.5.13–29: The function of the *pṛṣṭha* belongs to one [specific hymn], while the function of the *parisāman* belongs to the others.
In the Viśvajit sacrifice characterized by all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras (sarvapṛṣṭha),
there is an extended application (*atideśa*) of the six *pṛṣṭha* stotras belonging to the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*).
Regarding the *pṛṣṭha* (the *bṛhat* chant of the Hotṛ priest), there is a restrictive rule in certain modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).
This should be understood in the context of the passage beginning, "In the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the Vājapeya, [there are] optional [elements].
For the purpose of the *pṛṣṭha* [laud], there is something other than the *rathaṃtara*, because its source (*yoni*) is different and because it is distinguished from the *svāhā*.
In the Vaiśyastoma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "The Kaṇvarathantara is the *pṛṣṭha* [laud].

Regarding the inquiry as to which *yoni* (source-verse) that Kaṇvarathantara should be sung from, the author states the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) view: The Kaṇvarathantara, which is heard as distinct from the Rathantara for the purpose of the *pṛṣṭha* stotra, should reside in the *yoni* of the Rathantara, namely "abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ. Because it is preceded by that *yoni*, the very same *yoni* which exists for the Rathantara in the Jyotiṣṭoma becomes its *yoni*.
"Of the Kaṇvarathantara"—this indicates that the Kaṇvarathantara is preceded by its own source-hymn (*yoni*).
Now, one might object: since the Vaiśyastoma is preceded by the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Kaṇvarathantara should also have the *Bṛhat* as its source-hymn.
This is not so.
Because the verses of the *kaṇvarathantara* are distinct from those of the *bṛhatsāman* due to their separate division,
the term "rathantara" applied to the *kaṇvarathantara* is based on a common property (*dharmanimitta*).
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is that in the *vaiśyastoma*, the *kaṇvarathantara* sāman should be sung upon the source-verses (*yoni*) of the *rathantara*.
Or rather, it should be sung in its own source, because it is designated as such.
Setting aside the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) which was indicated by the sūtra through the word "or" (vā), he states the established conclusion (siddhānta):
the Kaṇvarathantara should be sung in its own source.
[Regarding the verse] "punānaḥ soma yojathe" (as stated in the *iti-ku*):
because it is designated as "all," the term *kaṇvarathantara* denotes that which is qualified by all its specific attributes.

The name *kaṇvarathantara* applies to the entire [sāman] which possesses the *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratihāra*, *upadrava*, and *nidhana*, and which includes all the *stomas* and the repetition of the time-measures.
In this regard, the *yoni* [verse] is also a qualifying factor.
Therefore, it should be sung in its own *yoni*.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Regarding the purpose of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra]:
if it is argued that it is for the sake of pacifying the *pṛṣṭha*, like the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

If the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) should argue: "The term *rathaṃtara* in the *kaṇvarathaṃtara* is applicable because it possesses the characteristics (*dharma*) of the *rathaṃtara*, just like the term *yūpa* [is applied to a post]; just as the word *yūpa* is employed for that piece of wood in which the characteristics of a sacrificial post exist, so it is here."
No, because of its connection with a ritual action.
The word *kaṇvarathaṃtara* does not function [as a name] due to a connection with a ritual action, unlike the word *yūpa*.
For the word *yūpa* functions by virtue of its connection with a consecratory rite (*saṃskāra*).
However, the term *kaṇvarathantara* is not like that; rather, this word is a conventional designation (*rūḍha*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *kaṇvarathantara* should be sung in its own source-text (*svayoni*).
(Ke.)

In passages such as "The Ukthya has the Vairūpa-sāman; the Ṣoḍaśin has the Vairāja-sāman," according to the principle stated in *Pṛṣṭhārthe vā prakṛtiliṅgasaṃyogāt* (10.6.6.16), since the Sāman serves to indicate the Pṛṣṭha-stotra by signifying that the Vairūpa and others are the means for the Pṛṣṭha, any dependence on the Sāman itself is far removed. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, p.
894). [This refers to] the limit of the Pṛṣṭha.

Furthermore, because the back is repeatedly bent when looking at various objects situated on the ground that are contrary [to one's expectations], it is designated by the term *pṛṣṭhakoṭi* by way of that general characteristic.
(In the *Sāhasrī*, however, there is a distinction regarding the *pṛṣṭhakoṭi*, and the meaning is also different).
Vārttika 2.1.7.32.

*Pṛṣṭhakoṭa*: the striking (*ākoṭa*) or curvature of the back (*pṛṣṭha*) in this ritual operation; that is *pṛṣṭhakoṭa*. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 670). What, then, is the region of the back? That interval above the *mādhyaṃdinapavamāna* and prior to the *maitrāvaruṇasāman* is the region of the back.
The Bhāṣya (on Jaimini Sūtra 10.6.15.13) states:

"The properties of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] are general properties such as the syllable *hiṃkāra* and so forth; the specific properties are those such as 'when the *rathantara* is being chanted, one should meditate on the earth in the mind,' and 'in the *bṛhat*, the ocean,' and so on.
(Bhāṣya on 7.3.135).
