In the case of the *pṛṣṭha* and *pratipad* [verses], which are respectively characterized by the *upavattī* and *apriyavatī* [mantras], there is no performance of these occasional (*naimittika*) elements in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) such as the *saṃsava*, even though they belong to the original (*prākṛta*) form.

The word *pṛṣṭha* indicates the mantras associated with the *rathaṃtara* and other [melodies] from the context of the fire-altar construction (*agnicayana*); it does not extend the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the hymns (*stotra*).
"He stands near with the *pṛṣṭhas*.
The word *pṛṣṭha* is the name of specific stotras occurring in the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. (Vi. 1.4.13)
The word *pṛṣṭha* in the expression "he worships with the *pṛṣṭhas*" denotes a specific substance;
the word *pṛṣṭha* refers exclusively to the hymn (*stotra*), not to the chant (*sāman*). (Mīmāṃsākośa 327)
The word *pṛṣṭha* denotes a specific type of hymn (*stotra*).
A *stotra* is a praise accomplished by means of chanted mantras.
Regarding the passage "They praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*," [Vi.
2.1.5], the word *pṛṣṭha*— referring to the seventeenfold (*saptadaśa*) chants— is a name, not an injunction of a quality.
Bhāṣya 1.4.13:
The *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*. [The injunction states:
"Having completed the sacrificial session (*satra*), they should sacrifice with the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*, a *jyotiṣṭoma* involving a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."
This is not a *sattra* sacrifice;
therefore, even the thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) does not deserve to be omitted.

Following the conclusion of the *sattra*, the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* (or *udavasānīya*) rite must be performed by a single *satrin* alone through the engagement of other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and not collectively.
The conclusion of the sacrificial session (*satra*) occurs through the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha, p.
1539). In the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*, the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is for the purpose of their formal hiring (*parikraya*).

In the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice, agency does not belong to the *satri*s solely by virtue of their being sacrificers (*yajamāna*); rather, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are not sacrificers are the agents.
In that case, even for the *satri*s, there is no fault in [their acting] solely as officiating priests through the act of hiring (*parikraya*). (Ke.
In the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice, the other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are distinct; they are not those same ones [from the preceding sacrifice].
In that case, one should choose different officiating priests.
Commentary: We shall now describe the sūtra concerning another topic of inquiry that intervenes.

In this very example, this point is doubtful: are those same performers of the sacrificial session (*satrin*) the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), or should others be chosen? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? They themselves [should be the priests]. Why? Because a common agency is understood from the expression "having departed, they should sacrifice."
There arises the conviction that those very ones who are the *udavasātṛ*s (those who have moved up) are themselves the *yaṣṭṛ*s (the sacrificers).

Just as, by the authority of the direct statement (*vacana*), the state of having many performers (*bahukartṛkatā*) occurs—setting aside the state of having a single performer (*ekakartṛkā*) obtained through the general rule (*codaka*)—so too, by the authority of the direct statement, those very persons must be [the sacrificers], setting aside the other priests (*ṛtvij*) obtained through the general rule.
This being the position reached, we reply:
Regarding that, it says, "they should choose other officiating priests.
For it is not the case that those who have emerged from the sacrificial session (*satra*) at the *pṛṣṭha-śamanīya* rite are enjoined as the performers;
it has already been stated that there is no injunction for them as things to be adopted.
And that which is not prescribed does not become unknown;
nor does there arise a state of deficiency when others who are inferior are present.
Furthermore, there are other officiating priests (ṛtvij) obtained through the force of the injunction (codaka).

Moreover, in this case, those alone are the performers who receive as much of the fruit of the action as is dear to the performer. This is the principle of the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice; this very point is understood from the specific use of the middle voice (*upagraha*).
Furthermore, the fruit of the action [of sacrifice] is not intended for the agent with respect to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Therefore, they are not the agents when it comes to the office of the priest;
rather, their agency is understood only in relation to the primary sacrifice (*pradhānayāga*).
"But other priests perform [the subsequent rites]," [it is argued].
Dvivedagaṅga replies: "Those very ones who are the performers at the conclusion (*udavasāna*) are prescribed as the performers for the *udavasānīya* rite.
(If, however, other performers were to exist for the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*, then) there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)."
(Thus the prima facie view being reached,) it is said in reply:

For the statement regarding common agency (found in the word "they should sacrifice") applies only to the principal act; indeed, no qualification is heard stating that "it should be performed with the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* [rites].
In the absence of such a statement, why would it apply when obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer)?

Even if the primary agency (i.e., the agency of the activity of the principal sacrificer) is involved, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is indeed possible. (Therefore, other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are to be chosen. [Objection: "In that case, would the officiating priests be those who have themselves performed the sacrificial session (*satrin*), or others? This reasoning is futile."
Those very same individuals who perform the priestly functions (*ārṭvijya*) in the primary sacrifice are also the priests in the subsequent [concluding] rites.

Bhaṭṭa: Whether they are non-members (*anaṅga*) or members (*aṅga*), the priestly functions must be performed by the sacrificers themselves (*yajamāna*) in accordance with the requirement that the concluding rite (*udavasāna*) have the same agent as the main sacrifice.

Nor can it be argued that this is justified because the intention refers only to the principal act; for since the scripture prescribes the same agent for the entire rite including its subsidiaries, and because in cases such as "they move the Adhvaryu among the waters," the sacrificer's agency—which is directly taught (*aupadeśika*) like that of the Āhavanīya fire—is present even in the subsidiaries, thereby precluding the agency of the priests. Furthermore, the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is also justified as having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

This being the case, since the status of the sacrificer as the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) is established here in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), there is no evidence for the presence of other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the subsidiary rites—even if they were to exist—or in the *saurya* and similar sacrifices where the priests would be obtained through extension (*atideśa*), as in the case of the *ājya-stotra*. Thus, the scriptural mention of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) is consistent with this view. Maṇḍana [says]: "Therefore, others would be the officiating priests."
Śaṅkara: "(In that case, the authority belongs to each individual—) if there are a thousand [sacrificers], then there are that many priests.
This follows the logic of the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* rite.
Because the *udavasānīya* rite requires the appointment of different priests, the status of agent belongs to each individual."
However, according to their statement, there would be a simultaneous performance, as in the case of the two sacrifices.

The Bhāṣya states: this very passage serves as an illustration: "Having emerged from the *satra*, they should sacrifice with the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* Jyotiṣṭoma accompanied by a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇa*).
In that context, the following point has been established: that the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* is not an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the *satra*.

Now, this is being considered: should that be performed by them acting together, or by each one individually? What is the prima facie view? That it is by acting together. Why? Because of the scriptural mention of plurality (*bahutva*) as something to be adopted when the speech is enjoined.

If it were performed by only one person, the performance associated with plurality would not occur—as in the case of the "two-sacrificer" ritual, as in the text: "By this [rite], a king and a domestic priest, desiring prosperity, should sacrifice together.

Even though the king and the domestic priest are mentioned merely as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, the sacrifice itself is presented as that which is to be undertaken (*upādeya*) by the phrase "they two should sacrifice."
And this agency is heard in the sacrifice [in the texts] "the two should sacrifice" (yajeyātām) and "they should sacrifice with the Pṛṣṭhaśamanīya.
Therefore, they should employ the Pṛṣṭhaśamanīya collectively.
Thus, for the time being, the matter remains unsettled.

Dupū: (by means of the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* [concluding rite]) because they are heard in the scripture as something to be undertaken (*upādeya*) with the injunction "they should sacrifice," the plurality is intended to be significant.
But surely, at the time of the *udavasāna* (the concluding departure), they are independent of one another?
In the same way, the *udavasānīya* sacrifice is prescribed for those who remain [in that state]; therefore, it too belongs to those who are indeed independent.
True;
although they are independent at the time of the departure (*udavasāna*), they are nevertheless dependent [on one another] during the sacrifice, as in the case of the *dviyajña*.
(For example,) the King and the Royal Priest are primary with respect to the fruit [of the sacrifice], yet they are subordinate with respect to the sacrifice (and thus dependent on one another).
How so? (The answer: For the sacrifice, being enjoined, requires an agent.
In that context, the number [two] is heard in its own word within the sacrifice (in the form "the two should sacrifice").
And therefore, the agents are dependent [on something else].
It is that very number which is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice (and not the agent).

How, then, is the performance carried out? To this he says: since the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (due to the specific use of the *ātmanepada* verbal suffix), the action will be performed for that purpose.
In such a state, the dual number is intended to be expressed.
If the king and the domestic priest were to be uttered for the sake of qualifying the dual number, then no one would perform the sacrifice as the primary element.
Therefore, the sacrifice is enjoined therein as a subordinate element (*aṅga*), just as in the injunction, "One who is dirty should bathe."
Moreover, at the time of the word [pada],
when one does not look at the word "having concluded" (*avasāya*) but rather at the time of observing the word "they should sacrifice" (*yajeran*), the expression denoting plurality is enjoined;
and such [plurality] is heard in connection with another word.
Therefore, plurality is intended [in the context of the sacrifice].
And by virtue of that, the performers are dependent [upon one another] (the performers become so at the conclusion of the sacrifice).
However, each individual [may perform it alone] because there is no prohibition and because in the archetype there is a connection with a single [performer].
Commentary: This is the reply to what was previously stated.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
They should not perform the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice collectively.
What then? [It applies] to each one individually. Why? Because there is no contradiction.
For at the time of the *udavasāna* (concluding rite), individuals are specifically indicated.
Regarding the phrase "those who dwell having concluded the sacrifice" (*satrād udavasanti*): since even a single person among them may be one who has concluded the sacrifice,
and since the sacrifice is likewise characterized by the act of concluding, the performance of the sacrifice is prescribed for each individual as well.
And it is not prohibited by anyone;
therefore, even a single person may perform the sacrifice. [Objection: But surely the performance for many is prescribed?
Therefore, it does not belong to each one individually.
This is not a fault; for it is not denied that it belongs to each one as well.
Therefore, by the force of the injunction, one should sacrifice alone. [The opponent] says:
"A performance connected with many cannot be accomplished by a single person."
Even so, there is no fault;
for here the expression of plurality is not being enjoined. The sacrifice belongs only to those who are departing from the sacrificial session (*satra*).
And they are many;
this is a restatement of those many who have arrived here. And even by each one of them individually, they are those who depart.
Therefore, their sacrifice will be exactly like that;

just as at the conclusion of the ritual (udavasāna), there is a mention of them being many while they are not acting in concert, so too at the sacrifice it will be for those who are not acting in concert.
To this, it is replied:
The mention of plurality is not a restatement (anuvāda),
because it is not already established.
For the mention of plurality is not established in the sacrifice such that it could be restated.
But was it not just stated that the sacrifice belongs to those who have completed their residence, and that they are many?
It is replied:
their plurality pertains to the completion of the residence, not to the sacrifice.
[Objection: But surely, by the power of the sentence, it will apply to the sacrifice as well.
[Reply: No, he says;
for a word, being complete in itself, requires another word, and from that a sentence arises.
Moreover, this sacrifice was already established by the expression denoting plurality;
at that stage, the *udavasātāraḥ* (those who depart) were not obtained through the sentence,
yet at that time, the plurality is indeed taken up.
Therefore, that which is connected with plurality takes precedence over what is situated in another word;
consequently, the performance must be carried out as connected with plurality,
as in the case of the Dviyajña and the Satras.
He said: "It is not so.
Where an explanatory restatement (anuvāda) is possible in some manner, there it may be either an explanatory restatement or an injunction (vidhi)."
Although an injunction is superior to a restatement because it conveys what was not previously known, nevertheless, in this case, it must be a restatement of the plurality.
For in that way, the connection of the sacrifice with many [offerers] is not rendered superfluous;
in that regard, there is a visible purpose. In the other alternative, if the plurality were connected to the sacrifice, an invisible result (adṛṣṭa) would have to be postulated.
Therefore, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
(He himself says: "He said"—it is said.
That same [conclusion] applies even in the case of two sacrifices, and likewise in the case of *satra* sessions.
To this it is replied: there is a distinction here;
[the rule] is that "having moved out [of the sacrificial ground], they should sacrifice."
"The king and the domestic priest should sacrifice together," and "Those desiring prosperity should perform the sacrificial session.
Where there is a word ending in the suffix *ktvā*, two performances are understood there,
precisely because they are heard as having identical phonetic forms.
In that case, by the statement of the subsequent application (*uttaraprayoga*), only the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is enjoined;
its substratum, the performance (*prayoga*), the agents (*kartṛ*), and the number associated with them—all of these are merely restated (*anūdyante*) here as things already established.

However, in the case of the *dviyajña* and *satra* sacrifices, the meaning of the verbal root is enjoined, as well as the performance, the agents, and the number associated with them; all of these are indeed unestablished (*aprāpta*) there.
For one cannot say "the king and the priest" (*rājapurohitau*) and thereby express their agency (*kartṛtva*), nor their number (*saṃkhyā*).
The same applies to the phrase "those desiring prosperity" (*ṛddhikāmāḥ*).
Therefore, in such cases, number is heard as being something to be taken up (*upādeya*).
Therefore, in the case of the *dviyajña* and other such rites, this is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
In those cases, the performance must be carried out in connection with plurality;
however, it is not so here.

Therefore, each one should perform the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice individually. [Dvaidhasūtra: At the conclusion (*udavasāna*), the performers are independent of one another, because the conclusion is established by the very nature of the purpose; since it is a non-existence [of the sacrificial state], those who are the performers at the conclusion are exactly the same as those at the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*.
Therefore, even in that case, the expression denoting plurality is intended to be significant.
But was it not said that they are independent in one instance and dependent in the other, like the king and the domestic priest?
And since the word "they should sacrifice" (*yajeran*) is heard directly, plurality is understood by depending upon another word.
Truth is understood, but it is not enjoined. How so? Because [the number] is already established. Why is it established? Because there is an attainment [of it].

From the hearing of the suffix *ktvā*, two applications (*prayoga*) are understood. It is also understood from that very source that those who are the agents in the first application are the same in the subsequent one.
And in the first sacrifice (namely, the application of the *sattra* called *udavasāna*), they are independent of one another; exactly the same [is true] for the subsequent application.
What, then, is enjoined? To this he says: "A specific action;
that alone which has not been previously established is enjoined (and not the number).
As for the plurality, however, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those who have departed."

The *pṛṣṭhaśamanīyanyāya*: 2612. When the *pṛṣṭhasāman* chants are performed by the Soma-sacrificers and the priests together, there is a connection because even the state of having a single agent is requested here.
As for the meaning of the *sūtra*: there should be a joint performance (*sahaprayoga*) by those sacrificers (*sattriṇaḥ*), because of the plural expression "they should sacrifice" (*yajeran*).

Just as in the case of "The king and the domestic priest should sacrifice" (*rājapurohito yajetām*), where the dual number indicates a joint performance by two, so it is here. [Objection: "In this case, the sacrifice may be performed either simultaneously or one by one; moreover, because of the plural expression, let there be another [sacrifice] for the sake of obtaining plurality, just as in the case of the two sacrifices, or like the Soma."
[The opponent argues: "It is like the plurality of the *ṛtvij* priests.

[Bhāṭṭa: Even though [the plurality] is not an auxiliary (*anaṅga*), they must act together; for the plurality conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is intended to apply to the agents who are the objects of the injunction (*upādeya-kartṛ*), as in the case of the *satra* sacrifice.

Furthermore, even if [the plurality] were somehow already established, the injunction is justified by accepting a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*) in order to ensure that the performance is carried out collectively—just as in the cases of "he lays down the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks" or "one should sacrifice with *soma"—and thus to achieve the intended purpose.
(That which was established remains concluded.

... [following] the establishment: There is no collective performance (*saṃhatya-prayoga*) in the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice, because plurality (*bahutva*), being already established, cannot be an object of injunction (*avidheyatvāt*).
For at the conclusion (*udvasāne*), the agency of multiple performers of the *satra* is already established.

Therefore, precisely because of the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) with that [preceding action], it applies even to the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice; thus, this is indeed a restatement (*anuvāda*). For by the force of the grammatical rule, the suffix *-tvā* must express not only anteriority in time but also the identity of the agent.

Nor should it be argued that because this [suffix] functions as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and since the action denoted by the suffix *ktvā* possesses the capacity for being a state (*bhāva-śakti*), its connection with a subsequent action—just like its quality of preceding in time—is logically accounted for through the relation of "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) as a relational property (*saṃsarga-lakṣaṇa*), and thus those two [properties] do not possess a distinct power (*śakti*) of their own.
For this would contradict the principle that Pāṇini and others, who are engaged in teaching the meanings of words (*padārthānuśāsana*), do not intend to express relational properties.

Furthermore, it must be discerned whether it is the meaning of the root itself, as conditioned by the suffix *ktvā*, that connects with the subsequent action—wherein *ktvā* is said to be the indicator of the intended relation (*saṃsarga-tātparya-grāhaka*)—or rather, that the abstract state (*bhāva*) which is the meaning of *ktvā* itself connects with the subsequent action through an implicit relation.

In this regard, the first [alternative] is not tenable: if singularity were to serve as the indicator of *tātparya* (speaker's intention) merely by being a cognition of singularity, then even a convention (*saṃketa*) regarding the number three would result in indicating *tātparya*. If, on the other hand, it were by being a cognition having "the state of being an indicator of *tātparya*" as its qualifier, then that would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Furthermore, since the dative case ending (*dvitīyā*) and others, which establish singularity and so forth, can be accounted for simply as indicators of the *tātparya* regarding relations such as "objecthood" (*karmatva*), it would follow that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) would be construed with the action through relations such as "objecthood," and it would also follow that the dative case ending and others could not have "objecthood" and so forth as their primary denotation (*śakya*).

For this very reason, it cannot be anything else; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of number itself being construed with the action through relations such as coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and objecthood (*karmatva*).

Therefore, by the force of grammatical authority (*anuśāsana*), objecthood and so forth must be the denotations of the suffixes, and the same applies to priority in time (*pūrvakālatva*) and the like.
Or, even if that were not the case, there would still be no fault.
Therefore, this is first of all a restatement (*anuvāda*).

When several [persons] are mentioned by means of a single word, the perceived association of agents (*kartṛsāhitya*) is not intended as a qualifying attribute of the subject (*uddeśyatva*), because it serves as a qualification of the causal condition (*nimitta*); furthermore, even though there is collective agency in a sacrificial session (*satra*), agency persists even when that [association] is abandoned, without the association itself.

For when a property such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a quality that resides in a collection (*sajyavṛtti*), its absence exists even in each individual; how much more so when, in a *sattra* sacrifice, because the plural number is mandatory, agency belongs to each person individually and there is merely a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the agents? In that case, when that [conjunction] is abandoned and there is an absence of association (*sāhitya*), what doubt can there be? As for the association understood from the plurality expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), it is indeed not intended to be significant if the plurality itself is not intended to be significant.

For at the conclusion (*udavasāna*), the agents are understood to be independent; it is precisely such [independent agents] who are understood to be present at the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice by virtue of the requirement of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*).

Therefore, because independence (*nairapekṣya*) is understood from the very first [cognition], there is no intention to express concomitance (*sāhitya*). Nor is it possible to intend both plurality and the concomitance understood therein—on the grounds that the agent of the gerund (*lyabantopāsa*) is the same—as if one were not accepting independence; for we accept the restatement (*anuvāda*) of a plurality that is already established, out of fear of the complexity (*gaurava*) of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
For this very reason, there is simplicity of injunction (*vidhilāghava*) since only the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice is enjoined.

Nor should it be argued that—just as one resorts to a qualified injunction for the sake of establishing the purpose of Soma and other substances (such as their exclusion from the ritual) due to the impossibility of another way of prescribing the performance—one should likewise resort here to an intentionality regarding plurality for the sake of establishing simultaneity (*sāhitya*).

For even if such a resort is made there to avoid the redundancy of the word "Soma" and so forth, in the present case, plurality is unavoidable because its mention is justified as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
Therefore, the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifices must be performed by a single person; thus, the original performers do not apply there.
Maṇḍana: "One should perform that [rite] individually. That [rite] is the *udavasānīya* sacrifice, which follows the *uttara*. Śaṅkara: "In that case, the entitlement belongs to each [individual]."

In that context, regarding the *udavasāna* [concluding rite], the Vārtika states that in the case of an occasional (*naimittika*) act—such as in the passage "as many portions as one might receive" (*yāvato 'śān pratigṛhṇīyāt tāvataḥ*)—the mention of the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* [rite] is not intended to be significant because it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
(Bhāṭṭadīpikā 5.2.2). The term *pṛṣṭhasāman* refers to the Sāmans sung during the *pṛṣṭha-stotras*.
(Viṣayānukramaṇikā 10.6.5). Through the six *pṛṣṭha-sāmans*, the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) is accomplished.
(Ke. Vi.
10.6.5) Regarding the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*s: for the *pṛṣṭhya* [sacrifice], the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*s are indeed applied with the *pṛṣṭha-sāman*s; the *rathantara* becomes the *pṛṣṭha*.
Bhāṣya 10.6.15: Regarding the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, the *vairūpa* is prescribed for the *ukthya* sacrifice alone;
and that same [sāman] is prescribed as the *vairāja* in the place of the Mahendra-stotra and in the *ṣoḍaśin*.
"The *ukthya* has the *vairūpa-sāman* and the twenty-one-fold chant (*ekaviṃśa*); the *ṣoḍaśin* has the *vairāja-sāman*."
In the Vaiśyastoma sacrifice, there is a Pṛṣṭha-stotra called the Kaṇvarathantara.

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states that the ritual properties (dharmas) of the Bṛhat and Rathantara—which are optionally substituted for one another in the archetype (prakṛti) at the Pṛṣṭha-stotra—should be adopted in the Vaiśyastoma according to the rule of option (vikalpa) where they are not contradictory, and by way of combination (samuccaya) where they are not. The Vārtika, however, maintains that both sets of properties are to be taken only by way of option.
9|2|16. At the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), following the *pavamāna* laud, there are four *pṛṣṭha-stotras*, each having the seventeenfold chant (*saptadaśa-stoma*).
Among them, the first hymn is the *rathaṃtara*, consisting of the *pragātha* "Abhi tvā śūra," wherein the former [verse] is a *bṛhatī* and the latter is a *paṅkti* (specifically a *sat-paṅkti*).
The second [hymn] for Vāmadeva is "akayā naś citra" (1.165);
therein are three *gāyatrī* verses.
The third is the *pragātha* form "nauparṇaṃ taṃ vo dasmṛtīṣam" (1.87).
In that [section], there are two *bṛhatī*s and two *paṅkti*s (*bṛhatīsat-paṅktī*).
The fourth [section] consists of the *pragātha* form "kāleyaṃ tarobhir va vidadvasum";
in that case as well, there are two *bṛhatī*s and two *paṅkti*s (*bṛhatīsat-paṅktī*).
In that regard, regarding the *pragāthas*, there is the accomplishment of the state of being a *ṛc* through effort [9.2.6, Section 2].
Regarding the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, the simultaneous application (*samuccaya*) of the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [Sāmans] occurs in the *saṃsava* and *apaciti* sacrifices [10.6.24–26].
In the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* at the *gosava* sacrifice, one should perform both; thus, there is the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the two *Sāmans*, the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara*.

And in that case, although the hymn (stotra) is one, there is a determination of the ritual properties (dharma) due to the difference between the two Sāmans. (JS 9.2.17). Regarding the Pṛṣṭha-stotras in the Jyotiṣṭoma, both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara are optional alternatives; however, the properties of both apply.
There is neither a fixed restriction nor a confusion [of the two].
The characteristics of the *Bṛhat* [Sāman] are: "It should be sung loudly," "It should be played forcefully," and "While the *Bṛhat* is being praised, one should meditate with a mind full of success.

The characteristics of the *Rathantara* [Sāman] are: "It should not be sung loudly," "It should not be played forcefully," and "While the *Rathantara* is being introduced (*prastūyamāna*), one should close one's eyes.

(Vi. 9.2.15). In the *Pṛṣṭha-stotras*, there is the seventeen-fold hymn-form (*saptadaśa-stoma*). Its sequence is as follows: in the first repetition, "three verses, one verse, one verse"; in the second repetition, "one verse, three verses, one verse"; and in the third repetition, "one verse, three verses, three verses."

The *kaṇvarathaṃtara*—which is prescribed in the *vaiśyastoma* as a means for accomplishing the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*—is to be sung in its own source-hymn (*svayoni*), namely "punānaḥ soma" (10.4.22.44–47). It is not to be sung in the two subsequent [verses] of the *rathaṃtara*, but rather in the two subsequent verses of its own source-hymn (10.4.23.48–49). By the very name "the six-day period consisting of *pṛṣṭhas*" (*pṛṣṭhyaḥ ṣaḍahaḥ*), the collection of cups (*grahamālā*) connected to the six-day period is obtained in the *gavāmayana*.
*Ṣaḍviṃśabrāhmaṇa-bhāṣya*, 10.5.25.85, p. 1980. Regarding the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*: in the *Gavāmayana* sacrifice, it recurs every month with an intervening separation.
Therefore, as it recurs, the consumption of *rasa* (liquid food), which is occasioned by the completion (*saṃsthā*) [of the rite], also recurs every month.

10.6.19.31. In the passage "The *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, two *svarasāman*s," there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the characteristics of the *svarasāman*s belonging to the *Gavāmayana* to the *svarasāman*s [of the *ahīna* sacrifice].
The section concerning the *Svarasāman*, the one-pot-sherd offering (*ekakapāla*), and the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*).
[Jaimini Sūtra] 7.3.10.27. The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite consists of the six days beginning with the second day of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*). Vi.
8.2.15: The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite belonging to the twelve-day rite is the archetype (*prakṛti*) for the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite belonging to the *gavāmayana*.
10.6.3: The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) is of two kinds: that which ends with the *trayastrimśa*, and that which has the *trayastrimśa* at its beginning.

The *pṛṣṭhya* [six-day period] is characterized by the *stomas* of *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, *saptadaśa*, *ekaviṃśa*, *triṇava*, and *trayastrimśa*. [This concludes the section on] the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period.
The term *triṣad* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, not a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva*.

Even when those two—the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara*—are divided according to the distinction of days (*aharbheda*), the expression "*bṛhadrathantarasāman*" remains uncontradicted and is not inconsistent.
It is just as in the case of: "Devadatta is to be fed with both ghee and oil for a month."

When this is said, [the rule] "for half a month with ghee, for half a month with oil" is thus rendered consistent; that is the meaning. Furthermore, the acceptance of the *codaka* (the general injunction) is not contradicted;
the sense is that if this division is accepted, there will also be favor toward the *codaka*.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that there is indeed one *sāman* for each day. [Objection:

If the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha] were merely for the purpose of providing the essence (*rasabojana*), it would occur on the thirty-third day, because of its immediate succession and because it is like the archetype (*prakṛti*).
In the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which begins with the *tridaśa* [stoma], there occurs a six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) consisting of the thirty-three-fold stoma.
Regarding that, it is heard in scripture: "When the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* has been completed, one should eat honey or ghee.
Now, let us not deliberate upon the first fortnight as it proceeds in direct order (*ānulomyena*) within the *gavāmayana*.

But when the subsequent six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) proceeds in reverse order (*prātilomyena*), then upon the completion—that is, the conclusion—of the first and last *pṛṣṭhya* six-day periods on the thirty-third day, there should be the consumption of *rasa* (juice) and honey on that very day. Because of its immediate sequence, in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the consumption of *rasa* follows after the thirty-third day; since this is the archetype, it is the same here as well.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the consumption of the *rasa* should take place on the thirty-third day, following the performance of the ritual.
Or rather, it should be at the end, because its time has been fixed.

The word "or" (*vā*) in the prima facie view is to be explained as indicating the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), which he states: "This is not the case—that the consumption of the *rasa* occurs after the thirty-third day."
However, it should occur at the end of the *pṛṣṭhya* [period].

Because the time for the honey-food (*rasabhojana*) has been fixed—since it is established by the scriptural injunction, "When the six-day period has concluded, one should eat honey"—its timing is determined;
its time is fixed at the conclusion of the six-day period.
And when the six-day period proceeds in reverse order, it begins with the thirty-three-fold [stoma] and ends with the nine-fold [stoma].
When that is completed, the consumption of honey should take place, not at the end of the thirty-three-fold.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that the eating of honey occurs when the six-day period ending with the nine-fold stoma has been finished.
10.8.11.23–28: Regarding the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *agni* and *atigrāhya* cups.
In the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite, when it has been taught, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the performance details extended by the consumption of honey and so forth.

Bhāṣya 10.4.1–2, Section 1: Regarding the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* occurring within the *gavāmayana*, on the first, third, and fifth days of the first fortnight (*pūrva-pakṣas*), the *rathaṃtara* should be sung; on the second, fourth, and sixth days, the *bṛhat* should be sung. On the first, third, and fifth days of the second fortnight (*uttara-pakṣas*), the *bṛhat* is to be sung, and on the second, fourth, and sixth days, the *rathaṃtara*.
*Soma* 10.6.3: In the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* occurring within the *Gavāmayana*, there is the performance of either the *Bṛhat* or the *Rathantara* [sāman] on each successive day.
See Mīko., p. 1550, under the entry “*gavāmayane pṛṣṭhye*”.
In the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* occurring within the *Gavāmayana*, whether in the *saloma* or *viloma* arrangement, honey is to be consumed at the end.
10.6.9. The fire-altar can be constructed during the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period.

Bhāṣya 10.8.12.23–28: During the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, when the thirty-three-fold [stoma] begins and concludes (at its end), there is the consumption of honey or the consumption of ghee; however, it is not at the conclusion of the thirty-third day. This occurs in the northern wing of the *gavām ayana*.

10|6|12–28. On the second day of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which consists of a six-day period of *pṛṣṭha* chants, there occurs the *viśvajit* stoma in the fifteen-fold (*pañcadaśa*) *bahiṣpavamāna*; this results in the state of "five fixed [verses]" (*dhruvapañcatva*).
This is the middle position between the *anurūpa* and the *paryāsa*, both of which are obtained through the general rule (*codaka*) of that ritual manual (*kalpa*).

(Vi. 5|3|4). In the six days of the twelve-day sacrifice consisting of the six-day *pṛṣṭha* period, the *sāmans*—namely, the *rathaṃtara*, *bṛhat*, *vairūpa*, *vairāja*, *śākvara*, and *raivata*—are to be chanted in sequence.

Śābarabhāṣya 10.6.3: When the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, as part of the Dvādaśāha, has been completed, the consumption of honey must be performed by those who have been initiated (dīkṣita), even if they are celibate students (brahmacārin), because it is prescribed in the ritual manual (kalpa).
10.6.12: In the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, six Sāmans—one for each day—are [recited]: the Rathantara, Bṛhat, Vairūpa, Vairāja, Śākvara, and Raivata.
These are the six Pṛṣṭha-stotras according to the Taittirīyas.
VI. 7|3|3. In the Gavāmayana, during the six-day period consisting of the *pṛṣṭha* chants, there is the performance of either the *Bṛhat* or the *Rathantara* [sāman] on each day.

10.6.3. 4–5. Furthermore, regarding the statement heard in connection with the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* sacrifice—"When the six-day period has concluded, one should eat honey"—the Bhāṣya states that because this prescribed eating of honey serves a different purpose, there is a combination [of the two] with the original milk-vow (*payovrata*) on that day. However, since the eating of honey is for the sake of sustaining the body and thus cannot logically function as a substitute for the physical effects of the milk-vow, the objection raised by the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) lacks a basis; therefore, that argument is disregarded due to the absence of the milk-vow in a comparable case. Or, let that too be taken as an example here.
(Bhāṭṭa-dīpikā 10.4.1).
In the case of the Ukthya sacrifices within the Pṛṣṭhya days, there is an option regarding the *atigrāhya* cups, not an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
This is to be seen under Saṃkarṣa 3.3.4 and Mīko, p. 989, in the section beginning with "even though the *atigrāhyas* are lateral."

In the Gavamayana sacrifice, there is no cessation of the consumption of honey and other such items from the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, because of the statement regarding a different ritual action [at the end of it].
(10.6.11.31). Due to the statement of a distinct Pṛṣṭhya in the repetition of the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, there is no grinding of the Soma for the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha. (2615)
The *āhuti* [offering] at the Gavāmayana is also [to be performed] by him;
see Mīko., p. 1553, under the entry "vijātīya in the Gavāmayana."
At the conclusion of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* within the *Gavāmayana*, there is the performance of either eating honey or eating *vṛta* (clarified butter) as an optional alternative.
See Mīko., p. 1552, under the entry: “In the *Gavāmayana*, at the end of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.”

In the case of the repetition of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, the eating of honey occurs only once at the end of the entire *ṣaḍaha*, and not at the end of each individual day, as is the case in the *Gavāmayana*.
(See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1554, under "In the *Gavāmayana* and other rites, upon the repetition of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*").
This is to be observed there.
Among the *sāmans* such as the *Rathantara* occurring in the *ṣaḍaha* (six-day rite) of the *pṛṣṭhya*, only the *Vairūpa* is to be placed for the *hotṛ* priest in the *Viśvajit* sacrifice.

[Jaimini Sūtra] 10.6.12–14. Section (*peṭikā*) 10.12.1–7. Regarding these seven sections, the inquiry concerning the *kṛṣṇala* oblation (*caru*) is present; because the "jewels" (*ratna*) of the section on existence (*sattādhikaraṇa*) reside within this section, the author of the *Rasāyana* has called it the "Section on the *Kṛṣṇala*" (*kṛṣṇalapeṭikā*).
Although the sections at 8|18 and 10|12|1 also concern the consideration of *kṛṣṇala* weights, they are not included within this section (*peṭikā*) because they belong to different locations.
Now, what is the *kvapeṭikā*?

It is so called because, in the four topical discussions (adhikaraṇas) from 4|3|12–15, it is investigated whether subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) is understood through the suffix *-balāka* or whether it refers to time; thus, this is named the *kvapeṭikā*.

Now, having treated the section from *sūtra* 1.4.12–23 as a constituent part of the *tatsiddhapaiṭikā*, the grounds for figurative application (*gauṇavṛtti*) have been analyzed; thus, this group of six topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) is called the *tatsiddhapaiṭikā*. Next, since the discussion concerning the substitute (*pratinidhi*) alone is carried out across sixteen topical sections from 6.3.4–20, this is the extensive *pratinidhipaiṭikā*.

Now, since the discussion concerning the consumption of the *soma* remnant occurs exclusively within the ten topical sections (adhikaraṇas) from 3.2.9 to 3.2.18, this group of ten topical sections is called the "Section on Insertion" (*prakṣepa-peṭikā*).

Furthermore, since in the topical section at 3.1.7 the investigation of the means of application (*viniyojaka-pramāṇa*)—namely *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth—is conducted entirely through the consideration of their relative strength (*balābala*), this is called the "Section on *Śruti* and the Rest" (*śrutyādi-peṭikā*).
Thus, although there is unity in the [number of] sūtras, there are indeed many intermediate topical sections.

Now, since the discussion concerning the *ṣoḍaśin* cup occurs within the six topical sections (adhikaraṇas) from 10.5.9 to 10.5.14, this group of six sections is known as the "Ṣoḍaśin-chapter" (*ṣoḍaśagrahapeṭikā*).

Although there is also discussion regarding the *ṣoḍaśin* itself in the two sections at 5.1.18 and 10.6.16, nevertheless, because those two are located in different places, they are not considered to be included within this chapter.

In that case, would it not follow that the first chapter is the "Box on Means of Proof" (pramāṇa-peṭikā), the second the "Box on the Differentiation of Rituals" (karma-bheda-peṭikā), the third the "Box on Subservience" (śeṣatva-peṭikā), the fourth the "Box on Application" (prayukti-peṭikā), the fifth the "Box on Order" (krama-peṭikā), the sixth the "Box on Entitlement" (adhikāra-peṭikā), the seventh and eighth the "Box on Extended Application" (atideśa-peṭikā), the ninth the "Box on Modification" (ūha-peṭikā), the tenth the "Box on Sublation" (bādhā-peṭikā), the eleventh the "Box on the Principal and the Subsidiary" (tantrāvāpa-peṭikā), and the twelfth the "Box on Occasional Application" (prasaṅga-peṭikā)? The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: there should be a carrying of all [the fees] every day, because all of them constitute the remainder of the entire sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and because in the original archetype (*mūlaprakṛti*), the Jyotiṣṭoma, the carrying of the sacrificial fee is observed at the midday (*mādhyaṃdina*) [rite]. Or rather, it should apply to the entire [sacrifice] once it has been divided, because the consecration is accomplished all at once; and because of the attainment of what was stated regarding each midday [rite], it should occur every day. Since all [the days] are identical to that, they should be divided like the twelve-day sacrifice.
Regarding the *pauṇḍarīka* sacrifice, there is one doubt: is this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā-dravya*) to be brought once, or is it to be brought every day?
Furthermore, regarding that second alternative, there is a second doubt: is the entirety of it to be brought every day, or is it to be brought in divided portions?

The first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, because the ritual preparation (*saṃskāra*) is accomplished [once], the leading forth (*nayana*) should occur only once. The second position is that, because it is obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*), the leading forth should occur every day; even then, since the image is one, all of it should be led forth on the first day. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that, as in the case of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), the leading forth should be performed by dividing [the task] each day.

In the *Ahīna* sacrifice, because the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is subordinate (*guṇatvāt*), the ritual act should be performed daily; there would be a distinction [between the two]. Commentary:
There is the *Pauṇḍarīka* eleven-night sacrifice, [prescribed] thus: "One desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the *Pauṇḍarīka* eleven-night sacrifice.
In that context, it is heard: "Ten thousand [cows] at the *Pauṇḍarīka*, and twelve thousand plus eleven at the eleven-night [sacrifice]."

In this regard, a doubt arises: should ten thousand and a thousand horses be given every day, or should one set of ten thousand and a thousand horses be given once? What is the prima facie view? In an Ahīna sacrifice, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be distributed according to each day. Why? Because the sacrificial fee is subordinate, whereas the days are the primary elements.

When a quality such as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is enjoined by means of a term denoting a collection (*samudāya*), it indicates the members of that collection; thus, the injunction would apply separately to each principal element (*pratipradhānam*).
This is just as when bathing or anointing is enjoined for a group (*gaṇa*), it pertains to each individual member of the group.
The same principle should be understood to apply here as well.
Furthermore, the injunction that determines the specific ritual action is thus supported;
and because of the abundance of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), there will be an abundance of results.
Therefore, it is understood that there is a distinction [between the rites].
Because all [the rites] constitute a single performance.
The Commentary states: "It is not the case that there is a different sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) every day;
rather, exactly ten thousand and one thousand are given."

Why? Because of the unity of purpose (*aikakarmyat*). For the single purpose of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) is the arrival of the priests; and since that [arrival] has been accomplished for the sake of the performance of the sacrifice along with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga-ṛtu*), there is no further need for it in the interim, and thus it is not performed again.
As for the claim that an increase in the number of subsidiaries results in an increase in the fruit, that holds true when the status of being a subsidiary is established, but not otherwise.
Furthermore, it has been stated that the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a subsidiary of the whole collection, not a subsidiary of its individual parts.

Now, as for what was said—that the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) applies to each individual action because it terminates with each action—the injunction of the sacrificial fees is established by means of direct scriptural statement and by their being accepted as subsidiaries of the whole collection; thus, the *codaka* is set aside, and there is no fault.
Or rather, this scripture concerning the qualities should be like the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter) offering.
The Commentary states: "And it is not to be given only once;
what then? Separately."
Why? Because a specific distinction among the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and the *prāsa* offerings is stated for each day; therefore, it must apply to each day individually.

Just as in the case of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), where the injunction "he sacrifices the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) with speckled butter" prescribes the quality of being speckled (*pṛṣattā*) such that it varies with each after-offering, so too should it be understood here.

Since the sacrificial fees belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, and because all [the days] constitute a single ritual action, they follow the model of the archetype (*prakṛti*); therefore, there should be a modification (*vikāra*) of those fees.
The Commentary states: This is not the case; it is not a matter of distinction.
What then? It is by way of the *tantra* (the common application), all at once.
How so? For in the Jyotiṣṭoma, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are given having accepted the entire mass of rites along with its subsidiaries.
Regarding those offerings which, being of such a nature, consist of a continuous collection, another distinction is stated:

when the distinction "a thousand" or "ten thousand" is mentioned, it is understood that this is a modification (*vikāra*) of the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) given here; it excludes their internal unity. Therefore, there is a single offering.
As for the statement regarding the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), it is correct that there is a distinction of substance (*dravya*) in the after-offerings.

For in a sacrifice, the substance is enjoined as a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*). Because those sacrifices are distinct, what is performed for one does not benefit another; thus, it is distinguished.
But here, it is stated that there is only one *ānati*.
Therefore, the illustrative example is dissimilar.

However, in the case of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), because of the scriptural injunction, there is a distinction of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) each day; since this [the *ekāha*] is its archetype (*prakṛti*), there would be a modification of their number on the subsequent days.
Commentary: This is not the case, that there is a single performance. This distinction differs every day.
Why? Because in the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, there is a statement for each day: "Every day he gives one hundred and twelve [cows]."
And the Pauṇḍarīka has the Dvādaśāha as its archetype.

Therefore, since the fees (dakṣiṇās) applicable to each day of the Pauṇḍarīka are established through the force of the extended injunction (codaka), when another specific rule regarding them is stated, it is understood that this constitutes a modification of those elements of the ritual designated as parts of the action. Consequently, the distinction regarding the fees is one of difference [from the archetype].
"Or rather, there would be a modification of the whole due to the division of the preparatory acts.
The Commentary states: "And this is not the case, that there is a difference in the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
What then? The sacrificial fee should be given only once."
Why? Because of the distribution of the ritual service (*parikriyā-vibhāga*), the entire sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) would have to be modified.
For the sacrificial fees are prescribed with reference to the sacrifice as a whole.
How so? Because that much [of the fee] serves the purpose of the person [performing the sacrifice].
That which possesses a fruit is what a person desires to perform.
And regarding one who is performing that [act], this specific term "purchase" (parikraya) is used for the non-appropriation of assistance.
Furthermore, a single component does not possess the fruit; rather, the fruit is produced from the aggregate.
Furthermore, when the purchase (*parikraya*) is performed by accepting the whole aggregate and continues until the end of the session (*āsada*), it is considered completed;
thus, it is not performed again in the interim.
Moreover, since a specific form of purchase is mentioned in connection with the word *pauṇḍarīka*, it is understood that this applies specifically to that which is denoted by that term.
Furthermore, the whole (samudāya) denoted by the word *pauṇḍarīka* is not a part;
for that whole is indicated by the word [as a secondary meaning]. In that case, the fault lies precisely in what is being indicated.
For figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is resorted to only when the primary sense is impossible;
but here there is no such impossibility.
Therefore, accepting the collective whole [of the priests], it follows that all the priests together should perform the sacrifice.
Therefore, there is a single purchase.
And when the purchase is made once, there is compliance with the injunction regarding the performance (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, because of the rapidity of the performance, the scripture possesses a broad scope.
Therefore, it is logical that [the gift] is indeed [one].
But there is a distinction, because of the connection with specific qualities.

The Commentary: That which was stated—that because the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice has the Dvādaśāha as its archetype, and since there is a difference in the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in the Dvādaśāha, a specific rule is here stated for that very same [gift]—that must be refuted.
To this it is replied:
even in that case, because the season (*ṛtu*) is one, there is a single purchase (*parikraya*).

However, due to a scriptural injunction, there is a distinction based on the purpose of connection with the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing) and the purpose of the consecration of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); yet, when that [distinction] is performed, the unity of the purchase is not divided.
Śā—In this regard, [the prima facie view is: "Since the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) occurs day after day, it undergoes differentiation every day.
[But the final view is: "However, because it falls within a single performance (*ekaprayoga*), it is understood as one through the principle of *tantra*."

Soma: Since it is established that the *ahīna* sacrifice—which is distinct from the *sattra* and performed by other agents—involves a consideration of the distribution of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) separately for each primary rite (*pradhāna*), the meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: in the *ahīna*, such as the Pauṇḍarīka and others, there should be a separate distribution of the fee for each day because of the difference between the primary rites, since the fee is a subordinate element (*guṇa*).
They say that the general mention of "in the *ahīna*" is intended to illustrate this by means of the example of the Pauṇḍarīka.
Vi— "Ten thousand [recitations] and so forth should be performed daily, or once, according to one's capacity.
The first [method] would be the primary practice; however, if the capacity is unified, it may be done once."
Therefore, the gift is given only once.
(The Bhaṭṭa commentary—see the unified explanation in the 17th and 18th sections of the Bhāṣya.
The Pauṇḍarīka is a one-day sacrifice (ahīna) consisting of eleven nights.
In that regard, it is heard in the scripture: "The sacrificial fee consists of ten thousand cows and eleven thousand horses."

In this regard, when considering whether one thousand horses and ten thousand cows are to be given every day, or whether they are to be divided and given once [for the entire period], although the *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) is prescribed in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is likewise established for the *dvādaśāha*—which is of the nature of an *ahīna* sacrifice—that "one gives twelve hundred every day. Because of this injunction of twelve hundred for each respective day, the *dakṣiṇā* belongs to the entirety of the performance; therefore, since this *dakṣiṣṇā* serves its purpose through the *prasaṅga* (incidental application) across those days, no other [fee] is given beyond that.

And therefore, even in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, since the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is obtained through extended application (atideśa) as distinct for each pressing, the thousand horses and the additional [gift] being enjoined would likewise result in twelve hundred, just as in the case of the separate [fees].

In reality, even in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, although the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is established as being for the sake of the entire ritual—including both the primary and subsidiary parts—by virtue of its being a constituent of the performance, the scriptural statement "The fee belongs to the Soma [sacrifice]" determines that it is intended solely for the primary sacrifice. Consequently, in the Dvādaśāha sacrifice as well, since the fee is understood to be for the primary acts alone due to the distinction grasped through the differentiation of the archetypal rules (codaka) applied to each individual rite—just like the Savanīya offerings—the injunction "Every day he gives one hundred and twelve" does not indicate that the fee is for the sake of the primary sacrifice; rather, it serves solely as an exclusion (parisaṃkhyā) of anything in excess of the one hundred and twelve.
The phrase "every day" (*anvaham*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the primary purpose obtained through extended application (*atideśa*).

Consequently, as in the previous case, since the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is obtained separately for each extraction (*pratissutyam*) even from the archetypal model (*prakṛti*), the thousand horses being prescribed therein would also be obtained separately.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): in the Jyotiṣṭoma, although the sacrificial fee serves the purpose of the primary rite alone, its status as serving the purpose of the primary rite is established solely through its inclusion within the single performance of the primary rite, and not directly.

For this very reason, there is no separate performance of that [gift] for the subsidiaries (*aṅga*). Even though it serves the purpose of the primary sacrifice alone, the practical consequence is that it is not extended (*anatideśa*) to modifications of the subsidiaries. Consequently, even in the case of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), although the "one hundred and twelve" [cows] are obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) as belonging to each individual day, they are obtained here only as a single unit within the performance of each respective day.
And for this reason, even in the case of other principal acts (*pradhāna*), a separate performance would not be required.

Consequently, due to the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), the single gift of one hundred and twelve [cows] offered at the beginning or at the end accrues to all the principal acts.
And thus, "every day, twelve..."

In the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, by the statement "one hundred [cows] as the sacrificial fee for the Pauruṣeya," since the previously established sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) would otherwise be rendered redundant if it were merely enjoined again as a subordinate part (*aṅga*), the word "daily" (*anvaham*) serves to introduce the consideration of its repetition, which would otherwise be understood as a single performance. Otherwise, if it were intended as an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the horse and other items, the word "daily" would result in meaninglessness.

And that non-repetition does not apply to the "one hundred and twelve" [cows] themselves; for since they are given on a single day as a mere auxiliary to the *sutyā* (pressing), it is necessary that they serve as an auxiliary to another *sulā* (pressing) through their application elsewhere. Rather, it concerns the sublation of the "one hundred and twelve" as a means—which is obtained through the determination of other applications—and which follows in its wake; thus, one must conceive of the "one hundred and twelve" as a collective whole (*samudāya*) throughout the entire *sutyā* as being the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

Furthermore, that sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), being established as the means of payment for each respective performance, is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) that benefits all [the days] through a single application (*tantra*). However, since one hundred and twelve [cows]—which constitute its constituent parts—are distributed and given daily according to scriptural injunction, this distribution is also an auxiliary in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Therefore, here in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice as well, even though ten million, a thousand, or a hundred thousand [cows] are prescribed in place of that [standard fee], they are likewise accepted through a single application as the means of payment for each respective performance.
The daily portion must be given by dividing [the total] part by part, precisely according to the division obtained through extended application (*atideśa*).

For this very reason, the two prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣa*) stated in the root-text commentary on Sūtra 18.1.69—namely, "the full ten thousand and one thousand should be brought forward daily until the day of the *mārgaśīrṣa* sacrifice," or "on some single day"—are disregarded, because there is no authority for a division other than that obtained through extended application.
However, another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be considered for that purpose.
(As stated in the Bhāṣya at 17.62–68 and 18.69–72:
Furthermore, that distribution is not for the sake of the primary purpose [of the sacrifice] in the sense of being "daily," such as "a thousand cows and a thousand horses on each of the eleven days.
This is because the *Mānava Sūtra* prescribes the thousand horses on the tenth day, stating: "Day by day he gives thousands; on the [day of the] Catuṣṭoma, a thousand horses."

For thus the arrangement of the days in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice has been stated by him [Āpastamba]: "One desiring the highest merit should sacrifice with the Pauṇḍarīka consisting of eleven nights; it is a repeated sacrifice. Six days consist of three *chandomas*, an *anuṣṭubh* *agniṣṭoma*, and a *viśvajit* *atirātra*.
Therefore, on the tenth day, having given a thousand horses, there is a distribution of thousands of cows for the remaining days. Maṇḍana says: "The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed once."
Śaṅkara: "One [is required];
it is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
18. Regarding the *pauṇḍarīka-barhis*: "Strew with red lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*)."

Human authorship (*pauruṣeyatva*) consists in belonging to the same class as a true cognition whose object is a produced effect. This is because [human authorship] is impossible in the case of the *Mahābhārata* and similar works.

However, it may instead consist in being a sentence produced by a desire to utter it, or being a sentence generated by a cognition of its meaning, or belonging to a class that does not depend on a prior utterance of a similar kind.
In the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other texts, the term "of the same class" (*sajātīya*) is used to exclude others.

*Maṇi*, p. 7–8. "Being of human origin" (*pauruṣeyatva*) means being produced through human oversight or dependence. *Su.*, p. 532. "Being of human origin" with respect to a sentence refers to its employment for the purpose of conveying its own meaning by depending on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it does not mean being an effect of phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth.

*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 34: Since human statements have as their purpose a meaning already known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they themselves do not constitute independent means of valid cognition; therefore, defects such as "splitting the sentence" (*vākyabheda*) and so forth simply do not arise.
*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 32: Human sentences possess a twofold nature.
One of these consists in the capacity to ascertain that the speaker possesses knowledge of the meaning of the sentence being uttered.
Just as in the case of the words of those with outflows (*āsavākya*), the determination of meaning occurs through the knowledge of each preceding speaker,

in the case of the words of those without outflows (*anāsavākya*), however, it is difficult to establish that the foundational knowledge of the speaker is correct; therefore, there is simply a lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*) therein— this is another [view], according to Vaidyanātha.
11|2|2, pp. 16–17. In the case of human-authored statements, the establishment of certainty regarding the meaning depends upon the weight of ascertaining the source (*mūlāvadhāraṇagaurava*).
1|1|2|2, p. 16. It is understood that the entire section concerning the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsakāṇḍa*) is designated as "paurauḍāśika.

Vārttika 3|1|7|4, p. 855. In the section designated by the name "paurauḍāśika," within the sequence for the *sānnāyya* offering, the mantra for purification, "aśundhadhvaṃ daivyāya karmaṇe" (Purify yourselves for the divine rite), is recited.

Because of the greater force of *krama* (order), it should be employed for the cleansing of the *sānnāyya* vessels, and not for the cleansing of the *puroḍāśa* vessels on the basis of *samākhyā* (name/designation).

Bhāṣya 3.1.7.4, p. 855. A mantra recited in the section of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) designated as *paurauḍāśika*, while situated within the general context (*prakaraṇa*), is not assigned [to the *puroḍāśa*] by *krama* because it lacks the indicative mark (*liṅga*) [for that purpose]. Rather, since it would otherwise apply to the *puroḍāśa* itself by default, it is enjoined by direct statement (*śruti*) as being subordinate to the *sālā* (shed) for the sake of the *sānnāyya*: "With the words ‘For food, thee,’ he cuts the shed."
(Therefore, direct audition is stronger than name.

Vārttika 3.1.7.4, p. 836. [In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice], during the Sutyā [pressing] day, the acts belonging to the cake-offering (puroḍāśa), such as sprinkling and so forth, must precede those belonging to the Soma ritual.
5.1.13.25–26. The principle of the cake-offering and the butter-portions (ājyabhāga).
The principle of the *ājyabhāga* offerings:
the *ājyabhāga* and other such rites, which provide only minor assistance elsewhere, must be performed in the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) sacrifice.
According to Jaimini, because there would be the contingency of falling under another’s system, there should be a prohibition of the independent [system].
Commentary: Regarding that very animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), there is this inquiry:
should the two butter-portions (ājyabhāgau) be performed, or not? He says:
Therefore, this must be examined: is the injunction (*codaka*) set aside by the incidental application (*prasaṅga*), or is it the statement of performance (*prayogavacana*)?
If the injunction is set aside, then the two [rites] need not be performed;
if, however, it is the statement of performance that is set aside, then they must be performed.

What, then, is the correct position here? That the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) is sublated. What is the reason? The *codaka* is inferential (*ānumānika*), whereas the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*); and the perceptual is stronger than the inferential.
It is logical that the weaker is sublated, not the stronger.

If this were so, then those two [rites] should not be performed; for they would be obtained through the general rule (codaka), and that [rule] is absent here because it has been set aside. This being the position reached, it is replied:
The view of the teacher Jaimini is that the two *ājyabhāga* offerings must be performed.
Why? Because there would be a prohibition of one's own independent procedure (*svatantra*) due to the occurrence of another's procedure (*paratantra*).
For when the performance of one's own procedure results in the occurrence of another's procedure, there should be a prohibition of that [former].
Just as the ritual for the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) follows that of the cake-offering (*puroḍāśika*),
so too it is not logical to prohibit something that does not serve any of one's own purposes;
just as when Devadatta’s carriage is stopped upon reaching Yajñadatta’s, it is not his clothes or ornaments that are stopped.
Furthermore, no animal-related subsidiary (pāśuka-aṅga) is required here for the two butter-portions (ājyabhāgau);
therefore, its prohibition would not be logical.
Consequently, there is an exclusion of the cori.
As for the claim that "the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) is directly perceived," there is no application of the injunction of performance here at all;
for it would indeed have to include the subsidiaries as well.
The two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśau) possess limbs by means of the very same [limbs] belonging to the animal sacrifice;
for even though this [animal sacrifice] is directly perceived, it does not take the two butter-portions (ājyabhāgau).
A limb that is proximate within the context (prakaraṇa) is grasped by the injunction of performance (prayogavacana).
"Those two, O gentle one, are neither in the lower [world] nor in the sacrificial animal.

Furthermore, it has been said: the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) is the grasper that seizes by name what has already been produced; the extended application (codaka) is also a grasper in its respective domain.
Therefore, that [position] is stronger.
Dvivedaganga says: "According to Jaimini, there would be a prohibition of independence because of the resulting dependence on another.

(Showing that the example given by the author of the Bhāṣya is for the sake of illustration, he says: Of this very [Paśupuroḍāśa], those things which do not exist in the animal sacrifice, such as the portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), the pouring out (*nivāpa*), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and so forth—that must be performed, and not...

Thus arises the doubt: therefore, for the sake of resolving it, this [Bhāṣya] says: "Is the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) set aside by the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance), or is the *prayogavacana* set aside by the *codaka*? [Note: these are not the third-person singular forms of the verb *chid*, but rather refer to the co-operation (*sahaprayoga*). Is the cake-offering (*puroḍāśayāga*) performed together with the *prayogavacana* and not lost, while the *codaka* is lost; or is it the reverse?
If the *codaka* is primary, there would be no performance of [acts such as] threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth.
But when there is a conflict with the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), the *karaṇa* [is the deciding factor].
In that case, because it is inferential (*ānumānika*), the general rule (*codaka*) is sublated, but not the injunction of performance, because that is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).
This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that a portion of the *prayogavacana* pertaining to the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*) is sublated by the *prayogavacana* pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) (not the sublation of the whole).
Which is that portion? It is said:

(Upasaṃgraha: The statement of performance. In this context: the prefix *upa* signifies proximity; the prefix *sam* signifies totality; and the root *grah*, meaning "to take," signifies "to perform" (i.e., the act of execution).
Thus, the statement of performance consists of these three parts.
In this context, this [term] (*prayogavacana*) has the nature of apprehension (*grahaṇa*).
The others, however, [refer to] proximity and totality (the printed text reads *samīpasakalye*; the manuscript *ḍupa* reads *samīpakaraṇasākalyakaraṇe*), and to qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).
By means of those two [proximity and completeness], that [injunctive statement] is perceived as qualified in all cases.
(In this regard, he shows the portion to be set aside: The qualifier is apprehended through the principle of "otherwise being inexplicable" (*anyathānupapatti*).

The other [the injunctive statement itself] does not think, "I do not exist as qualified by proximity and completeness"; rather, it brings about proximity and completeness [not by being heard, but by its own nature].
And here, by the procedural injunction (*prayogavacana*) pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*), proximity is established for certain elements such as the *prayāja* offerings;
thus, the requirement of their otherwise inexplicability (*anyathānupapatti*) is exhausted.

However, for those elements—such as the *ājyabhāga* offerings, the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), and the threshing (*vahanana*)—for which proximity to the animal has not been established, the procedural injunction indeed establishes that proximity through the force of their otherwise inexplicability.

Therefore, by way of *prasaṅga* (extended application), that portion of the instrumental case denoting proximity which pertains to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth is set aside for that [performance-injunction].
Now, as for what was said—that because the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) is inferential, it is weak and thus sublated—that is not correct;
for the *codaka* is not weak.

Why? If the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) does not effect the application [of details] at the time of origin (*utpatti*), then for what would there be the creation of proximity, or for what would there be the complete inclusion?

Therefore, even though it is directly perceived, the statement of performance (*prayogavacana*) is weaker than the *codaka*, because it occurs at a later time; thus, the statement of performance is set aside.

Furthermore, when there is an impeller (*codaka*), a contingency arises [which gains its own status]. For instance, if the impeller prescribes the *āghāra* and other rites up to the *patnīsaṃyāja* as being related to the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*)— meaning that they do not provide assistance to the *āghāra* and so forth [in their own context]— then subsequently, the injunctive statement of performance (*prayogavacana*) brings them into proximity.

And since that bringing together is performed by the *pāśuka* (application-injunction), [it does not perform it itself]; thus, the establishment of the *prasaṅga* (extension/application) occurs [and not otherwise]. To explain why: if there were neither the production nor the presence of the subsidiaries (*aṅgas*) for that *puroḍāśa*, then, because they are unproduced [due to the absence of subsidiaries, as their accomplishment would already be established through the *pāśuka* injunction and the *codaka*], the application-injunction would lack the very power to bring them together.
Furthermore, because there is no act of bringing [the elements] together, it is not at all tenable that proximity was established by something else, since there is no such requirement.
As the Śāstra states: "In that case, the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) prevails because it is directly perceived;
however, the extended application (*codaka*), being inferential in nature, is weak and must be set aside"—this is the reasoning of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
This being the position reached, we reply:
"When the subsidiary rites [of the model sacrifice] have been connected with the sacrificial cakes by means of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer),
the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance) subsequently prescribes them as qualified by those [cakes]."

Therefore, that portion of the injunction regarding the performance which pertains to the *prayāja* offerings and the like is set aside; however, even that is not set aside in the case of the *ājyāni* offerings.
[Regarding the *soma* sacrifice: because it depends upon the previously mentioned *prasaṅga*, there is a logical connection (*saṃgati*).

The Prābhākaras, however, maintain that even in the case of the *ājyabhāga* offerings and the *prayāja* oblations, the injunction pertaining to the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*) exerts its influence; since that location also serves as the motivator (*prayojaka*), there is sublation (*bādha*). Because an injunction has the singular nature of being a motivator, its status as such is not lost merely by being enjoined within the ritual framework (*tantra*) of another; thus, although the injunction itself is a motivator, it relies upon the motivation provided by another due to its placement within that framework, and therefore there is no separate performance.

However, this does not imply an absence of causal efficacy (*prayojakatva*) on the part of the injunction; for if that were the case, there would be no distinction between the injunction of the *puroḍāśa* and other offerings which are the subject of the context (*prasaṅgin*), and the injunction of the *vājina* and other offerings which are not its cause.

Thus he says: the meaning of the Sūtra, according to the view of the teacher Jaimini, is that when something dependent occurs in the place of something independent, there is a prohibition of the latter;
however, nothing from the sequence of the animal sacrifice (*pāśukrama*) occurs in the place of the *ājyabhāga* and other such offerings.
[Objection: "The two *ājyabhāga* offerings do not exist in the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice; this is its *codaka* [extended injunction].
Therefore, they do not [apply] from that [source]. [Reply: Not so, because that would result in the sublation of the *prayogaśāstra* (the manual of ritual performance).

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding those auxiliary elements such as the *ājyabhāga* offerings and the *āghāta* which do not exist in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), there arises the inquiry whether they should or should not be performed in the cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*). In this consideration, since the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) of the cake-offering requires a procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and since the assistance arising from the application of the archetypal rules (*codaka*) pertaining to the proximate animal sacrifice is already present, the requirement for a procedure is satisfied merely by postulating that [the archetypal elements] produce a fitness conducive to the generation of its own transcendental result (*apūrva*). Therefore, it is not necessary to assume an independent extension (*atideśa*) through the injunction of the cake-offering, as that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Therefore, just as in the case of the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, because there is no requirement for the *ājyabhāga* offerings when their established auxiliary benefit is absent, the assumption of an extended application (*atideśa*) does not arise; so too in the present case, since there is no requirement due to the presence of established benefits, the assumption of an extended application is untenable. Consequently, there is no evidence for the status of the *ājyabhāga* and other such elements as being auxiliaries.
