For this very reason, even the injunction regarding the performance of the cake (*puroḍāśa*) following the performance of the [main] action operates only with respect to the primary rite itself, and not with respect to the auxiliaries or for the sake of the benefits produced by them; thus, there is also parsimony (*lāghava*).

Nor is it the case that even in this way the assumption of extended application (*atideśa*) is based solely on the expectation of the directly contributing subsidiaries (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) that produce the eleven potsherds; for if that were so, the same would follow for the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice as well.

In reality, however, according to the principle of the *anuvāsa* section (7.1.12–9), since the eleven potsherds are understood as established in common worldly practice, there is no necessity to procure them during the course of the performance.
The distinction, however, is that in the Gṛhamedhīya, because a few specific directly contributing subsidiaries are recited in the text, they must be performed during the course of the ritual.

Therefore, the *ājyabhāga* and other such rites are not performed for the sake of the *puroḍāśa*. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the following is stated]: although the auxiliaries of the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) actually produce a capacity conducive to the generation of the *apūrva* of the *puroḍāśa* by virtue of being of that same class (*tajjātīya*), there is no assumption (*kalpanā*) of a word expressing a causal relationship between them in the form: "one should bring about the capacity through the auxiliaries related to the *parvan*, which is the primary part of the *puroḍāśa*. For if that were the case, it would follow that even the *apūrvas* produced by the subsidiaries of the animal sacrifice would become generators of this specific capacity. And this is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Since even the *apūrvas* (unseen potencies) produced by the subsidiaries of the Jyotiṣṭoma generate benefit for the *savanīya*, the extension (*atideśa*) of the *daikṣa* [rules] would apply there as well.

Furthermore, because the status of being a "benefit" belonging to a subsidiary connected to a preceding *parvan* is sublated in the case of the *apūrva* produced by the *puroḍāśa*, and because it would be over-extensive (*atiprasakta*) in the case of the benefit produced by the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth, it is impossible to assume such a term [for the benefit].

Therefore, there must necessarily be an upward displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the connection with the clarified butter (*ājya*), which is established through its association with the animal (*paśu*) that is its own primary element, and which is not sublated by the absence [of such a connection] produced by other factors.

One must state that the postulation is simply: "one should effect the fitness for the etymological derivation. In that case, it is better to postulate: "one should effect the fitness for the etymological derivation by means of the relationship with the Āgneya and Upāṃśuyāja cakes, as well as the five-fold assistance arising from their own association.
And therefore, the extension of the ritual details (*iṣṭika-dharma*) to the *puroḍāśa* cake is indeed logical.

And by virtue of that universal assistance, when the items have been obtained through their connection with it, at the time of the extension (*atideśa*) of the constituent elements (*padārtha*), the extension of those elements is necessarily a supplement to the injunction for their performance (*prayogavidhi*) in that specific context; therefore, it is entirely appropriate in the case of the *ājyabhāga* offerings and so forth.
However, regarding those auxiliary acts (*aṅga*) that are obtained from elsewhere, there is no extension because there is no purpose for extension in their case.
But in the portion concerning the non-assistance of the constituent elements, that [extension] certainly applies.

Although there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the benefit (*upakāra*) itself due to the complexity [of such a process], as well as because the definition of extension applies to other [elements], nevertheless, by means of a single extension, the objects (*padārtha*) are understood through the medium of the archetypal benefit (*prākṛtopakāra*) as being subject to optionality; and since the benefit itself is established through its connection with the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it too becomes an object of extension. Thus, in the case of *prasaṅga* (incidental application), extension occurs only when the benefit is obtained from another source through the medium of the archetypal benefit via extension, because the injunction of the objects is contingent upon that. In the absence of such [benefit], even if the connection with the benefit were established, there would be no injunction of the objects; therefore, no extension takes place.
Furthermore, because the constituent elements (*padārtha*) themselves are not things to be performed, there is no injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) either.

For this very reason, in all cases—whether in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*)—the meaning of the sentence in the injunctions regarding subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is as follows: "If assistance is not obtained from another source, then accomplish the requisite fitness by means of this subsidiary.

Therefore, even in the case at hand, since assistance is obtained through *prasaṅga* (incidental application) when the performance occurs in the midst of the extensive performance of the ectype, there is no performance of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.

Furthermore, even in the case of the *paśupuroḍāśa* (the cake-offering for the animal sacrifice) performed as part of the *daikṣa* [initiation], when it is carried out according to one's capacity by performing eleven *prayāja* offerings as a constant rule, the performance of five *prayāja* offerings is for the sake of the *puroḍāśa* itself; and in that case, the two feet [of the animal] also possess the status of *prasaṅga* (incidental benefit), because there is no distinction in obtaining assistance from another source. For this very reason, even such factors as "falling within the middle of the *tantra*" are merely indicators for obtaining assistance. Therefore, it is established that where assistance is obtained from another source, there is neither an extended application (*atideśa*) of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) that produce it, nor an injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavidhi*); however, in other respects, both [the *atideśa* and the *prayogavidhi*] apply.

Nor does it follow that there is no distinction [between *prasaṅga* and other types of application] simply because there is an absence of an injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) even in the case of what is not a motivator (*aprayojya*), since *prasaṅga* is distinct from that due to the presence of an injunction of performance in the locus of *prasaṅga* when benefit is obtained from another source. In reality, however, even the fourth [type of application] consists in being a non-motivator precisely when benefit is obtained from elsewhere; such is the appropriate form of *prasaṅga*, and thus there is no lack of designation. It should be understood that the very state of being a non-motivator is itself the nature of *prasaṅga*.

As for the Prābhākara view that both the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) and the *prayoga-vidhi* (performance injunction) exist [in the case of modified sacrifices], yet there is no performance because of a lack of purpose—that is disregarded; for if the *prayāja* and other rites, which are enjoined by the injunction as qualified by specific qualities, were not performed, it would be impossible to obtain the result due to the absence of the enjoined qualities.
In this view, however, the logic of the "portion of the cake-offering" (*pauroḍāśika-yāga-bhāga*) applies.
The distinction is simply that because the qualities are enjoined on the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), there is no deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) [in the performance].

As for the fact that in this section the root text treats the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) as the subject matter and formulates the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of the abolition of the extended application (*codaka*), and formulates the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by accepting the *codaka* while treating it as merely the injunction of performance— that has been disregarded because it is devoid of logical justification and lacks purpose.

Maṇḍana: "In that case, there is something additional, such as the *ājyabhāga* offerings," referring here to the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*). Śaṅkara: "But in the case of the cake (*puroḍāśa*), it is not non-existent."
3. That which does not exist in the archetype (*prakṛti*) is not employed, whereas that which exists there is indeed employed.

However, when there is a determination of the occasion (*nimitta*) at the time of the fourth performance (*caturthakaraṇa*), it is stated in the *Tantraratna* (on *Soma* 10.1.1, section 3) that [the rite] must be performed according to the principle of the sacrificial portion of the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika-yāga-bhāga-nyāya*) during the invocation of the deities (*devatā-āvāhana*).

In the case of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (āmīṣomīya-paśu), the release of speech (vāgvisarga) must be performed at the call to the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt-āhvāna) for the purpose of the rites concerning the sacrificial cake (pauroḍāśika-karma).
See Mīmāṃsākośa, page 122, under the entry "Release of Speech in the Animal Sacrifice to Agni and Soma."
The term *pauroḍāśika* is not Vedic because it is not recited in either the Mantras or the Brāhmaṇas; thus, there is no relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin) between them.
Nevertheless, even though the word is non-Vedic, it is authoritative because it is an eternal designation (*anādi-saṃjñā*) and because it is rooted in an existing Smṛti.
That the word *pauroḍāśika* denotes this [collection] is not beyond the reach of the senses.
Vārttika 3.1.7.4, p. 857:

Although the *prayāja* and other rites mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa designated as *pauroḍāśika* (pertaining to the cake-offering) would, by virtue of that designation, appear to serve the purpose of the cake-offering alone, it is established through the context (*prakaraṇa*)—in its general sense—that they also serve the purpose of the *pāṃśuyāja*. Context is more powerful than designation (*samākhyā*).
At the time of summoning the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation) for the *pauroḍāśika* rites, there is the release of the silence (*vāgyama*) maintained during the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*).
In the *iṣṭis* belonging to the Full Moon sacrifice, the *brāhmaṇa* [text] itself undergoes postponement (*utkarṣa*) regarding the *aiṣṭika* and *saumya* offerings.
Regarding the matter of whether the *āghānīyā* sacrifice precedes or the *soma* sacrifice precedes, there is indeed an option even for the Brāhmaṇa [class].
By the term "full-moon oblation" (*paurṇamāsa-havis*), the *āmīṣomīya-puroḍāśa* is understood; it is precisely this that is postponed for the Brāhmaṇa until after the *soma* sacrifice.
Regarding the *upāṃśuyāja* as well, the *āmīṣomīya* [offering] must be performed by the Brāhmaṇa priest before the *soma* sacrifice;
however, the *prājāpatya* or *vaiśvadeva* [offerings] must certainly be performed, so there is no displacement (*utkarṣa*) of that [latter group].

The *paurṇamāsī* is the aggregate of three sacrifices: the *āgneya*, the *upāṃśuyāja*, and the *āgnīṣomīya*. The *amāvāsyā* is the aggregate of three sacrifices: the *āgneya*, the *aindra-dadhi*, and the *aindra-payaḥ*.
(Ci. 2.2.3) The *paurṇamāsī* is not a modification (*vikāra*) of the *darśa*, nor is the *darśa* a modification of the *paurṇamāsī*.
5|1|16. The Full Moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī) has two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) after the Soma sacrifice, but before the Soma sacrifice it has only one sacrificial cake.
Bhāṣya 10|8|18|62: Before the Soma sacrifice, the Full Moon sacrifice is devoid of the Agni-Soma sacrificial cake and consists solely of the cake for Agni;
and in that case, the Upāṃśu sacrifice must also be performed as being dedicated either to Viṣṇu or to Prajāpati.
In the phrase "the full moon day" (paurṇamāsīm), there is an injunction regarding the composite whole of the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice.

(Regarding the two sentences within the context: "One should sacrifice with the *agnīṣomīya* on the full moon day" and "Moving toward the new moon day [one should sacrifice]"): In the first sentence, it is the very *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice under discussion that is enjoined for a separate result, just as in the case of the *aveṣṭi*, because there is extreme parsimony (*lāghava*) in the second injunctive statement.
Thus, like the injunction regarding the *aindravāyava* cup, this [sacrifice] is both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*).

This being the prima facie view, since it would result in the redundancy of the word *paurṇamāsī* as a term denoting a collective whole, the fourth mode of injunction is more appropriate according to the reasoning stated above.
(Saṃkarṣa 1.2.17):
"He sacrifices on the full moon" (*paurṇamāsīṃ yajate*) and "He sacrifices on the new moon" (*amāvāsyāṃ yajate*)—these two words are restatements (*anuvādita*) of the rites under discussion.
There is no deliberation regarding what is unprecedented.
2.2.13–8. Prior to the full moon day of the Mādhyā [sacrifice], the initiation for the Gavāmayana begins with four draughts.
6.5.9.30–37. On the full moon day, the hall need not be constructed for the purpose of casting the fires.

Bhāṣya 4.2.4.10–13: Since it is enjoined that [Soma] accompanied by Agni [is to be offered] on the full moon day, the presentation of Soma alone was refuted in the section concerning Mahendra (Mahendrādhikaraṇa).
Vārttika 3.1.1.2–3:
On the full moon day, there is a restriction regarding Agni because there is no distinction [in the injunction].

Regarding the statement, "They should undergo initiation four days before the full moon," there is no fixed rule as to which month's full moon is intended in the Gavāmayana sacrifice. Since no specific distinction is mentioned and no particular full moon is specified, there would be no restriction as to which full moon the cups are to be taken; this is one preliminary position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
On the full moon day;
however, because of its immediate sequence, it should be the Caitrī full moon day.
The word "tu" (but) serves to refute the first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

It is not that there is no fixed rule; rather, it should be the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) of Caitra, occurring in the month of Caitra and conjoined with the Citrā constellation. Why? Because of the immediate sequence.
Immediately after the aforementioned statement, it is heard in scripture: "The mouth of the season is indeed the full moon of the year, which is the full moon of Caitra.

According to the principle that "in cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence," it is concluded that this full moon is the one of Caitra; such is the second prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Alternatively, it is the full moon of Māgha, because of the scriptural mention of the eleventh day.
Having set aside the two preceding prima facie views by means of the word "or" (vā), he states the established conclusion:
that full moon day (paurṇamāsī) should be the Māghī, belonging to the month of Māgha. Why? Because of the scriptural mention of the eleventh [lunar day].
For regarding the purchase of Soma, there is a scriptural statement concerning eleven:
"The purchase of these is accomplished by means of the eleventh.
For one who has been initiated four days prior to the full moon of Māgha, the purchase can be performed on the eleventh day—that is, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that it is the full moon day of Māgha.
If it is argued that other [full moon days] are also intended, [the answer is] no;
it must be the full moon day [of Māgha].
In the section concerning the full moon sacrifice, that time at which the performers of the sattra are afflicted is the "afflicted" time;
and they become afflicted by the cold.
And it is cold in Māgha, not in Caitra.
Likewise, [the text says]: "Those who undergo initiation on the eleventh day speak of these [months] as being inverted for the year.
By the word "inverted" (vyasta), the delimitation of the solstice is expressed.
Furthermore, the determination of the solstice occurs in the months of Māgha and Phālguna, not in Caitra.
Likewise, it is said: "Not rejoicing in the waters, they proceed to the avabhṛtha bath.
If the mountain [the sun] were at the end of Māgha, there would be no rejoicing in the waters if one did not go to the avabhṛtha bath.
But in the month of Caitra, they should approach the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) while rejoicing.

From these indicative marks it is known that the initiation for the Gavāmayana occurs on the fourteenth day prior to the full moon of Māgha, and not prior to the full moon of Caitra. On which full moon or new moon should the modified sacrifices (vikṛtis), such as those dedicated to Indra-Agni, be performed? They should be performed on either the full moon or the new moon, because of the scriptural statement: "He who is about to sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, an animal sacrifice, or a Soma sacrifice, should sacrifice on the full moon or the new moon."
On the full moon day, because the place, time, and agent are one and the same for the Āgneya and other offerings, they are performed by way of *tantra* (simultaneous performance).
Even on the full moon day when there is only a single *puroḍāśa* cake, the *upāṃśuyāja* is still performed.
See Mīmāṃsākośa, page 1165, under the entry "Upāṃśuyājaḥ ekapuroḍāśāyām.
The Upāṃśuyāja occurs only on the full moon day (paurṇamāsī).
In that rite, Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, and Agnīṣoma are the deities in alternation.
On the full moon day, fourteen oblations are offered; on the new moon day, thirteen.
(There are five *prayājas*, two *ājyabhāgas*, the *puroḍāśas* for Agni and for Agni-Soma, the *upāṃśuyāja*, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and the thirteen principal offerings—thus making fourteen.
On the new moon day, because of the absence of the *upāṃśuyāja*, there are thirteen: the offering to Agni and the *sāṃnāyya* for Indra.)
Bhāṣya 4.1.110: On the full moon day, there is the touching of the oblation with the Caturhotṛ formula;
the mantra beginning with "Pṛthivī hotā" (Earth is the Hotṛ) is the [formula] for that Hotṛ.
'One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī [offering] on the full moon day'—this is an injunction prescribing a time, not a mere restatement. Bhāṣya 4|2|9|23–24."

In the injunction regarding time, "One should sacrifice with the Full Moon [offering] on the full moon day," since it is understood that several primary rites along with their subsidiaries (sāṅga) are to be performed, a restriction of the constituent elements (padārtha-niyama) is established for the sake of accomplishing them.

At the time of the *praṇayana* (carrying forward of the fire) on the full moon day, there is the selection of the Brahman priest (*brahmavaraṇa*); on the new moon day, it occurs as before. *Soma*, 5.1.2.
Bhāṣya 12.1.18.39: By the injunction "One should sacrifice on the full moon day" and so forth, the connection of the time with the Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual is prescribed; it is not a separate ritual.
VI. 2|3|123: On the full moon day, because there is no branch for the driving away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*), the cutting of a branch need not be performed.
Among the *añjara* vessels, some wood must be taken up for the purpose of placing the potsherds (*kapāla*).
At the recitation of the *sūktavāka* on the full moon day, the deities of the full moon are excluded and the deities of the new moon are connected.
And in the other case, there is the mention of the other deities;
thus, in the other instance, the mention of the other deities is purposeless.
On the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), even when there are only two sacrificial cakes (*ekapuroḍāśā*) due to the absence of Soma, the *upāṃśuyāja* must still be performed.
On the full moon day, the preparation of the altar (*vedikaraṇa*) occurs after the placing of the oblation materials (*havir-ābhimarśana*).

Bāla. pṛ. 19. When the full moon sacrifice has been omitted and an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has been performed, if one performs only the new moon sacrifice (*darśa*), the *vaimṛdha* offering should not be made as part of that new moon rite.
Soma.
The section concerning the Full Moon [sacrifice].
The principle of the Full Moon [sacrifice].

Since the section on sacrifice (*ijyādhikaraṇa*) [4.4.11] would otherwise constitute a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) without the section on the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsyādhikaraṇa*), the latter is commenced as the necessary prerequisite for the former.

Su. P. 732. The section concerning the *Vārttika* is connected with the section on the Full Moon sacrifice (*Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*), because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to indicate that the "Injunctions of the Knower" (*vidvadvākya*) refer to separate rituals; thus, although the application of mantras is not possible there [in the *vidvadvākya*], it is possible in the case of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices. Consequently, the doubt arises as a further objection that these two [mantras]—"The *vārtraghna* is recited at the Full Moon, the *dhṛvatī* at the New Moon"—are intended for the purpose of restriction (*vyavasthā*). [Kau. 3.1.13, p. 211]. By the section on the Full Moon sacrifice, an exception to the principle of repetition (*abhyāsa*) will be established, because they are restatements of a collective whole (*samudāyānuvāda*).
The *upāṃśuyāja* (2.2.4), *āghāra-agnihotra* (2.2.5), and the *paśu-soma* sections (2.2.6) constitute exceptions (*apavāda*) to the *paurṇamāsī* section.
Vārttika 2.1.12, p.

371: In the *paurṇamāsī* section, it was established that [the injunction] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) because it connects with a prior action characterized by the introduction of multiple qualities.

Su. Pṛ. 827. In the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa* (2.2.3), because the occurrence of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) would result from enjoining multiple subordinate qualities (*guṇa*), it is accepted that these are restatements (*anuvāda*) of the collective group.
Vākyārtha-pṛ. 20.

In that very same *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*, since it is impossible to enjoin multiple qualities in a rite already established by another source, the distinction based on those qualities is demonstrated.

In the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*, by means of the two sūtras, "But it is a quality because of its connection with the scriptural statement" (*guṇastu śrutisaṃyogāt*) and "Or rather, it is an injunction, because of the simultaneous teaching of the qualities" (*codanā vā guṇānāṃ yugapacchāstrāt*), there is the refutation of the objection (*prasaṅga*) regarding the injunction of multiple qualities within a single action through another means of knowledge.
This occurs in the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*.
The *paurṇamāsī-nyāya* (the principle of the full moon sacrifice) is found at *Ku.* 2.2.12–13.

It is stated in the *Kaustubha* under the section on the *paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa* that in the *āgneya-vākya*, the *āgneya-dravya* (the material for the offering to Agni) consists of the full moon and new moon sacrifices (*paurṇamāsy-amāvāsyātmaka*).
Bhaṭṭa 8.1.6:

First, regarding the *āgneya* sentence, since it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) by enjoining multiple qualities—namely substance and deity—while restating an already established action, one must accept that the action is enjoined by the quality itself which causes the syntactical split, as was stated incidentally in the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*. (Kauṣītaki-bhāṣya 2.2.122, p. 266). Furthermore, in the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*, it was established that the names *Darśa* and *Pūrṇamāsa* possess well-known meanings.

Bhāṭṭa 4.4.11: It has been stated in the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa* (Kau. 3.1.123, p. 212) that the absence of those two (*liṅga* and *krama*) is not due solely to the sentence’s partiality toward non-abrogation, but also because of the assumption of the parsimony (*lāghava*) of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*).

In passages such as "He who [performs] with the *iṣṭi*," where the performance is already established, it is stated in the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa* that there is an injunction of application (*viniyogavidhi*) regarding the time-component by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the ritual action.

Where the qualification of the qualifier cannot be established without the operation of multiple injunctions, there arises a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the repetition of the injunctive suffix (*vidhyāvṛtti*), because of the distinct operations of the injunctive suffix for the purpose of establishing the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified and for the purpose of enjoining the qualified entity as a whole. This occurs, for example, in the *Paurṇamāsī* section (*adhikaraṇa*), where the actions enjoined by the *vidvadvākya* are the objects of subsidiary injunctions (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the *Āgneya* and other rites.

Where, due to the existence of a previously unestablished cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is only a single qualification of the fruit of the injunction, and because those qualifications are enjoined by another injunction as being things to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there is repetition; this is clear from the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa* (Kau.

2.2.156, p. 199). However, where the occurrence [of the relationship] is through the connection of being a factor of action (*kārakatva*), as in "the *Āgneya*" and so forth, since there can be no connection with the status of a factor of action without a prior connection with the action, and since the occurrence can be justified even as a subsequent relationship, the connection with the eight-potsherd cake (*aṣṭakapāla*) does not occur at the very beginning.
Rather, this [connection] occurs solely through the mediation of the relationship with the meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).
This will be explained in the section on the Full Moon Sacrifice (paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa) for the purpose of establishing the distinction between sentences (vākya-bheda).

On page 38, in the Vārttika commentary on [PMS 2.2.1], the view that there is a temporal restriction between the two [actions] of *vardhati* and *yati* has already been refuted in the very same section on the Full Moon Sacrifice.

On page 211, under sūtra 3.1.123, it has already been stated in the *Paurṇamāsyadhikaraṇa* that the fixed order (*vyavasthā*) of the *vārtraghnī*, *vṛdhanvatī*, and *mantra*s is determined by the ritual action (*karmakṛtā*), and not by time (*kālakṛtā*). On page 212, under the same sūtra (3.1.123), even greater care is taken to refute [the opposing view] regarding the acceptance of the composite whole (*samudāya*) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* as the means of accomplishing the fruit (*phalasādhanatva*).

The discussion concerning the restatement of the aggregate (*samudāyānuvāda*)—which serves as the basis for the distinction between repetition (*abhyāsa*) and the cause [of a separate act] (*animittabheda*)—is carried out in the section on the *Paurṇamāsī* (Full Moon Day) within the *Vidvadvākya*.
This is the principle stated in the *guṇasūtra* concerning the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) section:

when an action has been enjoined by another sentence, since subordinate elements (*guṇa*) exist for the sake of that action, there is no mutual relationship [among them] and thus no mutual qualification; consequently, because it is possible to enjoin one subordinate element as qualified by another, each respective subordinate element is taught as something to be performed.

Regarding the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the establishment of a single performance (*ekaprayogatā*) for each set of three [rites] is proven; this is appropriately demonstrated in the *Vārttika* on the section concerning the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) from the eleven [chapters], as stated in *Bālamanoramā*, p.
13. This concludes the section on the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices.
The principle of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī-nyāya*).
The words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* denote the ritual acts themselves, not the sacrificial offerings. (Vi. 3.7.4)

According to the logic of the term *paurṇamāsī* (as in *paurṇamāsī-nyāya*, ŚBh 2.2.3), since it is determined that the words *ācāra* and *agnihotra* denote each individual form, the status of being a ritual action (*karmatva*) must be predicated of each individual form. And that [status] is already known. (Su.
Some maintain that even on full-moon days and other festival days (*parvan*), there is no restriction regarding the time for the *soma* sacrifice when the *soma* is established;

however, the true principle is that there is indeed no regard for seasons, lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), and so forth, due to the force of the double negative (as in the rule: "one should not ask about the season or the lunar mansion"). Nevertheless, one must certainly observe the festival days and the fortnights (*pakṣa*).
Bhāṭṭa 5.1.5:
The *anumārjana* (smearing) is not prompted by the collection [of rites] such as the *Paurṇamāsī*, but rather by the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
Bhāṣya 9.1.5.

The time for the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) and the optional deity Viśvadeva are associated with the *upāṃśuyāja*. Regarding the *āgnīṣomīya* oblation belonging to the full moon sacrifice, there is a view that for a Brāhmaṇa, it is like one who has recently died after [the consumption of] Soma.
Some maintain that there is only a postponement (*utkarṣa*) of the full moon sacrifice itself.
The Paurṇamāsī Principle. The two sentences concerning the knower (*vidvadvākya*) are restatements (*anuvāda*) of two composite groups.
But the context [belongs] to the full moon sacrifice, because its form is not stated [elsewhere].

The Bhāṣya says: For they recite thus: "The cake for Agni on eight potsherds which is never omitted at the new moon and the full moon"; "Those two, Agni and Soma, one should worship with clarified butter in a low voice at the full moon"; "To those two he offered this cake for Agni and Soma on eleven potsherds at the full moon; curd for Indra at the new moon; milk for Indra at the new moon."
Likewise: "He pours the libation (āghāra)," "He offers the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga)," "He cuts off for the Sviṣṭakṛt," "He performs the Patnīsaṃyājas," "He offers the Samid-yajus.

Similarly: "One who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the Full Moon," and "One who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the New Moon. Regarding this, there is a doubt: are all these equally principal acts, or are the [offerings] beginning with the Āgneya and ending with the Payas the principal acts, while the Āghāra and others are merely auxiliary rites (ārādupakāraka)?

Likewise, the phrases "he who, knowing thus" (*ya evaṃ vidvān*) are either restatements (*anuvāda*) of the previously mentioned rites connected in this manner, or they are injunctions (*vidhātṛ*) for two new rites—as in "he who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon" (*paurṇamāsī*) and "he who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon" (*amāvāsyā*). In that case, these would be injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*). What is the prima facie view? That because of the difference in words (*śabdāntaratva*), the Āgneya and other rites are equally primary (*samapradhāna*).
This being the position, we reply:
The context, however, pertains to the Full Moon sacrifice; the two [formulas] connected with the Full Moon and the New Moon are restatements of the Agniya and other sacrifices under discussion.
Why? Because there is no mention of their specific forms.
In the statement, "He who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice named the Full Moon," not all sacrifices are being referred to.
That which is designated by the name "Full Moon" (Paurṇamāsī) is what is being enjoined.
However, we do not understand in this way what the specific form of such a sacrifice is;
therefore, we grasp nothing at all.

Therefore we say that [the two terms] are meaningless when applied to the preceding [section] during the process of investigation. However, if they are intended as restatements (*anuvāda*) of the subjects under discussion, then it is understood that their form refers to the sacrifices connected with the *Paurṇamāsī* and *Amāvāsyā* which are present in context;
in that case too, the statement serves its purpose.

But how, it may be asked, can a word ending in the singular number denote many? It is explained that this is understood by virtue of its being a collective term (*samudāyaśabda*). For the sacrifices previously mentioned are possessed of form (*rūpavantaḥ*), and there exists for them a collective aggregate (*samudāya*) enjoined by the suffix.
This word "form" (rūpa) is used with reference to that [collection].
Therefore, there is no fault in its having the singular number.
For a word ending in the singular can indeed refer to many things when it depends upon a collective whole, as in the examples: "the herd," "the forest," "the family," or "he recites."
When the terms *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* denote the collection of the Āgneya and other sacrifices, then they are designated by the words *darśapūrṇamāsa* themselves.
Consequently, these [sacrifices] have a connection with the fruit; and because they are connected to the fruit, the Āghāra and other rites are *ārādupakāraka* (indirectly contributing) causes.

Alternatively—having cited all the injunctions for the sacrifices within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the Commentator initiates an inquiry: "Do all of them possess the status of being primary (*pradhāna*), or only some?"
To this it is replied: "This consideration regarding the subordinate and the principal is not within the scope of the fourth chapter;
by what occasion indeed has it been introduced here in the section defining the distinctions [of sacrificial acts]?"

Now, without considering the distinction based on number—which is a further internal difference characterized by repetition—how can one reflect upon the meaning that is not conducive to the definition? Some say: "This too is indeed for the sake of the definition," because of the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "Immediately thereafter, the primary and secondary [meanings] are examined" (*Bhāṣya* 2.2.1.1, p. 371).
But that is incorrect;
for, having raised that very objection, the statement is explained in quite another way.
For that third established object, which consists of the cognition of a previously unknown distinction,
has been stated here to be "presented.
However, this relationship of mutual subservience (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) among ritual actions is not in any way reconciled.
This will be established with great effort in the fourth [book], in the section concerning the statement "the sacrifices of the New and Full Moon [rites]";
and because of its clarity, it cannot be interpreted otherwise.
Therefore, this matter need not be deliberated upon here.

The statements "one who knows thus" (*ya evaṃ vidvān*) and so forth are either restatements of what has already been introduced (*prakṛtānuvāda*), or they are injunctions of new rites (*apūrvakarmavidhi*); in either case, everything [stated] in the commentary, such as "in that regard, these are injunctions of subordinate qualities" (*tatrete guṇavidhayaḥ*), does not cohere with the framework of the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) as it was presented.
Furthermore, if this very point is what is being deliberated, then the preceding [arguments] should not have been introduced.
Moreover: "And when there is a difference [of action], their observed capacity is for the sake of establishing equal primacy."
How are the repetition of another word and the repetition [of the same word] described as being the cause?

"The difference [between the two] is stated on account of the difference in words and the absence [of certain marks]; furthermore, their status as equally primary is established by these very same [arguments]"—this is an unprecedented reasoning (*apūrvā yukti*).

Nor are distinct positions and reasons for the body of the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) observed, by which one could conclude that these two investigations were undertaken through a single systematic framework (*tantra*).
Therefore, it must be supported in this manner:

In this context, when the section (adhikaraṇa) is commenced for the purpose of refuting the claim that there is no difference characterized by repetition, two examples from among those cited are as follows: "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon day" and "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon day.

Regarding these, the doubt is: do these two words "yajati" (sacrifices) enjoin two entirely new rites (apūrva-karma), or do they merely refer back (anuvadanti) to certain sacrifices already under discussion, being qualified by the words "paurṇamāsī" and "amāvāsyā," which denote specific times inherent to their own designations?

In that context, since the distinction among the others— namely the Āgneya and so forth— is established through their qualities (*guṇa*), the Prayāja offerings and so forth through repetition (*abhyāsa*), and the Āghāra libations and so forth through difference of words (*śabdāntara*), their presentation here is for the purpose of the two positions of the section concerning the state of being equally primary (*samapradhānatva*) and the absence of the injunction of non-existence (*ajñābhāva*), and not as the subject matter of the body of the section itself.
For it has been stated that the two positions of the section are neither the state of being equally primary nor the absence of the injunction of non-existence.

In this regard, one position is as follows: [1] the fact that the sun is connected with the full moon and new moon days (*paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā*), [2] the resulting distinction between the rites denoted by those terms, and [3] the equal primacy of all the *āghāra* offerings and so forth; these three are linked as a single thesis because they stand in an inseparable relationship as successive results.

Likewise, there is another triad in that same manner: [1] the status of those two [terms] as mere restatements (*anuvāda*), [2] the distinction between the rites expressing them, and [3] the non-distinction of the *āghāra* offerings and so forth with respect to the *āgneya* and other sacrifices.

Since each triad is inseparably connected with the other two, the establishment of one necessarily entails the establishment of the other two; thus, in both of these positions, having considered that the desired conclusion is achieved by whatever has been proven, the third part—which constitutes the result—is presented.
Furthermore, although difference and non-difference are already implied by the sense of the argument, they are shown again at the end for the sake of clarification.
But why were difference and non-difference presented at the beginning through the door of the absence of equal primacy between the two separated [principles]?
Why? Some say: "For this is the style of the Teacher" (meaning that introducing a topic through a trivial door is the method of the Commentator).

For instance, he introduced the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) in exactly this same way even in the two preceding sections. (He offers a rebuttal according to his own view, based on the essence of the observation of indicative marks: Alternatively, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) which he will state in the fourth sūtra—namely, "In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the *prayāja* offerings and others are seen"—will, while being incapable of directly refuting the [view of] distinctness (*bheda*), refute the state of equal primacy (*samapradhānabhāva*).

And when that [the existence of difference] has been refuted, the two types of positive injunction (*vidhi*) are also necessarily refuted due to their inseparable connection; thus, this presentation is made by depending upon that [refutation]. However, if only difference were presented, that [refutation] would be impossible.
In that regard, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) will be twofold.

One [view] holds that, by way of equal primacy (*samaprādhānya*), while the *Āgneya* and other rites are indeed injunctions of action (*karmavidhi*), there is an injunction of actions distinct from those connected with the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices; another view, however, maintains that those two alone are injunctions of action, whereas the others are for the purpose of enjoining accessories (*guṇavidhāna*).
First, he adopts the position of distinction (*vyatirekapakṣa*) with the words: "Because of the difference in wording (*śabdāntaratvāt*), the New Moon sacrifice has equal primaries."

Although these two reasons—the distinctness from non-sacrifices due to being a different word (*śabdāntara*) and the repetition (*abhyāsa*) from sacrifices—do not directly coalesce as equally primary, nevertheless, because they are connected with the distinction that is implied by the acceptance of that [repetition], they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*).
This is what is meant: "There is a distinction from non-sacrifices because it is a different word, and from sacrifices because of repetition; therefore, they are equally primary.
Furthermore, there is no purpose whatsoever for a collective restatement (*samastānuvāda*).

Furthermore, nothing is heard regarding the names of those [acts] characterized by specific qualities, wherein one might expect the injunction of the nature of the ritual action to depend upon the excellence of the injunction. Nor is this designation well-known among any of the rituals under discussion.

Furthermore, even when [the act] is already present, there is an injunction such as "He offers the *samidh*s" (*samidho yajati*) by means of one of the following: the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*), an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), or the optative suffix (*pañcamalakāra*).

And even when there is the connection with the word *yat* (as in "That which belongs to Agni is on eight potsherds," *yad āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*), there is no loss of the power of injunction, just as in the aforementioned case. Nor is there an option between injunctions (*vidhivikalpa*) as in the case of different schools (*śālāntarīya*), because other scriptures are meaningful insofar as they are intended for the instruction of different persons.

However, there is no purpose here in postulating a separate ritual action; nor is it possible for this to be a praise of any other injunction, because there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*). What, then, are the substance and deity of these two rituals? That is now stated.
The substance is fixed and common, while the deity is indicated by the wording of the mantra;
because it possesses a form, the sacrifice is enjoined as something distinct.

"Indeed, this [clarified butter] is taken for the sake of the entire sacrifice"; because it serves all purposes, just as the *śrauva* clarified butter is the substance for the *upāṃśuyāja*, so too is it for these two sacrifices.
Furthermore, in the sequence of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, four *anuvākyā* verses are seen: two addressed to Agni and two addressed to Soma.

These are set aside by a stronger syntactical statement (*vākya*) and prescribed for these two rites: "The one containing the word *vātra* is recited at the full moon, and the one containing the word *vadhu* at the new moon."
For by the words "full moon" (*paurṇamāsī*) and "new moon" (*amāvāsyā*), nothing other than these very rites is mentioned here.
[Objection: But surely these two terms are used here to denote time. [Response: What indeed is the connection between time and the mantra?
In the case of visible rites, such as the *samidhenī* offerings, there is only a primary [action].
As it is said: "One should abandon that action by which one desires to go.
Therefore, since the two *anuvākyā*s are of equal purpose and are subject to option (*vikalpa*), a corresponding *yājyā* must also be formulated.

(If the invitatory verse [anuvākyā] belongs to Agni, the offering verse [yājyā] must also be assigned to Agni; if it belongs to Soma, the offering verse must be assigned to Soma— this is one established principle regarding the Full Moon sacrifice.)

Furthermore, when "upapatti" (arising) is used as a term for time, the locative case is employed because that time is everywhere the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), not the object (*karman*). Since it cannot logically be the locus [in the sense of being produced], it would have to be conceived in some other way.

As for the question, "What is the purpose of the mantra’s connection with time?"—if there were only one type of relationship characterized by being for that purpose (*tādarthya*), and if that were not present here, then it would be appropriate to speak in that way. However, in this case, while the status of being for the sake of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings is established, and since a confusion [of mantras] might otherwise arise, a restriction is made regarding the two mantras employed at different times: "The *vārtra-ghnī* is for the two *ājyabhāgas* occurring at the full moon."
"The Bṛdhanvatī verses [are prescribed] for the two Amāvāsyā sacrifices.
Furthermore: "Because their deities are well-known, they have a visible purpose and involve only a minor injunction."
In my view, the following conceptualization would apply to you:

everywhere, a connection is preceded by an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Since the two *ājyabhāga* offerings have well-known deities, they take up the mantras by virtue of having an expectancy for mantras capable of denoting those [deities].
In your view, however, regarding two previously unknown rites,
it is joined with the performance of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices together with one another, and with a single *Amāvāsyā*.

Because of the restriction that "in whichever moment one sacrifice, having been commenced, reaches completion, in that very same moment the others [do so]," the performance of each triad by way of a common procedure (*tantra*) is established.
However, if one follows the original time [of the primary rite], there would be a performance of those [subsidiaries] that are separated from their specific parts; thus, there is a distinction.

But if this were the case, since two groups joined together would constitute the instrument [of the sacrifice], there would be no mutual requirement between them—just as there is no requirement for the combination of auxiliary parts (*aṅga-sāhitya*). (The two negatives, "not... not," reinforce the original sense. Thus, just as there is knowledge of the auxiliaries at that time, so too the Full Moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) would imply the New Moon day (*amāvāsyā*), and the New Moon day would imply the Full Moon day; consequently, both would apply elsewhere, or else there would be no contradiction regarding the time of their origin and performance, since they would be performed even there.
For one who performs [the sacrifice] on the full moon day does not thereby fail to perform the new moon sacrifice, nor likewise the full moon sacrifice.
Nor is another time prohibited by the originative injunction, since that injunction is exhausted merely by establishing its own specific time.
To this, it is replied:
"For one whose true nature is not known at the [proper] time, yet does not perish,
there is no fault in calling Time a limiting adjunct (upādhi) imposed from without."

For the *amāvāsyā* sacrifice, having no requirement for a time of origin, does not await the time of the *paurṇamāsī* for the sake of its association with it; likewise, the *paurṇamāsī* does not await the time of the *amāvāsyā*. Thus, if these two groups were separated by another time, there would be a contradiction with their original form, resulting in an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) and a deficiency in the sacrifice (*apūrṇatva*). However, because the subsidiary acts (*aṅgāni*) have an indeterminate time and thus possess a requirement [for a specific time], and because there is no contradiction with their time of origin, there is no separation [of the subsidiaries] in the view that they are performed together (*sāhityapakṣa*). This is the [proper] time.
He said: "Because for the ignorant, this time exists even without this statement due to its being the primary time;
therefore, this statement has no causal role here."
It is said:
"The primary time for those who are ignorant is not established by the Mānavas;
for this very statement is that [scriptural] passage, by the force of which this is asserted."
[Objection: "But surely those situated at a distance cannot provide assistance.

[Another says: "Is it not established that assistance must be rendered to what is proximate? In all cases, whether something assists or does not assist is understood by following the specific scriptural injunction.
In that regard, there is no evidence whatsoever to suggest that what is remote cannot assist simply because there is no mention of proximity."

But is it not the case that this application of the *tantra* is established by another very statement, such as "he who [performs] with an *iṣṭi*, with an animal sacrifice, or with Soma," since there too the instrumental case-ending is employed? In that case as well, because the *iṣṭi*—as a whole together with its subsidiaries—is taken in relation to the time, such an intention is obtained.
True, it is obtained; however, the desired application is not thereby established.
For instance, does the word "*iṣṭi*" refer to the whole [collection] or to each [individual part]?
One should not think that the activity [of the mantra] consists merely of those three.
First of all, the term *iṣṭi* does not intend to denote the triad [of sacrifices] collectively.

Since the word *iṣṭi* applies to each one individually by virtue of its being a sacrifice (*yāga*), the performance would occur on either the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) or the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) for each one separately; thus, the correct performance of the ritual as a whole is not established.

Now, if it is argued that because the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the entire names such as *Āgneya* and so forth has somehow already occurred, they are taken up [as wholes]—just as in the case of the injunction "the *Soma* sacrifice proceeds"—even so, because the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*) is a single unit, both groups would have to be performed either on the full moon day or on the new moon day; in that case, there would be the same contradiction with the doubt regarding their origin (*utpatti*).

If it is argued that one should resort to a fixed option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) in accordance with that [single performance], even so, due to the requirement of the aforementioned [injunction], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of performing only one [of the two groups].

Likewise, because there is no basis for distinction among those who are ignorant [of the specific details], the performance of the *Paurṇamāsī* and *Amāvāsyā* sacrifices would occur in one place at one time. Therefore, the sentence "He who [sacrifices] with the *iṣṭi*" does not have the same purpose as those two (*Paurṇamāsī* and *Amāvāsyā*), because it is not included in the original archetype (*prakṛti*); thus, it proceeds toward its own time only in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

Now, one might object: by this, the performance of the ritual as a single unit (*tantra*) would be established, since in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* on level ground," the coexistence (*sāhitya*) is intended because the location is something to be prescribed.
To this it is replied:
"The state of being a common substratum (*tantratā*) is established as both collective and individual;
therefore, [the teaching] is to be practiced and received by all together, not by many individuals separately."
For even when [the subsidiaries] are performed separately, their status as *tantra* (common performance) is established merely by their occurring in the same location.
Thus, due to mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), at the very moment one sacrifice is joined with the common performance, the other is likewise joined; this is what is called *tantratva*.
This being the case, since all six [sacrifices] are undertaken simultaneously, they are capable of being performed in that very manner, and thus that same contradiction arises.

If, however, one proceeds in accordance with the requirement of simultaneous origination (*utpattikāla*), then since each [act] is connected to its own time, their simultaneity must be accomplished in relation to the whole; thus, in the event of a lapse, the performance would have to be completed on the full moon or new moon days.

Furthermore, the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) for those [acts] whose time has elapsed must be performed as they are adapted to that duration, and thus they might be performed at any point within the interval.
Alternatively, because it is logical that each primary act (*pradhāna*) is accompanied by its own subsidiaries, even a single primary act is performed together with its entire set of subsidiaries.

If, however, it were determined that one should perform an equal connection simultaneously, omitting only as much as would be contradictory at the time of origination, then when two triads are being employed on the very same full moon or new moon day, the unknown [mantras] would have to be employed in proximity to whichever one [of the two triads] they please;
or else, for that purpose, on some day within the interval between those two months.
For all of this is the time of the principal rite; and the occurrence of the oblation at the time of the principal rite is what must be intended, not absolute proximity, because that is impossible.
Therefore, by this [argument] as well, the accomplishment of the intended performance is not established.
By this very [point], the statement regarding the result is also refuted, since the result, like the location, is not something to be undertaken as a subordinate factor (*anupādeya*).

Once it is established that all [the constituent parts] are joined together in mutual dependence (*itaretarayukta*) and possess their respective subsidiaries (*sāṅga*), the establishment of a single performance (*prayoga-tantratva*) does not follow; for indeed, a single result is accomplished by means of [acts] separated by vast intervals of time. If it should be argued: "The result must come into being, and thus the principal acts along with their subsidiaries are heard in scripture as being to be performed simultaneously at the time the result arises; therefore, they are not separated by long intervals," even in that case, there is the fault of necessitating the simultaneous performance of two distinct groups (*samudāya*).
By the very originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), as in the previous case, there is a connection with each individual performance (*prayoga*).
Nor is the time for the offering (*havana*) non-existent;
for that too is delimited precisely by the time of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the *prayāja* offerings.

Furthermore, by observing the time of their origination (*utpatti*), the duration of the performance (*prayoga*) that encompasses both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary rites (*pradhāna*) is exactly the same as the duration of the production of the result (*phala*). To that extent alone does such simultaneity (*yogapadya*) exist; thus, in every respect, the completion (*apavarga*) of the two [sets of rites] along with their subsidiaries occurs on the full moon or new moon days. Alternatively, due to the principle of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), it might follow that the performance of the subsidiaries occurs either in proximity to a single aggregate (*samudāya*), or within the interval of half a month, or at some other time. This is not the case; for it is established by another scriptural statement (*vākya*) that each triad of rites, together with its subsidiaries, must be performed at its own specific time.
Therefore, the injunction regarding time—“One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī [offering] on the full moon day”—is meaningful.
But if this is so, then the connection with time in the original injunction (*utpatti*) would be purposeless.
How could it be purposeless? Behold: “If the connection of the sacrifices with time were not prescribed in the original injunction...”
The status of being a restatement of a collective whole cannot be established without a basis.
It is accepted that the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* are restatements (*anuvāda*) of the three points of time denoted by themselves.

In their absence, however, it would not be known which is the *paurṇamāsī* and which is the *amāvāsyā*. Due to that ignorance, because the terms *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* would fail to qualify the specific sacrifices under discussion and would instead refer to all sacrifices in general, it would follow that all [the sacrifices] are equally primary (*samapradhāna*).
Therefore, there must necessarily be a prior connection with time.

For this very reason, even the non-originative statement (*anutpattivākya*) of the *upāṃśuyāja* has been cited as being connected with the *paurṇamāsī*. Furthermore, because of the observation of a specific distinction, this [connection] applies to the former; for if they were equal, there would be no application [of the rule].
Commentary: Furthermore, if all [the elements] were to be equally primary, the *prayāja* offerings would not be seen in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
Yet they are indeed seen, as in the injunction: "At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain.
This is possible only if the *prayāja* is subordinate to the *āgneya* offering.

Therefore, not all [elements] are equally primary (*samapradhāna*). Or rather—if these two were separate acts (*karmāntara*), then the *āghāra* and other elements would be equally primary. Consequently, by the principle that "since an action does not originate [without a result], there must be a difference in the agent, the collection of factors, and the fruit," the *prayāja* and other offerings would fall into the category of instruments (*karaṇa*), like the *āgneya* sacrifice. Thus, because they would function as instruments prescribed for a modification (*vikṛti*) through the requirement of the "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*), and because the name [of the act] is grasped as part of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the injunction of the *kṛṣṇala* berries by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the established *prayāja* would be untenable.

Therefore, how could the *prayāja*s and other rites possess the quality of being dedicated to Agni? [The answer is that] they are restatements (*anuvāda*) of the two groups [of sacrifices]. "But the accessory [is enjoined] because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement" (Sūtra).
The Commentary says: "It is not the case that these two are restatements of the two groups as connected with the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices."
But rather, they are the enjoiners of two unprecedented actions (*apūrva-karman*);
thus, the word will not be a term of definition (*lakṣaṇa-śabda*).
Is it not the case that there is no [independent] form?
We shall understand the form [of the sacrifice] through another statement:
"On the full moon day, there is a cake on eight potsherds.
This which is the rite of the full moon—its form consists of the Abhivarta as the deity and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) as the substance.
Therefore, a quality is enjoined by means of [the words] *āgneya* and so forth.
Alternatively (*vā*), the singular number in the word *paurṇamāsīm* will belong to the meaning of the nominal stem itself, not to the aggregate indicated by it.
Furthermore, since the sacrifice (*yajati*) is directly heard, there will be no difficulty regarding the connection between the substance and the deity on either side for multiple [deities].

Or rather, since there are multiple [actions], their *apūrva*s are also multiple; because these are restatements (*anuvāda*) of a collective whole, they possess the character of injunctions (*vidhi*) as well as the quality of being descriptive. Thinking that even the observation of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth can be easily resolved—either by means of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) where there are statements of constant restatement, or by means of an injunction regarding the qualities of the *prayāja*s belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*)—he states the following rebuttal to the objection: "In the sentences concerning the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) and others, since the words 'Full Moon' (*paurṇamāsī*) and 'New Moon' (*amāvāsyā*) denote the ritual acts themselves, the possession of a form (*rūpavattva*) is established by the sentence itself."
Or rather, it is an injunction of the accessories, because when they are taught simultaneously in the scripture, that [injunction] is for their sake.
Bhāṣya: Or rather, the injunctions of action (*karmacodanā*) would be those concerning the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices.
Why? Because the accessories are taught simultaneously.

In this case, you intend to enjoin multiple qualities by means of a single sentence. However, when an action has already been enjoined by another word, it is not possible to enjoin multiple qualities unless they are mutually related.

How so? If, first of all, the intended connection were "there is an eight-potherd [cake] on the full moon day," then the meaning would not be that "the eight-potherd [cake] is connected by way of its mere existence."

What, then, is the case? The *aṣṭākapāla* (the cake on eight potsherds) is connected with the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*). In that context, at that time, the sense of the verb *bhavati* (it becomes/is) applies.

At that time, because the term *āgneyaḥ* (dedicated to Agni) has also arrived in its proximity, and due to the existence of a connection with *bhavati*, it cannot be connected with this [the *aṣṭākapāla*] in the manner of "the *aṣṭākapāla* becomes dedicated to Agni."

Now, if it is intended to state that "the offering belongs to Agni at the full moon," then, since there would be no connection whatsoever between the offering and the cake dedicated to Agni, the description of its form would remain as it was; thus, it would be a mere restatement (anuvāda).
And for this reason, by implication—
"When there are three [lunar days] on the full moon day, or two in the domain of the new moon,
then the singular number and so forth must be understood as referring to the *ādhānīyā* [day].
Furthermore, 'or rather not, another...'"
Since there are principal oblations, their number is then established;
therefore, this sentence is completed within the context of the ritual action,
and not otherwise.
Thus it is established that [the term] is a restatement of the aggregate.
And it has been said: "Because its own meaning is not complete in terms of form, it requires another sentence," as in the case of *aṣṭakapāle*.
In this context, the power of the word is intended [to denote] the material cause;
it exists in that very form, and thus this is not an operation of the person (puruṣa),
nor is it an operation of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
And because it is a restatement of a collective [group],
it is possible to enjoin only the measure, since there is no distinction in the act of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This being the position reached, it is replied:
In that case, if there were the injunction of another action, one would have to assume a specific human effort regarding what is to be cut off, and thereby assume a sacrifice;
consequently, all [actions] would become primary.
However, it follows that these two are merely restatements of a collective whole.
In this regard, although it is not logical [to assume something] when perception is available—
[for] these two are considered to be of the nature of formlessness (rūpābhāva)—
and even if a substance might somehow be obtained through the conceptualization of an inferential deity, nevertheless, in this case...

The *Paurṇamāsī-nyāya* (2640): Because it is well-known as being like the *Paurṇamāsī*, there arises a doubt regarding the dual number (*dvivacana*) and the nature of the collection of the *svādhyāya*: does it refer to the plurality of the constituent sacrifices already under discussion, such as those dedicated to Viṣṇu and others, since the status of being a constituent member of a collection exists; or does it refer to a previously unmentioned sacrifice? Since [the dual] would have to indicate plurality through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it must be a restatement (*anuvāda*). Or rather, does it refer to a new, unprecedented sacrifice?

Now, it is precisely the indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*)—by way of establishing a collective whole (*samudāya*) that constitutes the relationship of capability—that, through three topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*), serve as the two *vidvat*-sentences when the restatement of the collective whole (*samudāyānuvāda*) mentioned in the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa* is to be performed.

Otherwise, in the absence of the two *vidvat*-sentences, one would have to begin a different internal prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the sacrifice at two times, based on the single-sentence inclusion of only the *upāṃśu* substance, while relying upon the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa* concerning the *Āgneya* sacrifice in its entirety.
In this [new] prima facie argument, there arises the contingency of the connection with the fruit for that which is already joined [with the procedure].

And just as in the case of "That which belongs to Agni (āgneya) [is] the eight-potherd [cake]"— where, through the mention of the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), the substance for the Āgneya is established by means of the "potherd" (*kapāla*) and so on— it has been explained in the *Kaustubha* itself that, because the pair of sentences concerning the two knowers (*vidvadvākya*) mentioned in proximity lacks a specific form (*rūpa*), [the same principle applies].
Therefore, it was accepted that because the connection of the six [limbs] with the fruit is established, this is an injunction for a subordinate purpose (*upasarjanārthavidhi*).
However, in this case, there is a disparity because the intermediate statement can be understood as an injunction (*vidhi*).
Therefore, it is only the intermediate sentence [that possesses injunctive force], whereas the sentences concerning Viṣṇu and the others are merely explanatory (arthavāda).
As it has been said: "Once the connection with the sacrifices to Viṣṇu and the others is established, the sacrifice would follow by implication;
however, this is not tenable when [the deity] is mentioned as a subordinate element in the direct Vedic statement."

Thus (Vārttika, p. 491). Therefore, since the sentences concerning Viśvajit and others lack the character of injunctions in every respect, it is established that the intermediate sentence is an injunction of a ritual act (*karma-vidhi*) and not a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

The practical application (*prayojana*) is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the Vaiṣṇava and other rites are to be performed; according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, only one [of them] is to be performed.

The Sūtra, however, states that there is an injunction regarding the action in the passage concerning obstacles (*antarāya*), because it is not divided by a single action, just as in the case of the passages concerning Viṣṇu and others.
As it has been said: "Because those under discussion are not non-existent, they are not understood as mere restatements (*anuvāda*);
for the sacrifice is enjoined by the sentences connected with Viṣṇu and the others."
Thus (Vārttika, p. 490).
On this point, some [hold that] "the sequence [of the two sacrifices] exists only because they are performed by the same person on the full moon day, and not merely because of their similarity."

The principle of the relative strength of what precedes and what follows applies only when [the elements] are of a light nature; for that rule operates only in such cases. (Ku. 3.1.12) Precedence and sequence.

According to this principle, the optional (*kāmya*) rite sublates the obligatory (*nitya*) rite. (In the prima facie view: when the twelve-potsherd offering has been produced, the eight-potsherd offering and others are sublated.)

[Objection: According to the principle that "the later [rule] prevails over the earlier" (*paurvāparya*), since both [statements] have their meaning established in accordance with the subsequent injunction of prohibition (*bādhividhi*) through the two explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), the charge of futility (*ānarthakya*) is avoided.
Such is the doubt.

Page 1600. According to the maxim *paurvāparya* (the sequence of prior and posterior), even those notions such as being an agent or an enjoyer—which are apprehended first—are sublated by the subsequent knowledge of Brahman as the Self. (Upadeśasāhasrī, Prakarana 2, Śloka 3; Rāmatīrtha).
According to the principle of "priority and posteriority" (*paurvāparya*), it was stated at the beginning of the treatise that the authority belongs to the *Śruti* alone.
— *Kalpataru*.

4|1|2|3 Brahmasūtra: Now, by this principle of "priority and posteriority" (*paurvāparya*), even though [the knowledge] has arisen from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it sets aside the primary Vedic knowledge and only pure knowledge is grasped.
Or rather: at page 806, verse 3.1.12, the directly obtained meaning (*sākṣāt prāptārthaḥ*)—namely, loudness (*uccaiṣtva*)—is understood most rapidly.

However, after the subsequent apprehension of the injunction of performance (*prayogavacanagrahaṇa*), the primary property (*pradhānadharmah*) therein—namely, whispering (*upāṃśutva*)—is sublated by the sequence of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*).
Thus it is contradicted.
Page 811, 3|1|12: *paurvāparya* (sequence).
Because this maxim concerns objects produced by cognitions that are mutually independent, it does not apply to inferential marks (*liṅga*) and the like, which are dependent.
Su. Pṛ. 1220. Regarding the sequence of priority and the weakness of what precedes due to its being the original state (*prakṛti*):

In a performance of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, when the *udgātṛ* and the *pratihartṛ* among the priests who are walking while holding onto one another in the manner of an ant-line for the sake of the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant undergo a simultaneous interruption (*apaccheda*) in some order, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated in response to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by the interruption that occurred first must be performed, and not that occasioned by the subsequent one.
When there is a sequence between two instances of *apaccheda*, it should be understood that the former is weaker—that is, the former is weaker in comparison to the latter.
Consequently, the latter *apaccheda* is stronger;
therefore, the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by the latter *apaccheda* must be performed.

That which pertains to the archetype (*prakṛti*) occurs first, and that which pertains to the modification (*vikṛti*) occurs later. In this regard, it is not possible for that which pertains to the modification to proceed without setting aside that which pertains to the archetype.
For example, the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) is the archetype, while the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) is the modification.
In the animal sacrifice (paśu) following the New Moon sacrifice (darśa), five fore-offerings (prayāja) would otherwise apply;
however, eleven fore-offerings are specifically prescribed for the animal sacrifice.
In that case, the modified number of eleven applies only by setting aside the original number of five, and not otherwise.

Similarly, even when there is a subsequent disconnection (*apaccheda*), only the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by the later disconnection must be performed, not that occasioned by the earlier disconnection.
Where both [expiations] are applicable in a sequence of priority and posteriority, there is no possibility of contradiction in performing both; in such a case, this principle does not apply.
As stated in the subsequent section: "In a sequence of priority and posteriority, there is the sublation (*bādhana*) of that which was established first."

Vārttika 3.6.13.10, p. 1033: In the case of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, or obligatory and optional (*kāmya*) rites, as well as between archetypal (*prākṛta*) and modified (*vaikṛta*) rites, there is sublation of the former by the latter according to the principle of sequence (*paurvāparya-naimittika-nyāya*).
Tantravārttika 6.5.19.54: The principle of sequence (*paurvāparya-nyāya*); the principle of the superiority of that which comes later (*paurvāparya-balīyastva-nyāya*).
See Mīmāṃsākośa, page 495, under the entry ‘apacchedanyāyaḥ’.
There is a suspicion that even the senior authority (jyeṣṭhapramāṇa) may be sublated by the principle of priority and posteriority (paurvāparyanyāya).
— Kalpataru.

Brahma Sūtra 1.1.1, p. 9; Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 117: In the first performance where only the *dvār* (gatekeeper) is disqualified, and in the second performance where only the *pratīhartṛ* (usher) is disqualified, the rule of priority (*paurvāparya*) applies.
Merely by virtue of proximity in sequence, the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṃkhyakrama*) is more powerful.

In the section on optional *yājyā* mantras, although the two mantras belonging to the *aindrāgna* formula would apply indifferently to both sacrifices due to the sequence of proximity, their application occurs according to the order of enumeration because they are proximate through absolute spatial correspondence.
Vārttika 3.3.7.14, p. 840: "In that case, indeed, the superiority of the subsequent over the prior is perceived, where there arises the birth of cognitions that are mutually independent.

For when contradictory meanings are heard that reside in different sentences and are independent of one another, the rule of the superiority of the subsequent over the prior applies; because the former attains its own nature only by being set aside by the latter, whereas the latter cannot attain its own nature without setting aside the former."
But where there is the hearing of mutually dependent elements as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), that [distinction] does not apply there;
for in such cases, the unity of the sentence arises by virtue of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
And what has been previously cognized expects what follows to be either consistent with itself or something additional.
And therefore, that which is neither additional nor conducive [to the purpose] does not exist at all in that sentence, because it is not required by it.
Nor can there be a sublation of what precedes by means of what is not present; thus, the preceding [rule] possesses greater force.
Vārttika 3.1.12, p. 806.

By the principle of "the later being weaker than the earlier" (*paurvāparyavalīyastvanyāya*), even though the grinding of the offering for Pūṣan (*pauṣṇaṃ peṣaṇam*) might—through the mediation of the assumption of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and so forth—contradict the authority of *liṅga* and the other means of proof, it is nevertheless proper that the opposite conclusion holds. This is because the assumption of a *śruti* and so forth, which is unavoidable through its connection with the fact of being mentioned in a Smṛti and its position within a specific sequence, depends upon the aforementioned assumptions; thus, it functions only after the *śruti* and other means have already operated. Furthermore, even though it requires an assumed *śruti*, it does not depend on a *śruti* that would cause contradiction; therefore, by the very principle of "the later being weaker than the earlier," the reversal [of the initial view] is indeed logical. (6.1.19)

Su. Pṛ. 1198: Regarding the *pauṣkala* Sāman, it was stated in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it should be chanted during the third pressing (*tṛtīya savana*), at the Ārambha-pavamāna, upon the two-hymn sequence consisting of the *kakubh* and *satobṛhatī* meters, beginning with "pavasva madhumattamaḥ" (6.92–93).

However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it was stated that the *pauṣkala* should not be chanted on a triplet (*tṛca*), but rather on a single verse alone, because of the specific injunction using the singular number in the word "kakubhi" (on the *kakubh*).

VI. 9.16, Section 3: The grinding of the offering for Pūṣan occurs only when he is the sole deity of the animal sacrifice, but not when there is a dual divinity as in the case of Somāpauṣṇa and Aindrāpauṣṇa [in the Rājasūya]. The grinding for Pūṣan applies only to the cooked rice (*caru*).
That [grinding] is for all purposes because there is no distinction.
The Commentary states: It was said in the preceding section that the grinding of Pūṣan, though heard in the archetype (*prakṛti*), applies to the ectype (*vikṛti*).
In this regard, there is a doubt: does it apply to the cooked rice (*caru*), the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), or only to the cooked rice?
What, then, is the prima facie position? That [procedure] should apply everywhere—in the *caru*, the animal sacrifice, and the *puroḍāśa*.
Why? Because there is no distinction;
no specific distinction is adopted.
"Therefore, in all cases"— or rather: "that [is] for all purposes, because there is no distinction" (only the aphorism has been recited,
it has not been explained).

Or rather, [the grinding] should apply to the *caru* (cooked rice offering), because in the case of the *puroḍāśa* (cake) there is a contradiction of purpose; it would not apply to the animal sacrifice.
Bhāṣya: The grinding should be applied to the *pauṣṇa-caru*.
As for the *puroḍāśa*, the grinding is already obtained by the very nature of the thing itself.
The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) does not become otherwise;
it is for that purpose that the statement exists.
Furthermore, it would not apply in the case of the animal sacrifice (paśu).
If the heart and other organs were to be ground, their characteristic forms would be destroyed.

What fault would there be in that? [The rule] "One cuts from the heart first" would then be violated by cutting from the heart [in a different manner]; likewise, other portions (avadāna) would not be cut according to what is prescribed in the scripture.
But surely, even from flour, one could cut out portions for the heart and other organs?
We say: no;
the heart and so forth are forms, not pieces of flesh.
This has been stated:
that the word-meaning is the generic form (*ākṛti*). Even though an object possessing that form is produced, nevertheless, with respect to the place of its production, it occurs repeatedly.
