Therefore, there is this statement: "In the case of the *caru*, the grinding for Pūṣan shall take place. Or rather: "In the case of the *caru*, it is implied by the purpose (*arthākṣepa*).

If someone should object that since the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) can be accomplished even by employing ordinary flour, the grinding is not necessarily implied by the purpose, then the following is said in reply to him.
"Meaning" (artha) refers to a natural benefit.

In the archetype (prakṛti), grinding was the means for that [benefit]; therefore, since that [means] was already established by prior application, grinding is prescribed for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). Furthermore, in the case of the animal sacrifice (paśu), there would be a deficiency in the primary rite.

For that [offering] must indeed be accomplished by means of something having the shape of the heart and so forth, and from which [the portion] has been cut out; and when [the substance] is ground into flour, that specific shape is not present for the purpose of cutting the portion.
Even if one were to recreate that shape, there would still be a deficiency, just as in the case of clay or other materials, because it would be a mere figurative imitation of the original form.
And it is heard in the scripture: "One cuts [the portions] from the place of production.
Furthermore, in the case of the heart and other parts that have been ground, it would not be known by which specific part of the animal these were originally stated to have come.
Therefore, since grinding is neither prohibited in the case of the *caru* nor is it naturally required there, it is prescribed specifically for that very purpose.
But surely, because there is no distinction in the reason— "for he is toothless"— it would follow that this applies to the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) as well; thus,
the offerings of the substance and its remnants would be given after being ground,
and the grinding would not take place merely for the sake of disposal (prātipatti).
It is said:
since the offering of the substance constitutes the primary procedure, it is not proper for there to be an interruption by grinding in the middle;
furthermore, it will be explained that the explanatory statement (*hetuvannigada*) serves merely as a praise.
Therefore, this is a rule for the grinding itself within its own context.

Furthermore, grinding is mentioned as a mere restatement in the case of the *puroḍāśa* cake because it is already established; it is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) in the case of the *caru* oblation where it would otherwise be excluded; and in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), it is a rule that establishes a different mode of application than what was previously obtained.
Moreover, these various forms cannot be understood as belonging to a single sentence.
In that regard, since uniformity regarding the fault is accepted for the sake of parsimony and because it is meaningful, the very nature of the counter-exception (*prati-prasava*) must be determined.
Thus, it is established that there is indeed the state of being a solitary wanderer (*kevalacara*).
If it is argued that this applies even when one is with a companion (*carau*), [the response follows].
The Commentary: If you observe this, [you might think] it is for the sake of the meaning because of the contradiction in meaning.
But is there not also a contradiction in meaning regarding the *caru*?
People apply the word *caru* metaphorically to rice that has been clearly cooked.
For when being ground, it indeed attains the state of being ground, just as a living being [attains death];
if you say that it moves within the vessel—so be it.
(Only the framework of the aphorism has been provided.
No, because it is merely the name of a bird.
Commentary: To this, it is said:

It is true that the word *caru* is applied to rice (*odana*) when it has been clearly prepared; however, this is due to the explicit mention of its being "clearly prepared," and not because "being clearly prepared" is the etymological cause for the application of the term.
If it were the cause for the clear accomplishment [of the result], one would not employ flour in the accomplishment of the sacrificial cake;
yet it is indeed employed there as well, in the statement, "a sacrificial pap made of flour is prepared.
Therefore, that which is common to these two is the cause.
This is logical, because it is the name of a cooking process;
there is no contradiction regarding the *caru*.
How so? Because it is the name of a cooking process.
It moves as a state of being cooked;
it is unstable within and its form is not fixed, yet it becomes that which is to be produced by many factors. The word *cara* is expressive of this.
Therefore, the usage occurs in the sense of "moving" (*carati*) with respect to both ground meal (*piṣṭa*) and clear rice-gruel (*viśadaudana*).

The purpose is exactly as stated for the position [of the proponent]. In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the grinding applies even to the animal sacrifice; in the final conclusion (siddhānta), it applies only to the oblation of cooked rice (caru).
Or rather—it is not so, because it is the name of the digestive process.
Nor is there a contradiction regarding the meaning of "moving.
How so? Because the movement of all things is established through worldly convention.

In that context, the specific degree of cooking is determined by the term *cara*. Since the word *cara*—applied here to *odana* (boiled rice), *piṣṭaka* (flour-cakes), and *caru* (sacrificial porridge)—is observed to have multiple meanings, it is understood as denoting the commonality of both.
And the commonality between those two is the state of having an unstable internal consistency.
Therefore, there is no contradiction;
the purpose stated for the position has been declared as the fruit.

Such is the nature of this Samādhi: even though there is no distinction [in the context], the purpose is not for the sake of the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake), but rather for the sake of the animal (*paśu*). Śābarabhāṣya: When it is argued that [the rule] should apply everywhere, it is replied as follows.
In the case of the *puroḍāśa* cake, [the grinding] is established by another source; in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), there is the destruction of the form [by grinding].

Therefore, for those two, there is no need for an injunction [of grinding]. However, in the case of the *caru* oblation, since it does not destroy [the form] and is not otherwise obtained, it is enjoined therein.

Soma: This is a contextual connection (*prāsaṅgikī saṃgatiḥ*). Viśvarūpa: "Regarding the cooked rice (*caru*), the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), is there grinding only for the cooked rice? Or is it prescribed for all of them, since no distinction is observed?
[It is] not for the sacrificial cake, because it is already established [as being ground], and because its firm shape would be destroyed [by grinding]."

"Grinding does not apply to the animal; by process of elimination, it applies only to the *caru*. (Bhaṭṭa): Regarding the consideration of whether that grinding should apply to the *caru* dedicated to Pūṣan, as well as to the animal and the *puroḍāśa*, or only to the *caru*—since there is no distinction among those things that are to be consumed—it follows [that it applies] everywhere. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the Siddhāntin replies]: First, in the case of the *puroḍāśa*, prescribing grinding before baking would be redundant since it is already established; however, if it were done after baking, there would be the undesirable consequence of destroying the specific form (*ākṛti*) denoted by the word *puroḍāśa*.
The same applies to the *paśu* (animal sacrifice) and the *dṛṣad* (grinding stone) and so forth,
because even those are present in the form of meat characterized by specific shapes.
Furthermore, in neither case is there an injunction for grinding subsequent to the offering of the food, since grinding was absolutely unestablished [prior to that point].
This is established. Now, however, a doubt arises:
does this apply to a [sacrifice] for Pūṣan dedicated to a single deity, or also to one dedicated to two deities?

What is the example for a sacrifice to two deities? In the Rājasūya, regarding the latter two offerings connected with the three [deities], it is said: "The cake on eleven potsherds for Soma-Pūṣan, and the dark-colored [animal] for Indra-Pūṣan; the sacrificial fee is a dark-colored [cow].

In that context, the offering to Indra-Pūṣan is the example. What is the prima facie view? That grinding applies to the one deity, because of the connection with a single [deity], just as in the case of the fourfold division [of the cake].
Or rather—because of the connection with one [deity] in a single case.

Now, when there is a doubt as to whether the grinding occurs in the *aindrāpauṣṇa* oblation (offered to Indra and Pūṣan) when accompanied by the final [deity], or only in the case of one [deity], he begins with the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) itself, starting from the point that this applies even in the case of the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*).
Because of the scriptural mention of a connection with "one" in the word "Pūṣan," it should be so in such a case.
And because of the contradiction of ritual properties (*dharma*).
The Commentary states: In a sacrifice for two deities, the ritual property would be contradicted;
namely, the grinding of the offering belongs to Pūṣan, not to the other deity.

In that case, if the portion for Pūṣan were to be ground, then the other [portion] would also have to be ground here; there would thus be a rule of grinding. And since the word *caru* (cooked rice) is based on the fact of being cooked, it would be contradicted.
Furthermore, thinking there is no contradiction, they might grind [the grain] for another portion as well; thus, there would be confusion regarding the portions.
What is the fault in that? One person's portion would be offered to another, and thus the ritual would be performed contrary to what was prescribed in the scripture.
Therefore, for this reason as well, there is grinding in the case of an offering to a single deity.
Or rather—this follows from another point: [grinding applies] to that which has a single deity.
Why? "In a caru-offering for two deities, do you grind the whole or only a portion?"
In the former case, there would be uneven cooking; in the latter, there would be a confusion of portions.
For when grinding the ingredients together, the ground portion would be cooked more quickly than the other by means of the milk.
Consequently, if the mixture were removed from the heat immediately after the ground portion was cooked, the other portion would remain uncooked.
Furthermore, because even the flour that has been left unattended for a long time dissolves [in water], it would follow that it is not *acarā* (solid);
for through uneven cooking, even flour becomes *caru*.
And this [undesirable consequence] does not occur in this view.

Now, if one were to first throw in the rice grains and subsequently throw in the flour, then the simultaneity that is understood [from the scriptural injunction] would be subverted. (Because both portions—the flour and the rice—serve as the means for a single sacrifice, they constitute a single oblation; and since the entire oblation must be poured in simultaneously, the simultaneity understood here through extension [of the rule] would be subverted—Su.

p. 1329). Furthermore, if, out of deference to Pūṣan, the portion belonging to Indra were also ground, there would be a confusion of portions; and when the portion belonging to one is given to another, a deficiency in the ritual results.

But surely all of this is equally applicable even to you regarding offerings to dual deities. For it is said: "When the sacrificial pap, the animal, or the cake is being offered to two deities, a confusion of portions arises because the oblation is initially a single unit."
And that [position] has been accepted, because there is no contradiction in offering a mixed oblation (*miśra-haviḥ*) simultaneously by designating it for mixed deities.
It is said:
"This would be so regarding the properties (*dharma*) if they were prompted by the unseen potency of the sacrifice (*yāgāpūrva*)."
According to your view, this grinding is considered to be a property of the deity;

however, in our position, the grinding is prompted by the sacrifice dedicated to Pūṣan occurring on the new-moon day. Since that [sacrifice] does not exist in the case of a dual-deity offering, there is simply no application [of the grinding].

Furthermore, even in other offerings where two deities are involved, this same principle applies; thus, the deity is subordinate. Since it is accepted that the principal element should not be repeated merely for the sake of a subordinate quality, when everything is performed together at once, there is no recourse to the fault of confusion (*saṃkara*).

On the other hand, according to your position, since it is impossible to assert grinding in a dual-deity offering while accepting our view, you must necessarily accept that the grinding is caused by the deity.
Furthermore, because the two deities are primary, each one is requested for its own portion unmixed with the other; therefore, the offering must be made in that very manner.
Moreover, it has been determined from the outset that the portion is intended for grinding;
consequently, there would be a flaw in the alternative position.
Now, if even the portion consisting of rice grains is ground for the sake of uniform cooking,
we say:
as long as the rice grains and the husks are not separated, to what extent can it be said that one part belongs to one and another part to the other?
Thus, because there is no lack of attention, the fault of confusion (*saṃkara*) does not arise.
However, if a distinction were merely conceptualized, then because of the verbal injunction, there would again be the occurrence of unification; consequently, one would arrive at an unmixed offering.
In that case, if a portion belonging to one [deity] were offered to another, a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) would result.
If it is argued that one sees [the distinction] through the difference in vessels, we say no.

For, since the *caru* is intended as having a singular number—being enjoined with respect to the sacrifice (*yāga*)—to resort to a basis for division based on the vessels would result in the contradiction of the scriptural injunction.
Therefore, grinding characterized by prohibited properties can never occur in the case of an offering to two deities; thus, it must not be performed.
Alternatively, it may be accompanied by a second [deity], because it is dependent upon a deity.
The Bhāṣya states: This grinding is heard as being caused by a deity;
namely, "Pūṣan is to be made the recipient of the ground portion."
And even when the portion belonging to two deities is being ground, how can it be understood [as belonging to one]?
It is not as in the case of the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*);
for there, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) occurs independently, and not with reference to a second [deity].
Even the compound *indrapīta* (drunk by Indra) applies to that which is independent, not to that which has a companion; however,
in this case, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound of the indeclinable word *prati* with the word *pada*,
and this [compound] also occurs only when the two members are semantically related (*samartha*).
But here, in the case of an offering to two deities, there is no defect whatsoever of the same kind [as in the case of a single deity].
Therefore, whether it be a sacrificial pap (caru) for one deity or even for two deities, its portion must indeed be ground;
or rather—even when compounded—the grinding must certainly be performed in full.
Why? "If there were an oblation for Pūṣan, or likewise one for the Aśvins, then, because it is not mentioned [otherwise], there would be no grinding in a dual-deity offering.
This grinding is caused by the presence of Puṣan; it is not caused by the specific nature of the substance itself.

Furthermore, because the status of being a deity is fixed [vyāsañjitatvāt], there would be no distinction of the flower in a rite dedicated to two deities; it does not mean, however, that Pūṣan or his portion does not exist.
As he will state regarding the Manotā (Bhāṣya, p. 1939): "In that case, Agni is not a non-deity, but rather he is not unconnected [asamaveta].

Therefore, since Pūṣan’s status as a deity here is merely a secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) by virtue of his connection, it is understood from the principle "it should be equal, as there is no scriptural statement to the contrary" (*samaṃ syādaśrutatvāt*) that Pūṣan has a share in the offering even when it is being offered to two deities.

While that grinding is being performed, if— according to the principle of one who eats from a bronze vessel— the grinding of the other portion is also performed with the thought, "for him as well," then that is indeed the grinding for Pūṣan;
it is the grinding for Pūṣan.
The intention (*saṃkalpa*) cannot be designated by either one [of the two deities] alone.

Just as the taking up of the *aindrāgna* sacrificial cake involves the taking up of both [deities] by means of the two words *āgneya* and *aindrāgni*, so too is there the taking up of the portion of Pūṣan in the case of the *aindrāpauṣṇa* and other offerings.

And although here there is no objection regarding the formation of the compound based on the utterance of such words, nevertheless, because the very object to be grasped by the word "portion" (*bhāga*) does not exist, there is no application [of the term].

And although both meanings, as they attain the status of deity, employ their constituent parts for the sake of establishing the conventional meaning of the whole, nevertheless, because the mental resolve (saṃkalpa) cannot be designated by either one [of the two meanings] alone, it is established that [the specific form] is not a defining characteristic.
The state of ending in "ad" is merely a reason.

Commentary: As for what was stated—that the phrase "for he is toothless" indicates a quality of the deity—that is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), which remains applicable even under the other view. Or rather: as for the claim that because of the presentation of a reason in the words "for he is toothless," this must be a quality of the deity; [that is not so].
To this it is replied:

because it has the sense of being an illustration (nidarśana) like a reason (hetu), it is not contradictory that its purpose is solely to praise the qualities of the sacrifice; therefore, it is not a [valid] cause [for the injunction], as the statement is merely supplementary.

The Commentary (Bhāṣya): Now, as for the other reason that was stated—namely, that "it is not ground" (anemapiṣṭam)—this indicates grinding when there are two deities, by showing the characteristic of the deity in the passage: "Half is ground, half is unground, because there are two deities.
To this, it is replied: if this were so, this statement would be [redundant] regarding what is already established.
But surely, it follows that a single sentence would enjoin multiple meanings.
It is said in reply: when there is an alternative position involving the injunction of multiple meanings, the difficulty is resolved by resorting to that alternative position.

Furthermore, in the absence of any other alternative, one must accept that a sentence has multiple meanings in order to avoid the undesirable consequence of [the injunction] being merely for the purpose of recitation.
Therefore, it is established that grinding applies when there are two deities.
Alternatively, in cases such as "half-ground" (nemi-piṣṭa), the statement will serve as a descriptive reference (*vācanika*) because there is no possibility of its application [otherwise].
Furthermore, because there is an injunction of a qualified entity, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Just as in the case of "one who is red-purchased" (*aruṇayā piṅgākṣyā*), there is a prescription of everything through mutual restriction (*parasparaniyama*).
And while a qualified injunction is weaker when compared to an unqualified injunction, such a deficiency does not exist here.

Therefore, the mark [of gender] pertains to the deity and not to the sacrificial substance. Śabara says: "Because there is no context of a sacrifice and because it is not heard in the sentence, this grinding is a property of the deity, and not a property of the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) or anything else."
"Since that [grain] possessing its own nature exists even when there are two deities," this being the position reached, it is replied:
"The deity is not at all the motivator for the grinding."

And the *upādāna* (the material substance) is understood by the word "portion" (*bhāga*) because its primary meaning is possible; for here, by means of the sacrifice, it will indicate [the substance] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
This word "portion" is heard in scripture; therefore, let it not be something that is not a material substance.
Vi— "Even in the case of a dual divinity, should one grind [the offering], or only when Pūṣan is the deity?
Even in the case of a dual divinity, because Pūṣan exists as a participant in the grinding,
the grinding would not be performed because the divinity [in that case] is rendered fruitless."

"Because the portion (*bhāga*) is mentioned in relation to the essence (*tattva*) of the sacrifice, that [grinding] does not apply to another sacrifice. (20) "In the sense of being the motivator (*prayojaka*) for grinding. Bhaṭṭa: In the case where Pūṣan is the deity accompanied by another—as in the Rājasūya sacrifice, where there is the offering "to Indra and Pūṣan"—should grinding be performed there as well, or only where he is the sole deity? Upon such deliberation, because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "for he is toothless" leads to the understanding that grinding constitutes the very nature (*svarūpa*) of Pūṣan, and since that nature exists even when he is accompanied by another, grinding is indeed appropriate.

For this very reason, the statement "one desiring cattle should offer a *caru* of rice for Soma and Pūṣan, half-ground" is also consistent, because the meaning denoted by the word *nema* (half) is indeed ground.

If, however, it were argued that based on the ninth chapter [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras], since there would be pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) regarding the form of Pūṣan, one must necessarily assume a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*), then let it be so; for by the method previously stated, there exists another indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhikā*)—namely, the name (*saṃjñā*) "Pūṣan-involved sacrifice"—which applies to those [other sacrifices] as well, and thus it [the indication] resides in the word *pūṣan*.

However, according to the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), since the deity presided over by Pūṣan is employed prior to the other deities, this indicative mark (*liṅga*) establishes that grinding is appropriate even when there are two deities.
And just as the successful cooking is achieved in such a case, one must strive for it either by preventing interference, by placing the portions in sequence, or by using separate vessels.

This being the position reached, [the following is established]: in order to avoid the fault of meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), it is necessary to understand the term through an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of that which brings about the *apūrva* (transcendental result); furthermore, because the status of being the medium (*adhiṣṭhāna-dvāratva*) must be postulated, this is untenable without the presentation of Pūṣan as the deity. Once he is presented, the fault of meaninglessness is avoided simply by postulating his role as the medium. Moreover, according to the principle of the section on the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa-adhikaraṇa-nyāya*), when there is a dual divinity, Pūṣan alone cannot possess the status of deity; therefore, the grinding (*peṣaṇa*) occurs only where Pūṣan is the sole deity.

Nor should it be argued that because the deityhood—which serves as the means for a previously unestablished [result]—is presented by the word *pūṣan* as a qualifier (*prakāra*) over Pūṣan, and because a wise person intends to express the essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*) itself as the mode of connection (*saṃsarga*), and since that [deityhood] exists in its entirety in even one of the two deities (Pūṣan), its non-duality is established, so how could there not be grinding?
For the principle is that a relation residing in only one [of two entities] cannot logically function as the mode of connection when a property residing in both is intended as the qualifier.
Otherwise, there would result the verbal cognition of expressions such as "one possesses duality" or "one is two," just as one might say "one possesses the time of two.

Therefore, since the deityhood (devatātva) residing distributively (vyāsajyavṛtti) cannot function as a qualifier (*prakāra*) through the relation of pervasion (*paryāpti*)— as in the case of the grinding for Pūṣan (*pauṣṇapeṣaṇa*)— and because that [distributive deityhood] is precluded in the case of Pūṣan alone, the grinding and so forth apply only where deityhood resides solely in Pūṣan, with that [exclusive deityhood] serving as the qualifier.
However, the state of not being ground (adantatva) is not contradicted because it is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda).

Furthermore, since even the "not-ground" (nemi-piṣṭa) status is likewise to be enjoined, there is no syntactical split (avākyabheda) due to the injunction of a qualified productive operation (viśiṣṭabhāvanā); thus, it must be understood as being traditionally handed down.
Maṇḍana: "There is no grinding for the offering to Indra-Pūṣan."
20. Śaṅkara says: "But that [grinding] is not considered [to apply] to the offering to Indra and Pūṣan.
That refers to the state of being ground.
20. Although the grinding for Pūṣan is heard in the archetypal ritual (*prakṛti*), it [applies] to the modified ritual (*vikṛti*).
The grinding pertaining to Pūṣan should be understood as belonging to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), because of the injunction [found] in the archetype (prakṛti).
Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they recite: "Therefore Pūṣan has a share in the ground [grains], for he is toothless.
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the grinding pertaining to Pūṣan belong to the archetype or to the modified sacrifice?
And this investigation has its purpose already established by the previously mentioned principle of *saṃtardana*.
For there exists a deity named Pūṣan in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices;

yet, the deity of the Darśapūrṇamāsa is not indicated here through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because of the presence of an explanatory statement (*hetuvannigada*) stating, "for he is toothless."
For the toothlessness of Agni and others is not found anywhere in the Veda or the Purāṇas;
however, the toothlessness of Pūṣan is recognized both in the Veda and in the Purāṇas,
and in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), Pūṣan is indeed the deity of that particular oblation.
Therefore, because it serves a purpose, the grinding is displaced by the force of the sentence.

It should be understood that although this was established by the previous principle (*pūrvanyāya*), it is now introduced for the sake of the subsequent discussion. As for the Sūtra, the previously mentioned *saṃtardana* (piercing) and *peṣaṇa* (grinding) are displaced in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

"In the archetype (prakṛti), there is no injunction for it," meaning there is no prescription. According to the Tautātitamatatilaka: "The grinding of the offering to Pūṣan is understood to apply to the ectype (vikṛti) because of the injunction, not to the archetype.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, it is stated: "Therefore, Pūṣan has a share of the cooked rice, for he is toothless"; thus, the grinding pertaining to Pūṣan—that is, the grinding for the deity Pūṣan—is prescribed.
That [mantra] is understood to belong to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) having Pūṣan as its deity; it is displaced from the archetype (prakṛti),
because there is no injunction for Pūṣan in the archetype, that is, due to the absence of an injunction.
The dark-colored (śyāma) animal dedicated to Pūṣan is the fourth among the eleven animals in the Aśvamedha and the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices.

Regarding the verse "One desiring progeny should sacrifice a dark-colored animal to Pūṣan," in the case of the cake (*puroḍāśa*) for Pūṣan, the grinding (*peṣaṇa*) must be performed, according to the rule: "Pūṣan has a share in the ground [grain], for he is toothless.
This is the section concerning the grinding for Pūṣan (*pauṣṇapeṣaṇādhikaraṇa*).
The grinding (*pauṣṇapeṣaṇa*) mentioned in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is to be transferred to the sacrifice dedicated to Pūṣan (*pauṣṇayāga*).

The grinding for Pūṣan is understood as applying to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), not the archetype (*prakṛti*), because of the injunction. Commentary: Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, they recite: "Therefore Pūṣan has a portion of ground [grain], for he is toothless."

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the grinding of the offering for Pūṣan belong to the archetype (*prakṛti*), or to the ectype (*vikṛti*)? What is the prima facie view? That it belongs to the archetype. Why? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
But is it not the case that in the archetype (prakṛti), they do not record Pūṣan as the deity of any sacrificial offering?
It is said in reply: the word "Pūṣan" will denote some deity from the archetype.
This being the case, we reply:
where there is an offering to Pūṣan, there its grinding can be enjoined;
however, Pūṣan does not exist in the archetype (prakṛti).
Therefore, the grinding is for the sake of excellence.
As for what was said— that the word *pūṣan* will denote some deity or other—
it might be so if *pūṣan* were not [the specific deity] elsewhere as well.
Indeed, by doing so here, the context becomes coherent; or rather, there is no doubt at all on this point—
it is stated exactly as it has been established.
"The grinding for Pūṣan applies in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), not in the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛti).
There is no injunction for Pūṣan in the archetype. For what purpose, then, is that which has already been established being stated?"
The subsequent discussion proceeds.

Alternatively—by the very principle of *saṃtardana*, since there is a conflict between the syntactical statement (*vākya*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*), that which is established for the sake of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is now commenced for the purpose of the following investigation.

*Soma*—Since the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "the placement [of the grinding] is within the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices according to the context" is weak, this is not a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*). Rather, it is performed by this sūtra merely as a preliminary (*prasakti*) to establish the incidental nature (*prāsaṅgikatva*) of the grinding, so that the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the grinding by means of the sentence may be established. This is because there is no direct connection to the inquiry about whether the placement is everywhere or only in the *caru*, which will be discussed later; for that [latter inquiry] concerns the consideration of non-contradiction when sentence and context are in conflict. *Vi*—"The one whose portion is ground" (*prapiṣṭabhāgaḥ*) [is mentioned] in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or in the ectype (*vikṛti*)? In the case of the *pūya* [offering], is it in the archetype or the ectype? [End of fragment].
It is appropriate that [the rule] applies to the archetype (*prakṛti*) precisely because of the context of the desired section;
however, like the *saṃtardana* and other such cases, it applies to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by virtue of the direct statement (*vākya*), since Pūṣan is not present there.
The restatement of what is already established is intended to express something additional.

18. Bhāṭṭa — In the section on the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "Pūṣan has a share of the ground [grain], for he is toothless. In this regard, is this an injunction for a separate rite as an auxiliary to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices themselves, or is it the grinding [of grain] in the sacrifice to the deity Pūṣan? This is the topic of the *pauṣṇapeyaṇādhikaraṇa*. 2652. It has been explained.

Regarding the inquiry as to what constitutes the *mātrāvidhi* (the injunction concerning the measure): first of all, it is not an injunction prescribing the act of drinking (*peyaṇa*) with reference to a sacrifice indicated by the word "portion" (*bhāga*). This is because it would result in the violation of the principle of "single thrust of expression" (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*), and because there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if [the sacrifice] were qualified by a subordinate term (*upapada*). Furthermore, it is impossible for the act of drinking—which has the fruit, the effort, and the substance as its subordinates—to be connected with the sacrifice.

For this very reason, the word *pūṣan* cannot be intended merely to express the deity indicated by the primary meaning of the word, nor the sacrifice indicated by the secondary meaning; moreover, since Pūṣan lacks a connection with the sacrifice performed by Agni, there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the presentation of that sacrifice.

Therefore, since this is an injunction for a distinct ritual action qualified by both a material (*dravya*) and a deity (*devatā*) due to these qualities, such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). In response: By the term *prapiṣṭabhāga*, through the etymological derivation meaning "that which has a portion (*bhāga*)—that is, that which is to be enjoyed or served (*sevyam*)—by him," even if actual service is impossible, a mere relationship between the ground-meal (*prapiṣṭa*) and Pūṣan is understood, as attested by common usage. And since that [relationship] is untenable without a sacrifice, it leads to the inference of a sacrifice; on this much, there is no dispute between the two parties.

Furthermore, since it is illogical for the injunction of a qualified [action] to be based on the obstruction of a mere injunction of qualifiers, there is no inference of a new, distinct sacrifice in the absence of evidence;
this has already been understood from the outset.
Therefore, and consequently...
However, it does not obstruct the injunction for the renunciation (*tyāga*) that occurs in the *iṣṭi* sacrifice where animal substances are desired.

Likewise here as well, the word "who" (*yaḥ*), being connected to an agent qualified by the act of knowing—as in "one who knows thus"—obstructs only the injunction of the act of knowing, not the injunction of the act of sacrificing.
Similarly, even in the word "thus" (*evam*), in the phrase "knowing thus," it refers only to the act of knowing and does not refer to the act of sacrificing.

Thus, this alone is indeed the nature of the injunction. Nor can there be meaningfulness for the restatement (*anuvāda*) in the absence of the performance of the entire collection required by the qualification, because—as in the case of the *rājasūya*—the formation of the collection is possible through the very sentence stating the result.

Furthermore, this being the case, there is no contingency of using the expression "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa" (instead of "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa-sacrifices"), as one uses "by means of the Rājasūya."
Because of the rule "substitutes for case-endings (sup) become case-endings (sup)," that which is employed in place of the singular ending possesses the same meaning as the singular itself.
Therefore, just like the *samit* and other [offerings], this pair of rites is enjoined precisely as delimited by the names of the sacrifices, such as the *Paurṇamāsī*.
Nor is it the case that it cannot be a name due to the absence of a basis for its application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*).

Just as in the case of the *agnihotra* and other rites, when examining the connection with deities not mentioned in the injunctions, the status of the two names is established by observing the grounds for the application of the two sentences to be enjoined regarding the connection with time: "One should sacrifice with the *Paurṇamāsī* on the full moon day" and "One should sacrifice with the *Amāvāsyā* on the new moon day. Nor should it be argued: "How can there be an injunction regarding time by reference to those names if the names themselves are not yet established? This would involve mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)."

Since the status of [the term] as a name is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*), just as in the case of "He performs the *agnihotra*," its specific basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is determined solely by a supplementary injunction (*mādhikālavidhi*) that mentions it; thus, there is nothing improper in this.
Now, one might object: "The form (*rūpa*) of a ritual action consists indeed of the substance and the deity, yet here there is no deity."

Nor does the sacrifice possess a definite form (*rūpavattva*) by virtue of having Soma as its substance and deity through a general injunction regarding the unmanifested [sacrifice], because an independent injunction cannot depend upon one that is dependent.
In this case, the injunction for Soma depends on the ritual action by way of depending on the injunction for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices through the subsidiaries such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*.
If the injunction for the Darśapūrṇamāsa were likewise to depend on that [Soma injunction], then there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
How then can there be a lack of injunction regarding the action?

It is not so; for by the scriptural statement within the context, "Indeed, that which is the clarified butter (ājya) in the *dhruvā* vessel is taken for the sake of every sacrifice," there is indeed a substance [for the action] derived from the sentence concerning the *dhruvā*.

Nor does a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) occur when, by a single sentence, both the connection of the *ājya* with the *dhruvā* and its connection with the sacrifice are enjoined; this is because the phrase "that which is the *ājya* in the *dhruvā*" merely restates the connection with the *dhruvā* and enjoins only the connection with the sacrifice.
If there exists another sentence providing the connection between the *ājya* and the *dhruvā* [ladle], then this [text] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on that [connection].

If, however, such a sentence does not exist, then it is not inconsistent for this to be a restatement of that which is obtained through a sentence inferred from the internal inconsistency of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Furthermore, the attainment of the deity is also derived from the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*).

By these two very sentences—“The *vātrghnī* is recited at the Full Moon sacrifice; the *dhruvantī* at the New Moon sacrifice”—the pair of verses denoted by the term *vātrghnī* and the pair of verses denoted by the term *dhruvantī*, although listed in the sequence of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, are enjoined as belonging to these specific rites by virtue of the sentence itself, thereby overriding the sequence.
Of these two, one is dedicated to Agni (*āgneyī*) and the other to Soma (*saumī*).

In that regard, because both mantras are applied simultaneously to each rite and thus present two deities simultaneously, there is indeed a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the two deities in each individual rite.
That being the case, there is indeed a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the two mantras as well.
And it is not untenable that this non-attainment (*aprāpti*) occurs from the *Dāśatayī*.

Therefore, there is a fixed determination of time (*kāla-vyavasthā*) regarding the *ājyabhāga* offerings themselves; thus, the two statements will stand exactly according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

"The two *ājyabhāga* offerings at the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) are accompanied by the two mantras containing the word 'dhruva'; the two *ājyabhāga* offerings at the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) are accompanied by the two mantras containing the words 'dhruva' and 'tya'.

This is not so; for in the former position, there are two sentences prescribing the time, and because the single prescription of time for the ritual action and its substance—which are already enjoined—would result in a redundancy.

Since the time for the *ājyabhāga* offerings is already established as the full moon and the new moon, those [sentences] do not serve to fix that [time]; rather, they must be understood solely as prescriptions for the mantras.
As it has been said: "The substance is directly heard [in the text], while the deity is [known] from the words of the mantra;
therefore, two sacrifices possessing distinct forms are enjoined."
Thus (Vārttika, p. 405).

Regarding the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, however, by means of a statement in the form of a past precedent (*purākalpa*)—namely, "For whichever deity the oblation is prepared, let us first sacrifice for him with clarified butter alone"—the status of Agni and Soma as deities is established here as well.

Although there is no direct mention of Agni and Soma here, nevertheless, because they were established as being referred to by the word *nau* ("for us") in the passage "In that case, for us, Agni and Soma [are the deities] of the clarified butter alone," they are understood here too by that same word *nau*.

The first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, having set aside those [verses] obtained through the sequence of the *yājyā* and *anumantraṇa*, the pair of *anuvākyās* alone is enjoined elsewhere by a direct statement;
furthermore, the acquisition of the *anuvākyās* occurs from the *Daśatayī-kāṇḍa*.

Alternatively, the requirement for the specific form (*rūpa*) will be fulfilled because qualities are enjoined in connection with the two rites—beginning with the *āgneya*—by means of the very statements [of the *āgneya* etc. themselves.
Nor is there the fault of enjoining multiple procedures regarding an already established action;

for, upon considering the purificatory injunctions such as "he mixes the *puroḍāśa*" and "he carries fire around the *puroḍāśa*," since the substance such as the *puroḍāśa* is already obtained, there is only the injunction of deities such as Agni.
Alternatively, the fault characterized by the repetition of an injunction (*vidhyāvṛtti*) occurs only when multiple things are enjoined through the employment of distinct words.
There is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

For example, in the case of the statement "he buys with a garment," there is a syntactical split because multiple qualities are enjoined by the sentence concerning the red color (*aruṇā*) and so forth.

However, in this case, since the substance such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) qualified by the deity Agni is presented by the single word *āgneya* itself—without requiring any other [word]—and since the single deity is enjoined by the suffix (*pratyaya*), there is no syntactical split characterized by a split in the sense of the root (*dhātu*).

However, where the substance and the deity are mentioned as separate words—as in "In that case, Agni and Soma [should sacrifice] with clarified butter alone" and "Men should not sacrifice on the full moon day"—these do not constitute injunctions because they take the form of *purākalpa* (ancient narratives).
Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) results in two ways:

in one case, there are eight rites, consisting of the six rites enjoined by the sentences concerning the Āgneya and others, together with the two rites enjoined by the pair of sentences [concerning Agni-Soma].
Furthermore, because qualities are enjoined in other passages such as "āgneya" and so forth, there are indeed two distinct rites enjoined by the pair of injunctive statements.

Thus, even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* is well-known in reference to a particular rite, and since the root *yaj* is well-known as referring to sacrifice in general, the two terms are in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and therefore denote sacrifice alone. As it has been said: "The well-known is the qualifier that limits the unknown."
Therefore, the meaning of the name is determined here in accordance with the Yajurveda.
Thus (Vārttika, p. 436).
This being the case, since the name of the sacrifice under discussion is prescribed for the sake of the fruit, all the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s are equally primary, just like the *rājasūya*.

An objection is raised: "If this is so, since there is no extended application (*atideśa*) of the primary [sacrifice] itself, how can there be an extended application of the *prayāja*s in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)? It is replied: "By means of a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*)," as in: "At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* [gold grain]," and so forth.
In this case, it is not improper [to say] that the *kṛṣṇala* oblation is enjoined precisely by means of the mention (*avāda*) of the *prayāja*s.

Now, why is there no injunction regarding the fruit for those two when they are enjoined as a pair of deities on the full moon and new moon days? If that is so, then since those two are recognized even in the collective sense according to the final position (*siddhānta*), how can there be an injunction regarding the fruit? If [it is argued that] in the final position the collection is not presented through the medium of the name, but rather through the medium of time—then [the answer follows].

If that is so, then this is indistinguishable in both these sets of rites, because it has been stated that the prescription of time is made by the two sentences: "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day" and "One should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day.
Therefore, since these two alone are applied by the sentence stating the result, how can there be equal primacy?
This is not so.

Because it is impossible to determine which sacrificial substance is to be taken— given that the connection with time is common to all six [substances], beginning with those dedicated to Agni— it has been said: "Since the connection with time is the same for the six [substances] beginning with those dedicated to Agni and for these two [others], there can be no definitive determination."
Thus [Vārttika, p. 477].
Nor should it be argued that this solution is simply impossible in the case of two objects (*dvikarmapakṣa*);

for even in the case of eight objects (*aṣṭakarmapakṣa*), if this were so, there would be no application of the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) themselves to the fruit by way of time, and thus they would possess equal primacy alongside the *prayāja* offerings and the rest.

For [the author] adopts a sentence that is already well-known as being itself the statement of the result (*phalavākya*), but not a sentence whose primary purpose is to establish a connection with a result. Furthermore,
he is capable of inducing a different meaning for even a subordinate word (*upapada*) by means of another mode of derivation (*vṛtti*).
Therefore, here too, the word *darśapūrṇamāsa*, which denotes time, is capable of bringing to mind the sacrifices associated with that time through secondary indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).

Consequently, because the subordinate term (*upapada*) lacks an established meaning [independently], its status as denoting the sacrifice is determined by its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), whose meaning is well-established.

In the final position (*siddhānta*), however, since the subordinate term serves an established purpose within the sentence stating the result (*phalavākya*) when it is a restatement of the aggregate (*samudāyānuvāda*), the result is enjoined for the entire aggregate simultaneously.
"And since such equality does not exist here, even in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is indeed equal predominance.
This being the position reached, it is replied:

There would indeed be a difference in ritual acts due to the repetition of the injunction, provided that the word *evam*—which possesses both the expression of the agent (*kartṛ-yukti*) and the expression of the act (*vidhi-yukti*)—did not become a restatement (*anuvādaka*) through its connection with the word *evam*.

As for the claim that the word *yaḥ* connects with the agent of experiencing (*vedana*) and not with the agent of sacrifice (*yāga*), that is incorrect; because the status of being the agent of experiencing is established without deviation, it is precisely what must be qualified by the word *yaḥ*.

In the case of "he who is initiated" (*yo dīkṣitaḥ*), however, since the status of being the agent of sacrifice is common to both the initiated and the uninitiated, the phrase "he who is initiated" is not a qualification [of the agent of sacrifice].

Furthermore, in this context, that which is devoid of sensation—that is, the insentient—cannot possess the status of being the agent of a sacrifice. Therefore, since the qualification [of the agent] would otherwise be redundant in the sense that "he who is the experiencer of sensation should sacrifice," the word *yaḥ* (who) functions specifically as a qualifier of the sacrificial agent. Consequently, the word *evam* (thus), which is co-referential with it, is likewise [a qualifier]; because it restates that [agent], it possesses only injunctive force (*vidhāyakatvam*). As it has been said: "When connected with a single verb of action, the word *yaḥ* does not obstruct the injunctive power."
That very [act], when connected with an agent, is a restatement (anuvāda) of what has been obtained from another source.
Thus [Vārttika, p. 488].
Furthermore, due to the absence of a form (rūpa), it cannot be an injunction for a sacrifice.
Even if, in that case, the acquisition of a substance were somehow possible, the acquisition of a deity is not possible in any way whatsoever.

Nor is there the attainment of a deity based on the wording of the mantra, because the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras are recited in the sequence of the *ājyabhāga* offerings and thus lack that specific purpose. Nor can the connection of the mantra with two separate rites be established by syntactical statement (*vākya*) overriding the sequence (*krama*), because the direct statements regarding the primary times— namely, "the *vātrghnī* is recited at the Full Moon sacrifice" and "the *dhruvāntī* at the New Moon sacrifice"— are intended to refer to the rites themselves, not the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Because it is the context;
as it has been said: "First, time alone is conveyed by these two words."
"And subsequently, because of its connection with that [time], the action is understood at this time" (Vākyapadīya, p.

Nor can there be a reference to the action through the medium of time by means of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā); for since the primary meaning is tenable—given that the two Ājyabhāga offerings themselves determine the application of the mantras by virtue of their connection with the full-moon and new-moon times—it is impossible to accept a secondary sense by subverting the sequence.

Nor should it be argued that because the times of the full moon and the new moon are already established for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, the statement cannot serve to determine the application of the mantras;

for according to the final position (*siddhānta*), the times of the full moon and the new moon are indeed obtained precisely through the two performances [of the sacrifices] together with their constituent parts.

Likewise, even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since among all the factors that accompany [the sacrifice] as its primary elements, the connection with time is explicitly heard for eight of them, when the connection with time is postulated for the others as well, the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*)—because that very time has already been transformed in the intellect—postulates a connection with that same time.

In that regard, since there is no means of certain determination (*vinigamanāpramāṇa*) between the times of the Full Moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the New Moon (*amāvāsyā*), when the performance occurs according to one's preference, this statement serves to establish a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*).

When there are the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) at the full moon sacrifice, then [the verses] *vāryantī* and *anuṣṭhye* [are used]; when there are the two offerings at the new moon sacrifice, then *vṛṣantī* and *anuṣṭhye* [are used].

Therefore, because they lack a form due to the absence of a deity mentioned in the wording of the mantra, they constitute injunctions of ritual acts. Furthermore, these two ritual acts must be performed as delimited by their respective names.

Nor can it be said that the terms *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* lack the status of names simply because they lack a basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Nor should it be argued that in a sentence primarily intended as an injunction of time, the status of being a name arises from observing a connection with time due to the absence of a general injunction;
for it is precisely in the originative injunction (*utpatti*) that time serves as the basis for the application of the name.

Furthermore, in the two sentences devoted to the prescription of time (*kāla*), no action is perceived as being manifested by the original injunction (*siddhānta*). Therefore, the connection with a name does not belong to that which has the same nature [as the original], nor does the connection with time belong to that which has the same nature; likewise, the connection with time does not belong to that which has the same nature, nor does the connection with a name belong to that which has the same nature. However, in the case of the *agnihotra* and similar rites, the production (*utpatti*) occurs in such a way that the very same nature is maintained, because the nature of the oblation (*homa*) contained in the original injunction—such as "If one does not offer to Agni and Prajāpati in the evening"—is understood. Thus, due to this difference, there is no inconsistency in the presentation.
[Objection: "In that case, since the deities alone are enjoined by the sentences concerning the Āgneya and other offerings, the requirement for a specific form (*rūpa*) is satisfied.
[Reply: Not so; for when an action is already established, enjoining multiple qualities such as substance and deity would result in the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no sentence-splitting because the substance is obtained through the consideration of the preparatory (*saṃskāra*) sentences, while the deity is enjoined [in the main injunction].
Because it is impossible for something to be a *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) without the existence of a substance (*dravya*).
Otherwise, by the maxim "when substances are connected with an action, they are related as subordinate factors (*guṇa*)," it would follow that [the offering] is a primary action (*pradhānakarman*).

Furthermore, even granting for the sake of argument that a substance is obtained, there would still be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the injunction of both the placing of the fire mentioned in the word *āgneya* and the eightfold nature mentioned in the word *aṣṭākapāla*.

Thus, what was stated—that there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because of the injunction of a substance qualified by a deity conveyed by a single word—is also refuted. For since the injunction of the number conveyed by the term *aṣṭakapāla* is necessary, the syntactical split remains as it was. Accordingly, the Sūtra states: "Or rather, it is an injunction [of the accessories] simultaneously; for when they are enjoined together, they are for the sake of that [principal], and thus there is no fault in the instruction."

Thus [it is argued]. But surely, even in the Siddhānta, if one were to enjoin the connection between the substance and the deity, as well as the conjunction with time, by means of a single sentence, the fault of *vākyabheda* (sentence-splitting) would be exactly the same.
This is not so, because in the injunction of a *bhāvanā* (efficient force) qualified by all its attributes, there is no lack of the sense of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*).

And this being the case, there is no separate injunction of the qualifiers, because it is impossible for there to be an injunction of a qualified entity [without its qualifiers]; rather, the qualifiers are enjoined along with the injunction itself. As it has been said: "If there were a multiplicity of direct verbal operations, there would be excessive complexity for the words; but by unifying them, there is no contradiction in the implication of the meaning."
"When an action is already established, more than one accessory cannot be enjoined;
however, when it is not yet established, even many accessories may be enjoined with a single effort" (Vārttika, p. 485).

Objection: Just as a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) depends upon an injunction for the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇavidhi*), so too an injunction for the qualifier must depend upon the qualified injunction to obtain its object; thus, due to mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), even a qualified injunction would be impossible. Reply:
This would indeed be the case if the qualified injunction were to function only after depending upon the comprehension of the injunction for the qualifier.
What then? [The operation of the injunction] proceeds by depending on the cognition of only those specific qualifiers that are required, proximate, and capable.

And these qualifiers are indeed presented by the words within the very sentence of the qualified injunction; however, since the duty to perform the qualified action as conveyed by the injunction does not conclude merely with the duty to perform the qualifiers themselves, the injunctions for the qualifiers—which depend on the duty to perform those qualifiers—are all established as being inferred through *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard).
Therefore, in a qualified injunction, the injunctions for the qualifiers are utilized solely by virtue of their prior connection [with the primary injunction].
Just as the existence of a living person outside [the house] follows from his absence from the house;
or just as, when a substance and its property arise, the nature of the individual (vyakti) is first understood because it is observed in linguistic usage,

whereas the nature of the form (ākṛti) was previously understood as being merely co-referential with existence, but is later determined to be the very essence of the individual through non-concomitance and non-deviation— thus there is no circularity— so it is here as well.
As it has been said: "The section on qualifiers is a [distinct] section."
"This deliberation (*vicāra*) is understood even later" (the reading in the printed edition is *viśeṣaṇavidhikṣāyam*),
"nevertheless, according to the principle of the form of the word (*lākṛtyanaya*), it arises prior to that," so [says] the Vārttika (p. 485).
Consequently, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the injunction of a qualified apūrva-bhāvanā by means of the sentences beginning with "āgneya" and so forth.
Therefore, the pair of "vidvat" sentences has as its object precisely the collection of rites enjoined by those sentences.

As it has been said: "Because the injunction [of the new form] is unprecedented, the verbal power [operates] upon the archetype [only] when [the result] lacks a specific form" (the reading *arūpatvāt* is found in the printed edition).
"In that very case, because of the attainment of form, it is a restatement of a collective whole" (Vārttika, p. 489).
However, this must be stated here.
What, then, is the purpose of restating the collection [of acts]? It is said:
for in the sentence concerning the result, because of the expression "by means of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa," the status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) arises for two [sets of acts].
And that [instrumentality] does not depend upon the specific nature of the ritual acts, because there are many of them.

Nor does it depend on a result, as in the case of the *rājasūya* sacrifice; for if that were so, there would be the consequence of using the singular number, just as in the expression "by means of the *rājasūya*.

Nor does it depend on the two times mentioned in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), because even then, by virtue of its being an internal factor (*antaraṅga*), the same consequence of the singular number would arise.

As for the statement that "the singular number [is used] here in place of the plural according to the rule *supāṃ supo bhavanti*," and that this constitutes a dual in this sentence—it was resorted to merely for the sake of formal correctness of usage (*prayogasādhutva*), since the grammatical correctness of the meaning (*arthasādhutva*) was otherwise impossible.

In this case, however, since the word *āditya* is not heard as part of a compound established by the pair of statements of the learned, and since there is a connection with the correctness of the meaning, one does not rely merely on the correctness of the usage.

For instance, because the three sacrifices—the Āgneya, the Āgnīṣomīya, and the Upāṃśuyāja—are connected with the single time of the full moon, and likewise, because the three sacrifices—the Āgneya, the Aindra-dadhi, and the Aindra-payaḥ—are connected with the single time of the new moon, there is a restatement of the groups (*samudāyānuvāda*) for the purpose of establishing the duality required by the two *vidvadvākya* (declarations of knowledge) which depend upon the sentence stating the result; thus, this [restatement] certainly possesses a purpose. As it has been said: "Just as the originative sentences possess the character of injunctions for performance, so too do these [two *vidvadvākya*s], because they adopt those [groups], thereby establishing their duality."
Thus (Vārttika, p. 479).

Now, is it not the case that the unbroken collection consisting of the *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* sacrifices is denoted by the two words *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*? To this it is replied: here, by the word *pūrṇamāsa*, its derivative form, the word *paurṇamāsī*, is indicated through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). If that is so, then by the word *darśa*, the *amāvāsyā* is conveyed precisely through the indication of the opposite (*viruddha-lakṣaṇā*), because [the moon] is no longer seen (*adarśanāt*) [at that time].
So it is said.

In that case, what offense has been committed by the grammatical rule "supām supo bhavanti" (the case-endings of the preceding word become the case-endings of the following word), such that a dual or plural ending would take the place of a singular? Do not say so.

For the two sentences which are restatements of the whole (*samudāyānuvāda*) serve no purpose other than to establish an injunction (*vidhi*) whose result is the presence of the word *darśapūrṇamāsa* in the dual number within the sentence stating the fruit (*phalavākya*). [Mīmāṃsākośa 333]
Since [the teacher] taught [the texts] solely for the purpose of attaining proficiency (*prabhṛtisiddhi*), even the exertion involved in their acquisition does not constitute a fault.
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, there is no such motive; this constitutes the difference.

Furthermore, since only these six [sections] are enjoined as being connected with a fruit, the others—beginning with the *ādhāra*—become subordinate to them by the principle of proximity to that which possesses a fruit (*phalavatsannidhi-nyāya*); such is the purpose of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The Sūtra, however, uses the term *prakṛte* (in the context), which refers to the subject matter (*prakaraṇa*); by this, the ritual acts such as the Āgneya and others are denoted.
By the phrase "on the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsyām*), the pair of *vidvadvākya* passages associated with the full moon day is indicated.
Therefore, the meaning is this: in these two sentences, it is the very rituals under discussion that are to be understood, not the two [sacrifices] mentioned previously.
The meaning is that because of the mention of *rūpa* (form), there is an absence of words that establish a connection between the substance and the deity. Tautā [says]:
"But the context [applies] to the Full Moon sacrifice because of the non-mention of *rūpa*."

The following sentences connected with specific times are heard in the scripture: "That which belongs to Agni, offered on eight potsherds, is constant on both the new-moon day and the full-moon day"; "Therefore, O Agni and Soma, we two shall sacrifice to you both with clarified butter alone in a low voice on the full-moon day"; "He performs the Upāṃśuyāja immediately after"; "To those two [Agni and Soma], he presented this cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni-Soma on the full-moon day"; "Curd dedicated to Indra on the new-moon day"; and "Milk dedicated to Indra on the new-moon day."

Likewise, there are sentences not connected to a specific time, such as: "He pours the Āghāra libations," "He performs the two Ājyabhāga offerings," "He performs the Sviṣṭakṛt offering," "He performs the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings," and "He offers the Samidh-yajus.
In proximity to these, it is heard: "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon day" and "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon day.

The inquiry is: are all of these principal acts (*pradhāna*), or are only those beginning with the Āgneya and ending with the Payas offering the principal acts, while the Āghāra, the two Ājyabhāgas, the Sviṣṭakṛt, the Patnīsaṃyājas, the Samidh-yajus, and so forth, are merely auxiliary acts (*aṅga*) that provide indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*)?

Thus, there arises the inquiry: do the two "vidvat" (knower) sentences—"He who, knowing thus..."—serve as restatements (*anuvāda*) of the rites under discussion, or do they enjoin two previously unknown rites, while the other [sentences] are injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*)?
Regarding this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) states: the term "on the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsyām*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).

In both the "vidvat" sentences containing the word "paurṇamāsī" and those containing the word "amāvāsyā," only the collection of rites such as the Āgneya already present in the context is restated; no new, distinct rites are enjoined.
Because of the non-statement of form— that is, because the form of the sacrifice itself, consisting of the substance and the deity, is not stated, not determined, and not cognized—

in the case of a restatement (anuvāda), however, the forms [of the sacrifices] are understood as the Agneya and other sacrifices already present, which are connected with the full moon and the new moon.

Therefore, since the words denoting the collection [of sacrifices]—such as *Āgneya* and the rest—refer to those sacrifices and their purposes, and since they serve to enjoin various qualities, the two collections, namely the *Paurṇamāsī* and *Amāvāsyā*, are understood again and again. These two alone would be taught or expressed by the suffix;
however, that is undesirable.

Therefore, the two groups [of rites] are denoted by the words *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*, and the connection with the fruit [is established]; furthermore, in the sentences concerning the *āgneya* and other offerings, there is no injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
Rather, an injunction of action (*karmacodanā*) alone is understood through the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*).
Consequently, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) states that these [individual acts] are without fruit [unless combined], as they are connected to the fruit [only as a collective].
The established conclusion is that the *ādhāra* and other such offerings are remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*).
The designation [of them as such] is likewise.
Furthermore, because a specific distinction is observed, there would be no application of the former [auxiliaries] to those that are equal.
Indeed, these oblations at the new moon are [the same as] those at the full moon. 4.

They are resorted to such that the first [offering] belongs to Agni, while the two subsequent ones—curd and milk—belong to Indra; thus, even though there is an absence of primary status (*prādhānya*) for the offerings to Agni and the others, as well as for the *āghāra* libations and so forth, the designation of "primacy" (*prādhānya*), which is synonymous with being the principal element (*upamya*), is established for these three in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the same manner.

However, in the case of the *upahomas* (subsidiary offerings) mentioned in proximity to the modified (*vikṛti*) rite, although the context (*prakaraṇa*) exists—defined by the expectancy (*kathaṃbhāva*) of the modified ritual procedure (*bhāvanā*) qualified by their own mention in proximity—their status as subsidiaries to that [modified rite] does not arise. This is because the expectancy for the "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*) has already been satisfied by the archetypal (*prākṛta*) auxiliaries previously connected [to the rite] as providing the required assistance (*kalpopakāraka*). Consequently, the aforementioned context, which must be invoked for the application (*viniyoga*) of the *upahomas*, is absent. Rather, their subsidiarity arises from the proximity to the person [performing the rite], which generates an expectancy for the modified rite, and it is precisely from that [expectancy] that their subsidiary status is established.

Nor does this result in an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of *prakaraṇa* (context) to the desire for production (*utpādyākāṅkṣā*), because that too is included within the scope of the definition as being a *prakaraṇa* of the type known as *sthāna* (position).

It should be understood, however, that the objection regarding the undesired consequence of treating the subsidiary elements of the *upahoma* offerings as belonging to the context (*prākaraṇikāṅgatva*) is to be refuted by the fact that, just as with mantras enjoined by indicative power (*liṅga*), the application of the term "belonging to the context" is governed solely by the presence of a well-established expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in the form of "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*).

The modern [scholars], however, maintain that *prakaraṇa* (context) is that which resides in a word-meaning established by a proximate sentence, which has as its result the destruction of [the doubt regarding] what has been understood, and which—referring to an object not previously known through other means of knowledge—is characterized by its own mode and requires [further] procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
And such [a context] exists in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth within the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice.
The qualification "having a connection with a result already understood" is applied to the word-meaning in order to exclude the status of *samidh* as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of *tanūnapāt*.

The qualification "established by a proximate sentence" (*saṃnihitavākyapramita*) is included in order to exclude the status of the *prayāja* offerings and others as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices merely through their presence in the context (*prakaraṇa*).

For it is stated in the tenth book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] that even for a subsidiary, there is no application of the context (*prakaraṇa*) when its procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—which is unknown because it has not been previously understood through prior means of knowledge—and which lacks the greatness [of purpose] established by direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), such as in the case of *prokṣaṇa* and other rites.

Regarding the statement "one sings the Vāmadevya [Sāman]," and so forth, although the stotra—whose connection to the result is known through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—requires the manifestation of the syllables of the *ṛc* verses that serve as its own means, and thus possesses subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) within the context (*prakaraṇa*), the qualification "as the procedure" (*itikartavyatātvena*) is used because, even though it requires the Sāman for the sake of manifesting the syllables of the *ṛc*, it lacks the nature of being a procedure when there is a requirement for a Sāman that is already established. Thus they say.

In this context, since it is possible to exclude the status of *tanūnapāt* as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *samit* and other offerings, as well as the status of *prokṣaṇa* and others as subordinate elements of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices through the method previously described, the qualifiers "having a connection with a known fruit" and "being unknown—that is, not having been understood by previous means of knowledge"—in the definition of *prakaraṇa* (context) as a factor for application (*viniyoga*), serve solely to specify the particular subject matter to be applied by *prakaraṇa*, just like the qualifier "not being connected [by another means].
Alternatively, let there be the qualifier "having a connection already understood" within the definition of *prakaraṇa* regarding *tanūnapāt* and so forth.

However, for the sake of the conventional usage of "context" (*prakaraṇa*) regarding sprinkling and so forth in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices, it is indeed inappropriate to employ a qualifying term intended to exclude those [cases], because such usage is established by the experience of everyone. Alternatively, since there is no conventional usage of "context" for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth in relation to the *godohana* vessel and the like, one might say "unknown by a means of knowledge not previously operative" (*svapūrvapravṛttapramāṇānavagatājñātatva*). But this does not mean "not known by that which is designated as *śruti*, *liṅga*, or *ākhyāna* prior to the context," for otherwise the conventional usage of "context" for sprinkling and so forth in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices would be impossible.

Furthermore, because the status of the *prayāja* offerings and other such elements as being subsidiary (*aṅga*) is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*)—which consists of the nature of the expectancy regarding the "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*) of the previously commenced *darśapūrṇamāsa* performance, arising from the expectancy regarding the "how" of the *godohana* vessel's performance—the designation of "context" is not applied to the *godohana* and similar items.
Therefore, this is the definition of context as the basis for its conventional usage;
however, the definition of context as a means of application (*viniyojaka-prakaraṇa*) is exactly as stated by Asada.

The essential point is this: although there exists a *prakaraṇa* (context) that assigns *samit* and the other items to the *tanūnapāt* and other [offerings], it is possible to preclude the status of those [items] as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to them by means of the aforementioned method.
Some, however, maintain: "Context (*prakaraṇa*) is the mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*).
And that is the expectancy regarding the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*), qualified by the expectancy for a result (*phalākāṅkṣā*).

And this distinctness [of context] is by way of the relationship of being based on a mental impression (*bhāvanā*) that is proximate to the mental impression residing in its own substratum, and not by way of being understood from the same recitation (*pṛṣṭha*) or similar criteria.
Therefore, the *Viśvajit* sacrifice and others are not to be indicated by the context of the *Darśa-pūrṇamāsa*.

The essential point is this: when there is a requirement for "how" (*kathambhāvākāṅkṣā*)—characterized by a desire for a result—that pertains to something whose status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) has been determined or not yet determined through the aforementioned relationship (the relationship of context), that [requirement] is the context (*prakaraṇa*) which serves as its applicator (*viniyojaka*).
For it has been stated: "That which is not connected [by direct statement] is [determined] by context (*prakaraṇa*), because it is of the nature of a procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

Here, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*), it is concluded that context is indeed the expectancy regarding the manner of performance (*kathambhāvākāṅkṣā*). Furthermore, they say: "The term *asaṃyukta* (unconnected) establishes the state of having expectancy for a result (*phalākāṅkṣatva*), but it does not serve to exclude those elements that are directly subsidiary (*saṃnipātī*)" [Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra].
That is exceedingly weak.

To explain: Is this the definition of *prakaraṇa* (context) as that which brings about the result of application (*viniyoga*), or as the state of being fit for its true nature? Not the first, because it would be over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) with respect to the *bhāvanā* of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, which do not bring about the result of application. For when there arises an expectancy regarding the "how" (*katham-bhāva*) residing in the *bhāvanā* of threshing and so forth—which has been determined to have the status of a means (*upāyatva*) by virtue of being heard as the end (*bhāvya*) qualified by the expectancy for a result in the *bhāvanā* of the *prayāja*s, and which resides in a *bhāvanā* connected through the relation of "residing in a *bhāvanā*" that is proximate to the *bhāvanā* having itself as its substrate—there occurs an expectancy regarding the "how" in the *tanūnapāt* offering, even though its lack of subsidiarity (*anaṅgatva*) has been determined. This is because, once the principal sacrifice is understood to possess a result through the context (*prakaraṇa*) in the form of the expectancy regarding the "how," the expectancy regarding the "how" in the *tanūnapāt* offering arises [subsequently] through the aforementioned relation.

Because there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) due to the qualification of desiring the fruit of the *tanūnapāt* oblation; nor [is it the case that] when both the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices result in being [mere] sacrifices, the status of being a sacrifice belonging to the *paurṇamāsī* [full-moon day] follows from the sentence, since the fact that the fruit belongs to the *tanūnapāt* oblation is understood through its connection with the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*) of the primary sacrifice.
Thus it has been stated in the *Balābalādhikaraṇa*. This concludes the examination of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Furthermore, once it is understood that even the *samidh* sacrifice possesses a fruit, the expectancy for a fruit ceases; therefore—
