Murāri, pp. 1189–1195. When there arises an expectancy (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) regarding the manner [of performance] for the fire-oblation (*tanūnapāt-yāga*) occurring at a later time, it cannot be said that its [the latter’s] procedure (*prakrama*) belongs to that [former].
This is because its procedure is established through the knowledge of the meaning in both worldly and Vedic contexts.
The relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is well-established in the case of an inference produced by the consideration of a light [as a mark]. (Su., p.

111). By means of the relation of being the subject matter of the treatise (*prakaraṇapramāṇatva*), there is the qualification of the past consideration of smoke (*atītadhūmaparāmarśa*) through the aforementioned relation.
...immediately following.

Vārttika 3.1.7.4, p. 852. [The word] *prakaraṇam* [is used here]. Since there is no sublation [of the connection], the specific desire for the fruit of the *samidh* oblation belonging to the past [context] prevails over the *tanūnapāt* oblation by means of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), because there is no obstacle to its presence within the context of the fire-installation (*agnyādheya*) when there is a requirement for the "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*).
But if the Pavamāna oblations were primary, [and] the [other] offerings were subordinate,
then— in order to avoid the aforementioned defect within the scope of the delimiting factor for being produced by the recollection of smoke— one must [include] one's own... [text truncated].

3|1|21|22. Setting aside the *prakaraṇa* (context), by means of the *vākya* (syntactical connection), just as there is the inclusion of the relationship between being "twelve" and "subsequent," so too here there is the inclusion of the simultaneous existence of the *ahīna* sacrifice itself, and not of the *jyotiṣṭoma*. If it is argued that there is an inclusion of its relationship [to the *jyotiṣṭoma*] because its knowledge has been determined, [then the following applies].
15–16. Context (*prakaraṇa*).

The primary context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) of the principal [action] is useless, because the requirement for the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) has already been satisfied by the aforementioned connection. In the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is established as beyond doubt; however, in the case of the ectype (*vikṛti*), there is a state of uncertainty.

Because there is no over-extension [of the definition] due to the absence of the qualification of desiring the primary fruit; for the context (*prakaraṇa*) pertains only to the principal [act], not to its subsidiaries (*aṅga*). This is because that [context] is intended by you as the means of establishing that [connection]. *Bālabodhinī*, p. 110. *Vivaraṇa*. *Tasya* (referring to the context) functions as the establisher of that [relationship]. *Tvadabhipretatvāt* (because it is intended by you).
Not the second [alternative], because of the *prakaraṇa* (context).

Where there is a discussion of ordinary ignorance (*prākṛtājñāna*), the injunction serves to fulfill the expectancy of "how" (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) by means of the *prakaraṇa* consisting of the primary application (*pradhānaviniyoga*) in its form of fitness;

or where there is a *saṃdaṃśa* (sandwiching), it is the applicator in that very modified rite (*vikṛti*). But elsewhere, due to the absence of the nature of the primary fruit-expectancy and its auxiliary factors, [the application of] the *tanūnapāt* [mantra]...

It is proximity alone. Bāla., p. 119. Context grasps all the requirements of "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*) for all the subsidiaries simultaneously, even when there is a context for the application of the *samidh* offerings.

Bhāṭṭa 10.7.9, p. 823: Due to the absence of the auxiliary factor of the requirement for a fruit (*phalākāṅkṣā*) by the sentence within the context (*prakaraṇa*), there would be the contingency of [the *samidh* offerings] not being subsidiary (*aṅgatva*). This is consistent and meaningful. Bhāṣya 3.1.19: When the exclusion [of the fruit] is established through the context, there is no room for the inclusion of the qualification of the requirement for a fruit. It is determined—
It is sublated by the direct statement (*vākya*).

The animal (*paśu*) dedicated to Agni and Soma is [sublated] by the direct statement; for it is impossible [for it to belong elsewhere], and its inclusion as a non-member [of that context] would be purposeless. If both were to be included, they would belong to the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the animal sacrifice.

4|1|21|27. Even in the case of the *prakaraṇa* (context), it serves to prevent the *prayāja* offerings and others from being subordinate parts (*aṅga*) of the *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) by means of the requirement for a fruit (*phalākāṅkṣā*).
Having postulated *vākya*, *liṅga*, and *śruti*, [the *prakaraṇa*] becomes the applicator (*viniyojaka*).
However, *vākya* is [considered first] because the necessity of postulating its status as a cooperative factor (*sahakāritva*) is more immediate; such is the direction [of the argument].

Having postulated two indicative marks (*liṅga*) and two scriptural texts (*śruti*), [the opponent] claims that these are the means of application. However, because this context (*prakaraṇa*) possesses expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) by its very nature, it presents [the connection] directly;
therefore, syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*). (Vi.
3.1.9) Since [context] lacks independent authority, its validity arises solely from the postulation of syntactical connection.
For instance:
context (prakaraṇa) is a means of application;
this is the section concerning context.
3|1|4. The requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) residing in the primary sacrifice is the cause for the performance of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.
Context (*prakaraṇa*) is not capable of subverting a directly stated material (*dravya*).
This is because the sentence concerning the *prayāja* and the sentence concerning the primary sacrifice are both accompanied by such requirements.

347: When a connection with another [substance] is enjoined—even though the respective individual sentence-meanings of the substance are complete—that does not constitute the purpose of the context (*prakaraṇa*); such is the meaning.

Or rather, a sentence is postulated through the proximity of the end of a word or a sentence. Even in the case of words used in common parlance (*pāribhāṣika*), by means of the presentation of their own meanings, they [contribute] to that which resides in other unexpressed words through the context (*prakaraṇa*) of what is proximate, fruitful, and whose status as a constituent part of the known meaning has been understood.

In the case of the object [of the injunction], there is an expectation [of the procedure] as being the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance). (As for the function of the word, however, it should be understood from the *Bhāṭṭa* perspective in the *Prakaraṇādhikaraṇavindu*, namely that it occurs by means of an inference based on the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of suitability conducive to conceptualization as the *itikartavyatā*.)

Bhāṭṭa 3.1.4: Regarding the group of defects such as "being expressed" (*vācitva*) and so forth, [the conclusion is] that it is to be inferred from scripture (*śruti*). Thus, through this indirect sequence, the context (*prakaraṇa*) possesses authority in establishing the eightfold nature [of the *prayāja*]. Context is stronger than the mere recitation (*samāmnāya*); therefore, [the *prayāja*s] are established by the context rather than by the recitation belonging to the *pauroḍāśika* section.
And there is the section concerning the conceptualization of sentencehood through sentences.

Even though the *prayāja* offerings and others, which are not mentioned in the *brāhmaṇa*, obtain their application through *samākhyā* (name/designation) alone—such as "He offers the *samidh*s" and "Thus one should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*"—their status as sacrifices is set aside by *prakaraṇa* (context), and they are instead understood to serve the purpose of the *sāṃnāyya* and *upāṃśuyāja* offerings. For this very reason, [it is said] in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*: "Having concluded the *paurṇamāsī*..."
It is established by the *mīnā*. Context (*prakaraṇa*) is the successful establishment of a fruit that possesses expectancy.
This is because, by the injunction "one should perform the Vaimṛdha," the [Vaimṛdha] which is situated in the middle of the Vaimṛdha [section] is [established] through context.
Su. Pṛ. 1477. Context (*prakaraṇa*) is general; it occurs in connection with a cause (*nimitta*).
[It is] context;
[it is] by means of context.
By context;
of the context. And the specific is stronger than the general.

Bhāṣya 316–317: Context (prakaraṇa) is stronger than position (sthāna). Although rites such as the dice-game (videvana) are recited in proximity to the consecration (abhiṣecanīya), they are not subsidiary to that consecration; rather, by virtue of context, they are subsidiary to the Rājasūya sacrifice. The Mīmāṃsā [commentators] define context as the statement of that which is to be performed and which possesses an expectancy for the manner of performance (itikartavyatā).
*Kaṇikā*, p. 316: "But surely context (*prakaraṇa*) does not sublate either syntactical connection (*vākya*) or direct statement (*śruti*). True, it does not sublate them;
however, your position is abandoned because it lacks a result."

Since that [injunction] is not applicable due to its lack of purpose, the injunction for sprinkling and other such acts will be established by the *prayogavacana* (the statement of performance) which possesses the context (*prakaraṇa*), provided there is no obstacle.
(For those whose application is obstructed by lack of purpose, the opposite holds true regarding their relative strength;

Bhāṣya 9.1.9.12). Indeed, in the absence of an originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there is no context for actions, because context—consisting of the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*)—only extends from the point after the connection with a result has been established, and thus depends upon the *prayogavākya*.

Vārttika 2.1.5.15, p. 499: Regarding those [offerings] belonging to the Vaiśvadeva-parvan which are prescribed by direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), it is understood through the sentence that the Viśvedevas are the deities, and by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*) that these are the Āgneya and other [deities].

(The Vārttika states: "By virtue of the context, this must be inferred: one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice consisting precisely of those [deities] such as the Āgneya, and not with any other.
Furthermore, this cannot be an unequal option (*viṣamaśiṣṭa-vikalpa*).
For context is not capable of subverting a substance that has been directly stated [in scripture].
Bhāṣya 1.4.10.14; as for the section on context (prakaraṇādhikaraṇa) regarding the new-moon sacrifice and so forth, [it is stated] at 2664.
The conflict and non-conflict between *prakaraṇa* (context) and *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya* are deliberated upon [from 3.3.8 up to 3.6.6].

Vārttika 3.3.8–15, p. 862. Regarding the conflict between two *prakaraṇas* (in the sense of being a subordinate element): when there is the contingency of *abhikramaṇa* (the stepping forward) and so forth being subsidiary to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices by virtue of the *mahāprakaraṇa* (great context), its status as subsidiary to the *prayāja* offerings arises from the *avāntaraprakaraṇa* (intermediate context).

However, regarding the state of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*), such a case occurs where, within a single composite whole, a certain property is obtained for one part through the *mahāprakaraṇa*, while properties contrary to that are obtained for another part through the *avāntaraprakaraṇa*.
Kau. 3|3|7|14, p. 363. When there is a conflict between two contexts (*prakaraṇa*), the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) is stronger than the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*).
"He offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāmaṃ juhoti*) is the illustrative example.
For by the great context, this [offering] is connected to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
However, by means of the intermediate context (avāntaraprakaraṇa), there is the status of being a subsidiary to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth;
that [intermediate context] is stronger.

For in that case, because of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), even before a connection with the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) has been experienced, a relationship resembling that of a syntactical unit (*vākya*) is established.
Vārttika 3.3.7.14, p. 840: "The displacement of sections from their place of origin.
Vārttika 3.6.7.18, p. 1043: "When the purpose of a section has been established, it is not possible to impose expectancy upon those [words] that are already devoid of expectancy."

Bhāṣya on Sūtra 3.3.7.14, p. 853: Regarding the sūtra located in the Oṣṭhyamāṃsādhikaraṇa, the author of the Bhāṣya cites the sentence read within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, "That which is burnt belongs to Nirṛti," and states: "In a case where there is no [other] context, two contexts would not be postulated, for that would render the injunction purposeless. Thus, the injunction of an action is rejected by the argument that "wherever there is [the deity] Nirṛti, there the state of being burnt is applied"; therefore, this arthavāda in the form of an injunction of action—namely, "that which is burnt belongs to Nirṛti," etc.—is set aside.

*Bāla*, p. 55: For in the case of a *prakaraṇa* (context), there is observed merely a mutual requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) between those [elements] that fulfill their own purposes and those called "limbs" (*aṅga*), based on the relationship of helper and helped. But in the case of a sentence (*vākya*), the connection is directly perceived.
*Vārttika* 3.3.7.14, p. 833: The section on *prakaraṇa*.
Context (*prakaraṇa*) is a means of application (*viniyojaka*).
That which is not connected by other means is applied through context, because it resides in the sphere of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
The Commentary states: "The causes of application have been stated—direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*)."
Direct assertion (*śruti*) is the accusative case-ending in "with the verse addressed to Agni (*ainyā*), [one approaches] the *gārhapatya* fire.

Indicative mark (*liṅga*) is the capacity of the words in mantras, as in "I cut the sacrificial grass, the seat of the gods (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*). Syntactical connection (*vākya*) is as in "He purchases [the Soma] with a ruddy cow (*aruṇayā krīṇāti*)."
Now, are these alone the causes of application? No, it is said.
By the very question, "What other cause is there? it has been stated.
And indeed, a discussion often begins with a question itself.
For example: "What is the name of this river?", "What is the name of this mountain?", or "What is this fruit? To this it is replied:
It is unconnected [to the ritual context], because the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) does not reside within the immediate context (*prakaraṇa*).

That which is not connected by direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), or syntactical connection (*vākya*), [is connected] by context (*prakaraṇa*), because the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) remains unestablished.
When a complete and capable statement occurs in proximity to that which requires the procedure, it enters into a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the preceding [text].
Therefore, it is applied to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
"What is the example here, and what is the purpose?

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "He offers to the *samidhs*," "He offers to *tanūnapāt*," "He offers to the *iḍas*," "He offers to the *barhis*," and "He offers with the *svāhākāra*.
These [mantras] are applied there [in the Darśapūrṇamāsa] by virtue of the power of the context (*prakaraṇa*), and not in the Agnihotra or the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Or rather—thus, first of all, *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya* have been explained through various examples as having for their objects the distinction between the primary [meaning] and that which is mixed with the knowable.

Among these, since *śruti* consists of injunction, application (*viniyoga*), and denotation (to be defined as the one who enjoins, the one who applies, and the one who denotes), and since the capacity for application belongs to this *liṅga*, and because *vākya*—consisting of the proximity of other words—is necessarily present due to the absence of usage otherwise when [the word] is used alone, it is essentially already included [within the others] and was therefore not explicitly mentioned by name in the Sūtra.

Alternatively, since the rule "Or [it belongs] to the Veda, because it is seen mostly so" (*vedo vā prāyadarśanāt*) determines that the characteristics of the Veda apply in every respect based on the beginning and conclusion [of the section], this very sūtra regarding the application of a sentence (*vākya-viniyoga-sūtra*) must be explained as the sentence's power of application residing solely within the preceding [section].

As for the passage beginning with "aruṇayā" cited by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), even there, one could say that the direct hearing of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) itself is the means of application, just as in the case of the *aindrī* verse.
If, however, the intention is that when [the word] is heard in connection with an action in general, the specific relationship is established by the sentence (*vākya*), then that is so.
That [word] is equal even to the *aindrī* [mantra].

For there too, because the *aindrī* mantra requires only something to be approached (*upasthātavya*), and because the word "the *gārhapatya*" requires only an instrument (*sādhana*), the specific connection [between them] occurs through the sentence (*vākya*) alone.
Therefore, since it can be shown to be included within both, it belongs to both the direct statement (*śruti*) and the sentence (*vākya*).
Both have been illustrated.

Now, as the consideration of relative strength (*balābala*) is imminent, he demonstrates the three means of proof (*pramāṇa*) in their essential nature and their capacity for application (*viniyoga-sāmarthya*) in what follows.
Among these, he introduces *prakaraṇa* (context) by way of the most general commonality regarding the object of doubt concerning application.
As long as anything else is being spoken, there is ignorance;
or else, even though it exists, there may be doubt because of the absence of occasion;
or else, there is no hearing of the syllables at all.
There exists another category of word distinct from those words whose proximity to other suitable meanings is desired for the sake of following their capacity;
therefore, context and the like are separate means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This being the position reached, it is replied as follows.
"When that which is recited regarding the primary act occurs within an uninterrupted context of 'how' (the manner of performance),
yet the action has an undetermined fruit, it is known from the context.
[One should accomplish heaven by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.]

How so? When this expectancy regarding capacity remains unfulfilled, there arise those rites whose purpose has not been explicitly heard, such as "He offers to the Samidhs," "He offers to Tanūnapāt," and so forth. Consequently, some form of assistance must be established for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and the *prayāja* offerings and others must have something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Furthermore, we do not perceive, through the five means of knowledge beginning with perception—namely, perception, inference, analogy, verbal testimony, and non-apprehension—any established assistance provided by the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices within their own words, their own sentences, or other contexts;
nor do we perceive it through the Vedic word itself as a mode of perception such as direct observation.
Likewise, in the case of the Prayāja offerings and so forth, there must necessarily be some [source of assistance] for both [the primary sacrifice and the subsidiaries] by means of one or the other.
But if we do not understand [the relationship] through any means whatsoever, then we shall understand that it does not exist.
And there is indeed a means of knowledge for this: the context (*prakaraṇa*).
For a single cause of connection is not something that is entirely isolated.
For as one thing after another is not obtained in close proximity, so the power of the Vedic injunction shifts toward that which is more remote.

Thus, in this case, since the proximate means characterized by "being helpful" (upakārakatva) is not found, even the remote one is permitted; consequently, it is understood solely through the force of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) that "this Darśapūrṇamāsa requires something helpful, and that is surely accomplished by these Prayājas and other subsidiaries.
And whatever purpose the Prayājas and others require, that is the assistance rendered to the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
Thus, for neither of these two is there anything else proximate;
and as for any other [entity] that might be postulated, since it has already become free from expectancy through its connection with another, no further expectancy for a connection exists here.
Therefore, there is no postulation of a fruit for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, as there is for the *viśvajit* sacrifice and others;
nor do they follow upon the fruit of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

For when a relationship characterized by mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) is absent, a relationship characterized by one-sided expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*) is accepted, provided that [the former] is not possible.
Therefore, just as in the case of the word *naśa*, mutual restriction is established.

For what purpose is the inclusion of the term "unconnected" (*asaṃyukta*)? It is for the purpose of precluding application by means of context (*prakaraṇa*) even when there is no assignment by direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), or syntactical connection (*vākya*), such as in the case of the number five mentioned in connection with duality and plurality.
Alternatively, it should be understood that "unconnected" refers to that which contradicts the context.

In the case of those [injunctions] connected with non-conflicting elements— such as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*), and "he buys [the Soma] with a red cow" (*aruṇayā krīṇāti*)— it is appropriate for them to be included within the context (*prakaraṇa*), as they are connected with the acts of threshing and buying mentioned in the scriptural context. Since this is established by the force of the evidence itself, it was not explicitly stated by the author of the Sūtras.

Śā—(Now, the meaning of the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" is: "There is an obligation (*kārya*) regarding the sacrifice for one who desires heaven. And the status of the sacrifice as the object (*viṣayatva*) of the obligation is nothing other than its being the content (*vidhatva*) of the volition (*kṛti*) that qualifies the obligation. Consequently, the meaning of the word is simply the volition having the sacrifice as its object; it is not a volition for heaven having the sacrifice as its instrument.)

Therefore, raising the objection that the fulfillment of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is untenable according to the reasoning stated above, [the author] refutes it following the Prābhākara school: "But surely, by the word *yajeta* ('one should sacrifice'), an effort (*kṛti*) having the sacrifice as its object is expressed.

[The reply: What is this "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*)? If you say it is "being the goal to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*), no; for here heaven (*svarga*) is connected as the goal to be accomplished, not the sacrifice.
For it is not possible [to say] that one should perform a sacrifice in order to produce heaven (*svarga*)— [where "heaven" refers to the world of women; according to the Prābhākara school, however,
it refers to the *apūrva* which grants heaven].

Now, as for the claim that "one should bring about heaven by means of an effort (kṛti) directed toward sacrifice"—this could indeed be so if the nature of effort were established by the suffix; however, this is not the case.

The meaning of the suffix here is simply "effort" (kṛtyā). The statement "it is accomplished by effort" is merely an explanation of the meaning already expressed by the suffix, using a different form of the word "effort."
And because of the phrase "one should perform," heaven is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), not the sacrifice.
Now, if you argue that being an object consists in being a qualifier, it is true that the sacrifice is indeed a qualifier; however, we must determine by what means it is brought about.
It is not, first of all, by way of such identity as in the case of "blue lotus," because of the difference between the sacrifice (*yāga*) and the cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Therefore, by virtue of being a factor of action (*kāraka*), the sacrifice functions as a qualifier of the action, just like *soma* and other substances.
And in that case, since there is an absence of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the relation is solely that of being a means (*sādhana*).
Therefore, the meaning of the word is simply the production of heaven (svarga-kṛti) having sacrifice as its instrument (yāga-karaṇikā), and not the performance of the sacrifice itself.
In this way, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the name [of the rite] is possible, and not otherwise.
Consequently, there remains the requirement: "Of what is the production? (kiṃ-pratyayā kṛtiḥ).
In that context, as long as that expectancy persists, from the statement "He offers the *samidh* oblations," it is understood thus: "This is the operation by which heaven results from the sacrifice.

And while the status of being the object of the sacrifice is possible for the *samidh* and other [subsidiary acts] through an unseen medium (*adṛṣṭadvāra*), for threshing and the like, it is through a seen medium (*dṛṣṭadvāra*).

Furthermore, once the sacrifice has been performed, because it is not [yet] a substance (*asattva*), it is incapable of producing the fruit; therefore, the performance of the sacrifice is understood by implication (*artha*), not from the word itself.
Therefore, this is the meaning of the sentence: "One should bring about heaven by means of sacrifice.

As for how—by what manner (i.e., by what operation)—heaven arises from the sacrifice, he says in that regard: "He offers the *samit* oblations," "He threshes the rice-grains," and so forth. The meaning of this is as follows: [heaven is produced] through the *samit* and other offerings by way of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), through threshing and the like by way of the refinement of the substance and the deity, and by way of the substance and the deity...
It is occupied with the sacrifice by way of bringing about its own form;
such is this operation.
By means of it, heaven arises from the sacrifice, and the sacrifice becomes oriented toward the commencement of the fruit.
"Benefit is simply the orientation toward the commencement of an action"; thus, the fuel-sticks (*samid*) and so forth are the means (*karaṇa*) for the fruit, which is the sacrifice (*ṛtu*).

(The Prābhākara objects: "But in this way, even in the case of the injunction 'one should produce the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) by means of the fuel-sticks and so forth,' there would be an expectancy [for further information] due to the need to fully understand the specific action. (The reply: "Who would find this undesirable?"
For this very reason, a separate intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*) is accepted.

Now, [an objection]: if this were so, then because the *prayāja* offerings and others lack a deity, there would be an extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual properties (*dharma*) belonging to the Soma sacrifice.

[To this, he replies: Why, according to your own view, is there no extension of the Soma-sacrifice properties to the Pitṛyajña, which does possess its own qualification (*sādhikāra*)? If you argue that it is because [the Pitṛyajña] has a time [for performance] prescribed by direct scriptural statement (*vācanika-kāla*) and thus occurs as a matter of course (*prasaṅga*), then the same applies here as well.

Moreover, even if there were an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), it ceases—this is its connection with what follows—by means of the scripturally enjoined substances such as the *jauhava* and others along with their purificatory rites, by the deity mentioned in the *mantra*-text, and by the altar, the sacrificial grass, the *barhis*, the ritual properties (*dharma*), and so forth, together with their purificatory rites, which are common to both the primary and subsidiary acts; [as stated in the rule:
"In another context, [the connection occurs] in another context."
"One should sacrifice for a month with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," and so forth.

Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the month prescribed as the time for the obligatory Agnihotra and the obligatory New and Full Moon sacrifices, or is it a separate ritual distinct from the obligatory Agnihotra and the obligatory New and Full Moon sacrifices? Having concluded the discussion on the five means of establishing difference (*bheda*), the determination of difference through "another context" (*prakaraṇāntara*), which is now reached in its proper turn, is being explained.

The intention here is as follows—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that since the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are well-known, the verbs *juhoti* and *yajati* mentioned in proximity to them must refer to those same acts; however, because they are heard in a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), like the act of pouring (*secanavat*), they must have a different meaning.

For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even words such as "limb" (*aṅga*) and so forth, whose meanings are established in common worldly usage, would have different meanings in the Veda.

Therefore, where a word recognized in its worldly sense does not have a different meaning in the Veda, it follows that in cases where it does have a different meaning, this occurs solely by virtue of being in a different context within the Veda itself.

Whence is this [known]? It has been said: "That which was previously taught as ritual action by means of terms such as *agnihotra* does not assume a distinct form merely through its connection with the word *vipra*. (Vākya-pada, p. 613).

Therefore, one offers in that very same ritual action; by means of the sentence [beginning with] *yajati*, the quality known as "month" (*māsa*) is enjoined, having set aside the context (*prakaraṇa*) through syntactical connection (*vākya*).

Nor should it be argued that a duration of time in the form of a month cannot be enjoined because of a contradiction with the scriptural injunction of "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*); for there is no contradiction, since [the monthly injunction] pertains to the optional (*kāmya*) performance.

Alternatively, even within the context of a lifelong obligation (*yāvajjīva*), it is logical that the distinction between capable and incapable subjects is established precisely through an *vyavasthita-vikalpa* (a restricted option).
On this point, some describe the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) as follows: "Having performed the *upasads*, one offers the *Agnihotra* for a month"—this is the sentence in question.
Here, several subsidiary elements (*guṇas*) are heard: the state of being subsequent to the *upasads*, the plurality of performers, and the duration of a month.
Furthermore, these qualities do not exist in the obligatory *agnihotra*.
Since it is impossible to enjoin multiple qualities when a ritual act is already established, this must be the injunction of a different ritual act characterized by multiple qualities.
And in this case, one should not say that the distinction arises solely from the qualities and not from the difference of context (*prakaraṇāntara*).
For that which is non-contextual is indeed a different context; and non-contextuality is characterized by the interruption of the mental continuum (*buddhi*).
As for the power of a name here to bring [an object] to mind, that has been refuted by the many undesirable consequences (*iṣṭi*) that serve as its counter-arguments.
And since that [objection] has been refuted, it is precisely another context (*prakaraṇāntara*), acting as an opposing factor, that serves as the differentiator.

Nor should it be argued that in the case of "for a month, by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," this established conclusion (*siddhānta*) does not even apply here because of the presence of multiple subordinate qualities (*guṇa*);
for in neither the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) nor the established conclusion is there a connection of the month-long time with either the oblation (*homa*) or the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
In the former case, because the times of evening and morning are already occupied; in the latter case, because it constitutes a different context within a different context.
Because the times of the full moon and the new moon are already occupied, and because there is a requirement for another time, what then [is the case]? It is something other than the *upasad*s.

Therefore, even in the passage "for a month with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s," by means of syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*), just as in the case of being other than the *upasad*s, one performs the *agnihotra* after having performed the *upasad*s for a month, and one should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s after having performed the *upasad*s for a month.
Therefore, in both of these examples, it is indeed a difference of context (*prakaraṇāntara*) that serves as the differentiator.
Nor should it be argued: "If this is so, since the distinction is established even by way of a quality (*guṇa*), what is the use of a difference of context?
For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not function to convey what has already been understood; rather, it must be independent (*anapekṣa*).

Furthermore, even regarding the hearing of multiple qualities, there is the observation of a difference in ritual action based merely on the fact that [the action] is not the subject under discussion, as in the rule: "And the result [is assigned] when not in proximity to a ritual action.

Therefore, it is established that this is a separate means of proof (*pramāṇāntara*). This [position] is now being challenged: if that were so, it would follow that the quality itself constitutes the difference [in the ritual].

For instance, in passages such as "The cake on eight potsherds belongs to Agni," it is observed that when an action is already established, the injunction of multiple qualities serves as a differentiator of the action (*karmabheda*), rather than being a mere interruption of the cognition (*buddhiccheda*).

Therefore, in this case, to abandon the perceived capacity [of the sentence] and instead assume a capacity not yet perceived—namely, the injunction of multiple qualities for the *Agnihotra* while disregarding its dependence on that context—would appear highly unseemly to the mind, as it would result in a lack of support (*anāśrayatā*).
Furthermore, there are cases where even when an action is present within the context (*prakaraṇa*), the injunction of multiple qualities functions as a differentiator.

In that regard, to claim that a quality introduced merely by a subordinate name serves only as a cause for the cessation of a mental conception [of the action] and does not differentiate the ritual action is truly laughable.

Furthermore, how could there be a connection with the *upasads* through syntactic extension (*anuṣaṅga*) in the case of "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa for a month," since there is an absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)?

Nor can there be a connection with the word "month" due to the relationship between the month and a shorter duration of time, because the ritual actions—the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices—have no expectancy regarding time once they have been completed by the prescribed times of the Full Moon and New Moon.

The phrase "yatastu" (but because) serves as a restrictive rule for one of the two [alternatives]. It functions to eliminate the requirement for another *tithi* (lunar day). Now, an objection is raised: since the sentence "māsaṃ darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta" (one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices for a month) is sufficiently accounted for by its capacity to satisfy the requirement for time—just as in the case of "māsād iti" and so forth—and since there is no need for syntactic ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) and thus no injunction of multiple subordinate qualities (*guṇa*), the sentence concerning the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices cannot serve as an example [for the point at hand].

Nor is there any impossibility of [the action] being subsumed [under the Agnihotra], because of its connection with two actions: by the force of the word *upasaddhi* (with the Upasads), and by the injunction of the month through the root *juhoti*.

Furthermore, since the Commentator, disregarding even the fruit associated with a single quality that he heard, cited only this much—"He performs the Agnihotra for a month"—that too is not understood; thus, saying "the Commentator was overcome by sleep," this is merely something trivial. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated exactly as a logician would state it:
everywhere, a quality related to an action is of two kinds—either something to be adopted (*upādeya*) or something not to be adopted (*anupādeya*).

In that context, because that which is to be adopted (upādeya) has already been previously established, and because it depends on the substance characterized by qualities such as being "sharp" or "intense" (as expressed by the word *yaccha*), it is fit for prescription; therefore, even when referring back to a distant ritual act (*karma*), the syntactical form is: "Wherever this [act] exists, there this [quality] should be performed. On the other hand, that which is not to be adopted (*anupādeya*)—being independent and already established as it is—is made the subject of reference (*uddeśya*) by means of the word *yat* for the purpose of connecting it with something else.
Therefore, wherever that specific mode of expression exists, there the action must be performed.

As it has been said: "Due to the distinctions of cause, fruit, refinement, and time, the non-prescriptibility [of certain factors] is traditionally taught for the purpose of enjoining subsidiary actions."

And this injunction of action (*karmavidhi*) with respect to that which is not to be adopted (*anupādeya*)—namely, place and time—is [an injunction] solely by way of delimiting the performance (*prayoga*), because they serve as the delimiters of the performance through being enjoined [as factors] for it; just as threshing and so forth are enjoined for rice and other grains for the sake of the *saṃskāra*, or as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices are [enjoined] for the sake of heaven, since in those cases the action itself is enjoined there by virtue of its being the object of the injunction.

O seeker of truth! However, from the mere injunction regarding the *nimitta* (occasioning cause), there is only its status as a qualification for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), but not an application (*viniyoga*) of the ritual act (*karman*) therein; for it is not adopted as something to be accomplished (*kāryatvena*). Rather, it is merely this much: "When that [cause] exists, [the rite] must be performed.

Therefore, even where the phrase "in that very place" occurs, it does not refer to a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), but rather refers to the fact that the performance of what is to be undertaken depends upon what is not to be undertaken, because of the distinct nature of the fruit and the occasioning cause.

Regarding these two—performance (*prayoga*) and application (*viniyoga*)—when there is an expectation of an action (*karman*), if the expectation for performance and application pertains to that very [action] which has already been produced, then it must be stated that since the entire [action] is present within the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*), that very produced action is both performed and applied; thus, there is no distinct action (*akarmāntaratva*).
This is as in: "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices on level ground," and "One should sacrifice with the Full Moon sacrifice on the full moon day," and so forth.
However, when the production of such [an action] is not present, then because it is produced [anew], it constitutes a distinct action (*karmāntaratva*).

And since there is no such origination of a homa or a sacrifice present here in the context of the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, it must indeed be a distinct ritual act. Where a quality to be enjoined occurs within a different context, it is proper that there be no distinct ritual act; however, when there is a subject matter [of a different nature], there is a different ritual act.
Thus [Vākyapadīya, p. 616].
Nor should it be argued that here too, because names such as *agnihotra* have already been produced, this must be a distinct ritual (*karmāntara*).
For in the case of "he offers" (*juhoti*), the meaning of the verbal root is understood as a process consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior stages, which is not yet a substantial entity.
The connection with gender and number is established by the nominal word (*nāmapada*);
therefore, there is no cognition of the [action's] origination (*utpatti*) through this [word].
As it has been said: "Even in the case of the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), when heard as it is, it is understood as something not yet become a substance (*asattvabhūta*)."
"By a name denoting a sentient being, such [an action] is brought forward" (Vākyapadīya, p.

Nor is there a state of dependence on a subordinate name for the verb associated with that name; for, due to the requirement of a time that is not itself to be enjoined (*anupādeyakāla*), it does not bring about the presentation of what is already under discussion (*prakṛta*).

Furthermore, since both nouns are presented by a single verbal suffix (ākhyāta), it is not possible for one to prescribe the performance (*prayoga*) and the other the application (*viniyoga*), such that there would be a difference in purpose; rather, they possess a single function. For even in that case, because the verb is primary due to its denotation of the *bhāvanā* which constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), the nouns are necessarily subordinate to it. Therefore, in this context, the meaning of a noun uttered in proximity to an injunctive verb must necessarily be described in accordance with that injunction itself.
Furthermore, because the application [of the injunction] is directed toward performance (*prayoga*), it serves the purpose of performance.

It cannot simultaneously serve the purpose of origination (*utpatti*) for that very same act performed once; thus, there is no assumption of a separate originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) that would result in a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

In cases such as "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day," however, there is no fault, because the context (*prakaraṇa*) is recognized as distinct, and since the name-word (*nāmapada*) is intent upon the unity of performance, it lacks the dual character [of both origination and application].

However, where in another context it is heard—after stating, "The Atirātra sacrifice, the Prāṇīya day, the four Abhipravas, the six-day periods"—that "those desiring prosperity should perform the Satra," there the words containing the term *atirātra* refer to the previous rite.

In all such cases, because the verb (*ākhyāta*) is the enjoiner of everything, it is the previously presented rite that is enjoined; thus, due to the difference between the word that presents the rite and the word that enjoins it, there is a distinct rite.

If, however, even there the meaning of the verbal root *yajati* (to sacrifice) were heard as a subordinate element (*anuṣaṅga*), then, because that [meaning] would be an insubstantial entity (*asattvabhūta*), there would be no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of it by means of names such as *atirātra*; consequently, even in that case, it would indeed be a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

In that context, regarding the words *āsīran* and *upeyuḥ*, although a distinct action is understood through the form of the performance, nevertheless, because the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is present, the *bhāvanā* is indeed distinct due to the difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*).
And it is determined that this [distinct *bhāvanā*] is merely the previously established action introduced by the name, but qualified by its connection to a specific result.
As it has been said: "Only the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is differentiated; the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not understood [as distinct].
For that [root-meaning] is grasped by the noun (*nāman*), since the injunction regarding the *āsana* (seating) is prompted by the *āsyati* (he shall sit).
(Vākyapadīya, p. 617).

Regarding the statements, "The Darśapūrṇamāsa [are for] all [desires]" and "The Jyotiṣṭoma [is for] all," even though they are taught outside of a specific context (*anāramyādhīta*), there is no separate ritual action (*karmāntara*) with respect to either the non-adoptable or the adoptable.

For it is heard in scripture: "Other optional sacrifices (*iṣṭi*) are undertaken for a single desire; the Darśapūrṇamāsa are for all; other sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) are undertaken for a single desire; the Jyotiṣṭoma is for all."

And here, since the meaning of the word *anya* (other) must be determined by reference to another counter-correlative already previously understood, it is concluded—by observing its future application—that this [word] refers specifically to the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices.
Nor is it the case that [the word] depends only on the Darśapūrṇamāsa mentioned in the sentence of application (*viniyoga-vākya*) while occurring in another context;
for there is an extraction of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara-niṣkarṣa*).
The word [denotes] that which has a common form, because it stands in a correlative relation (*pratiyogitva*) to the referent of another word.
For when one says "another Brāhmaṇa," the correlative does not appear as a mere [undifferentiated] purity;
rather, it is precisely a Brāhmaṇa.

In this case as well, because of the reference to what was previously understood—namely, "other desires" and "other sacrificial rites"—the meaning of the word *anya* (other) must be defined in relation to those previously understood counter-correlates (*pratiyogi*).

Therefore, by the force of the word *anya* itself, since the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices are already present [in mind], the statements "The Darśapūrṇamāsa for all [desires]" and "The Jyotiṣṭoma for all [desires]"—even though they are intent upon assigning the respective fruits of those specific rites—are not intent upon projecting a separate ritual procedure (*upāyāntara*). Consequently, there is no establishment of a distinct ritual action (*karmāntaratva*).

In the case of the statement, "He who should sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, an animal sacrifice, Soma, or through propitiation, [should do so] on the new moon or full moon day," here too, because the status of being previously established is set aside by the very presence of the word *yat* (relative pronoun) joined with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), there is a distinctness of action (*karmāntaratva*).

However, regarding the statement, "Having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma," since the venerable Vārttikakāra himself has stated that this is heard within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, one should not maintain a distinction based on a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*).
When this is done, there is no comprehension of a prior action belonging to the time of the verbal suffix from any source; thus, a name (*nāmadheya*) cannot sublate [the connection].

Therefore, because the production of a distinct action occurs through the cessation of the notion of "appropriation" (*upādāna-buddhi*) regarding that which is not to be appropriated, the existence of a distinction [between actions] is established.

As for the name *agnihotra* and so forth, it is accepted as being merely figurative (*gauṇa*)—due to its similarity to the subject by virtue of its name and its observation of future application, marked by study—and thus nothing is untenable.

The purpose [of this discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there would be performance for a month of the *agnihotra* itself as the archetype (*prakṛti*), and of the two archetypes, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
In the Siddhānta, however, regarding the employment of the word [“agnihotra”], it refers to the performance of a distinct ritual action characterized by the month, such as the Agnihotra.
As for the Sūtra: “In a different context, there is a difference of purpose caused by the difference of context; this means it is a distinct ritual action. (Tautātita)

[Objection: But surely, a time cannot be enjoined with reference to another sacrifice that is not present in the mind, according to the principle that "in a different context there is a difference of purpose. [Reply: True; however, here, because the sacrifices are present in the mind through the word "sacrifice" in the passage, "This indeed is the first of sacrifices," they are enjoined as occurring after the Agniṣṭoma—thus there is no fault. (Ratnaprabhā 6.3.14, 39–42).
If the Gṛhamedhīya did not have the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, then by the principle of "a different context," it would constitute a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).
Dvādaśamīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa 10.7.9.27: A sentence heard in another context ought to be expressive of that [action] within whose context it is heard.

The Section on a Different Context (Prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa) | 2.3.11–24. This is to be seen under the heading "The Principle of a Different Context" (Prakaraṇāntaranyāya). In the Section on a Different Context, it is stated: "An action, being differentiated because its efficient force (bhāvanā) is not present [in the previous context], is not prevented from being distinct."

The reading "the production of the differentiation of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) according to the method stated in the Vārttika, 'it is determined as being differentiated'" (Soma. 7.3.1; cf. Mīmāṃsā-sūtra-bhāṣya-vārttika on 2.3.11.24, p.

In the section concerning "another context" (*prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*), the term *agnihotra* is described as being used figuratively precisely because of the split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). (Vākya-artha, p. 20) Since the injunction of time qualified by the meaning of the word "various" (*vividha*) is established in the section on another context—because the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the suffix in "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is enjoined with reference to the objective efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*)—the words "sacrifice" (*iṣṭi*) and so forth in the statement "He who would sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, an animal, or Soma, [should do so] on the new moon day" are merely restatements (*anuvāda*).

Regarding the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, it is stated in the *Kaustubha* under the section on "Different Context" (*prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*) that the *avabhṛtha* is a distinct ritual act from the Soma-related *avabhṛtha*; that in the case of the *tṛṇa* (grass), it is a primary act (*arthakarma*), and in the case of the *niṣkāśa* (remnants), it is a disposal (*pratipatti*).
(*Bhāṭṭa-dīpikā*)

In the *Viśvajit* sacrifice performed on the first day of the *Aṣṭra*, by means of the principle established in the *Prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*, it is a distinct ritual (*karmāntara*). Through the extension of the name (*nāmātideśa*), the properties of the *Viśvajit* recited in the eleventh book—namely, that its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of "everything"—apply here.
(Bhaṭṭa 6.7.8).
Upon examining the exposition of the *Prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa* (2.3.11–24), it appears that there are five [factors] which are not to be taken up as subordinate elements (*anupādeya*).
The sacrificer’s own singularity as well as his caste, such as Brāhmaṇa and so forth, are indeed non-essential (anupādeya).
Bāla. pṛ. 97.
Exposition of the determination of a different context (prakaraṇāntara).

In the section on "Different Context" (*prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*, 2.3.11–24), five types of non-essential factors (*anupādeya*) are stated: place, time, fruit, occasion, and consecration (*saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, the definition of "different context" is stated in all treatises as: "The proximity of that which is non-essential constitutes its non-proximity [to the primary action], which is different context.
This [definition] will be explained in the passage: "They go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with the dregs of the *vāruṇī* and the water used for rinsing."
For in that regard, a distinction is stated in another section of the Vārttika, in the *Prakaraṇāntara* (Different Context) section;

likewise, in the *Śāstradīpikā*, in the seventh book, in the section beginning with "Similarly, the *avabhṛtha* [is distinct] from the Soma" (7.3.4.13–16), it is stated: "By the word *yanti*, a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*) is enjoined on the basis of a different context."

On this point, Bhaṭṭasomeśvara offers the following resolution: "The aforementioned definition applies here; for in that case, because the removal of the *vāruṇī* liquor and the satisfaction of those who are thirsty serve as a benefit to living beings (*bhūtopayogitva*), there is an extraction [of the rite] into a different context (*prakaraṇāntaraniṣkarṣa*). This is by way of the principle of a different context (*prakaraṇāntaranyāya*), since [the act] is not something to be undertaken as a mere preparatory refinement (*saṃskāra*)."

This has been stated by him [Śabara]: "In the case of the third [sentence], 'Whatever may be smeared with Soma, with that the Adhvaryus go,' even though the *niṣkāsa* (the scrapings) is a means for the removal of the husks (*tuṣa*; note: the word *tuṣa* is not in Su.), because the *niṣkāsa* is a remnant of the *vāruṇī āmiṣā* [offering] (note: even though it is used in the *vāruṇī āmiṣā* sacrifice, it is not something that has reached its final purpose), and because the husks are remnants of the *āgneya* and other sacrifices (note: they are the sacrificial materials for the *āgneya* sacrifice), there is no contradiction in their being a *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) in the form of being something to be disposed of (*pratipādyatva*), just as in the cases: 'He sprinkles the oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*s' and 'Whatever may be smeared with Soma, with that the Adhvaryus go'" (Su. p. 954).
That is weak,
because it contradicts the *adhikaraṇa* (the topical section).

For in the eleventh [book], at this very same passage (11.2.15.63–65), having refuted by means of another injunction the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the temporal distance of the performance (*pracāra-viprakarṣa*) concerning the *savanīya*, [the author] establishes that it is a disposal (*pratipatti*).

Thus, another prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) has been stated: because the *tuṣanirvāpa* (the winnowing of husks) is mentioned as a preparatory act (*saṃskāra*), the objection regarding syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is avoided, and it is declared to be a primary act for its own sake (*arthakarma*).

For this very reason, the definition of "separation by context" (*prakaraṇāntara*) must be stated. Here, what is to be understood is not merely proximity to something non-enjoinable (*anupādeya*) in its own form—as in the case of "non-proximity" (*asaṃnidhi*)—but rather the impossibility of the injunction’s purpose being transferred to another object.
And just as that [non-proximity] occurs through the non-proximity of the object to be enjoined (*upādeya*), so too does it occur through the non-proximity of the [injunction] itself.

Therefore, the definition of *prakaraṇāntara* (separation by context) intended here is: "Non-establishment [of identity] aided by the impossibility of the transfer of the meaning of the injunction to the object to be enjoined.

For this very reason, it should be understood that even in cases such as "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," where there is no enjoined object to be transferred because only the name is heard, the distinction [from the original rite] arises solely from non-proximity, aided by the impossibility of transferring the meaning of the injunction.
For this very reason, in the case of the *Ujjit* and others, as well as the *Āgneya* and similar rites, the distinction is stated by name within the immediate context itself.
The same applies to passages such as "Now this is the Jyotis.

Furthermore, in the third [section], in the section concerning King Janaka, regarding the sentence—"Having spoken of the Agniṣṭoma, there are four threefold days"—where the qualities to be adopted, namely the four-fold *saṃsthā* and the threefold nature (*trivṛttva*), are heard, a distinction is accepted on the grounds of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), just as in the case of the *Tūṣṇīṃ-niṣkāsya* passage.

For this very reason, in the section concerning "another context" (*prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*), regarding passages such as "He performs the monthly *Agnihotra*," the statement in the *Bhāṣya*—"or when there is a non-enjoinable quality" (*anupādeyaguṇe vā*)—and the phrase "due to proximity" (*upasannidhiśritvāt*) refer to the presence of another enjoinable quality; thus, although syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) exists in its own right, it is mentioned in the *Bhāṣya* as a reason for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) only with reference to sentences containing two enjoinable qualities.

It should be understood that the Master (Pārthasārathi Miśra) refuted the irrelevance of that [syntactical split] to the establishment of the final conclusion only in the case of sentences like those concerning the month, and not in the case of the *Sārthatrika*.
Bāla, pp. 88–89:
The principle of a different context (*prakaraṇāntaranyāya*).
In the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, the Māsāgnihotra and other such rites constitute distinct ritual acts.
In another context, there is a difference in purpose.
The Bhāṣya states: In the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana*, it is heard: "One performs the Agnihotra for a month," and "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa for a month," and so forth.

Regarding this, a doubt arises: Is the month prescribed as the time for the established Agnihotra and the established Darśapūrṇamāsa, or is there an injunction for a different ritual (*karmāntara*) distinct from the established Agnihotra and the established Darśapūrṇamāsa?
What, then, is the established position? It is that there is indeed an injunction regarding time for those [acts] already established.
Why? Because the word "for a month" (*māsam*) is of the very nature of an injunction of time.
How is it of the nature of an injunction of time? That which is already known from the statement "he performs the *agnihotra*," namely "for a month," is what is not yet known.
In this way, the terms *agnihotra* and *darśapūrṇamāsa* will not refer to something other than [the well-known rites].
Therefore, it is an injunction regarding time.
But is it not the case that the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *kuṇḍapāyināmayana* overrides the sentence (*vākya*)?
Granted, let it be set aside;
for the syntactical connection (vākya) is indeed more powerful.
This being the case, we reply:
A sentence heard in another context must be expressive of that [action] to which it belongs by virtue of that context.
But is it not the case that there is a direct injunction of accessory details for the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa?
No, it is said in reply.

How so? By the phrase "having resorted to proximity" (*upasannidhiśritvā*), which is synonymous with "having performed the sacrifice" (*iṣṭvā*), this is stated. Furthermore, there is no such thing as "proximity" for the Agnihotra or the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Therefore, this is an injunction regarding the month of Akṣa.

Now, it might be argued that the *upasad* rites are also enjoined [by this sentence]. In that case, because multiple subordinate elements (*guṇa*) would be enjoined within this single sentence for the purpose of enjoining those qualities, the sentence would suffer from syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Furthermore, on this view, the word "Agnihotra" would not be connected [to the sacrifice], and thus it would not qualify the ritual action.
Therefore, there will be no split in the sentence.
Thus, it is established that this is a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

As for the discussion regarding the distinction characterized by accessories (*guṇa*), what kind of accessory, being impossible in the previous case, creates a split, or what kind of accessory is possible in that very same case?

Now, since the five causes of differentiation characterized by a difference in context have been concluded, the distinction [between rites] is being discussed. In that regard: "In the case of the Agnihotra and other such rites, the ritual action previously understood as non-differentiated does not attain the form of a distinction merely through remoteness."
Just as the word "agnihotra" and others, when uttered in Pāṭaliputra or elsewhere, do not convey a different meaning, so it is even in another context;
for another context does not indeed obstruct its denotative power.
This is the principle of another context (*prakaraṇāntaranyāya*).
The principle of "another context" (prakaraṇāntaranyāya) indicates this:
even the roots *yajati* (to sacrifice), *juhoti* (to offer oblations), and so forth, when qualified by that [context], do not function with a different meaning.
Nothing becomes meaningful without another meaning;
nor is it impossible for an injunction to apply to those [acts] that have already been established,
because an option is logically tenable due to their being of equal strength with injunctions such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*).
Since the specific time for their optional performance (*kāmyaprayoga*) is not otherwise known, the prescription of the month as its measure is not defective.
Furthermore, it is accepted that a direct statement (*vākya*) overrides the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Alternatively, this is a counter-exception (*prati-prasava*) permitting even those acts prohibited on account of being initiated (*dīkṣitatva*) to be performed within the limit of a month.
However, that [performance] is indeed carried out in the midst of the ritual application (*prayoga*).

Alternatively, those very rites such as the *agnihotra* and others are presented here together with the *soma* sacrifice and enjoined for the sake of the fruit by means of the injunction for the performance of the *sattra*.
For Devadatta, who was previously eating alone, does not become something else when he eats in a row together with others.

And it has been stated that the connection with another result is not impossible without [the act] being a distinct ritual (*karmāntara*); this is the subject of the present section (2.3.2). Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that one must proceed only to the point where the sacrifice is completed; for even a principal act (*pradhāna*), when enjoined by its own word in an incomplete form regarding the instrumental aspect, is not contradictory.
Therefore, even in this case, those very same [rites] such as the Agnihotra and others [are intended].
This being the position reached, it is said:
"This Agnihotra is enjoined after the Upasads."
Nor are these [Upasads] present in the case of the *naiyamika* (the obligatory rite), so they are not distinct [from those in the optional rite].

For if the month were enjoined as pure [independent of other elements], then there would be a difference in cognition regarding the subsequent reference (*anuvāda*); however, this is not the case. Since it is heard [in the scripture] as following the Upasads, the time can be indicated by means of the existing Upasads.
Furthermore, those [acts] do not exist for their own sake or for the sake of others within the obligatory rite (*naiyamika*).

If, however, they and the month were prescribed as occurring subsequent to that [obligatory rite], then, because multiple actions would be enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

For this very reason, this injunction has been refuted—whether as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to what was prohibited by the prohibition of giving, sacrificing, and cooking for one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*), or as a part of the sacrificial session (*satra*).
For even there, since "the month after the Upasads" expresses a single purpose,
there would be the fault of multiple purposes if another ritual action were being enjoined.
Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya maintains that this is a separate ritual action.

However, this must be addressed here: if the status of being a separate rite follows from the consequence of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*), then that very cause of distinction would result, not "another context" (*prakaraṇāntara*).
Alternatively, if the distinction arises simply from the quality itself because it cannot exist in the previous [rite] due to its multiple natures, then there is no room for "another context."

For it is said: "Even if this [quality] might apply to that very subject in question due to that cause, nevertheless, because of its impossibility there, one should state that the quality belongs to another action.
Furthermore, "By this [argument], a distinction from the Agnihotra would have to be established with great difficulty."
But for the subsequent [rites], there could not be [such a status] without their connection to the *upasads*.

For in cases such as "He sacrifices with the New and Full Moon sacrifices for a month," since only the connection with the month is being enjoined, no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) occurs; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence that these are not distinct rites (*akarmāntara*).
To this, one might object:
Here too, [the opponent argues] that because of the ellipsis (*anupaṅga*) "having performed the *upasad* rites," there is equality with the *agnihotra*.
That is incorrect.
Why? Because: "Where the scriptural statement would be meaningless without an ellipsis..."

For indeed, the principle of *anuṣaṅga* (supplying an ellipsis) applies only where there is an incompleteness [of meaning] for those who have not yet accomplished their purpose, and that is not the case here.
*Anuṣaṅga* is appropriate only where, without it, nothing at all has been stated.

For example, in this very context, in passages such as "for a month, with the Vaiśvadeva [sacrifice]," until the word "he sacrifices" (*yajate*) is supplied, nothing at all has been stated; therefore, it must necessarily be supplied.
In this case, however, the sentences concerning the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices are already rendered complete in their own terms.
Furthermore, the phrase "having performed the Upasads" has already fulfilled its purpose in the preceding context and thus requires nothing here.
Consequently, there is no reason whatsoever for it to be supplied by way of syntactic ellipsis (anuṣaṅga).

If, however, one should desire *anuṣaṅga* precisely because of the contingency of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*), he might indeed perform that *anuṣaṅga*. But in that case, since there is an injunction of the word "paritvā" [repeated] again, it would follow that the *anuṣaṅga* of the *upasad* and so forth must continue as far as the *anuṣaṅga* extends.
And this is undesirable, because there is no authorization from the Veda for such a thing.

Now, if it were argued that all the *anuṣaṅgas* (supplementary additions) are already accomplished by those performed previously for the *agnihotra* itself, then—in that case—the utterance of the words would likewise remain fixed as assisting the *agnihotra* and other rites in accordance with the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), and thus there would be no purpose for the *anuṣaṅga*.
Therefore, this interpretation is not tenable. It should rather be explained as follows: "Where a quality (*guṇa*) is to be adopted within a different context..."
In that case, it is logical that there is no separate action (*akarmāntara*), whereas when there is a different subject matter (*uddeśya*), there is a distinct action.
Here, first of all, a distinction does not arise from the existence of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*); it must necessarily be at the end.
What then? It arises from the interruption of the previous context.
For when the preceding action is not being modified, a distinction of the subsequent [action] is perceived in no way whatsoever;
however, even if there is a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), it does not contribute anything at all.
And we shall explain this under the sūtra: "And the fruit [is understood] when there is no proximity to an action" (*phalaṃ cākarmasaṃnidhau*).

Furthermore, in every case where there is a connection with a ritual action whose context has been interrupted, two types [of elements] are heard: that which is to be adopted (*upādeya*) and that which is not to be adopted (*anupādeya*).

Among these, that which is to be adopted—such as the *āhavanīya* fire, the introductory verses (*pratipad*), and so forth—can be prescribed even by means of a reference to another location. However, that which is not to be adopted—consisting of place, time, occasion, fruit, and preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*)—is subject to this verbal formulation for the sake of prescribing it in relation to a ritual action situated in another location: "The action must be performed right there."
The principle of context;
thus [is] the principle of context.

Furthermore, when an action is being enjoined for the sake of another [deity], if it is presented by another sentence of that very same form, then, because it is that very same [action], it is difficult to maintain that it is not a different action.

However, if it does not present itself due to even a slight concealment, then, because it is being enjoined as something further, the cognition of its distinctness from what was previously enjoined remains established; it cannot be sublated, and thus it becomes a different action.
For such is the nature of that injunctive [sentence].

In that context, the instruction is as follows: "With regard to the object to be denoted, this action is enjoined by me; and since that which is unproduced in its own nature cannot be enjoined, it is brought forward by implication.

Therefore, if anyone is able to produce such a thing, let him produce it, while I too perform the injunction here; but if he does not produce it, then let no one come along later and consider it my fault.
By this, it is meant that [the injunction] has been thus proclaimed (or made known).
Or rather, this may be the reading: if someone brings such [an offering], then he too performs that very same [act] in a particular place and so forth;
but if he does not bring it, then it is determined that he himself produces it.
Therefore, in this case, because of the mention of "months," it is not possible to enjoin [the act] by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to a distant oblation.
For no one is capable of bringing about the month right here merely for the sake of the *homa*.

Therefore, when the *homa* and other rites are enjoined with respect to the month— which is entirely independent and not something to be brought into being [as a subordinate element]— the originative injunctions, though situated at a distance,
effect the origination of the rite right now, provided that their power to produce it remains unimpaired.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for that which has already arisen to arise again, this is understood as an original injunction (*apūrvavidhāna*). But surely, when the origination of that rite is set aside by the word "Agnihotra" and so forth— which is associated with its [original] origination— this injunction would merely result in a connection with the month,
and its character as an originative injunction (*utpādakatva*) would be frustrated.

"If an action, though brought near by proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), does not arise again, then it certainly will not arise when brought near by a name (*nāmadheya*). Where even another sentence is not differentiated when recognized through mere proximity, how can it be that what is brought near by a name within its own sentence is not recognized? It is said in reply: [The text continues: "It is because of the difference in the names. Just as in the case of the sentences *vājibhyo vājinam* and *vājibhyo vājam*, although the word *vājibhyaḥ* is common to both, the two actions are not understood as identical due to the difference in the names *vājinam* and *vājam*. Similarly, here too, although the action is recognized through proximity, it is not recognized as identical because of the difference between the names *vājina* and *vājapeya*. Therefore, the sacrifice denoted by the name *vājapeya* is indeed distinct from the *vājina* sacrifice. Furthermore, the name *vājapeya* is not merely a synonym for *vājina*; rather, it is established as a distinct name based on the connection with a specific result. Thus, since the names differ, the sacrifices are distinct. Moreover, the *vājapeya* sacrifice is enjoined together with the result, whereas the *vājina* sacrifice is enjoined together with the material; therefore, they are distinct. Consequently, the *vājapeya* sacrifice is indeed distinct from the *vājina* sacrifice. This concludes the section concerning the *vājapeya*. Now begins the section concerning the *saubhara*. Here, the doubt is as follows: Is the *saubhara* a subordinate element (*guṇa*) of the *rathantara* chant, or is it a distinct rite? If it is a subordinate element, then it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *rathantara*. If it is a distinct rite, then it is an independent injunction (*apūrva*). In this context, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: The *saubhara* is a subordinate element of the *rathantara*. Why? Because of the proximity (*saṃnidhi*). Since the *saubhara* is mentioned in proximity to the *rathantara*, it is understood as a subordinate element of that very chant. Furthermore, the *saubhara* is a specific form of chanting (*gīti-viśeṣa*), and a specific form of chanting is a subordinate element of a specific chant. Therefore, the *saubhara* is a subordinate element of the *rathantara*. Moreover, the *saubhara* is enjoined as a means to produce a particular tone (*svara-viśeṣa*). If it were an independent rite, it would be enjoined as a means to produce a specific result. However, it is not so enjoined. Therefore, the *saubhara* is a subordinate element of the *rathantara*. This concludes the prima facie view. Now follows the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). The *saubhara* is a distinct rite. Why? Because of the mention of a specific result. Since the *saubhara* is mentioned as a means to achieve a specific result, it must be an independent rite. Furthermore, the *saubhara* is enjoined as a means to produce a specific tone, and it is not possible for one thing to be enjoined as a means to produce two different things simultaneously.
