"In whatever manner it is desired, even by means of a weak cause,
once the ritual action (*karman*) has been brought into proximity, that very [action] is performed there;
for since the action is understood to belong to the sacrifice and to a specific place and so forth through its presence (*saṃnidhāna*), it is presented in exactly that way and thus does not differ."

Furthermore, the name (*nāmadheya*), because it is subordinate to the verb (*ākhyāta*) from the very beginning, does not at all operate with respect to either difference or non-difference. The intention [of this statement] is as follows: since the name's capacity to bring about the prior action is based on its denoting that prior action, and since the verb's subordination to the name cannot exist without the name having the prior action as its object—and because, in the absence of such a basis, the name's status as a denoter of the prior action could not be determined, and thus its capacity to present the prior action would be untenable—the name does not constitute an obstacle to the origination [of the action].

And while that [root] remains awaiting the commencement of its verbal expression, when one considers only the connection with the word *yajati* (sacrifices) as grasped in the injunctions "he offers for a month" (*māsaṃ juhoti*) and "he sacrifices for a month" (*māsaṃ yajate*), there is no recognition of any other root such as *juhoti*, because it does not recur within the context of its own sentence. Furthermore: "By its name, only the meaning of the verbal root is brought to mind according to its capacity."

However, *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is determined to be distinct because it is not present [in the verbal root]. For all nominal designations are established as names for the meanings of roots by means of words expressing generality (*sāmānya*), but not for *bhāvanā*.

Therefore, at the time of determining whether *bhāvanā* is different or not, even though it is the meaning of the root, *bhāvanā*—lacking any other means of proof and not being brought forward by another verbal suffix—is in no way recognized; thus, it is established that its purpose is attained.

Alternatively, even the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is perceived in the verb (*ākhyāta*) as being a substantial entity (*sattvabhūta*), because it cannot be construed with gender and number [if it were not so]. Such a [substantial] form is not brought forward by a noun (*nāman*) which denotes a non-substantial entity; for here, the meaning of the verbal root, being non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), is what is to be delimited by the root *juhoti*.
Furthermore, that [action] is also distinct because it is not recognized as being denoted by words such as *agnihotra*, which denote the connection of a substance (*dravya*) with gender and number;
for there is no recognition [of identity].
However, where even in another context such a thing [is denoted] as something non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), [there is recognition].

It will not be taken up; nor indeed is the cultivation (bhāvanā) intended to be expressed merely as a mere imitation (of the model sacrifice), since its nature is colored by the meaning of the verbal root which has become non-substantial (asattvabhūta). In that case, since it is understood that the very same object (karman) is presented by one word and enjoined as a fruit by another, let it be a separate, optional action (kāmyakarman). This is as in the cases such as: "The Prāyaṇīya day belongs to the Atirātra sacrifice," "In the Caturaha there are the Āpivāḥ, the Ṣaḍahas, and the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha," and as in the Varuṇapraghāsas, where it is said, "They go to the Avabhṛtha bath."

But when it is determined that the injunctive character—connected with factors such as being the fruit of another context—is joined with the originative injunction and, being irresistible, is separated from it by a more powerful originative injunction that causes its abandonment, then even in such cases a distinction [between actions] is understood. However, because they are synonyms, "only the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is divided, not the meaning of the verbal root, since the word *yajati* is not heard [there]. For it is by means of the name (*nāman*) that that [action] is taken up, as in the case of what is expressed by the words *āsana* and *upāyi*."
For when one hears a name that is distinct [from others], there arises a difference in its meaning (Mīmāṃsākośa 135). However,

in the case of a *sattra* sacrifice, because the previously mentioned sacrifice is recognized through the mere presentation of its name upon hearing it, there is no difference in the name of that which is denoted by it.
Therefore, it was rightly stated by the author of the Sūtras: "In another context, there is a difference in purpose.

The Commentator [should be understood] as showing that the time characterized by the phrase "having heard the Upasandhi" is itself of an imperceptible nature, serving as the cause for the distinction.

Furthermore, the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "Now, it might be said that the *upasads* are also enjoined" is to be supported as an *abhyupetyavāda* (an argument conceded for the sake of argument), just as in the *Abhyāsa-adhikaraṇa*. Just as in the *Abhyāsa-adhikaraṇa* Bhāṣya (p. 472)—which states, "And that which is performed by means of the connection with the *samits*"—the point was established by conceding the argument on the grounds that, because words such as *samit* do not denote a deity, there is no distinction among the substances (*dravya*) even when there is a distinction among the qualities (*guṇa*). It is to be supported in that same manner as an *abhyupetyavāda* by others.

The purpose (*prayojana*)—according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—is that in the well-known *Agnihotra*, there is an option regarding the month as an alternative to the lifelong period and other times, and there is the performance of the *Agnihotra* within the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana*.
According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, both of these are absent, and so forth.
In the Sūtra, the word "purpose" (*prayojana*) refers to the state of being maintained (*dhāryatva*).

Vi—It has been stated that because the injunction "He offers the Agnihotra for a month" possesses the capacity to enjoin, it cannot be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *upāṃśuyāja* offering; thus, by the principle of a distinct context (*prakaraṇāntara-nyāya*)—due to the difference in the non-enjoinable intermediate time—it is declared to be an injunction of a separate ritual action.
Su. Pṛ. 753. However, some maintain that the distinction [of the *āgneya* substance] is established by the principle of a distinct context (*prakaraṇāntara-nyāya*).

For instance, if the quality itself were the differentiator even when it is not to be adopted because it does not enter [into the primary action], then in the case of "māsaṃ juhoti" (he offers for a month) as well, that very [quality] would suffice as the differentiator; thus, there would be no need for a separate context (*prakaraṇāntara*).
Therefore, it must be accepted that, with respect to that which is delimited by non-adoptability, the separate context alone is the differentiator.

And even so, they say: "Since there is no proximity (*asaṃnidhi*), how can it have the capacity to differentiate? For at the time when the differentiation is being expressed, there arises the contingency of the non-proximity of the presentation of the action that serves as its counter-correlate; this is equal here as well, just as in the case of the *māsāgnihotra*. To this we reply: In the section on the *gavāmayana*, regarding the statement "The *prāyaṇīya* day occurs," the status of it being a separate action follows precisely from the absence of any determining factor (*vini-gamanāviraha*). *Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Bhāṣya*, 2.3.13, p. 166.

The statement regarding "difference" (*bhedokti*) according to the logic of other treatises by the author of the *Bhāṣya* is to be explained as being based merely on proximity (*asaṃnidhi*), characterized by the absence of a quality to be acquired that has not yet been obtained. [Śābara-bhāṣya on] 2.3.12, p. 83. In the section on defects, regarding the injunction "one should touch the calf" (*vatsam ālabheta*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) establishes that this touching is a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) by virtue of its connection with a quality to be acquired for the purpose of purification, according to the logic of "another context" (*prakaraṇāntara*).

[Śābara-bhāṣya on] 2.3.6.17. Furthermore, there is no suspicion of it being a distinct ritual act by virtue of "another context" in the case of [the text]: "He who, having not sacrificed with this [Agniṣṭoma], performs the Aśvamedha... [Śābara-bhāṣya on 2.3.6.17].
By the explanatory passage (arthavāda) beginning with "eṣa vāva," other sacrifices such as the Udbhid and others are brought into proximity.

Regarding the Bhaṭṭa school's position (5.3.14): one should not argue that even in the final view (siddhānta), because of the principle of a different context (prakaraṇāntara), there is no repetition of the six-day period (ṣaḍaha) due to the sacrifice being a distinct rite (karmāntara) requiring the well-known six [days], but rather that—as in the case of other distinct rites—there is only a repetition of the Viṣuvat day within those [six].
This is because, in cases of this kind, there is no difference in the nature of the ritual act (karman).

Soma. 8|13: Now, in passages such as "Now this is the Jyotis," since it is possible for the word *atha* to refer to what is about to be mentioned, the non-proximity (*asaṃnidhi*)—acting in conjunction with a result that is an unenjoined quality (*anupādeyaguṇa*)—is capable of effecting a distinction through the principle of "another context" (*prakaraṇāntara*). Kau. 2|8|8|21, p. 248. However, in the present case (the sentence concerning the Dākṣāyaṇayajña), because there is no interruption of the previous cognition and because the "context" (*prakaraṇa*) which serves as the indicator is present, there is no distinction by way of "another context."

Page 39, 2|3|18: Since the fruit (phala) is not something to be undertaken as an object of action (*anupādeyatvena*), it is impossible to undertake the ritual act (*karman*) with reference to that fruit; because the injunction intended for the sake of the fruit must take up the ritual act by way of the fruit; and because, by the principle of "separation of context" (*prakaraṇāntara*), it concerns the essential nature of the ritual act itself.

*Sūtra-bhāṣya*, page 820: Where there is such an application within one Veda, and in another Veda there is a connection with a verb (*ākhyāta-sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—even in cases such as "In spring, the Jyotiṣṭoma [is performed]" which involve the determination of time and place—it should be understood that because these are injunctions of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), the accent is based precisely upon that.

Because verbal co-referentiality (*ākhyāta-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [with the previous action] exists, the principle of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara-nyāya*) would result in the action being a different ritual (*karmāntaratva*).

However, by the word "they go" (*yanti*)—as in the passage from the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, "They go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with the scrapings of the offering to Varuṇa and with the husks"—a different ritual is enjoined by means of the principle of a different context. (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 3.3.10, p. 326).

Śābarabhāṣya 7.3.4: In proximity to the *savanīya* [offering], by the scriptural statement, "Having taken the *āśvina* cup and having gone out, he winds the rope around the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," a second winding of the sacrificial post is enjoined for the sake of the *savanīya* sacrifice—either as a distinct context (*prakaraṇāntara*) or through repetition (*abhyāsa*)—and this serves to produce the status of the post as a *yājñika-yūpa* (a post belonging to the sacrifice).

According to the *Bhāṭṭa* school (Bhāṭṭa 4.4.9), because the *āghāra* and *paryagni-karaṇa* lack the status of being enjoined as originating factors (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), they cannot be considered stronger [than the *āghāra*]. Furthermore, regarding the injunction "He offers the oblation in the evening and in the morning," since it mentions time—which is not a subordinate factor (*anupādeya*)—it is understood from the context of a different section (*prakaraṇāntara*) that this is an injunction for a distinct ritual action (*karma-vidhi*). (Su. p. 431). In the *Soma* sacrifice, there is a vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) during the night of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Since the vigil of initiation serves the purpose of the heart [as a preparatory rite], it is impossible for it to be a case of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Even if that [vigil] were for the sake of the day, there is no evidence to suggest that two heterogeneous vigils produce a single unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) through the principle of a different section (*prakaraṇāntara*).

Bhāṭṭa 12.1.8: "He cuts off from the heart first," and so forth—by virtue of being in a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), this independent act of cutting (*avadāna*) is enjoined with reference to the heart and other parts (this is the prima facie view). Kau. 2.2.16, p. 208: Regarding the statement, "With this *udavasānīyā* sacrifice, which is equal to the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*), one performs the *agnihotra*," this injunction, by virtue of being in a different context, either prescribes a separate ritual as subordinate to the Soma sacrifice or as a distinct rite consisting of the *udavasānīyā* itself (this is the prima facie view).
Bhāṭṭa 6.1.3: Nor can it be argued that, because of the difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*), there is no possibility here of an injunction regarding time for other sacrifices.

This is because, in the passage "This indeed is the first of sacrifices" (*eṣa vāva prathamo yajño yajñānām*), the word "of sacrifices" (*yajñānām*) brings other sacrifices to mind as well; thus, there is an absence of a difference in context characterized by the non-recurrence [of those other sacrifices].
Soma 5.3.14: "He worships with the *pṛṣṭha* hymns."

One might object: "Let this simply be an injunction for the well-known act denoted by the word 'pṛṣṭha'; why resort to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) to establish an injunction for a thousand rites? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that, because of the difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*), according to the principle of "difference of context" (*prakaraṇāntaranyāya*), this is an injunction for a distinct rite (*karmāntaravidhi*), citing a counter-example to the principle of difference of context.

(Regarding this prima facie view) | 7|3|14. The Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice is heard of in the context of the Vājapeya; therein, because it occurs in a different context, it is enjoined as a distinct ritual act.
— Kalpataru.
1|2|11 Vas. p. 68. The nature of *prakaraṇāntara* (difference of context).

Even though there is a commonality regarding the goal (*upeya*) [shared with the *abhyāsa* section], there is no confusion regarding the nature of the principle of *prakaraṇāntara* [which differs from the nature of the principle of the *abhyāsa-adhikaraṇa*].

For in the case of *abhyāsa* (repetition), the operation consists solely in establishing the status of being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) regarding the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), by accepting its status as something to be adopted (*upādeyatā*) through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).
In other contexts, however, the function [of the injunctive suffix] is not the induction of prescriptivity through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*),
because that is impossible given that even time and so forth are accepted as being prescriptive by way of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).

Rather, even when there is another thing to be prescribed, the induction of prescriptivity applies to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as well, for the sake of attaining co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the object to be acquired (*upādeya*) which has been induced [by the suffix].

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the Udayanīya is not a separate ritual action, because there is no "separation of context" (*prakaraṇāntara*) due to the presence of proximity (*saṃnidhi*). This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Bhāṭṭa 11.2.15: Even in the absence of a distinct context (*prakara�ṇāntara*), he says [the following] to demonstrate that the status of being "non-enjoinable" (*anupādeyatva*) entails the character of not being an injunction for a ritual action (*akarmavidhitva*).

Since the injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) refers to the occasion (*nimitta*), it is logically established that it does not constitute a qualification (*avacchedakatva*) that must be adopted; thus, because the connection with non-adoptable qualities (*anupādeyaguṇa*) is investigated for its differentiating or non-differentiating character, there is no application of the principle of a separate context (*prakaraṇāntara-nyāya*) regarding the reversal of the ritual action (*karma*). Nevertheless, even though the principle of a separate context is not applicable here, the investigation into the difference caused by non-adoptability is logically consistent, as it arises immediately after [the discussion of] non-adoptability and remains present in the mind. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 969). In the absence of a name (*saṃjñā*), since there is no interruption of the cognition of the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛtabuddhi*), the subject matter does not fall within the scope of the principle of a separate context, and therefore differentiation (*bhedakatva*) is not possible.

Su. Pṛ. 820: Since the Agnihotra is presented here as something to be excluded (*paryudasanīya*), and because the principle of a separate context (*prakaraṇāntaranyāya*) is inapplicable, it is logical that this is a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*). Consequently, when the performance of that very same rite would otherwise follow after the *avabhṛtha* bath, establishing a different time-limit (*avadhi*) results in parsimony (*lāghava*). Bhaṭṭa 10.8.7: Since only an injunction of an "unacceptable" (*anupādeya*) element serves as the basis for the application of the principle of a separate context, in the present case (such as "one should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," or "one should offer the *iṣṭi*"), its absence means there is no differentiation [of the ritual]. (This refers to the prima facie view).
The maxim of the counter-example regarding a different context (*prakaraṇāntarapratyudāharaṇanyāya*):
Non-essential factors such as place (*deśa*) and so forth, when present in the proximity of a ritual action, do not cause a distinction between ritual actions.
The non-injunction [of the *aveṣṭi*] would result in an improper fruit.
But because of its proximity, the repetition is for the sake of a specific fruit due to the distinction [of the context].
Commentary: There is the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice, beginning with the text: "There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni," and so forth.
Regarding that, there is a doubt: "Should one cause this [rite] to be performed by means of the Ācāryaka?

In that regard, there is a doubt: is it indeed a different ritual from the Aveṣṭi, or is it the Aveṣṭi itself? What is the prima facie view? It is a different ritual, according to the stated reasoning.
This being the case, we reply:
the repetition of the *aveṣṭi* in proximity is for the sake of a specific result; it is not a separate ritual action.
Why? Because there is no distinction.
The word "by this" (etayā) is not able to denote another sacrifice distinct from the *aveṣṭi*;
rather, this word is a reference back to what is proximate.
Therefore, it is the *aveṣṭi* itself that is enjoined for one who desires other [results].

What is the purpose? Whether the *aveṣṭi* consists of the oblations beginning with the *āgneya*, or whether it is a separate ritual (*karmāntara*) involving different oblations—this [discussion] is commenced for the sake of providing a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for all [the cases] where [the result] is not to be connected [to the original context]. The mention of the "result" (*phala*) is merely illustrative.

However, all factors such as place (*deśa*) and so forth must also be cited as examples: "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices on level ground"; "One should sacrifice with the Full Moon sacrifice on the full moon day"; "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices as long as one lives"; "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices"; and "From the remnant, he sacrifices to Sviṣṭakṛt. In every case, because [the action] is enjoined with respect to place and so forth by means of the preceding section, the status of being a distinct ritual act (*karmāntaratva*) is initially reached.

And it is said: "Since there is no injunction for that which has already been enjoined, it would follow that this is a mere restatement (anuvāda). That which is being restated is the subject (uddeśya), yet here the possibility of a subject does not exist;
for those actions which are being restated must necessarily be subjects."
Furthermore, the occurrence of things to be enjoined through the means of enjoining them is not possible.

For, if one were to assume that actions being enjoined by means of the injunction of place and so forth are merely restatements of their own nature, it would be improper due to the fault of simultaneous injunction and restatement. Therefore, these are distinct actions.
This being the position reached, it is replied:

"For in the case of *mitra*, there is similarity with an injunction regarding both origin (*utpatti*) and application (*viniyoga*). When a way [of interpretation] exists, those two would attain equality."
For by that very act of comprehension, both the origination and the application are effected.

However, when another means of knowledge is available, it is untenable for the applicatory injunction to serve as the originative injunction; thus, one understands merely the capacity for application regarding those [acts] which have already been originated and are present through some other means.
"Furthermore, being the object of a general enunciation (*uddeśya*) is not the cause for being a restatement (*anuvāda*);
nor does being obtained (*prāpya*) enter into the state of being that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), even when there is no formal prescription (*upādāna*)."

Although place and so forth are indicated because they are by nature not things to be adopted (*anupādeya-svabhāva*), nevertheless, since they have not been previously established, it is understood that they alone possess the character of being enjoined (*vidheya*).
Furthermore, regarding the action (*karman*) being adopted, because such an action is presented by another [means], it has the character of a restatement (*anuvāda*).

However, in the case of non-proximity (*asannidhāna*), because there is no presentation [by another means], it is an injunction (*vidhi*); thus, there is no contradiction, for it is not [an injunction] merely from the act of adoption itself.

This very thing is that; and it is expressed by the word "non-distinction" (avibhāga) precisely because it is the opposite [of distinction]. However, it is understood specifically through this word and its corresponding cognition.
Regarding the purpose, they raise this objection:

since these [offerings] are indeed characterized by that same desire even in another ritual action, and because of the perception of similarity, they are merely the *āgneya* and other oblations; thus, how can it be a sacrifice involving different oblations?
But that is untenable.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, since it is possible for this word to have its primary meaning as a direct denotation (*mukhyatva*), a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on similarity is untenable.
Therefore, it is quite clear that [the rite] is a different ritual (*karmāntara*) involving a different oblation (*anyahaviṣka*); thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya.
In this way, the six grounds for differentiation (*bhedakāraṇa*), including the *avadāna* (cutting-off), have been explained.

However, regarding a different substance (*dravyāntara*), the causes for differentiation—namely, a different word (*śabdāntara*), a different name (*saṃjñā*), a quality (*guṇa*), and a result (*phala*)—have been cited as applying only to that which is mobile [i.e., an action].

This is because repetition (*punaḥśruti*) and number (*saṃkhyā*) are included within "different word," and because "separation of context" (*prakaraṇāntara*) consists in the grasping of the fourfold set of results.
That, however, appears to be incorrect.
For the act of sacrificing (*yajati*), even when repeated five times, does not become a different word.
Nor is it possible for seventeen words *prājāpatya* to be uttered simultaneously in a single ritual context (*tantra*), because of the recognition of the same word-form.
Thus it has been said: "as in the case of the sun" and "due to the absence of number."
And he will state the unity of such things in the passage: “Or rather, because there is no difference, on account of the word ‘form,’ or because of the division.

Therefore, while there is indeed a single entity, it is through a different context that distinction is manifested. The difference in words arises from a difference in the intended meaning (*bhāvya*).

Furthermore, it has been stated that even if the difference between distinct contexts (*prakaraṇāntara*) is mentioned, it is not observed to be a differentiator in the absence of [distinct] results and so forth—as seen in such passages as “But because there is no division in proximity” (*sannidhau tvavibhāgāt*) and “The repeated mention of qualities in their proximity” (*tatsannidher guṇānāṃ punaḥśrutiḥ*).
Therefore, since the cognition of the favoring of a result is based on recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), it is disregarded even though a distinct context itself serves as a cause for differentiation.
Moreover, the result has not been examined as being included within the distinct context.

Although it was stated that the statement, "Or [the action is] one, because there is no difference in conjunction, form, injunction, or name" (*ekaṃ vā saṃyogarūpacodanākhyāviśeṣāt*), serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the fact that the reason for unity is seen to be the opposite [of the reason for difference]—the analysis of which is: "that which is the reason for unity and that which is its opposite"—nevertheless, this was not considered in the context of the present section because [the other reasons for difference] are impossible therein.

Therefore, it is now asserted that there are only the six reasons for difference as previously described; furthermore, regarding the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the distinctions between "name" (*saṃjñā*) and "different word" (*śabdāntara*), as well as between "quality" (*guṇa*) and "number" (*saṃkhyā*), ought to have been stated but were not, and thus they are being explained here.
“Because it does not denote its own form, a name is distinct from other words;
and because it inheres in a plurality [of substrata], number is distinct from other qualities.”

For *saṃjñā* (name/designation), being of the nature of a substance, differs from the five [categories] denoting action merely by way of exclusion (*viccheda*). Number (*saṃkhyā*) also, when co-arising with multiple things simultaneously, differs from other qualities (*guṇa*) due to its prior existence.
As for *śā* [the suffix]: "In this case as well, because of the mention of location (*deśa*) and so forth, there is an action directed toward that."
It would be something to be accepted, and likewise something to be enjoined; therefore, it is distinct [from that].

To this we reply: "In the case of proximity, the non-differentiation of the ritual action is understood through recognition; therefore, the repeated mention of that very same action is for the sake of its fruit and so forth. Although the ritual action must indeed be enjoined, nevertheless, it is not divided."
For there is no difference [in the result] when there is a difference in the procedure for production; and that difference does not exist here for us.

This section is presented as a counter-example to the previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) because it concerns the presence of place, time, indicative mark (*nimitta*), fruit, and preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*). This constitutes the "internal connection" (*antarasaṃgati*) by way of being a counter-example.

As for the purpose: in the case of the sentences concerning the *Paurṇamāsī* and other sacrifices, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is the injunction of distinct rituals (*karmāntara*), resulting in an increase in the number of rituals; however, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is no such increase.

If the sentence *etayā* were to enjoin a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), then because the ritual properties of the Soma sacrifice would apply to that action by the rule *avyaktāsu tu somasya*, a sacrifice with Soma as the oblation would have to be performed by one desiring food—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, it is clear from the *Vārttika* that [the sacrifices] have Agni and others as their oblations.
In the Sūtra, the meaning is "because of the division" (*vibhāgāt*) and "because of the reversal" (*viparivṛtteḥ*).
[The Sūtra states: *yajeta same paurṇamāsyāṃ yāvajjīvaṃ tathaitayā*.
In passages such as "one desiring food," is there a difference in the ritual action, or is it merely a subordinate quality (guṇa)?
Because the injunction and the material to be employed are one and the same, the [distinction of] place and so forth is untenable;
however, in the case of an injunction regarding the ritual act (*karman*), there must necessarily be a repetition of the scriptural statement due to their difference.
Since the connection with location and so forth is not established, there is a distinction between those two;
however, because the person and the word are all-pervading, that [distinction] is abandoned through redundancy.
Bhaṭṭa: Here are counter-examples for all five non-subordinate factors (*anupādeya*).

Regarding the four [factors] in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*: “One should sacrifice with the *paurṇamāsī* on the full moon day,” and “One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* on level ground.
Regarding the refinement of the form of the remnant (*śeṣa*), having established the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering: “One sacrifices the *sviṣṭakṛt* from the remnant.”

In all these cases, because [the action] is already present and because its occurrence within its own sphere is understood as being subject to an injunction, what is admitted for the purpose of defining the injunction is merely the performance of the action as qualified by time and place; however, the origin of the action (*karmotpatti*) is not enjoined. But where even the performance is already established—as in the case of "he who [performs] with an *iṣṭi*," etc.—there an injunction of mere time and so forth is possible by way of restating the already established performance.
Even though place and time can be things to be adopted (*upādeya*), there is an injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) insofar as they are subordinate members of the sacrifice.

indeed, there must be modification (*ūha*), which is to say, alteration.
Regarding that, the reason why an adaptation (*ūha*) must be made in this matter has been stated [in the sūtra]: "And because the meaning is not something to be produced" (1.3.11).
The *codaka* (the extended injunction) conforms to the meaning of the mantra, not to the syllables of the mantra;
for those [syllables] are subordinate to the meaning, and do not have their own form as the primary element.

Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that modification (ūha) must be performed. Regarding the indicative mark (liṅga) cited by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin)— namely, the injunction "Recite for Agni the omentum and fat of the goat"— which was offered as evidence that there is no modification, that [mark] refers to the desire for a mantra, because it is the desire for that collection of words, which serves the purpose of being a mantra, [to be modified].
Otherwise, that which has been modified would not possess the status of a mantra; consequently, the accomplishment of the modification by means of it would not occur.
Or rather, there is a restrictive rule because both parts share [the same nature].

In the absence of both [the previous reasons], another indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been stated by the proponent: "O Vāyu, this is for you; O Vāyu, these two are for you; O Vāyus, these are for you. This restriction is established;
otherwise, the touching of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) would be shared by both [mantras], and there would be a connection with all mantras without restriction.
Therefore, a specific mantra is restricted in each case according to whether "there is one post, two, or many."
Consequently, that too is not an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the absence of modification (*ūha*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that modification must be performed in the case of the *nirvāpa* mantra and others within the modified ritual (*vikṛti*).

In the section [of the *Tantravārttika*] beginning with "Or rather, in the archetype, because of being stated twice" (*prakṛtau vā dviruktatvāt*; there is also a reading *adviruktatvāt*; 3.6.12), two reasons for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) were stated: the occurrence of the fault of being stated twice and the discrepancy in time.

However, because these two reasons are mutually inconsistent, there is indeed the contingency of being stated twice through both direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*), due to the lack of dependence on the archetypal rule regarding the moment [of action], as well as the discrepancy in the time of attainment; this is shown in the counter-example stated by the author of the *Vārttika* at the very end of that section: "Prajāpati is seventeenfold; he was pierced in another way. Thus, even in that case, the fault of being stated twice remains.

Likewise, when it is stated that the *phalacamas* shares the same ritual rules (*sāmānavidhya*) as the *soma*, since its status as a modification (*vikṛti*) is established for both parties, a double-statement (*dvirukta*) is impossible. Furthermore, because a permanent rule (*nityavidhi*) operates first, whereas an occasional rule (*naimittika*)—like an occasional sacrifice (*iṣṭi*)—operates later, there is indeed a disparity in the time of their application. Therefore, in the section concerning the sharing of ritual rules with the properties of *soma* (3.6.13–16), it is said: "Moreover, the occasional [rule], because of its inequality, would not have the same ritual rules. Thus, the occasional [rule]...

"The fruit-cup (phalacamasa) will not adopt the properties of Soma; in that case, the properties, being common [to both], would be stated twice"—by this passage, the objection raised by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) regarding the contingency of redundancy (*dviruktatā*) in the case of equal injunction (*sāmānavidhya*) is indeed to be disregarded.

Now, one might ask: since the contingency of redundancy exists in the case of "Prajāpati is seventeenfold," and thus equal injunction is impossible, how can the author of the *Vārttika* state that as a counter-example?
It is said in reply:

The avoidance of futility in this case—just as in the case of *tadarthaśāstra* and so forth—should be effected by means of the purpose of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section [JS 1.2.40] beginning with "Or rather, in the archetype, because of the double-stating" (*prakṛtau vā dviruktatvāt*). In the case of the *parṇatā* (leaf-nature) and other such qualities as well, the same method of explanation is easily stated.
And here, the primary reason for the conclusion known to the experts of the Siddhānta is precisely the difference in the time of application (*prāptikālavaiṣamya*).
The reason for this is stated precisely because redundancy (*dviruktatā*) is not observed;

otherwise, there would indeed be doubt as to whether the redundancy resulting from the acceptance of the extended application (*atideśa*) must be avoided by making it synonymous with the original injunction, or whether it serves the purpose of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) even for things like the *parṇatā* (being made of *parṇa*-leaves) which are already obtained through extension.
Even if [the rite] were to be obtained through specific scriptural injunctions (*śruti-viśeṣa*), the doubt that it would be purposeless (*anarthakya*) would remain difficult to resolve.

For in that case, it has been accepted hundreds of times that even when a matter is already established by means of other authorities—such as extended application (*atideśa*) or mantras—it may be enjoined again for a specific purpose, as seen in passages such as *agre kṣayadvīreṇa* and so forth.

Furthermore, in the *Gavām Ayana* sacrifice, during the first two days, the *aindravāyava* draught is obtained because it is a constituent part (*bhāga-dharma*) of the injunction regarding the *aindravāyava* draught.
Likewise, there is the sublation by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of a mantra that would otherwise be obtained through an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).

Similarly, there is the sublation of the attainment of heaven as the purpose [of a rite] in the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices—which is already established by the principle of universal desirability (*sārvakāmya*).
In this way, there is the sublation of that which is already attained, even though it is being implied by an injunction because its purpose has already been stated in scripture.
The same applies here as well.

Therefore, the conclusion is that it is precisely the disparity in the time of attainment that must be relied upon to dispel doubt, as stated in the rule "or in the archetype, because of the lack of double mention.
Now, since the purpose of this section is not yet firmly established, it is explained as follows:

Although it has been stated elsewhere that "What is the purpose [of this rule]? If there is equal injunction (*sāmānavidhya*), then there is the application of those desiring specific qualities (*guṇakāma*)," nevertheless, that applies only to actions such as piling the altar (*cayana*), because in those cases the desire for qualities based on them is possible.
However, since a genus such as being made of *parṇa*-wood is not an action, a desire for qualities based upon it is not possible.
Therefore, another purpose must be stated.

Regarding this, Bhavadeva maintains: "In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since there is no distinction in the fact that the state of being made of *parṇa* wood and so forth is taught [in both cases], there is equality of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) when those are omitted in the archetype (*prakṛti*). In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, there is a distinction in expiation when there is an omission of what is taught versus what is extended by injunction (*atideśa*).
To this we reply: nowhere is a distinction in expiation seen to be prescribed based on a difference between what is taught and what is extended.
Therefore, the purpose must be stated. That is now explained:

in the first quarter of the first chapter (*vākya-pāda*), under the rule "The mantras are recited loudly" (*uccairmantrāḥ kriyante*) and so forth, as well as under the rule concerning occasional expiatory rites (*nemittika-prāyaścitta*) such as "If [the sacrificer] suffers a mishap from the *ṛc*, he should offer an oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire with the words 'bhūḥ svāhā'," the status of these as properties of the Veda (*vedadharma*) has been declared.

Then, in the second section (*adhikaraṇa*), regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that both [the high-pitchedness and the expiation] are based on the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that both are based on the applicatory injunction (*viniyoga-vidhi*); namely, that where the *Ṛgveda* and so forth are employed in accordance with an injunction, there the high-pitchedness and other qualities apply, and the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) pertains to the failure of that very [application].

Consequently, from the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice of the Yajurveda, its subsidiaries—including the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites—along with their constituent parts, are extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to its modification (*vikṛti*), namely the *śyena* sacrifice of the Sāmaveda. Among those [subsidiaries], there is the *juhū* ladle; regarding that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since it is enjoined and applied by a Yajurvedic injunction, when there is no difference [in its nature], a Yajurvedic expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed for that Yajurvedic subsidiary. However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), although that [ladle] was enjoined and applied by a Yajurvedic injunction in the archetype (*prakṛti*), in the case of the *śyena*, because it is applied by an extension from the Sāmaveda, a Sāmavedic expiation is to be performed for that Sāmavedic subsidiary.
Nor is there a lack of mantra-status for the *ūha* (modifications) and so forth, nor is there a lack of Vedic status for the extended application (*atideśa*).
For this very point—that the *ūha*-based pronouncements lack the status of mantra—was stated right here [in Sūtra 2.1.1].

The *avadāna* and other such [narrative] sections are like the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice; the *phala-pada* (words denoting results) in the *viśvajit* and other sacrifices are like [the results in] the *saurya* and other rites; and even the *ūha* (modification) and so forth—which consist of *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard)—are said to be "portions of the Veda" according to the rule: "Because [they are] a part of the assumption [of the text], they are [therefore] a portion of the Veda" (*Jaiminisūtra* 1.4.25). Furthermore, since it is stated that even in the *Āgama* (Smṛti), there is a twofold division into *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa*, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is introduced as a digression (*prasaṅga*) to state that this [twofold division] belongs only to the *Pratyak-Veda* (direct Veda) and not to the *Kalpa* (ritual manuals).
(Bālakrīḍā, pp. 104–106).

It has been stated that one should carry the sacrificial vessels (yajñapātra) for as long as one lives. Regarding the inquiry as to whether these should be carried starting from the commencement of the Full Moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī), or starting from the laying of the fires (anyādheya), the author states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):
"Starting from the Full Moon sacrifice, the sacrificial vessels should be carried even if one were to die."

Because they serve as the primary purpose (*prakṛtyartha*) and because they are stated without reference to a specific context (*anārabhyoktatva*), these [rites] belong to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Since it is said, "Of these, [the offering] on the full moon day," therefore, they should be maintained for the full moon sacrifice.

Or rather, one should maintain those [fires] from the time of the *agnyādheya* (the establishment of the sacred fires), because there is no prohibition; for death is not a fixed occasion [for cessation].
It is not that the maintenance [of the fires] begins only with the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*); rather, one should maintain them starting from the *agnyādheya*.

This being so, since death is an indefinite occurrence and lacks a fixed time, even if death should happen before the full moon, there is no prohibition—because there is no contradiction in the absence of the loss of the funeral rites (*śarīrasaṃskāra*).

Although the vessels are produced at the Full Moon sacrifice, nevertheless, by virtue of the extended application (codaka), those belonging to the archetype— namely, the base and the suffix— are obtained for the Pavamāna offerings in the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya).
Therefore, the established conclusion is that the carrying of the sacrificial vessels begins precisely with the *agnyādheya* (the establishment of the sacred fires).
This is an instance of a prohibition regarding an auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) action belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*), such as: "One should not employ [these vessels] at the first sacrifice."

The base and the suffix [together express the meaning].
(Pāṇini 1.4.13) The justification for the rule "the base and the suffix together express [the meaning]" is as follows:

On page 566, it is stated that "the base and the suffix together express [the meaning], and between them, the meaning of the suffix is primary. By this traditional authority (*smṛti*), the primacy of the meaning of the suffix as determined by the base is established as being common to all meanings of verbal suffixes (*su*).

*Rahasya*, p. 38: According to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating, "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together, but of these two, the suffix [expresses it] primarily," the meaning of the suffix is primary. Therefore, one should not ask how the meaning of the suffix—which is logically established—can possess the status of a qualifier (*viśeṣatva*). (Note: The reading *viśeṣatvāt* is adopted.)

This is because the primacy of this [action]—as delimited by the word *bhāva* (action)—is understood from the traditional rule of the *Nirukta*, "The verb has action as its primary meaning"; and because its being denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is understood from the grammatical tradition, "The mere, pure meaning of the root is called *bhāva*.

Furthermore, the general rule regarding the primacy of the meaning of the suffix is explained by the phrase "in the case of *suv*-suffixes, etc.," since that general rule is set aside by a specific traditional rule.

In reality, this traditional rule (*smṛti*) regarding the predominance of the meaning of the suffix does not regulate predominance by way of delimiting [it] to that which is the meaning of the suffix; for although gender, number, and so forth are meanings of the suffix, they are not admitted to be predominant.

Nor is it intended to establish a rule that whatever is predominant must necessarily be the meaning of the suffix; for according to the traditional rule "noun-stems (*nāman*) have substance (*sattva*) as their primary meaning," the referent of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), though predominant, is not the meaning of the suffix with respect to gender, number, and the like.

However, in cases where the predominance of the meaning of the suffix (such as instrumentality) over the meaning of the nominal stem is already established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this traditional rule (*smṛti*) merely restates that fact.
Thus, even if the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), there is no obstacle or contradiction to its being a qualifier.

Kau. 2|2|16, p. 96: The meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) conveys itself as a subordinate element within the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), which takes the form of a *kāraka* (grammatical participant). Furthermore, this general rule is in accordance with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the category of *kāraka* and so forth, but not regarding number (*saṃkhyā*) and the like; otherwise, it would be untenable for the meaning of the nominal stem to be identical with the property of existence (*sattva*).

2|1|2|15, p. 30: "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together; of these two, the meaning of the suffix is primary"—this is the teaching of the Teachers regarding the primacy of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha-prādhānyopadeśa*).

Su., p. 1417: "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together; of these two, the meaning of the suffix is primary"—this is the traditional rule (*smṛti*) regarding the primacy of the meaning of the suffix.

(If this is argued, it is replied: Since *bhāvanā* is established by its very nature as something distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the arguments for its primacy and its being the meaning of the suffix are difficult to refute. Thus, on page 547: "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together; of these two, the meaning of the suffix is predominant"—this principle applies even to the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), as there is no exception to it regarding its own meaning.

This is because it is established by those who know the logic [of grammar] that "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together, and between these two, the meaning of the suffix is predominant."

"That which [the grammarians] maintain—that both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) express the action (*saṃhṛti*) primarily..."
For when it is expressed by a negative particle alone, its predominance is stated by that [particle].

There exists a certain power residing in the word as a whole, distinct from the powers of its individual parts,

Thus, since even the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of meanings as already connected) has been refuted with respect to both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), there arises the doubt: "Does the suffix express its own meaning through connection? (Su. pṛ. 707–708).

Since it has been stated that "the base and the suffix express [their meanings] together, and of these two, the suffix is predominant," the suffix, which denotes the primary meaning, possesses predominance.

In that case, within the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), namely the Kṛttikādīṣṭi, the Nāriṣṭha-homa rite would be an addition—that by which a refinement is performed, specifically one characterized by a particular unseen merit (adṛṣṭaviśeṣa).
The subsidiary offerings (upahomas) are combined with the nāriṣṭha offerings because of their connection with the indicative marks of the archetype;
it is like the archetype.
This is the meaning.

Why? Because of the absence of connection with the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*), that is, because there is no connection with the effect (*kārya*) that serves as the mark of the archetype.

And thus, since there is no connection with the word "cooking" (*apāka*) in the archetypal effects, the ritual action characterized by the *upahoma* and so forth would be a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) that is additional to the archetypal; however, it is not [merely] what is expressed [by the words]. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Now, in the second interpretation (*varṇaka*), this sūtra is to be explained as a *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra.
The meaning of the words of the sūtra remains the same; the only difference is that the examples and the terminology are distinct.
Thus, the commentary states: "This is handed down in the tradition: 'One practicing sorcery should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) to Soma and Rudra, made of black rice grains.'"

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the *kuśa* grass [required by the model sacrifice] cease to apply or not? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Since both are known through authoritative means—namely, the *codaka* (the rule of extension) which establishes the *kuśa* grass, and the specific injunction "the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara* reeds" which establishes the *śara*—there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of both.
This is the prima facie position.
Now begins the third section.
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "He commences the Māhendra-stotra with the sound of a chariot.
And in the archetype (prakṛti), it is heard: "With [the words] 'Turn hither,' he commences the stotra with two blades of darbha grass."

In this matter, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)—which is the very meaning of the words of the Sūtra—is that both [the sound and the chariot] are the subordinates of both [the mantra and the dharma]: the sound is the subordinate of the mantra, and the chariot is the subordinate of the two dharmas.
When there is a connection with a sign (*liṅga*) of an injunction (*codanā*), its modification is understood due to the proximity of the archetype (*prakṛti*).

If it is argued that, just as in the passage from the Śaramāreya, "The sacrificial grass consists of *śara* reeds," the *śara* reeds exclude the *kuśa* grass, so too the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) in the Nakṣatreṣṭis exclude the Nāriṣṭha offerings—then [the author] states the disparity between the two cases as a counter-example.

Regarding the connection with an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in an injunction (*codanā*): when there is a connection with an injunction that contains an unerring indicative mark—namely, the word *barhis* (sacrificial grass), which is the means for preparing the sacrificial ground—in the case of the injunction "the sacrificial grass is made of *śara* grass" (*aśaramayaṃ barhiḥ*), because of the proximity to the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the presence of a word that sets aside the original rule, it is understood that *śara* grass is a modification (*vikāra*) of the original *kuśa* grass used in that context.
However, in the case of the *upahoma* offerings, there is no such indicative mark in the injunction; therefore, the *upahoma* is not a modification of the original *nāriṣṭha-homa* and others.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Now begins the second section. This is a sūtra of the established conclusion (siddhānta). The meaning of the words is the same as in the first section.
However, there is a distinction: for in that case, there is a connection with the word *barhis*, which possesses the gender of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, there is the displacement of the original [grass] made of *kuśa*.
Now begins the third section.
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "One introduces the Mahendra-stotra with the sound of a chariot.
In the archetype (prakṛti), it is heard: "With the words 'Upāvartadhvam,' one introduces the stotra with two blades of darbha grass.

In this case, neither of these two [the chariot sound nor the darbha grass] is a displacer of both; rather, the sound associated with the chariot displaces the mantra and the two blades of darbha grass.

"A chariot is not empty of sound, nor is the sound [empty] of the chariot"—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Thus, in the second and third expositions (*varṇaka*), this Sūtra is indeed a Sūtra of the established conclusion; it is not, as in the first exposition, a means of establishing the conclusion by way of refuting an objection.

It is not merely stated as a matter of family tradition that the world has Brahman as its material cause (*upādāna*), but rather it is asserted for the sake of establishing non-duality (*advaita*) through the principle of the non-difference between the material cause and its modification.

Kalpataru, p. 87: It is understood that the fulfillment of the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) occurs precisely through the logic of the non-difference between the material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikārāvyatireka-nyāya*).

This principle should be understood as having the same meaning as the principle of the non-difference between the material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikārāvyatireka-nyāya*).

(The prima facie view).
Māṭṭa 4|2|1|1: "Oṃ. Regarding the primary procedure (*pradhānatantra*) for the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*), it must be sought in Śrauta texts.
