(Setting aside the consideration for the sake of argument: If the archetype (*prakṛti*) were to have a common ritual procedure (*samānatantra*) with the ectype (*vikṛti*), then because [the ectype] is occasional (*anitya*), the [archetypal] procedure would become purposeless. The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): When the archetype and the ectype share a common ritual procedure, should the archetypal procedure be performed, or the ectype’s? But surely there is no such thing as a common ritual procedure between an archetype and an ectype.
If it is argued that this is a case of "common tantra" (samānatantra), then it is considered inconceivable.

What is the conclusion? If the original form (*prakṛti*) is employed first, then it is the archetypal (*prākṛta*); if, however, the modified form (*vikṛti*) is employed first, then it is the modified (*vaikṛta*). But what is appropriate here? The original form (*prakṛti*).
Nature is eternal; modification is adventitious.
It arises when a desire or a cause has appeared.
Furthermore, those who dwell in the prior state are stronger because of their posteriority.

Therefore, the archetype (prakṛti) is employed first; its ritual procedure (tantra) must be performed because it is of prior timing. Thus, it follows that the archetypal ritual procedure must be performed.
This being the case, we reply:

a new (*apūrva*) modified (*vaikṛta*) ritual procedure (*tantra*) is employed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), provided that it shares the same ritual procedure; for if it were not shared, it would be optional due to its non-permanence.
A modified rite is non-permanent, as it occurs only when a specific desire arises or when a particular occasion (*nimitta*) presents itself.
An occasional modification (naimittikī vikṛtiḥ) does not sublate the desire to perform the obligatory rite (nityāṃ cikīrṣām),
for that [modification] occurs only when the obligatory rite exists;
therefore, it does not arise to the exclusion of the primary rites.

If it were not set aside, the performed injunction would be purposeless. For one whose desire to act has arisen, there is first the performance [of the preparatory rite]. Therefore, the action is performed prior to the main ritual act.
And for that which has its primary ritual procedure (*tantra*) first, the manner in which that primary procedure is to be performed has been explained in the section on the *pūrva*.

Therefore, the modified (*aikṛta*) procedure is employed in the archetype (*prakṛti*). As for the archetype, it is employed at every new-moon and full-moon festival throughout one's life; the modified rites (*vikṛti*) also fall upon the very same festivals, whether by specific desire (*kāma*) or by a particular occasion (*nimitta*).
In this regard, having performed the application of the archetype and its modifications simultaneously (*tantra*), it is considered as follows:

since a modification (*vikṛti*)—whether prompted by a specific desire (*kāma*) or by a particular occasion (*nimitta*)—enters [the ritual] by setting aside the general desire to perform the archetype (*autsargikī nitya-cikīrṣā*), the procedure (*tantra*) of the modification alone is extended to the archetype; such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). The subject matter here consists of those modifications whose time is fixed on the *parvan* days.

Just as an animal sacrifice possesses the nature of a *tantra* (a composite ritual) because its joints are interconnected, so too is it here; this is the connection [of the argument] that has arisen. The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: If a modification (*vikṛti*) were to have the same *tantra* as the archetype (*prakṛti*), then an unprecedented modification would result, because it would be impossible for the modification to be established without that [archetypal procedure], and any other specific modification would be rendered purposeless due to the measurement [of the ritual] being identical. However, because of the commencement of the archetype and the modification [as distinct acts]... [2696] (Note: The final portion of the text appears to be a fragmentary reference to a specific section number, "2696," likely from a commentary.)

Vi— "It must be either the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*), for the *tantra* [system] depends on the archetype; this [archetype] is taught as being obligatory (*nitya*). Do not say so, for it is like the desire-offerings (*kāma-yajña*). Bhaṭṭa—As for those ectypes which are either optional (*kāmya*) or obligatory (*nitya*), since the time of the full moon or new moon (*parvan*) is prescribed for them by the rule "he who [sacrifices] with an *iṣṭi*," they are performed immediately at the *parvan*. Having thus established their immediate timing, there is no prescription of the archetype; therefore, the inquiry into *tantra* and *prasaṅga* does not apply there.

Even in cases such as an *iṣṭi* sacrifice performed on account of the breaking of a thunderbolt (*pavīnāśa*) and so forth, where the occurrence of the cause takes place precisely in the midst of the performance of the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is no dispute regarding that very [archetype] being the locus of the application.

In such instances, there is generally no need for the *sāmadasya* (the principle of commonality) and so forth; even if it were to exist, since it would have no scope, it should be understood that the archetype itself is the locus of the extension (*prasaṅgitva*) regarding the *prayāja* offerings and other parts, whereas the modified form (*vikṛti*) is the locus in other respects.

However, where an event such as the burning of a house occurs in the midst of the performance (*prayoga*), there the primary rite (*prakṛti*) alone possesses the status of a *tantra* (the governing ritual framework); for that [event], such as the falling of a cause (*nimitta*) like the death of a member of the assembly (*sadasya*), falls outside the scope of the performance itself.

But where the occurrence of the cause for a particular sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) is fixed at the very commencement of the primary rite, even then, in reality, having performed the modified rite (*vikṛti*) as one whose time is immediate (*sadyaskāla*), one must diligently perform the *pragātha* of three verses.
VI. 1.2.6, Verse-number 1. (The classification of *pragātha* according to the *Ṛgveda-sarvānukramaṇī*, Section 11).
The *bṛhatī* and *satobṛhatī* [metres] belong to the *bārhata* class.
If the *kakup* comes first, it belongs to the *kākubha* class.
The Mahābṛhatī, the Mahāsatobṛhatī, and the Mahābhārata;
the Bṛhatī and the Viparītā, and the Viparītottarā.
Anuṣṭubh,
two Gāyatrīs, and an Anuṣṭubh—
thus there are five [verses], beginning with the Pragātha.
(Ke.
By means of the *pragātha*;
then, by means of the *bṛhatī* and *paṅkti* meters of the two following [verses], and then by means of the *pramaya*.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the singing of the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [Sāmans] is performed upon verses composed in the *Kakubha* meter (6.2.25–28).

Although it is understood from the context that these belong to the *Aindra-pragātha* and from the fact that they occur in the Jyotiṣṭoma, when there is a requirement for a specific means of application (*dvāra*), [they are connected] with that which is called the *Pṛṣṭha*.
That [connection] is understood through the sequence of the door of praise (*stotra*).
Su. pṛ. 642. *pragātha-pra*...

The section concerning the Prajāpati-vows: "One should not look at anything other than the sun," and so forth; this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), with its fruit being declared in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
4|1|3. The *prajāpativratas*—such as gazing at the rising sun (*udyadādityekṣaṇa*), making a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and so forth—are for the sake of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
One should consult the summary (*bindu*) titled "The Section on the *Prajāpativratas*" (4|1|3).
The connection of the *prajāpativratas* with their fruit is stated thus: "By this much, one becomes joined with the *haṃsas*."

Bhāṣya 4.1.8.24: The Section on the Vows of Prajāpati. The vows of Prajāpati—such as not looking at the rising sun, making a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and so forth—are for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Upon their abandonment, [the conclusion is that] rituals are for the sake of the person, because the scripture is beyond doubt. Furthermore, the substance is intended to be employed; because it is connected with that purpose, the mention of the person (*puruṣa*) occurs in relation to the action.
Commentary: Here, the examples of the Prajāpati-vows are cited, such as:
"One should not look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting," and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt: are these Prajāpati-vows ritual acts (*karma*), or are they for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)?
What is established? That it is a *kṛtya*-suffix.
Why? Because in this way, a separate result need not be postulated.
But is it not heard that there is indeed a result for this [act], namely: "By this much, one becomes joined with swans"?
It is said:
this statement is not intended to prescribe a result; rather, this word is merely a description of the present state.
Therefore, this prohibition applies wherever the viewing of the sun has been established as required.
Where there might be some rule regarding sunrise or sunset for one who has undertaken ritual duties (karmābhr̥t),

such being the case, we reply: upon the abandonment of that [obligation], acts of this kind— such as giving pleasure, embracing, and so forth— would indeed serve the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha).
These [details] are taught with reference to the agent, not to the action.
The connection with an agent who is obtained through the force of the meaning is what is intended to be enjoined;
the connection with the action, however, does not exist at all [as something to be enjoined].
And the scripture is not to be doubted; it is a more authoritative means of knowledge than even the words of one's father or mother.
For one understands through it by oneself;
indeed, it stands in the place of the sense faculties.
Nor is any superior benefit to the substance accomplished by such [words] as these.
Therefore, because of its connection with that human purpose, it is the person who is heard [as the agent] in relation to an action of this very kind.
Moreover, the effort of the person is stated merely to indicate the injunction regarding the ritual object.
It should remain as it is of its own accord.
Now, as for what was said— that where the sight of the sun reaches, there [the mantra] is recited, while where it sets, there is a prohibition—
it is true that a prohibition is logical.
In that way, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) would be upheld; otherwise, a mere implied restriction (*lakṣaṇā*) would be assumed.
However, here a restriction is heard directly by the word itself in the phrase "his vow" (*tasya vratam*). Therefore, there is indeed a restriction: "The sun must not be looked at.
Furthermore, by the statement "By this much he becomes yoked with the *haṃsa*," the excellence of the person's faith is praised, not a connection to ritual action.

Therefore, the Prajāpati-vows are for the sake of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Likewise, [vows] such as "the cow-marks must be made on the hands" are also for that purpose. Regarding their abandonment, there is a scriptural statement concerning the person (*puruṣa*).

(If, because pleasure is inseparable [from the acquisition of wealth], even though the acquisition of property serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), its status as a human goal exists only when pleasure is relinquished due to the absence of any imagined fruit; then, since there is likewise an absence of any imagined fruit for the *prajāpati-vratas* which are outside of any specific ritual context (*aprakaraṇa*), let them be regarded as prohibitions (*kṛtyatva*). Thus it is introduced. Therein, demonstrating that their status as prohibitions is logical precisely because they are negations, he establishes their nature as prohibitions—) "One should not look at the rising sun."

The negative particle (*nañ*) is connected by the word expressing "that which is to be done" (the suffix, meaning the *pratyaya*), as in the case where the sun is connected as the object to be reached (*prāpyakarma*) and the act of seeing (*īkṣitādhātaḥ*) is connected as the instrument (*karaṇa*), such that one might reach the rising sun by means of seeing; likewise, the negative particle is also connected with that very [suffix] in the sense: "one should not reach the rising sun by means of seeing. Thus, when there is a connection with the suffix, the words are primary (*śrutivāci*) and not figurative (*lakṣaṇāvāci*).

But when there is a connection between the negative particle (*nañ*) and the verbal root (or the word [as a whole], according to the reading *nañ-upapadayoḥ*), then, having abandoned their own primary meanings, they indicate another entity (*vastvantaram*). (The plural number is used either with the intention of referring to multiple subordinate elements [*upapada*] or in view of the multiplicity of examples.)
Therefore, there is a prohibition [due to the defect of the definition].
And that [prohibition] is a nominal stem;
moreover, it is found as something already established in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices.
That [view] is refuted;
and thus, no fruit need be postulated.

Even though this is not a prohibition (but rather, what is called "non-looking" is a restriction of the form of a mental resolve of the internal organ), nevertheless, for fear of postulating a fruit, this must be a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) despite its being a *kṛtya* suffix.

[Objection: "By this much, one becomes joined with swans" (some read "liberated")—since the hearing of this result [of the destruction of sin] is present, no further result need be postulated; therefore, he says: "This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the result, not an injunction for a result.
This being the case, we reply:
"This is not a prohibition."
For, having introduced the subject with "His vow" (*tasya vratam*), there is the statement, "He should not look at the sun when it is setting.

And "vow" (*vratam*) is spoken of in a general sense as an action; that [general action], requiring a specific detail, is specified by this: "This is the action" (*tat idam karma*), namely, "he should not look at the sun when it is setting," and so forth.
For, regarding the prohibition, the previous section on the Prajāpati-vows is the section on the Prajāpati-vows.
It would remain expectant;

and by that, the specific ritual action (*karmaviśeṣa*) would be grasped without being interrupted. Moreover, because of this syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), two unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated (having been postulated previously, they would now have to be postulated again).
Thus, in this negation, there would be much inconsistency.
Therefore, because of this contradiction, the negative particle (*nañ*) is not connected with the delimitation of agency (*kartavyatā*).
Consequently, it is employed [as follows]: it is connected with "the seer" (*īkṣitṛ*).
Therefore, this restriction (*niyama*), consisting of non-looking (*anīkṣaṇa*), is heard as a duty of the agent (*kartṛ-dharma*).
There is a connection with the agent through that which is obtained by implication (*arthaprāpta*) but exists in a form contrary [to what is otherwise required].
However, because there is an absence of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, there is no connection with the sacrifices (*ṛtu*).

Since the objection might arise that "because the scripture is not to be doubted" applies equally even to things intended for ritual performance (*kratvartha*), this reason would not be conclusive regarding the human goal (*puruṣārtha*); therefore, to dispel that doubt, it is stated in the Sūtra: "And the substance is not intended to be prepared. (He then explains: Neither a substance intended for the ritual is consecrated nor transformed (this is an illustration that includes both preparation and modification), by virtue of which—through its connection with that [substance] and by way of mediation—it might indirectly serve the purpose of the ritual.
Therefore, these [acts] serve the human goal.
Now, a deliberation is undertaken as to whether these [rites] are optional (*kāmya*) or obligatory (*nitya*).

In this regard, some first say: "The instruction for these is for the purpose that they must be performed by one who desires a fruit" (just like the *Vidhijit* sacrifice and others). He refutes that: "No, the instruction is not for the purpose that they must be performed by one who desires a fruit."
What then? He says: "By way of its being obligatory, like the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Non-looking (*anīkṣaṇa*) is simply the absence of looking; since it is a non-entity (*abhāva*), how can it be enjoined here as a positive entity (*bhāva*) in the form of a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*)? Demonstrating this, he shows the relationship that serves as the basis for the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*): "In every case—whether in engagement (*pravṛtti*) or in withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) [that is, when something is to be done]—one either engages or withdraws by undertaking a mental operation (*mānasavyāpāra*)."
(Here too, while performing the non-looking: one forms a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that "the non-looking at the sun must be performed.
Therefore, the mental operation (termed *saṃkalpa*) is inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*) with the non-looking (which is the absence of looking).
Because of that inseparable connection, [the word] expressing the absence of looking is able to indicate it.
Just as a form [indicates] an individual object, so too, because the non-existence of touch and the rest is invariably concomitant with that [absence], there is no injunction for them [either].

(Furthermore, he explains the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "The effort of a person is *kṛti*": If [the action] were for the sake of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*), the injunctive [text] would be restricted solely to the origination of the rite (the mention of "origination" is also indicative of "application").

And this being the case, that very quality of the [text] which establishes its purpose for that [end]—meaning its quality of establishing the performance—would be lost, because it would have already been accomplished by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*).
Therefore, that position must be accepted wherein the prescriptive [text] is meaningful.
Since there is no distinction in the scripture, the fruits should accrue according to the literal scriptural statement.
The Commentary says: It is replied as follows.

If this were so, then these [other injunctions] would also be for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*): "He offers the *samidh* oblation," "He offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation," "He should not speak untruth"—and so forth.
In these cases too, there is a mention of human effort, and in these cases too, no material substance (*dravya*) is intended to be produced.
Alternatively, because the purpose [of the action] is not grasped as its cause, there is a connection to the locus of the object for that purpose.
The Commentary states: "The word 'api' (even/also) serves to exclude the previous position.
It is not the case that the *samid* and other such offerings would thereby result in being for the sake of the person."
If no reason were apprehended, the Prajāpati-vows would be for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
In that case, no reason such as direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) or the like is apprehended by which it could be understood that they are subsidiary to ritual acts (*karmāṅga*).
Therefore, they are for the sake of the person.
There is no connection between the purpose and the ritual acts in the case of the Prajāpati-vows; however,
in this context, the means known as *prakaraṇa* (context) is taken,
by which it is understood that these acts are for the sake of the ritual.
Therefore, these are mere illustrations;
and human effort, being thus [dependent], is merely a restatement,
as it is with those things that sustain the world.

The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): Even in common worldly practice, when people hear that certain actions—such as those performed for a completed task or those possessing a specific purpose—are not restricted by their results, they understand them to be for that very purpose. Thinking thus, they prescribe fasting and recitation (*japa*) and consider them to be for the sake of the ritual performance (*kṛti*), not for the sake of the sacrifice (*ṛtu*), [concluding] "this is the instruction for this purposeful act.
And others, thinking likewise, do not consider such statements to be ill-spoken.
Therefore, it is established that the *samit* and other such rites are not *prajāpati-vratas*.
Śabara: "In the case of a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), there is direct denotation (*śruti*); but in the case of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there is secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And a prohibition, seeking its object of application, would apply to the sacrifice.
This being the position reached, we reply:
Since the word "vow" (*vrata*), which denotes an action, is heard at the beginning [of the section],
there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) here even by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
and that [exclusion] pertains to the sacrifice (*kratu*).
One who hears [the teachings] outside [of this system], while desiring fruits, seeks the status of a human goal.
There exists no evidence here, such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth, for a connection with a ritual sacrifice;
rather, it is the fact that the subject matter is desired by the person that is made known by the injunction (*vidhi*).
What is directly required by that [act] is its fruit alone, and not the sacrifice itself;
therefore, it exists for the sake of the fruit, and this is to be understood from the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa).

Regarding *soma*: because pleasure is not perceived through direct observation in the same way it is in the acquisition of wealth (*dravyārjana*), the conviction is that it serves solely the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*). This constitutes the connection [of this topic] with the preceding one.

Because of the fear of having to postulate a fruit (*phalakalpanābhaya*), it can be argued that the status of serving the sacrifice’s purpose applies even to cases such as the *Viśvajit*, the *Rātrisatra*, and the "death of gold" (*hiraṇyamarana*); therefore, they say that these too fall within the scope of this section.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Even though that joy (*prīti*) is not perceived—just like the acquisition of wealth and so forth—the observances of Prajāpati (*prajāpativrata*) and others do indeed serve the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*). This is because the scripture does not contradict them when it teaches their status as *puruṣārtha*; therefore, there is no room for the claim that they are motivated by a lack of joy. Furthermore, he provides the justification for the scripture’s teaching that they serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), stating: "And not... (*na ca*).

In this way, the substance is not intended to be connected with the sacrifice through the ritual acts; that is to say, there is no connection of these [acts] with a substance for the sake of the sacrifice, by means of which they might serve the purpose of the sacrifice.

Therefore, because of the connection with that [substance] which serves the purpose of the person, the Vedic text [speaks] of the person as either the agent or the principal (śeṣin) in the act of looking and so forth. For example: "One should not look at the rising sun"—is this for the sake of the sacrifice, or is it for the sake of the person? [It is for the sake of the person. Or: "The fire should be kindled"—is this for the sake of the sacrifice, or is it for the sake of the person? [It is for the sake of the person.]
Because it is to be assumed as a result, that which is obtained in the sacrifice is prohibited.
By this statement, since it is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), the intention here is "not looking";
because it is not a subordinate part of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), it serves the purpose of the person for the destruction of sin.
Bhaṭṭa: Beginning with the words "His vow," and preceded by the mention of bathing, [it says]: "One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting;
nor when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky."
Thus, the *prajāpativratas* are heard in the scriptures.

Regarding those as well, the commentators and others—having raised the objection that, whether they be prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) or exclusions (*paryudāsa*), the assumption of a fruit would imply they serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*)—concluded that because they are not recited within the context of the ritual (*anārṣyādhītatva*) and thus lack a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) [linking them to the sacrifice], they cannot serve the purpose of the sacrifice; therefore, accepting them as exclusions, they established that they serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatva*).

That too is required because, according to the logic of the prohibition against eating what has been offered (*kalpyabhakṣaṇapratiṣedha-dhāraṇanyāya*), the suspicion that they serve the purpose of the sacrifice is untenable.
The deliberation here must be conducted in this very manner:

is this a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) or an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)? In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), [the action] is motivated by the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); since that [fruit] would be absent in the case of a prohibition, there is currently a lack of consistency.

In this context, since the negative particle (*nañ*) cannot function as a mere exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—because it is untenable for it to denote the primary object [of the sentence] through its characteristic features and so forth—it follows that this is indeed a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) consisting of looking at the rising sun as prompted by passion, just like the prohibition against performing the *kalpa-kṣamaṇa* and other such rites.

Consequently, because looking [at the rising sun] is established by the prohibition as a means to an undesirable end, there is no expectation for another result; thus, the assumption of a further fruit based on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), such as "by this much one does not become joined with swans," is untenable, and therefore the [prohibition] is not motivated by such an explanatory fruit.
However, the *arthavāda*— because it makes known the absence of a cognition produced by [direct] observation—
does not sublate the proximate cognition in the section concerning the leading forward (*praṇayana*). In the section concerning the leading forward, the proximate cognition remains unsublated.
Now, as for what was said— that it will have the status of the word "tīrtha"—
to this we reply:
even the word "tīrtha" denotes merely a tīrtha.

Having stated, "He has gone on a pilgrimage (tīrthayātrā)," several sacred fords (tīrthas) are enumerated; from this, it is understood that the word [tīrtha] possesses that specific meaning. However, where it is used alone, it denotes merely a sacred ford, as in: "A kinsman is a sacred ford (tīrtha); for he becomes a sacred ford among his equals."

Moreover, when the direct meaning (śrutyartha) is possible, a metaphorical meaning (lakṣaṇārtha) should not be accepted; and in this case, the direct meaning is indeed possible. Therefore, a metaphorical meaning is not to be accepted.
[The purpose of the statement] is for the sake of restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*), for the sake of a quality (*guṇa*), or it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
The Commentary says: Regarding that which was stated, "the other is indeed inexpressible," what is the rebuttal? It is said:
It may be for the sake of restriction, as in "they lead [the fire] in two [cases], not in four."
[The statement] "Therefore, with two [fingers]" is either for the purpose of a quality (*guṇa*) or for the purpose of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*).
In that regard, first, if it were a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*), there would be three defects;
furthermore, no quality whatsoever is being enjoined.
By process of elimination, it is for the purpose of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*).
Furthermore, even the eulogy would be purposeless because the act of leading [the fire] has already been established.
We shall explain the purpose of the eulogy in the subsequent section: "The middle boundary from the *gārhapatya* fire" (Sūtra 25).

(The commentary *Laghuṭupṭīkā* on this point, Mi. Ko., p. 1688, is included under the heading "The Carrying Forward of the Shovel (*abhripraṇayana*) in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices," as it is common to both sections; therefore, it should be consulted there.)—As for the connection [of the present discussion]: although the Soma-related acts such as the *nirmanthya* fire do not effect transference (*atideśa*), it was stated that the word "carries forward" (*praṇayati*) will effect transference; hence the connection. The meaning of the sūtra is: the carrying forward related to the Soma sacrifice is similar to that of the Soma sacrifice; the other, however, is the archetypal (*prākṛta*) one obtained through the *codaka* rule, and thus need not be mentioned [separately].

Vi—The carrying forward of the fires (*praṇayana*) should be either *saumika* (pertaining to the Soma sacrifice) or *prākṛta* (archetypal), for it is heard [in the scripture] in connection with both; however, since the former is not otherwise established, it is not so. "Vādagīḥ" refers to a statement intended as an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*).
Bhāṭṭa—In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, there are four sections (*parvan*) known as Vaiśvadeva, Varuṇapraghāsa, Sākamedha, and Śunāsīrīya.
In this regard, it is heard in the scripture: "They lead forth two; for two.

Regarding this, the Commentator explained two distinct topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) through seven sutras (the first section by four sutras and the second by three). Among these, in the first [section], the question is whether this leading forth (*praṇayana*) is the same as that belonging to the Soma sacrifice along with its specific characteristics, or whether it is the original (*prākṛta*) one to be brought from the Gārhapatya fire by the Adhvaryu priest.

When this thought arises, since the ordinary [method] is already obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), the injunction would otherwise be rendered purposeless; therefore, for the sake of making the statement meaningful, this term *praṇayati* refers to the Soma-sacrifice method of carrying forward the fire (*saumika-praṇayana*), and it is intended to enjoin that specific procedure.

For this very reason, since the *uttaravedi* (high altar) exists there [in the Soma sacrifice], its application is established, and thus the prohibition—"One does not scatter the *uttaravedi* in the Vaiśvadeva, nor in the Śunāsīrīya"—is also consistent as an exclusion of that [altar].
Consequently, in those two [sacrifices], the ritual details of the Soma-sacrifice method of carrying forward the fire, excluding the *uttaravedi*, are to be performed.

However, just as there is no commencement of a substitute for optional rites (*kāmya*), so too one should not engage in a subsidiary desire (*guṇakāma*).

If, however, when some minor accessory (*guṇa*) has been lost during the performance, a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is employed, then because that constituent part must be completed, there is equality with the modification (*vikāra*) by means of the substitute; thus, "equality" (*samāna*) is the very purpose for the modification (*ūha*).
Soma—the purpose: [the formula] "I buy Soma from you," etc., is prior to the modification (*ūha*).
Vi—The defeat by *pūtīka* plants is either unequal or equal in praise; there is equality with Soma.

There is no equal substitute by way of being a mere signifier (*naimittikatva*), because [substitutes] such as *pūtīka* grass are equal to *soma* only through their capacity to overcome [the deficiency], and so forth. Bhaṭṭa: However, where there is an injunction for *pūtīka* and the like in the absence of the primary substance itself, since the performance of the sacrifice produced by *soma* equipped with all its constituent parts is possible first, and only subsequently does that [injunction for *pūtīka*] come into operation, there is no case of "equal injunction" (*samānavidhānatva*). For in this case, there is no restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the qualities inherent in the *pūtīka* acting as a substitute.

Since those [other plants] are similar to the *manda* plant, they too would not be obtained; furthermore, this would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of resorting to a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the parts within the word *pūtīka*.

Nor can that [figurative indication] be accepted on the grounds of the simplicity (*lāghava*) of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), because such an injunction is rendered ineffective by the principle of the *niṣādasthapati* section, as it serves merely as a result [of the injunction].

This being the position reached, [the author replies]: for the quality of being a *pūtīka* (i.e., *pūtīkatva*), which is the referent of the word *pūtīka*, is not heard here as being the instrument (*karaṇa*), since the word ends in the accusative case.

And therefore, in accordance with the parsimony of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), that [injunction] does not indirectly indicate (*lakṣyate*) that the state of being *pūtīka* is a direct means; rather, it indicates only the status of being a prompter (*prayojakatva*) which is inseparable from the means residing in its constituent parts. Thus, there is no indication of the constituent parts in the word *pūtīka*. Since this injunction does not operate until after the application of the principle that restricts [the choice] to similar things, the justification for the restrictive injunction is established. Consequently, even here, since the fact that certain constituent parts serve as the means is already established by the scriptural rule regarding *soma*, there is an equal application of the rule (*samānavidhānatva*). Maṇḍana says: "Even a fragment of *pūtīka* possesses the prescribed properties."
Śaṅkara says: "It is exactly the same even in the case of the *pūtīka* [substitute]. 16. The rule of equality:
even in the case of a substitute, the performance of the primary attributes must take place."
The primary and its substitute are subject to the same injunction.
Commentary: There is a substitute when the prescribed substance is unavailable. For example, when rice is unavailable, wild rice (*nīvāra*) may be used.
In this regard, there is a doubt: are the wild rice grains subject to the same injunctions as the rice, or not?
What is established? That the substitute is like that [the occasional rite].
Just as the occasional rite has a ritual procedure not identical with that of the obligatory rite, so too is the substitute;
because they are not equal.
What is this inequality? It is that [the rule] is prescribed for *vrīhi* rice, not for *nīvāra* wild rice; thus there is inequality.
For while [the rule] is prescribed for *vrīhi*, the *nīvāra* becomes the offspring of the noble [rice].
Or rather—the same principle applies even to a substitute (*pratinidhi*).
Not so, because the purpose is one.
The Commentary states: This is not so; the substitute (pratinidhi) does not have the same injunction (asamānavidhāna).
It would be like that [the original] only if it were explicitly heard in the text (śruta);
there is no relationship of archetype and modification (prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva).
Why? Because rice is indeed the cause for the properties of rice [to apply] to the individual instance of rice.
Furthermore, it is not heard in scripture that the nature of *nīvāra* takes the place of the nature of rice (*vrīhitva*).
Therefore, there is no relationship of original form and modification (*prakṛti-vikārabhāva*).
How, then, do the ritual properties (dharmas) apply to wild rice (nīvāra)? It is said:
those individual grains of rice (vrīhi-vyakti) which are delimited by the nature of rice exist in the wild rice;
it is for them that those properties are performed.
And this same rule applies equally to those individual instances of rice.
What is the equality? Both are likewise characterized by the term "rice. Therefore, they are subject to the same injunction.

Or—if the *nīvāra* grains were, by their own inherent power, the means for accomplishing the ritual action, then the ritual properties (*dharma*) would be connected to them through the principle of functional necessity (*kāryāpatti*).
However, there is no evidence whatsoever for their being the means [of accomplishment]. As for those ritual properties belonging to the *vrīhi* rice:

Only a few [properties] are seen [to apply], because the person, while acting, does so as a necessary consequence (*anantarīyakatvāt*) of that [primary injunction], not by virtue of being an agent of action (*karmijñatayā*).
However, the properties of the rice (*vrīhidharmāḥ*) are enjoined individually by the word "rice" and are thus subject to the same rule (*samānavidhānāḥ*).
For the cognition of rice does not cease from the threshing-floor; as he will say: "That is the commonality, for it is drawn along by that."
Therefore, that deity proceeds together with it,
because it is not characterized by the scriptures.

Commentary: For this reason as well, there is no substitution [of a proxy] in relation to that which is directly enjoined (*śruta*), because of the relationship with the function of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Why? Because it is characterized by its purpose (*artha-lakṣaṇatvāt*).
A substitute is employed for the sake of the purpose.
Furthermore, it is not possible to understand this as "the state of being *nīvāra* takes the place of the state of being *vrīhi*.

Therefore, a substitute does not possess the status of performing the primary function (*prakṛtikārya*) alongside that which is prescribed by scripture. Or rather—the substitute is employed because it is not enjoined by the sacred teaching (*śāstra*).
Therefore, some maintain that this [substitute] is a *kāryāpatya* (one who takes on the function) due to a restrictive rule (*niyama*),
and not a substitute (*pratinidhi*) in the technical sense of the scriptures,
because it arises from the completion of the primary rite.
Or, if it were not characterized by the scriptures, it might still be performed;
and there would be no fault whatsoever from its non-performance.
Therefore, the Sūtra must be explained in this manner.
Furthermore, because the Ārāya does not possess the characteristics of the original scriptural injunction (*śāstra*), there is no substitution of its function (*kāryāpatti*).

However, those properties of the *vrīhi* rice which were adopted by the injunction for the *vrīhi*—incomplete though it may be compared to the full set of properties belonging to the primary injunction—are indeed subject to substitution of function, because they do not constitute a different entity.

[Soma: The practical application is as follows: this [substitution] cannot take the form of engaging in a desire for a specific quality (*guṇakāma*), because just as there is no procedure for a substitute in the case of a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya-karman*), so too there is no possibility of a procedure for a substitute in the case of desires for qualities.

Therefore, since those desiring the qualities [of the primary substance] who proceed by means of the principal substratum cannot proceed by means of a substitute, it is clear from the Vārttika on the subsequent section (though not in this specific section) that the purpose of the *ūha* and *anūha* is precisely [the modification of mantras such as] "O cloud, [rain] for the rice" (*vrīhīṇāṃ medha*). Viśvarūpa states: "Is the rule regarding substitutes such as *nīvāra* unequal or equal? As before, it is unequal; there is equality because the 'rice-ness' exists through its form."

Bhaṭṭa: Even if there is a cognition of similarity to *nīvāra* and other grains when rice is absent, there is no lack of commonality of injunction (*asamānavidhānatva*) because the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) is understood prior to the injunction regarding the refinement (*saṃskāra*). This is because the ritual scripture (*karmaśāstra*) implies that [the grain] when a performance of the sacrifice produced by *vrīhi* grains endowed with all required qualities is possible.

This being the position, [we reply]: It is true that there is an implication of that [means] at a later time; nevertheless, at the very moment of considering that which is to be accomplished by *vrīhi*, once the universal property (*jāti*) of *vrīhi*-ness is understood to be the means to the sacrifice, it is delimited by the fact that [the sacrifice] could not otherwise be accomplished. Furthermore, the status of being a means for those *yava* grains that constitute the beginning of that [act] is also implied.

And therefore, since the genus (*jāti*), the individual substance (*dravya*), and the status of being a means (*sādhanatā*) have already been understood [for the *vrīhi*], even though the grasping of only some [of these] occurs at a later time due to their impossibility [in the case of *nīvāra*], it is logical that they are subject to the same injunction (*samānavidhāna*) by virtue of their essential nature as previously apprehended.

For those [grains] are not taken up in the form of *nīvāra*-ness, such that there would arise the consequence of a lack of common injunction because the cognition of their status as a means in that form were posterior; rather, they are taken up as possessing a certain number of constituent parts similar to those of the parts that constitute *vrīhi*.

Therefore, although those [grains] must necessarily be taken up in order to achieve the status of being a means residing in the parts of the rice (*brīhi*), there is no contradiction in their being subject to the same injunction (*samānavidhāna*), because the status of being a means residing in the parts has already been established prior to the injunctions regarding the consecrations (*saṃskāra*).

For in the case of the injunctions regarding consecrations, since the very status of being a means residing in the parts—which is delimited by the fact that the substance is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) used in the archetype—is the intended object (*uddeśya*), there is no conflict even when the status of being a means residing in the parts differs from one part to another.

Thus, where there is no substitute because the constituent parts are not identical, there is neither an equal injunction (*samānavidhānatva*) nor an acquisition of ritual properties (*dharmaprāpti*) through the principle of functional equivalence (*kāryāpatti*). For instance, when threshing is replaced by plucking with the nails, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites do not apply to the nails; likewise, in the case of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), even if one uses ordinary grass as a substitute for the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) for spreading, the purpose is already fulfilled. However, in the case of the fruit [of the sacrifice], the inference of an extended application (*atideśa*) arises solely from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) inherent in the words of the text, such as "one should give that food to him"—this is the distinction.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: regarding the mantra "O cloud, of the rice-grains," according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there would be an omission [of the word 'rice-grains'].
According to the established conclusion (siddhānta), there is no modification (anūha).

This is because it is appropriate to employ the words such as 'rice-grains' contained within the mantra—even though they imply being the means of accomplishment—also in the case of the parts [of the grain], just as in the case of things that possess the implied status of being means of accomplishment.

Maṇḍana: "The instruction regarding the dharma applies to the substitute. Śaṅkara: "The equality [of the substitute] pertains to the subject of the substitute. 15. When a substitute has been employed for the consecrated animal, even if a piece of *khadira* wood is used, one must not perform the binding again with a *khadira* tree.
VI.
And because there is no modification in the case of a substitute.

Regarding the deliberation as to whether the mantra, "O grain, you are fragrant and well-disposed," should be applied with modification (*ūha*) or without modification (*anūha*) when *nīvāra* grains are taken as a substitute for *vrīhi* rice in the event of its unavailability, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
When a substitute, such as *nīvāra* rice and the like, has been employed, the term "no modification" (*ūha*) is understood to carry over.
No modification should be made regarding the substitute; because there is no alteration, it is to be used exactly without change.

In the case of a substitute (pratinidhi), let the mantra proceed as if there were a figurative application (upacāra) of the original; the word "ca" (and) serves the purpose of providing an illustration, such as "like the wife" or "like the Agnihotra."
"Because it is not recited in the scripture, there would be a lack of scriptural authority due to the absence of the other.

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) sets aside the established conclusion (siddhānta). "Lack of scriptural authority" means being devoid of an inferred scriptural statement; this would occur either because [the injunction] is not recited in the scripture, or because of the absence of the other [alternative].

If the word *vrīhi* were not recited in the mantra, or if there were an absence of the other substance, *nīvāra*, which serves as its substitute, then there would be a lack of scriptural authority (*aśabdatva*).
However, in this case, the word *vrīhi* is indeed recited;
yet, in practice, the *vrīhi* grains are unavailable and *nīvāra* grains have been taken instead.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the designation of the *nīvāra* grains, the word *nīvāra* must be substituted in place of the word *vrīhi*, as in the mantra: "O cloud, being well-disposed toward the *nīvāras*.
Thus, modification (*ūha*) must be performed;
such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Or rather, it may bear that name because it is for the sake of that [purpose], since it is not distinguished from the original materials by means of the consecrations (*saṃskāra*).
The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

When the *nīvāra* grain is taken as a substitute in place of the *vrīhi* rice, one must not perform the modification (*ūha*) in the mantra "I have measured the *vrīhi*s," changing it to "I have measured the *nīvāra*s."

How so? Because the *nīvāra* grains have that same purpose—that is, they serve the same purpose as *vrīhi* rice—the substance consisting of *nīvāra* is designated by that very name, *vrīhi*, and the ritual refinements (*saṃskāra*) are performed upon it.
And those ritual refinements are what is denoted by the word *vrīhi*.
They exist even in wild rice (*nīvāra*).
And thus, the wild rice is not distinguished from [other grains] by its ritual preparations (*saṃskāra*);
it is designated [as such].
For this reason as well, the substance *nīvāra* is designated by that very name.

Therefore, the *nīvāra* grains, acting as a substitute, must be spoken of by the word *vrīhi* itself. Consequently, no modification (*ūha*) should be made; such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

And it has been stated regarding the principle of "that thou art" (*tattvamasi*): that rice (*vrīhi*) possesses a specific quality in relation to wild rice (*nīvāra*) is explained in the verse, "The universal is indeed the object of that desire" (6.1.127).
Wild rice is extremely similar to rice.
Furthermore, wild rice (*nīvāra*) is inferred [to be a substitute] for rice (*vrīhi*) by virtue of their similarity.
Therefore, when wild rice is accepted as a substitute, there is no modification (*ūha*) of the formula to "May the clouds [rain] for wild rice.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Even when a substitute (pratinidhi) such as the *pūtīka* plant is prescribed, the primary ritual properties (*mukhyadharma*), such as purchase (*kraya*) and pressing (*abhiṣava*), must still be performed [with that substitute].

3.6.15. Even when a substitute capable of receiving the ritual consecrations (*saṃskāra*) is obtained, if the primary substance itself, which is likewise capable of receiving the consecrations, becomes available, the primary substance alone must be employed.
See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2186, under the section "The Adhikaraṇa on the Conflict between Substance and Consecration" (*Dravyasaṃskāravirodhādhikaraṇa*).

Even when a substitute (*pratinidhi*) capable of performing the consecration (*saṃskāra*) is available, that which is incapable of the consecration—even if it is capable of the primary act (*pradhāna*)—must be adopted as the primary substance itself. 6|1|19. Regarding the modification (*ūha*) of the model form (*sthānin*) in the case of a substitute, this should be understood from the rule: "The modification of the model form occurs in the case of a substitute" (9|2|1239).

When a substitute material is taken in place of the primary substance, although there is a difference in the substance, there is nevertheless no difference in the sacrifice. (6.1.11–12). This is the section concerning substitutes.
Even in the case of substitutes, the performance of the primary ritual duties must take place.

3|6|14|37–39. By the phrase "the established reason in the section concerning the nature of a substitute" (*pratinidhidharmādhikaraṇasiddhahetu*), which is "because of the unity of purpose" (*prayojanaikatvāt*), it is intended that the injunction itself is what is meant by the collection of doubts regarding the two-fold [application].
*Rasāyana*, p.
156. In the employment of a substitute, only that which is similar to the primary [substance] possesses the status of a substitute.
There is no substitute because of equality.
The commentary states: This is now investigated.
When the prescribed substance has been procured but then lost or destroyed, it follows that one should perform the ritual by taking a substitute.

When that substitute has also been destroyed, killed by the enemy, then what should be taken up: something similar to the substitute, or the very thing that was originally obtained but subsequently destroyed?
What is the prima facie view? When the substitute has been destroyed, something similar to it should be taken up, according to the previous principle.
This being the position, we reply:
There can be no substitute for a substitute.
Why? Because of their equality.
Just as the original substitute was undertaken out of a desire to perform the enjoined rite, and not out of a desire to employ a substitute.
Thus, this [substitute] is also intended for the sake of fulfilling what was heard [in the scripture], not for the sake of fulfilling a mere substitute.
Therefore, that which is similar to the substitute should be adopted;
for it is only when the primary substance has been adopted that something similar to it should be sought.

Regarding the *soma* and *pūtīka* plants: even when substitutes are employed, if those too fail, one should take something similar to the *pūtīka*, and not something similar to the *soma*. This constitutes the connection (*saṃgati*) because it raises a challenge to the purpose of the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: when a substitute fails, another substitute that is similar to that [first] substitute is not to be taken; for even when a substitute fails, the taking of another substance is equal [in principle], since the desire to obtain the specific part mentioned in the scripture remains the same. Vi— "But upon the failure of a substitute, [one should take] either that [original] primary substance or something equal to it."
The former [is so called] because it has already commenced; the other [is so called] because of obtaining a portion equal to what was heard.
Regarding the metaphorical treatment of a substitute (*pratinidhyupacāra*), the Bhaṭṭa school has established a single topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) consisting of the sūtras 3.1.34–39.
Thus, this is not distinct.
Maṇḍana says: "It is similar to the perception of the primary.
That which is the apprehension of the similar is "similar to the perception of the primary" (mukhyadṛk-sadṛk), and not similar to a substitute.
Śaṅkara: "He is not a substitute for you.
A substitute is considered a substitute; it is not regarded as being identical to the original. This is the maxim of the 'refutation of the substitute' (pratinidhikhaṇḍanyāya)."
This should be seen under the principle of the "substitute" (*pratinidhinyāya*).

Since the principle of the substitute is established, and since the combination (*samuccaya*) of the two [daily] offerings is more appropriate, why is this section (*adhikaraṇa*) commenced? It is said: because [the case is] different.
10.8.8.126, p. 2069: A substance that is optional [as an alternative] does not function as a substitute (pratinidhi).
(For example, when *khadira* wood is unavailable, *pālāśa* and the like are not substitutes; or when *vrīhi* rice is unavailable, they are likewise not substitutes.
6.1.128–30: Substitute-hood applies only to that which is similar to the prescribed substance in the event of its unavailability.

6|1|1127. When there is the total destruction or defect of the *havis* (sacrificial oblation), clarified butter (*ājya*) serves as its substitute. 6|1|1119. There is no status as a substitute for prohibited substances such as *māṣa* beans and the like.
"And that which is prohibited is indeed without distinction; for such is the scriptural statement.

Commentary: Now, as for that which is prohibited—such as "Varaka grains and Kodrava grains are unfit for sacrifice" and "Māṣa beans are unfit for sacrifice"—does that serve as a substitute in the event of the loss of the prescribed substance, or not?
What is established? That there is a substitute in this manner;
for the scriptural injunction is without distinction.
This being the case, we reply:
that which is prohibited cannot serve as a substitute.
For there is no distinction made in the Vedic revelation; it is stated without qualification that *māṣa*, *varaka*, and *kodrava* beans are unfit for sacrifice.
The connection of these with the sacrifice is prohibited;
it should not be understood that these are to be excluded from the sacrifice. Furthermore, if they were to be substituted, they would be reduced to the status of mere subsidiary parts.
Therefore, these are not substitutes. [Objection:
It is prohibited. [Response:
The taking up of *varaka* and other such items is for the purpose of performing the action with the prescribed substance; they are not enjoined as being of equal status.
And since being an auxiliary part has been prohibited,
therefore items such as the *varaka* grain should be adopted.
This being the position reached, we reply:

That is to say, where something has attained the status of being a means for the sacrifice (*yajñasādhana*), that is prohibited there. (In the *Asmallita*, however, the reading is in the plural: "those things which have attained the status of being means for the sacrifice there are prohibited.

Regarding Soma—since its functional efficacy is directly perceived here, let it be a substitute; thus, the connection [of this topic] is established through direct perception. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: even prohibited items such as *māṣa* beans and the like should not be used as substitutes, because the scriptural prohibition applies without distinction to anything merely connected with the sacrifice.
Vi— "Beans (*māṣa*) and the like may indeed serve as substitutes, because they prevent what has been prescribed;
or rather, they are not eligible [as primary materials], because of the statement that they are unfit for sacrifice (*ayajñiya*), which serves to exclude them.

Bhaṭṭa—Since the statement heard outside of a specific context, "Beans, *varaka*, and *kodrava* are indeed unfit for sacrifice" (*ayajñiyā vai māṣā varakāḥ kodravāḥ*), prohibits the very nature of beans and the like for use in sacrifice, the prohibition applies only where there is a direct injunction for their use, serving the purpose of establishing an option (*vikalpa*).

Alternatively, where there is an injunction by way of a general property such as "grain-ness" (*dhānyatva*), there is a prohibition of what is obtained through one's own desire, such as *māṣa* beans and so forth, just as in the case of the rule, "Silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass. Consequently, although *māṣa* beans and the like may serve as substitutes or means of accomplishment, because they lack the specific quality of being *vrīhi* rice (due to conflict with the ritual scripture), there is no prohibition against them in that context. Furthermore, according to the reasoning to be stated later, when *māṣa* beans and the like serve as substitutes for the form of the substance due to conflict with the scriptural injunction regarding the substance itself, they are included under the category of "rice-ness" and so forth; since their inclusion is unavoidable, they are taken up, and thus there is no prohibition because the required substance is not entirely absent.

Thus, they too [might be considered] substitutes. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: by the term "unfit for sacrifice" (*ayajñiya*), which conveys the sense of unfitness, there is a prohibition of their status as mere means (*sādhanatva*) in all cases other than those specifically prescribed; thus, it establishes a prohibition of *māṣa* beans and the like. Therefore, they are not to be used as substitutes.
However, it should be understood that in the absence of any substance whatsoever, they are indeed to be accepted.

And here, because the prohibition of *māṣa* beans is enjoined by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with reference to the sacrifice, there is no violation of the principle of non-duplication (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*).
Maṇḍana says: "That which is prohibited is not accepted [as a material].
Śaṅkara says: "Nor is there [the acceptance] of that which is prohibited."
Even for that which is prohibited, there can be no substitute.

Even when a rite is performed by means of a substitute, the name "Darśapūrṇamāsa" and so forth, as employed by the ritualists (*yājñika*), does not bring about non-difference [between the original and the substitute]. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 344). Furthermore, they consider that the principle expressed in the rule "because there is no difference" (*apīḍā-vyatirekāt*, 6.1.12) applies equally even to those rites prescribed in the *Vidhyanta* section, regarding the subject matter of rites performed with substitutes.

The Principle of the Substitute (pratinidhinyāya): In the case of the obligatory rites such as the Agnihotra, when the prescribed materials are unavailable, they are to be completed using substitutes.

Because the Veda is the authoritative means of knowledge, in the absence of what is prescribed by the Veda, there is no substitution for another, since there is no scriptural injunction [to that effect].
Commentary: Obligatory rites such as the Agnihotra are the examples here.

When there is a deficiency in these regarding the materials prescribed by the Veda, a doubt arises: should the performance be carried out by taking a substitute, or should the rite be abandoned at that point?
What is established? In the absence of a disciple, there is no transmission for anyone else; it would follow that [the teaching] is non-existent. Why? Because it has not been taught.

That which is heard as having rice (*vrīhi*) as its quality and being fruitful becomes fruitless when performed with *nīvāra* as its quality; therefore, it is a substitute (*pratinidhi*) for that [rice]. Dūṣaṇa says: It is a substitute for that [rice] in the absence of rice.
For the attainment of the fruit of the observance follows the sequence of what has been heard [in scripture].
Therefore, in the absence of the fruit (due to the absence of the scriptural injunction [or] the absence of the substance), there is its abandonment at the end;
because some [authorities] have so prescribed.
14. Commentary: In some cases, it is prescribed as a substitute.
For example: "If one should not find Soma, one should substitute Pūtīka plants.
This is the principle of substitution (pratinimitta).

Bhāṭṭa: Regarding the question of whether a substitute exists for a substance or not—the answer is that it does not exist, because there is no authoritative evidence [for its existence]. However, since there is an injunction for the performance of the rite which implies the necessity of a substance, when the prescribed substance is unavailable in a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), or even before the commencement of a compulsory rite (*nitya*), a deliberation arises as to whether another substance should be used as a substitute or not. In this regard, although one may perform the rite by offering a substitute due to incapacity, there is no authoritative basis for actually adopting such a substitute as a formal constituent (*aṅga*) of the ritual.

For instance, it is not the case that the treatise on substances (*dravya*) and so forth [is the source], because that [treatise] prescribes [the substance] as delimited by *vrīhi*-ness (rice-ness) and the like, and thus does not prescribe *nīvāra* (wild rice) and the like;
for *vrīhi*-ness does not exist in those [other grains].

Nor is the treatise on ritual action (*karma*) the impeller of that [substance], because when a substance is impelled, it is impelled as something unique to a specific pair [of materials], and since *vrīhi* and the like are prescribed, it would result in [the substance] being unique to that specific pair.

For the scripture concerning rice (*vrīhi*) is not a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) by virtue of its verbal form; rather, it is so by implication, through the prevention of [the use of] other [grains].
