First of all, since the investigation of the meaning of the Veda consists solely of the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no introduction here of any other topic, such as the definition of difference; thus, its commencement is deferred to a later time.

Even therein, the relationship of subsidiary and principal, the relationship of purpose and that which serves the purpose, and ritual action belong to distinct entities; therefore, [the definition of] qualification (*adhikāra*) is not commenced before the definition of difference.
Likewise, qualification can be determined only when the nature of the ritual action has been ascertained through its suitability; thus, the definitions are perceived in this sequence.

Therefore, since the latter hexad depends on the knowledge of the teachings because it is the subject matter of the extended application (*atideśa*), its accomplishment is dependent upon the knowledge derived from the teaching;
and since the whole [latter hexad] requires the entire preceding hexad,
this relationship of the definition of differentiation (*bhedalakṣaṇa*) is established by elimination, and thus it is commenced here.

(The purport of the second chapter—) The Commentary: Herein, sixfold differentiation of action (*karmabheda*) will be explained: difference of words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), accessory quality (*guṇa*), context (*prakriyā*), and name (*nāmadheya*).
What is about to be explained is first briefly mentioned so that what is being stated may be easily grasped as it is demonstrated, and the intellect of the listener may be composed.
This they call the "definition of non-action" (*akarmalakṣaṇa*); this is the purport [of the chapter], while everything else is incidental or relevant to the incidental (*utpātaprasaktānuprasakta*).
Or rather—[the phrase] "the sixfold division of action" [is used] by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) for the division of the means (*sādhana*).

Since the number must be stated differently in accordance with the sequence of the sūtras to be explained later, it was stated here as "beginningless existence" (*anādisattva*), even though it should have been stated as "number.
The two particles *iti* are used in the sense of providing a reason (*hetvartha*).
The sixfold division of action is due to these causes; that is to say, [it is due to] these reasons.

Alternatively, having derived the word *bheda* (division) in the sense of "instrument" (*karaṇa*), one will explain the other categories—beginning with "difference in words"—as being in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
We shall discuss the dependence of names and differences in words, as well as number and quality, in their respective places.
Furthermore, their primary intent at all times is merely to demonstrate that distinction;
anything else follows by way of introduction (*upodghāta*), incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), or a further incidental discussion (*anupra-saṅga*).
Regarding these, it is said: "They call an investigation for the sake of establishing the subject at hand an introduction (*upodghāta*)."
The relevant and the incidental arise from what has been introduced.

"Just as this present topic will serve as an introductory discussion (*upoddhāta*) for the purpose of establishing the inference of the distinctions among the various *apūrvas* produced in connection with the primary sacrifice (*prakṛti*).

(The term *anunirvartya* is derived from the root *anu-sṛ* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the agent; thus it should be construed as: "for the sake of establishing that distinction of action which follows the distinction among the various *apūrvas* produced in connection with the primary sacrifice.
From which word, when connected with the fruit, are the distinctions and non-distinctions of the *apūrvas* to be inferred?"

(And by this, the meaning of the section [adhikaraṇa] has been indicated: whether the meaning of the noun is the instrument for the production of the result, or rather the meaning of the verbal root. The Commentary: (The Section on Each Word) — First of all, this is considered there. In the first chapter, it was stated: "Dharma is a purpose characterized by an injunction (codanā)."
An injunction (*codanā*) is a sentence that expresses an action (*kriyā*).
Within a sentence, there are the meanings of the words (*padārtha*).
In this regard, does dharma [arise] from each individual word, or is it only one [dharma] produced by all [the words] together?
What, then, is the prima facie position? That "dharma" applies to each individual word.
This being the position, it is replied:
when one [word] precedes another, then the other will exist for its sake; thus, it will be established by the very application of the eighth inference, which is more subtle.
Therefore, there is only one *apūrva*.

Or rather—if both the sentence and the meaning of the sentence were partless—then the inquiry, "Is *dharma* [the result] associated with each individual word? and so forth, would be entirely irrelevant.
Hence, the *Bhāṣya* says: "And the meanings of words reside in the sentence."
Here too, an objection is raised:
"When the meaning of the sentence is established as being characterized by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*),
how can it then be questioned that *dharma* is expressed by every single word?"

For if the essential nature of dharma were being denoted, then the inquiry "What is expressed by each word? would be appropriate; however, since it is figurative (lākṣaṇika), that [inquiry] is improper. It is said:
"The property of being dharma (dharmaness) belongs to the word-meaning itself, because of its connection with the fruit."
Therefore, it is proper to investigate which among all these [causes] is the one intended.
Nor is it investigated here whether every single factor (*dharma*) is expressed by each individual word.

What, then, is being investigated? Is that which is expressed by each word a factor understood as the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) subsequent to its connection with the result, or is it a single factor grasped from among the meanings of the individual words? This is what is being considered.
And thus, it is established that all [actions] share the nature of *dharma*,
because it is accepted that the nature of *dharma* belongs solely to that which directly accomplishes the fruit;
however, there is no single *dharma* common to all of them such that one could maintain that they are "one" in that sense.
And regarding that which is connected with the word "fruit" (phala), they consider its meaning to be the means for accomplishing dharma.
Therefore, the inquiry arises: are all words connected with the fruit, or is it only one? What is the prima facie position? That it is for each individual word.
Why? "Because a connection with the principal [element] is established through uniformity;
therefore, every word is connected solely with the word denoting the result."

For if a distinction were perceived such that "this one is connected with the fruit, while this one is not," then only a specific portion would be so connected. However, since no such distinction is perceived, all words are connected with the fruit.

Furthermore, if it were assumed that one word is connected with the fruit while the others are merely related to it, then—according to the logic of the *Vājapeya* section—there would arise the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) caused by the dual nature of the sentence: because for one [word], there would be the status of being an injunction of qualification (*upādāna-vidhāna-guṇa*) toward the fruit, whereas for the others, there would be the status of being a subject of reference (*uddeśa-anuvāda-prādhānya*).
However, because all those things being enjoined are uniform with respect to the result, their connection as a *tantra* (common procedure) is established.
And when a possibility exists for all [the factors] to be connected, a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is always connected primarily with the principal (*pradhāna*).
Therefore, because all are connected to the result, they possess the nature of dharma.
In this regard, does each [element] individually accomplish the entire fruit like the *sannāyya* offering, or do they act together like the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices?
Likewise, one may conceive as desired whether they function by way of option (*vikalpa*) or combination (*samuccaya*), and so forth.

In that context, because the abundance of the fruit is paramount, because there is no mention of the word "one" (*eka*), and because it is understood that each possesses the power of accomplishment like the *sannāyya*, the position is that the fruit results separately from all of them.
Alternatively, according to the principle of the "Dawn and Sun" (aruṇādinyāya), because they are presented within a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*), the fruit belongs to them collectively.
Or rather, because there is a single lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*), the connection with the other [subsidiary] cannot occur at that very moment; therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
To this, it is replied: "From that which has a connection with the fruit, the transcendental result (*apūrva*) is postulated."
And when that [explanation] is established by means of fewer [assumptions], it is not logical to postulate many.
For if the sentence were intended solely for the purpose of establishing a connection with the fruit, then all [actions] might occasionally be connected with that fruit.
However, since this is not established by that much alone, another *apūrva* (unseen potency) must be postulated;
and that is based on the authority of logical necessity (*anupapatti*).
In this regard, since the postulation of a single *apūrva* is sufficient, there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for postulating further unseen entities.
For he who postulates many *apūrvas* must necessarily postulate at least one;
and once that one has been postulated, the explanatory necessity (*anyathānupapatti*) of the sentence is exhausted, as its purpose has been fulfilled.
It does not constitute a means of knowledge for a distinct *apūrva*.
Therefore, there is only one connection with the fruit, and from that, it is established that the other [action] is an *apūrva* that assists in the production of the fruit.

Nor will there be any contradiction here, because the name [of the sacrifice] serves as the resolution; or else, by resorting to possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)—as in the case of "He cleanses the cup with the *daśāpavitra*"—the status of the root-meaning as an instrument is established through the portion of the goal (*sādhya*) implied by the sense.

This being the case, as to which one [of the two] should be retained—since it is necessary to avoid the assumption of multiple unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*) in every respect, and thus a state of non-restriction would otherwise result—it is said: "The subordinate [element] is connected with the fruit; that which is connected with it is expected [to be the primary]. The status of being a subordinate part belongs to one [element], and its oneness is not assumed."

For it is not logical that within a single sentence the very same thing should sometimes be the primary element due to its connection with a result, and sometimes be a subsidiary element due to its assistance to that which possesses the result; this is because the nature of a philosophical conclusion (*siddhānta*) is fixed. Therefore, the cognition of the *apūrva* arises necessarily from either a verbal root (*ākhyāta-pada*) or a nominal stem (*nāman-pada*). Śā—Whatever injunction is to be postulated for the sake of human ends—whether it be optional (*kāmya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or pertaining to a substance, a name, or a quality—it is all an example [of this].
(He sets forth and refutes the Prābhākara view: Some, however, cite injunctions concerning qualification (*adhikāra-codanā*) as examples.

They say that since all such [injunctions] involve the occurrence of two sets of three contradictory factors (*viruddha-trika-dvaya*), the name itself must be the qualifying adjunct (*upapada*); therefore, they maintain that names and their adjuncts alone are the examples.
This is incorrect.
Even if we grant that the injunctions regarding qualification (*adhikāra-codanā*) alone are the examples, nevertheless, not every word in them is necessarily a name (*nāmadheya*).

For only that which possesses etymological derivation (*yaugika*), syntactic distinctness (*vākya-bheda*), a corresponding suffix (*tat-pratyaya*), and a designation for that [quality] is a name; whereas anything else, even if arrived at through the statement of qualification, serves only to indicate a quality (*guṇa*).
Just as in the passage, "He who desires, 'May a hero be born to me,' should offer the *bahuhotra*," the term *bahuhotra* denotes a mantra and is not a name;

likewise, in the passage, "If they should carry away this [Soma] while it is pressed and [the sacrifice] is incomplete, one should offer the *daśahotr* with four-drawn clarified butter (*ājya*) into the *āgnīdhra* fire," the *ājya* mentioned in connection with a contingent obligation (*naimittika-adhikāra*) is not a name.

Nor does there arise the fallacy of two incompatible triplets (*viruddha-trika-dvaya*), because a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*) is possible through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*).

And a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) is preferable to the postulation of an unestablished meaning; for otherwise, [in the case of] "with soma" (*somena*), there would be the same problem as in the section concerning the *pratipad* verses.
"The word *soma* in [the injunction] ‘one should sacrifice’ (*yajeta*) and so forth would be a name (*nāmadheya*).

Even in the originative statement (*utpattivākya*), there is figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) on the side of [accepting] a quality (*guṇa*); this was stated by the author of the commentary himself in the section on repetition (*abhyāsādhikaraṇa*, 2.2.2) with the words beginning ‘by the enjoining of a sacrifice’ (*yāgavidhānena*) and so forth.
This is not correct."
"Even though another *apūrva* is not perceived, nevertheless, that very thing is denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*).

And since the sacrifice is the instrument for that [result], it would follow that it is a name (*nāmadheya*) due to the equality of the fault; however, this is not tenable. Furthermore, this is analogous to the injunctions: 'One desiring spiritual luster should offer a *caru* to Sūrya,' and 'One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu.'"

In this context, the author of the *Nibandhana*, who maintains the doctrine of the connection between distinct words (*śabdāntarabandhavādī*), considers that "moving" (*caran*) and "white" (*śvetam*) are words denoting substance and quality, while the word "sūrya" and so forth denote the action (*bhāvārtha*) and constitute the object of the injunction (*niyogaviṣaya*).
Therefore, that [example] is also an illustration here, because it is an injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāra*) connected with the meaning of the action (*bhāvārtha*).
Likewise, in the case of "gold is to be worn" (*hiraṇyaṃ bhāryam*), it is because there is no [expressed] verbal suffix (*apratyayatvāt*).
"Like the Viśvajit and others"—this is the example here.
"The words *caru*, *śveta*, *hiraṇya*, and *saurya* denote substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and deity (*devatā*); they are not names (*nāmadheya*).
Therefore, it is stated that only those instances where a name is accompanied by a qualifying term (*upapada*) constitute the examples.
"This [view] is contrary to the Bhāṣya.

For the author of the Bhāṣya, while stating the purpose of the section on "the meaning of the verbal root" (bhāvārthādhikaraṇa), declares that in the established conclusion (siddhānta), when a substance is heard [in the injunction], the taking up of a substitute (pratinidhi) is the purpose.

For if [the word] were a name (nāmadheya), for what would there be a substitute? Furthermore, it is not necessarily only injunctive passages concerning entitlement (adhikāra-codanā) that serve as examples; for even in cases such as "one should sacrifice with Soma" (somena yajeta) and "one gives gold" (hiraṇyaṃ dadāti), the inquiry "whence [does this lead to] the unprecedented (apūrva)? is possible.

"Even though, due to the suspicion that these [words] are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of what is already primary, no new *apūrva* is initially perceived, nevertheless, the consideration arises as to whether it is reasonable for something being perceived even from the perspective of the alternative view (*pakṣa*) to be established.

[Objection: But surely, since that [new *apūrva*] is subsequently postulated as a subordinate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) of the specific factor (*kāraka*)—the object (*karman*)—which has been grasped by the grasper (*grāhaka*), it will be determined solely as having the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) as its domain; thus, there is no occasion for further deliberation."

"It might be so," [one might argue], "if it were established that the object (*karman*) is grasped by the grasper (*grāhaka*) prior to its status as a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*); but that is not established. For it is precisely here that this is deliberated: do all words become the objects of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) through the mediation of the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*), or is it rather a word specifically qualified by other words, while setting aside the relationship between action and its factors?
Even when there is only one [such word], is it a word for a substance (*dravya*) etc. qualified by the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), or the reverse?"

In this regard, because the relationship between action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*) is understood even prior [to the specific application], and because there too the substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) are heard as being *kārakas* by virtue of having the meaning of "being" (*bhāvārtha*) as their essence, and because they possess the nature of producing something else, the *apūrva* arises from the meaning of "being.

Furthermore, when this principle—that the relationship between action and its factors is not abandoned—is present, the "taking up" (*grahaṇa*) by the grasper (*grāhaka*) also belongs exclusively to the meaning of "being," because that alone has the nature of producing something else and possesses the status of a *kāraka*, whereas substances and qualities do not.
Consequently, the *apūrva* would also arise from that very [meaning of "being"] alone.

"If, however, this principle did not exist, then both the giver and the receiver would grasp the gold with mutual regard for their connection; or else, the gold would be subordinate to the act of giving.
Consequently, even the *apūrva*, when being postulated as something subsequent, would have to relate to both [the giver and the receiver] or to the gold alone.
Therefore, even in that case, the fact that the *apūrva* has the efficient force (*bhāvārtha*) as its object depends upon this very section; thus, it is appropriate that it be cited as an example."

Therefore, every example cited has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). [The commentary] states: "In an injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*), everything is first conveyed by all the words; [only then] is that entire conveyance accomplished by each word individually."

Because they are connected with the result; because all [the words] are distinct from the primary [meaning]; because of parsimony, as in the case of a single cognition; "but that which is subordinate to it" is another word.
"Therefore, only one [word] is the signifier of the word-meaning.
Bhaṭṭa: "Thus, since the means of knowledge for dharma and adharma have been determined, their nature is now being determined.

Although that [nature] is indeed already understood insofar as it is the object to be established by these many means of knowledge, nevertheless, because it has not been understood in terms of its unity, plurality, and so forth, it is here determined in that form."
In this context, the meaning of the chapter is precisely the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) whose existence is established by means of proof such as "another word" (*śabdāntara*) and so forth;

whereas the distinction between the meanings of verbal roots (*dhātvartha-bheda*) is investigated in some cases merely for the sake of establishing that [cultivation], and the distinction of the *apūrva* is also treated as its result—therefore, those two are not the primary subjects of the chapter.

"Even the distinction between [actions] that have already borne fruit depends upon the distinction between the means to the *apūrva* (the unseen potency); thus, when there is an inquiry into those means, since the *apūrva*—which is the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) of the very pursuit of heaven and so forth—is the means toward it, there arises a deliberation as to whether the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) toward the result such as heaven, or whether the meaning of the nominal stem (*upapadārtha*), such as *soma* and the like, is also [the instrument]. Since the initial connection with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is accepted even by the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the subsequent connection with the result is also equally applicable to all. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [we reply]: because it would entail the postulation of multiple unseen potencies (*adṛṣṭa*) if all were instruments, the status of being the instrument defined by the result belongs to only one; whereas for the others, their status as instruments is established solely through the mode of being desired (*iṣṭavidhi*).

"In this case, when the meaning of the verbal root itself is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the result, the *soma* and other materials serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) precisely by being the producers of that [root-meaning].

And when the *soma* and others are the instruments, the meaning of the verbal root serves a visible purpose precisely by being their substratum (*āśraya*); thus, there is no assumption of multiple unseen effects (*adṛṣṭa*).
Maṇḍana says: 'A single category (*padārtha*) produces the *apūrva*.'"

Śaṅkara says: "Dharma" [is the subject], "not at every step," but rather [it was established] in the section on the first quarter (2.1.1). In the first chapter, the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) has been completed.
In this regard, the section concerning each word (*pratipadādhikaraṇa*) follows the method of injunction (*vidhi*). This is the section concerning each word.
"Those [matters] have been determined according to reality.
The injunction regarding qualities and the status of names have also been examined.
In that regard, it was stated that for those things whose meaning is doubtful, the determination of the sense is made from the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa)."
In this regard,
after having briefly introduced [the subject], the primary and secondary [categories] will subsequently be examined as to whether they are distinct or non-distinct;
it is precisely this point that must be described, and no other.
"This very [section] is the connection concerning superimposition (*adhyāsa*).

Herein, the sixfold distinction of action (*karmabheda*) will be explained—namely, difference of word (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), context (*prakriyā*), and name (*nāmadheya*)"—thus the topics to be discussed are announced. By thus announcing what is about to be shown, it will be easily grasped, and the listener's intellect will be properly prepared. Therefore, they call this chapter "The Definition of Nameless Actions" (*anāmakarmalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, following the introduction and the incidental discussion, this is first considered: it was stated in the first chapter that "Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā).
And "injunction" is a sentence that expresses an action.

"In a sentence," [it is asked], "is the meaning of each word [the dharma]? Or is it one [dharma] expressed by all [the words together]? This is the *pratipadādhikaraṇa* (Topic on Each Word), Sūtra 2728; the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *pratipadādhikaraṇa*.
There is a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

And here, because of their status as instruments (*karaṇa*), there is no simultaneous coexistence of the two in a manner that is subordinate to the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*)—which is to be accomplished by the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) and has the fruit as its object—due to their being mutually compatible.

For when the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), having been already accomplished, serves as the object to be accomplished by the efficient-force, it remains directed solely toward the realization of its own essential nature.

Likewise, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) must be stated. The name’s meaning functions as an instrument precisely through the verbal root-meaning—which serves to bring about the verbal root-meaning—without the need for possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), and by its own nature alone. And that [instrumentality] occurs prior to the verbal root-meaning itself.
For that which has already been accomplished as the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) cannot be connected as an instrument (karaṇa).
Therefore, the meaning [of the sentence] is this: "By means of this, there exists the state of effecting the sacrifice, which is the meaning of the verbal root; therefore, it is established."
"Let it not be that he should perform [the action]";

for this being the case, at the stage of application (*viniyoga*), there is a coexistence (*sāhitya*) of the meaning of the noun with the verbal root-meaning in terms of their essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), whereas their joint performance will occur in terms of the task to be accomplished (*kāryatva*). This is because the verbal root-meaning, such as the sacrifice which is the duty of the qualified person (*adhikārakartavya*), functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). For instance, at the very moment the verbal root-meaning is produced by the meaning of the noun, since an instrument cannot have another instrument, that coexistence is produced within the *apūrva* (unseen potency) in accordance with the previously understood relationship; therefore, the metaphorical indication of possession (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) does not entail any fault.

Therefore, because it is simpler to postulate a single *apūrva* (transcendental result), and because the requirement for their coexistence is satisfied, conjunction (*samuccaya*) is appropriate. And this—being postulated through the otherwise inexplicable nature of the instrumentality understood from the word, whether from the sacrifice itself or from the deity—is established as being free from fault.
As it has been said: "From that which has a connection with the fruit, [the *apūrva*] follows."
That is correct.

This would indeed be so if the *apūrva* were postulated as the fruit of only two [factors]. However, since that *apūrva* must be established, it is not logical that the multiplicity of instruments (*karaṇatva*) should be based solely on the Vedic text; rather, it is postulated through the requirement of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).
(Vārttika, p. 373).

This is the Tautātitamatatīkā. In that context, the status of the proximate meaning of the verbal root as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) must be inferred from its connection with the production of the result (*phalabhāvanā*).

Since the meaning of the name has its instrumental function established and operates as a locus for the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) of the action, it is determined that the result arises from a single [action]; thus, a connection with the efficient force of the result must be postulated for that which is not remote [from the action].
When such a connection is being postulated, because it depends on the intellect, the *pratipadādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning individual words) is commenced by way of its production.
It is appropriate to postulate precisely that [connection] wherein there is no assumption of multiple unseen principles (*adṛṣṭa*).

Ku. 2.1.2, p. 121: It has already been stated that for the sake of establishing a combination (*samuccaya*) by means of both [the primary and secondary] functions of the *pratipadādhikaraṇa*, one must necessarily assume an unseen potency (*apūrva*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "those [mantras] are to be meditated upon" (2.1.2.6). Furthermore, when assuming only one [potency], no other [function] is possible there, because the non-inclusion of the others is established through their non-connection with the rest. Ku. 2.1.2, p. 2: The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *pratipadādhikaraṇa* (the very nature of the reasoning) is as follows: [The mantras are not merely descriptive, but have a prescriptive function]. Because they do not grasp anything else, the non-connection of the others is logically established.

This [is stated] according to the understanding of the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*): "If, out of a desire for proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) from that one [root] alone, then the *apūrva* arises from that alone, but not from all [roots]. (Soma. 2.1.1, p. 97). Thus, the status of the meaning of the nominal stem as an instrument resides precisely in the meaning of the verbal root.

Now, by virtue of the desire for a scriptural instrument (*śrautakaraṇatva*), it is established in the section concerning individual words (*pratipadādhikaraṇa*) that "the *apūrva* arises from one [root]."

Even though the meaning of the noun (*nāmārtha*) is remote, it possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*). In that case, since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is already connected [to the result] precisely by way of being its operation (*vyāpāra*), there is no need to postulate an instrumental status for it as well. As it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "That which [produces] the unseen potency (*apūrva*) from one [element], that alone is for the sake of that [result]. Furthermore, the contingency of postulating multiple unseen potencies (*adṛṣṭa*)—which was raised in the *Pratipadādhikaraṇa*—does not apply here. Thus, the connection of *soma* and other such substances with the fruit is established in order to prevent the meaning of the verbal root from being displaced from its role in the production of the fruit (*phalabhāvanā*), and the meaning of the noun from being displaced from its role in the verbal root-meaning. [Otherwise,] even if the *Agniṣṭoma* sacrifice were unified with the *Ājyapeya* because of the injunction regarding *soma*, [that connection] would remain untenable.

In such cases as "one should sacrifice for the sake of avoiding that" (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 2.1.3, p. 8), if one resorts to the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), then indication itself is the fault; thus, regarding the theory that the word's power (*śakti*) resides in its connection with another [word], the view presented in the *Pratipadādhikaraṇa* is preferable, namely, the postulation of a new transcendental result (*apūrva*). To this, it is replied:

The nature of the principle of the *pratipadādhikaraṇa* is as follows: "The origin (*utpatti*) [of an action] due to its being previously unknown (*apūrvatva*) is not merely the essential form of the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha-svarūpa-mātra*), because it is not observed at the stage of application (*viniyoga*). Since a sentence is sufficiently accounted for by assuming only one [thing], there is no assumption of many, even though the knowledge of the essential form of the verbal root-meaning is likewise present; rather, the knowledge of the essential form of the verbal root-meaning is [obtained] through its being the means to the accomplishment of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). In that regard, although the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) is the regulator there—since it is where [the action] arises because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the primary effect (*kārya*), and thus the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) does not present itself as something to be accomplished by its own inherent power (*svasvadhā*)—nevertheless, because this non-concomitance (*asāhitya*) can function as a means (*sādhana*), there is an application to multiple [entities] through option (*vikalpa*), as in the case of the sacrifice (*yāga*) and the *soma* according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *pratipadādhikaraṇa* (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2.1.4–5). For, because it is stated without qualification—that is, by way of the general property of being *māṣa* and so forth—the scriptural prohibition is expressed in such texts as: "Verily, *varaka* and *kodrava* are unfit for sacrifice," and "Verily, *māṣa* is unfit for sacrifice."
Therefore, substances such as mung beans (*māṣa*) and the like are not to be substituted.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to provide an illustration by means of the deity and other factors.

Just as there is no substitute whatsoever for the deity and so forth, so too it is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that substances such as mung beans cannot even be conceived of as substitutes.
In the case of performing what is prohibited, an undesirable consequence follows.
(Bhāṭṭa: Prohibition)
There is no substitution of prohibited substances such as mung beans (*māṣa*) and the like. This is because there is a prohibition.
Indeed, a prohibition must pertain to the act of procurement (*upādāna*), not to the qualification for the rite (*adhikāra*).
Straightforward. Page 31. Prohibition is of two kinds: perceptible and inferable.
The perceptible will be explained as being of many types.

The inferable is also remembered as being of seven kinds: that which is inferable from tradition (smṛti), that which is inferable from custom (ācāra), that which is inferable from a prohibition (niṣedha), that which is inferable from an explanatory passage (arthavāda), that which is inferable from a mantra, that which is inferable from expiation (prāyaścitta), and that which is inferable from punishment (daṇḍa).

Among these, that which is to be inferred from Smṛti is, for example, "one's own gotra woman is not to be married," and so forth. That which is to be inferred from custom (ācāra) is, for example, the prohibition of breaking the fast at a time designated as Harivāsara.
That which is to be inferred from a prohibition is, for example, the prohibition of a qualifier [implied] by the prohibition of a qualified object.

The assumption based on explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is of two kinds: that which is assumed from independent explanatory passages, and that which is assumed from explanatory passages supplementary to another injunction.
The first of these is also twofold: that assumed from explanatory passages concerning defects, and that assumed from explanatory passages consisting of statements of established facts.
An example of the first is the Smṛti rule: "In the case of false swearing, there is a defect equal to that of one who speaks the truth twice over."
And by speaking falsely, one incurs the fault of false accusation.

The second type is as follows: in the context of the *agnihotra*, there is the statement, "Therefore, they burn the calf for ten nights after it is born. Since it is stated as an established fact that the cow should not be milked for ten nights following the birth of the calf, a prohibition is inferred because such a description would otherwise be inexplicable; this is like the injunction: "The cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni is never omitted on the new moon and full moon days."

A prohibition that is to be inferred from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) as a supplement to another injunction is, for example, the prohibition of *māṣa* beans inferred by the passage "Indeed, these [beans] do not take up the sacrificial offering" (*na vā ete māṣān havir gṛhṇanti*), which serves as a supplement to the injunction "Therefore, one should resort only to forest [food]" (*tasmād āraṇyam evāśrīyāt*), just like the injunction "For he holds [the ladle] above for the gods" (*upari hi devebhyo dhārayati*).

Furthermore, a prohibition inferred from a mantra is also twofold, like an injunction: first, by inferring the status of a prohibition from the very negative particle (*nañ*) occurring within the mantra itself as a statement of the present; second, by inferring another sentence containing a prohibition.
The first example is the *mṛtpa*.
The second type is, for example: "The unintelligent man finds his food in vain.

That which is determined by expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is, for example: "If one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should happen to encounter impurity due to birth or death (*sūtaka*), what is the expiation in that case? He should offer an eight-potherd sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) to Agni Tantumat.
That which is determined by punishment (*daṇḍa*) is, for example, as stated in the *Karmapradīpa*: "On the day of the sacrifice, if the moon is seen in the direction of the Śraddhāruṇī..."
Having offered oblations there with the Vyāhṛtis, one should give a staff to a twice-born man.
Thus [it is said].
This is not a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), because there is no officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).

And in this case, since the rule regarding the staff (*daṇḍa*) is to be understood as applying specifically to the preparatory rite (*anvādhāna*) on the preceding day, it is by that very rule that the prohibition is established.

Prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), negation (*niṣedha*), is of four kinds according to its possibility, having as its objects genus (*jāti*), individual (*vyakti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*), even when it is to be inferred from the Smṛti and other sources.
Among these, the first is, for example, the prohibition of chickpeas (*caṇaka*) and so forth at a *śrāddha* ceremony.
Marīci states: "Kulattha beans, chickpeas, and kodrava grains should not be given at a *śrāddha*."
The prohibition of a specific individual is, for example, the prohibition of those afflicted by disease and so forth at the *śrāddha* ceremony itself.
Yājñavalkya states: "One who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is one-eyed, and likewise the son of a remarried woman... and so on.
Because words such as *rogya* are etymological (*yaugika*), they denote individual instances (*vyaktivācakatva*).
An example of the negation of qualities (*guṇaniṣedha*) is found in the *Marīci*: "And all *kaṅkakā* [birds], as well as those that are tasteless."

An example of the prohibition of action is as stated by Vriddha-Manu: "Even when enjoined during the fertile period, one should never approach a woman. Furthermore, this prohibition—derived from the Smritis and other sources—is twofold: that which pertains to ritual duties (*kṛtya*) and that which pertains to human ends (*puruṣārtha*).
Among these, the first [type] is exactly as previously stated, being fourfold.
The human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is also fourfold, based on the distinction between the objects of genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*).
Among those, an example of the prohibition of a genus as a human goal is the prohibition of *masūra* beans and the like.

For just as facing eastward is prescribed as dependent upon eating, but not the act of eating itself, so too here, it is only the lentils and such that are prohibited as dependent upon the act of eating, but not the eating itself.
This is a prohibition of a substance held by a person, as in the rule: "One should not eat what is left over" (*ucchiṣṭa*).
This is because the word *ucchiṣṭa*, being etymological (*yaugika*), denotes a substance.

A prohibition of qualities for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is, for example: "One should not eat what is white. This is because a substance that has become moldy through the passage of time possesses the quality of being white. A prohibition of action for the sake of the person is, for example, the Smṛti rule cited by Manu: "Wine is indeed the impurity of foods, and evil is called the impurity."
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink *surā*.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, prohibition—such as that found in the Smṛtis and other sources—is of two kinds:
that which has a visible purpose and that which has an invisible purpose.
Everything previously cited pertains solely to matters of invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
An example of a matter of visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) is [the prohibition of marriage] with a woman who lacks the *Arohiṇī* [signs], and so forth.
As stated by Vijñāneśvara: "In the case of women who are diseased and the like, there is indeed a contradiction with visible reality."
Prohibition (*niṣedha*), such as that prescribed in the *Smṛtis* and other texts, is also twofold:
that which has as its object merely human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) and that which has as its object duty alone (*kṛtya*).
The first is, for example, the prohibition of sexual intercourse and so forth during ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), religious observances (*vrata*), and the like.
The second is, for example, the prohibition of meat even though it is prescribed for the *śrāddha* rite:
"In the Kali age, one should avoid these five: an unmarried girl (*akṣatā*), a cow, meat at a *śrāddha*, honey, and procreating a son through a brother-in-law."
Thus says the *Nigama*.

Likewise, [it says]: "And for Brahmins, the *śāmitra* [fire] alone. However, the prohibition found in the *Smṛtis* and other sources regarding the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is of a single kind, pertaining solely to the domain of the human goal.

The prohibition of human goals (*puruṣārtha*) concerning objects that are merely human goals is of two kinds: those concerning objects obtained through passion (*rāga-prāpta*) and those concerning objects obtained through injunction (*vidhi-prāpta*). The first is, for example, the prohibition of liquor for humans as cited from the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra].
The second is, for example, the prohibition of Vedic study for women in the sixth book, in the section beginning with "Of her, only what is stated" (*tasyā yāvaduktaṃ*, 6.1.6.24).

The scriptural prohibition (*śrauta-niṣedha*) is perceptible; it is also fourfold: prohibition of a genus (*jāti*), prohibition of an individual (*vyakti*), prohibition of a quality (*guṇa*), and prohibition of an action (*kriyā*).
Among these, an example of the prohibition of a genus is: "Therefore, silver should not be given outside [the sacrificial ground].
An example of a scriptural prohibition of an individual is: "One who has not performed the *Agniṣṭoma* sacrifice should not perform the *Sāṃnāyya* offering."

Because the term *asomayājin* is etymological (*yaugika*), this is a prohibition of the agent (*kartṛniṣedha*) alone, not a prohibition of the action (*kriyāniṣedha*). This is because, as in other cases, there is a prohibition of an enjoined action; thus, in the tenth [book], the option established by that very [prohibition] is resolved by a counter-exception (*prati-prasava*) in the rule "one should bring that at the *samiṣṭayajus*," since otherwise there would be no option due to the lack of a possibility of performance. An example of a scriptural prohibition of an accessory (*guṇaniṣedha*) is found in the sixth book, seventh pāda, tenth section (*adhi0 10*), regarding the *āghāna* (fire-consecration): having prescribed "one cow should be given... twelve cows should be given," etc., it then states, "an unlimited number should be given."

In that regard, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), this is a negation of all the previously mentioned numbers; however, an example for this must be sought elsewhere. An example of a scriptural negation of an action (*kriyāniṣedha*) is: "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice."

The scriptural prohibition (śrauta-niṣedha), moreover, is of two kinds: that pertaining to ritual action (kṛtya) and that pertaining to human purpose (puruṣārtha). Among these, the scriptural passage cited previously is one pertaining to ritual action. That pertaining to human purpose is also fourfold, based on the distinctions of genus (jāti), substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), and action (kriyā).
In that regard, the prohibition of a class for the sake of human purpose is as stated in a general injunction: "One should not eat *kalañja*, nor garlic, nor *gṛñjana*.
Here too, the prohibition applies to the class alone, according to the reasoning given regarding the prohibition of *masūra*.
A prohibition of a substance is perceptible, as in: "One should not converse with a woman in her courses," because the term *malavadāsā* is etymological (*yaugika*).
The prohibition of a quality serves a human purpose when it is perceptible, such as the prohibition regarding quantity: "One should not drink from a vessel that is entirely full.
A scriptural prohibition serving a human purpose is the prohibition of action, as stated by the author of the Vārttika in his commentary on the word *nañ*: "One should not harm any living beings.
Every perceptible prohibition has only a visible purpose; indeed, there is no such thing as a perceptible prohibition with an invisible purpose.

The scriptural prohibition (*śrauta-niṣedha*) for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*) is threefold: that which has as its object merely what pertains to the person (*puruṣārtha*), that which has as its object merely what pertains to the ritual, and that which has both as its object.

The first type is also twofold: that which concerns an object obtained through natural inclination (*rāga-prāpta*) and that which concerns an object obtained through a mandatory injunction (*vidhi-prāpta*).
Among these, the first is, for example: "Even though [the eating of] meat from a black antelope and so forth is for the sake of the person..."
Prati-pratiṣedhaḥ means negation.
The prohibition is an auxiliary part of the ritual here, by virtue of its dependence on the context.
This was stated in the section on grammatical derivation (*vyākaraṇa-adhikaraṇa*; Vārttika, p. 284).

A prohibition that pertains to both the person's own purpose (*puruṣārtha*) as established by an injunction and the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) is, for example: "The initiated one does not give gifts, he does not offer oblations.
One that pertains solely to the purpose of the sacrifice is, for example, as already cited: "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* [sacrifice]."

The prohibition concerning both that which is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and that which is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is as follows: the scriptural prohibition for the sake of the sacrifice is, for example, "One should not speak untruth," which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

Here, the prohibition is also of two kinds regarding its purpose: first, when one has resolved upon barley (*yava*) for a sacrifice but then uses rice (*vrīhi*), the untruth consisting in that resolution—which is for the sake of the sacrifice—is prohibited; second, it also applies to the speaking of untruth obtained through worldly desire, which is for the sake of the person. This was stated in the third [book] at the sūtra: "An action not connected with a sacrifice would be a restatement of a connection based on a fixed rule" (*akarma kratusaṃyuktaṃ saṃyoganniyānuvādaḥ syāt*). Thus it is said.
However, a prohibition concerning a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) based on Vedic scripture is of only one kind:
that which has as its object a human goal in general.
There is no such thing as a prohibition concerning a human goal that has as its object a mere thing (*artha-mātra*), because such an example is impossible.

For even though it is studied as an independent injunction (*anāramyādhīta*), it does not have the person as its purpose, because that would entail the necessity of postulating a separate fruit. It is, however, rightly understood as having the sacrifice as its purpose, since the sacrifice is brought to mind through the prohibition of an action that is otherwise practiced during the performance of the sacrifice. Furthermore, a prohibition concerning the person as such is of two kinds: one whose object is obtained through natural inclination (*rāga-prāpta*) and one whose object is obtained through a scriptural injunction (*vidhi-prāpta*).
The first is, for example: "One should not harm any living beings," and likewise, "One should not eat *kalañja*; therefore, one should not touch the *upa*.
These two prohibitions—against the eating of *kalañja* and the touching of the *upa*, which are prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*)—are for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
The second is, for example, the prohibition of the *sānnāyya* offering for one who has not performed the *Soma* sacrifice;
that too results from the prohibition of the agent.

Furthermore, prohibition is sixfold: general prohibition, specific prohibition, counter-prohibition (*pratiprasava*), prohibition in the form of permission (*abhyanujñā*), prohibition in the form of a restrictive conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), and prohibition in the form of a systematic restriction (*vyavasthā*).
Among these, the first is, for example: "One should not harm any living beings.

The second is, for example: "One should not kill a Brāhmaṇa. The third is as follows: when there arises a conflict—such that the injunction "one should not harm" would preclude the injunction "one should not kill a cow," and the cow would thus be excluded—the counter-exception (pratiprasava) is made in the Kali age by the rule: "The cow and the sacrificial animal are unblemished."

A prohibition in the form of permission is, for example, found in the second Āraṇyaka of the *Aitareya* Upaniṣad: "This is the path; this is the action... therefore, one should give at the right time, and one should not give at the wrong time.

Here, the statement "one should not give at the [wrong] time"—referring to states such as poverty—does not establish a fault in the act of not giving. For it is not logical that a fault should attach to one who eats himself when guests and others have arrived, even if he has only enough for his own meal; otherwise, it would contradict such traditional narratives as: "O Brahmins, a sacrifice performed with a single measure (*prastha*) of barley flour is not considered equal [to other sacrifices]."
Therefore, "one should not give at the wrong time" is merely a permission; thus he gave there. It was a slight fault.
A prohibition in the form of a summary is as follows: "There is no following the dead [in death] for a Brāhmaṇa, according to the injunction of the Veda"—this is a general prohibition.
"Having ascended a separate funeral pyre, a Brāhmaṇa ought not to go [to the other world]"—[this is a specific one].
By this, [the rule] is restricted to specific cases.

As for the example regarding what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), Paiṭhīnasi states in the Hemādri: "Nālikā, potīka, kusumbha, and aśmantaka—these, when smeared with ghee, are among the vegetables that are not to be eaten.
This [statement] prohibits the eating of those [vegetables] when they are smeared with ghee.

"One should not avoid the *kandūḍha* white eggplant or the *kūṣmāṇḍa*," thus it is restricted to specific cases by the statement of Devala. Furthermore, the prohibition is established in seven ways: by place, by time, by agent, by action, by occasion, by preparation, and by result.

In this regard, a prohibition established by place is as follows: "Certain [sects] do not accept the month beginning with the dark fortnight," according to the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana*. A prohibition established by time is as follows: "The twice-born must perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) in the evening and morning, as enjoined by the Veda."

"One should not eat in between [the two meals]. This prohibition is restricted by the agent (*kartṛ*), as in: "One who has not performed the *Soma* sacrifice should not offer the *Saṃnayya*. An example of a prohibition restricted by the ritual action (*karman*) is found in the *Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra*: "For one desiring offspring, the first is the nine- or seventeen-night rite called *Navasaptadaśāhorātra*; for the eldest son born of an eldest wife, the second is the rite called *Viṣuvat*."

The third is named Gaura for one who has rivals; the fourth is named Āyu for one desiring heaven or one free from deceit; the fifth is named Jyotiṣṭomātirātra for one desiring prosperity; the sixth is named Viśvajittirātra for one desiring cattle; the seventh is named Triṣṭutirātra for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); the eighth is named Pañcadaśāhorātra for one desiring valor; the ninth is named Saptadaśāhorātra for one desiring food; the tenth is named Ekaviṃśatirātra for one desiring stability; the eleventh is named Asoryāmātirātra; ... the twelfth is named Abhijittirātra for one with rivals; and the thirteenth is named Sarvastomātirātra for one desiring to enjoy all things. Thus, having introduced the thirteen nights with the phrase "thirteen Atirātras," the prohibition of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup—which is established in four ways by the sūtra stating, "Of these, the first four have the *ṣoḍaśin*"—is performed.
The negation by way of a cause is a negation.
The prohibition is established as follows: "The abandonment of Smārta rites [occurs] except for Rāhu’s [eclipse] during impurity (*sūtaka*).
This means that, other than Rāhu’s [eclipse], there is an abandonment of Smārta rites during other forms of impurity; this is understood through the force of the meaning.

Now, an alternative meaning for this was stated previously (Bālakrīḍā, p. 16, ll. 3–4). True; nevertheless, because the capacity to convey two meanings is grasped through the sentence's internal coherence and its intended purport, and since both meanings are consistent, Hemādri has explained it accordingly.

The restriction established by way of specific ritual application (*saṃskāra*) is as follows: in the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*, after prescribing the spreading of grass (*paristaraṇa*) everywhere for those performing the *dharma*-oblations with the words "having spread [the grass] around," it states, "the spreading of grass is optional in the case of oblations of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*). Here, the word "optional" (*akṛta*) expresses a prohibition, while the restriction is stated for other cases.

The prohibition is established by way of its result, as for example: "Whoever should threaten a Brāhmaṇa, him one should punish with a hundred; whoever should strike him, with a thousand; whoever should draw blood, for as many years as the scattered dust particles he might gather, for so many years he shall not recognize the world of heaven. Therefore, one should not threaten a Brāhmaṇa, nor strike him, nor draw his blood. For the results of the prohibited acts are indeed the results of the prohibition; and in these cases, the prohibitions are established by those very results.

This sixfold general prohibition is further divided according to the distinctions of *śrauta* (Vedic), *smārta* (traditional), and so forth, as well as by the distinctions established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Among these, we have provided examples of *śrauta* and *smārta* prohibitions as far as possible.

Likewise, since the distinction between that which is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and that which is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is also applicable within the sixfold general prohibitions, we have occasionally provided some examples of *kratvartha* and *puruṣārtha* prohibitions as far as possible.
The others also are to be sought.

Regarding the prohibition of actions for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthakriyā*), there is a scriptural classification of prohibitions; that which was previously mentioned as "having bathed" (*snātau*) is also sixteenfold, because the action for the sake of the sacrifice is of sixteen kinds.

To illustrate: in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*), the modified rite (*vikṛti*), and the rite consisting of neither archetype nor modification (*aprakṛtivikṛtātmake karmaṇi*), the prohibition is of equal application, as in: "He who, having purchased [the Soma], performs the work of a servant falls like iron."
Thus, in all cases, negation is taught in these forms:
namely, the negation of an indirectly contributory (ārādupakāraka) action and the negation of a directly contributory (saṃnipatyopakāraka) action.
Of these, the first is also threefold: pertaining to the archetype (prakṛti), the ectype (vikṛti), and pertaining to an unprecedented rite (apūrvakarman).
Among these, the first is as follows: "One should not perform the first two [offerings].
That which pertains to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is also twofold: that which concerns what is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) and that which concerns what is directly enjoined (*upadeśa*).
The first is, for example, the prohibition of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings: "One does not perform those two offerings."

A prohibition concerning an *ārādupakāraka* (remotely contributory) rite taught in a modified context (*vaikṛta*) is, for example, found in the Kātyāyana Sūtra regarding the Agnīṣomīya animal sacrifice: after prescribing two remotely contributory offerings made while looking at the animal with the two mantras "Svāhā to the gods" and "To the gods, svāhā," it prohibits them with the statement, "And he does not offer these.

A prohibition of an *ārādupakāraka* action taught in connection with a new rite (*apūrva-karman*) is, for example, the prohibition of the singing of the Vāravantīya and other Sāmans in the Agnyādheya rite, expressed as: "The Brahman priest does not sing the Sāmans."

In this context, since the singing of the *sāman* by the *brahmán* priest is not otherwise established, it might be suspected that because the passage is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) and does not prohibit the *sāman*-chanting, the *sāman* must be sung constantly. However, it has been stated in the tenth book (10.8) that since a mere restatement would be purposeless, this is indeed a prohibition of the *sāman*-chanting; the word "brahmán" (*brahma*), moreover, is a restatement referring to the Brāhmaṇa priest.
Furthermore, the prohibition of an action that provides direct assistance (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) is also threefold:
pertaining to the archetype (*prakṛti*), pertaining to the ectype (*vikṛti*), and pertaining to a rite that is neither an archetype nor an ectype.

The prohibition of actions pertaining to the *prakṛti* (archetype) that arise from a combination [of factors] is also twofold: having as its object an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and having as its object a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

That which has a visible purpose is also twofold: having as its object the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of a substance distinct from the disposal (*pratipatti*), and having as its object the disposal itself.
That which pertains to an original action (*apūrvakarman*) is likewise threefold, and that which pertains to a modified action (*vikṛti*) is likewise threefold.

That prohibition, though threefold according to its relation to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), is further divided into two types: that which has an explicitly taught subject (*upadiṣṭaviṣaya*) and that which has an extended subject (*atidiṣṭaviṣaya*).
Thus, twelve distinct varieties of prohibition are established.
The illustrative examples for these twelve are now stated.

In this context, (1) there is the prohibition of a direct (*saṃnipatyadṛṣṭa*) purposeful action inherent in the nature [of a substance], as in: "In the *madhuparka*, in the *soma*, in water, and in the *prāṇāhutis*, a twice-born man does not become impure by remnants.
Here, because *soma* is a male substance, the prohibition applies to the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*), which is a direct auxiliary (*saṃnipāti*) intended for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

(2) The prohibition of an act performed for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) that is incidental (*saṃnipātika*) and distinct from the disposal (*pratipatti*) belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*): for example, after prescribing "having approached the fire" (*agnim upasthāya*) when the *agnīṣomīya* animal has been sacrificed, the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* states, "Therefore, one should not approach it," thereby prohibiting the incidental act of approaching for the purpose of purifying the fire. (3) The prohibition of a disposal belonging to the archetype: for example, the prohibition in the Kali age [of the rule] "licking the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle."

(4) The prohibition of a *saṃnipātin* act with a visible purpose occurring in a rite that is neither a primary (*prakṛti*) nor a modified (*vikṛti*) form, as in the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*: "One should not perform the shaving, the seasonal rites, the collection [of materials], the *sāman*, the four-footed [verses], the *ājya*, the forest [products], the full [oblations], the *anvārambhaṇīyā*, the serpents, and so forth," which prohibits shaving during the *ādhāna*. (5) The prohibition of a *saṃnipātin* act with a visible purpose other than the disposal (*pratipatti*) occurring in a rite that is neither a primary nor a modified form, as in the very same *Kātyāyana-sūtra* mentioned above, where there is a prohibition of waking at night—which is a *saṃnipātin* act serving a visible purpose for the sake of observing the ritual details.

(6) The prohibition of the ritual practice pertaining to the body of one who has undergone a transformation not inherent to their nature is as follows: In the passage, "They cremate the fire-maintainer with this fire and the sacrificial vessels," the consecration resulting from the rite of *ādhāna* is prescribed as a form of ritual treatment for that body. However, regarding such a person who has committed suicide, the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*—after mentioning self-destruction and other acts in the verse beginning "Death by one's own will, O Brahmin"—prohibits the performance of funeral rites, including cremation, stating: "For them, there is no [need for] purificatory baths or consecrations. Thus, the cremation is forbidden.

(7) The prohibition of a concurrent action taught for the sake of an auxiliary element belonging to a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), such as the prohibition of taking the *ṣoḍaśin* cup in the *atirātra* sacrifice.

If the proponent (siddhāntin) should say this,

In the phrase "not in the *anuyājas*," the word "not" (*na*) is a supplement to the sentence; specifically, it is a supplement to the word "anuyāja"—which constitutes a portion of the sentence—and not a supplement to the word "he performs" (*karoti*).

Consequently, the negative particle (*nañ*) here does not signify a simple negation (*pratiṣedha*), but rather signifies an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), due to its nature as mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).

Because an option (*vikalpa*) is illogical; for if there were a connection with the negative particle (*nañ*) and the verb *karoti*, an option between injunction and prohibition would have to be accepted,

Therefore, so that the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*) does not arise, the word *anuyāja* and others, accompanied by the negative particle (*nañ*) in that context, function as injunctions; they would constitute a partial modification of [the original injunctions] such as "he chooses. The established conclusion regarding prohibitions is as follows: in sentences stated as prohibitions, such as "One should not eat *kalañja*," or "One should not eat garlic," because there is no [independent] action—since they are not subordinate to an injunction for a ritual act (*kalpa*) that contradicts eating—there would be an action [of avoidance]. Regarding these *prājāpatya* penances, there are three scriptural statements: "His vow," "He shall not look at the rising sun," and "By this much he becomes released from injury. Because of the meaningfulness of the prohibition; for only in that case does the prohibition of those [sacrifices] ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* and those known as the *anujñājña* become purposeful and effective, and not in the previous state of ending with the *iḍā*.

Therefore, the established conclusion is that the preceding Śāṇḍilyavidyā ends with the Śākvara hymn. Furthermore, because the prohibition is characterized by urgency, it cannot apply to another location.
For this reason as well, the preceding Śāṇḍilyavidyā must end with the Śākvara hymn.
Because this prohibition is characterized by urgency;
this prohibition was stated with a sense of haste:
"They performed the Prāyaṇīya offering."
"That was concluded with the *śaṃsad* [the *śaṃs* formula].

Then the Asuras, thinking 'Let us sacrifice,' hurried; having made it end precisely with that *śaṃsad*, they attended to it in haste," and "They offered the *ātithya* [hospitality rite]; that ended with the *iḍā*.
