And this state of being characterized by haste is possible only when the preceding [rite] ends with the *śaṃsad*.

Therefore, that prohibition of the *patnīsaṃyāja* and so forth does not belong to another region nor to a subsequent region, but rather belongs precisely to the preceding region. Consequently, it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that it terminates with the *śaṃyuvāka*.
[End of] Ke. [This concludes] the definition of the verbal productive force (*śabdabhāvanā*) of the prohibition.

Even the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*) in the form of prohibition is, in general, of the nature of turning away; and specifically, in its form as a prohibition, it must be established in the same manner as an injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, that [prohibition] is the cause of desisting, consisting of the property of the desister, in the form "I am causing this person to desist," because it functions as a mental cognition (*mānasapratyaya*) for the desister, just like an impulsion (*pravartanā*).

Furthermore, that [injunction] is threefold in the worlds by virtue of its superior, inferior, and middling authority through various means (*dharma*). Since there is no such thing as a "person" (*puruṣa*) in the Veda, and because it is impossible for [an injunction] to exist in the form of a specific intention belonging to such a person, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth alone possess the power of instigation (*pravartaka*). Therefore, a fourth mode, which is essentially contained within those [three], must also be admitted.

That very [fourth mode] is what is celebrated as "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*) or "negation" (*niṣedha*). However, in common worldly usage, the conventional employment of these two terms is merely metaphorical, being derived from the conventional usage of the term "injunction" (*vidhi*).

In that regard, however, this much is the distinction: there is no grammatical rule (anuśāsana) that establishes the expressive power (śakti) of the optative suffix (liṅ) for the purpose of prohibition, as there is for the purpose of instigation—namely, the rules [Pāṇini 3.3.161] stating "the optative is used in injunctions, invitations, and so forth."

Nevertheless, since beginningless *saṃsāra*, having observed that the cessation of the prompted [action] follows upon hearing a negative suffix (*nan*) whose meaning is not superimposed [upon the root], and having—through the method of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*)—concluded that the capacity for denotation belongs specifically to the negative suffix and so forth when they cause such cessation, the learner (*vyutpitsu*) comes to grasp the capacity for "causing cessation" (*nivartanā*). This occurs because the teacher’s conventional usage of terms like "I have been turned away by the teacher who turns me away" would otherwise be inexplicable; just as the capacity for "causing to act" (*pravartakatva*) is grasped through the inexplicability of the usage of "causing to act," so too is the capacity for "causing cessation" grasped through the inexplicability of the usage of "turning away. This [capacity] constitutes the function of that [negative suffix].

As it has been stated in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa-vārttika*: "The negative particle (*nañ*) is not a prohibitor when it is not connected with an injunctive [word]; for where it is joined with an injunction—as in 'one should not drink here'—it does not function there as a mere negation. (314) "In that case, the agent of non-existence certainly does not itself restrain the person."
(315) Thus [it is said].

Here, the capacity of the negative particle (*nañ*) for exclusion (*nivartanā*) is stated. However, in the *Nañvāda* (Vākyapadīya 2.237, p. 212, lines 8–10), in the passage beginning with "For a prohibitive injunction is indeed another kind of injunctive" and ending with "or else there would be the contingency of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by the meaning of the suffix," it is further stated that by the term "injunctive" (*vidhāyaka*), the optative suffix (*liṅ*) itself has the sense of prohibition.

And likewise, when there is an intention to express the verbal suffix (*liṅ*) as that which is to be negated, it is said that the repetition applies to that very suffix and not to the negative particle (*nañ*).
However, in the passage beginning with "But for those who," the previous view is also stated.

In this regard, although there is no difference in the fact that the suffixes such as *liṅ*—which denote an instigation (*pravartanā*) whose object is not the state of non-existence (*amāva*)—are capable of expressing abandonment, and likewise, in the view that particles such as *nañ* express cessation (*nivartanā*), the suffixes such as *liṅ* (when combined with *nañ*) merely restate an instigation already obtained through passion (*rāga*) and so forth; and in the view that the suffixes such as *liṅ* express cessation, particles such as *nañ* merely restate the absence of activity toward the meaning implied by them—nevertheless, in the first position, there is parsimony (*lāghava*), because one need only postulate four distinct powers for the four indeclinables in the rule "amānonāḥ pratiṣedhe" [Pāṇini 2.2.6], rather than postulating a separate power for each individual word.

Because it would result in the cumbersome assumption of multiple additional capacities for the suffixes *liṅ*, *loṭ*, the fifth mood (*pañcamalakāra*), and the various *tavya*-type suffixes, the position that the capacity [of negation] resides in the suffix is not tenable. Thus, the author of the Vārttika, by expressing this twice, indicated his preference for the view that the capacity [of negation] resides in the particle *nañ*; this is what is implied [in the Bālamanoramā, p.
...]. A rule of prohibition (*pratiṣedhavidhi*) culminates in the meaning of *nañ*.
The *bṛhatī* [verse] consists of the *gāyatrī* as its foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*). There are 8 syllables in each quarter-verse (*pāda*). Example: "āpaḥ pṛṇīta meṣajam" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.9.7).
One desiring a firm foundation (pratiṣṭhā) should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the Tryahi-śenātirātra.
Bhāṣya 10.4.10.20: For one desiring a firm foundation, one should recite twenty-one *sāmidhenī* verses at the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
twenty-two—
For one desiring stability, he should recite [the verses] either in the case of the *pratihoma* sacrifice; (10.5.8.27).
For one desiring stability, (6.5.12).

The *pratihomas* (substitute offerings) are not to be performed when there is a displacement [of the sacrifice]. A twenty-one-night rite has been prescribed by Kātyāyana (*Bālambhaṭṭī*, p. 34), because even in that case the initiation (*dīkṣā*) has already been performed and the prohibitions regarding the *homas* and other rites have not been observed.
For one desiring stability (*pratiṣṭhā*), one should lead [the water] with an earthen vessel (*mārtika*).
(Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya 4.3.14).

Retrospective oblations (*pratihoma*) are not to be performed; this is the position of Jābālaka regarding the *udavasānīya* [concluding rite] and the rites to be remedied (*pratisamādheya*). This applies even when there is a displacement from the *agnihotra*. See Mīko., p. 116, under "rites such as the *udavasa*."
See *Mīmāṃsākośa*, page 282, under the entry "Even when there is a postponement of the *sānnāyya*, [the rule] regarding the *pratihomas*";
and see the same work under the entry "The qualification (*adhikāra*) regarding the *agnihotra* and so forth."
The *homās* are not to be performed when there is an extension (*utkarṣa*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*. [Sūtras 6.5.12.40–41]. The *pratihartṛ* is a subordinate (*puruṣa*) of the *udgātṛ*;
he is known as belonging to the third group.
Mīko., p. 1844: "In the case of the displacement of the Jyotiṣṭoma, the counter-oblations (pratihomas) are directly perceived" (2742). Because of direct instruction, this [is] the blue dawn.

Bāla, p. 131: By means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and [other means] such as verbal testimony (*śruta*), those [elements] such as verbal testimony that are obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) are sublated. Vārttika 3.1.14, p. 841: Direct perception lacks the capacity to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding *dharma*.
1.1.4: In the case of direct perception, the sense organ (*indriya*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and its contact [with the object] is the operation (*vyāpāra*).

Maṇi, p. 19: The principle is that when there is perception, what need is there for inference? Since perception and inference consist of cognitions that differ in their degree of immediacy, perception is more powerful. Sāhasī, 162: When perception is available, it is not proper to resort to inferential construction.
Or [as stated] at Vārttika 2.1.6, page 488: "Smṛti inferred on the basis of a gross [evidence] that contradicts perception is sublated.
Therefore it is said: 'Having recognized Smṛti as being based on conduct, one regards it as equivalent to Śruti;
thus, their authority, being separated by an intervention, is cast far away.'"

According to the *Vārttika* (of Kumārila), section 1315, part 2: There is no absolute rule that whatever is determined as a duty through perception and inference must necessarily be completed once it has been commenced. However, if there is the perception of undesirable consequences (*aniṣṭa*) from not completing it, then it must indeed be completed; this is because of the direct instruction (*pratyakṣopadeśa*) based on perception and inference [Sūtra 2.1.4]. This is the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
The designation (*samākhyā*) is also indeed primary because it has no other scope; therefore, there is a combination (*samuccaya*).

In cases such as "of the *udgātṛ*s" and so forth, because that [designation] denotes them and because it expresses consumption, by that statement there is no non-specification, no exclusion, and no sublation of the agent of the cups (*camasa*), such as the *hotṛ* and others; for a single sentence cannot have the dual purpose of both injunction and prohibition.
And because another [agent] is seen in the case of the cup (*camasa*).
In the Siddhānta, this sūtra is intended to refute the objection regarding the reason [stated in the previous sūtra]:
"He distributes them at the Camasins' [rite], and he carries them away with the vaṣaṭ-offerings. This is because, in that statement, other Camasins are seen in relation to the cup (camasa).
For if there were only one [Camasin], only a single cup would need to be offered with the vaṣaṭ-offerings.
In this context, it is stated that many cups (camasas) are to be brought forward;
therefore, it is understood that there are multiple consumers in respect of the cups.
Consequently, the combination [of the cups] is indeed based on the occasion of consumption.

In the phrase "from the observation of others" (*anyadarśanāt*), the compound is to be analyzed as "from the observation of others" (*anyeṣāṃ darśanāt*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to indicate another reason.

Which [reason]? Because of direct instruction (*pratyakṣopadeśāt*); that is, its superiority [over inference] consists in its capacity to produce immediate understanding, as opposed to an inferred extension (*kalpyātideśa*).
VI. 213|8. The Determination of Direct Perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*).
First of all, the definition "direct perception is cognition produced by the sense faculties" is not [correct], because all cognition whatsoever is produced by the mind (*manas*).
Therefore, the author of the Sūtras states: "Perception is knowledge produced by the connection between a sense faculty and its object.

The ancient teachers maintain that there is no over-extension [of this definition] to the perception of the Lord (Īśvara), because the cognition of the Lord is distinct from perception, just as it is distinct from inference.
According to them, perception is knowledge whose instrument is another cognition.
This is because inference, comparison, verbal testimony, presumptive testimony, and recollection possess the nature of cognition due to having cognition as their instrument (*jñāna-karaṇaka*).

Nor should it be argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) and perception of a qualified object through its qualifier (*viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya-pratyakṣa*), since those two have indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) as their instrument;

for an uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇa-kāraṇa*) possessing an operation (*vyāpāra*) is the instrument, and while indeterminate cognition and the like may be causes, they are not instruments because an operation is defined as that which is produced by the cause and itself produces the effect.
Alternatively, it is the state of being a cognition devoid of the universal (jāti) of "retention" (dhṛti) produced solely by a cognition that is itself produced [by another].

Since the sense organ is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in every perception and its contact is the operation (*vyāpāra*), such properties as inferentiality (*anumititva*) and so forth are absent in perception; thus, the definition is consistent.
However, qualities such as conceptualization (*savikalpakatva*) are not universals (*jāti*).
And that perception is twofold: non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

Among these, magnitude (*mahattva*) is the cause for perception in general. Furthermore, it [magnitude] exists by way of inherence (*samavāya*) in the perception of a substance; by way of inherence-based co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the perception of qualities, actions, and universals; and by way of inherence in that which is inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamaveta-samavāya*) in the perception of qualities, actions, and universals.
In the case of visual perception (*cākṣuṣa*), the cause is manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*) and the conjunction of light with a manifested, non-overpowered color.
Regarding this, some maintain that "in the visual perception of time and so forth, largeness, manifested color, and the like are not causes.
In the case of tactile perception (*sparśana*), however, it is manifested touch (*udbhūtasparśa*) [that is the cause], and not color as well.
Therefore, air (*vāyu*) is also perceptible by the sense of touch (*tvak-pratyakṣa*).

Thus, being the object of a substance-perception produced by an external sense-organ is not delimited by the effect of manifested color (*udbhūta-rūpa*); rather, it is simply the presence of visual perceptibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth—this is parsimony (*lāghava*).
Some maintain that "even in mental perception (*mānasa*), magnitude (*mahattva*) is a cause."
[The action] must be inferred. Some, however, say that action is not perceptible, but is instead inferable from disjunction and subsequent conjunction;
therefore, they claim that magnitude (*mahattva*) is not the cause for its perception.

*Maṇi*, pp. 19–21. Inference based on a relationship perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣato dṛṣṭasaṃbandham anumānam*) is, for example, the cognition of another form (*anyākṛti*) upon seeing the form of smoke.
Where the relationship is grasped between two particulars (*viśeṣa*) themselves, that is called an inference concerning particulars (*viśeṣaviṣaya*) based on a perceived relationship.
Vaidyanāthī: Furthermore, because they are preceded by perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference, analogy, and verbal testimony have no causal efficacy regarding *dharma*. Bhāṣya 2.1.4.

It has already been stated in the section on the "Abundance" (*bhūmādhikaraṇa*, 2.1.17) that, just as with the hearing of a perceptible [text], the mantras—excluding those words heard in the context of bricks—are restricted to those very [mantras] denoting bricks.
Bhāṭṭa 5.137. The definition of perception: Perception is direct cognition.
Direct cognition is cognition of the thing-in-itself (svarūpa).

"One's own form" means its unique, specific form (*asādhāraṇarūpa*). That cognition which functions by means of the very unique essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a given object is direct perception (*sākṣātpratīti*).

If it is argued that conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), being qualified by universals (*jāti*) and so forth, would not be perception because its object is a common form (*sādhāraṇākāra*), we say no; for even in that case, the unique form is also taken as an object.
In this context, the definition [of perception] is the unique form (*asādhāraṇākāra*), not the exclusion of common forms (*sādhāraṇākāravyāvṟtti*).
In inference, however, because there is a cognition of a relation through a common pervading form (*sādhāraṇabhūtavyāpakākāra*), there is no directness (*sākṣāttva*).
Alternatively, direct cognition is a cognition preceded by positive concomitance (*anvayahita*).

If it is argued that the cognition of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) would not be perception because it is mediated by the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*), and that the first mental cognition (*manasapratyakṣa*) would not be perception because it is mediated by a preceding cognition, [we reply: by "unmediated" (*avyavahita*) we mean not being separated by another cognition whose object is included within its own object; thus, the definition is consistent. Or alternatively: the definition of perception is the direct awareness of the existence of an object as it is determined at its own time; that is, the definition of the perception of an object is that the cognition belongs to the same time as the object with which it is connected. (Pratyakṣasūtra 2745)
The meaning is "the object.
However, in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is no fault, because it also has as its object an entity connected with its own time.

If it is argued that inference would then be perception because it concerns the present, [we reply: no, for even that [inference] is delimited by its own time; rather, it is delimited precisely by the time of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

However, the capacity of inference has been established as being delimited by the time of the pervasion (*vyāpti*); otherwise, if it were not so, one would have to postulate a separate capacity for the inference of the past or the future, which would be a fault.

Therefore, it is established that perception is direct cognition (*sākṣātpratīti*). (Pravi. p. 26) By the term "perception," since there is an understanding of the concomitance (*sāhitya*) of all cognitions at a single time—just like the concomitance of the primary acts according to the rule of performance—it follows that each individual cognizer must perform all the primary acts simultaneously; such is the understanding of the meaning, because of the synthesis of the constituent elements (*padārtha*).

The example is as follows: regarding the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, one performs the *upākaraṇa* (preliminary consecration) for all the animals together, saying, "Having performed this for all the animals, the *niyojana* (binding) is to be done. This is *padārthānusamaya* (the performance of each individual ritual act for all objects).
According to the Bhaṭṭa school (Bhāṭṭa 5.1.21), because of the explicit scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavacana*), the general injunction (*codaka*) is weaker.

When there is an explicit statement (*pratyakṣavacana*) and the alternative is otherwise untenable (*anyathānupapatti*), there is no recourse to a scriptural text obtained through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Vārttika 2.1.3, p. 589. An explicit injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*) is not [itself] a non-injunction (*avidhi*).

1. An injunction regarding the mere meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha-mātra-vidhi*); 2. An injunction regarding the meaning of the verbal root along with its qualities (*saguṇa-dhātvartha-vidhi*); 3. An injunction regarding the meaning of the verbal root having some specific object (*kiñcid-uddeśyaka-dhātvartha-vidhi*); 4. An injunction regarding the meaning of the verbal root as qualified by something having some specific object (*kiñcid-uddeśyaka-viśiṣṭa-dhātvartha-vidhi*); 5. An injunction of another [element] which has the meaning of the verbal root, etc., as its purpose (*dhātvarthādy-artha-anyavidhi*); 6. An injunction regarding the relationship between two other [elements] within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthe anyayoḥ saṃbandha-vidhi*); 7. An injunction regarding the relationship between two other [elements] through the verbal root being subordinated (*dhātvarthāvṛta-prakṛtyena anyayoḥ saṃbandha-vidhi*); 8. An injunction regarding the relationship between two others, setting aside the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthaṃ muktvā anyayor eva saṃbandha-vidhiḥ*). (Bālakrīḍā, p. 22). Direct injunction (*pratyakṣa-vidhi*) is stronger because of its abundance.

When the *puroḍāśa* is directly enjoined in the middle of the ritual procedure (*tantra*), even though there are many *devasū* oblations, they are established by *prasaṅga* (extended application) through the properties of the *puroḍāśa*.

This is because of the contradiction with the principle stated in the *Vārttika* (213.14, p. 589): "Since [the requirement] is established by a direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*), that which is based on inference (*ānumānika*) is not obtained" (the reading 'kaḥ' appears in the Ānandāśrama edition). Thus, when there is a direct injunction for sacrifice in the form "One should sacrifice with Soma," there is no room for the [inference of] substance and deity in the sentences concerning the Aindravāyava and other cups.
The *Pratyakṣa-sūtra* [is defined as]: cognition;
the meaning of cognition.
It will effect that much;
nor does it produce anything else.
For the suffix, enjoining the sacrifice for the sake of the fruit, is not displaced.
And one who is intent upon non-arising will not conceptualize arising. [2.2.129, p.
561] What, moreover, is this "condition" (*pratyaya*) which is correct knowledge? It is that which is expressed through association with name, genus, and so forth.
*Bṛhatī*, page 38:
[A name] by connection with a name, as in "Devadatta";
by connection with a genus, as in "This is a cow."
By connection with a quality, as in "this is white";
by connection with an action, as in "he cooks";
by connection with a substance, as in "the man with a staff."
The suffix (such as the optative *liṅ*) is straightforward; it impels the person toward the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) in its own sense.

Therefore, although the suffix sometimes occurs in connection with a sacrifice, the efficient force—which is the meaning of the suffix—does not accept the sacrifice within itself [as its object], even though the sacrifice is proximate.
A suffix denoting a *kāraka* (participant in an action) would denote it by means of its capacity alone, not by way of a substance (*dravya*), because the latter is not itself a *kāraka*.
Vārttika 3.4.143, p. 933.
The base and the suffix together express the meaning of the suffix.
239 (this sentence appears many times in various editions; it should be consulted under the section "prakṛti-pratyayau").
By means of the suffix (*pratyaya*), both the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) and singularity (*ekatva*) are indicated.
In that case, when there is proximity to a single causal factor (*kāraka*), the relationship occurs first, as in the injunction: "One should sacrifice an animal" (*paśumālabheta*). (Vi. 4.1.5)

Designation by means of a suffix with a specific [meaning] is not contradictory, even when a qualifier has already been expressed previously, because of the difference in the powers (*śakti*) of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).
For, having heard [the word], the existence (*sattā*) of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is expressed by the suffix.

Bhāṣya 10.4.6.9: In view of the absolute non-existence of the suffix, it is more appropriate for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) to possess a definition characterized by not abandoning its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā*). Since there is no abandonment of the primary meaning through a definition that does not abandon its own sense, this [ajahatsvārtha] alone is logical according to the maxim of the "one who eats from a brass vessel" (*kāṃsyabhojinī-nyāya*), as in the example: "The man rose up. (Soma 3.5.7).
The suffix expresses the related [meaning], while the others express only their own forms;
however, in reality, there is no such thing as the expression of a related meaning at all. (Bālamanoramā, p. 43)

The employment of the suffix and the base alone is impossible; that is, the occurrence of the base and the suffix in isolation is impossible. Consequently, the suffix must necessarily be repeated for the purpose of connecting it with the verbal root. (Vārttika on Pāṇini 2.2.11, p. 463). Because the base and the suffix function only toward their own respective meanings, the connection between them is understood as occurring in the interval [between those two].
The rule is that "suffixes convey their own meanings as connected with the meaning of the base" (pratyayānāṃ prakṛtyarthānvitasvārthabodhakatvam).

In the case of a suffix (*pratyaya*), there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by dissimilarity (*vairūpya*): [on the one hand], in the act of cleansing (*saṃmārjana*), "the cup" (*graham*) is subordinate with respect to the singular number; [on the other hand], by means of the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyāvibhakti*), there is primacy (*prādhānya*) in the object to be indicated (*lakṣya*) with respect to the cup. (Bālamanoramā, p. 181). The meaning of the suffix is primary, not the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

According to Yāska’s traditional teaching that "names have substance as their primary meaning" (Nirukta 1.1), because the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is predominant, and because its connection with the primary element is more highly esteemed, it is by virtue of the word-hearing (*padaśruti*) that the number is connected only with the animal (*paśum*), and not with the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) by virtue of the affix-hearing (*pratyayaśruti*).
Nor should it be argued that grammarians maintain the predominance of the meaning of the affix;
for that [predominance] is established as pertaining specifically to the domain of the verb (*ākhyāta*).
Furthermore, in order to prevent number (*saṃkhyā*) and other such factors from being primary, it is necessary to restrict the application of that [general] recollection.

Thus, since even the connection of number with the *kāraka*—which is understood through the direct hearing of the suffix (*pratyayaśruti*)—must be abandoned, its status as an auxiliary to the sacrifice (*yajñāṅgatva*) becomes impossible to attain by resorting to the sentence (*vākya*).

Nor should one suspect that, when oneness (*ekatva*) connects with the animal (*paśu*), because the animal itself is connected with the *kāraka* while qualified by oneness, oneness too must be an auxiliary to the sacrifice; for [the animal] is already [connected] as something distinct [from the oneness].

Since it is impossible for a cognition to cease its operation [after one function], the word "one" first conveys the relation of oneness with the animal; however, because it is impossible for that same word to subsequently convey the relation of the case-role (*kāraka*) to that very entity as qualified by oneness, there must be a simultaneous connection between both number and the case-role. Consequently, since it is logically untenable for the case-role to connect with the animal as qualified by number, the case-role connects only with the animal itself.
To this, it is replied:

If the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) were predominant, then because that [meaning] would be subordinated to the *kāraka*, the *kāraka* would become a subordinate attribute (*guṇa*). Consequently, the *kāraka* expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix could not be construed with the action (*kriyā*).
Therefore, the meaning of the nominal stem is not predominant; rather, it is only the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) that is so.
Even there, since a sentence has the action as its primary focus and the *kāraka* exists for the sake of that [action], the predominance belongs to the action alone, and not to number and the like.
However, the traditional statement of Yāska regarding cases such as "the cow is white" (*gauḥ śuklaḥ*) refers to instances where there is no connection with a verb.

Nor should it be argued that, because the agent (*kāraka*) is already restricted by the number [denoted] by the suffix (*pratyayaśruti*), there could be no connection of the animal (*paśu*) with that agent by means of the weaker word-hearing (*padaśruti*);

for when it is stated that "one must sacrifice with an agent characterized by a single number," there exists an expectancy for a specific detail—namely, "of what kind is that [agent]?"—and thus, since the animal is compatible [with this requirement], its connection is not contradicted even though it is established by a weaker means of knowledge.

Based on the view that the suffix expresses both the *kāraka* (grammatical relation) and number separately, the meaning of the suffix is [the *kāraka*], because the *kāraka* expressed by a single suffix is more proximate than the nominal stem expressed within a single word. This is the meaning of the suffix.
Furthermore, because it is the primary factor, number is connected only with the *kāraka* (case-role) and not with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
In reality, however, number and the *kāraka* are not denoted separately; rather, it is the *kāraka* itself as already endowed with number that is expressed.
Consequently, since the number is already integrated with the *kāraka* at the very stage of its expression, there is no possibility of its subsequently connecting with the nominal stem.
Thus it should be understood;
Soma. 4.1.5, p. 352. Maṇḍana holds that the meaning of the suffix is *bhāvanā*.

Page 109, Vārttika 2.2.11, page 380: The Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas) maintain that the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the substratum of the operation (*vyāpāra*) and the substratum of the result (*phala*). Maṇi, page 109: Maṇḍana holds that the meaning of the suffix is the favorable operation (*anukūlavyāpāra*).
Page 109: The Naiyāyikas maintain that effort (*yatna*) is the meaning expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

Page 106: The author of the *Ratnakośa* holds that production (*utpādana*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix. Page 107: The established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that *bhāvanā* is the effort denoted by the suffix, whether as suchness (*ākhyātatva*) or as effort-ness (*yatnatva*).
Page 110:
The meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is not obtained in isolation.

Since both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix are traditionally recorded as expressing their own respective meanings, and because of established usage, the suffix—occurring among those who understand it when its form must necessarily be employed as preceded [by the base]—expresses its own meaning only as being joined with that which has already been formed [by the base].

Therefore, the meaning of the suffix is never obtained in its pure form. (Vārttika 2.2.11, p. 465). "Even though the meaning of the suffix is the same, it is differentiated by the difference in the verbal root. (Vārttika 2.2.12, p. 468). "The base and the suffix always express the meaning of the suffix together."

"Because of its predominance, the meaning of the suffix is determined to be *bhāvanā*. (2.2.11, p. 380). For by means of the meaning of the suffix, the "manner of performance" (*itikartavyatā*) is required; [the suffix] expresses that which is to be done.
Bhāṣya 9.1.1.1, p. 1639: For the procedure (itikartavyatā) is connected with the meaning of the suffix, not with the sacrifice.
Rather, the sacrifice—being composed of prior and subsequent stages—grasps the procedure, not [the sacrifice] in its completed form.

Thus, the principle has already been described. (For it is stated in the Bhāṣya at 9.1.1.1, p. 1639: "Indeed, the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*) is required by the meaning of the suffix; [the suffix] tells what is to be done, not that 'what kind of sacrifice is it?'"—*Ḍup.* 11.1.210).
The expressibility of the meaning of the suffix as *bhāva* has been established [Vākya-p.
Regarding the suffix-meaning of *bhāvanā* in relation to the base-meaning (*prakṛti-artha*)—[the rule] "the base and the suffix... [Vākya-p. 2.2.19].

Since primacy (*prādhānya*) is taught by the traditional rule (*smṛti*), "But of those two, [the meaning] of the suffix is primary," and since primacy is thus understood—as in the case of "he threshes rice" (*vrīhīn avahanti*)—the status of the sacrifice as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) [of that action] is established by the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) itself.
(Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Bhāṣya 2.2.15, p. 90).

Regarding *soma*: since the cognition that "the remnant (*śeṣa*) must be set aside for the sake of the subsidiary rites (*śeṣakārya*) precisely at the time of the primary performance" exists as the cause for setting aside the remnant, and because the setting aside of the remnant necessarily follows while that cognition persists, the setting aside occurs immediately after the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) has been satisfied by that very [cognition].

However, in the view of the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*), although there is no setting aside of the remnant due to the requirement of the subsidiary rites, and thus the setting aside of the remnant lacks the character of being occasioned (*naimittikatva*), there is no obstruction of the occasion; therefore, at the time of the subsidiary rites, all [of them]...

They say that, just as in the case of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) and the like, there is the postulation of a collection of words expressing the injunction of the qualifier and so forth, or rather, the postulation of another sentence that conveys non-difference (*abheda*).

In every respect, it is established that the primary meaning [of the noun] possesses the status of a qualifier (*prakāratā*) in relation to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) through a relation of difference, a status common to the second case endings and others.

By this, the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), which holds that the referent of a noun such as Caitra—or the referent of the nominative case—is construed with non-difference (*abheda*) with the agent and so forth expressed by the verb (*ākhyāta*)—is also refuted.
This is because there is no evidence for postulating a separate semantic derivation (*vyutpatti*).

As for the argument that in cases such as "he cooks slightly" (*stokaṃ pacati*), in order to ensure the non-difference relation (*abheda-anvaya*) of the nominal object "slightly" with the act of cooking, there must necessarily be a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) such that: "the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a word co-occurring with the aforementioned noun is the cause for a verbal cognition delimited by being a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of a noun co-occurring with a meaningless case-suffix (*sup*) through the relation of identity"; and that by this very rule, the non-difference relation of Caitra and others with the agent and so forth is established through fitness (*yogyatā*)—that is not correct.
The nominative case following the word *caitra* cannot be meaningless, as that would contradict Pāṇini and other authorities, and it would also contradict the actual text.

The meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) *stoka* is "smallness" (*stokatva*). Although the meaning of the accusative case serves as a secondary indicator (*lakṣaṇā*) for the object [of the action], and although the cognition produced by a word whose gender is coreferential with that object is a cause [of verbal cognition] by way of its being the qualificand of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), this is possible because, even when there is no mention by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the specific [qualificand] is established through the force of another cause, namely the form of the cognition itself. This is the general direction [of the argument].
*Rahasya*, pp. 57–67. Regarding the three *upasad* days beginning with the first: as in the *agnicayana* sacrifice, there are six *upasad*s. (5|1|2).
In the modification of the *sāmidhenī* verses, the completion of the required number is achieved by repeating the first and last verses three times and inserting the remaining names [of the deities].
(10|5|8|27–33). However, in all cases, the primary motivator (*prayojaka*) is simply the agent’s utterance.

Whether that [genitive] is of the nature of agency (*kartṛtva*) in general or a specific type of agency is another matter; this is the first consideration regarding the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the nominative case (see *Rahasya*, p. 38). Furthermore, even if the aforementioned type of presentation (*upasthiti*) arising from a word ending in the nominative case is accepted as a cause—by virtue of being common to both number and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)—what, according to your view, is the motivator for the nominative, the third person, and so on? It cannot be the expression (*abhidhāna*) of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth as the motivator, because you do not admit such [an expression].

Nor is there [a distinction] between the expression and non-expression of number; for in all cases, the primary meaning of the first case (*prathamā*) is the presentation [of the object] as devoid of any qualification by number.

It is precisely this [qualification by number] that motivates the use of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth, while its absence is what motivates the use of the first case—such is the consistent rule.

Even so, if one does not intend to express instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and the like as a mode (*prakāra*), then in your view, since wood (*kāṣṭha*) and other factors would enter into the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) through the relation of instrumentality and so forth, there would arise the undesirable consequence of such usage as "Caitra cooks wood, pot, and rice" (*caitraḥ kāṣṭhāni sthālī odanaḥ pacati*). [Objection: Since those [wood, etc. do not connect with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) for you, and because the meanings of nouns connect with that [verbal meaning] only through the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*), such an application of the usage does not occur. [Response: Even so, just as in the case of "He sees curd" (*dadhi paśyati*), the occurrence of usage characterized by the instrumentality of wood (*kāṣṭha-karaṇatva*) must certainly be prevented.

It should not be argued that, according to the *Mānamanohara*, since everything is construed with the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*) alone, and since even the referent of a noun such as "Caitra" is admitted there to be connected [to the action] through a relation of difference (*bhedasaṃbandha*), it follows that even things like firewood would logically be construed [with the verb]. For precisely out of fear of such an undesirable consequence (*prayogāpatti*), I too postulate a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for words expressing kārakas (factors of action) as expressed by me: that when a non-different nominal referent (*abhinna-nāmārtha*)—characterized by its own gender and number—is connected to an action, the requirement is for the presence of case-endings such as the accusative (*dvitīyādi-vibhakti*), which are distinct from the connection of gender to the inflected word (*subanta*). This is because [the nominative ending] serves the purpose of indicating the gender [of the noun] itself.
It is clear that [the definition] is intended to refer to its own syntactic relation (*anvaya*).

Here, even in cases such as "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*), where the referent of the noun (*nāmārtha*)—namely Caitra and so on—is directly related to the action, the phrase ends with "is distinct from" (*bhinnam iti antam*).

In cases such as "Bring the cook" (*pācakam ānaya*), although the case-role (*kāraka*) is expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix and the like, when the word "cook" (*pācaka*) is related to the effort conducive to bringing, it is necessary that the status of being the object (*karmatva*), presented by the accusative case-ending, serves as the medium; therefore, it is stated that [the noun] "denotes its own [referent]" (*svabodhakatva*).

Since it will be explained later that even in cases such as *pācaka-pada*, there is an understanding of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is necessary for the wood and other factors to be construed with that [operation] by means of case-endings such as the accusative, which express their status as instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth.

For this very reason, in accordance with this view, the *Kaustubha* and other works do not accept the direct connection of the nominal stem-meaning (*prātipadikārtha*)—which possesses a gender relation conveyed by the case-ending—with the productive operation.
Therefore, they maintain that in expressions such as *pacati-kalpam*, the nominative case occurs when there is an intention to express the mere meaning of the nominal stem.
That is not so;

for even in this case, since there is a desire to express a relation of difference between the *bhāvanā* expressed by the suffix *-kalpa* (when used in an *īṣadasamāsa*) and [the action], the occurrence of the genitive case would be unavoidable.

Furthermore, even in an *īṣadasamāsa*, because such a nominal stem-meaning stands in a relation to the aforementioned action, it would involve a deviation [from the rule] due to being mediated by the meaning of the accusative or other case endings.

Therefore, we consider it logical that although grammar elsewhere functions to convey the *vṛtti* (the specific relation between stem and suffix), in the present case it is intended solely to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). Some, however, hold that in expressions such as *pacatikalpam*, because the verb *tiṣṭhati* is supplied, the meaning is "the activity of cooking (*pākabhāvanā*) persists slightly [less than expected]";

and according to this view, even the word *pacati* connects with the meaning of the suffix *kalpa* through the relation of difference (*bheda*), since they are both presented within the same syntactic unit.
Therefore, they say that even though the suffix *kalpa* is denotative (*vācya*), the first case ending is justified because it is construed only with the verb "he stands" (*tiṣṭhati*).
That is not correct;
for if plurality were intended to be expressed, the form *pacanti-kalpaḥ* would also result.
Thus, it is established that in this [view], the attainment of the form of being the motivator for everything is easily achieved, whereas it is not so in your view.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that having offered the Āśvina, the Aindravāyava should then be offered.
Or rather, because it is the principal act and the others are subordinate, the placing [of the oblation] is likewise [not to be postponed].
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the prima facie view;
the offering is not to be deferred.

Because the offering (*pradāna*) is the primary element; for the offering is not subordinate to the drawing (*grahaṇa*). However, the placing (*sādana*) is indeed subordinate to the drawing, and therefore it is postponed accordingly.
Therefore, there is no withdrawal of the offering;

Why? Because the offering is primary, as it is the means for the attainment of the fruit.

Thus it is heard in the Śruti: "Having piled the fire-altar (*agni*), one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī," and "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava."

In that regard, there arises the following deliberation: Is the Sautrāmaṇī to be performed only within the framework (*tantra*) of the *Cayana* sacrifice, or at its own specific time? Regarding this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) argues as follows: Because the subsidiaries are conjoined with the principal rite, and because there is a constant relationship between the subsidiary and the principal, the subsidiaries must share the same time as the primary rite.
Those whose time is the very same as the time of the principal [rite] are called "mukhyakālāni" (having the principal's time).

That which is the time of the principal is indeed the time for the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). Therefore, in the case of the *agni-cayana* and other such rites, the *sautrāmaṇī* must be performed even when [the principal rite] is not yet completed.
"But when [the Sāmidhenīs] have ceased, the injunction [should apply], because of its similarity to them, at the proper time.
By the word "but" (*tu*), he sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
When they have ceased—that is, when the *sāmidhenī* verses in the sacrifice or the Vājapeya rite have concluded—the injunction [of the *ṛc*] applies.

By the expression "having piled" (*citvā*), which denotes the priority of the time of piling, it is indicated that the Sautrāmaṇī is to be performed after the completion of the piling along with its constituent parts; likewise, by the expression "having sacrificed" (*iṣṭvā*), there is an injunction that the Bṛhaspatisava is to be performed immediately after the completion of the Vājapeya along with its constituent parts.
Therefore, the performance of the Sautrāmaṇī and other rites does not occur in the middle of the piling and so forth;

"Having the same time" (*sakāla*) means having the same [ritual] occasion due to the commonality of their *prakṛti* (archetype).

Because the Sautrāmaṇī is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *iṣṭi*, its "same time" is the time of the *parvan*. And because the Bṛhaspatisava is a modification of the Jyotiṣṭoma, its "same time" is the spring.

Bāla, p. 81: The primary action (pradhānakarma) is that which directly provides assistance [to the agent]. Ku. 2.1.4.9: Because it is for the sake of the primary action (pradhānakarmārthatvāt). 2767: Because it is for the sake of the primary action.

The *stotra* and *śastra* are principal acts (*pradhānakarman*). Vi. 2.1.5. Principal acts serve the purpose of the person; they belong to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Bhā. 3.8.2.4. Since the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) exist for the sake of the principal acts, there would be a distinction of acts in performance due to that distinction [of the principal].

Since the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) exist for the sake of the principal rites (*pradhānakarman*), due to their distinction—and because of the distinction between those principal rites in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*)—there would be a difference in the performance, that is, a difference in the execution, of the auxiliaries.
The performance of the auxiliaries must be carried out separately for each principal rite;
thus, "there is no difference for each principal rite" is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Furthermore, there would be a disruption of the sequence if simultaneity were to occur.

If the subsidiaries were performed simultaneously by adopting a single performance for the sake of all primary rites, there would be a disruption—that is, a contradiction—of the sequence of the primaries.
Thus, the Āgnīṣomīya sacrifice would begin before the Āgneya sacrifice, along with its subsidiaries, had been completed.
The *Sāṅgāmeya* section is concluded. Therefore, if the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] were performed after the *sāman*, there would be no violation of the sequence (*kramakopa*).

By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that just as the actions such as removing the embers (*aṅgārāpohana*) and those involving contact (*saṃsparśa*) differ for each primary rite (*pratipradhānam*), so too do the *āghāra* libations and other such elements.
However, for equal [subsidiaries], simultaneity (*yaugapadyam*) should occur because they are taught by a single term and no distinction is perceived.
The word "tu" (but) introduces an alternative view:

there is no non-distinction with respect to each primary act; rather, there would be simultaneity—that is, performance all at once—of those acts that are equal to the primaries by virtue of their agent, location, and time.

Because of the instruction by a single word—namely, because of the instruction of the principal acts by the single expression "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—and because no distinction is apprehended, that is, because no distinction is stated or known;
it is not known whether these rites belong to the Āgneya sacrifice or to the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice. Therefore, there is no non-difference [of the procedure] for each principal act.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
There would be a single purpose and a common substratum (*dravyāvaya*).
Regarding what was stated—“there is a subversion of sequence if there were simultaneity”—he says in response to that:

Because they have a single purpose—that is, because they share one aim or produce a single result—the principal acts perform their function collectively. However, for the sake of performance, there must be non-interruption, which constitutes a sequence. Therefore, there is an order in their application.

Whence is there a violation of the sequence? Since even the auxiliary parts (aṅgas) perform their function through cooperation, there is no violation of the sequence even with respect to the assistance rendered.
Thus, Kāmukāyana cites the observation of another scriptural purpose;
and likewise, there is no repetition of the auxiliaries for each primary act.

Regarding this, the teacher Kāmukāyana held the view that there is an observation of another purpose [in the scripture]: “Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day, thirteen on the new moon day.
Because that is the logical principle, there should be a sequence of performance for the sake of the refinement (*saṃskāra*), since the refinement is for that purpose.

As for what was stated regarding the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*)—namely, that there should be repetition even for those factors that assist from a distance (*ārādupakārin*), just as there is for those that act by direct contact (*saṃnipātin*)—[that is rejected].
Regarding this, he says:
because they follow that principle; according to the principle that "those who act in combination perform the action together," there is no repetition of the subsidiaries for each primary rite.
Those subsidiaries which possess that principle are "tanyāyāni"; it is because they are of such a nature [that there is no repetition].
Because of incapacity—that is, because it is impossible—there would have to be a sequential performance of actions such as the removal of embers;
for it is not possible to perform the cooking of another sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) by means of the removal of embers intended for one.

Since the refinement consisting of the removal of embers and so forth is for the sake of that [cooking], and since the purpose is the cooking itself, it is proper that this action be performed for each individual sacrificial cake.
Therefore, even when there is a repetition of the *saṃnipātin* (indirectly contributing) [auxiliaries], there is a repetition of the *naropakarins* (human-performing auxiliaries).
Even one who is not directly touched [by them] is [included] because of such a nature.
That which is touched is the *saṃnipatyopakārin* (directly contributing auxiliary).
That which is non-contacting (*asaṃspṛṣṭa*), distantly assisting (*ārādupakāraka*), such as the substratum (*ādhāra*) and so forth— even though it is non-contacting and distantly assisting—
is that which must be repeated for each primary act (*pradhāna*).
Because they are for that purpose— that is, because the subsidiaries exist for the sake of the principal— or because of their capacity, like a lamp. To this, it is replied:
These auxiliary elements (aṅgas), even when performed in the presence of only one [principal], are capable of benefiting all the principal acts.

This is like a lamp: just as a lamp lit in the presence of only one Brāhmaṇa dining in a certain place benefits all of them, so too, due to the pervasive power of the auxiliaries, there is no repetition for each individual principal act.
The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. However, in common worldly usage, it would apply according to the injunction for each primary element.
The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says:
In the world, it is observed that even a single lamp serves the purpose of illuminating many things;
therefore, it is logical to proceed from that purpose.
But in the present case, it is by virtue of the injunction (*vidhi*).

Because [the subordinate action] exists for the sake of the primary action (pradhānakarma), the definition of the primary action is established by the injunction itself; thus, it is taught that [the subordinate action] may be either beneficial or non-beneficial. Consequently, there would be a distinction between the substratum and other factors for each primary action.
Kāmukāyana [holds that] the sacrifice is performed once, because of the contradiction regarding the measure.

Because of the contradiction with the stated measure of oblations—namely, "fourteen on the full moon day" and "thirteen on the new moon day"—the teacher Kāmukāyana held that the Āghāra and other offerings should be performed only once.
This restatement of what was previously mentioned is for the sake of the subsequent argument:
"But because the injunction serves another purpose, there would be a single performance, which would constitute a departure from the scriptural text."
Regarding this, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says:

"It is enjoined"—here, by the word 'vidhi' (injunction), the subsidiary (aṅga) is meant. Since the subsidiary of the injunction exists for the sake of another, that which is recited in its proximity is for the sake of the primary; therefore, there would be a single transgression of the scriptural audition (śruti), for a single audition is contradicted [by such an interpretation].
If, however, the reading is *asakṛd ijyā*, then there should be repeated sacrifice (*asakṛd ijyā*).
Otherwise, if it were a single sacrifice (*sakṛd ijyām*), there would be a transgression of the revealed scripture (*śruti*); this is how the construction should be understood.
Regarding the statement, "Fourteen [oblations] on the full moon day, thirteen on the new moon day," the oblation (*āhuti*)...
Because it is the principal element, there is an injunction regarding the substance that has become the principal: the mantra "O Agni, eat of the Soma.

According to the principle stated in Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 64—"Since it is possible for the principal to be the qualificand (viśeṣya), it is improper [to treat] the qualifier as the qualificand"—it is appropriate to conceive of [the deity] as the qualificand.

*Rahasya*, p. 41: "Even when there is a difference in the primary [acts], there is a *tantra* (commonality of procedure) for ignorant persons in a single ritual action" (*pradhānabhede'py ekasmin karmaṇi ajñānāṃ tantraṃ*);

1.1.12.14–67. The maxim of the "overthrowing of the chief wrestler" (*pradhānamallibarhaṇanyāya*): Wrestlers are those skilled in hand-to-hand combat; among them, the "overthrowing of the chief" refers to the manner of bringing him down to the ground, specifically the joining of his back with each of the other primary wrestlers.
The meaning of the maxim is that just as one who desires victory seizes the primary opponent, thereby making the defeat of the others—who are weaker in comparison—easy;
so too, in the *Sāhasrī* (2.1.3), beginning with the words "He sees [but] not the sound," the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause was repeatedly raised and refuted by the Sūtras themselves.

Therefore, following the maxim of "striking down the champion wrestler" (*pradhānamallibarhaṇa*), he extends this principle to all other views by stating: "By this, all [theories of causes such as atoms and the like] are explained."
Śāṃbhā. 1|4|8|28: In the optional sacrifices (kāmyeṣṭi), the low-voiced recitation (upāṃśutva) is for the sake of the primary rite alone.
3|8|19|35-36: The purificatory rites for the sacrificer (yajamānasaṃskāra) are for the sake of the primary rite alone.
3|7|16: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the initiation (dīkṣā) and the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) are for the sake of the primary rite alone.
3|7|116–12. Even though it possesses the status of a primary substance capable of functioning as the principal factor, it is that very [substance] which is the material cause.
6|1|2|140–42. Ignorances have a single effect consisting of the form of the principal [cause].
Bhāṣya 1|1|12|15–10. The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the reality of the phenomenal world (prapañca) alone is logical.
The Vedāntins maintain that [the ultimate reality] is characterized by being distinct from both existence and non-existence (Maṇi, pp. 48–51).
Regarding the Smṛti statement, "A water-station (prapā) should be established" (Bhāṣya 1.3.11, p.
160), it is understood that water-stations and tanks are for the benefit of others, not for the sake of religious merit (dharma).

And so it is seen in scripture: "Like a watering-place on a desert path" (RV 6.45.31), and "They gather water from the pits" (ŚB 5.3.5.19). This is the principle of the analogy of the watering-place (*prapāmelananyāya*). 1.3.12, p. 166. The Principle of the Analogy of the Watering-Place.

Just as at a *prapā*—a water station—many living beings from various directions meet, and in the second moment they depart by different paths, so too do transmigrating souls (*saṃsārin*) meet and separate. [This is] like the repetition of a collective recitation (*samūhāvṛtti*), such as when students desiring to master a *prapāṭhaka* (a section of a text) recite each part repeatedly. *Sāhasrī*, 898. This refers to the repetition of a group [of verses]. Just as students wishing to repeat a *prapāṭhaka* recite each individual portion many times, so it is here.
VI. 10|5|25. Regarding the root *vas* preceded by *pra*: this is the application when one who has set out from his own place dwells elsewhere.
Su. p. 772: In the case of "prapra," the word *praprī* itself should be employed, according to the principle of the *irā* passage.
This is the purpose of the preceding section (and not of the eighteenth section).
Duhkha 1.1.9.18: A strong [element], merely because it is strong, does not take up that which is employed by a weak [element], but rather only when there is a conflict.
*Parākrama*, p. 26: A modification (*vikṛti*) based on desire (*kāmyā*) is *tantriṇī* (governed by its own procedure), because desire operates swiftly;
however, the archetype (*prakṛti*) is that which causes the operation [of the procedure] (this is a hypothetical discussion, *kṛtvācintā*).
A means of valid cognition is indeed a means of valid cognition.
Only the capacity to reach an object not previously apprehended should be accepted as the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Logicians, however, maintain that *prabhākara* is the means of valid cognition,
and its nature as *prabhā* consists in being a veridical experience.
And correctness (*yāthārthya*) consists in having that [object] as its qualifier (*prakāra*), delimited by not having anything else as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
Furthermore, the nature of experience (*anubhavatva*) is a specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*),
because it would be untenable [to apply it] in a sequential or reverse order.
Bhāṭṭa 1.1.2:
[The sequence of] the means of knowledge with respect to the object (or purpose) is established by its logical necessity in the proper order and its impossibility in the reverse order.
Bhāṭṭa 1.1.2.
A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is defined as that which brings about contact with the object.

When a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) arises toward it, a counter-cognition (*pratipakṣavijñāna*) arises having that very [subversion] as its cause. (Bṛhatī, p. 19). An example of such a means of valid cognition is the Smṛti text: "Having sipped water, one should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*)," and so forth.
VI. 1|3|4 | First, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the Mīmāṃsakas are of many kinds, distinguished according to their divisions.

To explain: they are sixfold—namely, perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), verbal testimony (*śabda*), comparison (*upamāna*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and non-existence (*abhāva*).
In that regard, perception is sixfold, distinguished as visual and so forth.
Inference is twofold: that based on general observation and that based on specific observation.
Each of these two types is further twofold: for one's own sake and for the sake of others.

However, a distinction between purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) and purely negative (*kevalavyatireki*) [inference] is not accepted, because it is stated in the *Ślokavārttika*, Anumāna 167: "And the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) would likewise [be required]; it is not that which is delimited by the three forms. This is because it is declared that a mark devoid of the three forms cannot function as a logical reason (*liṅga*).
Furthermore, for the logicians, the inferential statement for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) does not consist of five members (*pañcāvayava*).
However, there are only three.

As it has been said: "Regarding that [fivefold reality], some say it is fivefold, others say it is twofold, and we say it is threefold—up to the point of illustration, such as the illustration itself."
Thus [it is said].
Perception, along with those called comparison, presumption, and non-existence, are merely the four worldly [means of knowledge].
Presumption, moreover, is the presumption of an unperceived object.
And there is presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*). The subsequent [presumption] is also of two kinds: worldly and Vedic.
Word (*śabda*) is also of two kinds: worldly and Vedic.
The Vedic [scripture] is also of two kinds, distinguished by direct instruction (upadeśa) and extended application (atideśa).
Direct instruction is also of two kinds: injunction (vidhi) and prohibition (niṣedha). Furthermore, direct instruction is of many varieties.

There are six factors that differentiate ritual acts (*karman*), namely: difference of word (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), name (*saṃjñā*), quality (*guṇa*), and a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*). There are six factors that determine application (*viniyojaka*), namely: direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), order (*krama*), and name (*samākhyā*). There are six authorities for determining order (*krama*), namely: direct statement (*śruti*), meaning (*artha*), order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), order of position (*sthānakrama*), order of the principal (*mukhyakrama*), and order of performance (*pravṛttikrama*). These are the six authorities pertaining to the five elements.

The five means of proof for the transference of ritual details (*kāryāpatti*) in the ninth book are: direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*), injunction by negation (*abhāvavidhi*), modification (*vikāra*), the word itself (*svaśabda*), and restatement of a prohibition (*niṣedhānuvāda*).
The sevenfold types of extended application (*atideśa*) will be explained later. These are the means of proof.
The Veda is the authority regarding dharma (Bāla, p.
8). Perception is not an authority regarding dharma (Bhāṣya 1.1.4).
An authority does not depend upon another authority for the determination of its object.
However, even a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) requires yet another means of valid cognition for the determination of its own nature. (Rjuvimalā, p.
66). That which does not present an object independently is not a distinct means of valid cognition.
Page 160. Authority (pramāṇa). That by which something is correctly cognized is an authority. Bhāṣya 1.1.5, page 59. Authority.

Even by investigators, worldly means of valid cognition (*laukika-pramāṇa*) must be followed. *Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 73. "Valid cognition is the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). *Vivaraṇa* 1.3.4, Section 2. Valid cognition.

A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that functions swiftly becomes established and serves as a sublater (*bādhaka*) for that which is not so. However, where even a swift means of valid cognition—such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the like—even when it has arisen, becomes itself unestablished due to defects such as distance and is thus uncertain, there a determination of the contrary object occurs without doubt, even by a slower means. *Ratnākara*, pp. 364–365. "Valid cognition is right conduct (*sadācāra*)."
Bindu 1.3.4: "Indeed, what is called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is an instrument (*karaṇa-kāraka*).
Rju-pṛ. 94: 'Whether worldly or Vedic, every means of valid cognition that is free from defects is relied upon for its own purpose; and in this [Self], there is no possibility of defect.'"

"Or [it may be otherwise]. (Vārttika 1.2.125, p. 784). The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding dharma and adharma are eightfold: injunction (*vidhi*), explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), mantra, tradition (*smṛti*), custom (*ācāra*), name (*nāmadheya*), supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), and capacity (*sāmarthya*). (Bhāṭṭa 1.4.20). These are the means of valid cognition. For perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone is not the only means of valid cognition; indeed, inference (*anumāna*) and the others are also means of valid cognition."
Furthermore, non-existence (abhāva) is determined as being nothing other than a form of direct perception (pratyakṣa) by means of the sixth [means of knowledge].

Vātsyāyana Bhāṣya on Nyāyasūtra 2.1.16–18, p. 452. There are six worldly means of valid cognition (pramāṇa): perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), comparison (upamāna), verbal testimony (śabda), presumption (arthāpatti), and non-apprehension (anupalabdhi).

There are six means of valid cognition regarding Dharma: injunction (vidhi), explanatory passage (arthavāda), mantra, name (nāmadheya), traditional law (smṛti), and the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra).
There are six factors that differentiate ritual duties (*dharma*): difference of word, repetition, number, name, quality, and a different context.

There are six means of proof for the knowledge of ritual duties: direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*).
There are six means of determining sequence: direct assertion, meaning, textual order, position, primary function, and customary practice.

The means of proof for extension (*atideśa*) are threefold: statement (*vacana*), name (*nāma*), and indicative mark (*liṅga*). The means of proof for modification (*ūha*) is one: displacement (*sthānāpatti*). The means of proof for annulment (*bādha*) are threefold, consisting of substitution (*pratyāmnāna*), prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), and loss of purpose (*arthalopa*).
Thus, there are thirty-one non-worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Some maintain that these means of valid cognition possess merely the status of auxiliary factors (*sahakāritā*), like the conjunction of light and so forth; others hold that here, positive injunction (*vidhi*) alone is the authority.

Maṇi, p. 13: The means of proof (*pramāṇa*) that assist the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) are sixfold, consisting of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*).
Mīmāṃsā: The means of proof are five, beginning with perception (*pratyakṣa*), for the purpose of cognizing real entities (*vastu*).

Or: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are exactly six: perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), verbal testimony (*śabda*), presumption (*arthāpatti*), and non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*)," according to the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "O Rāma, these six are joined together in the world; by them, everything is set ablaze. (Maṇi, p. 62). All means of valid cognition, whether they concern an object currently being utilized or not, bring about the manifestation of the self within their own scope; and for that very reason, the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference are described as their results.

Vā. 1|2|12|1, p. 106: When [an action] has been rendered free of expectancy by a stronger means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is the performance of that which possesses a weaker means of knowledge. 3|6|7|9: By the respective six means of knowledge, even all six means of knowledge are sublated; here, the sublation occurs through precedence (*prāsa-vādha*). 3|1|7|4, p. 860: The means of knowledge itself is primary; the means of knowledge itself is also the means (*upāya*).

Regarding the means of performance and the means of knowledge for the meaning of the Veda, there exists a relationship of primary and subordinate; the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is subordinate and not primary.
(Vi. 1.1.3) The function of the means of knowledge is characterized by the determination of the object.

*Ṛjuvimalā*, page 94: Even where a weaker means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is absolutely useless due to the absence of a subject matter, there the stronger [means] undergoes sublation in the form of a restriction, and thus the weaker attains predominance. For example, regarding the cup of the sacrificer (*yajamānacamas*), which is obtained by the name (*samākhyā*) through the delimitation of the *pratipad*—which is more powerful than the *vaṣaṭkāra* and other causes—the name, finding its scope elsewhere, results in the fact that it serves to consecrate a portion of the Soma, because another drinking [of Soma] performed by the sacrificer is enjoined for the purpose of consecrating the Soma.

Kau. 3|3|7|4, p. 367: It is accepted that even a weaker means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), when its object is a particular, may effect a restriction (*saṃkoca*) of a stronger means of knowledge whose object is a general one.

This is because, according to the principle of the relative strength of the objects of knowledge (*prameya-balābala-nyāya*), the restriction of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) regarding seasonal sacrifices by the Smṛti stating "In whatever region the deer are black" has been established.
1|3|17: An examination of the means of knowledge concerning Dharma.

1|2|3. The function of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is solely the comprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya*), and not the comprehension of a purposeful object; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the status of being an end (*upeyatva*) could never be comprehended. *Soma*, 1|2|1, p. 5. The non-sublation of a means of valid cognition (meaning its state of being unsublatable).
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3.1.7.4, page 829: When both means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are sublated, which one is to be examined as a valid cognition?
Since the object of consciousness is not established, there is the sublation of only one.

*Bṛhatī*, p. 204. Regarding two means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) of equal strength, when there is a conflict, a determination must be made based on relative strength. *Vārttika* 3.6.2.9, p. 1030: When two means of knowledge proceed together, that one which reaches the place of application later constitutes a "distraction" (*vikṣepa*) which causes weakness. However, once the application has been determined, even if [the contrary] becomes easily available through inference afterwards, there is nevertheless no such remoteness (*viprakarṣa*).

3|3|7|4, p. 831: It has been stated (at 3|3|7) that for means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose basis is established, there is sublation by what is already perceived, but not for those whose basis is merely hypothetical.
3|1|23|15: The establishment of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Su., p. 179:
Sublation characterized by the non-arising of a means of valid cognition occurs in cases of conflict between direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth.

Vārttika 6.1.9.14: The status of being a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntaratva*) is based on the inclusion of a unique cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*). *Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 74. A pseudo-means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*) is sublated by each of the six means of valid cognition according to its respective nature; here, sublation occurs through anticipation (*prāsavādha*). Vārttika 3.1.7.4, p. 860. Sublation by a pseudo-means of valid cognition does not always apply to a [genuine] means of valid cognition alone.

Vārttika 3.1.7.4, p. 829: The course of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) should be adopted in such a way that, when two possibilities exist, it does not contradict another means of valid cognition. Vārttika 3.4.1.9: The first section (lakṣaṇa) is for the purpose of investigating the means of valid cognition; the subsequent eleven sections, however, are for the purpose of investigating the objects of valid cognition (prameya). Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 533: The establishment of the determination of the objects of valid cognition is dependent upon the means of valid cognition.

Kaṇikā, p. 306: By means of the logic of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), although there is mutual dependence through the differentiation of the two parts, there is no mutual contradiction;

for both valid cognition and reasoning become firm [only] when taken together. Parimala, 3.4.1.1–5: *Vas.* states that being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) is the state of being a source of light (*prabhākaratva*).

Su. Pṛ. 2. Acceptance of five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-pañcāṅgīkāra*): [In the view of Prabhākara, there are five means of valid cognition excluding non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). Rju. Pṛ. 160. The nature of the examination of the means of valid cognition: The basis (*nimitta*) [of Dharma] need not be examined. For perception and the other [means of knowledge] are well-known means of valid cognition, and the scripture (*śāstra*) is included within them; therefore, that too need not be examined.
To this it is replied:

In the *prayāja* offerings, the injunction regarding the deities is based on the wording of the mantras;
however, words such as *samidh* and so forth are names of the ritual acts themselves.
Bhāṣya 9.2.20.59–60: In the *prayāja* offerings, there is no complete oblation (*sarvahoma*).
This is because, by the very injunction for holding the remnant of the *prayāja* as a means for performing subsequent rites, it follows that the remnant remains for other purposes.
In the animal-sacrifice *prayājas*, four [additional offerings] are added; they are, respectively, modifications of the four original [offerings].
In the other [six *prayājas*], namely the fifth through the tenth, three [additional offerings] are added; these are modifications of the fourth and fifth [original offerings].

Regarding the eleven *prayāja* offerings, it might be argued that because they are performed with the act of looking, there are modifications consisting of equal *prayājas* through division—some being one and others being two.
This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: due to the commonality of the first four, there are four modifications in sequence;
likewise for the others.

Among those six ordinary *prayāja* offerings recited between the *anyā* and *upānyā*, because there is no commonality of deity, the modifications of the fourth and fifth [offerings] themselves occur in sequence as modifications, according to the principle that "it should be equal" (*samaṃ syāt*).
*Saṃkarṣa.* 2.3.6 states that among the *prayājas*, the *barhis* offering occupies the fourth position.
When it is stated, "He brings [the butter] back for the fourth offering," it is said, "Having passed over this *barhis*, he brings it back.

(Bhāṣya 5.1.13). In the *prayāja* offerings, there is an injunction regarding the deities based on the wording of the mantras. This is the section concerning the *prayāja* offerings (*prayājādhikaraṇa*).
9|2|20|58-59. See *Mīmāṃsā* p. 2052: "In the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *prayāja*s are *ārādupakāraka* [indirectly beneficial].
This is the section concerning the *anumantraṇa* mantras of the *prayāja*s.

In the fifth [chapter], in the section "There is no restriction elsewhere" (5|1|13), regarding the *prayāja-anumantraṇa*s recited according to different *śākhā*s, [it is stated]: "One for me, and one for her..."

Having established the combination (*samuccaya*) of the *prayājānumantraṇa* mantras—such as "of its subsidiary parts ending with the *prayājas*"—and the [mantras] such as "I gratify Vasantam among the seasons," someone asks: is there a fixed order (*krama*), or is it unrestricted? This is what is being considered.
In this regard, a doubt arises.

Now, if the *anumantraṇas* have an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose, then there would be a contradiction with the section on mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*). Likewise, there would be a contradiction with the statement in [PMS] 3.1.12, "And the order [is determined] by the commonality of location," where it is said: "The application (*prakriyā*) of those whose indicative marks (*liṅga*) are not known does not effect the connection;
and the capacity of the word 'asi' has been concluded in its proximity"—this being an assertion that the *anumantraṇa* serves a visible purpose.

Likewise, there is a contradiction because [the act] possesses the characteristic of *anumantraṇa*, as defined by the statement: "One should proceed by reciting the mantra while perceiving it as the meaning of the mantra; having become one whose mind is fixed on that [meaning], this constitutes *anumantraṇa*."
Now, if it is argued that they have a visible purpose, then the consideration of their sequence is not appropriate in the absence of a collective performance (*samuccaya*).
On this point, some say:
the visible purpose of mantras is indeed remembrance (*smṛti*), just as it is for the *stotras* and *śastras*.
Smṛti, however, like the *stotra* and *śastra*, has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa*).

Even though in the case of the *anumantraṇas* of the *prayājas* there is no Smṛti that contradicts the sequence of the Śruti, nevertheless, because its purport is grasped through the technical name (*samākhyā*) "anumantraṇa," that [Smṛti] must necessarily be accepted.
As for the statement that even Smṛti has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) in the section "And the Sequence" (3.1.12):

In the text [of the Vārttika, pp. 819–820], it is stated: "Because [the mantra] has a visible purpose through its application to the original sacrifice (*prakṛta-yāga-pratyavekṣaṇa*). That too is merely a claim based on relative dependence (*apekṣāvāda*). That is not correct;

for if that were the case, even in the mantras addressed to Pūṣan and others, there would be no invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*), since their recitation (*anumantraṇa*) could be displaced (*utkarṣa*) when the drawing of the cup (*grahaṇa*) is possible within the context of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa-prakaraṇa*).
