Therefore, where the mantras, by virtue of their indicative power (*liṅga*), reveal a meaning inherent in the ritual action, there the Smṛti rule also serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Moreover, this very extent constitutes the typical definition of an *anumantraṇa* (subsequent recitation), because it functions as an indicator. Consequently, on that basis, the mantras for the *prayāja-anumantraṇa* do not have the Smṛti as their purpose through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); rather, they serve solely an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

The *Vārttika* passage beginning with "the original sacrifice" (*prakṛtayāga*) refers exclusively to the subject of recitation for the sake of memory (*smṛtyarthānumantraṇa*), and is not a hypothetical argument (*abhyupetyavāda*).
However, the subsequent *Vārttika* passage, "even though its purpose is unseen" (*satyapi cādṛṣṭārthatve*), is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*).

Alternatively, the phrase "by way of being the meaning of the mantra" (which is a term intended to define the characteristic of *anumantraṇa*) does not mean "by way of being propounded by the mantra," because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of instrumental mantras (*karaṇamantra*).
However, the word *amya* has the sense of "purpose" (*prayojana*) due to its etymological derivation.

Consequently, in some cases it is not to be expressed, while in others it is to be expressed; the meaning is that *anumantraṇa* is that wherein the remainder (*śeṣin*) is remembered as the purpose of the mantra.
And thus, the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) in the expression "while uttering the mantra" is justified as having a present-tense meaning.

Since the recollection of the mantra occurs after the recitation of the mantra, it is logical that one should recollect while uttering the mantra. Consequently, because the status of being a subsidiary (*śeṣatva*) is possible at the time of recitation for both the recollection of the *Āgneyī* bricks—which has a visible purpose—and the recollection of the *Prayāja* offerings—which has an invisible purpose—it is appropriate that they function as recollections later on as well.
Furthermore, because they serve an invisible purpose, their combination (*samuccaya*) is desired.

Because the intended meaning is "when there is the state of being a direct object (*ṛjvavastu*) [of the action] and not being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*)," there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the instruments.

Furthermore, regarding the word "uttering" (*uccārayan*), the suffix *śatṛ* is used according to the rule "in proximity to the present, it may be treated as the present"; thus, "by way of the mantra's purpose" means "by way of being what is expressed by the mantra.

Consequently, even in the case of the *anumantraṇa* (recitation following an act) of the *prayāja* offerings, although its visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) is established through the designation (*samākhyā*) of "recitation" itself by means of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the statement will serve the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*), just like the mantra for taking hold of the firewood (*abhyādānamantra*).
Or they say it is due to *kṛtācintā* (the consideration of what has been done).
(Bāl. pp.

112–113) Regarding the *prayāja-anumantraṇa-mantras*, such as "I please the spring among the seasons; may he, being pleased, please me," there is no fixed order because there is no fixed sequence of recitation. (Vi. 5.1.3)

The *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are subsidiary acts (*aṅga*) and are not prompted by a specific fruit; in that regard, the mention of a fruit is merely for the sake of praise (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, they are for the sake of the *āgneya* and other primary sacrifices.
The prayājas and anuyājas are for the sake of the sacrifice;
and their connection with the sacrifice is established by the context (prakaraṇa).
These *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings—both those belonging to the *pāyuka* and the *pauroḍāśa* cakes—are indeed part of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
In that context, the terms *prayāja* and *anuyāja* are well-known; they are obtained here by the rule of transfer (*codaka*) and are present as proximate elements.
Furthermore, it is logical that a word should refer to its relevant context;
nor is it proper for a single word to have multiple meanings.
Therefore, these [rites] belong to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Their assistance as well belongs specifically to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
for that is well-known to them. Bhāṣya 12.1.14, p. 2220.
The clarified butter contained in the *aupabhṛta* ladle serves the purpose of the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s.

In the passage "That [butter] is for the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s," there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), according to the method explained in the *Kaustubha* following the principle established in the section on the singularity of the vessel (*grahaikatva-adhikaraṇa*).
(Bhaṭṭadīpikā 4.1.16)

In the phrase "prayājānuyājebhyastat," there is no fault if the analysis (*vigraha*) is taken as "from the *prayājas* and from those that are to be permitted" (*anujñeyebhyaḥ*). (The analysis is performed using the fully established case endings. Bhaṭṭa 4.1.15.
In animal sacrifices and the like, the number eleven and so forth of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings must be accomplished in its entirety.
This is to be seen under the principle known as "the logic of the eleven *prayājas*.
Furthermore, there is the displacement (*apakarṣa*) of the entire set of auxiliary rites ending with the *prayājas* in the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice within the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

In the statement, "They perform the *prayāja* offerings while the animal victim stands," the rule regarding the eleven *prayāja* offerings is heard even in the absence of offspring; and that [rule] applies not only to offspring.

VI. Where it is heard in scripture that "in the absence of offspring, the clarified butter for that purpose is not taken; those *upasads* are without *prayājas*; those are without *anuyājas*" (Bhāṣya 5.1.16.54), [the rule applies].
The bringing together of the clarified butter (*ājya-samānayana*) for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the clarified butter contained in the *aupabhṛta* vessel;
this is to be seen under the section "On the Bringing Together of Clarified Butter" (*ājya-samānayana-adhikaraṇa*), Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 808.
In the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, the vessel for the *anuyāja* offerings is distinct from the vessel for the *prayāja* clarified butter.
The *prayāja* offerings and so forth assist by means of the existence of an invisible benefit (*apūrva*);
the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and so forth assist by means of holding the materials for the sacrifice.
Others [contribute] by way of preparing the substratum;
however, the agents assist through the accomplishment of the action.
The *prayāja* and other such rites are indeed the means for accomplishing the primary *apūrva* (transcendental result) by way of their own intermediate *apūrva*.
(Vi.
3.7.1). The *prayāja* and other rites, which are prescribed in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, are extended (*atidiṣṭa*) to the *saurya* and other sacrifices as well.
The *prayāja* and other such elements are subsidiary (*śeṣa*),
because they are [performed] in succession, like the *bhūyas* and other [repetitions].

Although the *prayāja* offerings and others are grasped by a single injunction of performance (*ekaprayogavacana*), they do not enter into mutual connection with one another, according to the principle "And because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another" (3.1.12).
Vārttika 3.7.14.
The *prayāja*s and other such rites are qualities (*guṇa*) of the Vedic *apūrva*.
Bhāṣya 7.4.14.

Through the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) such as the *prayāja*s intended for the animal sacrifice, the requirements for the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) are fulfilled by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*).

The status of the *prayāja* offerings and others as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) arises from their context (*prakaraṇa*), not from their being primary acts (*pradhāna*).
See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2664, under the section "The Topic on Context" (*prakaraṇādhikaraṇa*). Vi. 3.1.4.11.

The *prayāja* offerings and others do not require the postulation of a fruit as in the case of the *viśvajit* sacrifice, nor is there an attachment (*anuṣaṅga*) to the fruit of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. (Vārttika 3.1.4.11, p. 818).

Since the *prayāja* and other rites require something to be benefited (*upakārya*), and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices require the benefit (*upakāra*), and because neither is yet fully accomplished, their subservience to that purpose (*tādarthya*) is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) regarding that benefit. (Sūtra 3.1.12, p.
In the *prayāja* offerings and others, the number eleven is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) in the case of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice.
See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 107, under the entry "In the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, regarding the *prayāja* offerings and others.
The *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are to be performed only once during a single performance.
This should be examined under the section titled "The Topic of the Fruit and the Stages" (*phalabhūmādhikaraṇam*).
The location, time, and order of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are the same as those of the primary sacrifices (*pradhāna*).
The properties (*dharma*) of the *prayāja* and so forth are prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) itself.
The properties such as the *prayāja* offerings are prompted by the *apūrva*.
This is to be seen under the principle of *atideśa* (extended application) on page 236 of the *Mīmāṃsākośa*.
By means of direct instruction (*upadeśa*), the properties of the *prayāja* and other offerings serve the purpose of the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*).

The Principle of the Eleven Prayājas: In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, the number eleven for the prayājas and anuyājas must be accomplished in its entirety. Because the acts are distinct, the quality of being offered with ghee (*pṛṣadājyatva*) is prescribed for each individual one.
Commentary: Regarding the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "He performs eleven prayājas; he performs eleven anuyājas."
In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, it is stated: "He performs nine Prayājas; he performs nine Anuyājas. Here it is further heard: "There are six Upasads.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the number eleven for each individual Prayāja (and similarly the number nine in the Cāturmāsyas, and the number six in the Agnicayana Upasads), or is it that the number applies to the total collection?
What is established? That the number varies with each principal act.
For those acts are distinct, and the number is heard in relation to those principal acts.
And when a subordinate element (guṇa) is enjoined in the proximity of a principal element (pradhāna), it is repeated for each principal element.

Just as in the case of the injunction "He sacrifices the after-sacrifices with the *pṛṣadājya* [speckled butter]," the subordinate element of *pṛṣadājya* is repeated for each after-sacrifice, so it is here as well.
As for the statement "He sacrifices eleven *prayāja*s," the number eleven is enjoined as a property of the *prayāja*s themselves.
And because they are being designated as such, their association is not distinguished;
therefore, each one is connected with the number eleven.
Or rather, it should be the number of all [the items], for that modification is what is perceived.
Commentary: A number should be conceived as pertaining to all [the items].

Why? For a number resides in distinctness; in the absence of distinctness, it would have to be conceived through repetition, and it would be repeated only as long as there is no possibility of difference.
It is only logical that the number resides in distinctness for as many items as are possible.

They are joined; and as for the other numerical location, it is indicated by the performance characterized by the *prayāja* offerings. Therefore, the number is to be accomplished through all [the offerings].
As for the statement regarding the *pṛṣadājya*, it is rightly set aside [by this rule].

To this he says: "In that case, the fore-offerings (*prayāja*) do not possess separateness (*pṛṣaktā*); it is not possible for one [act] to have [separateness], nor does that [number] reside in separateness.

The number heard [in the text] is heard for another purpose; it is uttered for the sake of something else. And an action performed for one [purpose] does not benefit all [others] by way of a common application (*tantra*)."
Therefore—
(it might be so, but that is not tenable)—
furthermore, (there is this other fault: it must necessarily be broken.
But by means of the *tantra* method, the number is accomplished;
it depends on the others.
When the *prayāja* is uttered once, it is connected with the number, for that [number] occurs in the performance (*prayoga*).

This being the case, the application [of the word] would entail simultaneity; however, it is not possible for both the direct denotation (*śruti*) and the indicative mark (*lakṣaṇā*) to be employed simultaneously. Therefore, the statement will be accepted as being figurative.
Therefore, in both of these two positions, there is the assumption of what was not heard: that number resides in separateness (*pṛthaktva*).
In that regard, substances fall within the scope of the principle of the eleven *prayāja* offerings; [this concerns] the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings.
By the principle of the eleven *prayājas*, the repetition of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) sacrifice is established.

However, the injunction "he offers three oblations" does not fall under the scope of the principle of the eleven *prayājas*; for prior to the injunction of the number eleven, the *prayājas* in the archetype (*prakṛti*) already possess a determined number, whether as individual acts or as a collection qualified by a suffix.
In the present case, however, the number is inferred, because it is directly heard in the scripture (*pratyakṣaśruta*).
Kau. 2|2|7|20, p. 224: For the purpose of the *prayāja* substances, one should pour the clarified butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū* ladle in its entirety, and not less than half.

Bhaṭṭa 4|1|17 (regarding the *avabhṛtha* of the Varuṇapraghāsa): Since the residue of the *āmikṣā* offering, namely the *niṣkāsa*, cannot function as an offering material (*havis*) in this rite, it should be treated as a disposal (*pratipatti*) according to the logic of the *prayāja* (specifically, the logic of the sprinkling with the *prayāja* residue at 4|1|14).
Thus, the *niṣkāsa* is consecrated [as a disposal].
This being the prima facie view:

[Sūtra 1.1.2.15]—when the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is postponed at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), since the postponement of the end of that [sequence] occurs by virtue of the postponement of the *prayāja*s (according to the principle of the postponement of the end of a sequence, 5.1.12), it follows that even the subsequent [rites] should be postponed. This being the prima facie view:

VI. 5.1.14. After the bringing forward of the Soma-fire (*saumikāgni-praṇayana*), because of the connection [in the text] stating "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*) as being an auxiliary to the animal sacrifice (*paśvaṅga*), the cutting of the post—though [normally] performed during the consecrations (*dīkṣāsu yūpaṃ chinatti*)—is drawn forward by the logic of the *prayāja*s (the logic of drawing back to the end of that section, VI. 5.1.12), thereby drawing forward even the preceding ritual items such as the *abhīṣṭoma-praṇayana* and others.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): In the *prayāja* formulas, the deities are indicated by the words "Samidhs," etc., as in: "O Agni, may the Samidhs partake of the clarified butter" (*samidhaḥ samidho agne ājyasya vyantu*), and so forth. (Bhāṭṭa-dīpikā VI. 5.1.14)
VI.

Regarding the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*) mentioned in the *prayāja* injunctions, its application is restricted to the *prayājas* alone, and not to the entire context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
The statement, "He sprinkles the oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," pertains to both the subsidiaries and the primary sacrifice.

Vārttika 3.1.15: Regarding the statement, "He sprinkles the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) with the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings," although there is an extended application (*atideśa*) of that [remnant] to them, it is determined to be a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*) because it is useful for the ritual function. (PMS 1.3.8.27, p. 284). The meaning of the scriptural injunction, "He sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings" (*prayājaśeṣeṇa havīṃṣyabhidhārayati*), is that he causes the remnant of the *prayāja* to flow over the oblation. (Kaṇikā, p. 284). The sprinkling of the oblation with the remnant of the *prayāja* is both a disposal (*pratipatti*) and a purification of the oblation (*haviḥ-saṃskāra*); it is a purification of the oblation that has already been used or is currently being used.
Bhāṣya:

Regarding the sprinkling with the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings, the sprinkling of the *āgneya* cake with the *prayāja* remnants must be performed first, followed by that of the *sāṃnāyya*, because the order follows the sequence of performance (*pravṛttikrama*) and such order possesses greater force. Bhāṣya 4.1.4.12–14: The sprinkling with the remnants of the *prayāja* is optional for the omenta of the *prājāpatya* animals.

*Bāla*, p. 163. Discussion of the section concerning the sprinkling with the remains of the *prayāja* offerings (*prayājaśeṣābhighāraṇādhikaraṇa*): Something is said regarding the section on the sprinkling with the remains of the *prayāja* offerings in the fourth book (*4.1.14.33–39*).

"He takes four portions in the *juhū* for the *prayājas*"—thus the fourfold portion (*caturgṛhīta*) is intended for the *prayājas*. By the statement, "This [portion] was indeed fourfold; having made an offering (*āghāra*) three times from it, he performs the *prayājas* facing eastward," it is concluded that the portion is for the purpose of the *prayājas*. Therefore, when the rule "he offers with the *juhū*" prescribes the oblation, the entire [fourfold portion] must be offered.
[Objection: But surely, out of regard for the disposal (*pratipatti*) consisting of the sprinkling of the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings, there would be an incomplete oblation (*akṛtsnahoma*).
[Reply: No, because disposals do not necessitate [the performance of the primary act].

Nor should it be argued that while those [passages] lack the function of enjoining production (*utpatti-prayojakatva*), they may nevertheless possess the function of enjoining maintenance (*dhāraṇa-prayojakatva*). This is because it would contradict four sections of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā*. To explain: [1] Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in *Sūtra* 3.5.6.19, "And because of the scriptural statement, [the cup] is not enjoined," where the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established by the statement "He offers a small amount" (*alpaṃ juhoti*) despite the application of all oblations through the rules "He offers with the *grahas*" and "He offers with the *camasas*"; that [conclusion] would be subverted. For if the partial offering were established by logic (*nyāya*), the statement regarding the "small amount" could not function as an injunction.

[2] Likewise, regarding the sūtra *ājyācca sarvasaṃyogāt* (3.1.11), there would be a contradiction with that section, for even though the *upāṃśuyāja* has been performed using the fourfold-drawn (*caturgṛhīta*) clarified butter from the Vedic injunction *caturgṛhītaṃ juhoti*, the remnant would have to be set aside in accordance with the requirement for the disposal of remnants (*śeṣakārya*). [3–4] Similarly, the established conclusions (*siddhānta*) of the two sections concerning *sākaprasthāyya*—namely, *sviṣṭakṛdidaṃ ca tadat* (3.1.12.3)—and *sautrāmaṇyāṃ ca graheṣu* (3.1.12.4)—would both be undermined.

Furthermore, there is not merely a contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*); rather, by means of the principle that the various ritual acts (*pratipattayaḥ*) serve as the motivators (*prayojaka*) for the disposal of what has been offered, just as it is established that they lack the capacity to motivate the production of the object to be disposed of, so too is it established that they lack the capacity to motivate the avoidance of the total oblation (*kṛtsnahoma*) which would otherwise result from the scripture.

As it is stated in the *Śāstradīpikā* under the section (3.5.6.19): "Because of the word 'in the oblation' (*home')"; [the commentary continues]: "Now, if it is argued that [the remnants] are used because they are the objects of the disposal-rites (*śeṣakārya*), then since those [disposal-rites] are themselves motivators..."
"Even in cases such as the removal of defects from the remnant (*śeṣa*), there would be the transition to another sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
(Regarding the word *śeṣyeta*, the Nirṇayasāgara edition reads *śiṣyeta*.
...In cases such as the removal [of defects], and even in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth, there is the sacrificial oblation.)
And such is the reading.

Therefore, since there is no scriptural statement such as "he offers a small amount," and because the entire [substance] from the *jauhava* ladle is offered by means of the three *prayāja*s, there is no residue of the *prayāja*s at all; thus, the sprinkling with the residue of the *prayāja*s is negligible.
To this we reply:
One must infer that "this [procedure] applies to them" even though it has not been stated by any authors of the texts;

or rather, since a complete oblation (*kṛtsna-homa*) is prescribed by the scripture, if one should offer with a remainder due to negligence, then this disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remainder is enjoined—thus, one must infer it as being established as a constant rule (*nityavat*). And by the very injunction for disposal, the deficiency arising from the absence of a complete oblation is also remedied.
Thus [it is stated]. Bāla., p. 108–109. The Principle of the Sprinkling with the Remnant of the Prayāja Offerings:

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, a separate vessel for holding the remnant for the purpose of sprinkling the sacrificial oblation (havis) with the remnant of the prayāja offerings need not be prepared.
There is no sprinkling with the remains of the *prayāja* offerings over the omenta of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati.
If there were such sprinkling, it would entail a separation [of the ritual acts], and consequently, as in the case of the *anuyāja* offerings, there would have to be a separate vessel.
Commentary: There is the Vājapeya sacrifice, [enjoined] by the text: "One desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the Vājapeya."
In this regard, it is heard: "One sacrifices seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati; Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold; [this is] for the attainment of Prajāpati.

It is stated that there is a combination of those dedicated to Prajāpati with those having fixed numbers, according to the rule: "And because of the scriptural mention in the case of the Prājāpatya [animals].
However, in the archetype (prakṛti), there exists the injunction: "He sprinkles the oblations with the remnant of the prayāja offerings."

In this regard, there is a doubt: Should another vessel be produced for the purpose of holding the remains of the *prayāja* offerings in order to sprinkle the omenta (*vapā*) of the *prājāpatya* animals with them, and then the omenta of the *prājāpatya* animals should be sprinkled with that [remnant]; or rather, should the remnant not be held, and thus the omenta of the *prājāpatya* animals should not be sprinkled at all? What is the prima facie view? A vessel is produced for the purpose of holding the *prayāja* remnant for the sake of sprinkling.

The remnant of the *prayāja* offerings at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) remains until the distant time of the midday pressing (*mādhyandinasavana*), at which point it is heard in the scripture that "having performed the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite for those [animals] dedicated to Prajāpati,
they release them at the time of the *brahmasāman*";
furthermore, the *juhū* ladle becomes overflowing.
Therefore, another vessel must be produced.

Just as in the case of the *pṛṣadājya* offerings, a vessel is produced for the purpose of holding the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), based on the scriptural injunction, "He performs the *anuyāja* offerings with *pṛṣadājya*," so it is here as well.
Mīmāṃsākośa 349: "Or rather not, because of unworthiness; but worthiness [of sprinkling] exists because of being a part.
Commentary: Or rather, the omenta (vapā) of the Prājāpatya offerings are not to be sprinkled with clarified butter.
Why? Because they are remnants (śeṣa).
If it is asked how there is the state of being a remnant, it is because of unworthiness. How is there unworthiness? Because it is only a single part.
For that [portion] is a single part (*ekadeśa*) of the *ājya* butter which has been taken for the *prayāja*; it is the remnant (*śeṣa*).
What follows from this? If it is so, then because it would result in being a single part, the [remnant] as it is heard in the text does not enjoin the whole (*avayavin*) as something to be taken up.
He says:
It does not enjoin the production [of the substance], but rather, by implication, it will enjoin the maintenance of that which has been produced. It is said in reply:
because it is a part [of the whole], the mention of "maintaining" means that it does not actually employ the substance itself.
This single portion of the substance whose purpose has already been accomplished is being offered; therefore, the act of sprinkling (abhighāraṇa) would be purposeless.
[Objection: But surely, because of the use of the accusative case-ending for the oblations (havir), they must be the primary objects.
[Reply: No, it is said.
For an assistance is provided by the oblation through eight [acts].
However, when clarified butter (*ājya*) is predominant, the visible purpose is the emptiness of the *juhū* ladle.
The purpose of the empty *juhū* is for the sake of the *ājyabhāga* portions so that there is no mixing with the clarified butter, and not with the intended oblation.

Therefore, for the *prājāpatya* offerings, there is no need at all for the clarified butter that has been sprinkled; for what purpose, then, should the remnant be retained? [The opponent replies: Even though the *prakṛti* (archetype) is under discussion, the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice) is cited here because its possibility exists; the author of the Sūtras has included these indicative marks (*liṅga*) as evidence for that very point. [He states the Siddhānta: The very utterance of the words "with the remnant of the *prayāja*" demonstrates that it has already been employed elsewhere as a remnant.
Therefore, this [portion] should be used elsewhere as a remnant (*śeṣatvena*), and it is not employed by another [rite], just as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is for the sake of what follows.
Because the oblations (*haviṣām*) are being taken up, their number is intended to be significant (*vivakṣitā*). [This reading is found in three manuscripts of the Anānandāśrama edition;

following that, the *Tantraratna* states: "If the oblations were being taken up, then the number would be intended to be significant, but that is not the case; thus this statement of the author must be explained [otherwise]."]

However, the reading found in the Ānandāśrama edition—“Because they are not being taken up [as a whole], the number of the oblations is not intended to be significant”—is more appropriate, even without the statement of *avītokti*.
*Avītokti* means a solitary statement (*ya-rekokti*). Furthermore, there is a purpose for the *juhū* ladle being empty.
Since that [pair of *ājyabhāga* offerings] will be offered with that [sacrificial ladle], how could it be untouched by the remains of the *prayāja*?
Therefore, there is a requirement for a disposal (*pratipatti*).
However, since the refinement of the oblation (*havis*) is not required [at this stage], the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) must be postulated as the purpose of the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*).
Consequently, the sacrificial oblations (*haviṣi*) would be purposeless.
(If so, how then is there the accusative case in the word "haviṣi"? To this, he says:
[It is] by means of the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings...
By the principle of the *prayāja* remnant (2788), by the principle of the *prayāja* remnant (2789), the determination of application:
Maṇḍana—“The sprinkling is for the sake of the *prayāja*s”;
Śaṅkara—“Likewise, the pouring over the oblations.”
17. Likewise, it is not purposeful.

According to the principle of the sprinkling with the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings, since the act of eating (*bhakṣa*) or the rule regarding its specific performers serves as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the performer, there is no eating of the specific sacrificial oblation (*havis*) nor even of that which qualifies it.
This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Bhāṭṭa 6.1.47: Regarding the statement "He performs the *upayāja* with the tail," since the tail has already been employed [in the sacrifice] and thus requires a disposal (*pratipatti*) according to the principle of the sprinkling of the remnants of the *prayāja*, it would follow that a separate sentence must be assumed for the disposal by means of the remnants of the *upayāja* consumption.

Bhāṭṭa 12.4.4: Even if the injunction "He performs the *patnīsaṃyāja* with the tail" were merely a restrictive rule (*niyama*), it is impossible to assume—on the basis of the principle of the sprinkling of the *prayāja* remnants—that the restriction itself serves the purpose of purifying (*saṃskāra*) the tail.
12|4|6: "That which is the consumption [of the Soma] effecting a refinement (*saṃskāra*) effects a refinement of the agent for the purpose of discharging its potency, flavor, and fragrance.
This is the determination of application (*prayukti-nirṇaya*). 2790: The proposition concerning the investigation of application (*prayukti-vicāra-pratijñā*):
although it is worldly (*laukika*), it is nonetheless prescribed by Smṛti as a means for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth.

The state of being desired (*kāmyamānatva*) is like the cause for the acquisition of wealth; however, we shall explain in the section on *arthavāda* that the state of being desired is not possible when the object is either known or unknown to be doubtful. If it is argued that since teaching is accomplished by mere study, there can be no impulsion toward a specific type of study, [we reply]: first, initiation (*upanayana*) is understood to be a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of teaching because it enters into the ritual (*kratūpapatti*); furthermore, study is prescribed with reference to initiation.
Therefore, the impulsion toward specific study follows as an inseparable consequence of the impulsion toward initiation.
But there is no such thing as a remotely contributing factor (*ārādupakāraka*).
[Objection: Is it not the case that the student's study is determined by the hearing of the accusative case-ending?
The superiority of the accusative case-hearing was stated in the passage: "Having encircled the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), he performs the introductory rite (*upākaroti*)."

This is not so; for it is logical that initiation (*upanayana*), being a constituent part of the act of teaching (*adhyāpana*), serves as the means (*dvāra*) by virtue of being a constituent part of the student (*māṇavaka*), just as the threshing of rice (*vrīhi-saṃśrava*) serves as the means for the *apūrva* (transcendental result) which is a constituent part of the sacrifice. Furthermore, there is another Smṛti text: "Having initiated the disciple, the Guru... and so forth. Moreover, even in the absence of an injunction for teaching, the application of its own injunction is not possible, because its application is established through the injunction of the ritual sacrifice (*kratu*).

And this being the case, the entitlement to study would belong to one who merely desires heaven according to the Vedic injunction; furthermore, the prohibition against those not initiated (anupanīta) would apply only to those of the three higher castes who are proximate [to the study of the Vedas];
and the prohibition regarding Śūdras and outcasts (ucchista) would likewise apply only to matters obtained through worldly inclination (rāga).
It is not a matter of contradiction, as in the case of the injunction "one shall not kill.

However, in the view of the non-existent (asat), [the means] are delayed relative to the person to be impelled (*prayojya*), relative to the specific requirements of the sacrifice, relative to the expectation of the fruit for the person to be impelled, and relative to the means for the ignorant.
Or rather, there is the procedure for becoming an Ācārya, namely: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa for study" and "One should teach him.
Here, the application is for the purpose of becoming an Ācārya.
This is clear from the application [of the rule].
Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that there is freedom of choice regarding the number of performers.
Alternatively:

even though it is not stated by the word and even though there is no contradiction, because it has a different meaning— since it is cognizable through other means of valid cognition such as perception—
the primary [entity], the Puruṣa, does not exist for the sake of the qualities (guṇas).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "because the agent is primary, when there is the sense of being for that purpose" (*tādarthye*).
Or rather: "thus. Or else: "alternatively."

Regarding the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*): once it is understood that heaven is what is desired by the person, it is impossible for the person—who is the seeker of that [heaven]—to regard either heaven or the sacrifice as being for the sake of a subordinate element (*guṇārthatā*).
If this principle were not stated, there would be an intention to express the number [of the agent].
However, the principle established regarding the singularity of the cup (*grahaikatva*) has already been stated: that the number residing in the principal [element] is not intended to be expressed.

Furthermore, it is not possible for both the intention to express and the non-intention to express a number to coexist, because they are distinct objects; that is, due to the difference in their referents (*arthabheda*). This difference in referents has been stated to entail the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Since the agent is the primary element, the term "primary" (*pradhāna*) refers to that which has the state of being primary as its principal meaning—that is, primacy itself.
The term *bhūtam* (become) refers to that which has been attained from the root *rudh* etc., meaning "that which has been reached.
Because it has attained primacy (*prādhānyam*) by virtue of being the principal factor,

and because it has attained primacy for the single person who is the agent of the sacrifice, characterized by being the enjoyer of the fruit, there is no distinction between persons (*puruṣabheda*) in the present context.
Therefore, the number is not intended to be significant. Thus [says] Ku.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) states that, in reality, there is no subordinate status at all.

The injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" is a single prescriptive mandate (*codanā*). If it enjoins either the production of the fruit or the production of the sacrifice, then the agent does not act for his own sake.
But when he acts for his own sake, then the sacrifice or the fruit exists for that purpose.
And this does not occur simultaneously.
Therefore, the person is not subordinate either to the sacrifice or to the fruit.
Consequently, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that one, two, or many may perform the sacrifice.

Or rather, when there is a connection with a desire, [the agent] would be prescribed for the performance because of that connection; for the scriptural injunction is directed toward each individual purpose.
The phrase "or rather" (*apivā*) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

When a connection with a desire—that is, with a desired fruit—is understood from the expression "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*), then because of that connection, and because of the singular number in the word "he should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) which connects it to a single agent, only one agent would be prescribed for the performance—that is, the execution—of the sacrifice, not two or many.
However, where multiple matters are to be expressed, there is a separate scriptural injunction for each matter.
This is like the case of the horn (*vipāṇā*).

For example, in the statement "He scratches with the black antelope horn," there is a separate injunction regarding scratching performed by means of the horn; and in the statement "He throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit," there is a separate injunction regarding the throwing of the horn as the object of the action.

In the present case, however, there is no separate scriptural injunction; therefore, the singular number in either "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*) or "he should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is indeed intended to be significant.
Consequently, there is only one agent.
The word *hi* (for/indeed) serves to indicate that the example of the black antelope horn is well-known.

In this context, by the word *kartṛ* (agent), only the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is to be understood. Regarding this, the following words from the Bhāṣya establish the meaning of the Sūtra: "The repetition of the fifth [case ending] in the word *apīva* indicates that the agent is taught for the sake of the performance [of the ritual], and not for his own benefit."
Because of the connection with desire (*kāma*), the desire's relation to the self is understood from that very connection.
One who desires a result desires the result for oneself alone, not for another.
However, where both meanings are to be expressed, an injunction (*vidhi*) is heard for each respective meaning.
As in the examples: "He scratches with a black antelope horn" and "He throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit.
Now, for the *Subodhinī*: the word "of this" (*asya*) is to be supplied [to complete the compound] as "of this selfhood" (*ātmatvasya*).

Regarding "in connection with desire" (*kāmasaṃyoge*): that in which there is a connection (*saṃyoga*) between desire (*kāma*)—that is, the object of desire (*kāmya*)—is "connected with desire" (*kāmasaṃyoga*), such as the sentence "One who desires heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*).

In that sentence connected with desire (*kāmasaṃyoga*), because the verb (*ākhyāta*) is related as a constituent part, it is taught and heard as having the person as its primary referent for the sake of performance.
The sense is that the number of the verb is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*).

Regarding the object of each [verbal suffix], in the sense of predominance and in the sense of being that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), the scriptural injunction (*vidhiśruti*)—that is, the intention of the injunction—is not present here in the same way as it is in the case of the [injunction regarding] horns.

Now, as for curiosity: where both the subordinate (guṇa) and primary (pradhāna) states exist as injunctions, there is a separate injunctive scriptural statement (vidhiśruti) for each respective object, just as in the case of the "horn. The word "viṣāṇa" (horn) possesses all three genders.

In a sentence connected with desire (*kāmasaṃyoga*), when one is enjoined as the agent (*kartṛ*)—both by way of being a person and by way of being singular—in order to employ the sacrifice for its performance, it is not the case that he would merely obtain the result [as a subordinate element]; rather, he is enjoined as the primary element, characterized by being the locus of the result (*phalavyāpyatva*).
Why? Because of the connection; for, by the very nature of the matter, since the attainment of heaven is impossible otherwise, the result must necessarily pertain to him.
Thus it is said.
If it is argued that this applies to another as well: the proponent says— if the proponent should say, "Someone else, desiring heaven, might perform a different sacrifice."
The connection with the name is for the sake of another [purpose].

The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) says: Even though one who desires heaven might not be directly denoted by the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), nevertheless, when the performance is for the sake of another [purpose], [the name applies].
Regarding the application:
if the application were to arise [independently], there would be no connection between that [application] and the other result, namely heaven.

The *ātmanepada* ending is prescribed only when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent; since the verb *yajeta* here is used in the *ātmanepada*, [it follows that the result goes to the sacrificer]. Because one person desires heaven for the sake of another, there is neither a connection with the agent nor an identity [between the two].
This is to be supplied [from the commentary] because of the hearing of the *ātmanepada* ending—thus it is stated in the *Subodhinī*.
The term "of another" (*anyasya*) is carried over from the preceding sūtra.
This is the sūtra: "There is no connection with the object" (*nārthenābhisaṃbandhaḥ*).
There is no connection—that is, no state of being pervaded—of another with the object, which is the result (*phala*).
Because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is prescribed when the fruit accrues to the agent;
thus says the *Kutūhala*.
If it is argued that the desire for the fruit is the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), [we reply:]...
The proponent says: The fruit of heaven is one fruit; whereas the "desire for fruit" (*phalakāmaḥ*), though itself being desired, refers to the desire for incidental fruits.

The fruit mentioned in the *sūkavāka*—such as "this sacrificer desires long life, he desires good offspring," and so forth—being what is desired by oneself, would be the occasion (*nimitta*) for the middle-voice ending (*ātmanepada*) in the injunction "one should sacrifice."
If the proponent should say this:

"The word 'one who desires heaven' (*svargakāma*), signifying the desire for a result, is the occasioning condition (*nimitta*); the middle voice ending in 'yajeta' indicates that this is the occasioning condition.
If he should say this:
Thus says the *Subodhinī*.
If it is argued that "one desiring the fruit" (*phalakāmaḥ*)— meaning one who desires the fruit of the auxiliaries residing in the agent— is the cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*),
[this is addressed] in the *Kutūhala*.
"Not so, because it is eternal.
(Sūtra 11) The proponent of the established view (siddhāntin) refutes the doubt raised by the opponent (pūrvapakṣin):
It is not only the desire for incidental results that is possible.
Whatever belongs to the primary fruit of an action must also belong to that same agent as its incidental fruit;
for the fruit of the principal sacrifice accrues to the performer, since the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here invariably.
Therefore, one should perform the sacrifice desiring the fruit of the sacrifice for oneself alone, not for another.
And that performer of the sacrifice is only one, not two or many. If it is argued that the ritual act is likewise [singular], the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) raises this doubt.

If the opponent should argue: "In the *Bahispavamāna* [laud], it is heard: 'For you two are the lords of heaven' (*yuvaṃ hi sthaḥ svarpatī*); one should employ this as the *pratipad* for two sacrificers. And 'These [two] are the delighters in the waters' (*ete asu-abhinandaḥ*) should be employed as the *pratipad* for many sacrificers. Thus, in a ritual involving two sacrificers as well as one involving many sacrificers, when the *pratipad* is prescribed, the rite would be exactly the same for both cases of two sacrificers; consequently, there would be freedom of choice regarding the number of sacrificers."

Regarding *kutūhala*, however, it has been explained that only if the number of sacrificers (*yajamāna*) is indeed not intended to be significant (as per Mīmāṃsākośa 350), then the performance of the *bahiṣpavamāna* rite— which is prescribed as being accompanied by remnants (*śeṣayukta*)— would be consistent in the case of the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice involving two or many sacrificers. [This is not so], because of the connection (*samavāya*).
What was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view is not correct;

for such a *bahiṣpavamāna* is connected with the *ahīna* sacrifices, owing to its connection with them. Indeed, in certain *ahīna* sacrifices and *satras*, as well as in the *kulāya-yajña*, there is the presence of multiple sacrificers.

In each respective case, there is a specific injunction; in each case, it is included therein. Therefore, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Jyotiṣṭoma, and other such rites, the singularity of the sacrificer is indeed intended to be significant.

Therefore, one person alone should sacrifice, not two or many. Why? Because place, time, and the agent are auxiliary elements of the performance (*prayoga*), not subordinate parts of the injunction (*vidhi*). For time is an auxiliary element of the performance, serving as a benefactor to the ritual acts.

The very principle (*nyāya*) of the knowledge of application (*prayoga-jñātṛtva*) is the fundamental reasoning for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the locus of the desire to perform (*cikīrṣā-adhikaraṇa*) [Sūtra 3.1.3.17, p. 9]. Su.

3.79, p. 9. The eleventh chapter is for the purpose of investigating the extent of the performance (*prayoga-iyattā*), following as a consequence of the discussion on the extent of the subsidiary elements (*śeṣa-iyattā-prasaṅga*).
Because there is no scriptural injunction regarding the production of linguistic usage, there would be no fixed determination among words.
Words such as *gauḥ*, *gāvī*, *goṇī*, and *gopotalikā* serve as examples.
The doubt is as follows: just as the word *go* is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, are words like *gāvī* and the others likewise, or not?
In this regard, is there one word that has an uninterrupted tradition for denoting its meaning while the others are merely corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*),
or are all of them beginningless?

On this point, Prabhākara, out of a desire for consistency, disregarded the example provided by the author of the *Bhāṣya* on the grounds that "the example need not be strictly adhered to," and instead examined the word *adhvan* occurring in the injunction (*codanā*) "one should sacrifice a horse" (*aśvam ālabheta*).
In the world, the word *aśva* is seen to be used for both a horse and a pauper;
in that case, it is not known where this [usage] is correct and where it is incorrect.
Furthermore, the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is not a basis for a definitive conclusion.

Since its validity is impossible due to its lack of a foundation, the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that an injunction such as "one should sacrifice a horse" (*aśvam ālabheta*), containing words whose meanings are established otherwise, is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is that because the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇa-smṛti*) is based on beginningless usage, it is a valid authority. Therefore, according to that [tradition], this word *aśva* belongs to the *tālavya* class [of dentals] in grammar.

The word *sādhu* applies only to the horse (*turaga*). Regarding the derivation from the use of the dental *sa*, [the rule] "the production of usage" (2694) is appropriate; and by the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) "one who does not possess [anything] in himself," the word *sādhu* means "poor" (*daridra*), and it is not joined with the palatal *śa*. Thus, the injunction (*codanā*) "one should sacrifice a horse" (*aśvam ālabheta*) is indeed authoritative (*pramāṇa*), because its meaning is firmly established.
This is incorrect. For, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since grammar lacks a foundational basis, correctness must be asserted everywhere solely on the strength of usage.
Since this is no different in both cases, when the word *aśva* is employed for either a horse or a poor man, it is indeed correct.

And this being so, just as in the case of words with multiple meanings and the like, determination [of the specific meaning] is possible through context and the subject matter; therefore, there is no lack of authority due to non-determination.

Thus, the present topic is introduced according to the sequence of the Vārttika. Having previously established in every way that Dharma consists of Smṛti and custom (ācāra), we now, by way of a relevant digression, examine whether or not the Smṛti of Grammar possesses authority regarding the correctness of words; specifically, it is examined how the term "correct" (*sādhu*)—as in the phrase "this is correct" (*sādhum imaṃṣita*)—is utilized for the sake of Dharma.
This alone is the ultimate doubt here.

However, it should be understood that the Commentator has presented the resulting doubt: "Are all words such as *go*, *gāvī*, and so forth correct (*sādhu*) with respect to the object possessing a dewlap and other characteristics, or is only the word *go* correct while *gāvī* and others are corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*)? In this regard, the intention of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) would be an authoritative means for distinguishing between correct and incorrect words regarding terms such as *go*, *gāvī*, and the like, provided that its foundational source (*mūlabhūta-pramāṇa*) could be inferred, just as is done for the traditions of Manu and others.

In this regard, perception cannot be the basis [for the knowledge of grammatical correctness], because its object is the correctness (*sādhutva*) consisting in a denotative power that transcends the mere nature of the phonemes.
Nor can it be perception assisted by the traditional grammar (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*), because the traditional grammar lacks a foundation and thus cannot function as an auxiliary.
Nor can it be analogy (*upamāna*), because there is no mark (*liṅga*) invariably concomitant with it.
Nor is it verbal testimony (*śabda*), because if it were of human origin, it would suffer from the defects of the current tradition;

and if it were of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*), it could not possess authority regarding an established object, since its function lies in the domains of engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*).
As for analogy (*upamāna*), however, because its object is similarity, it is simply not even to be considered as a candidate.

Nor can it be established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because that too arises from the impossibility of understanding a meaning otherwise, and thus it would apply without distinction even to words such as *gāvī* and the like.

Therefore, since none of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apply, it is established that the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) has non-existence (*abhāva*) as its very basis for invalidity.
Furthermore, grammar is not a valid authority regarding correctness (*sādhutva*), because it involves a contradiction with one's own words.
The sūtra is *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.30).
Here, by the word *jani*, "the act of being born" (*janana*) itself is intended.
Therefore, the meaning is this: that which is the source (*prakṛti*), i.e., the producer, of the agent of birth—the one who is being born—receives the technical designation *apādāna*.

Furthermore, the act of birth is not denoted by the word *jani* alone in the world, for that has been explicitly prohibited by Pāṇini himself in the rule "itikṛtyatṛcaḥ dhātunirdeśe" (Pā. 3.3.172). Likewise, the compound *janikartuḥ* is also untenable; for by the rule "tujakābhyāṃ kartari" (Pā. 2.2.15), a genitive compound with the word *kartṛ*, which ends in a *tṛc* suffix, is itself prohibited.

Likewise, because this [rule] prohibits a genitive compound even for that which ends in the *akrac* suffix, the genitive compound of the word *prayojaka* ending in *akrac* with the pronoun *tad-*—as in the rule *tatprayojako hetuśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.55)—is also untenable.
Thus, due to the lack of determination regarding its meaning and other such factors, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

To explain: regarding the rule "bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ" (roots begin with bhū), what is the ground for the application of the term *dhātu*? It cannot be the recitation in the list of roots (*guṇapāṭha*), because then even the word "sattā" in the entry "bhū sattāyām" would result in being a root.
Nor can it be the state of denoting action (*kriyāvacanatva*), because then "bhū" itself would incur the consequence of not being a root.
For this very reason, even the two taken together cannot be the ground for the application of the term *dhātu*, since in the entry "bhū sattāyām" there is an absence of the denotation of action.

Therefore, there is a lack of authority even because of the determination of the meaning. Likewise, the definition of an agent provided by the author of the grammatical treatise is also entirely incoherent. For instance, the definition of an agent is: "The independent one is the agent."
And here, autonomy itself is not understood.

If autonomy consists in being the locus of will and effort, then there would be the undesirable consequence of [inanimate objects like] wood and a cooking pot lacking the status of agent in such cases as "the wood cooks" and "the pot cooks.

Alternatively, if agency consists in being the substratum of the operation denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), then since the operation—beginning with the cleaning of the pot and ending with the transformation of the rice into a cooked mass—is determined by the root *pac* in the expression "he cooks," there would be the undesirable consequence that all the case-factors (*kāraka*s) would also possess the status of agent.
In this way, it has been stated—even though not elaborated here for fear of prolixity—that everything from action (*karman*) up to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is likewise difficult to define;

thus, since grammar is non-eternal (*aśāśvata*) with respect to the production of correct words (*sādhuśabda*), correctness does not reside in those words that merely follow [the rules of] it. Therefore, the traditional authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the grammatical smṛti does not extend toward correctness.
Thus [ends the argument].
This being the position reached, it is replied: "The word shares in the occurrence of error because it is produced through effort"—this is the intended meaning.
This would indeed be so if the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) were not an authoritative means of knowledge regarding the correctness of words.
Nor is it invalid because of being rootless, for perception itself is its root.
To explain: what is called "correctness" (sādhutva) is a distinct form of a word that possesses an innate power of expression with respect to a particular meaning.

And that [correctness] which is established by the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) through the medium of roots, suffixes, and so forth, is indeed perceived quite clearly as the nature of correctness—distinguished from incorrect words—by auditory perception aided by that very grammatical tradition. This is just as the status of being a Brahmin is perceived by visual perception aided by the memory of one's relationship with one's parents, or as the quality of being a gem is perceived by visual perception aided by the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) combined with knowledge of the science of gem-testing.

Therefore, since correctness (*sādhutva*) is perceived by auditory perception—augmented by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the recollection of earlier grammars—even for ordinary people, the tradition of grammatical memory (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) cannot be said to be rootless.
Nor can it be [rootless] due to a lack of a continuous succession, because there is no temporal sequence between memory and perception; [the tradition] is beginningless.
As it has been said: "Just as one might [mistake] rubies and other gems mixed with glass and crystal..."
Experts recognize excellence, and others likewise do as well.
Thus (Vārttika 1.3.8.27, p. 282).

Therefore, because the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is rooted in perception assisted by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) devoid of other [contradictory] traditions, its authority is indeed established.
Nor is there a lack of authority due to self-contradiction in rules such as "the source (*prakṛti*) of that which is produced is the agent" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.4.30), and so forth.
For it is observed everywhere in the sūtras of the authors of the sūtras that their usages are indeed figurative or based on secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Just as in the case of Jaimini himself, when the eternal is to be expressed, there is the usage of a word based on a limiting condition (*aupādhika*), so too with the word *jani* in the sense of the verbal root-meaning; to take it as having a secondary meaning (*lākṣaṇikatva*) in the sense of "birth" would bring about a fault.

Likewise, even the hearing of the prohibition of the genitive compound in the rule "with [words ending in] *tṛc* and *aka*, in the sense of the agent," is solely for the purpose of demonstrating that the prohibition is optional.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the [Pāṇinian] rule *abhūvādayo dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.1) lacks authority because the meaning of the term "dhātu" (verbal root) is not fully understood—that is incorrect. For "dhātutva" (the state of being a verbal root) consists precisely in being the base (*prakṛti*) for suffixes such as *tiṅ*. This very point was demonstrated by Pāṇini himself through the two sūtras beginning with *pratyayaḥ* and *paraśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.1–2). Moreover, as for the claim that the definition of an agent (*kartṛ*)—namely, "the independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*)—is untenable due to the difficulty of defining independence—that too is incorrect. For independence (*svātantrya*) is simply the status of being the instigator of the factors of action (*kāraka*) conducive to the accomplishment of an action.

And that [agency] is sometimes imperceptible and sometimes imperceptible. As it was said by Bhartṛhari: "That which is the master over the causal factors (kārakas) in either their engagement or their withdrawal—whether unassociated or associated—is called the agent (kartṛ), the causal factor par excellence."
Thus [it is said].

As for the designation of an agent in cases such as "the pieces of wood cook," which involve insentient things, that must be understood as being merely figurative (vaivakṣika). In the same way, the status of being the most desired (īpsitatama) should be inferred for the object and other [kārakas] as well.

Therefore, since it is rooted in auditory perception, the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*)—by virtue of the correctness of words—is indeed an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, only words such as *gavā* and so forth are correct. As for words such as *gāvī* and the like, they are corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*) of original words; their capacity to convey meaning follows the intended original word when that original is intended, but when it is not intended, they possess no expressive power at all. The practical application (*prayojana*) is this: if the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) holds, one may employ even corrupt forms in ritual contexts, such as in sentences involving the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding the performance of a rite.

In the Siddhānta, however, it is by the word *sādhu* itself, as in the expression "this [word] is well-said" (*sādhum imaṃṣita*). As for the Sūtra: when a word is manifested, because that manifestation has its production dependent upon effort, the state of being corrupted (*apabhraṣṭatva*)—which is the absence of correctness—is due solely to a defect in the manifestor; this is the intended meaning. (Tautā)
Because words arise from usage, there would be no fixed rule regarding arbitrary terms.

In the case of words such as *gauḥ*, *gāvī*, *goṇī*, and *gopolatikā*, there would be no established rule that "this meaning is correct and one must communicate by means of this alone," or "this is incorrect and one must not communicate by means of this.
If it is argued that the rule would be established by the traditional grammar (*vyākaraṇa-smṛti*), we say no; for that [grammar] is itself a scripture whose origin lies in usage.
The rule regarding the origin of usage [is not established] because that usage is non-eternal and lacks a foundation in the sacred scriptures (śāstra).

Alternatively, the "origin" (utpatti) of usage refers to its systematic establishment; thus, this "origin of usage" is the grammatical tradition (vyākaraṇasmṛti). Because this origin of usage is non-eternal and devoid of a foundational revelation (mūla-śruti), it lacks authoritative validity (aprāmāṇya).

Alternatively, since the usage "this is good" (*sādhu*) or "this is bad" (*asādhu*) arises from the fact that the rule governing pronunciation is not inherent to the word itself, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that any word whatsoever may be employed in the accusative case and so forth. [The Siddhāntin replies:
Since a word is produced through effort, it is subject to error.
The proponent says:
It is true that the determination of correctness and incorrectness is not easy. Why? Because a great effort is required for the utterance of a word.
Driven by the vital air (*vāyu*), [the sound] expands in the chest, turns upward in the throat, strikes the head, and returning there, moves within the mouth and manifests various sounds.
Thus, when a sound is to be uttered, because the sound is produced or manifested through the effort of the speaker, it partakes in the possibility of error.
Error must necessarily occur.
From that, words such as *goṇī* arise;
and thus, because error is possible, it cannot be said with certainty that all [words] are beginningless.
Alternatively, there is a word division: "because the production of a word results from effort."
For one who manifests a word with unerring effort,
all [instances] would be of the same type, arising from the mere utterance of the word at the time of usage, due to the production of usage handed down through tradition.
But when it is possible for even the production of a word to occur without effort, then, because of the possibility of a change in form caused by error therein, not all words possess the same status.

Alternatively, whether it be the production of a word or the effort directed toward a word, an error is observed even among the most skillful whose organs of articulation are flawless, let alone those with unskillful organs.
Therefore, correctness (*sādhutā*) belongs to those words manifested without error.
This rule regarding the wickedness of those who have committed offenses was established by him.
(Vārttika, p. 275):
"Because both [the general rule and the specific exception] share in the occurrence of an offense, both possess their respective scope:
the commonality [of the general rule] and the fixed necessity [of the specific], as well as the application of the remedial rite."
This being the case, it is logically established that grammar and other such sciences serve as the regulating factors for determining correctness (*sādhutva*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that only correct words (*sādhavaḥ*) should be employed, and not incorrect ones (*asādhavaḥ*).
When a word such as *gavi* is used, there is a participation in fault, namely, the fault of improper pronunciation.
*Bhāga* means participation (*bhajana*) or activity (*pravṛtti*).

By virtue of the relation of being a producer (*janakatā-sambandha*), that speech is the *bhāga*; its state (*bhāva*) is *bhāgitva*, which is to say, the state of being an instigator (*pravartakatva*).
This is because of the accomplishment of effort—that is, through a specific effort, there is the proper manifestation of the very nature of the sound.
Thus ends the curiosity.
[Now follows] the section on the multiplicity of words for a single object. If it is asked, "Why is it not accepted that all [words] are denotative?", he says in response:
"From multiple words": that which has many words as its designators for a single object is "anekaśabda"; the state of being such is *anekaśabdatva*.
That is illogical (*anyāya*). It is called *nyāya* because it is led (*nīyate*) [to the conclusion].
The suffix *ghañ* is applied to the verbal root *kṛ*.
Since it is stated that words ending in *ghañ* are masculine, this word is necessarily masculine.
Furthermore, in a *nañ*-tatpuruṣa compound, the gender of the final member prevails; thus, the masculine gender is maintained.

It is not logical for a single meaning to be denotable by multiple words, because [otherwise] there would be no emergence of the appropriate meaning, other words would be rendered useless, conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) would arise, or distinct meanings would result; furthermore, it is sufficient that a single word, which is the substratum of the denotative power delimited by denotability, suffices for this very purpose. It should be understood that by a modification of this very aphorism, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "the state of having multiple meanings is improper" (*anyāyyānekārthatvam*) has been set forth.
In that regard, the true nature [of the relationship] may be established through specific application (*abhiyoga*).

But surely, what is the decisive criterion (*vinigamaka*) for establishing that only words such as *go* and so on are correct (*sādhu*) denoters, whereas words such as *gavya* and so on belong to those ignorant of the grammatical treatises? To this, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) replies:

In that regard, the knowledge of the true nature of correctness (*sādhutva-tattva-jñāna*) concerning words such as *go* and *gavya* would arise from a specific application of effort (*abhiyoga-viśeṣāt*).
Through the repeated hearing of the definitions, application proceeds;
by that, there arises knowledge of other objects of definition, which is designated as its specific excellence.
(Vākyapadīya, p. 278):
Through hearing and the repeated practice of grammar as a system of rules (*lakṣaṇa*), a specific proficiency arises.

By means of that proficiency—having heard and practiced the rules by taking the linguistic data (*lakṣya*) as examples—one gains knowledge of other linguistic data that follow the same principles, even if they do not have names distinct from those already encountered.
And thus, the excellence of practice consisting in the repeated hearing of the definitions constitutes a specific application;
through that, the knowledge of the true nature of words arises.
Accordingly, with respect to the incorrectness of words, grammar serves as the decisive criterion.
Because it conforms to the capacity of that [convention].
Now, one might object: how can the well-established fact that words such as "cow" convey meaning through *śakti* (denotative power) be possible without it? To this, he says:
"Incapacity": there is no incapacity of those words, such as *gavī* and so forth, with respect to the object *gavya*; rather, they possess the capacity [to denote it].
However, their status as signifiers of the meaning arises from their conformity to the word *go*, that is, from their similarity to the word *go*.
The underlying point is this: someone desiring to utter the word *go* may, due to a defect in the sense organs, utter *gavī*.

Another person understands that what he intends to speak of possesses a dewlap and other such features. Having learned this, others also utter the word "gāvī" when something possessing a dewlap is intended to be spoken of.
Thus, words such as *gāvī* convey their meaning by means of the recollection of the correct (*sādhu*) word.
Furthermore, because it is a part [of a word], a suffix would arise even in the case of an indeclinable.

For example, when asked, "From where have you come?", and one ought to say, "I am coming from the Aśmakas," someone might instead say, "I am coming with the Aśmakas. In that case, since the nominal stem *aśmaka-* is a part [of the full form], and because the word *aśmakebhyaḥ* is recalled [from that partial form], the respondent understands the answer to the question despite the corruption.

Just as in the case of *aśmakebhyaḥ*, even though there is a corruption of the case ending—as in *aśmakaiḥ*—the intended meaning is still understood, so too from words such as *gavya* and others, the comprehension of the meaning occurs through the recollection of the expressive, correct word (*sādhuśabda*).
However, the word *gavya* and the like are not themselves expressive or correct.
Therefore, the knowledge of the correctness and incorrectness of words is derived from grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).
It is established that only the correct form (*sādhu*) should be employed, not the incorrect (*asādhu*).
At the time of performance, the presentation of the object of the rite is the purpose of the mantra's recitation;
it is understood that the object presented by the mantra is what must be performed.
Bhāṣya 12.1.125:

"Because there is no injunction for usage, as in the case of oneness due to non-separation. Now, regarding the doubt as to whether words such as "cow" (go) are the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the form (*ākṛti*) or for the individual (*vyakti*), it is said in reply: The word "cow" and others—do they denote the universal form or the individual? Since there is doubt on this matter, the following is stated. [Note: The commentary explains that because there is no scriptural injunction requiring the use of a word for a specific individual, the word must refer to the universal form, which remains constant across all individuals.]

First, let this be examined: are the very same words that are worldly (*laukika*) also those that are Vedic (*vaidika*), or are they different? When they are the same, the doubt arises as to whether their meaning is also the same or different. In this regard, Prabhākara—desiring a direct connection [to the main subject] even while accepting that the investigation of whether the worldly and Vedic words are identical or distinct is a subordinate matter (*uddeśya*)—has presented a separate connection by stating the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) on the grounds of non-authoritativeness (*aprāmāṇya*).
And this [treatment] appears like a "token gift" even for one accompanied by a son-in-law who has been drenched with the essence of excessive generosity;

for indeed, even an introductory section (upodghāta) does not require a separate connection, since it is connected by virtue of its very connection to that [main topic], being intended for the sake of establishing the manifest deliberation. Thus, the topical section (adhikaraṇa) is introduced exactly as it follows in sequence.

For, in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), having established that words such as "cow" (*go*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), the determination of the denoted object (*vācya*) is commenced by way of that same context: is it the generic form (*ākṛti*) that is denoted, or is it the individual (*vyakti*)?

Anticipating the objection that this inquiry might be purposeless, its utility is now investigated by way of an introductory discussion (*upoddhāta*): are the very same words used in common worldly usage (*laukika*) also those used in the Veda (*vaidika*), and are their meanings the same, or are they different?

In this regard, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Having stated, "Now begins the instruction of words," [the author] says, "Of which words? Of both worldly and Vedic ones. From this, a distinction is first understood due to the observation of different designations by those experts who know words (namely, the authors of the *Mahābhāṣya*).
Likewise, a distinction is also understood from the difference in form.
For instance, in the Veda they read "adhakāpālaḥ."
In common usage there is "a cake on eight potsherds" (*aṣṭakapāla*);
likewise, in the Veda there is "Agniṣṭoma," and in common usage there is "Agniṣṭoma. Similarly, in the Veda there is "guhyāmi," and in common usage there is "guhyāmi."
Likewise, a difference in meaning is also observed.
It is heard in the Veda: "The divine cows indeed carry [the offerings] while lying on their backs," "The tree has golden leaves," and likewise, "Clarified butter is honey.
And yet, such things as these do not exist in the world in the same manner as the actual objects denoted by words like "cow" and so forth.
Therefore, even in cases such as the words "cow" (*go*) and so forth, where no difference in form is perceived, there too the difference between words arises solely from the difference in meaning;
and the determination of identity is merely a statement of similarity.
Even where there is a difference in form, there too there is likewise a difference in meaning.
However, the comprehension of meaning in the Veda is precisely because it differs from the worldly [usage].

Therefore, since words and their meanings differ in the world and in the Veda, the investigation into whether worldly words such as "cow" denote the class (*ākṛti*) or the individual (*vyakti*) is of no use for establishing the authority of the Veda.
This being the case, it is replied:
this would indeed be so if there were a difference between worldly and Vedic words;
however, because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), the worldly and Vedic [words] are one and the same.

Those very words such as "cow" and so forth that are recognized in common worldly usage are also recognized in the Veda. Nor can it be argued that words such as "eight-potherd [oblation]" or "Iṣṭi sacrifice" are not recognized because of some difference in their application.
Because the word *go* (cow) is recognized as being unmodified, just like the word *nalāṅgala*.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that common worldly words such as *aṣṭakapāla* and others could not share the same unmodified meaning as their Vedic counterparts, such as *aṣṭakapāla*.

Or, let it be granted that some words are different; yet this is not the case, for there is no reason whatsoever for words such as *go*, which are recognized as being unmodified, to be considered different.
The difference in designation, however, like that between a "Brahmin" and a "wandering mendicant," is based solely on their inclusion within Vedic sentences of distinct forms.

As for the statement, "Indeed, the divine cows carry [the offerings] while lying on their backs," that too is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), because its purpose is to extol the specific action of carrying on their backs—a fact already established in common worldly experience.
Thus, other examples as well are intended solely for the sake of praise.
This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "Those very words that are worldly are the same as those that are Vedic, and their meanings are the same.

The purpose [of this discussion] is that the commencement or non-commencement of the Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa (the section concerning the genus) depends upon the positions of the *pūrvapakṣa* and the *siddhānta*.

The Sūtra, however, states that there is identity between the form of the word and its meaning in both the worldly and Vedic contexts, because they are recognized as identical and because there is no distinction between them.

And this being the case, there would be the existence of injunctions for the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices. [Tautātita-sūtra: "Because of the absence of injunctions for performance, there is oneness due to non-distinction."

Regarding the inquiry as to whether the words such as "cow" (*go*) and so forth, along with their respective meanings, which are worldly, are the very same as those in the Veda or whether they are different, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) states:
"Unity of meaning" (*arthakatvam*) means the oneness of the meaning—that is, the identity of the denotative word and the denoted object.
Those very same words and meanings that exist in the world are the ones found in the Veda, and not others.

Because there is an absence of injunction for usage (*prayoga-codanā*) regarding words and their referents in both worldly and Vedic contexts, Vedic words would lack grasped connections (*agṛhīta-saṃgati*). Consequently, the utterance of sentences for the sake of understanding Vedic sentence-meanings would be impossible. A "sentence" (*vākya*) is that which is used (*prayujyate*);
its "injunction" (*codanā*) is its utterance; because of the existence (*bhāvāt*)—that is, the presence—of such an injunction [for worldly sentences, the same applies to Vedic ones].
And thus, for the sake of establishing the injunctions regarding ritual application, the identity of words and word-meanings in both worldly and Vedic usage must necessarily be accepted.
But is this not merely a practical purpose?
Let the reason be stated.
It is stated: because of the non-separation of the word and its referent.
Since they are not perceived as distinct or separate, the unity of meaning is established.

If, however, there were a difference between words and their meanings, then because the relationship of all Vedic words would remain uncomprehended, there would be an absence of knowledge regarding their meaning; consequently, there would follow the non-existence of injunctions for usage consisting of the connection between action and its factors (kriyākāraka).
Thus, the word *abhāvāt* is to be split in two ways—as both "because of existence" and "because of non-existence.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that words and their meanings are identical in both the world and the Veda.
Now, regarding the inquiry as to whether the meaning of a word is the *ākṛti* (form) or the *vyakti* (individual), he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*):
the individual is the meaning of the word, not the form.

This is because, if the form were the referent of the word, there would be an absence of injunctions for practical application; that is, injunctions for performance such as "He threshes the rice" and "He sacrifices the animal" would become impossible, resulting in their non-existence.
For neither riding nor immolation is possible for a genus;
therefore, the individual is the meaning of the word,
