because [the word] does not denote a substance.
The manifestation (*vyakti*) of a word must be accepted as residing only in the individual (*vyakti*), not in the genus (*jāti*).

For if the genus were the referent, there would follow the consequence that the word would not denote a substance (*adravyaśabdatva*), because it would lack the status of being a word denoting a substance; this would entail the consequence that the word lacks the capacity to express a substance. Furthermore, in injunctions prescribing sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) such as "one cow is to be given," "six are to be given," or "twelve are to be given," words such as "six" could not be construed with the word "cow" (*go*), because the genus "cowness" (*gotvajāti*) is a single entity.
And because another [animal] is seen:
in the statement, "If the animal should escape while being cooked, one should immolate another for that purpose," we observe another animal in place of the first animal that was accepted.
If the word *paśu* (animal) were denotative of the generic form (*ākṛti*), then the immolation of another would not be logically possible.
The same form belongs to any other animal as well;
therefore, one must accept that the word denotes the individual—this is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
But the form (ākṛti) [is what is denoted], because [the sacrifice] is for the sake of action.

When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been reached—that the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) is the denotable meaning (*śakyārtha*) of words—the aphorism of the established conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*) follows.
The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside the prima facie view.
"Form" (*ākṛti*) refers to what is called form, namely the universal (*jāti*).
The meaning of words is the genus (*jāti*), not the individual (*vyakti*), because only the genus serves the purpose of action.
This is evident in sentences such as "Construct the *śyenacit*," which refer to the construction of a specific sacrificial altar (*sthāṇḍila*) shaped like a hawk.
Because it is possible for [the word] to convey actions such as "blue" and so forth, whereas that would be impossible if the individual (*vyakti*) were the denotable object.
If it is argued that "there would be no action," and thus the injunction applies to another thing and not to the substance;
or if it is argued that "the power of the word resides in the form (*ākṛti*)," then in that case, actions such as carrying a load would not be possible.

If it is argued that actions such as the immolation of an animal (*ālambhana*) are possible only in the case of an individual (*vyakti*) and not in the case of a genus (*jāti*), [we reply: if the position were that of the *ākṛti* (genus/form), then in the case of the injunction, "If the animal consecrated for sacrifice should escape, one should immolate another animal in its place," there would be no prescription of another object—that is, another individual—because the *ākṛti* remains the same even in that other instance. Regarding the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position that the word's expressive power (śakti) resides only in the individual (vyakti) and not in the form (ākṛti), the answer to the reasons stated in the sūtras beginning with the thirtieth up to the twenty-fourth is given by this [present] sūtra:

because the usage—such as the usage of "carrying" and so forth—is for that purpose, meaning it is for the sake of the individual; since [the word's application] is established in the form through the medium of the individual, there is no contradiction.
As for "non-distinction" (avibhāga): because there is no absolute distinction between the universal (jāti) and the individual, there is therefore no contradiction.

Even though [the word] denotes a genus (*jāti*), because it is through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that there is the application of the individual (*vyakti*), the injunction for usage (*prayogacodanā*)— that is, the rule of application (*prayogavidhi*)— is established as the means of cognition; thus, the performance of threshing and other such acts is logically justified.
The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the denotative power of the word resides only in the form (ākṛti).

Regarding this, the Vārttika states: "Because it is for that purpose; because it is for the sake of the *apūrva*. Since sacrificial acts such as immolation (*ālambhana*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) must be employed as means for accomplishing the *apūrva*, and since it is the substance (*dravya*)—not the form—that is the means for accomplishing the *apūrva* because it is required by the sacrifice for its own fulfillment, whereas the form is incapable [of such action]."

That denotation [of the word] must be understood as being for the purpose of restricting the substance (*dravya*), and not for its own sake, because it depends upon the universal (*jāti*) and because it would otherwise result in having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*). Furthermore, since the instrumentality of the universal—which is denoted by the nominal stem—is perceived, that too is only through the restriction of the substance and not directly, due to its inherent unsuitability. Therefore, since the denotation of the form (*ākṛti*) has that [restriction] as its purpose, and since [the universal] serves to restrict the substance, and since in the case of the substance there is the possibility of [performing] acts such as immolation (*ālambhana*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), as well as [grammatical relations like] number, kāraka, and coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is no invisibility [of purpose].
Thus it says: "The non-distinction of the ritual application" (sūtra).
Even in the view that the universal (*ākṛti*) is the primary meaning, the ritual application such as the act of immolation (*ālambhana*) is inseparable from the substance (*dravya*).

Since there is no absolute difference between the universal and the individual, sometimes the substance is denoted in its individual form and sometimes in its universal form, according to the speaker's intention; for the word has both forms as its object (*tadarthatvāt*).
Even if the individual instance (*vyakti*) is not denoted, no distinction in ritual application (*prayoga*) is obtained;

nor is there any need for such a distinction because, since there is no absolute difference between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual, the properties (*dharma*) belonging to the individual are effectively established in the universal itself.

Furthermore, since both the form (*ākṛti*) and the individual serve as the purpose of the sacrifice, and since the properties performed in whatever serves as a means to the sacrifice are purposeful, they are inseparable from the substance (*dravya*). Thus, there is no utility in distinguishing them in practice.

Therefore, since even in the view that the word denotes the form (*ākṛti*), the possibility of [the form being] the whole (*ālabhya*) and so forth exists, it is established that the form alone is the meaning of the word. [Question: How can there be the accomplishment of the ritual action (*karma-siddhi*) without the determination of usage (*prayoga-pariccheda*)? [Answer: Usage is the inclusion [of the details] within the injunction. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 856).
The word *upa* signifies proximity; the word *sam* signifies totality; and the word *grahaṇa* signifies the act of grasping.
Thus, the three together constitute the term for application (*prayoga*).
Among these, this [term] has the nature of grasping.

(The sense is that among the three components, that which serves the purpose of ensuring the performance is the very nature of the *prayogavacana* [the injunction of performance]. The other two, however, are qualifiers regarding its proximity and completeness;
by means of these two, the whole is perceived as qualified.)

Ḍupa. 1211 2|7. It has been stated by [the author] himself in the section on the conflict between the subordinate and the primary (3|1|2) that the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) is weaker than the extended application (*codaka*) because it occurs at a later time;
this will also be explained by the Bhāṣya at this point (5|1|1–10|18).
Vārttika 3|1|2|15 states in the twelfth book (1|2|12|7) that the injunction of performance is weaker in relation to the extended application.
*Soma*, 5.1.10: The injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) brings about those constituent elements (*padārtha*) which possess the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).
Bhāṣya, 5.1.10.17: The injunction of performance is the collector of those [elements] already obtained;
the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), however, is the producer and the bringer of the ritual properties (*dharma*).

Therefore, the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), occurring at a later time, is weaker due to its remoteness from the purpose. (9.1.2.15). The injunction of performance encompasses everything. (6.1.4.10; 3.4.26). Regarding the items that are to be performed together, the injunction of performance permits only as much temporal extension as occurs through one's utmost capacity for one who is not hurrying for the sake of all the items.
If one who is capable were to allow even a moment’s distraction, the injunction of the performance-statement (*prayogavacana*) would not tolerate it.
Vārttika 1.3.16 states that, by virtue of being a performance-statement, all constituent elements (*padārtha*) must be kept proximate to the time of the principal act (*pradhāna*).
This is because, through the single word of the performance-statement, both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the principal are expressed together.

Bhāṣya 10.1.16: Because of the performance-injunction (*prayogavacana*), which effects the collection of what has already been produced, the originative injunction (*utpādaka*) and the applicatory injunction (*prāpaka*), as the *codaka*, are stronger.
Therefore, when there is no [other] assumption to be made, the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the Bārhaspatya sacrifice come first, and the properties of the Sarasvatī sacrifice come later.
5.1.10.17–18: The function of the performance-injunction is "collection" (*upasaṃgraha*).
After the operation of the *codaka* (the rule of extension), there is the inclusion (*upasaṃgraha*). [Dupa.

1211/13] That which depends on the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance) is sublated by that which depends on the *codaka*, just as in the case of the *syena* sacrifice, where the role of the *udgātṛ* priest regarding the archetypal (*prakṛta*) auxiliary rites is sublated by the plurality of officiating priests obtained through the *codaka*.
[Bāla. p. 141] That which is based on the *prayogavacana* is sublated by that which is based on the *codaka*, because it has not yet been established [by the latter].

This [is stated] at Vārttika 3.1.14, page 860: "Because they depend upon the *prayogavacana* (the statement of performance), the primary [order] and the sequence of transgression (*vyatikrama*) are weak; however, because they depend upon the *codaka* (the injunctive transfer), the direct statement (*śruti*), the sense (*artha*), the order of recitation (*pāṭha*), and the section (*kāṇḍa*) are stronger.
At *Dvādaśādhyāyī* 5.1.10–18: "By means of the *prayogavākya*, actions whose essential forms have been determined are grasped."

Vārttika 2.1.2.11, p. 466: The injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) is that which causes the execution of multiple constituent elements (*padārtha*) by a single agent. Soma, 5.1.9, p. 406: The injunction of performance is that which [establishes] the state of being achievable through volitional effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*). [Page] 2800: The treatise on performance (*prayogaśāstra*).
The *bodhaka-vidhi* (informative injunction) [is stronger].
Bhaṭṭa, p. 151. The *prayoga-vidhi* (injunction of performance) is weak even regarding the matter of sequence (*krama*).

Since the *prayoga-vidhi*, which consists of its own conceptualization, would have its own conceptualization cut off [by a stronger injunction], it does not possess the capacity to conceptualize another sequence.

*Soma* 5.1.10: The injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavidhi*) is weaker than the extended application (*codaka*), because the injunction regarding the performance depends upon the attainment of the constituent elements (*padārtha*), and that attainment depends upon the extended application. Thus, based on this [logical] inconsistency, the offering of the outer [oblation] occurs first, followed by the offering of the clarified butter (*ājya*) to Sarasvatī.
5.1.10: The injunction regarding the performance is weaker than that which relies upon the extended application.

5|1|10|17-18. Even in the case of obligatory (nitya) entitlement, the injunction of performance (prayoga-vidhi) mandates the principal act as qualified by all its constituent parts. Su. p. 532. An injunction of performance is an injunction that makes known the performance together with its auxiliary parts. Furthermore, it is friendly toward the obligatory rite and dependent upon the originative injunction (utpatti-vidhi) and the injunction of application (yoga-vidhi).
Nor should it be asked for what purpose that conceptualization is made;
for since [the result] cannot be obtained by any other means due to having the same location and agent,
that [conceptualization] is necessary in order to obtain it.

Others maintain that the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) is precisely the cognition of the distinction between the auxiliary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) sentences (Maṇi., p. 99). Just as ritual items (*padārtha*) are enjoined by the injunction of performance according to their application through direct statement, indicative mark, and so forth, so too sequence (*krama*) is enjoined by the injunction of performance because it has been applied by direct statement and the rest (Soma., 5.1.1, p. 406). Since the injunction of performance is dependent upon a causal condition (*nimitta*), there can be no sublation of the scriptural statement of that condition in accordance with it.

Su. Pṛ. 532: In the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*), because the *prayāja* offerings and other such elements function as subordinate factors (*guṇatva*), there is no syntactic connection with each individual action.
Bāla. Pṛ. 165: The weakness of that which is dependent upon the injunction regarding performance has been established in various places.

Bhāṭṭa. 1112/7: When something is prompted by the injunction regarding performance, its performance follows as long as it is possible; however, when it is impossible, it is to be omitted in accordance with the scriptural statement of the occasion (*nimittaśruti*).
Bhāṭṭa 6.2.7:
"If it is argued that they are treatises on ritual practice (prayogaśāstra). Here, the *kalpasūtras* are the examples.
The *Māṣaka*, *Hāstika*, *Kauṇḍinyaka*, and other such works are characterized by doubt as to whether they are authoritative (*pramāṇa*) or non-authoritative (*aprāmāṇa*).
Regarding this, the section (*adhikaraṇa*) is described as follows, based on its connection with the subject of illumination (*prabhākaraṇa*):

Just like the Vedas, the *Kalpasūtras* also possess the nature of being Vedic because there is no difference in their status as subjects of formal study (*svādhyāya-adhyāya*), nor in their form and so forth, and because there is no difference in their content; furthermore, the titles of the *Māṣaka* and other such works are justified as being due to specific recensions (*pravacana*), similar to the *Kāṭhaka* and others; therefore, they possess the status of the Veda.
Moreover, if they possess the status of Veda, a mutual contradiction is observed here.
For instance, the Kalpasūtra states, "The Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices are performed on all lunar days," whereas the Vedas state that they are performed only on the full moon and new moon days.
Furthermore, an option between these two, as is possible in the case of rice and barley, is not admissible here.
For when two things of non-conflicting meaning are mutually contradictory, an option (*vikalpa*) arises.

Here, since the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are applicable to all lunar days (*tithi*), including both the full moon and the new moon, there is the possibility of an option; however, because these two contradictory meanings would result in mutual annulment, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they lack authority altogether.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: it would indeed be so [if they were truly contradictory].
It might be argued that [the authorship] is merely a matter of designation (samākhyā), as in the case of the *Kāṭhaka* and so forth;
however, because there is a continuous and most firm tradition of memory regarding the authors such as Madhu and others, it must indeed be their composition.
This is because, being equal to the Veda, it is invariably associated with unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) due to its recitation by those who are designated as "Vedic" (*vedamin*).
Therefore, since the Kalpasūtras are of human origin, they must simply be disregarded due to their contradiction with the Veda.
This is incorrect;
for there is no lack of authority in two texts of mixed content merely because of their mutual contradiction.
If that were the case, then there would be the undesirable consequence of invalidity even in passages such as "one [offering] for the goddess" and so forth.

If, however, it is argued that in those cases there is no contradiction because one may assume a greater abundance of results, then here too the mention of the full moon and new moon days must be for the sake of a greater abundance of results; thus, the section (adhikaraṇa) is introduced exactly according to the Vārttika.

Having previously cited the Smṛtis of Manu and others and established their authority—on the grounds that they are rooted in Śruti through the same logic applied to the Kalpasūtras and Purāṇas—the present section now cites the Kalpasūtras themselves. It raises the objection that these very texts possess independent authority equal to the Vedas, and by refuting this, the principle of the *Smṛti-adhikaraṇa* (the section on Smṛti) is further explained.

Nor should it be argued that [the *kalpasūtras*] fall under that same principle as the *smṛtis* such as those concerning the *aṣṭakā*, on the grounds that "since dharma has its root in the Word (*śabda*), that which lacks the Word would not be authoritative," for in the case of those *smṛtis* whose root words are perceived, they are indeed subject to that principle. But how can the *kalpasūtras* also be subject to that principle when their roots are directly perceived? For it is not the case that all *smṛtis* have unperceived roots;
this is because *smṛtis* such as those concerning the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) find their basis in the directly perceived Veda.
Nor is it the case that all Kalpasūtras are based directly upon the Vedas as their source;
for, due to the objections raised regarding the various Vedic recensions (śākhās), there is no recovery of the Vedic texts that would serve as the root for those Kalpasūtras.
The only distinction lies in the fact that some have been studied more extensively than others.
Nor does it become the subject of that principle merely by this much.
As for the statement that the *Kalpasūtras* alone were cited as the primary example, that should not be respected, as it was made in accordance with the *Bhāṣya*.

Here, the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) is as follows: because the *Smṛtis*, the *Purāṇas*, and the *Kalpasūtras* concern supersensuous matters that are accepted and revered by great men, they possess the very status of *Veda*, just like the injunctions regarding the *Agnihotra* and other rites.
Likewise, it is understood from the Veda itself that the word of the Teacher (ācārya) is authoritative;
and this is only consistent if those [Vedic texts] are eternal.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction due to the conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal, and because designations such as "Māśaka" and so forth could just as well be explained as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth based on the act of teaching alone.
Furthermore, the designation of an author (*kartṛ-vyapadeśa*) is justified by the mention of "makers of mantras" (*mantrakṛt*) and the like;

for just as in the Veda there is the mention of "makers of mantras" regarding the originator of mantras, such as in the passage, "Śiśu Āṅgirasa was a maker of mantras among the makers of mantras" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 13.3.124), so too in common worldly usage there is the designation of an "author" regarding originators such as Māṣaka and others.

This being the case, even though the Buddha and others are not [directly] perceived, their status as authoritative sources on Dharma is intended by the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*), because they are indistinguishable from the Vedas in terms of the same logical principle and the fact that they are treatises on ritual application (*prayoga-śāstra*).
This being the case, it is replied:
"No, because of the lack of restriction.
This is the intended meaning.

This would indeed be the case where the status of being a Veda could be established for something that has as its object supersensuous matters accepted by the reverence of great men, even in the absence of [being] a Veda.
And that status is possible in two ways: both as a Veda and as being rooted in the Veda.

In this regard, because it is impossible for it to be a human-authored Veda due to the continuous and very firm tradition of remembrance regarding its author, it is established as being equivalent to the Veda according to the settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *Smṛti-adhikaraṇa*.

As for the claim that, even if [the Veda] were eternal, there could be an instruction regarding an agent (kartṛ) just as there is regarding the place of the mantra-composer (*mantrakṛt*), that is inconsistent; for a mere mention, like that of the mantra-composer’s place, can be explained away in some way or another.
However, in the case of the most firm recollections of an agent, no explanation whatsoever is possible without admitting non-eternality. And such a recollection does not exist in the Veda.
If that were the case, it would follow that the Veda itself is non-eternal.
And this being so, even the traditional designation (*samākhyā*) would be based on human authorship, rather than being based on recitation as in the case of the *Kāṭhaka* and other texts.

As for the claim that the Veda itself establishes the eternity of the *Kalpasūtras* and similar works by stating, "The word of the teacher is authoritative," otherwise there would be a contradiction regarding the conjunction of the eternal with the non-eternal—this is incorrect.
For this Veda is not the subject of the *pravacana* (recitation) in the form of *kalpa-sūtras* by Māśaka and others; what then? This refers exclusively to the word of the *ācārya*.
And the *ācārya* has been defined by Manu and others:
"A twice-born man should teach the Veda to a pupil who is to be initiated (*upanayanīya*)."
One who possesses both the ritual manual (kalpa) and the secret teachings (rahasya) is declared to be an Ācārya.
Thus [Manu 2.140].
And his word is indeed authoritative regarding the subject matter of students.
As it has been said: "Of one who explains the meaning of the Vedas and himself recites the Vedas..."
Because there is no other means of knowledge regarding disciples, the word of the teacher is authoritative.
Thus [it is stated in Vākyapadīya 1.3.6.14, p. 242].
Nor is there a contradiction regarding the conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal;

for the suffix -aṇ is applied to the word *ācārya* by relying on its status as a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) which serves as the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), because it possesses an eternal meaning in cases such as *pāśaka*.
Alternatively, based on the etymological derivation that "he who gathers (ācinoti) the intelligence of the listeners," it is not at all unreasonable to consider the Veda itself as the *ācārya*.
For this very reason, because there is a more firmly established tradition regarding its authorship, even the scriptures of the Buddha and others do not possess independent authority.

However, there is this distinction: the authority of the *Kalpasūtras* and similar texts is due to their being rooted in the Veda, whereas those [other scriptures] lack authority precisely because they are rooted in what is unreal.

The purpose [of this discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), even for one who has studied the *Kalpasūtras*, there would be a Vedic expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for transgressions; whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is because they are not the Veda.

As for the Sūtra: "The status of being the Veda does not belong to the *Kalpasūtras* and so forth, because they were composed by Māśaka and others through a restrictive compilation of what was previously non-existent.
(Tautā.)
If it is argued that they are *prayogaśāstra* (manuals of performance):
regarding the inquiry as to whether the *kalpasūtras*—such as the *Māśaka*, *Hāstika*, and *Kauṇḍinyaka*—are authoritative or not, the proponent states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

If it is argued that the *prayogaśāstra*—the manual (*śāstra*) or instructor (*śāsaka*) concerning the sequence of items to be performed (*anuṣṭheya-padārtha-paurvāparya*)—is authoritative by its own authority.
"Not so, because of the lack of restriction.
The proponent of the established view (siddhāntin) refutes the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa):
"The Kalpasūtra is not an independent authority, because there is no restrictive rule [to that effect]."
"This is not a sound basis because of the absence of [proper] accents," so says the Bhāṣya.
"Because it was composed by persons such as Bodhāyana and others who were previously non-existent, and because it was produced according to rule after rule"—this is the curiosity [of the opponent].
[The answer is: "Because there is no supplementary statement (avākyaśeṣa)."
In the Siddhānta, he states another argument:

just as there are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as supplements to sentences in the Veda, such do not exist in the Kalpasūtras. Thus, because they lack sentence-supplements—that is, due to their being devoid of sentence-supplements—the Kalpasūtra is not an independent authority like the Veda.
The meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) is that it is also because [the Kalpasūtras] provide instructions regarding the present *kalpa*.

The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) refutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), which asserts that the *Kalpasūtras* are independent authorities because they are the words of those whose speech is truth and because they are applied everywhere as well as being proximate scriptures.

[The refutation is as follows: In the *Kalpasūtra* statement, "In the *pūrvapakṣa*, on all lunar days (*tithi*) there is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)," the word *amāvāsyā* is employed in reference to all the lunar days of the *pūrvapakṣa*; therefore, it is stated that the performance of the new-moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā-yajña*) is to be carried out on every such day.
In proximity to the *amāvāsyā* sacrifice, there is indeed a scriptural statement from the Śruti: "One should sacrifice on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).

Since [the Kalpasūtras] are employed in this manner everywhere and because of their proximity to the scriptural injunctions, the author of the Kalpasūtra does not establish himself as one who speaks only the truth [independently]. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the authority of the Kalpasūtras is independent.

Regarding the *prayogaśāstra* (2802), the motive for this inquiry is as follows: the word "ca" (and) signifies a reason (*hetu*), namely that the *kalpasūtras* are authoritative only because they are rooted in the Veda, and not independently; therefore, they are non-authoritative when in conflict with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣaśruti*).
As for the second doubt, the word "ca" serves to include other subject matters, such as the topic beginning with "or both, because there is no distinction" (*aviśeṣād ubhau vā*).
The *apūrva* (transcendental result) is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the auxiliary parts belonging to the *agnihotra* and other rites; by means of it, the modification (*ūha*) is established.
The *apūrva* is the motivator for the auxiliaries that provide direct assistance (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), just as it is for those that provide indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*).
[Bhāṣya 9.1.1.2–3] The *apūrva* is the motivator for the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the mortar and pestle.
9|1|12–3: The *prayojaka* (the motive) for the new (*apūrva*) is the praise by means of the *caru*, the *hautra*, and the *hotṛ-mantra*, but not the aggregate of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
9|1|5|11–19: The *prayojaka* for the new (*apūrva*) is the mantra "parīcchan trīn," but not the state of being a *paridhi* in the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

In the case of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, the discarding of blood and so forth, or the seizing of the animal, is not the motive.

In this regard, the mention of a fruit is merely a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*).
[Śabara-bhāṣya 4.1.1–4]: The fruit is not the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the constituent acts (*karma*), such as the *āghāra*, the *ājyabhāga*, the *prayāja*, and the *anuyāja*.
And those ritual acts are for the sake of the sacrifice;
in that regard, the mention of a fruit is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) concerning the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

Furthermore, the motivator is of two kinds: that which is a motivator for its own sake (*svārtha-prayojaka*) and that which is a motivator for the sake of another (*parārtha-prayojaka*).

The first case is as follows: the principal element (*śeṣin*), such as heaven (*svarga*) and so forth, impels the subordinate element (*śeṣa*), such as sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, for its own sake and not for the sake of another.

The second case is as follows: when there is a cause (*nimitta*) such as living or cutting, the subordinate element (*śeṣabhūta*) such as the ten [days] and so forth, as well as the *medana-homa* and so forth, do not impel [the action] for their own sake. (Cāla., p.
107) The impeller (*prayojaka*) is indeed the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), as it is known from the Veda.

4|1|38-9: The status of being a motivator (*prayojaka*) or non-motivator (*aprayojaka*) is treated in the fourth chapter.
Vārttika on 2|1|1, p. 372: The status of being a motivator or non-motivator does not exist apart from the relationship of the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*).

Ṭup. 7|1|1|1: For the status of being a motivator (*prayojaka*) or a non-motivator (*aprayojaka*) follows from [the rule] "there is inequality regarding the purpose" (4|1|8|29); thus, from 2804 onwards, the discussion concerning the purpose has been directly considered starting from the examination of the *āsomalipta* (4|2|8|20–22).
Ratna. 5|2|1|9: Because they are both motivators and non-motivators, there is no fixed order.
The definition of the motivator and the non-motivator is the subject matter of the fourth chapter.
In the fourth [section], the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the non-instigator (*aprayojaka*) are defined.
Therein, the instigator is of such a nature, and the non-instigator is also of such a nature.
[1] A certain [type] is an instigator even of arising, as well as of the appropriation (*upādāna*) and of the maintenance (*pālana*).
For example, in the case of the Agni sacrifice, the sequence of the sacrificial vessel (*kapāla*), the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*), and so forth, is determined by their respective verbal injunctions.

[2] Some things are non-efficient with respect to all three stages; for instance, the scattering of husks (*tuṣopavāpa*) is not the efficient cause for the production of the vessel, nor for its acquisition, nor for its preservation.
Rather, it merely takes as its instrument a vessel that has already been produced, acquired, and preserved for the sake of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

[3] Something may be non-efficient with respect to the production of something else, yet efficient with respect to its appropriation and preservation. For example, the threshing of grain is not the cause of the production of dust, since that is established by its very nature; rather, it is the cause of the appropriation of those particles already existing in a state of equality, in the form of their being gathered, and of their preservation. Similarly, the morning milking of a cow is not the cause of the production of milk that has not yet been drunk or heated, but it does prompt the appropriation of the milk already situated in the udder in the form of milking, as well as its preservation.

The *vājina* sacrifice (*vājinayāga*) is also not the cause of the production of the *vājina*, because that production depends upon the bringing of curd for the sake of the *āmikṣā*; however, it is indeed the cause of the acquisition and preservation of the *vājina*.

[4] Some things are causes only of production, and not of acquisition or preservation; for example, the *āmikṣā* is the cause of the production of the *vājina*, but not of its acquisition or preservation.
Likewise, a result such as heaven is the cause only of the production of the sacrifice, and not of the acquisition or preservation of the sacrifice.
Because it is impossible for there to be a material cause (*upādāna*) for a sacrifice distinct from its production, and because preservation is impossible for that which is momentary:
[5] some [agent] is the instigator only of production and material cause, but not of mere preservation; for example, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth are the instigators of the remnant (*śeṣa*).

[6] Some [agent] is the instigator only of the material cause, and not of production or preservation; for example, in the case of placing the seventh footprint on the grinding stone (*grāvan*), the act of sacrificing the axle is the instigator only of the taking up of the unrefined dust, and not of the production or preservation of that dust.

Thus, in the case of the pouring of husks (*tuṣopavāpa*) into the cooked rice (*caru*), it is the very act of taking [the husks] by hand that is the motivator (*prayojaka*), not the production or the preservation of them.

Similarly, in the case of the animal sacrifice for Agni and others (*āgneyādi-gāgo*), it is the very act of taking [the animal] through the mental determination (*uddeśa*) of the deity that is the motivator, not the production of the deity or its preservation.

[7] Some thing is a motivator only for production and preservation, but not for taking, as for example: heaven and other fruits are the motivators for the production of the *apūrva* (unseen potency), and also for its preservation, as in the case of the discourse on the destruction of merit and the destruction of karma at the beginning [of their fruition].

For when the production [of an action] has been accomplished, there is no further material cause (*upādāna*) for the *apūrva* distinct from that production which could be impelled by a fruit such as heaven.

[8] A certain [impeller] is an impeller only of the production and the material cause, not of the maintenance; for example, in the modification of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, when the *nirvāpa* (offering) has not yet occurred, the giving of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest while the sacrificer is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) is an impeller of the production and the material cause of the staff, but not of its maintenance, because it already existed previously.
Thus, the impeller is of seven kinds, counting the first division and the third and subsequent divisions.
It is established that even the non-efficient [cause] is sevenfold by counting the second, third, and subsequent varieties.
Furthermore, the efficient [cause] is of two kinds:

some prompts for its own sake, as for example, the *śeṣin* (the principal), such as heaven (*svarga*), prompts the *śeṣa* (the subordinate), such as sacrifice (*yāga*), for its own sake, and not for the sake of another.

Someone employs something for the sake of another, not for their own sake; for example, the breaking of a vessel and so forth, which has become a *nimitta* (occasion), or the *darśa* sacrifice and the *bhedana-homa* (oblation for breaking) are not employed for their own sake, but rather for the sake of the *śeṣa* (subsidiary purpose), such as the destruction of sin or the assistance to the ritual (*ṛtu*).
As it was said by the Teachers: "In the same way, the oblations are employed due to occasions such as breaking or spilling;
it is not considered that these oblations have [the occasion] as their subsidiary."
Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, the non-efficient (aprayojaka) is of two kinds. One is that which is non-efficient even with respect to its own constituent part (svāṅga); for example, the scattering of husks (tuṣopavāpa) is non-efficient even with respect to the potsherd (kapāla), which is its own constituent part.

Some [subsidiary acts] are not the motivators (*aprayojaka*) of another subsidiary, even if that other subsidiary is beneficial to them. For example, the *vājina* sacrifice is not the motivator for the bringing of the curd; or, for example, the immolation of the animal is not the motivator for the leading-in of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), even though the former is accomplished by the latter. Or, for example, the disposal (*pratipatti*)—such as the removal of the blood-clots, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, and the throwing into the *cātvāla* pit—is not the motivator for the blood-clots, the remnant (*śeṣa*), or the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*) and so forth, which are the objects of disposal.

Likewise, even though the animal-cake sacrifice (*paśupuroḍāśayāga*) and others occur in connection with it, they are not the *prayojaka* (instigator) of the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and so forth, which are its own subsidiaries and provide assistance to it.

*Prayojakatva* (the state of being an instigator) consists in being invariably antecedent (*niyatapūrvavṛttitva*), provided that there is a relationship of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekavattva*).
Maṇi, p.
45: "The status of being an instigator (prayojakatva) is twofold: when [the substance] is prepared in parts, or when it is held [as a whole], as in the case of rice (vrīhi) and so forth.
Vārttika 3.8.188.
The state of being a prompter (*prayojakatva*) is the quality of that for whose sake something is performed in order to achieve its accomplishment.
(Vi. 9.1.1, Section 2).
Furthermore, the state of being a purpose (*prayojanatva*), as defined by the prompter, is examined in the fourth chapter.
Bhāṭṭa 4.1.1.
Discussion of Purpose (Prayojana-adhikaraṇa), verse 2805: "The sequence of the primary [rite] and the sequence of performance depend upon the causal agent and the effort."
Or rather, as stated in Vārttika 3.1.1, page 651: "Even a dull-witted person does not engage in activity without aiming at a purpose"—this is the maxim. This maxim has been elaborated by Bhaṭṭācārya.
For instance: "Even a dull-witted person does not engage in activity without aiming at a purpose."

"For one who creates the world, what indeed would not be accomplished? (Ślokavārttika, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra-prakaraṇa: 'For one creating the world, what desired object would not be achieved? Even a fool does not act without aiming at a purpose. "

According to the maxim, "Even a fool does not act without a purpose," it may be doubted that activity—such as the creation and maintenance of the world—toward the Supreme (the Paramātman) is impossible without a motive. [To this, the answer is:
In the *Sanatsujātīya* (Nīlakaṇṭha’s commentary on 1.29), it is stated:
"A purpose may arise even from what was not previously intended, just as by a single utterance one may reach a hundred, and then by repeating it again."
Bhāṣya 5.1.11: The purpose (*prayojana*) need not be stated in a deliberation on a hypothetical discussion (*ācintā*).
Purpose (i.e., the objective) is the authority for the [proper] order, because it would be untenable in the case of a reversal of that order.
Bhaṭṭa 5.1.2.
"The purpose of all sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) is [the attainment of heaven]," and so forth, is the *ānandana* (pleasing statement).
Bhāṣya 10.3.9.71 states: "The purpose need not be stated in the case of a definition.
The Naiyāyika definition is: "That object aiming at which one acts is the purpose" (Nyāyadarśana 1.1.24).
Su. Pṛ. 449; Kaṇikā Pṛ. 339:
"Everything, at the time of its injunction, expects a purpose.
At the time of the operation of this sentence, "He takes the *caru* for Indra and Agni," there arises the expectation as to what its purpose is.
Vārttika 2.2.6.9, p. 519: There is a rule that the *pakṣa* (the thesis) must be stated solely by means of its purpose (*prayojana*).
The purpose of the purpose itself is not stated;
rather, it is the purpose of that which is to be employed [as the thesis].
Bhāṣya 10.1.137:
The Section on Purpose.
In a *sattra* sacrifice, each participant has the entitlement to the entire fruit.
Because it accomplishes the goals of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*), it would thus have that [status as a primary injunction].

The Commentary states: "One desiring offspring should cause him to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite" (*dvādaśāhena prajākāmaṃ yājayet*); "Those desiring prosperity should undergo [the initiation]" (*ṛddhikāmā upeyuḥ*).
"Likewise, in various instances, those desiring such [results] entered into a *satra* sacrifice.
"At least ten, up to twenty-four, should sit for a *satra*.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: does the entitlement to the *satra* belong to that individual who desires its entire fruit, or does the entitlement belong to the assembly (*parṣad*) that desires it?
He says: "But surely, those who desire [prosperity] are indicated as being characterized by a large number; how then can there be eligibility for each one of them individually?

It is replied: Since the injunction "those desiring prosperity" (*ṛddhikāmāḥ*) and so forth applies to all those seeking prosperity—whether collectively or individually—it cannot be restricted to a specific subset by the plural marker.
Therefore, a doubt arises as to whether this refers to each individual person or to the assembly (*parṣad*).
What, then, is the conclusion? Each individual is not capable of performing a *sattra* sacrifice that requires many performers.
However, we understand that the assembly (*parṣad*) is both the agent and the one desiring the result; and a result does not accrue to one who is not the agent.
And yet, no single person desires to perform [the entire rite] alone.
Therefore, the fruit belongs to all collectively, while for each individual it is but a portion of the fruit; thus, the middle [position] would be that the whole fruit [accrues to each].
This being the case, we reply:
Consequently, the entire fruit for that seeker is accomplished through the sacrificial session (*satra*).
Why? Because from a single performance, the accomplishment of each individual human purpose occurs;
when the *satra* is performed as a single integrated act (*tantra*), it accomplishes each individual human purpose through that unified procedure.
And the fruit belongs to the agents, and each one here is an agent.
[The opponent] says: But has it not been stated that a single individual is unable to perform an action involving many agents?
[The respondent] replies: It is said.
It is possible [to speak of each one] when there is a desire to express their independence.
When each one acts independently, then he is urged by means of conciliation and other methods to exclude others [from that action].
Thus, one person accomplishes the human goal, while the others do not.
Therefore, all [the participants] shall be performers; they will have mutual requirements in the *sattra*.
If all are performers, they will be endowed with the fruit individually. [Objection:
But surely, even when joined with one another, each performs [the rite] while the others also perform it?

Therefore, there is no distinction regarding the performance (*prayoga*). The consideration of qualification (*adhikāra*)—whether one is pervaded by the entire fruit or by three fruits—is appropriate [only] for the agent (*kartṛ*); it is like an examination of a crow’s teeth, because there is no distinction in the performance itself.
It is said:

Is the instruction regarding sacrifice intended for one who desires the entire fruit, or is the instruction such that it applies even to one who desires only a portion of the fruit? Thus, the qualification (*adhikāra*) itself is being considered.

(In the *Tantra-vārttika*, this is explained as follows: "That very instruction concerning ritual action which pertains to the qualification of those desiring prosperity (*ṛddhikāma*) is what is being considered."

By breaking down the compound *adhikāre* as a locative case ending (*saptamyanta*), one can also explain it as "it is considered in the chapter on qualification (*adhikāra*)," and thus there is no lack of consistency within the chapter. How do we know this?
Because even when [verbal and physical] performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) exists— Ke. — [the following applies].

Regarding the specific point [of the mental recollection]: is it a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) whose scope is the entire fruit, or is it a subordinate part of that [fruit]? This is the appropriate inquiry.
By this, the connection with the definition (*lakṣaṇasaṃgati*) has been shown.
Alternatively, in one view the fruit of an action accrues to the agent, while in the other view it does not accrue to the agent.
(This is stated by one who is primarily a proponent of the *pūrvapakṣa*.

For he, considering it a *pūrvapakṣa*, thinks that in his own position the fruit goes to the agent; whereas in the position of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because each [individual] is an enjoyer and they are not agents, the fruit does not go to the agent.

Thus he says with a single intention: If this were so (that is, if it were as the *pūrvapakṣa* considers), then because the collective whole is the agent, those [individual members] would not be the agents.
In this way, when there is the cognition of a collective agency (in the performance), there is a distinction.
For instance, if the agency belongs to the group as a whole, then if one person dies during the performance, another cannot be brought in.
But according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since agency belongs to each individual, [if one dies] another is brought in to complete the required number.
[Objection: But surely, the completion of the number is equally [unrestricted] in the other case as well (i.e., in the prima facie view).
[Reply: It is said: in that case (the prima facie view), the number [is determined] by the difference of substances, not by the difference of agents.

If this is so, then just as in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the injunction "one should offer seventeen [animals] to Prajāpati"—where, upon the loss of one animal, the entire group of animals is repeated because the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), being a collective whole, has been lost—so too here, when one [animal] is lost (along with that which was brought to complete the number), they perform the sacrifice again from the beginning, having become seventeen; for such a case refers to the expression of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

(Thus, having established the doubt, he states the prima facie view: What, then, is the conclusion? The connection is with each [individual] as a constituent part of the single fruit; not with the entire fruit. Why? Because if each one were to obtain the entire fruit, then there would have to be separate performances.

Therefore, multiplicity [of results] is not tenable; hence, the injunction regarding the constituent parts of the fruit pertains to the *sattra* sacrifice. Furthermore, as for a rite (such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*) where multiple fruits are enjoined, it has been stated (in the *Yogasiddhi* section, 4.3.99) that even such a rite accomplishes only a single fruit in a single performance—how much more so in the case of one where only a single fruit is enjoined (such as the *sattra* and others).
Thus, by the force of the simultaneous performance understood from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), it has been stated that there is also a collective unity with respect to the fruit.

Now, because the word *kāma* occurs many times, the meaning is not grasped as being [the same for all]; thus he says: Furthermore, in the phrase "those desiring supernatural powers" (*ṛddhikāmāḥ*), this is a *ekaśeṣa* (a grammatical retention of one term).
In that case, if those joined with the others desire the fruit, then the *ekaśeṣa* is justified as demonstrating that connection with the others.
For this *ekaśeṣa* is based on a *dvandva* compound.
Therefore, because mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is perceived by this [word], the result is indeed produced simultaneously.

Now, one might object: since they are being mentioned [as individuals] and because those desiring supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) understand them as a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*), there would be no intention to express mutual conjunction. To this, it is replied:

True; although the mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is not intended to be expressed in this word, nevertheless, it is logical that the connection with the result belongs only to those [factors] whose status as means (*sādhanabhāva*)—that is, their status as agents (*kartṛbhāva*)—is understood [from the verb], because the result accrues to the agent. And since they are understood by the verb to be means through mutual conjunction, therefore they are connected with the result precisely while remaining mutually conjoined.
The mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) understood from the word "kāma" (desire) has been stated as being merely supplementary (*abhyucyamānatva*).
This being the position reached, we reply:

By the principle stated in [PMS] 4.1.2.12, "In that which there is pleasure for a person," since the fruit is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), the sacrificial session (*satra*) is enjoined as the means for each individual who desires the entire fruit; they are not enjoined with respect to the *satra* itself (because, since they are merely being referred to in relation to the *satra*, their collective association is not intended to be significant).
Therefore, they are each treated as independent agents.

Consequently, the entire fruit belongs to each one individually. Regarding this very point, he states another reason: "The *ātmanepada* occurs when the fruit of the action accrues primarily to the agent (*kartṛprāye kriyāphale*); and agency (*kartṛtva*) belongs to each one alone. Furthermore, if each one were an agent, then because there would be many agents, it would be illogical for there to be [only] a singular number [of the verb].

Otherwise (if there were no individual agency), since the assembly (*pariṣad*) would be the agent and it is a single entity, there would be an absence of diversity among agents; and due to the absence of diversity among agents, the plurality [of agency] conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) would be untenable. If, on the other hand, the plurality heard [in the text] regarding agency (the form of the agent) is postulated as residing in the substances (*dravya*), then this very same fault arises: that what is heard in one place is postulated in another.

The meaning of this [Bhāṣya] passage, "when one employs [the sacrifice] by means of conciliation and so forth," is as follows: for one who desires a result, the sacrificial session (*satra*) is prescribed as the means; and that [session] is capable of accomplishing the result through many performers (since the plurality denoted by the verbal suffix is intended to be significant).

In that case, one who is acting independently, seeing another also acting independently, says: "You must sacrifice together with me, not with anyone else. Regarding this restriction concerning a companion (*sahāyaniyama*), the means beginning with conciliation (*sāma*) are employed, just like travelers; for example, those setting out upon a difficult road, though all are independent, become companions to one another. If agency belongs to one [who is] independent, then the others are merely [factors of] number.

They would be [merely] for the purpose of filling [the number of] officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); consequently, because they lack independent agency (*svatantra-kartṛtva*), the plurality [of agents] would be absent—this is the very same fault mentioned in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Therefore, the meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is exactly as stated.

As for what was said—that if each were an agent individually, there would be an absence of plurality due to the difference in performance (*prayoga-bheda*)—it is replied: that very performance is identical for each individual [agent therein] (it is not distinct); no distinction is perceived there, such that "the performance belongs to one and not to the other."

(How is it not understood? To this he says: The resolve regarding a substance intended for a deity is common to each [deity] individually. And this being so, since the status of agent is established for all [deities] within a single performance, a distinction between performances is not obtained (it would follow that there is none).
Moreover, just as the perception of existence occurs because of the connection with the originative injunction, so too the state of being [the object] would exist without division.
The Commentary states: Furthermore, this is not the case—that "a single action is performed by many.
If it were so stated, it would be contradictory; for once the action has been performed by one, what could a second person do? To this, it is replied:
If the action were performed sequentially, such a fault would arise;
however, in some cases, the action occurs through *tantra* (simultaneity).
Just as there is the perception of a sentient being, so too would existence be non-differentiated.

Just as when each individual elephant or horse is seen, the whole [process] is accomplished by one [person], even so would there be a *tantra*-nature in a *satra* sacrifice. The substance is common to all. The Adhvaryu sits upon the central Āhavanīya fire.
In that case, all [the factors] become agents; however, there is no conjunction with what has already arisen. Rather, for the sake of origination, number is conjoined with the action.

For if that which has already arisen were to be joined [with the result], then the statement "for the sake of multiple connections" would be understood; however, there is no such connection with what has already arisen. Therefore, each individual [act] is connected with the entire result.
Ratna: This is a sūtra consisting of subsequent words [of the objection]:
"But surely, in a single performance, the agency of many is not possible, because when an action has been performed by one, another cannot be joined as an agent.
To that, the answer is: "And also because of the connection with the origin [of the action]."

(Dup—this commentary is for the purpose of explaining the words of the sūtra, *utpattisaṃyogāt*: "In this case, there is no connection by way of origination; rather, the action is connected with the number precisely by way of its origination.

(He explains that: In the very sentence of origination (*utpattivākya*)—that is, in the sentence stating the result (*phalavākya*)—the number pertaining to the independent agent (*kartṛ*) is heard in the expression "those desiring prosperity" (*ṛddhikāmāḥ*).

If [the number] were heard in the sentence describing the qualities (*guṇavākya*) and not in the sacrifice being produced (*utpadyamāna*), then there would be no connection of each individual [sacrifice] with the fruit of the action.

In that case (where the connection is established upon production), they would not be pervaded by the fruit; it is for this purpose that the plurality is stated. What, then, is its purpose? It is stated for the purpose that the sacrifice is to be performed as qualified by the number of plurality.

However, because there is no powerful contradiction to the plural number in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) which denotes independent agency, the plurality belongs to the agents themselves; therefore, the fruit accrues to each [agent] individually.
Śabara [says]: "Since the agency belongs to the collective (*samudāya*), the entire fruit attaches to it.
But the connection with the parts of the fruit would belong to each member of the collective."

This being the position reached, it is replied: "Even if the agency belonged to the collective whole, nevertheless, because each individual possesses the entitlement (*adhikāra*), they would obtain the fruit in that very same way;
moreover, their agency is understood to belong to each one individually."
For multiplicity resides in the agent; otherwise, it would reside in the substance.

In the first section (*pāda*) concerning the Soma sacrifice, the qualification (*adhikāra*) was defined through the determination of the scope of the section on the desire for heaven (*svargakāma*). Here, however, qualification is defined by means of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

They say that because the verbal suffix conveys number which was previously unapprehended, and through that [number] the cognition of the person (*nara*) is obtained, there is a difference between this *pāda* and the previous one, as well as immediate succession (*ānantarya*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: there should be a separate entitlement for each individual, because the fruit that is the human goal is established individually—that is, it is established for each person separately. As stated in the Viśeṣa: "In a Sattra sacrifice, the acquisition of the fruit belongs either to each individually or to all together; agency belongs to the collective group.
However, [in other cases], it belongs to even a single individual, because of the nature of the act itself and because of the plurality [of participants]."

The Bhaṭṭa [position]: Regarding such passages as "Those desiring prosperity (*ṛddhikāmāḥ*) should perform the *sattra*," there arises an inquiry as to whether, from the performance of a *sattra* involving multiple agents, the single fruit is enjoyed by all the agents in its entirety, or only partially. Although the agency of all may be either individual or, like that of a husband and wife, collective, in both cases—since a single performance of the *sattra* serves as the cause for multiple fruits, and because even in rites like the *darśa*, an infinite number of heavens arise simultaneously or sequentially from a single performance—one must necessarily accept that a single performance yields a single fruit; thus, the single fruit is enjoyed by all in parts.

This being the case, it is first of all impossible for there to be primary constituent parts (*mukhyāvayava*) of a single composite whole (*phalavayavin*), because such a whole— consisting in the accomplishment of its purpose— is the locus of purposes such as pleasure, and thus cannot possess constituent parts.

It must simply be stated that the delimitor of being produced by Satrajan (satrajanyatvāvacchedaka), such as "cognition-ness" (buddhitva) and so forth, merely does not subsist pervasively (avyāpyavṛttitva) across the cognitions residing in all those persons; yet there is no evidence for this, because words such as "śruta-kalpanā" and so on are intent only upon propounding the result [of the action]. Even in the case of a postulated entitlement (kalpyādhikāra) that propounds the enjoyment of the result residing in the performer who desires prosperity (ṛddhikāma), since the subsistence of the desire for prosperity in a collective manner (vyāsajyavṛttitva) is contradicted, and there is no evidence for accepting a mode of existence distinct from that which subsists collectively, it is determined that the desire for prosperity resides in each individual, and thus the result accrues to each individually.

For in that case, by the term *ṛddhikāma* (desiring prosperity) with a plural ending, what is not being established is that those delimited by plurality possess the desire for prosperity—which would lead to the consequence of [the property] residing distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*).
Rather, it is the plurality of those delimited by the desire for prosperity, as in the case of [the word] *paśūn* ("animals," etc.).

Nor does the fact that agency (*kartṛtva*) is distributed imply that possessing the fruit (*phalavattva*) and possessing the unseen potency (*apūrvavattva*) are likewise distributed; for although the general agency involved in granting a fruit may reside in each individual, there is no evidence for such a restrictive rule.

Therefore, even if [the agency] resides in both husband and wife collectively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), it must be stated that the *apūrva* (unseen potency) and the fruit are indeed distinct, or rather that the substratum in which the property delimiting the state of being produced (*janyatāvacchedaka-dharma*) is fully present (*paryāptyadhikaraṇa*) is distinct.
In the present case, however, because the plural number is heard in the verbal suffix, agency alone is understood [to reside in each individual];
there is no inclination toward postulating that the possession of the fruit and so forth reside collectively.
Nor does it follow that multiple fruits do not arise from a single application;

for it is postulated that, by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), the state of being a fruit acts as an obstacle to [the production of] anything delimited as a fruit, and there is no sublation of this rule in other cases.

Nor does the consideration of individual occurrence (pratyekavṛttitva) serve as a restrictive factor even in this case, because there is no burden (gaurava) or other such objection in postulating that the fruitfulness (*phalavattva*) and so forth reside in the collective whole (*vyāsajyavṛttitva*). This is because, if one were to postulate that the property delimiting the state of being produced (*janyatāvacchedakadharma*) resides in the collective whole, then one would have to postulate as the locus-delimiter for its pervasion (*paryāptyadhikaraṇatāvacchedaka*) the quality of "having as its produced fruit [something] residing in all the performers" (*yāvatkartṛniṣṭhajanyaphalakatva*), which would result in excessive complexity (*gaurava*). On the contrary, since it is simpler to postulate that the very nature of the fruit produced by the *sattra* resides in each individual, the fruit belongs to each person individually.
The practical purpose (*prayojana*) is the corresponding mental resolution (*saṃkalpa*) based on such an understanding.

Being "prompted" (*prayojyatva*) consists in being pervaded by an activity (*kṛti*) that proceeds for the sake of another.

Furthermore, this "pervasion by activity" takes the form of being "to be performed" (*anuṣṭhāpyatva*), which distinguishes it from time (*kāla*) and other such factors; this has been established precisely in the *Kaustubha* regarding the instrumental role of the *Vājapeya* sacrifice and so forth.
Consequently, although time and the like may be related to the activity as its causal factors (*kāraka*), they lack the status of being "prompted," just as a jar or similar objects do not possess it.

Therefore, when something is pervaded by an activity that has commenced in a particular place, it is *prayojya* with respect to that [activity], as for example, the bringing of curd (*dadhyānayana*) and the *prayāja* offerings are *prayojya* with respect to the *āmikṣā* and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices respectively.

If it is asked, "What is the proof for dissolution (*pralaya*)?", the answer is: none is required. The establishment of *khaṇḍapralaya* (partial dissolution) is achieved through the following two inferences: 1. The production of the potsherds [from a jar] is the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of the effect-substance, because it is an absence, like the absolute absence of the self's death in another world. 2. A jar is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of a destruction that occurs in a locus of the effect-substance which is not a locus of the effect-substance, because it is a positive effect (*bhāvakārya*), like sound. Intellect (*buddhi*) is the counter-positive of a destruction that does not coexist with its own prior non-existence, because it is a positive effect (*bhāvakārya*), like a primary merit (*adṛṣṭa*) existing at a time immediately preceding [the experience]. Sound is the counter-positive of a destruction of a conjunction that does not serve as a substrate for odor, because it is a produced quality (*janyaguṇa*), like an experience that does not produce a mental impression (*saṃskāra*); by way of negative concomitance, it is like space (*ākāśa*).
All atoms (*paramāṇu*) are individually possessed of a continuous series of complete effects, because they are initiators (*ārambhaka*), like an atom initiating a wind that has already perished.

They say that the continuity of suffering is absolutely severed because it is a continuity, just like the flame of a lamp falling [out of existence]; thus, through this inference demonstrated by the Teacher (Ācārya), as well as through the Mahāpralaya (the Great Dissolution), the validity of Puranic expressions such as "the Kṣatriya clan rejoices" is established.
