Furthermore, this does not concern the second or subsequent performances; for in those cases, the performance is already established by the very originative injunction (*utpattivihita*) of the *Pravargya*, which states: "They perform the *Pravargya*. Therefore, this is a counter-exception to what was prohibited in the first performance. Consequently, because it is both enjoined and prohibited in that context, there is an option (*vikalpa*).

Regarding the first day of the *atirātra* sacrifice, however, there is indeed the obligatory performance [of the *agniṣṭoma*], because the injunction for the first day of the *atirātra* is optional; for in that case, there is an extension of the prohibition [against it], and since the sacrifice lacks the *agniṣṭoma* form, there is no extension of a counter-exception (*prati-prasava*).
On this point, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* has stated two objections.

Regarding the tenth [sūtra]: "There is no prohibition; since another is being enjoined, there would be an option because [the action] is both obtained and prohibited" (10.1.14). By this, according to the principle that "even a weak injunction becomes equal in strength to a prohibition dependent upon its non-activation," if "one should not go forth [as a renunciant] at the first sacrifice" were a prohibition, and if "they perform the *pravargya* when they go forth" were also a prohibition, then—precisely because of the extension (*atideśa*)—an option would result even for the first performance of the *atirātra*, just as in the first performance of the *agniṣṭoma*; thus, the status of a mandatory performance would not be established. This is the second defect.

But [the author] himself has established that the statement "not at the first sacrifice" is not a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), but rather an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) which forms part of the originative injunction for the *pravargya* rite—"when they proceed with the *pravargya*"—and that the sentence concerning the *agniṣṭoma* is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to that exclusion.

Now, it may be argued that since what was stated as non-obligatory is restated as obligatory, this constitutes a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*); furthermore, since an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) cannot possibly be intended to express non-obligatoriness, and because the *sūtra* "vidhinā-mekadeśaḥ syāt" (10.8.1.4) will establish in the tenth book that the whole [of the injunction] applies—not just a part—in order to avoid optionality (*avikalpa*), it is not logical for there to be a counter-exception in the form of an exclusion.

For this very reason, even an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the first performance of the *agniṣṭoma* is improper; because the general injunction is restricted (*upasaṃhāra*) to the second and subsequent performances alone by means of a prohibition (*paryudāsa*) that excludes both the necessity and the non-necessity [of the rite] for one who is seated [in the first performance]. If it is argued: "But since there is no injunction for the first performance, when its performance is [otherwise] established, the mere performance of what is prescribed for the *agniṣṭoma* would be accomplished therein," [we reply:
True, elsewhere a prohibition does not have the purpose of stating non-performance; nevertheless, in this case, that purpose must necessarily be accepted.

Otherwise, since the two sentences concerning the *agniṣṭoma* would be established as *anārabhyavāda* (general injunctions) by means of the mere exclusion of the obligatory performance during the first application,

both of them would be rendered purposeless. However, if the exclusion is made meaningful through the obligatory performance— as in the case of the rule "not at the *anūyāja*s"— then a further injunction is required.
It may be so.

Therefore, since the purpose here is to state that [the act] should not be performed by means of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), it is to be optionally combined with the injunction again; and it is logical that this constitutes a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*). As for the objection that if it were a prohibition (*niṣedha*), there would be the contingency of an option regarding the *Atirātra* sacrifice—that too is not the case. Because the exclusion, which serves as a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the general rule in the archetype (*prakṛti*), is extended (*atideśa*) to the *Atirātra*, it is established as being to be performed invariably; thus, the counter-exception, whose purpose is to provide an option, is not extended to it.
This view of Someśvara is also untenable.

First of all, the claim that even a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion) here serves the purpose of stating that something is not to be performed is an invention never seen or heard elsewhere; for if that were so, an unavoidable option (*vikalpa*) would likewise arise there in the case of the first performance of the *atirātra* sacrifice as well.
As for the argument that because a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) intended to provide an option is not extended [to this case], there is no permanent non-performance, that too is incorrect.

An option (*vikalpa*) is not indeed the meaning of the sentence regarding the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*); rather, its purpose lies in determining the intent (*tātparya*) that [the act] is not to be performed through the method of exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Consequently, because the capacity to grasp the intent is present even in the non-extension (*anatideśa*), the determination of the intent—that it is not to be performed—is established by that very [exclusion]. Since the exclusion pertains only to a matter already determined, and since there is a mutual contradiction in the sense that the intent regarding non-performance applies to the archetype (*prakṛti*) but not to the modified rite (*vikṛti*), the meaning would be inconsistent and improper; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of an option even in the *atirātra* sacrifice, as it would be appropriate to state non-performance there as well.
Even in that case, it is difficult to avoid [this conclusion].

It has been established [in the Śābarabhāṣya] that "it is not logical for a scriptural injunction, which has been determined in the archetype (*prakṛti*) to have one purpose, to be understood as having another purpose when it is extended by transfer (*atideśa*) to the ectype (*vikṛti*). (This is a restatement of the *arthavāda* from the Śābarabhāṣya.)

Therefore, if the purpose of the statement "it should not be performed" is to express a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), then in order to avoid the contingency of having to choose between alternatives even when the *Atirātra* is the first performance, the purpose of the statement must be the exclusion of the other; however, if the purpose of the statement "it should not be performed" is not to express an exclusion of the other, then there would be the contingency of its mandatory performance in the first application of the *Agniṣṭoma*, and thus the establishment of an option (*vikalpa*) would follow. This is a "rope with nooses on both ends," resulting in the contingency that the *Agniṣṭoma* scriptural passage would become meaningless. If it is asked: "Even if the critique by Bhaṭṭa Someśvara is thus [invalidated], how can the two aforementioned critiques in the view of the author of the Vārttika be considered most faultless? To this we reply: [The response follows: ... [the critique remains valid] because the *Agniṣṭoma* passage is indeed meaningful, as it serves to establish the option for the *Atirātra* sacrifice when the *Agniṣṭoma* is the first performance. Thus, the two critiques are not flawed.

The prohibition "not at the first sacrifice" is indeed a restriction; and since that [prohibition] pertains to the domain of scriptural performance (*vaidhakriyā*), an option (*vikalpa*) is already established, and it is not something to be obtained from the sentence concerning the *agniṣṭoma*. This is the rebuttal of the criticism regarding the section on the *pravargya* rite. This is the rebuttal of the criticism regarding the section on the *pravargya* rite.

Nevertheless, the two objections raised by Bhaṭṭa Someśvara—that the sentence concerning the *agniṣṭoma* would be rendered meaningless and that such an option (*vikalpa*) would result in the *atirātra*—are to be resolved as follows: the *agniṣṭoma* sentence is for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*). It serves to exclude the option that might otherwise apply between the first day’s performance of the *agniṣṭoma* and the *atirātra*, specifying that it applies only to the *agniṣṭoma* and not to the first day’s performance of the *atirātra*.

Furthermore, this *agniṣṭoma* sentence also functions as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), because it enjoins what was previously understood as something not to be done, thereby establishing its necessity.

Nor is there any contradiction between being a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) and being an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*). Alternatively, by virtue of its similarity to what was previously stated, the term "counter-exception" is used figuratively to denote an exclusive specification.

If it is argued that an exclusive specification involving an option (*vikalpa-parisaṃkhyā*) is fulfilled merely by the performance [of the alternative], and thus the performance itself would not be established—this is not so.

In this case, there is no verbal exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of an alternative; rather, it is an implied exclusion (*ārthī parisaṃkhyā*) by way of excluding the performance of the *pravargya* rite, in the sense that "one should retire [from household life] only during the *agniṣṭoma*, not during the *atirātra*. Thus, the obligatory performance [of the *pravargya*] in the *atirātra* is established. If one were to say that such a method of excluding alternatives is nowhere observed, then where has the method of *paryudāsa* (exclusion by negation)—which serves to state that something is not to be done—ever been seen? [This refers to Someśvara’s response.]
If that [subsequent] is postulated right here, then the former one is also postulated right here; thus, the objections regarding exclusion (*paryudāsa*) and the responses to them are equal.

[Objection: But surely, if this were a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) stating that one may go forth only in the Agniṣṭoma and not elsewhere, then the *pravargya* would not be performed anywhere else—in the performance of the Atirātra and other sacrifices, nor in any other modified rites (*vikṛti*). In that case, since there would be a restriction solely to the optional *pravargya*, the restriction would apply only to the *pravargya* of the first day of the Atirātra because it is optional there; however, there is no authority for a restriction that applies only to the optional *pravargya*. [Reply: It is said:
By virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*), its intended meaning is obtained.

"One should go forth [into the life of a wandering ascetic] only at the Agniṣṭoma, and not elsewhere"—this is indeed a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*). Alternatively, it is a prohibition (*nivṛtti*) of the *pravargya* rite elsewhere. Where, due to the extension of rules from the archetype to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), such as the first day of the Atirātra, the performance of the *pravargya* might optionally apply, if this [injunction] is heard even in that other alternative case, there is conciseness (*lāghava*). However, where the optional application of the *pravargya* is not even suggested—such as in the second or subsequent performances of the Atirātra, or in other modified sacrifices—if a restrictive injunction were understood there, it would result in extreme prolixity (*gaurava*).

Just as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) fulfills only that unestablished alternative of threshing and so forth while remaining indifferent toward the alternative where it is already established, so too does an exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) fulfill only that unestablished alternative regarding the non-performance of the *pravargya* rite while remaining indifferent toward the other alternative. And just as the injunction "one [should sacrifice] with rice" operates by fulfilling that unestablished alternative precisely where rice is not otherwise obtained— in the *āgneya* and other such sacrifices in the sixth book, and not in the *upāṃśuyāja* and so forth— because even though rice is generally prescribed there, it is not obtained in that specific context.

Furthermore, in the tenth book (10.1.12–17), it is stated that even a sentence which applies generally may have a specific application based on parsimony (*lāghava*). For example, regarding the animal sacrifice dedicated to Vāyu, where it is heard in the scripture: "He offers the *āghāra* oblation with [the mantra] beginning 'Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre'," this applies specifically to the northern *jauhava* *āghāra* offering. This is because there is parsimony in the restriction of the mental visualization (*dṛṣṭi*) produced by the archetypal mantra "Indra ūrdhvo'dhvaraḥ" to that very instance.
Conversely, in the case of the southern *āghāra*, such a restriction would entail the fault of postulating something not previously established (*asiddha*).

If it is argued: "Even so, this would be a *prāptapari-saṃkhyā* (an exclusion of what is already obtained), and since that is impossible to avoid the three faults, it is not accepted anywhere," [we reply]:
because this too is, in reality, an *aprāptapari-saṃkhyā* (an exclusion of what is not otherwise obtained).

For instance, in the case of the *haraṇa* (carrying) ritual, regarding the mantra "imāmagṛbhṇan raśanāmṛtasya" and so forth, if this [exclusionary injunction] did not exist, then—based on the indicative power (*liṅga*)—one would have to assume an applicatory statement (*viniyojaka-vākya*), and consequently, the mantra would apply even to the taking up of the donkey’s halter. However, when this [injunction] exists, the assumption of such a statement based on indicative power is itself precluded. Similarly, if there were no exclusionary injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) stating "one should not perform the *pravargya* in the *agniṣṭoma*," then—in the first performance of the *atirātra* sacrifice—an option (*vikalpa*) would arise due to the assumption of two extended applications (*atideśa*): namely, "they perform the *pravargya*" and "one should not perform the *pravargya* in the first sacrifice. But when this [injunction] exists, because the extended application is blocked, no option occurs in the first performance of the *atirātra*.

Thus, everything is faultless. "Having not understood that which was taught by the author of the Vārttika in the Śāstra as a result of its full ripening, Someśvara here speaks much out of partiality. Therefore, having understood it, I have brought my own nature into accord with the doctrine of the Vārttika; knowing this, the wise, who are like Indra among the learned, will not consider me at fault. Thus ends the rectification of the refutation regarding the *Pravargya* section.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *Bhāṣya* is that in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the *pravargya* rite is prohibited in the first performance, but there is no prohibition in the second and subsequent performances.

For a performer who follows the *Śrauta* tradition, the *pravargya* is optional (*vikalpa*) in the first performance of the *agniṣṭoma*; for other sacrificers (*yajamāna*), however, its absence is mandatory (*nitya*) in the first performance of the *agniṣṭoma*.
In the first performance of the *atirātra* sacrifice on its first day, there is always a non-performance [of the *sādana*].

However, since there is no "first performance" at all in other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), there is no prohibition regarding them. Furthermore, the phrase "not at the first sacrifice" (*na prathamayajñe*) is not an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), but rather a direct prohibition (*pratiṣedha*).

Thus is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the author of the Vārttika. This is the extraction of the essential point (*paṇḍoddhāra*) from the section concerning the extension (*pravardhya*) of the Agniṣṭoma; [it is] the principle of *pravardhya* (2814).
In the first performance, the application is mandatory for one who has studied the Veda (*anucāna*), while for others it is subject to restrictive rules (*niyamaprayoga*).

However, in the case of the *atirātra* sacrifice being the concluding rite (*pratyāhāra*), there is no application whatsoever for anyone; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the author of the *Śāstradīpikā*.
In the first performance characterized by the *agniṣṭoma* form, the performance is mandatory both for one who has studied the Veda and likewise for one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
By the context, "śrotriya" refers to one who has mastered the Veda and its meaning;
this is because the word "kāma" (desire) denotes an optional rite (*prakalpa*).
Therefore, even when the *agniṣṭoma* is included among those minor rites, it is not to be performed as a mandatory obligation.
Since there is no counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding the exclusion [of the *atirātra*], its non-performance is indeed obligatory.
However, in the case of a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it must always be performed even during the first performance.

As for what was stated in the *Vārttika*—that there is an option only for those who have studied the Vedas (*anucāna*), while for others there is an obligatory non-performance—that is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*).

If, however, there is a persistent insistence that this very point must be established, then, because of the appearance of an option (*vikalpa*) and because the *agniṣṭoma* injunction is subsumed by that [option], the option should be established as belonging only to one who has studied the Veda (*anūcāna*).
This is the opinion of the author of the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*.
"Let there be a systematic arrangement of injunctions and prohibitions according to the difference in qualified persons (*adhikārin*)."

"This prohibition applies only to the first performance of the Agniṣṭoma when it is performed by a person other than an Anūcāna"— this is the view of the author of the *Śāstradīpikā*, following the opinion of the author of the *Vistara*.
This is the principle of *pravardhya* (the rule concerning the increasing).
The section concerning the prohibition of the *pravargya*:
the prohibition of the *pravargya*—which is prescribed in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—applies only to its first performance as an *agniṣṭoma*, when it is performed by a person other than the *anūcāna*.
That which is associated with a number should belong to the sacrifice because of the context.

The Bhāṣya states: Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma, having introduced the *pravargya* rite, it is recited: "One should not employ it at the first sacrifice; one should employ it at the second or the third. In this regard, there is a doubt: should the *pravargya* not be performed in all performances of the Jyotiṣṭoma, or is the prohibition restricted to the first performance?
What, then, is the prima facie view? The prohibition applies to the Jyotiṣṭoma. Why? Because of its connection with sacrifice;
by the word "first," the Jyotiṣṭoma is denoted as the sacrifice.
For its very first connection is thus recorded: "This indeed is the first of sacrifices, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma; he who, having not sacrificed with this, should then sacrifice with another.

Since it is the first among sacrifices, it is established by the word "first"; [thus] it has been stated that [the example] is untenable as a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the Agniṣṭoma passage.

Even in the sentence concerning the *atirātra*, if these [rites] were performed at the time of fulfilling the duties pertaining to that [sacrifice], then they would be its subsidiary (*śeṣa*). However, it is not stated thus, because the terminuses (*saṃsthās*) do not share the same injunction (*asamānavidhāna*), and because no prohibition is heard within the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).
For this cannot be a subsidiary of the word "having the *atirātra* as its archetype" (*atirātraprakṛtitva*), which is separated by other sentences containing multiple interwoven elements.
Therefore, this is understood as a prohibition alone, just like the rule "na tau paśau" (not those two on the animal sacrifice).
However, even though it is a prohibition, it does not apply only to the primary model (prakṛti);
for it would indeed apply there, were it not possible [for it] even in the modified form (vikṛti).

But that prohibition, because it depends merely upon the occurrence [of a grammatical operation], operates in both cases regardless of whether it is an original rule (*upadeśa*) or an extended application (*atideśa*). (It permits that its scope be restricted to the original base alone—) for it could indeed be argued here as well: "Or rather, it applies only to the original base, because [the operation] has already been stated twice.
Now, this would be appropriate only if the two cases had identical meanings.

And here there is indeed a difference in meaning, because [the practice] is optional in the archetype (*prakṛti*), whereas in the *atirātra* sacrifice, there is a permanent prohibition of what is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*).
This is not so (even though it appears to be a double statement).

For he will say this: "In the case of a specific injunction (*pradeśa*) and in the case of an unattached injunction (*anārabhyavidhāna*), since there is both a prescription and a prohibition, there would be an option" (10.8.11).

(He establishes the meaning regarding the sun: For that which has no attainment [of application] in its own branch, since it is impossible to prohibit it without first permitting its attainment, one must necessarily accept that even the injunction intended by that prohibition is itself present.
If that is accepted, then because there is no difference in their status as belonging to the branches, they are equal [to the specific injunctions].
Therefore, in every respect, there must be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the *atirātra* sacrifice.

Therefore, because of the double mention and because of the difference in the time of application between the original instruction (*upadeśa*) and the extended application (*atideśa*), it is better that [the term] refers only to the archetypal form (*prakṛti*).

But if this is so, since the status of being the archetype is already established by the statement "he sprinkles [the grains] in the Agniṣṭoma," the isolated injunction (*anārabhyavāda*) would become purposeless.
This is not a fault.
By that [statement] there is the origination [of the rite], and by this [statement] there is its application; thus, there is a distinction in their functions.
Alternatively, the *anārabhyavāda* (unattached statement) will have as its scope matters other than the *agniṣṭoma*.
But is it not the case that it is restricted by the *agniṣṭoma* sentence?

This cannot be restricted [by general rule]. That indeed is restricted by a specific statement where, being incapable of serving a purpose in that context, it is connected in some way through an indirect application (*parokṣavṛtti*), as in the case of the *sāsadasya*.

Therefore, it will apply to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*); and this being so, the statement "not at the first sacrifice" from the independent injunction (*anārabhyavāda*) becomes appropriate in the case of the first performance of the *atirātra*.
The application of the restrictive rule (*niyamaprayoga*): In the Agniṣṭoma, because it is touched by a purely prescriptive injunction, its performance is obligatory.

For it has been stated that even the remainder of that sentence does not mean "this [is optional]. (The proponent of a partial view refutes the idea that the *anārabhyavāda* is for the sake of the modified sacrifices [*vikṛti*]: Only this much can be determined here: this *anārabhyavāda* does not enter into connection with the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*).
If he were to go [to the Soma sacrifice], then he would also have to go to the *iṣṭi* and *paśubandha* sacrifices;
yet he ought not to go there, because the restriction of place expressed by "prior to the *upasads*" would be inapplicable in those cases. Therefore, he goes only where the *upasads* occur.

Furthermore, because of the disparity in the time of their occurrence, those *upasads* exist in the archetype (*prakṛti*) even without an explicit statement; how much more so when there is a clear statement?

It has been explained in the fourth section (*adhikaraṇa*, 3.1.16—as stated in the marginal note) that even for such [texts] which have a manifest general connection, there is a restriction (*upasaṃhāra*). Therefore, there is no redundancy solely due to the extraction (*utkarṣa*) and application (*viniyoga*).
This being the case, there will be a coherent meaning together with those [elements] whose recitation occurs within the context itself.

(He refutes the view of a certain partial proponent: If, then, because both [statements] form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), the meaning "one initiates the consecration at the Agniṣṭoma" is established, then there would be no contradiction whatsoever for the statement "not at the first sacrifice," which would thus apply to the Agniṣṭoma that is not the first sacrifice; consequently, according to the previous position, the rite would necessarily never be performed.
Therefore, he says—[in order] to explain the sentence regarding the Agniṣṭoma as establishing an option—it must be explained in this way.

Since the status of the *anārabhyavāda* (unattached statement) as being for the sake of the archetype (*prakṛti*) is established, the statement "he anoints at the Agniṣṭoma" is understood to serve the purpose of reviving what was prohibited, because it has another purpose.
But was it not said that this is not a prohibition at all?
We reply: it is indeed a prohibition, because its meaning consists in being connected with the Agniṣṭoma.
For it has been shown that a *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation) with this [term] is not possible;

nor is the *anārabhyavāda* (independent statement) intended for the non-*agniṣṭoma*, since a *paryudāsa* regarding that subject would be untenable. Therefore, both [the *paryudāsa* and the *agniṣṭoma* statement] have the *agniṣṭoma* as their scope.

And therefore, although this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), nevertheless, by the force of both [the general rule and the exception], it must indeed be an option (*vikalpa*). Why? "For if this were performed constantly, the exclusion would be useless;
or if it were not performed constantly, the injunction would be purposeless."

And therefore, since a partial exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is resorted to because of the suffix *-ikta*, that [exclusion] applies even when that [condition] is present; thus, it is better to resort to a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) based on the very nature of the word.
By that, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the first performance in the *agniṣṭoma*.
Even in that case, when for some...

Regarding the statement, "But one who is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) and a *śrotriya* may, if he so desires, perform [the rite] after having extracted [the portion]," since this counter-exception (*pratiprasava*)—which functions as an option—is directed toward a specific agent, the option applies only to that subject; for others, there is an absolute absence [of the rite].

But how can a non-*śrotriya* engage in the ritual action, such that he is heard of as a qualifying attribute? True; however, a restatement of what is already established would be purposeless if its result were merely that much. Therefore, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), it is understood as referring to excellence (*prakarṣa*).

Just as in the expression "a maiden should be given to one who is *abhirūpa*," it is understood to mean "to one who is more handsome (*abhirūpatara*)," so too the mention of the *anucāna* (one who has studied the Vedas) will serve to exclude the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, because the term is connected with Vedic recitation (*anuvacana*), which pertains to the Brāhmaṇa. This same principle applies even in the case of the *atirātra* sacrifice.

In that case, because of the prohibition "not at the first sacrifice" (*na prathamayajñe*) and because there is no counter-exception (*prati-prasava*) due to its being an *agniṣṭoma*, it must never be performed [at the first performance]. In other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), since a "first performance" is impossible, it must always be performed.

[Objection: But even there, since the rule "not at the first sacrifice" applies by extension (*atideśa*), and since the specific nature of the *agniṣṭoma*—which is the cause for the counter-exception—is absent, its non-performance would necessarily follow at the first performance.
This is not so;
for the word "first," which remains unexhausted and applies everywhere, does not apply elsewhere [in this context].
Therefore, it is established that this prohibition refers exclusively to the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
This prohibition is not a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice due to syntactical connection (*vākya*) or context (*prakaraṇa*);
rather, it is stated that it is a subsidiary part of the performance (*prayoga*) because of the syntactical connection itself, since performance is considered primary.
Thus, in the performance of the Agniṣṭoma, the recitation by one who has studied the Vedas (*anūcāna*) is mandatory, while for others, its non-performance is mandatory.
However, in the case of the *atirātra-prathamāhāra*, there is no application for any of them at all.
[The opponent objects: "Just as in the previous case, because of the conflict between the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the sentence (*vākya*), the context is set aside by the sentence;
here, however, since there is no such conflict, the context should not be set aside. This constitutes the connection [of the objection] based on such a counter-argument.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Since the first place [of the *pravara*] is connected with a specific number and characterized by its priority, this prohibition—"not at the first sacrifice"—would, by virtue of the context, apply to the *kratu* (the sacrificial session). Viśvarūpa comments: "The prohibition 'not at the first sacrifice' does not apply when the *kratu* has been commenced; rather, the prohibition is properly applied to the *kratu*. For it has been stated that the *pravara* is prescribed for the *kratu*, and its application is established by the direct statement (*vākya*) of the injunction within the context of the *kratu*."
The prohibition regarding the first performance applies only in certain cases— namely,

when the Agniṣṭoma is performed for the first time by one who is not already an *anūcāna* (one who has completed his Vedic studies). Regarding this, the *Bhāṭṭa* school notes that the *pravargya* rite, which is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*) in the scripture stating, "He performs the *pravargya* with barley," [is subject to this rule].
And regarding that [Pravargya rite], there is an application as a subsidiary of the Jyotiṣṭoma based on the injunction: "Before the Upasads, he performs the Pravargya.
This is because its presence [in the context] is established by the principle of "repetition" (dviruktatva) assisted by its connection with the ritual for the purpose of exorcism (abhicāra).
Nor should it be argued: "Why could it not be a subsidiary of the Upasads themselves?"

Because, prior to the *upasad* rites, that which presents its own meaning cannot serve as the designator of the objective (*uddeśya*) by virtue of being a temporal correlate; for, since it is already present, there is no need to postulate another word to express it. However, if one were to accept its status as the objective, then—since the presence of the *jyotiṣṭoma* is necessary for the purpose of knowing that the *upasad*s possess a fruit—it would be more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to establish that [the *pravargya*] is for the sake of that [sacrifice].
Furthermore, in the *Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa*, the *pravargya* is mentioned within the very context (*prakaraṇa*).
And in that regard, it is heard in scripture: "One should not let the sacrificial animal be led forward at the first sacrifice" (*na prathamayajñe pra vañjyāt*).

Upon reflection as to whether the term "first sacrifice" (*prathamayajña*) denotes the Jyotiṣṭoma—which is the archetype (*prakṛti*) of all sacrificial forms and is necessary for all—as a whole, or merely its very first performance, [the conclusion is]: the word "first sacrifice" is indeed the name of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself. This is because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the statement, "This indeed is the first of sacrifices, the Jyotiṣṭoma," and because its being performed for the first time constitutes the ground for the application of that name.

Although, because other *saṃsthās* are designated by different terms and because the status of being a *jyotiṣṭoma* and the [specific] time are prescribed for them, the *jyotiṣṭoma* with all its *saṃsthās* is performed first; nevertheless, since that status exists in common with the *jyotiṣṭoma* nature as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), this prohibition or exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—namely, the statement "one sprinkles [the fire] in the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice"—is established through both syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) as delimited by the *jyotiṣṭoma* nature, and it serves the purpose of providing an exception (*pratiprasava*) to that exclusion.
And that [rule] is further restricted by the statement, "But one may indeed perform it for him who is an *anūcāna* and a *śrotriya*.

Consequently, the performance [of the *prathamayajña*] is obligatory for an *anūcāna* *śrotriya* in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice when it has the *agniṣṭoma* as its final stage (*saṃsthā*), it is not obligatory in other *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifices, and it is obligatory in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).

This being the position reached, we reply: since the understanding of the meaning is established through the perceptible [text] alone, there is no evidence for assuming anything additional; furthermore, because the word "first" (*prathama*) refers to the instigation of what has not yet been performed, it is understood to pertain to the very first performance.

And since the word *yajña* is used here in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote "performance," or rather, by accepting—on the basis of the context—that it refers specifically to the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the term "first sacrifice" (*prathamayajña*) refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma according to the principle of the fifth book (PMS 5.1.24), and also to that which has the *atirātra* as its final form, based on the scriptural injunction: "The sacrificer should perform the first sacrifice with the *atirātra*.
Therefore:
The *pravartyanyāya*: By the principle of *pravartyanyāya*, this statement constitutes either a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) or an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the *pravargya* rite in both cases;
it does not, however, constitute an alternative option (*vikalpa*), because in that case [the rite] would be obtained through both direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*).

Nor should it be argued that since primacy (*prāthamya*) is intended to be significant in relation to the neglect of a second performance (*dvitīyaprāyopekṣā*) in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, and since such primacy exists in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) as well—being the primacy occurring in the performance (*prayoga*) in relation to the neglect of a second performance—how could that [primacy] not be obtained there?
For, when primacy requires a defining correlate (*nirūpaka*), the second performance serves as that correlate;
and by the scriptural statement, "This indeed is the first sacrifice among sacrifices," this primacy is restricted specifically to every modification of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
For this very reason, it should be understood that the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself is the subject of the first performance (*prathamaprayoga*).

Thus, by virtue of the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) and Vedic usage, the word "first sacrifice" (*prathamayajña*) denotes the *jyotiṣṭoma*—the subject of the performance characterized by primacy relative to other *soma* sacrifices—through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*). Otherwise, if the word merely denoted a performance characterized by primacy relative to its own second performance, then in such passages as "The *āhitāgni*s take the fuel at the first sacrifice; they should perform the *satra* for seventeen [days]," the term would apply only to the period following the first performance within a *satra*.

For this very reason, it is said that the means of performing the *pravargya* rite apply only to the first performance of the two types of *jyotiṣṭoma*, because they have not yet been previously performed; the *sāman*s and other elements are likewise [restricted] as means of performance.

"But the purchase [of Soma] is as it is directly perceived" (Bhāṣya 10.2.8.25). "The nature of instigation (*pravartanātva*)—which is the delimitor of the capacity of the optative suffix (*liṅ*)—is the quality of being an instigator with respect to an object that generates activity residing in another" (Maṇi, p. 117). Maṇḍana holds that "instigation is simply the state of being a means to that [desired end]."
The Bhaṭṭas maintain that *pravartanā* (the impelling force) is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*).
The venerable teachers (*pitṛcaraṇa*) hold that *pravartanā* is simply the capacity (*śakti*) conducive to the expression of the objective productive urge (*arthabhāvanā*).
118. The nature of *pravartanā* (*pravartanatva*) consists in being an activity (*vyāpāra*) conducive to engagement (*pravṛtti*).
And being "favorable" (anukūlatva) consists in being a generator (janakatva). This [quality] exists in the world as residing in human goals (puruṣārtha);
however, since that is absent in the Veda, it should be understood that something distinct from desire (icchā) possesses the nature of an instigator (pravartanātva).

Pārthasārathi [holds that] the suffix *liṅ* and others denote, by way of being an instigation (*pravartanā*), that very thing called "denotation" (*abhidhā*) which is conducive to the realization of the object; having thus postulated that it is denoted by the *liṅ*, he maintains that the mere fact of the knowledge of that [instigation] being the cause for activity is what is postulated. (Rahasya, p. 11). For an injunction (*vidhi*) is of the nature of an instigation. (Bhāṭṭa, 4.1.1). "That word by which the cognition 'one should act' is produced..."
"And that [cognition] is called an injunction (codanā), or rather, it is a cognition whose fruit is instigation (pravartanā)," so it has been said.

The *Codanāsatra*, verse 13, states:

"The discourse that lacks logical justification (*niryukti*) is to be abandoned" (Maṇiprabhā, p. 12). Regarding the sacrificer who has gone abroad, there is a benedictory mantra for the purpose of attending to the *agnihotra* fire: "Being right here, [I offer] to those who are there; [I abandon] what is left behind."

Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3.8.6.16: "Perpetuity in a stream (*pravāhanityatva*) consists in the state of being entirely devoid of a homogeneous prior non-existence (*sajātīyaprāgabhāva*) and a homogeneous destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). (Maṇi, p. 175). There is no contradiction between this perpetuity in a stream and its being occasional (*naimittikatva*).

(The literal meaning of the maxim is: "Just as all the currents of the Gaṅgā and other rivers ultimately reach the ocean alone, so it is.

Commentary on Vārttika 3.1.2.2:
Regarding the phrase "even when [the rite] has commenced.

If, while the substance prescribed by scripture has been substituted and the ritual has already commenced—with some of the preparatory rites having been performed—if that very primary substance should become available, then the primary substance alone must be taken.

Regarding this, the *Ṭupṭīkā* states: "When certain preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) have been performed but the primary purpose has not yet been accomplished, that which is directly enjoined by scripture (*śruta*) must be undertaken.
There is no obligation to conform to the preparatory rites, because they are subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) of the substance.
Therefore, there should be a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of those preparatory rites that have already been completed [for the sake of the primary purpose]."
Thus, this becomes the sūtra of the established conclusion (siddhānta-sūtra). However, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) must be stated:
"Or rather, if it is argued that even when [the primary purpose] has been accomplished, the revealed text should be brought into practice," [this is the prima facie view].
When *khadira* wood is obtained, the ritual procedure is commenced with *khadira*.
The consecrations prior to the tethering of the animal [are performed with it].
Why?
At that time, a *khadira* wood was obtained.
This being the case, all the ritual consecrations (*saṃskāra*) must be performed again on the *khadira* starting from the beginning.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that after performing the tethering of the animal (*niyojana*) on the *khadira*, the remainder of the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) is to be brought to completion.

Regarding this, if it is argued that "even though [the animal] has not yet been set to work," the animal whose desire has been aroused is the recipient of the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) other than the binding (*niyojana*).
Alternatively, the animal whose desire has been aroused receives all the consecratory rites up to and including the binding.
Once the consecratory rites ending with the binding of the animal have been performed, the *khadira* wood is subsequently obtained.
Even then, the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that the entire ritual procedure must be performed again with *khadira* wood.

In that regard, the meaning of the sūtra in the first section is as follows: "If it is argued [thus]" (*iti cet*) refers back to the previously established conclusion (*siddhānta*). According to the principle that "when the primary is available, the primary [is to be used]," even when one has proceeded by means of a substitute, the primary material itself should be adopted.
Alternatively, there is no fault here because it is not purposeless.

When the primary substance, *khadira*, is unavailable and an animal has been tied to a substitute *kadara* tree, even if the primary *khadira* is subsequently obtained, it should not be taken once the act of tying has already commenced.

"Because of being purposeless," that is, because of being fruitless; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Why? Because, in the section concerning the *some* sacrifice (*some-adhikaraṇa*, 8.1.31), after presenting two prior positions (*pūrvapakṣa*)—namely, "since [the *some*] has not been previously enjoined, its performance should consist of the [rites] desired"—the established conclusion will later refute them by showing that the adoption of the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is due to their providing a ready-made assistance (*klṛptopakāraka*), and that the [former views] lack any intended meaning (*tātparya*) because they are fully prescribed [as alternatives]. Since those [prior positions] are thus absent [in the final view], [the reason given is] "because of being purposeless."

Because it has already commenced, the commencement [of the Soma sacrifice] should take place once the Iṣṭi has been performed; that is, the commencement of the Soma sacrifice should occur after the Iṣṭi, because [the preparatory rites] have already been set in motion.

The procedure of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) is operative in the Dīkṣaṇīyā, Prāyaṇīyā, Ātithyā, Upasads, and Udayanīyā offerings. Therefore, that same procedure should apply to the Soma sacrifice as well, since it occurs within that interval; such is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) view.
And because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Regarding the prima facie view that the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices applies to the Soma sacrifice, [the author] states an indicative mark:
"It has one hundred and one after-offerings (*anuyāja*). Thus, the ritual elements (*dharma*) such as the fore-offerings (*prayāja*) belonging to the iṣṭi are observed in the Soma sacrifice.

This is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the extension of the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice into the *soma* sacrifice. "Of that" means "of the *soma* sacrifice. The particle *ca* serves to combine the reasons.
"Or rather, there is originality (apūrvatva) because of the complete prescription.

By the word "or" (*vā*), [the author] sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—namely, that the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *iṣṭi* applies to the *soma* sacrifice—which was established by the two preceding sūtras, and states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The term "in the *soma*" (*some*) is understood to carry over from the previous context.
There would be something unprecedented;
he does not derive any properties from anything else,
because it is a complete injunction.
In the context of the Soma sacrifice, there is an injunction for all those duties that are to be performed;
therefore, this [sacrifice] possesses enjoined duties.
However, in the case of those sacrifices that lack enjoined duties, there is extension (atideśa).

Therefore, Soma is an independent archetype (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, because there is a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*) of the absence of sacrificial formulas (*ṛg-abhidhāraṇa*), the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) states that there is no ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) pertaining to the *iṣṭi* sacrifice in the Soma sacrifice, since it is independent. To this, the following objection is raised: "But surely [the text says], 'The gods, having made clarified butter their thunderbolt, struck at Soma; the two ladles were their arms.'"

Therefore, [the rule] "pure soma-oblation is not destroyed" and the prohibition "one does not sprinkle with the Soma-sacrifice" would be untenable, because a prohibition presupposes a prior application. Thus,
by the indicative mark (liṅga) of this prohibition, there is an application of the ritual pertaining to the iṣṭi in the Soma sacrifice.
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) replies:
The mention of the absence of both the pouring out (suc) and the sprinkling (abhidhāraṇa) would be a constant restatement (nityānuvāda).
It is a restatement of an absence that is already eternally established, not a prohibition of something that has been obtained.
Therefore, the rules of the *some* sacrifice apply here. If it is argued that this is a primary injunction (*vidhi*),
the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) replies.

If it is argued: "This prohibition regarding the pure Soma-vessel and the sprinkling of clarified butter (*ājya*) is not a restatement of an established fact, but rather an injunction in the form of a prohibition;
consequently, the archetypal ritual procedure (*aiṣṭikavidhyanta*) applies to the Soma sacrifice."
"Not so, because it is a supplementary statement.

The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) says: This prohibition regarding the placing of the Soma in the ladle and the pouring of clarified butter over it—which occurs in the context of the Soma sacrifice—is not an injunction; rather, it is merely a restatement of what is already eternally established.
Why? Because it is a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣatvāt*).
"The earth is indeed the limit of this Soma when they press it.
When they make his two arms the two *sruva*-ladles, and when they have placed the clarified butter near, [then] O divine Soma, may you who are the stalk swell in the hand. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the injunction "The stalk [of Soma] is in the hand," which occurs in the context of the statement, "They made that very oblation-food their *dhuri* (pole) and thereby cause it to swell," this passage—"The gods, having made clarified butter (*ghṛta*) their thunderbolt, struck at Soma with the two ladles (*srucau*) as their arms;
therefore, the Soma-oblation is not destroyed in the ladle, nor does one sprinkle the Soma with clarified butter"—is its supplementary explanatory passage (*vākyaśeṣa*).
Because this is a supplementary explanatory passage for that injunction, it is not possible for it to be an injunction in the form of a prohibition.
Therefore, the prohibition is merely a restatement of what is already established. Consequently, there is no application of the *iṣṭi* sacrificial procedure (*vidhyanta*) to the *soma* sacrifice.
And one might object on the grounds of not fasting.

Regarding the *soma* sacrifice, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is indeed unprecedented (*apūrva*), and thus the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *iṣṭi* does not apply there; he states another reason for this:
"Because of the absence of cremation (*anupoṣaṇāt*), there is doubt"—this is the additional reason.
"Cremation" (*upoṣaṇa*) means burning outside [the body].

Thus it is stated; thus it is declared. If the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *iṣṭi* were to apply to the *soma* sacrifice, [the rule] would not apply because fasting (*upoṣaṇa*) is already established [there], and because there is no fasting [in this case].

And because of the absence of fasting, the *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* raises an objection: "If one should depart without having fasted, they would be led away by the *śrīvabrahmana* as if marked by a sign" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 3.1.8.1).

Therefore, the *vidhyanta* (procedural details) of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice apply to the *soma* sacrifice. The view that the *iṣṭi* *vidhyanta* applies to the *soma* sacrifice is supported by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the statement, "Its hundred and one *anuyāja* offerings are born," as stated in the sūtra *Liṅgadarśanācca* (8.1.3.4) by the proponent of the final position (*siddhāntin*).
The "observation" (darśana) mentioned refers to the observation of the indicative mark (liṅga); it should pertain to the sacrificial rites (iṣṭi) belonging to the Soma sacrifice.
That number belongs collectively to all the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and after-sacrifices (anuyāja) performed in all those rites, such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā and others, within the Soma sacrifice.
Furthermore, even a subordinate part of a subordinate part can be referred to by the word "of that" (tasya), just as one says, "the sacrificial post (yūpa) of the Vājapeya."
And thus, that characteristic mark (*liṅga*) is not a means of establishing the *vidhyanta* (procedural details) of the sacrifice pertaining to the *iṣṭi* in the case of the *soma*. [Question:

Now, if it is argued that the procedure for all the *āgneya*-type offerings applies because the *soma* sacrifice is a specific form (*rūḍhi*) of them, and because of the principle of "application due to what has already commenced"—as in the statement "the application [of the *iṣṭi* details] occurs in the *soma* because [the *iṣṭi*] has already commenced"—then there would be an inclusion of what has already been introduced.
(Regarding the word *iṣṭi*): Vārttika 2.2.3, p.
482 states that because the selection [of the priest] has already commenced, the selection of the *hotṛ* should be performed for each individual sacrifice (*vatra*).
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Hotṛ’s formula is prescribed as: "Agni, the divine Hotṛ, shall worship the gods.
This is extended to the iṣṭi rites that constitute parts of the Soma sacrifice.
The Soma-related Hotṛ’s formula is prescribed as: "He chooses the Hotṛ, saying: 'Abhi is my Hotṛ; O Hotṛ, you are my Hotṛ.'"

In this regard, since it is established by the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the selection (*varaṇa*) of the Hotṛ priest performed at the Soma sacrifice already effects his appointment (*ānata*), one might think that the selection for the New Moon sacrifice (*dārśika*) need not be performed.
However, the selection of the Hotṛ must be performed for each ritual procedure (*tantra*) and for each offering (*iṣṭi*).
Why? Because the selection is made when the rite has commenced; since the New Moon selection is performed after the rite has begun, it is not for the purpose of initial appointment.
What then? It is merely the ritual action.
If that [recitation] were not performed, there would be a deficiency in the quality of the rite.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the recitation of the Hotṛ priest must be performed separately for each individual ritual action.
If it is argued that even Brahmā [is subject to this], it is a commendation regarding his prior engagement.
Bhaṭṭa 5.1.7:
The cause of engagement is precisely the comprehension that [an action] is a means to what is desired.
[This] is the cause for activity.

The apprehension of a portion qualified by the reality [of the object], as opposed to the discourse of others regarding misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), serves as the cause for activity and so forth.

Nor does it follow that there would be a confusion between the deluded and the non-deluded due to the resulting activity of Maitra from the cognition, "Caitra possesses the cognition of silver, because he possesses the cognition of the state of being an effect"; for such a consequence would not arise.
This must be stated:
for the absence of activity [toward an object] is established simply by the sublation (*bādhā*) of that error.

This is because we accept that activity arises even from a cognition having "silverness" as its qualifier (*rajatatva-prakāraka-jñāna*)—occurring after a moment's delay—in one who possesses a cognition of another person’s cognition having "silverness" as its qualifier; or alternatively, because we accept activity based on a cognition that does not have [the object itself] as its content (*jñānāviṣayaka-jñānatvena*).

Alternatively, there is no inconsistency whatsoever, because [the cognition] is the cause of an activity directed toward silver, by virtue of being a cognition possessing a primary objecthood (mukhyaviśeṣyatā) residing in silver as qualified by the modehood (prakāratā) of silverness.
(Maṇi, p. 27).
This sequence of activity applies even in the case of extended application (atideśa).
It is not only within the scope of direct instruction (*upadeśa*).

For, by means of the actual performance (*pravṛtti*), the sequence of the preparatory rites (*upakaraṇa*) and so forth, which was not determined in the archetype (*prakṛti*), is determined in the case of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatya-paśu*).
Section on Praise (Praśaṃsādhikaraṇa):
7.1.12. There is no *prasaṅga* (extension/application) of the waking at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma to the waking pertaining to the Darśa sacrifice.

12.1.8.17. There is no *prasaṅga* in the Jyotiṣṭoma of the sacrificial vessels used for the *savanīya-puroḍāśa* and other offerings—namely, the large cups (*camasa*) belonging to the Soma ritual—to the sacrificial vessels of the Darśa sacrifice, such as the *juhū* and others.

And there would be an application [of the rule] to the vessels (*pātra*), because they serve the purpose of offering (*homa*). The Commentary states: Regarding those very vessels used for the *soma* sacrifice which are based on the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as their archetype—such as the *sāvana* cup, the *sāvana* sacrificial cakes, and the *saumya* oblation—it is deliberated whether the offering of these should be performed with the *graha* and *camasa* vessels, or rather with the *darśa*-type vessels such as the *sruva* ladle and so forth.
To this it is replied: there would be the same contingency regarding the vessels.
Why? Because they serve the purpose of the oblation.
Those vessels are for the purpose of the *homa* offering;
and that *homa* is accomplished even by means of the *graha-camasa*.
The ritual acts are subordinate to the *soma* procedure (*somatantra*).
In those [offerings], the oblation should be performed either with the *graha* vessels or with the *camasa* cups;
for it is logical that the [latter] should be used, since they have already been employed [in the primary rite], whereas if they were not used, there would be a lack of connection (*prasaṅga*).
The Commentary states: "Or rather, the [vessels] belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) should be used, as it is logical."
The oblation is performed by them.
Why? Because they have been employed;
they exist as having been employed.
"If they were to set down the vessels of clarified butter (*ājya*) after having drawn them out, they would strike the sacrificer;
but since they set them down after having drawn the *ājya*, they do not strike the sacrificer"—this is first their application:
the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the wiping (*saṃmārjana*), which constitutes the drawing of the *ājya*.
Those very [auxiliaries] are found to be employed in connection with the clarified butter (*ājya*). There would be an extension (*prasaṅga*) [of the application] to that which is not so employed.
When an auxiliary belonging to the middle [section] is not employed, the performance of its function and the auxiliary occasioned by it are extended [to other instances].
For in the absence of one's own [means], even that belonging to another is utilized;
for when one's own vehicle is not present, Devadatta mounts the vehicle of Yajñadatta,
but when his own is present, he travels by his own vehicle alone.
For in that [chariot], there is a certain ease of movement by its own independence which is not found in another vehicle;
likewise, the excellence of the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) when using the vessels prescribed for the New Moon sacrifice (*darśika*) is not matched by the *graha* and *camasa* cups.
Furthermore, in that [other vehicle], the natural species of wood and the purificatory rites such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) are not obtained.
The absence of those [vessels] is in the case of the *graha* and *camasa* cups;
even those belonging to the Soma sacrifice have no connection with the *puroḍāśa* cakes.
Furthermore, if the vessels used at the New Moon sacrifice (*dārśika*) were not employed [here], would it follow that the *graha* and *camasa* cups should be used? We say: no.
Only those belonging to the Darśa sacrifice would apply.
Where an auxiliary performed for one purpose also serves as an auxiliary for another, there is *prasaṅga* (incidental application),
as when the *pāyuka* fore-offerings (*prayāja*) being performed also serve the purposes of the cake-offerings (*pauroḍāśika*).
But here, when the cup for the draught (grahacamasa) is employed, the other [subsidiary] vessels are not thereby employed;
for when the Soma is being offered, the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) have not been offered.
Therefore, there is no extension of the scriptural injunction (śāstraprasaṅga).
What, then, is meant by this statement, "there would be an undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) if [the procedure] were not applied"?
The meaning is that if the application of these [elements] were not possible, or if it were prohibited, then there would be an undesirable consequence.
Furthermore, the elements belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are logically appropriate, not the great *camasa* cup.

What is their propriety? They are explicitly mentioned by word in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Therefore, they are extended by analogy to the cake (puroḍāśa), and thus there is a direct contact with the scriptural text. Furthermore, it follows from the sense as well.
Even in the absence of a word [expressing it], the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) occurs.

And he demonstrates these vessels: "I yoke the earth for thee with light," [saying this] he touches the *dhruvā* ladle; "I yoke the wind for thee with the intermediate space," [saying this] the *upabhṛt*; "I yoke speech for thee with heaven," [saying this] the *juhū*.
Therefore, the oblation must be performed with these.

Śābarabhāṣya: Regarding the question whether, in the case of the *iṣṭi*-type rites involving Soma and Agni, only the vessels belonging to the Soma sacrifice should be employed, or whether the *juhū* and other vessels must be used separately—when this doubt arises, it is considered that the requirements of the *iṣṭi* rites are fulfilled by the very vessels of the Soma sacrifice intended for oblations; thus, there is *prasaṅga* (extension of application). If the functions of the *juhū* and other vessels, such as the offering of oblations, were performed by other [Soma] vessels, they would become defective (*viguṇa*).
Furthermore, the oblations and other rites were not performed here by others alone—such that they would not need to be performed again, as in the case of the *pṛṣadājya* offerings at the *anuyāja*s.
Therefore, since the oblations and other rites ought to be performed, why should they be performed deficiently when it is possible for them to be complete in their qualities?
Consequently, there is an application of the vessels.

Soma: If even for the purpose of the *pracāra* [the ritual procession], the accomplishment of the placement of the original oblation (*prakṛta-havis*) is established through the altar (*vedi*), then what need is there to say that the accomplishment of the original *homa* [offering] is achieved by means of vessels having the same purpose as those used for the *homa*? This is the connection [of the argument]. Viśvarūpa: Is this *homa* belonging to Soma to be performed with the vessels belonging to the Soma-sacrifice (*saumika*) or with those belonging to the Iṣṭi-sacrifice (*aiṣṭika*)?
It should be performed with the *saumika* vessels because the purpose is accomplished thereby; otherwise, due to the deficiency [of the other], it would belong to both.

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the vessels for Soma, such as the *graha* and *camasa*, after they have been placed on the *khara* altar, those which are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *iṣṭi*—namely, the *savanīya-paśu* and others—the purpose is accomplished by those [Soma-vessels] already provided; therefore, there is no implication (*ākṣepa*) of the original (*prākṛta*) *juhū* and other vessels. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: First of all, the offering of the oblation (*havistarpaṇa*) is not accomplished by the pouring of Soma into those [Soma-vessels], because a separate *juhū* and so forth are required for that. Furthermore, in the case of the offering of the oblation and the like, the *graha* and other vessels are not established by authority (*prāmāṇika*) as the instruments in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), due to the absence of both direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*). For it is only in the case of the eight [fore-offerings] such as the *prayāja* that there is a relationship of assisting the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

While it is logical that those [elements] already established by extension (*atideśa*) should subsist upon what is already established, in the present case there is no evidence for such an extension to the earthen vessels (*bhaumika*). Furthermore, just as with the great altar (*mahāvedi*), there is no evidence that the cups and bowls (*graha-camasa*) possess the nature of *juhū* and other implements characterized by specific shapes and the holding of oblations. Moreover, since the vessels subject to extension are already included at the time of the foundational rite (*ādhāna*), the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) does not apply here; thus, there is no establishment of "incidental benefit" (*prasaṅga-siddhi*) in this instance.

For this very reason, the touching of the vessels used in the *iṣṭi* sacrifice is enjoined by such texts as, "With the words, 'I yoke the earth with light,' he touches the *sruk* ladle," and so forth.

For this same reason, the view that the *grahas* and other vessels are for the purpose of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice—based on the injunction of the *grahas* and so on occurring within the context of the general statement regarding the act of pouring (*prakṣepa*) which is common to both subsidiaries and the main rite, just as in the case of the injunction "the *srucs* are made of gold"—is also refuted by direct instruction (*upadeśa*) regarding the pouring of different oblations. Otherwise, the mention of the *dhruvā* and other vessels would be purposeless; furthermore, there are other indicators that the *grahas* and so on are intended solely for the *soma*.
Maṇḍana: "The perpetual fire-oblation (naiṣṭikahoma) is desired [to be performed] with the vessels used for the Soma-sacrifice and others.
Śaṅkara: "The vessels do not apply;
those belonging to the Soma-sacrifice [apply] at the initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth."
There is no logical consequence that the portions to be consumed as remnants of the hundred Soma-Agni sacrifices are covered by the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of the Soma sacrifice.
"If it is argued that the eaters of the remnants should likewise cease [from their duties] just as the *anvāhārya* [rice-offering] does," the Commentary states:
"It is said that they are for the purpose of performing the ritual service (*parikriyā*)."
No, because of the connection with ritual action. The Commentary states: These [mantras] would not cease [to be used], for they are intended for the purpose of ritual performance.
Because the purpose of the ritual is fulfilled by the *anvāhārya* rice being measured out,
these [measures] are prescribed for the majority of the ritual;
they are not intended for the mere measuring itself.
Therefore, those [acts] are not for the purpose of preparation (*parikriyā*), but rather for the purpose of consecration (*saṃskāra*);
hence, they must be performed for that purpose.
Śā—Previously, because the sacrificer’s consumption was understood to serve the purpose of sustenance, its cessation by means of the vow (*vrata*) had been suspected.

Now, it might be suspected that the consumption by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is superseded by the primary sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), since their purpose is to serve as a form of remuneration. However, that very suspicion is refuted by the fact that the consumptions are for the purpose of the disposal of the remnants (*śeṣapratipatti*); thus, they are not merely for the sake of payment.

Furthermore, in the tenth book itself—specifically at *Śeṣabhakṣāśca tadvat* (10.2.13)—the view that the consumptions are for the purpose of securing the services of the priests (*ānatyarthatva*) has been rejected.
This purpose of that [discussion] is stated here by way of a contextual application (*prasaṅga*).

Soma says: "If the propitiation is accomplished by the primary sacrificial fee (*pradhānadakṣiṇā*), then there is a cessation of the *anvāhārya* rice; in that case, there would also be a cessation of the portions for consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*)"—this is the connection (*saṃgati*) as it is stated.
In the Sūtra, it is likewise: "like the *anvāhārya*."
