Bhaṭṭa: Although the secondary portions (śeṣa) to be consumed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) serve the purpose of disposal (*pratipatti*)—as in the case of the rule for sprinkling the remains of the *prayāja* offerings—their consumption can also serve to provide strength for other rites yet to be performed, according to the logic of the *prayāja*-remnant. Since it is understood that this [strength-providing] function is the primary motivator (*prayojaka*) by way of inference, the extension (*prasaṅga*) of the twelve-hundred-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is indeed appropriate. This being the position reached, we reply: By the force of the injunction mandating the *anvāhārya* rice as the sacrificial fee, the consumption of the remnants is determined to be merely for the purpose of disposal, as indicated by the accusative case ending. Thus, the consumption of the remnants serves solely as a disposal act.

And as stated in the tenth book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras] and elsewhere, by the logic of the *prayāja* remnant, it is said that [the eating] serves the purpose of providing strength, which is synonymous with sustaining the life-force (*prāṇa*) of the officiating priests.

Therefore, even in this case, there is no establishment of *prasaṅga* (incidental benefit). Maṇḍana states: "Nor should the eating of the *iṣṭi* offerings be withheld merely because the sacrificial fee (*bhṛti*) has been paid through the medium of the *anati*."

Śaṅkara: "The sacrificial portions (*ṛtvig-bhakṣa*) should belong to those performing the *iṣṭi* sacrifice. There is an extension (*prasaṅga*) of the new-moon character to the collection of nights; however, the establishment of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) must be performed separately outside [the sacrifice], if it is for the sake of the deities.
Extension (*prasaṅga*) means that even when an action has been fully accomplished, it serves as a benefit to another."

The application of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *paśupuroḍāśa* [animal-cake offering] extends to the subsequent offerings (*anunirvāpya*) in rites such as the fire-piling (*agnicayana*), including the *devasuvā-havis* and others.
See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 383, under the section "Anunirvāpyādhikaraṇam."
The general rule (*prasaṅga*) is that when there is a specific application, there is a single performance.

And the specific application occurs by way of: the substance, the fruit, the desire for a result, the occasion (*nimitta*), the form, the number, the time, the mantra, and the agent. Bālakrīḍā, p. 149.

In the case of the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes, there is only the principle of *prasaṅga* (incidental application) of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) pertaining to the animal sacrifice, not an option;
this should be understood from the rule known as the "Savanīyādi-nyāya. There is also *prasaṅga* of the Soma-sacrifice altar (*saumika-vedi*) upon the New Moon altar (*dārśika-vedi*).
"In the same way, this consequence would follow if one's own rule were already established. The consequence applies to that very case;
however, this is the distinction: "if one's own rule were already established."
Even though another injunction might enjoin this [offering], it is not performed because its purpose is already fulfilled by the primary injunction.
Just as the *prayāja* offerings are obtained for the animal sacrifice by the *codaka* rule and are also applicable to the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*),
yet they are performed only for the sake of the animal sacrifice.
The consequence is that,
although they assist the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), they are not performed for its sake.
Bhāṣya 12.1.11: Furthermore, the contingency of *prasaṅga* does not arise when there is simultaneity.

For example, the modified (*vaikṛta*) sacrifices, although simultaneous with the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), do not depend upon the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
this is the domain of *prasaṅga*.
There is the principle of *prasaṅga*.
Its scope is now defined:

when, within a particular ritual system (*tantra*), another action of similar character occurs that is distinct from the first, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) belonging to that prior action is extended (*prasajyate*) to it.

Just as when the animal sacrifice is extended, the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) becomes applicable; its procedure pertaining to the animal sacrifice (pāśukītikartavyatā) follows accordingly. How so? That is now explained.
One should bring about [the result].
What? The state of being a Paśu. By what means? By the sacrifice of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
By the word "how" (katham), the operation inherent in the sacrifice [is indicated].

And that [operation] is sought through similarity by that which is characterized as being metaphorically indicated— the operation inherent in the sacrifice belonging to the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice].

Since that [animal sacrifice] has already been performed here by the injunction for the animal ritual (*pāśuka-prayogavacana*), it does not again bring the [details] pertaining to the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*) into proximity.
Therefore, the injunction for the cake-offering is omitted;
this is the principle of *prasaṅga* (extended application).
Ṭupṭīkā: Prasaṅga (incidental application) occurs because of the inclusion of specific details; it is the state of something serving another purpose by assisting yet another.

The *prasaṅga* (incidental application) is characterized by the statement "it follows" (*prāsaṅgāt*). It is twofold: primary incidental application (*pradhānaprasaṅga*) is one; subsidiary incidental application (*aṅgaprasaṅga*) is sixfold.
(Bālakrīḍā, p. 132).

Regarding the definition of *prasaṅga* (in the twelfth chapter): the animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśas*), which are commenced with subsidiaries intended for another purpose, do not bring about the inclusion of their own subsidiaries.
And that final [element] is not at all figurative.
Vārttika 3.6.1.10.
This is the connection by way of a relevant topic (*prasaṅga*).
Upon the completion of that investigation which was undertaken by way of a *prasaṅga* (incidental discussion), that very [conclusion] becomes established in the intellect.

That which is established by *prasaṅga* is as follows: in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the practice of beginning the meal with the food of the New Moon sacrifice (*dārśika*), which is obtained through the *codaka* (transfer rule) for the ritual acts belonging to the Iṣṭi class, is superseded by the milk-vow (*payovrata*) and other observances belonging to the Soma sacrifice.
12.1.14.30: The *dārśika* vow, established by way of *prasaṅga* (incidental application), applies to the *prāyaṇīya* and other rites through the *saumika* milk-vow (*payovrata*) and so forth.
See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 18.8, under the entry "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, regarding the *prāyaṇīya* and other rites.
The color of the *hotṛ* priest is not established by *prasaṅga* in the *iṣṭi*-type rites within the Jyotiṣṭoma.

That [procedure] must be performed according to its specific modifications (bheda). Bhāṣya 12.1.18–49: The common ritual framework (tantra) for the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) of the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana) is established by extension (prasaṅga) through the framework of the animal sacrifice (pāśuka); however, the frameworks for the sacrificial cakes of the midday pressing (mādhyandina-savana) and the third pressing (tṛtīya-savana) are established by extension either through the framework of the animal sacrifice or through the framework of the sacrificial cakes of the morning pressing.

Bhāṣya 12.1.130–32: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the selection of the Brahman priest (brahmavaraṇa) is established by extension; that which is obtained through the injunction (codaka) from the New Moon sacrifice (dārśika) is superseded by the procedure belonging to the Soma sacrifice (saumika) during the rites of the Iṣṭi type.

The invocation of the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation) is accomplished by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*) through the invocation for the sake of the animal sacrifice, [and thus applies] to the *savanīya-puroḍāśas*. The consumption of the remnants (*śeṣabhakṣa*), such as those belonging to the *iḍā*, which is obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) in the *aiṣṭika* rites within the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, is accomplished by way of incidental application because it is fit for the purpose of purification (*saṃskāra*). The purchase (*parikraya*) of the *anyāhārya* rice, which is obtained through the *codaka* in the *aiṣṭika* rites within the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, is accomplished by way of incidental application through the purchase pertaining to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*).

The *ārambhaṇīyā* [iṣṭi] need not be performed separately in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), as its purpose is fulfilled through incidental application (*prasaṅga*) from the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. The call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) for the *savanīya* animal sacrifice serves the purposes of the *savanīya* cake of the third pressing, the *saumya* caru, and the two-potsherd offering to the Aśvins; it need not be repeated separately.
There is incidental fulfillment (*prasaṅgasiddhi*) of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the *agnīṣomīya* animal cake for the ritual procedure of the *devasuvām* oblations.

The accomplishment by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga-siddhi*) refers to the common ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the subsidiary offerings (*anunirvāpya*) to the Devikās, which are to be subsequently offered;
see Bhāṣya 12.1.13–18.

The accomplishment by way of incidental application also refers to the sprinkling of the Upasads and the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice being effected by the sprinkling of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) at the Ātithyā ceremony.
See Mīmāṃsākośa, page 887, under the entry ‘ātithyāvahiḥprokṣaṇādinā’.

Accomplishment by occasion (prasaṅgasiddhi) occurs, for example, when the forest-food prescribed for the Darśa sacrifice is [consumed] during the Soma-sacrifice’s Prāyaṇīya and other rites through the milk-vow (payovrata) and similar observances.

Accomplishment by extension (*prasaṅgasiddhi*) occurs, for example, of the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) belonging to the Soma sacrifice in relation to the altar, fire, animal victim, and so forth, belonging to the [Dīkṣaṇīyā] initiation rite;
this is to be understood in the case of the phrase "of the Soma-sacrifice altar.
Accomplishment by extension also occurs of the *anyāhārya* fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in relation to the fee belonging to the Soma sacrifice, in rites such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā.
The phrase "of the Soma-sacrifice’s sacrificial fee" (saumika-dakṣiṇāyāḥ) is to be understood as referring to the dot (bindu).

There is no accomplishment by way of incidental application (prasaṅga) in the Jyotiṣṭoma, because the ritual procedure (tantra) following the Ātithyeṣṭi belongs to the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice. There is no accomplishment by way of incidental application in the Jyotiṣṭoma of the New-Moon sacrifice’s (dārśika) vigil by means of the vigil performed at the time of initiation (dīkṣā) for the Prāyaṇīya and subsequent rites.

There is no accomplishment by way of *prasaṅga* (incidental application) for the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), because of the [separate] *anvārambhaṇīyā*. There is no accomplishment by way of *prasaṅga* for the selection of the *hotṛ* priest at the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśika*) in the Soma-related *iṣṭi*s and animal sacrifices, because of the Soma-related selection of the *hotṛ*.
There is no accomplishment by way of *prasaṅga*.
The establishment by way of a logical consequence (prasaṅgasiddhi) regarding the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) in the animal-cake offering (paśupuroḍāśa).

There is no accomplishment by way of *prasaṅga* (incidental application) for the consumption of remnants at the *saumya* and *āgneya* offerings by the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of the *saumika* [sacrifice]. There is no accomplishment by way of *prasaṅga* for the *darśika* (new-moon) vigil by means of the *saumika* vigil performed at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
See Mīko., p. 1753, under the entry "jāgaraṇayāya."

There is no accomplishment by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*) for the vessels of initiation (*dīkṣāpātra*) in the *savanīya-puroḍāśa* and other offerings within the Jyotiṣṭoma, because they are already obtained through the Soma sacrifice. Nor is there incidental application for the *barhis* grass and the *anvādhāna* (placing of the fire-sticks), as these are specifically prescribed for the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*). Bhāṣya 12.1.15.18.

There is no establishment by implication (*prasaṅgasiddhi*) of the consumption of the remnants of the *iṣṭi* sacrifices through the consumption of the vow-food (*vratabhakṣaṇa*) of the *soma* sacrifice.

[Objection: "If it is argued that the consumption of the remnants is likewise [in both cases]," the Bhāṣya states: In the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there is the consumption of the remnants, such as the *ida*; and in the *soma* sacrifice, this is extended to the *iṣṭi*-type rites by the rule of transfer (*codaka*).
If it is argued that he also concludes with the vow pertaining to the Soma sacrifice, we say no, because of the difference in nature.
Commentary: No.
Why? Because it is not purposeless;
for it is not sufficient for the mere act of subsistence.

Its purpose is refinement (*saṃskāra*), because the portions to be consumed (*bhakṣa*) are remnants of what has already been used, and because of the use of the accusative case in the injunction: "The four priests with the sacrificer as the fifth consume the *iḍā*."
Therefore, it must be performed.
This very point was established in the sixth [book] itself (6.8.8).
However, this statement regarding its purpose is mentioned here because it arises as a relevant incidental discussion (this is the connection).

In the *Soma-sūtra*, the meaning of the word "likewise" (*tathā*) is that [the eating] is not to be performed, just like the eating of forest-dwellers (*āraṇya*). Vi—[The objection: "If the portions for consumption belong to the sacrificer, they do not exist, as in the case of the forest-dwellers. [Response: No; these are not for the sake of livelihood, but must be performed for the purpose of ritual disposal (*pratipatti*).

Bhaṭṭa: In that case, since even the consumption of the remnants (*śeṣabhakṣa*) performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) possesses the character of a refinement of the agent (*kartṛsaṃskāra*)—according to the principle of the sprinkling of the *prayāja* remnant—it is logical that it serves the purpose of sustaining life. Even though there is an accusative case indicating that the remnant is for the sake of disposal (*pratipatti*), the sprinkling of the *prayāja* remnant, which is inferred from the [textual] authority, is itself the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the sustenance of life; and thus, its requirement is met through the incidental fulfillment (*prasaṅgasiddhi*) provided by the milk-vow (*payovrata*).

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the conclusion is as follows]: because of the injunction of a restrictive rule regarding eating according to one's designation (*ākhyāśana-niyama-vidhāna*), it is understood that the sustenance of life must be performed by that very means. Since the sacrificer’s portion (*yajamāna-bhakṣa*) serves solely for the disposal of the remnant (*kevala-śeṣa-pratipatti*), and since there is no establishment of such disposal through incidental application (*prasaṅga-siddhi*), the sacrificer must indeed consume the remnant even in the *Prāṇīyā* and other offerings.

As Maṇḍana stated: "In this case, there should again be consumption of the remnant, as in the case of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*). And as Śaṅkara stated: "But the portions of the sacrificer should be separate."
The establishment by way of incidental application (*prasaṅgasiddhi*) pertains to the threshing of the sacrificial grain and the vow associated with the new moon sacrifice.

The establishment by way of incidental application refers to the animal cake-offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) being accomplished by means of the *prayāja* and other rites performed for the sake of the animal sacrifice.

The accomplishment by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*) occurs in the case of the animal-sacrifice *puroḍāśa* offerings and the subsequent offerings (*anuyāja*s) being accomplished by the subsequent offerings belonging to the animal sacrifice; [this is stated in] Vindusūtra 5.1.15.

Incidental application occurs when the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*) is accomplished through a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the modified rite (*vaikṛta*), provided that the archetype and the modification share a common ritual procedure (*samānatantre*).
(Setting aside for consideration) | This is to be seen under the rule: *mīko.* p. 2695, ‘When the archetype and the ectype share the same procedure (*samānatantra*).’

Accomplishment by way of incidental application (*prasaṅgasiddhi*) occurs when the ordinary practice of eating forest-grown food is extended to the *prāpaṇīya* and other rites by means of the Soma-related milk-vow (*payovrata*) and so forth;

this should be seen under the entry "The Principle of Eating Forest-Grown Food" (*āraṇyabhojananyāya*) on page 972 of the Mīmāṃsākośa. Accomplishment by way of incidental application also occurs when the *anvāhārya* sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is [replaced] by the Soma-related fee in the Soma and Agniṣomīya sacrifices and others.

The accomplishment by implication (*prasaṅgasiddhi*) refers to the binding of the wife (*patnīsaṃnahanam*) in the Soma sacrifices by means of the binding of the wife performed at the Soma-related offerings (*saumikeṣṭi*).
And there is the binding, because it has already occurred.

The Commentary states: "And the binding of the wife in the New and Full Moon sacrifices is prescribed up to that point [in the ritual manual] with the words, 'He binds the wife with the *yoktra* (girdle).'"
Therefore, even though it is extended by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) to the *iṣṭi*-type rites which are subsidiary to the Soma sacrifice, it should not be performed.
Why? Because it has already been completed (*vṛttatvāt*).

At the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), the girding of the wife for the sake of the Soma has already taken place, as it is recorded in scripture: "He girds the wife with the *yoktra* (girdle), and the initiated one with the *mekhalā* (waistband), for the sake of forming a couple."
The girding of the garment is for the purpose of wearing it and serves all purposes;
it is accomplished by the very rite of the Soma sacrifice through incidental application (*prasaṅga*) until the completion of the ritual.
Regarding "Soma"—the connection [of this topic] arises from its distinction from the previously mentioned *agnyādheya* (fire-consecration).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "And the girding of the wife should not be performed at the Soma sacrifice, because it has already been performed there. [The objection: "The girding of the wife must be performed because of the extended application (codaka). [The reply: No; for that is not so, since the binding and the wearing of the garment are already accomplished by means of the yoktra.

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the binding of the wife with a cord (*yoktra*), which is prescribed by the rule "he binds the wife with the yoktra," is accomplished through *prasaṅga* (extended application) by means of the well-known binding of the wife with the water-pot (*karaka*) performed at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) during the *Prāyaṇīyā* and subsequent rites; thus, it need not be performed separately. However, in the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice itself, it must indeed be performed.
Bodhāyana, however, has stated that even in that case it is not so.

For that [act] is not for an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose, such that it would be performed again according to the logic of waking; since a visible purpose exists in the form of the necessity of wearing the garment, it is improper to assume an invisible result. Nor does it follow here that it serves as a means for wearing the initial garment, as is the case with the *anvādhāna* rite.

It might be argued that since there is the possibility of being heard again even after having been performed once, the subsequent binding within the wrapping (*parivyāṇa*) is justified for the purpose of extending the firmness of the *savanīya* sacrificial post; however, this must be rejected.

For while one may assume a different purpose for the directly enjoined wrapping in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it is improper to assume a new function for the original binding—which already has an established purpose as securing the post against falling—by assigning it a different task in the modified sacrifice.

If, however, it is argued that the *saṃhanana* (girding) belongs to the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself and is not for the purpose of wearing a garment, but rather for the purpose of imparting strength for the rite about to be performed, even so, since strength is already established by the *saṃhanana* belonging to the Soma sacrifice, and since in the absence of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) it is logical that the same [Soma] rite serves as the archetype for the drawing [of water], there is a contradiction with the principle of "incidental establishment" (*prasaṅgasiddhi*).
Maṇḍana says: "The girding of the wife is certainly not desired here.
Śaṅkara says: "There is no girding of the wife at all."
The throwing of the *prastara* [grass-bundle] occurs at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), when the *anuyāja* offerings are being deferred upward from the fire-altar.

Furthermore, although the *śāstra* (recitation) was prescribed for the sake of the *tapas* that is subordinate to the *savanīya* oblation, it is not applied because of its *apūrva* (novelty), according to the principle of Vedic injunctions (*vaidikakaraṇanyāya*). Therefore, the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the [Soma] must be offered at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) itself, even without the *prastara* (grass-bundle).
It would belong to the *sānnāyya* option.

Regarding the statement, "He throws the *prastara* along with the branch," since the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the branch is not fit for the *prastara*, there is a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the branch present in the *sānnāyya* option;
thus, the *upaveṣa* would also exist only in the *sānnāyya* option.
Therefore, the conjunction [of the terms] has the purpose of indicating time.

However, in reality, because of the scriptural statements, "He places the potsherds after having placed the *upaveṣa*" and "He places the milk-pot over the fire after having placed the *upaveṣa*," the *upaveṣa* is for the purpose of the *sānnāyya* (curdled milk offering) and for the purpose of placing the potsherds.
In that regard, even though there is no milking at the Full Moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāsa*), the placement of the potsherds would necessitate the use of the *upaveṣa* for its own sake.
In that case, even in the absence of a shed, a support made from the vāraṇa tree must be used;
thus it is stated in the *Kutūhala*.
Ke.

The term "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is used figuratively for the *prastara* [grass-bundle], as in the passages: "The sacrificer is the *prastara*" and "The sacrificer is the single-pot-sherd cake" (Vi.
1.4.12). The offering of the *prastara* consists of the casting of the *prastara* into the fire with the *sūktavāka* mantra beginning with "This [is] heaven and earth" (*idaṃ dyāvāpṛthivī*).
VI. 3.2.5: The throwing of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the deity.
Regarding the throwing of the *prastara*:
"And the throwing does not subsist as a form of sacrifice (*yāga*)."
This is clearly a *homa* itself, because it is described as consisting of an act of throwing [the offering] into [the fire].
Just as the vessel and other implements attain the status of a *homa* by virtue of holding the substance,
so too does the act of offering (*praharaṇa*) attain the status of a *homa* by virtue of the act of throwing (*prakṣepa*).
Or [it may be] so. (Vārttika 3.2.5.12, p.
761): "The throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle is both a disposal (*pratipatti*) and a sacrifice (*yāga*).
Thus, the *prastara* is disposed of and the sacrifice is accomplished."
It is established through direct perception; by means of the scriptural statement, the sacrifice is accomplished.
Bhāṣya 3.2.5.15.
[This concerns] the throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle.

Since the substance of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is not mentioned as being the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) in this case, and since Agni and others are the deities, this act is understood to be a sacrifice (*yāga*). However, because it consists primarily of the act of throwing [the bundle] into the fire, it is determined to be a *homa*.
Along with the throwing of the *prastara*, the throwing of the *darśa* branch is a disposal act (*pratipatti*).
That [result] accrues only from one who is self-restrained, and not from one who is unrestrained.
The throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle has the purpose of providing a *prastara* for the placement of the *sruva* ladles.

In the *prastarapraharaṇa* (the throwing of the grass-bundle), according to the view that the section concerning the deceased (*mṛtādhikāra*) applies, the portion of the *sūktavāka* mantra intended for the sacrificer’s benediction—beginning with "This sacrificer desires... and so forth—is omitted.
(Kṛtvācintā) | Vi.
10.2.11 | In the offering of the grass-bundle (*prastarapraharaṇa*), the *sūktavāka* is a mantra in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; it is not a connection for the purpose of [indicating] time.
In the *sūktavāka* mantra used as the instrument for the throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle, the word "yajamāna" (sacrificer) must be modified when there is a change to a plural number.
Bhāṣya 9.1.14.1.
The throwing of the branch occurs at the time of the throwing of the *prastara* [bundle of grass].
(6.4.14). See Mīko., p. 2024, under the entry "Throwing of the Branch at the Darśa" (*darśe śākhāpraharaṇam*).
The *Prastarapraharaṇanyāya* (the principle of the throwing of the *prastara*, wherein the *sūktavāka* is an auxiliary to that act).
The principle of the *sūktavāka* should be consulted in this regard.
The *prastarapaṅkti* is a *paṅkti* [verse].
The syllables in its quarters are 12, 12, 8, and 8.
For example: "From her [came] the oceans" (*udā0* 'tasyāḥ samudrā adhi', *Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.164.42).

Regarding the *prastāva*: "One performs the *prastāva* for the first verse with an eight-syllable [meter], and for the two following [verses] with a two-syllable [meter]" (*ke.* prastāvaḥ 'aṣṭākṣareṇa prathamāyā ṛcaḥ prastauti, dvyakṣareṇottarayoḥ').
The *prastāva* is the second division of the *sāman*;
the *prastotṛ* sings it. (Vi. 3.1.8)
The Prastotṛ is the assistant of the Udgātṛ;
he belongs to the second group.
As a participant entitled to half the sacrificial fee, he receives six cows.
VI. 3|7|17: "The *prastotṛ* chants the *prastāva*.
3|7|9: He sings the second portion of the *sāman*, called the *prastāva*. 3|1|8: "The *pratiprasthātṛ* initiates the *prastotṛ*."
The *upagās* are indeed the *prastotṛ* and others; they are not some other persons.
(Vi.
3.7.14) The *prastotṛ* and *pratihartr̥* are the singers (*gātārau*), not the *udgātṛ*s.
Alternatively,
the throwing away of the *prastara* is both a disposal (*pratipatti*) and a sacrifice (*yāga*).
In that case, the *sūktavāka* mantra is the means (*aṅga*).
Or rather:
[Vārttika 3.2.6.15] The throwing [of the *prastara*] is the sacrifice;
it is an injunction regarding the deity based on the indicative mark (*māntra-varṇika*).
The *praharati* (the act of throwing) is a sacrifice (*yajati*).
Thus, the *prastara* (grass-bundle) can be thrown with the *sūktavāka* only if the *praharati* is a sacrifice and has deities such as Agni as its object.

Bhāṣya 3.2.5.13: The act of throwing away the branch is not the primary motive; the throwing away is not a contextual *arthakarma* (substantive act), but rather a *pratipattikarma* (disposal) in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices.
And that [act] does not exist in the Full Moon sacrifice.
The throwing away of the branch occurs at the time of the throwing away of the *prastara* bundle.
The throwing away of both the branch and the *prastara* is a disposal (*pratipatti*).

Bhāṣya 6.4.14.44: At the conclusion of the Soma sacrifice, the throwing (*praharaṇa*) of the *svaru*—which was taken up and employed as a common ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice—is not [governed] by the time of the subsidiary (*anubandha*).
Regarding the throwing, there is also the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *prastara* and the branch (*śākhā*).
Since the throwing would otherwise occur at an indefinite time, it is prescribed that they be thrown together, according to the injunction: "He throws the *prastara* together with the branch."
*Duṣprahāsa*: The description of something as being such [as it is] by one who knows it to be otherwise, without that purpose.
"Because there is no prior exclusion regarding a woman with soiled garments.

Regarding the injunction heard in connection with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—"One should not converse with a woman with soiled garments (*malavadvāsas*), nor should one eat her food"—there arises a discussion as to whether this prohibition against conversing with a woman with soiled garments applies only to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice and similar rites, or whether it is a prohibition for a person in all circumstances. In response to this inquiry, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): the prohibition against conversing and so forth with a woman with soiled garments—that is, a menstruating woman—applies to a person in all circumstances.
This [act] is for the sake of the person alone, not for the sake of the ritual act (*kratvartha*).

Because it is stated that "one whose wife becomes menstruating before the performance of the *Sāgnī* sacrifice should sacrifice after asking her permission," and because the prohibition [of the sacrifice] occurs precisely before that [period],
it is therefore for the sake of the person.

This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Furthermore, because of the prohibition of food for one who is "malavadvāsas"—that is, a woman in her menses—according to the Vedic text: "One should not eat her food; indeed, the food of a woman is ointment," there is a prohibition of sexual union (which is well-known among the Lāṭas as being for the sake of the deity) through the sequence of food and ointment; thus, it is established that the prohibition of conversation and other such acts pertains to the duty of the man.

Therefore, this prohibition is not a *kṛtadharma* (a duty pertaining to the ritual act), but rather a *puruṣārtha* (a duty pertaining to the person); it is thus established as an exception (*utkṛṣṭa*) from the context. [Kevalānanda: Before initiation, there is freedom of action, speech, and eating. [Dvivedagaṅga: This is the conclusion.
"The *jātakarman* (birth-rite) for a male is ordained before the cutting of the umbilical cord.
This is a Smṛti injunction according to Pañcamakāra;
see Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 40.
Because that *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick has its purpose fulfilled prior [to it],
the *citriṇī* and subsequent bricks are to be placed in the middle layer (*madhyamā citi*).
This was established in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*).
In the middle layer as well, the bricks called *lokaṃpaṇā* should be placed before [the completion of the layer], not afterwards;
for the purpose of that *lokaṃpaṇā* is fulfilled once the layer has been piled. The filling out of the piled layer is accomplished by means of the *lokaṃpaṇā*.
Therefore, whether it be one or many, that [brick] is placed only at the end;
after that, nothing else can be added.
Consequently, the established conclusion is that the *citriṇī* and other bricks must be laid down in the middle layer prior to the *lokampṛṇā*.

In some cases, that which is studied outside of a specific context (*anāramyādhīta*) is set aside by that which belongs to a specific context (*prākaraṇika*), just as the *sāmnāyya* oblation is set aside by the *pāśubandha* sacrifice (Bāl.
p. 141). This applies even to all the elements belonging to the specific context, such as the washing of the hands, the restraint of speech, the forming of a fist, and so forth.
Regarding the sacred thread (*upavīta*), its status as an auxiliary to the context is established in relation to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
As for the bricks' properties such as "not being black" (*akṛṣṇatva*) and so forth, they possess a commonality that applies both to those within the context and those outside the context.
The Citriṇī and others are also auxiliary parts of the fire-altar.
The same applies in the section concerning the limbs of the fire-altar (*agnyaṅga*).
The Commentary states: "Without reference to a specific context (*anārabhya*), it is declared: 'He lays down the *citriṇī* bricks; he lays down the *vajriṇī* bricks; he lays down the *bhṛt* bricks.

Yet, within that specific context (*prakaraṇa*), there are properties of the bricks, such as: 'One should make the brick devoid of testicles and black,' and likewise, 'One should join the bricks with ashes.'"
In this regard, there is a doubt: should it not be performed when it is outside the context?
Why? Because of its non-proximity.
This being the position reached, it is said in reply:
The subsidiary part of the fire-altar (*agnyaṅga*) should be exactly like that which is near it;
for syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*).
And this would be otherwise for these bricks.
This is the topical [application].
Regarding the principle of the "enclosure" (*prākāśanyāya*):

let it be that in the case of the *soma-sūtra*, if there is another [element] such as the *citriṇī* bricks during the removal, that too would be endowed with the ritual properties (*dharma*), just like the *āgrayaṇa-graha*.
They are not established in [words such as] *vi*, *akhaṇḍa*, *adīka*, *dhāmāṃśin*, *triṇya*, and so forth;
nor do they exist even in sentences spoken by non-Aryans.
Therefore, they are not [denotative] even from a sentence that is primary (*prakṛta*), unprecedented (*apūrva*), or auspicious (*dhanya*).

The properties such as *akhaṇḍatva* (integrity) and so forth exist otherwise in the *citriṇī* bricks and others. [Objection: Since the application of the *ihakā* bricks—which possess the properties of blackness (*kṛṣṇa*) and so on—to the *citriṇī* bricks is based on a non-Aryan source (*anārya*), they do not possess the properties of the primary context (*prākaraṇika*). This being the position reached, [the reply is: as before, because of the proximity of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*), either the connection with the *apūrva* produced by the *ihakā* bricks or the connection with the *apūrva* produced by those [black bricks] must be indicated; and since there is no distinction even in their being based on a non-Aryan source, here too they possess the properties of both.
Maṇḍana: "The bricks [of the altar] are distant from the *syena* and possess the same characteristics.
Śaṅkara: "There is one [type of brick] designated as *citriṇī*, etc.
3. According to the *Prākāśa*.
The notion that "this is a connection between a case-ending and a verb" is sublated by the observation of fitness;
for the vastness of space and light is seen through the word *urvī*.

As for what was said—that in connection with that [action], it would be the fifth [priest] in the future—this is true as far as the understanding is concerned; however, in the absence of that [action], there is no connection with the Adhvaryu.
For that [connection] is understood through the sentence.
He says: "The fourth [syllable] that is heard will set aside the sentence. No, for that which is not being enjoined is not capable of setting anything aside.
How then is it heard [in the scripture] regarding a recipient who is not intended to be designated?
It is by way of restating what is obtained through the force of the context;
therefore, there is no fault.

Or rather, it has been stated that the gift qualified by all its specific attributes is what is enjoined. Thus, when there is no desire for others [to receive], there will be favor toward the *codaka* (the extended injunction) insofar as the original form is maintained.
Therefore, the two *prākāśa* lamps are the displacers of the portion belonging to the Adhvaryu priest.
*Ḍupū*: The two *prākāśya* vessels do not exclude the entirety of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

Why? If, by restating the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇām anūya*), the two *prākāśyas* were enjoined [in the nominative case], then they would exclude the entire sacrificial fee—as in "the two *prākāśyas* are the sacrificial fee" and "they belong to the Adhvaryu" [whereupon the transfer of the person [to another priest] would occur later through a subsequent sentence], as in "a wooden cup for Soma is the sacrificial fee; it is to be given to the Brahman. But this is not the case.

How so? Because this is a single sentence: "He gives two *prākāśa* vessels to the Adhvaryu" (where the word *ca* indicates a reason). Furthermore, the word *prākāśyau* is not in the nominative case, as is the case with *somacamasaḥ*.

What, then, [is the case]? It is the accusative case. And that [accusative] is connected with the act of giving by the Adhvaryu (not with the act of giving alone), because of syntactical unity (the meaning being "because of syntactical unity with the word 'adhvaryu'").
And in that context, a connection between the Adhvaryu and the *prākāśa* vessels is enjoined by means of the act of giving (that is, by the injunction following upon the act of giving).

The word *adhvaryu* does not refer merely to the act of giving, because that would entail the fault of restating what is already known (*anuvāda*) and because it would involve a disjointed connection.
Rather, it means "the Adhvaryu himself gives to the Adhvaryu.
In that case, the *adhvaryu* ending in the dative case functions as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

The *prākāśa* nominal stem, ending in the accusative case, is subordinate with respect to the non-Adhvaryu priest; because of the connection between those two nominal stems, the dative case is obtained.
Now, it was argued that the two *prākāśas* are enjoined while taking up the act of giving (*dadāti*). To this, it is replied:

"Because of the connection with the word *adhvaryu*, that meaning which follows from it [the dative case] must be accepted; the connection between the *prākāśa* and the act of giving (*dadāti*) is not to be accepted"—this passage is found additionally in the Ānandāśrama edition (it is not found in our manuscript copy or in the *Tattvanirṇaya*). In that context, the connection with the *adhvaryu* expressed by the dative case-ending is to be accepted (this line is not present in the Ānandāśrama edition). [The *adhvaryu* is not [connected] in his own right.]

[Objection: Is it not the case that an action, once heard, connects with its factors of action (*kāraka*s)? Therefore, the connection will be between the verb *dadāti* ("he gives") and the *prākāśa* (the two mirrors), rather than between the *adhvaryu* (priest) and the *prākāśa*.
[Reply: It is said: because *dadāti* is not being enjoined, the syntactic connection (*vākya-sambandha*) alone is more powerful.

(He explains this very point: When an action is being enjoined, the factors of action (kārakas) possess manifested capacities; and they are connected with that action because they are factors of action. But when [the action] is not being enjoined, [the factors of action] do not possess manifested capacities.

In that context, when [the word] *avidhisthe* is heard, the very connection characterized by syntactical unity (*vākya*) which is perceived through immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) must be accepted; it is not [the connection] with the distant verb *dadāti*, because the two [words] *prākāśau* are separated by the word *adhvaryave*.

The passage from the Bhāṣya beginning with "The direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) does not depend on syntactical unity" is to be interpreted according to this very principle—that the direct statement is not intended as an injunction (*avidhi*).

(He explains the meaning of the Bhāṣya statement, "Capability is sublated by perception," by way of its underlying sense: The phrase "sublated by perception" (referring to the rule that "the case-ending [of the agent] is connected with the verb") must also be understood as applying precisely because [the connection] is not being enjoined.
(Therefore, due to the connection with the Adhvaryu, only his portion is accomplished.)

(Explaining the section [adhikaraṇa] beginning with "one, five," etc., he says: In the phrase "one cow" (*ekā gām*), the word "one" (*eka*) is connected with the word "cow" (*go*), not with the verb "to give" (*dadāti*), precisely because the action is merely being referred to (*anudyamāna*); this is the very same principle. (Staying within the subsequent three sections, he shows them in brief: The second section (the second with respect to the section on the *prākāśya*) holds that it is the sublater of the entire sacrificial fee (*dākṣiṇya*). [This is] the refuter of the view of Krudākṣi.
Regarding that, he states a specific doubt: "But it is commenced for the purpose of excluding [the application of] the indicative mark (liṅga) and the direct statement (śruti).

(As for the section concerning the *yajyuḥ* and so forth: It is not a modification of the whole, nor is it a modification of the end, (nor is it a modification of a part); rather, another [priest] is [appointed] for the purpose of consuming the portion of the Adhvaryu.

Śā—In the context of the Aśvamedha (though in fact it is heard in the Rājasūya: "He gives two *prākāśa* mirrors to the Adhvaryu"), there arises a doubt: do the two *prākāśas* exclude the entire sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), or do they exclude only the portion belonging to the Adhvaryu?
If the syntactical connection is "he gives the two *prākāśas*," then they exclude the whole.

Then, regarding the two [mantras] beginning with "prākāśyau," they belong specifically to that portion; for in that case, the connection with the *adhvaryu* supersedes what was obtained through immediate sequence.
By the force of the second hearing (*dvitīyā-śruti*), there is a syntactical connection with the action "he gives" (*adāti*).
Furthermore, the act of giving, which is obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*), is indicated;
and it is not possible for the Adhvaryu priest to specify that indication.

Therefore, the term *adhvaryu* in the phrase "he yokes the *adhvaryu*" is appropriately applied to the entire [priestly function] in some way (since it is a restatement, there is no fault in explaining it in some manner). The injunction regarding the two *prākāśa* vessels pertains to the act of giving alone; thus, there is a cessation of the entire [function]. (It is said: "The connection with the *adhvaryu* itself is enjoined for the two *prākāśas*—alternatively, the prior act of giving is qualified by the two [vessels]"). For fear of rendering the word *adhvaryu* meaningless, the injunction does not apply to the act of giving alone.

Therefore, that very relationship which arises subsequently between the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), namely the Adhvaryu priest, and the object to be given, namely the two *prākāśa* mirrors, caused by the connection with the ritual action, is what is being enjoined.
(Because of the dative case, the objective factor (*karmakāraka*) qualified by the two *prākāśas* is enjoined with reference to the recipient factor (*saṃpradānakāraka*) qualified by the Adhvaryu.
Since a factor of action requires a correlative, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) even though the referent is qualified by the Adhvaryu.)

Furthermore, since the relationship between the object to be given (*pradeya*) and the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is dependent upon the act of giving, the relationship that exists between the two [the *pradeya* and *saṃpradāna*] as expressed by the verbal root *dadāti* (to give) reaches its finality in an injunction (*vidhi*). Because it serves to denote the relationship between those two, it depends upon the act of giving which is required for that purpose; thus, the root *dadāti* is not entirely redundant. Some, however, maintain that the relationship of ownership (*svasvāmibhāva*) itself is enjoined between the *prākāśya* (the prize) and the *adhvaryu* (the priest).

And since that [act] occurs through the giving of the *prākāśas* to the *adhvaryu*, there arises the possibility of the *adhvaryu* being the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), the *prākāśas* being the object (*karman*), and the act being one of giving (*dāna*). Consequently, they say that the verb *dadāti* (gives) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) accompanied by the second and fourth case endings. However, the author of the treatise, dissatisfied with this—because the relationship of owner and owned, which is common to all actions involving giving, necessarily implies the act of giving and thus would itself have to be enjoined—has established that only the relationship between the factors of action (*kāraka*) is what is intended.

Alternatively, precisely out of a desire to avoid rendering the word *adhvaryu* meaningless, an entirely new act (*apūrva*) characterized by the manifestation of the *adhvaryu* is enjoined immediately after the gift.

Since this serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), the *adhvaryu*'s entitlement is established; consequently, his original share is set aside, and thus there is no total exclusion [of the *adhvaryu* from all shares]. (This "alternative" position is a bold assertion, because a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is only possible when a simple injunction (*kevalavidhi*) is not feasible).

*Soma*—The connection [of this section] arises from the following objection: since the *ekāgni* sacrifice bestows [the reward] due to its inherent nature (*anvābhāvāt*), even though the entire sacrificial fee (*dākṣiṇya*) is suspended there, here [in the *soma* sacrifice], because the connection with that [fee] is possible, there is a suspension of the whole.
Regarding the word *prākāśyau*: the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*) in the sense of "that in which one shines" (*prakāśate*).

The lengthening of the vowel of the prefix is according to Pāṇini 6.3.122, "The [vowel] of a prefix is often lengthened before *ghañ* when not referring to a human," or it is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
And therefore, Bhaṭṭabhāskara says that the two golden mirrors (*prākāśau*) [are the meaning];
in the Sūtra, the word *tathā* has the sense "like the flute" (*venu*), [meaning] those two which turn toward all [the priests].
Vi— "Are the two mirrors the sublaters (*bādhakau*) by themselves, or of the entire Adhvaryu ritual?"

"It is due to its connection with the act of giving as a whole, not due to its connection with a specific [recipient]" (the phrase "due to its connection with a specific" means due to its relation to the act of giving characterized by a specific recipient).
Some say that the two items are a lamp and a pillar.
Others say they are mirrors.
The Bhāṭṭa [position]: In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "He gives two golden *prākāśya* vessels to the Adhvaryu.
Therein, by means of the injunction of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-vidhi*), there is an injunction of the *prākāśya* vessels with reference to the act of giving (*dāna-anuvāda*).

Nor does the injunction of "goldenness" (*hiraṇmayatva*) result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because goldenness is already invariably established due to the fact that the substance of the object called "prākāśya" cannot be anything other than gold. Furthermore, since the act of giving—the subject of the injunction—is qualified by the term "adhvaryu," the word *adhvaryu*—having been interpreted in some way as referring to the entire [priestly class] based on the etymology "he joins (*yunakti*) for the Adhvaryu"—effects the exclusion of the ordinary sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in its entirety.

This being the case, since the term *adhvaryu* would otherwise be rendered meaningless, one abandons the third type of injunction and instead enjoins the *prākāśa* (the two mirrors) with reference to the status of the *adhvaryu* as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
Furthermore, since the status of being a recipient does not occur outside of an act of giving, the fact that the *adhvaryu* is the locus of the act of giving is established by logical fitness alone.

As for the statement in the root-text that "the relationship between the *prākāśa* and the *adhvaryu* is enjoined," its meaning is precisely this; it is not to be taken literally as enjoining some other relationship that is not itself a primary word-meaning (*apadārtha*).

Therefore, just as there is a multi-faceted injunction regarding a cow and so forth, or an injunction for curd with reference to Indra, so too here, even when the gift (*prākāśya*) is enjoined with reference to the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*), there is no lack of grammatical proficiency (*avyutpannatva*), because the relationship between the two—the referent (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*)—is indeed established.

If, however, it is considered that in all cases the requirement for being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) belongs solely to the nominal stem—such as "cow" (*go*)—and not to the status of being an object denoted by the case-suffix, nor to the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) denoted by the case-suffix, then for this very reason, even the Maitrāvaruṇa and others do not have the status of being the object of reference merely by virtue of being recipients; rather, although they are subordinate (*guṇa*) by virtue of their specific nature, there is the postulation of another word [to denote them], just as it was stated regarding the Adhvaryu. In that case, let it be that here, even by abandoning the method of prescribing the dative case (*caturthīvidhi*), there is simply the injunction of a distinct, qualified act of giving.

Nor should it be argued that, even so, because the connection with the manifestation (*prākāśya-bhāvanā*) is logically established through the fourth case— characterized as the object of the action— as the Adhvaryu priest is the intended recipient, it is not proper to conclude that this is an injunction for a different act of giving; for if that were the case, it would be impossible to treat the existing, permanent, archetypal act of giving itself as the subject of the restatement (*anuvāda*).

Therefore, when the acceptance of six distinct varieties is admitted, even after the act of giving, that which is distinguished by both the recipient and the excellence [of the gift] is enjoined as producing a different result (*adhvaryānati*), in accordance with the capacity of the injunction for the postulation of a separate ritual action (*padāntara-kalpanā*), since there is no evidence for the postulation of a separate ritual procedure (*karmāntara-kalpanā*).
Consequently, when the original (*prākṛta*) giving is repeated as a constituent part of that [new rite], the cessation of its specific portion alone follows.

In reality, however, because of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is accepted that the substitution (*ātadeśa*) operates prior [to the original]; thus, only the aforementioned practice of giving, qualified by the two mentioned attributes, is enjoined. This is for the purpose of establishing the non-transference (*anatisiddhi*) of the Adhvaryu as before. Consequently, even though there is no cessation of the original gift (*prākṛtadāna*), there is a cessation of the original singing associated with it (*prākṛtatadgāna*). In every respect, it is established that there is no cessation of the entire original consecration (*dīkṣaṇā*).
Maṇḍana says: "But in the case of the *prākāśa* [gift], there is not a total cessation in every way."

The lamp is that which is denoted by the word "light" (*prākāśa*). (Su. p. 769).

In a case where even one of low birth may attain renown through the exertion of his own virtues, it is there that this [rule] operates; thus he is bold.

In the section on the establishment of the sacred fires (*āgnidhana*), the *sāvitra* oblations are prescribed, as in the injunction: "He offers the *sāvitra* oblations. Following that, with great elaboration, the acts such as the touching of the *ulūkhala* (mortar) and so forth are enjoined.
Subsequently, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is prescribed: "One who is being initiated should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu."

In that context, because the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice is helpful to the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) within the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is remembered quickly in the case of the fire-altar construction (*cayana*). Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—which is contrary to the established rule—is reached, namely that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* should be performed first in the fire-altar site (*agnidhana*) and the *sāvitra-homa* and other rites afterwards, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to carry over the preceding sūtra, "That would be the place.

Since the *sāvitra-homa* and other rites are prior to the archetypal *dīkṣaṇīyā* rite, they must have the very same place as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, namely the space preceding it, and not at the end of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*.
In the *Agnikāṇḍa*, although the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are already established by the force of the general rule (*codaka*), they are recited again after the *Sāvitra* and subsequent rites;

therefore, the *Sāvitra* and others come first, and the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* comes later. Kaiyaṭa: "When there is a scriptural mention of a quality for that which is archetypal (*prākṛta*), there should be a designation by means of that which possesses the quality."

When there is a scriptural mention of a quality (*guṇaśruti*) in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) regarding a deity mentioned in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the deity should be designated by means of that name together with its quality during the invocations (*āvāhana*) and other rites.
It should be performed in this manner;
for example, in the case of the *pavamāna* oblations, one must say: "Bring Agni Pavamāna," "Bring Agni Pāvaka," "Bring Agni Śuci," and so forth.
But it is not the case that the word "fire" alone is devoid of qualities;
this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Alternatively, because the word refers to its meaning, it would be like a substance even in the absence of modification.

In the Pavamāna [stotras], regarding the formulas "I offer what is pleasing to Agni Pavamāna," "to Agni Pāvaka," and "to Agni Śuci," this entire designation of the deity belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*) should remain unmodified in the ectype (*vikṛti*); there should be no modification. The designation must be made without attributes.
The word *vā* is for the purpose of setting aside the alternative view.
Because they are words denoting the object: "the object and the word" are *artha-śabdau*; because of their non-departure—that is, the absence of any departure from them—[they remain as they are].
In this context, the referent is the deity and the word is the word "Agni.
Because it is the word "Agni," it must indeed be uttered.
Now, whether the qualifying words such as "Pavamāna" and so forth are present or absent, that same deity remains.
It belongs to the original state; there is no loss of that [quality].
It is like a substance, as in: "This very barren cow (vaśā) belongs to all the deities; one desiring prosperity should sacrifice it to Vāyu."

Thus, even when the ritual action is enjoined by the word *ajā* (goat) or *avaśā* (she-goat), the *nigama* verses employ the word *chāgā* (he-goat). In that case, neither the meaning nor the word is lost;

therefore, there should be no modification—this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). Furthermore, because of the connection with the commencement [of the sacrifice], the designation should be made according to what is enjoined; for since the meaning is connected to the direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), if it were not expressed [as it is], the teaching of the subordinate quality (*guṇa*) would be purposeless.
The word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Because there is no inherent connection (*samavāya*)—that is, no relation of the deity existing by its own form at the commencement of the ritual act—and because the object that is the form of the deity is connected through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), as in the injunction "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna," it is stated that the object in the form of the deity possesses the quality of being inherently present (*samavāyitva*) and has a direct relationship [with the rite].

Therefore, in the *āvāhana-nigada* (invocation formulas) and so forth, there should be the designation of the object in the form of the deity by means of the prescribed term for the deity together with its attributes (*saguṇa-devatāpada*), as enjoined by the Vedic rule.

If the deity were denoted by the word "Agni" accompanied by its qualities—that is, by the word "Agni" joined with terms expressing qualities such as "pavamāna" (purifying)—then the teaching of the qualities, namely the words "pavamāna" and so forth which function as qualifiers, would be redundant.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the *nigadas* and other such passages, the deity must be denoted by the word "Agni" together with its qualities, and not by it alone without its qualities.
[This is stated] in the sense of "beginning with substances" (*dravyeṣvārambham*), because of the capacity [of the word] regarding the modified form (*vikārye*).

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it was argued that in the Pavamāna sacrifices, the deity should be designated in the medhas (animal sacrifices) by using the word *agni* alone, without any qualifying term. This is what he expresses in the passage beginning with "in the substance, the commencement," and so forth.
