*Saṃkarṣa* 3.1.25. See *Mīmāṃsākosa*, p. 95, under the entry "The cooking of the animal for the Agnihotra.

Regarding the discussion on the *prājahita* fire, see *Saṃkarṣa* 3.1.21: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it should be that very [fire]. See *Mīmāṃsākosa*, p. 1830, under the entry "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it should be that very [fire]."
The clarified butter for the *upāṃśuyāja* at the New and Full Moon sacrifices is either dedicated to Prajāpati, to Agni-Soma, or to Viṣṇu (Bhāṣya 5.1.6.21).
The clarified butter for the *upāṃśuyāja* dedicated to Prajāpati or to Viṣṇu is to be performed by a Brāhmaṇa before the Soma sacrifice;
however, the clarified butter for the *upāṃśuyāja* dedicated to Agni-Soma is not to be performed before the Soma sacrifice. Thus, there is no displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *upāṃśuyāja*.

Although the seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati are introduced together with the seasonal animals (*ṛtupaśu*), they are nevertheless sacrificed at the time of the *brahmasāman* after a long delay following the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite; the seasonal animals, however, are sacrificed in the morning. In that regard, the formula "The divine immolators" (*daivyāḥ śamitāraḥ*) is to be repeated for each animal and is not a single performance for all (*tantra*). (Vi. 11.4.21). [This concerns] the seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati in the Vājapeya sacrifice.

In this regard, these are seventeen sacrifices, and not a single ritual action consisting of a group of seventeen animals. Regarding the scriptural injunction, "One desiring long life should offer a *caru* of rice cooked in clarified butter (*dhṛta*) for Prajāpati, consisting of a hundred *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces," there is the presence of grain (*auṣadha*) in that gold, but not of clarified butter (*ājya*).
8|1|1|8|13-39. "One desiring long life should offer a *caru* oblation of gold pieces (*kṛṣṇala*) dedicated to Prajāpati; he cuts off four *kṛṣṇalas* at a time.

Thus, the *kṛṣṇalas* constitute the sacrificial offering (*havis*). Bhāṣya 10|1|1040. Regarding the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, it is heard in scripture: "They release them after they have been circumambulated by fire (*paryagnikṛta*); they sacrifice them at the *brahmasāman*."

In that context, the former [sūtra] is for the purpose of prohibiting the subsequent purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), while the latter is for the purpose of prohibiting those very same rites at another time. (1.1.2.15–53). In the Vājapeya sacrifice, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the seasonal animals (*ṛtu-paśu*) with the animals dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatya-paśu*).
This is to be understood from the statement: "with the animals dedicated to Prajāpati prescribed in the Vājapeya. (10.4.136).

One view is that the Prājāpatya offerings possess the character of being performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). Another view is that, according to the injunction "one should meditate on Prajāpati with the mind," silence itself is the characteristic of Prajāpati.
(Vi. 10.8.17). The sacrifice of the Prājāpatyas is heard of as taking place at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), at the time of the *brahmasāman*.
Bhāṣya 4.2:
For the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, there is merely the postponement of the immolation at the time of the Brahmasāman.

At the abandonment of those animals for whom the fire-circumambulation has been performed, there is the abandonment of the ritual action for the Prajāpati animals; this is because of the commonality of the scriptural injunction, as in the case of the Āraṇa rite. Therefore, there should be a displacement of the injunction to the Brahmasāman.

Commentary: Regarding the Vājapeya sacrifice, with reference to the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, it is heard in the scripture: "They release them after they have been carried around the fire" (*tān paryagnikṛtānutsṛjanti*), and "They immolate them at the Brahmasāman" (*brahmasāmnālabhante*). In this regard, a deliberation arises: Is the statement "they release them after they have been carried around the fire" a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action, while "they immolate them at the Brahmasāman" is an injunction for a different ritual action? Or rather, is the former intended to prohibit the subsequent purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) following the carrying around the fire, and the latter intended as a re-enactment (*prati-prasava*) of those very same rites at a later time? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That it is the abandonment of the ritual action.

The meaning is the prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action (*karmaśeṣapratiṣedha*). This is because of the similarity of the scriptural statement, as in the case of the forest-dwellers (*āraṇyavat*).

Just as it was stated regarding the passage "They release [the animals] after they have been encircled by fire" that it signifies a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action—according to the sūtra: "Or rather, it is a prohibition of the remainder, because of the absence of purpose, as in the case of the *idānta* [sacrifice]" (9.4.13.52).

Thus, "śruti" means equal to the Veda. What is the object of praise for these two? In that regard, ritual actions are enjoined, such as: "One should offer a *kapiñjala* bird to the spring. In all of those [rituals], the archetypal (*prākṛta*) qualities are obtained.

When those [animals] have been brought forward, the section concerning the subsidiary rite of carrying fire around them (*paryagnikaraṇa*) is heard again in the statement: "They release them after they have been carried around with fire. Since a repetition of an action devoid of further qualifications serves to exclude others, it is understood as a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual procedure.

In the same way, for the rites enjoined by the injunction "One should sacrifice the animals dedicated to Prajāpati," this repetition of the section on the subsidiary *paryagnikaraṇa*—being itself devoid of further qualifications—serves to terminate the remainder of the ritual procedure, thereby prohibiting it in all subsequent stages.
And because it is so, there must be an injunction for a separate ritual action in the statement, "They obtain equality with Brahman.
This is a supplement to the preceding [text]: "They obtain equality with Brahman through seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati.
The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: "In the phrase 'they release them after the carrying of fire around them,' the procedure ending with the carrying of fire around them (*paryagnikaraṇa*) is enjoined."
In the same way, these [offerings] dedicated to Prajāpati are rendered complete, like the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice. "They slaughter the Brahmasāman" refers to a distinct ritual act;
in that case, whatever substance and deity were used in the preceding sacrifices are supplied here by extension.
Or rather, there is a prohibition of the preparatory rite (saṃskāra) because of the unity of the sentence and the commonality of the sacrifice.
Commentary: "Or rather, it is not a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action.

What then? It is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding the *brahmasāman*, having prohibited those purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) that had reached their proper occasion from that specific occasion.
What is the reason? Because of the unity of the sentence due to the commonality of the sacrifice.
This is a single sentence: "He releases them after they have been encircled by fire" and "He immolates the Brahmasāman [animal].
How is this known? Because in the statement "he immolates," there is no mention of a specific substance or deity;
and when the sacrifice is the same, there is unity of the sentence.
For in that case, it would have to be stated that only the animal is to be sacrificed, because the substance and the deity have already been mentioned.

Alternatively, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); consequently, the former [sentence] would prohibit the remainder of the ritual action, while the latter would enjoin a different ritual action. In that situation, the substance and the deity would have to be stated [again].
As for what was stated previously— that they "combine"— that is not the case here, because their purpose has already been fulfilled in that very manner. Therefore, it is a single sentence.

But surely, in a single sacrifice, the purificatory rites are prohibited by the former [text] and enjoined by the latter; thus, due to the difference in meaning, there is indeed a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
For when it is said, "He performs the *brahmasāman* sacrifice," the abandonment [of the rite] up to the end of the *paryagnikaraṇa* is established by implication alone;
it is not [thereby] enjoined.
"The animal is to be sacrificed after being led to the enclosure; it is to be drawn out alone"—there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) regarding the commonality of the season (*ṛtusāmānya*).
As for the *Ṭup-ṭīkā*: "The times [of the rites] are obtained according to their sequence" (the time for the *paryagnikaraṇa* belongs to that which is being sacrificed).

When such sentences are taught as "the purificatory acts (*saṃskārāḥ*) are not to be performed at this time (but rather during the *brahmasāman*)," we do not accept them as injunctions of subsidiary elements (*aṅgavidhi*).

(If that were the case, since there would be no mutual connection between these two acts,) there would be a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*); and from that split of the sentence follows a split of the ritual act (*karma-bheda*); and from the split of the act follows a total lack of unity—thus it would result in the fallacy of assuming eight [separate] injunctions.

For when the animal to be sacrificed (*ālambhya*) is prescribed for another time, then by logical necessity (*nyāya*), there arises the consequence of postponing (*utkarṣa*) all the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) to that other time, which is why they are prohibited [in this context].
(Therefore, the injunction is merely for the postponement [of specific rites], and thus there is syntactic unity.)
Therefore, the ritual up to the *paryagnikaraṇa* (the encircling with fire) need not be repeated on the day of Māgha;
for we observe that there is no pouring of clarified butter (*āghāra*) over the omenta (*vapā*).

The commentary states: "At this time, the omentum is indeed not yet sprinkled with clarified butter; the *brahmasāman* is indeed the Brahman. In that he seizes [the victim] with the *brahmasāman*, by that it becomes for him as if not sprinkled. If there is a prohibition of the consecratory rite (*saṃskāra*), then, because the *juhū* ladle has been emptied by the performance of the *savanīya* offerings, there is no remnant of the *prayāja* oblations.
Due to the absence of that remnant, its state of being unsprinkled is appropriate.
Now, if there is a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action, then the attainment of equality with Brahman would occur through another ritual action;
in that case, the *prayāja* offerings arise again,
and they possess a remainder.
Therefore, there would be an act of pouring [libations];
however, the observation of no such pouring is not tenable.
For this reason as well, there is a negation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

Ṭup—Even though the statement "he offers the Brahma-sāman" occurs after another ritual act, the *prayāja* offerings for that animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) are nonetheless incidental (*prāsaṅgika*), according to the principle: "And because of the displacement of the animal [offering], due to its being prescribed in the middle of the ritual framework.
Therefore, this view is incorrect;
for it is equal for both disputants [that there is no sprinkling of clarified butter] due to the absence of the *prayājas*.
Regarding this, some describe it as follows:
there are two positions concerning those animals (*paśu*).

According to one position, after the drawing of the *āśvina* cup and after performing the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite for the animals prepared together with the seasonal animals (*ṛtupaśu*), they are released; then, at the time of the *brahmasāman*, they are to be immolated.
The second [view] is that the conclusion occurs together with the seasonal animals (*ṛtupaśu*).
In this second position, the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) of the omenta (*vapā*) exists [because it is proximate].

And when they are to be immolated on the day of Māgha (*māghadina*), then that sprinkling which belongs to them is present; for at the time of the *prayāja* offerings, the omentum has not yet been produced.

In the view of Yājñavalkya, since that consecration by sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa-saṃskāra*), which was invariably experienced in the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), is no longer present [in the case of the vapā], the statement expressing doubt regarding a defect—namely, "But now it is indeed dried up"—is appropriate.

In the alternative view that it is a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*), that property [of sprinkling] would have never been experienced before; therefore, there would be no ground for such a doubt as expressed in "But now it is indeed dried up. Thus, because a suspicion of a defect is observed, it follows that this is not a separate ritual act.
This also is not tenable;

for even according to the proponent of distinct acts (*karmāntaravādin*), since the sacrificial oblations (*haviṣ*) are obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), the statement expressing the doubt—"they do not exist here together"—is indeed appropriate.
Therefore, it is precisely correct that this indicative mark (*liṅga*) should be interpreted as representing the opinion of another school.

Śabara: Therefore, [the rites] ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa* belong to the *prājāpatya* [sacrifices]. This is the reply to the one who considers that, based on the statement "the *brahmasāman* is performed after the [animal] has been immolated" and the rule "the remainder is with clarified butter," this is a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*). [The reply is: "An injunction for another ritual action is not appropriate, because it would entail the postulation of multiple unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*) and because it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, there is an injunction for displacement (*utkarṣa*)."

Soma: In the previous case, because of the difference in agents, [the rule] was not applicable; here, it is stated that it is "elevated" (*uccaiḥ*) due to the difference in time. This is the connection.
(In the Sūtra, regarding the *śruti* of the *prājāpatya*s: 2847, among the *prājāpatya*s...)

The meaning is that due to commonality—that is, due to the similarity of the words—there is a distinct injunction, which constitutes the prescription of a separate ritual act. As stated in the *Citrādhikaraṇa*: "In the case of the *paryagnikaraṇa*, the abandonment [of the animal], the *ālabhya* at the *brahmasāman*, and the prohibition of the remainder of the ritual act would constitute the prescription of a separate ritual act."

Or rather, what excellence remains for that which is left over? For there is the teaching of the *Araṇyaka-Upaniṣad*. The last [alternative] is excluded because of the absence of substance in the eightfold division of sentences.

Bhaṭṭa: In the Vājapeya sacrifice, with reference to the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, it is heard in the scripture: "He releases them after they have been carried around the fire" (*tān paryagnikṛtānutsṛjati*) and "He immolates the Brahmasāman animal" (*brahmasāmnālabhate*).

In this context, because the preceding sentence prescribes the performance of the ritual up to the point of the *paryagnikaraṇa* (carrying fire around), just as in the cases "he releases the animals after they have been carried around the fire" and "he releases the *pālīvat* after it has been carried around the fire," and because the subsequent rites are understood to be non-performable due to the *gṛhamedhīya* being a new independent act (*apūrva*), the statement "He immolates the Brahmasāman animal" is an injunction for a separate ritual (*karmāntaravidhi*), similar to the rule "He completes the remainder with clarified butter."
And in that case, the substance and deity are obtained through the syntactical connection (anuṣaṅga) of the very same [injunction]: "He offers seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati."

This being the prima facie position, [the following is established]: Since the injunction for the act of requesting (*prārthanā*)—which occurs at the time of the *Brahmasāman* and follows the *paryagnikaraṇa*—for the *Prājāpatya* animals that were prepared together with the seasonal animals (*ṛtupaśu*) after the drawing of the *Āśvina* cup has been made by the statement "He immolates the *Brahmasāman* animal," it follows by implication that everything up to the end of the *paryagnikaraṇa* is to be performed together with the seasonal animals. Because the release (*utsarga*) is thus established at the conclusion of that [act], the preceding sentence cannot be taken as having that same meaning, and since its purpose is already fulfilled, it becomes a single syntactical unit with the subsequent injunction. Otherwise, if one were to treat the preceding and subsequent sentences as distinct and accept the third type of injunction (a restrictive injunction, *parisaṃkhyā*) for the former, while accepting the sixth type of injunction (an injunction of a qualified action, *viśiṣṭavidhi*) for the latter—which would involve a specific substance and deity—there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, in this case, only the postponement (*utkarṣa*) of the immolation (*ālambha*) is enjoined.

And at that time, the excellence of the subsequent cognitions is obtained precisely through the maxim: "Or [the result is obtained] from the connection with that and so forth" (5.1.12.24). Consequently, since the *anārāyaṇa* maxim does not apply here, there is no repetition of the subsidiary rites ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa*.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The refinement (*saṃskāra*) is excluded in the case of the animal sacrifice."
Śaṅkara: "In the *Brahmasāman*, there is no performance of ritual acts (*na karmabhṛt*).
The vows belonging to Prajāpati have the person as their purpose (*puruṣārthatā*) [Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.3–6].
In the *Prājāpatya* sacrifice consisting of one hundred *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces, the procedural details (*vidhyanta*) belong to the vegetable offering."

8|1|12|35–39. Regarding the *prājāpatya* [sacrifices], the extension of the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *ekādaśinī* will be stated in the section on the group of animals with disjoined necks (*atatvapracchigaṇa*) at 8|1|8|16 (Su.

p. 813). Furthermore, regarding the *prājāpatyas*, in the section beginning with "and because they are mentioned in the *prājāpatyas*" (10|4|13|6), the combination (*samuccaya*) of those prescribed as *vājapeya* [animals] and those established as *prājāpatya* [animals] is stated (Bhāṣya 4|1|4|133; Bālakrīḍā p. 177). [Objection: One will state the combination in various places, such as "and because they are mentioned in the *prājāpatyas*," since there is no contradiction [between them]. (This is the doubt.)
Or [it is so] because they are prescribed among the Prājāpatya [animals].
In the archetype (prakṛti), the seasonal animals (ṛtupaśu) are prescribed; and in the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is enjoined: "He immolates seventeen Prājāpatya animals."
In that regard, because they are prescribed in the *Prājāpatya* section, there is a combination with the seasonal animals (*ṛtupaśu*).

For the seasonal animals are indeed prescribed in the *Vājapeya*: "The exponents of Brahman say: 'It is neither an *agniṣṭoma*, nor an *ukthya*, nor a *ṣoḍaśin*, nor an *atirātra*. Then why are all the sacrificial forms (*yajñakratu*) encompassed by the *Vājapeya*? One should reply: 'By means of the animals. When he immolates the animal for Agni, he thereby obtains the *agniṣṭoma*; by the one for Indra-Agni, the *ukthya*; by the one for Indra, the *ṣoḍaśin*; by the one for Sarasvatī, the *atirātra*; and by the one for Mitrā-Varuṇa, the *bṛhat-stotra*."

"Indeed, by means of this many sacrificial rites (yajñakratu), they obtain [the results] through animals"— this shows a combination (samuccaya). Therefore, in the case of the Prājāpatya [animals], there is a combination of the Prājāpatyas with the seasonal animals (ṛtupaśu).
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "mahānāmnī";
such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
In the case of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, the *kumbhī* is the common procedure (*tantra*).

Bhāṣya 11.4.11.39: In the case of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, regarding the formula "of the goat's omentum and fat," there is a modification (ūha) to "of the goats' omenta and fats. Bālakrīḍā, p. 127. In the Vājapeya sacrifice, among the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, the procedure (tantra) for the cooking pots, spits, and frying pans is common. 11.4.8.33: Regarding the sacrifices dedicated to Prajāpati, there is a doubt as to whether they are one or many.
The determination [of the ritual procedure] has been made according to the model of the original [archetype], by means of the remainder of the scriptural statement (*vākyaśeṣa*).
Vārttika 3.1.12, p. 650. In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the performance of the *prājāpatya* offerings occurs after all other Soma sacrifices.

Nor should it be argued: "How can there be a calculation of multiple sacrifices, given that—according to the logic of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the *Prājāpatya-adhikaraṇa* (2.2.12–13)—the heart and other organs are mentioned in a single word, and thus their connection with a single deity is established? This is because they are taken together as a group.
Prāṇabhṛd-ikāthau: 2850. At the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana), the mantras of the Prāṇabhṛt and Ikātha [sections] are indeed prayers for vital breath (prāṇa).

Having heard the passage beginning with "The vital breaths indeed belong to the possessors of vital breath" (*prāṇā vai prāṇabhṛtām*) concerning the sacrifice of the vital breaths, the mantras beginning with "They all enjoy the season" (*te ṛtum api bhuñjanti viśve*) are recited as related to that.
And their connection is one of mutual requirement (*parasparākāṅkṣā*), since, even though the mantras are fewer than the cups (*graha*), they can be completed through repetition.

This being the prima facie position, [the following is established]: because in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "The Brāhmaṇas who know the past say these are indeed the eldest," those mantras are praised as having the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of great seers (*maharṣi*); and because, within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the fire-piling (*cayana*), one finds only such mantras containing the names of Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, and others among the *prāṇabhṛt* mantras; therefore, even when taking only those [specific mantras], they possess the status of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*).

For this very reason, the praise of those bricks and the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks as being equal in their nature as "breaths" is appropriate in the supplementary injunction to the rule, "Having laid down the *prāṇabhṛts*, he lays down the *saṃdhi*s," namely: "Having piled the *prāṇabhṛts*, he joins the *saṃdhis*.

Furthermore, it must be stated that the denotation of the *prāṇabhṛt* mantras within fifty word-units (*pada*) is either the expressed meaning or the delimiting factor of their capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).
And the definition [of a word] is the nature of the phonemes that constitute the signifier;
for example, in the case of "kaṃsaḥ," it is the letter *k* and the letter *a* alone that are perceived in the word "kaṃsa."

In that case, the cognition of "hell" (*naraka*) arises from the letter *ka* accompanied by an anusvāra contained within the word *naraka*, and the cognition of "residing" (*samāśrita*) arises from the letter *sa* contained within the word *samāśrita*.

Therefore, it is precisely the possession of the letter *ka* with an anusvāra and the letter *sa*—as brought to mind by their respective bases—or the letters *ka* and *sa* themselves, that constitute the denotatum or the delimitors of denotability (*vācyatāvacchedaka*).
Likewise, even in a word such as *Amuṇḍā*, the three phonemes alone—by virtue of [denoting] the bringing of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa—are the denotatum or the delimitors of denotability.
In this way, in words such as *parīkṣita*, when [the meaning] is not exhausted, one should understand the respective caste (*varṇatva*) through expressions such as "born into an unexhausted family.

Since the relations of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*) are not established in these cases, there is no denotation of genus and so forth, nor is there a delimitation by words such as *yat* (relative pronouns), because the relation [of the suffix] is demonstrated.
Nor is there a derivative (*yaugika*) nature, because the word denotes that which is to be determined internally from the meaning of the whole (*piṇḍārtha*).
Nor is there indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because no relation [between the word and its referent] is apprehended.

While indication is appropriate in cases such as the word *durepha* [referring to a bee], since the cognition of the syllable *repha* exists within the word *bhramara*, here indication is not possible due to the absence of any such relation.

Since there would be an infinite number of moments of those [intermediate] cognitions, there would likewise be an infinite number of their arising and perishing; and thus, one must maintain that the ascertainment of the reality of the object occurs through itself alone.
Thus...
Because [otherwise] there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) due to conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

And thus, it is logical that even in the cognition of a jar and so forth, validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), and likewise, the production of a subsequent cognition regarding such objects as river-channels and the like is easily obtained.
Because of its existence;
therefore, it is established that its cognition is by that very cognizer of the knowledge itself.
Others, however, maintain that the self-validity (*svatastva*) of validity consists in a relationship characterized by pervasion between the commencement and the [cognition of] the object.
They say that its object is mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). Furthermore, they do not acknowledge its existence; moreover, cognition is not perceptible.
If it were perceptible, it would be indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*).
[We] go [to refute that].
To exclude perception, [the definition includes] being devoid of a mode (*niṣprakārakatva*), being devoid of a qualificandum (*nirviśeṣyakatva*), and being devoid of a relation (*niḥsaṃsargaka*).
Others, however, [define it as] the "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) residing in that substratum which is produced by the cognition of that [object].
However, since there is no decisive factor (*vinigamaka*) [to choose between them], one might assume that all three are obstructors;
yet even this would not apply to cases involving past or future objects,
due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*).

Nor can it be said that there is no determination of the qualifier when there is a mode of qualified-qualifier relation (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya-prakāratva*), nor that there is no determination of the delimiting mode (*avacchedaka-prakāra*) of the qualifier; for such [determination] exists therein. Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that the effect belongs to what is non-existent, or that the term "effect" is merely metaphorically applied (*upacarita*). This is because [otherwise] duality and so forth would not be established.
Because there is no sublation regarding its production from the day [of creation].

Nor should it be argued that in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceptibility for the conceptualizer (*kalpaka*) of a destroyed duality; for [the rule is] "in the qualificand... [and so forth].
It must be stated that it is a recollection (*smaraṇa*), because a recollection of duality is impossible for one who has not previously experienced it.
[This occurs] either in the manner of "six" or in the manner of "both in one. Such...

Nor should it be argued that "how can there be perception of duality without the perception of its substratum?"—for there is no causal necessity for a certainty regarding the qualifier-delimiting property (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka-prakāra*) in perception.

This is because, by parsimony (*lāghava*), such [certainty] lacks causality with respect to the perception of conjunction; consequently, the occurrence of a non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) of that [conjunction] would be unavoidable.

The cessation of pervasion occurs in the perception of the middle term (*madhyapratyakṣe*), because that [middle term] lacks the status of being a cause; and thus, since there is no necessary state of being an obstructor (*pratibandhakatva*) in this manner, it is more easily stated (*suvacatvāt*) than [the view requiring] conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

Nor is it the case that even in the absence of the perception of the substratum (*āśrayapratyakṣatva*), there is a perception of its gap (*tacchidrasaṃpratyakṣa*); for in the cognition of qualities residing in the self, knowledge itself [functions] through identity (*tādātmyena*) as merit and demerit (*dharmādharma*).
This must be said:
even though air is not perceptible, there is the apprehension of its apertures;
this is due to the conceptualization of a commonality [between them] based on the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and the observation of their similarity.
Since you yourself (as a Naiyāyika) have accepted this,
it is more appropriate to postulate that the obstruction consists precisely in the delimitation by duality and its universal (jāti).
Just as plurality resides in both future and past entities, so too do the experiences such as "I know" regarding objects produced by those respective cognitions possess the form "I am experiencing."
That [cognition] also has as its object a real entity (bhūtapadārtha) that has been manifested.
Nor is duality and so forth something merely removed from the mind;

for since a quality lacks an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), how could there be the production of two manifested things? And thus, because it is established in the object, the cognition is indeed established in that [object].
It should not be said [that this is so].
For when the effect of an action arises through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), identity (*tādātmya*) is inferred [in the following way]: "The jar possesses cognition, because it is cognized.
In that case:

Since it must be stated that a substance possesses the status of being a producer through a relation—namely, the causal relationship of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*)—number, like the object [of cognition], must be a distinct category (*padārthāntara*). Murārimiśra, however, maintains that following the cognition of a jar or the like, there arises the cognition "I know the jar"; since this [cognition] also lacks [an inherent relation] by way of inherence (*samavāya*), an inherent cause is necessary.

Thus, such after-cognitions (*anuvyavasāya*) arise; by means of them, there is the apprehension of validity in the form of having a qualifier (*prakārakatva*), namely: "I know the absence" and "there are two absences," which involve the objectness (*viṣayatā*) of the number two belonging to the particularity (*viśeṣya*) of potness (*ghaṭatva*). So they say.

Some maintain that one knows the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of a preceding cognition through the statement "there are twenty-four qualities," which refers to their residing in qualities such as absence (*abhāva*);

for in reality, since it is accepted that [validity] arises by way of its own essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) immediately after the activity prompted by the knowledge of water and so forth—following the ascertainment of water and so forth—a *samavāya* cause is not necessary.
Thus, one knows the validity in the preceding cognition.
Because of this,
there is no consequence of duality and so forth being characterized as momentary,
due to [their dependence on] relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi).

However, some [hold] that one proceeds toward validity after knowing [their own view], because being a producer does not necessarily entail being a determiner. But when the "apprehension of relation" (*apekṣābuddhi*) is manifested,
since there is the experience of doubt such as "is the cognition that has arisen valid or not?", there is no contingency of its [validity] occurring with necessity.

Nor is it logical that the ascertainment of intrinsic validity occurs merely through the cognition of a quality inherent in the effect; nor can it be argued that [validity] is extrinsic, for since there is no inference of anything other [than the cognition itself], how could there be eternality? Thus it must be said.
In some cases, the established doctrine (siddhānta) is not informative;

however, in other cases, because there is deviation regarding individual instances such as the "red" (*aruṇā*) when they are not treated as a unity, the apprehension of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) does not occur. In some cases, it occurs extrinsically (*parataḥ*); thus, validity is indeed uniform. This is because, due to the absence of favorable reasoning (*anukūla-tarka*), [the opposing argument] lacks probative force (*aprayojakatva*).
Furthermore, in the absence of a substratum (āśraya), the apprehension of an object cannot possess causal efficacy.
Therefore, it must be stated that since there is no doubt regarding the cognition produced by the Veda, what state could there be for [qualities such as] truthfulness and the like?

Upon the destruction of the [cognizing] head and so forth, intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) [is lost]; however, in the case of a cognition produced by something other than that, extrinsic validity (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is known.
Therefore, there is no sublation [of the position] even if objectivity (*viṣayatā*) exists for a mere moment, just as in the case of a jar or similar objects.

Thus, since validity arises precisely from the quality of being rooted in memory-generated cognition, we consider it logical that even in cases such as "the jar is known"—even when the object has perished—the validity is established;

for this is accepted even in the Siddhānta. This is because [validity] exists due to the occurrence of the cognition, and its status as residing in both the past and the future is merely a general direction.
For this very reason, because it is known (*jñātatva*) by virtue of being produced by cognition, the status of the object (*karmatva*) in the expression "I know the jar" is established. Therefore,
objectivity (*viṣayatā*) is something distinct [from the cognition itself].
Furthermore,
regarding the theory of the validity of knowledge (*prāmāṇyavāda*),

concerning all cognitions, it is considered that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) and so forth in the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) only when mental impressions (*saṃskāras*) possess the same object (*samānaviṣayakatva*).
Is both validity and invalidity understood intrinsically? Objectivity is something additional; that itself is "cognizedness" (jñātatā), and knowledge is likewise so.

Alternatively, even if one of the two [truth and falsity] is not determined by its own nature (*svabhāva*), yet the quality of the cause (*kāraṇaguṇa*) is apprehended, then the truth residing therein (*tanniṣṭhaprāmāṇyam*) is also [apprehended]; this is "self-validity" (*svatastva*). Is it rather that falsity is apprehended through defects (*doṣa*) and the cognition [of them], while truth is apprehended intrinsically? [Objection: But in that case, would there not be doubt as to whether "this cognition is true or not"? [Reply: No. Truth would be apprehended either from the cognition of the quality of the cause or from a corroborative cognition (*saṃvādajñāna*). For if the cognition itself is not grasped, there is no cognition of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*); and when it is grasped, [truth] resides in it.

If it is argued that validity is either understood from the cognition of successful purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), or that validity is intrinsic because truth (*pramātva*) is also apprehended [by the same means], we say no. This is not a doubt regarding truth arising from the cognition of a defect in the cause once [the cognition] has been obtained as qualified by the [cognition of] the object; rather, this is merely a doubt regarding the object itself.

"In the object present before one, [the cognition] is sublated by invalidity; thus, following the cognition of silver and the like, there arises the inquiry: 'Does silver-ness exist or not? This refers to the state of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*).

In that regard, because the capacity of all causes toward their own effects is inherent, and because upon recollection the cognition of silver and so forth is sublated, the possibility of doubt regarding it arises.
Some maintain that both cognitions are understood through their own natural force (*svarasa*) alone.
Even when there is knowledge, doubt arises merely from the contact of the sense organ with the object;
this is the view of the proponents of the theory of error (*saṃkāryavāda*).
For in their view, even when the cognition of validity (*prāmāṇyajñāna*) exists, the production of that [doubt] occurs solely due to the suspicion of a defect (*doṣaśaṅkā*).
The collection of effects arises as existent; thus, validity and invalidity, as well as defects and the state of being otherwise than that [validity], [arise] from the cognition of something else.
Therefore, it is not correct to say that [validity] is also intrinsically [established].
For knowledge is not conjoined with its own object; thus, the self-validity (*svatastva*) of validity [is established].

That which is capable of simultaneously cognizing both "as-it-is-ness" (*tathātva*) and "not-as-it-is-ness" (*atathātva*) is a heavy object such as a jar and so forth, and not knowledge itself—since this applies to all cognitions—due to contradiction.

Now, some manifestation of cognition [proves] its own validity by its own nature, because it accepts the threefold nature (tripuṭī) as its object; and since this triad consists of the cognition, the self, and the object, it makes [them] known.
Some [others] say that invalidity [is proven] in this way, yet even so, there is no contradiction in form.
Therefore, it is incorrect for the omniscient one [to have] such after-cognitions (*anuvyavasāya*) as "I know the jar," and so forth;
for if cognition itself were the apprehender independently of any other cause, [the aforementioned would be impossible].

Because the cognition itself apprehends its own status as having a jar or other object as its content, it is impossible to discern what [status] arises within that cognition; therefore, they say that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
Both [the cognition and its object] are unestablished by their own intrinsic nature;

therefore, according to the theory of intrinsic validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*), the validity consisting in the correspondence between the cognition and the reality of the object is ascertained intrinsically (*svataḥ*) alone, and is not to be understood through the cognition of excellences (*guṇa*), the cognition of correspondence (*saṃvāda*), or the cognition of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).

What is being established here is that invalidity—which consists in the non-correspondence with reality—is not apprehended by itself (*svataḥ*), but rather it is apprehended either through the cognition of a defect in the cause or through the direct cognition that "this is not so.
And it has been said:
"For by that [cognition], the notion that 'this is false' is destroyed."
"By that increase in the means of valid cognition, the object is likewise treated in conventional practice;
how could there be any alteration of it once it is established, except through another cognition?
Thus [it is said].
Likewise: "Furthermore, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed self-evident with respect to its own object;
its falsity cannot be apprehended without another means of valid cognition.
For the non-existence of an object is not [established] by the first [cognition] alone, just as its existence is not."

"For if it were already thus, then further cognition would be fruitless because it has already been apprehended; but if it were otherwise, then because it is not established [as such], its status as a means of valid knowledge would have scope.
Thus [it is said].
Likewise, at the commencement of the investigation: "Are the validity and invalidity of cognition intrinsic?
Or is even one of them not clearly determined by its own nature?
Because it depends on something else, one adopts one of the two positions without doubt."

By saying this, he has made it perfectly clear that it is precisely the determination of whether [cognition] is valid or invalid that is investigated as being "self-evident" (*svataḥ*) or "other-dependent" (*parataḥ*).
As for the objection: "But perception and the other means of knowledge are not apprehended as being 'valid';
and without such apprehension, practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is not possible."
"Because [the means of knowledge] is grasped [only] subsequently, it first exists in its own nature.

(Ślokavārttika, Codanāsūtra 82–83). This Vārttika states that perception and the other means of knowledge are not grasped as "this is a means of knowledge" because they are not grasped in the form "I am a means of knowledge. Thus he says.

Now, if validity (*prāmāṇya*) were apprehended at the time of the cognition's arising, then that which does not manifest as valid at its arising would be recognized as invalid; thus, even without a grasper of defects in the cause, invalidity could be determined through elimination (*pariśeṣa*) at the very moment of arising, and so invalidity too would follow as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
Do not speak thus.

For this word "self" (*sva*) is not employed here with reference to validity—meaning that validity shines forth from validity itself—nor is it employed with reference to the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For if it were so, then since validity does not appear in invalid cognitions, invalidity would be established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).
However, the word "itself" (*sva*) refers to cognition; thus, validity appears from cognition itself.
Therefore, even from the knowledge of that [cognition's] validity, validity alone is understood of the self [of the cognition], and thus there is no establishment of invalidity by way of elimination.
Invalidity, however, is recognized only after the fact, in the form of a report regarding the perceived validity.
As it has been said: "Since self-validity is established as the general rule everywhere, it is set aside by the cognition of a subverting factor and by the cognition of a defect in the cause."
"Established" means attained or realized.

"In all cases" means not only in the case of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but in the case of every cognition whatsoever. Likewise: "Even that which is not a means of valid cognition is, by its own nature, like a means of valid cognition with respect to its own object."
Thus it is said.

Nor is this inquiry concerning whether the validity of means of knowledge (*pramāṇas*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*) directed toward the final cognition of those very means of knowledge.

What then? This investigation concerns all those cognitions—such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth"—which are distinct from cognitions of doubt involving multiple mutually exclusive alternatives (e.g., "is this a post or a person? and from cognitions consisting of memory.
"First, let this object of all cognition be examined.
(Ślokavārttika, Codanāsūtra 63; the reading is *pratīkṣyatām*).
Thus the discussion begins.

If one were to investigate by taking only those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as the subject of inquiry, then— since the validity of those which are established as *pramāṇas* by both parties would be proven simply by the fact that they are accepted as such by both—

it would follow that the Veda’s own intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) would not have been established, because its status as a subject of inquiry depends on its validity being established for both parties.
In that case, an investigation into the validity of the Veda would be as futile as examining the teeth of a crow.

However, when intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) and extrinsic invalidity (*parataḥ-aprāmāṇya*) are being established with respect to cognition (*jñāna*) alone, then since the Veda is also a form of cognition, its validity—consisting in its nature as a means of knowledge—would be understood as intrinsic. Furthermore, because there is an absence of factors such as the cognition of defects in the causes [of the Veda], the doctrine of intrinsic validity remains firmly established; thus, this inquiry is purposeful. [Objection: But surely, validity does not consist merely in being a cognition, for otherwise it would follow that even memory (*smṛti*) would possess that same status.
[Reply: True, it is not merely that much.
In this context, we consider only this much: whether [validity] is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

For the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) refers to that which, by virtue of being apprehended and being assisted [by its object], consists in the ascertainment of a real object (*abhūtārtha*). The state of being that is validity (*prāmāṇya*).

And what is its nature? It is a triad combined: (1) the state of being subsequently connected [to memory] as having been apprehended by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*); (2) the existence of the object in that manner; and (3) the capacity of the cognition to produce the ascertainment of that [object]. This triad, taken together, constitutes the validity (*prāmāṇya*) denoted by the terms "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*), "cognition" (*buddhi*), and "word" (*śabda*). In this regard, that state of the object being subsequently connected as having been apprehended is understood through the non-perception of the means of knowledge (*anupalabdhi*), and not from the intrinsic nature of the cognition itself.
For the cognition of a jar does not establish the jar's existence as something previously unapprehended.
Nor is the cognition of that [object] derived from the knowledge of its qualities and so forth;
therefore, in that case, it is neither intrinsic nor extrinsic.

However, in order to refute the suspicion of invalidity—characterized by non-correspondence with reality—which was raised by the phrase "nanu atāttvikaṃ," it is established that validity, characterized precisely by correspondence with reality (*arthataiva*), is intrinsic.
As for the passage stating "the production of validity consisting of ascertainment," that too is not contradictory;
for indeed, that which ascertains the true nature of an object is precisely what produces the ascertainment of that very object.
For that which is a communicator (*jñāpaka*) with respect to the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is itself a producer (*janaka*) with respect to the cognition (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, certainty (*niścaya*) is indeed validity (*prāmāṇya*), because it is the ground for the application of the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).

Thus, the prima facie opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) who maintains that "validity, characterized by correspondence to the object, is ascertained through the cognition of excellence (*guṇajñāna*)" is not inconsistent. As for the statement: "The production of validity consisting of certainty, however, because it is the very nature of the thing, is self-determined (*svavyavasāya*) by virtue of being the effect of the cognition of excellence and corroboration."
If, however, this very point is stated explicitly—that "validity, which consists of certainty, arises intrinsically"—then it must likewise be said that invalidity also arises extrinsically;
otherwise, it would not even constitute its opposite.
[The position is: validity arises intrinsically, while invalidity is understood extrinsically.
Therefore, the meaning of this section is simply that both validity (*prāmāṇya*) and invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) are understood through themselves and through others;
for in this way, the logic of the treatise becomes consistent.

Thus, here is the summary of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final position (*uttarapakṣa*): because a jar and so forth are perceived along with the cognition of the jar, the jar can be ascertained by that [cognition] alone.

Therefore, it is precisely through the observation of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) that one first ascertains the reality of the jar, and thereby determines that the prior cognition of the jar arose from the jar itself.

However, the cognition of purposeful action cannot determine the validity of the prior cognition because its own validity is self-evident (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) due to its non-deviation regarding the purposeful action; it cannot establish the validity of the preceding cognition.
Likewise, corroboration by another cognition is not possible in the absence of the object's reality; thus, the ascertainment of the object's reality follows from that as well.
Likewise, since cognition produced by a cause possessing excellence is necessarily true to the object, its suchness can be determined even through the ascertainment of the excellence of its causes.

Therefore, the determination of the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of knowledge is extrinsic (*parataḥ*) alone, not intrinsic (*svataḥ*). It is not possible to determine its validity—characterized as correspondence with the object—inherently, because that would be inconclusive (*anaikāntikatvāt*). And since there is no validity when the object is undetermined, invalidity itself is the intrinsic nature of knowledge.
Furthermore, the absence of certainty cannot be produced by the cognition of defects, whereas certainty—being a positive entity—can be produced by the cognition of excellences and so forth.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) consisting in the true nature of the object is ascertained solely extrinsically (*parataḥ*).
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that cognition does not determine the object solely through the medium of sublation, but rather intrinsically (*svataḥ*) itself.

For if it were impossible to determine [an object] through itself, then, in that case, there would be a total absence of certainty, and consequently, the entire world would remain in a state of uncertainty.
Indeed, an object not determined by itself cannot be determined through another, because for the other as well, it would be equally impossible to establish.

For just as the cognition of a jar, being observed in relation to a jar that is itself indeterminate, is not itself determinative, so too the cognition of causal efficiency (*arthakriyājñāna*), being observed in relation to a causal efficiency that is itself unreal at the moment of its own existence, cannot determine that [efficiency] either; much less can it determine the jar in that way. Thus, it follows that the entire world would be unknown.

Now, if it is argued that by the cognition of causal efficiency what is meant is not the fetching of water and so forth, but rather the cognition itself which is of the nature of a thread (*sūtra*), and that all such "thread-like" cognitions are intrinsically valid (*svataḥpramāṇa*) with respect to themselves because they are non-deviant; [The opponent continues: ...[the rest of the argument follows].* *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow of the argument up to this point.)*

Even if that were the case, let it be granted for the sake of argument that there is certainty regarding the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); nevertheless, it is still not possible to ascertain the correspondence (*yāthārthya*) of the preceding cognition in that manner.
For even from what is non-correspondent (*ayathārthya*), such as the application of sandalwood paste and so forth in a dream, pleasure may arise.
Furthermore, the ascertainment of the object of the preceding cognition depends upon the causal efficiency whose inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) has been grasped.
For this inference has as its object the cause through the effect;
and it is not possible to grasp a relation when the related member has not been grasped.
Therefore, at the time of grasping the relation, one must necessarily admit that the ascertainment of the jar arises from the cognition of the jar itself.
The same should be said regarding the correspondence between qualities and knowledge.
For indeed, even a quality cannot be ascertained from the knowledge of that quality, much less the validity of the preceding cognition;
the same applies to correspondence as well.

Verification (*saṃvāda*) is indeed another cognition having that same object as its domain. Its distinction from the preceding cognition is that by means of it, the causal basis for the preceding cognition is determined.
Although this determination is produced by the thing itself (*vastu-lāñjanya*), nevertheless, it is produced by cognition alone and not by anything else.

Therefore, validity is established intrinsically (*svataḥ*), while invalidity is determined extrinsically (*parataḥ*) either through the cognition of defects or through the cognition of the sentence itself.
Now, it may be argued that since invalidity is produced by defects, and because those [defects] are non-existent, it cannot be ascertained from them. To this, it is replied:
We do not say that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is produced by defects (*doṣa*) in the form of a destruction of certainty; rather, it consists in the object being otherwise than it appears.
That [invalidity] can indeed be determined through the cognition of defects, because correctness is caused by the absence of defects, and because we observe incorrectness in defective causes.
Since this applies even to the Veda, its validity remains established, unrefuted due to the absence of defects.

How, then, is it understood that falsity is caused by defects (*doṣa*) and not by the absence of excellences (*guṇa*)? For in all cases, falsity is known whether the causes are possessed of excellences or are defective. In that regard, how is this distinction made—that the cause is the defect alone and not the absence of excellence? Therefore, even if the apprehension of non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*) is extrinsic (*parataḥ*), nevertheless, because its apprehension is possible through the mere absence of excellence—and because there is the presence of the excellence of being composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*)—the intrinsic validity (*svarasaprāmāṇya*) must be accepted for the sake of the doctrine of validity.
It is argued that the Veda’s status as a source of knowledge is undermined precisely because it contains statements regarding qualities (guṇa).
To this, it is replied:
a conceptual construction (kalpanā) follows what is actually perceived; it does not arise from things that have not been perceived.
Therefore, it is possible to postulate this in such a way that the intrinsic validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the Veda, which is established by its very nature, is not contradicted.
Consequently, it is not proper to postulate anything contradictory to that.

Thus, although in well-known cases of erroneous cognition (*ayathārthajñāna*), the absence of excellences (*guṇa*) and the presence of defects (*doṣa*) are observed, nevertheless—since validity is seen even in the absence of excellences in the case of the Veda—one must not allow that [intrinsic validity] to be sublated; rather, for cognitions such as that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, it is the defect alone that is postulated as the cause of their being non-correspondent with reality (*ayathārthatva*).

Otherwise, being non-correspondent with reality (*ayathārthatva*) would have to be assumed to be based on being a cognition (*jñānatva*), since cognition is observed in all means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In that case,
just as being non-correspondent with reality is caused by being a cognition because it is observed in perception and so forth,
so too the absence of excellences (*guṇābhāva*)— since it is observed in the Veda to be correspondent with reality— is not the cause of being non-correspondent with reality.

If it is argued that its correspondence with reality (*yathārthatva*) is unestablished, then from what source is the correspondence of perception and the other means of knowledge established? If you say it is "self-evident" (*svataḥ*), then the same applies even when there is a difference [in the object]; otherwise, one would fall into the error of dogmatic attachment (*abhiniveśa*). Therefore, there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for those who perform the *prāyaṇīyā* sacrifice.
However, words that are names of ritual acts do possess the quality of extended application (*atideśa*).
Vi. 7.3.1–2. In the *Prāyaṇīya* sacrifice, the properties pertaining to milk (*payas*) are not to be performed.

Soma says: it is not merely for the purpose of remedying a deficiency in the occasional rite (*naimittika*) itself, but rather for remedying a deficiency in the ritual action (*karman*) when that deficiency serves as the occasion (*nimitta*) for the injunction.

However, Bhavanātha (a follower of Prabhākara) states that they have a single purpose insofar as they are connected with the sacrifice in its general form, rather than by way of being specific *ṛc*-verses and so forth.
As for the meaning of the Sūtra: since in the case of expiations there is a connection with a deficiency that has already arisen, they therefore have a single purpose.

Therefore, there is an option (vikalpa) that the destruction of all defects occurs by means of one [of the two]. For the purpose of rectifying defects.

Bhāṭṭa: Expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) are intended for the removal of faults caused by deficiencies in ritual performance. Among these, even though they serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there is an option (*vikalpa*) between those that are prescribed by their respective texts as multiple independent [remedies] for a single deficiency, just as in the previous case.

For example, in one Vedic recension it is stated: "If the sacrifice should meet with failure through the Sāman, one should offer an oblation into the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra 'suḥ'"; here the oblation is performed by the Adhvaryu priest. In another, however, it says: "If the sacrifice should meet with failure through the Sāman, [one should offer] into the Āhavanīya with 'svaḥ'"; here the oblation is performed by the Brahman priest.
This identity of the sacrifice as being of a single kind necessitates these two distinct expiations for its remedy.

Likewise, when the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are omitted, in some cases the *Pāthikṛtīṣṭi* is prescribed, while in others the *Vaiśvānarī*. In these instances as well, it is understood—both from the force of the required injunction and from the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*)—that their purpose is to remove the mental affliction caused by the omission of the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Therefore, just like the case of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), since at the very time of the injunction for those specific rules one understands that each is a means to the end independently of any other subordinate effect of a single deficiency, an option (*vikalpa*) between them is appropriate here as well.

Nor can it be argued that because the causal capacity is differentiated by distinct species (*vaijātya*), and because intermediate distinctions between *pūrvas* (transcendental potencies) are necessary for the establishment of the respective dharmas, how could there not be a combination (*samuccaya*) as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings?

Even if they are distinct, due to the force of the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) which functions independently, the principle of the order of performance (*prāvṛttika-krama-nyāya*) applies to both of those unseen potencies (*adṛṣṭa*) regarding the expiations (*prāyaścitta*) that produce the destruction of the deficiency of one or the other.

Because, unlike the *prayāja* offerings and others, there is no perception of a combination [of the *japa*] with the subsequent performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*), as is the case with the eleven *uttarīyās* (11.1.5). For, just as the performance-injunction brings about the understanding of the concomitance (*sāhitya*) of all the constituent parts—the *prayājas* and so on—with respect to the single great task known as the assistance to the primary rite, there is no such understanding of concomitance even with respect to the intermediate tasks. If that were the case, it would result in the sublation of the independence established by the injunctions of origin (*utpatti*) and application (*viniyoga*). Therefore, since it is necessary for that [intermediate task] to be defined by the intermediate task as cognized through the sentence of application, an option (*vikalpa*) is appropriate.

Even so, in the present context, there is no lack of justification for independence (*nairāpekṣya*) being defined by those respective intermediate prior states (*pūrva*); furthermore, there is no evidence that it is defined by the destruction of defects (*vaiguṇyadhvaṃsa*). For that [independence], which is postulated for the sake of establishing the determination of properties at a later time—possessing both the nature of being defined by the destruction of defects and independence—is incapable of subverting that [definition].

by abandoning those intervening factors that are permitted, some additional excellence arises.

Therefore, since the first constituent element (*padārtha*) was commenced, that very one must be commenced next. Regarding the statement, "Having performed the Vaiśvadeva, they proceed with the Prājāpatya offerings": at this time, those [offerings] being taken up along with their required procedures (*itikartavyatā*) and joined with one another (because they are taken as the means of performance immediately following the Vaiśvadeva), it is understood that they are to be performed together; thus, the order of sequence is considered. In that regard, there is no fixed rule (*aniyama*) concerning the first constituent element.
It may be commenced starting from any animal whatsoever.

Regarding the second point (the sacrificial substance), however, there arises the doubt: must it be commenced from the very same point from which the first was begun, or is there no fixed rule even in that case?
Since there is no scriptural statement to the contrary, the prima facie view being that there is no restriction, it is replied: the restriction follows from the very commencement itself.
(The first object is determined by the very same sequence in which it was performed; that same sequence is restricted for the subsequent ones as well.
Why is this so? (This is the introductory statement of the question.
The meaning is: how can an activity occurring at a time subsequent to the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*) serve as a regulator of its operation?)
"Because of the commencement of that [principal action]" (this is the subsequent Bhāṣya).

For all constituent elements (*padārtha*) must not be separated from the time of the principal action (*pradhāna*). Indeed, the statement "the constituent elements are to be performed together with the constituent elements" implies that the connection of the purpose (*arthasaṃbandha*) should be understood as mediated in this way.
(How is there a connection with the intervening [passage]? The answer is: For there is the statement "it does not deviate from the time of the primary," which constitutes the justification.

Therefore, the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "the other two [subordinate elements] have a suitable object, for the primary is what is intended to be performed" should be seen immediately after the phrase "the remoteness [of the subordinate] is that which follows."

[Question: How can there be a statement [in the scripture] regarding the principal act together with its constituent elements, given that in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta*), only the principal act is heard? [Answer: The meaning of the word "should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is that it would cause you to hear [the result] through the sacrifice.

In that regard, at the very moment when the agent attains the status of being the performer of the production of heaven, at that same instant the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) also operate.
Therefore, by the word "should sacrifice," the necessity of performing all three—the fruit, the instrument, and the procedure—is expressed simultaneously.
The word is likewise thus: this very triad of garments.

If the past time were to be produced [as the primary], and the instrument (*karaṇa*) and procedure (*itikartavyatā*) were to belong to the future time, then these two would not possess the status of being the instrument and the procedure at all.
(For that which occurs later cannot be the instrument.)
Whether [the object] is yet to be, in the process of being produced, or already produced, this same fault applies to the instrument (*karaṇa*). For an instrument that has perished does not exist.
This same fault also applies when there is a temporal separation between the instrument and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Therefore, the word, the object, and the inference must be simultaneous.

In that case, if the time of the result were known, then its time would determine the delimitation of the instrument and the procedure. However, here the time of heaven is unknown, whereas the times of the instrument and the procedure are known.
By means of their time, the time of the production of heaven is delimited.

Consequently, when the primary acts together with their respective procedures (*itikartavyatā*) are to be performed simultaneously in a single moment, a single agent is incapable of performing multiple primary acts or their procedures all at once; thus, such a temporal separation (*viprakarṣa*) necessarily occurs.
Even when performed with such a separation, the constituent elements (*padārtha*) are nonetheless considered to have been performed together.
In that case, by the rule of proximity (*āsatti*) to the primary acts, the constituent elements—such as the preparation (*saṃskāra*) of the *Āgneya* and other offerings—are obtained.
In that case, proximity (*āsatti*), which might otherwise occur without restriction according to the direct statement (*śruti*) and other means, is excluded.
(The meaning is that the operation of *śruti* and the rest does not apply to the restriction itself, but rather to the nature of the sequence.

He says that in this treatise, the excellent commentary must be explained: "Since separation is inevitable, [the distinction is made between] that which is intended to be performed as the primary act and that which has already been performed as its cause. This establishes the rule: for acts such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), the primary act yet to be performed is the cause; however, for acts such as one's own desire (*svēcchā*), that which has already been performed is the cause.
Therefore, since such a temporal distance is inevitable, some constituent elements are required [by the primary act] as separated by a single moment, some by two substances, and some by many.
This same principle applies here in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) as well, because it is obtained through the *codaka* rule.
From the laying of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) up until the preliminary offering (*upākaraṇa*), that which is common to all [animals] is performed only once.

The preparatory rites (*upākaraṇa*) and others, which are directly contributory (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), must also be performed together with the animals, because they are enjoined as being simultaneous.

What is established? Because the Maitrāvaruṇa is mentioned in connection with the *praiṣa* (direction) and the *anuvacana* (recitation), it is impossible for there to be an intention to express a conjunction (*sāhitya*) of that which is being pointed out by the word itself; furthermore, the word as it is heard expresses mere conjunction (*samuccaya*), and not mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) or a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), because those two are always understood through compound formation (*samāsa*). Nor is the definition of "secondary addition" (*anvācaya*) applicable here, since both [the *praiṣa* and the *anuvacana*] are equal. Thus, it is mere conjunction. The word *prokṣaṇī* would be purely etymological (*yaugika*) when applied to the waters, because of its connection with the meaning—that is, because of its connection with the meanings of its constituent parts. The etymological derivation (*yoga*) is: "that by which one sprinkles" (*prokṣyate ābhiḥ*) is *prokṣaṇī*.
Whatever vessel is used for sprinkling is all designated as *prokṣaṇī*;
therefore, the conclusion is that the word *prokṣaṇī* is etymological (*yaugika*). Why? Because of its connection with the purpose [of sprinkling] (*arthasaṃyoga*). *Prokṣaṇīṣvarthasaṃyogāt*.
Regarding the word *prokṣaṇīḥ* in the injunction "Place the *prokṣaṇī*s," there is a doubt: is it a term for a consecration (*saṃskāra*), based on a genus (*jāti*), or etymological (*yaugika*)?
In this regard, the first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:

because the word *prokṣaṇī* is seen to be used for water that has not undergone consecration—just as in the case of *barhis* (sacrificial grass) or *ājya* (clarified butter)—it must indeed denote a consecration.
Thus is the first position.
That is incorrect;
let it not be employed in every case.
To begin with, it is employed in certain specific regions among those who are unrefined;
as the author of the Bhāṣya has stated: "In some regions there occurs the word *vakāraḥ* [for *vākyaḥ*] in the sense of 'those who are agitated by the sprinkling waters'" (p. 344).
Therefore, according to the principle of the *bahirajyāyanī*, it cannot for that reason be considered a term denoting a ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*).
Nor does it possess an etymological meaning (*yaugikārthatva*).

For the etymological derivation (*yoga*) based on the sense "that by which something is spoken with excellence" (*prakṛṣṭam ucyate anena*) applies equally to clarified butter (*ghṛta*), clay (*mṛd*), and so forth; thus, there is no definitive restriction (*vinigamana*) to the specific class of water.

Furthermore, the comprehension of the etymological meaning arises only after a delay, as it depends upon reflecting upon the meanings of the prefix (*upasarga*), the verbal root (*dhātu*), and the suffix (*pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the conventional usage of a whole depends solely upon the perception of the syllables and does not require a consideration of the constituent parts;
therefore, the conventional usage of the parts is more remote from it than that of the whole. As it has been said: "The conventional usage of the whole is bound by the syllables themselves."
"Because it withdraws the meaning [of the individual parts], the other [meaning] is set aside" (Vākyapadīya 3.4.18, p.
344). Therefore, by the force of the established conventional usage of the whole, just as in the case of *bahir* and *ajya*, it denotes the genus (*jāti*) alone.
This being the case, it is replied:
this would indeed be so if a conventional usage for the whole were already established.

For such a convention is only postulated where usage is observed in accordance with the meanings of the constituent parts, as in the case of the word *aśvakarṇa* when applied to a particular kind of tree.

As it has been said: "When the meanings of the constituent parts are non-existent, that which is employed for another meaning there succeeds as a whole by virtue of having no other recourse" (Vākyapadīya, p. 144).

Therefore, since a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) is not postulated, and since the usage of the word is established solely through the well-known powers of its constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*), the term *prokṣaṇī* is purely etymological (*yaugika*).
[Objection: But surely, because it would apply commonly to clarified butter (*ghṛta*), clay (*mṛd*), and so forth, such an etymology is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*).
[Reply: True.

From the root *vah* preceded by *pra*, the meaning is understood as follows: although only any liquid substance capable of sprinkling (*secanasamartha*) is initially apprehended, it is established that "water alone" (*āpa eva*) is the word-meaning due to the force of the plural number and the feminine gender.
Therefore, it is proven that the word *prokṣaṇī* possesses a derivative (*yaugika*) meaning for the sake of establishing the sentence-meaning of the injunction, "Bring the *prokṣaṇī* waters."

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: In a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), where it is heard that "ghee is the sprinkling" (*ghṛtaṃ prokṣaṇaṃ bhavati*) and the injunction (*praiṣa*) "bring the sprinkling waters" (*prokṣaṇīr āsādaya*)—which is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*)—if the word [prokṣaṇī] denotes a preparatory refinement (*saṃskāra*), then the unmodified form "bring the sprinkling waters" (*prokṣaṇīr āsādaya*) is used.
If, however, it denotes a genus (*jāti*), then by modification (*ūha*), the form "bring the ghee" (*ghṛtam āsādaya*) is used.

But according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because it is etymological (*yaugika*) and thus possesses the gender of its denoted object, and since ghee has a neuter gender, the form "bring the sprinkling" (*prokṣaṇam āsādaya*) is used.

The Sūtra, however, states that the term *prokṣaṇī* is used in its etymological sense because of its connection with the meaning—that is, because of the connection with the meanings of its constituent parts. (Sautrā. 11.4.190). This is the section concerning the *prokṣaṇīs*:

therefore, because these are equal [in status], they fall under the scope of the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*) alone. Among those, the example for time (*kāla*) has already been stated.

And here, although there is no hearing of the word *yaji* (to sacrifice) as there is in the case of the *Atithyā* and other rites, nevertheless, because the relationship between the substance and the deity cannot be established except through the act of sacrificing, these are indeed of the nature of the *Agnihotra* and so forth; thus, they constitute distinct rituals (*karmāntara*).

Regarding the occasion (*nimitta*) as well, such cases as "one should sacrifice with the *Viśvajit* when the *Sannāyya* is spoiled" and "the *Viśvajit* at the *Samyāna*" should be understood from the previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) itself.
In this case, however, there is something yet to be said regarding the fruit (*phala*) and the refinement (*saṃskāra*), and thus they constitute the subject of investigation.
Among these, the illustration of the fruit has already been stated;
by the same logic, that which was stated regarding the refinement should also be understood.
"The *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] belongs to Maitrāvaruṇa," and so forth.
Here, the following prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is intended:
first of all, because the fruit must be established by a well-defined operation, it is not something to be directly enjoined (*anupādeya*).
The preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer and others is likewise merely something to be adopted for the sake of accomplishing the ritual action.
Therefore, because these two are not things to be adopted [as primary objects], there is no difference in the ritual acts (*karma*).
Now, even if these two are things to be adopted, since they are already established [by other means] and thus not objects of prescription, it is the ritual act itself that must be prescribed.

And since that has not been prescribed, it is exactly equal to the Agnihotra and other such rites. Not so; for in the case of the Agnihotra, this is indeed a name [of the rite], and the performance is what is being enjoined by the passage beginning with "he offers."
And because that name is dependent on another, it belongs to the category of the origination of a previous action; thus, it constitutes a different action.

Here, however, since the action of the preceding section is presented through its connection with a material and a deity, that very same action—though not subject to injunction because the fruit is being desired and the means of attainment is already established—is not lost when an action is enjoined upon it; this is the point of distinction.

Similarly, regarding the statement "the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is the *maitrāvaruṇī*," because the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is heard in the injunction "one should sacrifice for a month with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s," and because the name *maitrāvaruṇī* does not end in the suffix *-tva*, it merely brings to mind the previously established *dhātavīyā* as being situated in its place.

Thus, setting aside the *prakaraṇa* (context), by means of the *vākya* (syntactical connection), the previously established *maitrāvaruṇī*—which is a *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite)—is enjoined as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* specifically as a purificatory rite for the sacrificer. (*The word 'kārya' is conjectured as missing.*)

Therefore, by the logic of the "separate context" (*prakaraṇāntara*), since there is no absence of the cognition of taking up what was previously not to be taken up, there is likewise no separate ritual action here as well.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
this would indeed be so, if [the distinction] were like that of place and time.
We maintain that even in the case of the result (*phala*) and the refinement (*saṃskāra*), their non-acceptability (*anupādeyatva*) is established by their very nature.
What then? It depends solely upon the correlative term with which they are syntactically connected. For it is said: "Non-acceptability indeed consists in being for the sake of another."
That [injunction] alone is supreme, established by its own nature, as it possesses place, time, and cause.
However, the fruit and the residual impression (saṃskāra) do not possess the status of being "to be undertaken" (upādeya) for the sake of the action expressed in immediate proximity.
What then? It is the production of the action itself for their sake; therefore, with respect to them, they simply lack the status of being "to be undertaken."
Nor can there be the presentation of a previously understood action through its connection with a substance and a deity;
for it is by way of inference that the connection between a substance and a deity establishes a sacrifice.
