And since it is impossible for the single word *yajati* (to sacrifice) to simultaneously function as the means (*karaṇatva*) both in the presentation of the previous [action] and in the application to the fruit, the action connected with the fruit—whether it be directly heard or inferred—is indeed a different action, just like the *agnihotra*, because of the two factors of being an "unacceptable" [object] and the presence of the word of "taking up" (*upādāna*).
Now, an objection is raised: in the statement "The *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa" (*maitrāvaruṇī dīkṣaṇīyā bhavati*), no verbal root for sacrifice (*yaj*) is heard;

nor can it be inferred through the connection of a material and a deity, because such a connection is absent. Furthermore, since the word *maitrāvaruṇī* does not depend on a finite verb, it cannot—like the *atirātra* and other such terms—be understood as referring back to a previously mentioned rite by virtue of being part of a single syntactical unit (*vākya*). How, then, can this be a separate ritual action? It is replied: [as follows].
This would indeed be the case if a single utterance of the word *maitrāvaruṇa* were capable both of recalling a previous action and of being employed for another purpose.

However, since the employment for another purpose is mandatory here, a distinct action (*karmāntara*)—which does not require the recall of the previous action—is what is enjoined. It has already been stated previously that this applies to cases such as the *Atirātra* sacrifices, where there is a cutting off of the application of the original injunction.

And this is the same as in the case of the statement "the Viśvajit [is performed] on the occasion of the Sāṃsthā," thus it is established that here too the distinction between rituals arises solely from the difference in context (*prakaraṇa*).

The practical application (*prayojana*) is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since [the rites] are prompted by the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there is no separate performance of them, as the two connections with the completion (*apavarga*) themselves constitute the further result.
However, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the properties of the Āgneya [rite] are distinct from the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
In the Siddhānta, the meaning of the Sūtra is that a result mentioned in proximity to no ritual action brings about a distinction between ritual actions.

The meaning of the Tautā [Tautātita] Sūtra is as follows: when heaven or the like is being experienced, the pleasure or satisfaction of the person arises; the desire for that is natural, characterized by its very purpose (arthalakṣaṇā).
"Because the fruit is experienced through pleasure.
[Vi—] "Is the fruit that which is to be enjoined, or not? Since it is distinct from the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), it is like anything else.
The portion consisting of the object of attainment (*bhāgyāṃśa*) cannot be what is enjoined, because one is prompted toward it by natural inclination (*rāga*)."
Bhaṭṭa: Alternatively, this is not intended as a definition;
rather, like the other two [the means and the agent], the result (*phala*) is also something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) because it is a qualification of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).
Even in the case of "one should not kill" (*na hanyāt*), there is no "being enjoined" apart from its being a qualification.

If, however, the injunction of a qualified *bhāvanā* (efficient force) enjoins both the purpose (*artha*) and the state (*tādavasthya*), then the result (*phala*) would likewise not be distinct [from the others].

This being the position reached, since the injunction of a qualified *bhāvanā* necessarily entails an implied injunction of its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), and since such an implication occurs only for those parts where there is no prior attainment (*aprāpti*), and because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for assuming the result—given that it is already attained through natural inclination (*rāga*)—the result is not something to be enjoined (*idheyatva*).

The practical application (*prayojana*) is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the sorcery (*abhicāra*) which is the fruit of the Śyena sacrifice would be subject to the injunction, and thus it would be something to be performed (*piṣṭeyatva*).
In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, because it is prompted by passion (*rāga*), it falls within the scope of the prohibition "one must not kill.

Nor should it be argued that since the word "killing" (*hiṃsā*) denotes an action conducive to death, and since such an action—characterized by having the result of killing an enemy—is prescribed [in this context], how could it possibly be subject to the prohibition?

From the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the injunction "one desiring to perform sorcery (*abhicaran*) should sacrifice," it is understood that the hawk (*śyena*) and the agent are identical. Since the word "sorcery" (*abhicāra*) denotes the act of bringing about death through means difficult to accomplish—such as by incantations—it follows that the hawk itself is the fruit [of the ritual]. Furthermore, because this [act] is necessarily undertaken out of passion (*rāga*), one must understand that the killing of the enemy occurs through the mental state induced by the hawk, and not directly by the hawk itself.

As for what has been stated by someone—that the meaning of the term *abhicāra* (malevolent magic) is simply an action intended for the death of an enemy, and since the patron (*yajamāna*) is the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) therein, he incurs sin even though the act itself is prohibited—this is not tenable, because the Śyena sacrifice itself is the instigating action, and since it is prescribed as such, it is illogical for the patron to incur sin merely by being its performer.

However, where it is heard in scripture that "one who desires to kill an enemy should sacrifice," it should be understood that even in the absence of worldly activity by the agent conducive to the enemy's death, sin arises precisely because of the desire for the cessation of the enemy's life. This is because it is remembered that rites of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) possess the nature of unrighteousness (*asaddharma*). Let it be the same in the present case as well.
And the fruit [of the sacrifice] occurs when there is no connection with a specific ritual action (*akarmasannidhi*).

This is heard in the context of independent injunctions (*anārabhya*): "One desiring splendor should offer [a cake] to Agni at the time of the lower [part of the day]," and "One desiring cattle should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," and so forth.

Regarding this, the author states the final conclusion (siddhānta) in response to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), which holds that a specific fruit is enjoined for the archetypal (prākṛta) rites such as the Āgneya and others.

When not in proximity to an action—that is, when heard in a different context (prakaraṇāntara) apart from the proximity of the archetypal Āgneya and other rites—a stated fruit becomes a differentiator of the action.
For if it were a mere restatement (anuvāda), it would be impossible to enjoin a fruit.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that these are distinct rites from the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Similarly, in the Aśvamedha it is heard: "The Dīkṣaṇīyā [offering] is the Dhaidhātavīyā.
There too, the Dhaidhātavīyā is indeed a separate rite intended for the purpose of purifying the sacrificer.

[The opponent says: "In the view that the *agnihotra* sentence is merely an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), it is only possible for the two sentences, 'He offers in the evening' and 'He offers in the morning,' to be injunctions of an action because they connect with a time that is not [otherwise] to be enjoined (*anupādeya*); however, this is not the case in the view that the *agnihotra* sentence itself is the injunction of the action. For in that case, even though the two sentences 'He offers in the evening' and 'He offers in the morning' connect with a time that is not to be enjoined, they do not enjoin separate actions, because the principle 'And when there is no proximity to an action, [the mention of] a result [indicates a separate action]' is the cause for the distinction between actions."

*Soma*, 4.1.4, p. 64. If [the result] were not something to be undertaken (*anupādeya*), then by the maxim "and when not in proximity to a ritual act, it is fruitless," it would be an injunction for a separate ritual act (*karmāntara-vidhi*) rather than a limit on repetition (*abhyāsa-vadhi*). This is as in the case of "it becomes a *śatokthya*," where there is a hundredfold repetition. 8.3.4. The fruit, moreover, benefits the person, not the ritual act.
For it has been stated: "And the fruit [is the purpose], because it serves the aim of the person" (3.1.16).

And in the Bhāṣya: "But the fruit [belongs] to that [injunction] which has that as its primary object" (4.3.13); thus, it will be explained that when an injunction is connected with the word *kāma* (desire), its purpose is that [fruit]—namely, the purpose of desire.

Or [as stated] at Vārttika 3.4.15, page 946: "But the fruit [of the action] is [conceived] together with the effort," just as in the case of threshing and so forth; this meaning should be applied here according to [Vārttika] 3.1.14.10: "Because there is no denotation of the word [for the fruit], it would [otherwise] occur in separation.
And at 3.1.8.17: "The fruit, place, time, occasion, and the object to be refined—this is the section on non-qualifiers (*anupādeya*)."
Foolish person, page 88. ❀ The fruit is not that which is to be enjoined.
In whatever a person finds pleasure, there arises a desire to obtain it; this is characterized by the object itself, because there is no distinction [between the pleasure and its cause].
4.1.12 (Section 2).

Śā—(With the underlying thought that the discussion of the definition in the *Vicāraśāstra* is not entirely consistent, he states another alternative, even though it was not mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*: ) Or rather, it is considered whether the fruit-portion (*phalāṃśa*) is the injunction (*vidhi*) or the motivator (*prayojaka*).

Since the fruit is a qualifier of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) which is to be enjoined, there arises the doubt that the fruit itself is also something to be enjoined, just like the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth. However, because activity is established through passion (*rāga*), the fruit is not something to be enjoined (*abhidheya*).

The purpose [of the discussion on *soma*] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the result of the *śyena* sacrifice—namely, malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) consisting of violence—is itself that which is enjoined, the prohibition "one shall not kill" does not apply there.
According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, that prohibition does apply. This is the result.
Because it serves the purpose of the fruit;
because it serves the purpose of the fruit;
[therefore] the fruit-cup.
Śaṅkara: "The object is not considered the fruit.
[This is] the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣaḥ).
However, if the reading is "because it has the fruit as its purpose" (phalārthatvāt), then it is the injunction of the ritual action (karman).
"Regarding the fruit, Jaimini holds that it is a subordinate element of the ritual action" (Bhāṣya 3.2.14).
The fruit is the motivator for the *godohana* vessel, not the sacrifice itself.
4|1|2|2 Section 2. Regarding the fruit: that which is declared in the mantra as "bhadra" (auspicious) goes to both the sacrificer and the priest in the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice at the *uparava* holes.
Vi. 3|8|16. As for the fruit, [it consists of] heaven and so forth resulting from acts such as sacrifices.
6|1|2|1–3. The fruit is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and is the primary element.
VI. 4|1|6. For in all cases, that which is being aimed at is the fruit.
Vārttika 4|1|58. The fruit is manifested through the performance of the action;
prior to the performance of the action, the fruit does not exist.
If it were so, action would be purposeless;
yet it occurs at the time when the action has been performed, and it is brought into being by that action,
as in the case of agriculture.

Bhāṣya 1.1.4.20: Since the fruit of the primary action belongs to that very person [who performs it], it follows accordingly; for this has been established here as well in cases such as "He sacrifices with the eleven limbs made of *nyagrodha* wood" and so forth, where the *vyaṅgya* (the modified form) and others apply. Furthermore, in the case where the *phalacamasa* (the fruit-cup) is to be prepared by some three [priests] among those previously mentioned, its purpose has already been fulfilled.

Nor can it be argued that the three [animals] are taken up for the sake of the purpose [of disposal]; having thus raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the author] replies: since the triad, which requires connection with the sacrifice, is necessarily (*nāntarīyaka*) taken up by means of the subsidiaries, there is no requirement for a further act of disposal (*pratipatti*). Consequently, because a compound with the term *pratipatti* is impossible, an intermediate relationship among the three [animals] within the eleventh [section] is established.

Furthermore, as for the implied [meaning], since the taking up of the remnants of the sacrifice is for the sake of the animal sacrifice, it is not possible to determine a general definition for the taking up [of the parts] as being merely for the sake of disposal; for such taking up would result in a mere scattering of materials (*ākīrṇakaraṇa*), and in the absence of a scriptural statement regarding a requirement for disposal, [such a conclusion] cannot stand.

What then? [The text says: "In the middle of the eastern half of the right foreleg," "from the middle of the molasses," and "from the hindquarters of the buttocks. Even though there is only one [injunction], a specific application (*pratipatti*) occurs here due to the distinction between the various persons (*puruṣabheda*). However, when the verbal statement exists, the application occurs exactly according to that statement. Therefore, because of the connection with the location for the consecration of the sacrificial substance (*yāgīyadravyasaṃskāra*), three [locations] are determined.

By those very same specific details, it was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that, because the connection between the drinking and eating [of the *phalacamasa*] would otherwise be inexplicable, the *phalacamasa* must necessarily undergo the same ritual treatment as the *soma*. Therefore, just as the *śara* grass must be conceived as a means for the sacrificial vessel, so too here, on account of the mention of the drinking associated with the sacrificer—namely, "If he [the sacrificer] drinks the *soma*, it is a modification (*vikāra*); likewise here also, the modification of the remnants of the sacrifice (*ijyāśeṣa*) by those not remaining from the sacrifice (*anijyāśeṣa*) would be exhausted"—it follows [as stated in *Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra* 10.1.3–11].

Therefore, even otherwise, since the purificatory act of the sacrificer’s consumption would be useless for the remainder of the fruit manifested by the result, it would be understood as a modification (*vikāra*) of the Soma remaining from the cup-offering (*camasenejyā*), not of that which has already been discarded. Thus, because the ownership of the sacrificial portion is established by that much alone, when the sacrificer’s cup exists, the Soma produced in the primary rite—the sacrifice—is indeed modified; it does not modify the Soma without an intervening act of taking up (*grahaṇa*). This is settled.
It will not be so.
Regarding the phrase "not Soma," since the consumption [of Soma] is established by the context as being occasional (*naimittika*), there is no fault even if a specific Soma is obtained.
And thus, because there is a sublation (*bādha*) by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the exclusion of Soma, this is also logical here.
When the purchase and other consecrations have been performed, that which is to be carried forward must be presented at the feet of the sacrificer.

Similarly, regarding the statement, "If one should not find Soma, one should press Pūtīka plants," some raise the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that, in the absence of Soma, the consumption of the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*)—which serves as a subsidiary means—is prescribed as a substitute for the pressing (*abhiṣava*) that is connected to Soma. However, these words of the *Vārttika* on the prima facie view have not been properly considered; for the very nature of the consecration (*saṃskāra*) is observed in the Pūtīka plants, which establishes their status as the means of sacrifice (*yāgasādhana*).
Furthermore, this position is not tenable even according to the logic of those who hold it, because it is marred by numerous defects. It must be understood through the correct reasoning.

For instance, the injunction "one should not consume" (na bhakṣaṇaṃ kuryāt) sets aside the consumption ending with the fruit-cup (phalacamasa) by means of a modification of the application (*viniyoga*).

Thus, the purpose regarding the Soma is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the consumption even in the sacrificer's cup is not replaced by the fruit-cup because it does not perform the same function, this [sacrifice] should not be performed with Soma.
However, the fruit-cup serves merely for the purpose of consumption.

In the Siddhānta, the word "soma" is not a restatement of what is already established by the sense of the context; rather, since the sentence is intent upon a prohibition, one must sacrifice with the *phalacamas* (fruit-cup) as in other cases.

The Sūtra, however, states that there is a distinction regarding the sacrifice due to the *phalacamas*. Furthermore, because of the prohibition against consuming the prescribed *soma*, there arises the contingency of a "twelve-fold fault" (*aṣṭadoṣa-duṣṭa-vikalpa*). Consequently, there is merely a modification of the *soma* for the sake of the purificatory rite consisting of consumption, which takes the form of eating.
Likewise, the fault of postulating eight defects has also been stated [by the Tautātitas]:
"because it is for that purpose" and "because it is a substance serving as a means for the sacrifice."—
Tautā.

In the context of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), that which is considered merely as a conceptual alternative (*pakṣavikalpa*) must indeed be regarded here as having been made the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by them.

Therefore: "The *phalacamas* [is] a modification of the consumption based on the scriptural statement; it is occasional (*naimittika*) because of its connection with the scriptural statement; the *phalacamas* is a modification of the consumption caused by the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya because of its connection [with them].
Thus [it is stated].
This being the case, it is replied:
"Or rather, there is entitlement to the sacrifice, because the preparatory rite is for that purpose.
This is the intended meaning:

This would indeed be so if the *phalacamasa* were heard of in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), such that [the Adhvaryu] might [be the one who consumes it] if he is a *rājanya*, due to the connection with the act of disposal (*pratipatti*).

For there are two kinds of substances that are "scattered-offerings" (*ākīrṇakara*); thus, one might perform a sacrifice for a Vaiśya. If that [Kṣatriya or Vaiśya] expects the ritual application of *soma*, because its purpose has already been fulfilled—just as one would desire to consume the *soma* juice after it has been used—one should cut down the shoots (*stimī*) of the *nyagrodha* tree, grind them, and mix them with curd to make an offering (*caru*), since they are taken up as an inseparable means for the sake of the ritual purpose—just as one would ask for food for the blind, not *soma*. *Vibhakṣayiṣyet* means "he would wish to consume.
*Nyagrodhānāṃ stimīḥ* refers to the sprouts (or the fruits) of the *nyagrodha* trees.

By this statement, the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) is prescribed for a *rājanya* or a *vaiśya*. (The meaning of the term *phalacamasa* and its ritual application should be consulted in the *Cintāmaṇi* under the entry "Phalacamasa: its nature and its application").

Is this a modification of the consumption (*bhakṣa-vikāra*), or a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyā-vikāra*)? Just as [the consumption] is established for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), is the meaning "the sacrificer who is a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should also consume" that he should consume the fruit-cup (*phala-camasa*)? Or is it a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the established prohibition "one should sacrifice with the fruit-cup"? From where is this seen? In the midst of this doubt—namely, "this is the meaning"—the Sūtra states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
It is occasional (*naimittika*), and there is the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) which establishes its being for the purpose of the sacrifice.

From this indicative mark—that it is prepared by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya—and from the scriptural observation, it is established that the fruit-cup (*phalacamas*) serves the purpose of the sacrifice, just like the Soma. It would be a modification of the act of consuming alone, not of the sacrifice itself.
Because of the expression "he should desire to consume" (*vibhakṣayiṣet*), the fruit-cup is a modification of the sacrifice, not a modification of the consumption.

[The fruit-cup] belongs to the Rājanya and the Vaiśya in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice because of the connection with the scriptural mention of "eating," as in the injunction: "One should offer the fruit-cup as food to him. It is not [the case that] the Soma-cup [belongs to them] because of the connection with the scriptural mention of the word "eating.
[This is so] because if one should officiate for a Rājanya or a Vaiśya, the qualification for the sacrifice [is established], since the purificatory rite is for the sake of that [qualification].

If he should desire to consume Soma, one should strike down the shoots of a *nyagrodha* tree, grind them, mix them with curd, and having strained them, offer that as the Soma-consumption for the blind man. The phrase "fruit-cup" (*phalacamasa*) refers to [cups made from] the *plākṣa*, *āśvattha*, or *audumbara* trees; the word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of excluding the consumption of [actual] Soma. This is the aphorism intended to establish the final conclusion.
*Phalacamasa*: a modification (*vikāra*) of the *soma-camasa*. [Bhāṣya 3.6] A cup (*camasa*) filled with fruits (*phala*) is indeed a modification of the sacrificial offering (*ijyā*).
The fruit-cup (phalacamasa) is for the sake of the sacrifice (yāgārtha); its nature and ritual application are as stated in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa;
it is not merely for the purpose of consumption (bhakṣārtha).

In the *Brāhmaṇa* concerning the purchase and address [of the Soma], it says: "The vessels for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) are made of Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Plakṣa wood, because that is their purpose—that is, because they are for the sake of the sacrifice. Similarly, regarding the Soma-cups, there are fruits; these are seen [in the text] prior to [the section on] him [the Kṣatriya, etc.]. Therefore, the fruit-cup is for the sake of the sacrifice.
(Already) before the purchase of the Soma, the necessary implements are prepared; then, after the *homa*.

They purchase King Soma. For those [priests], when the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, according to the procedure for the King [Soma] itself—that is, by the very path of Soma—up until the day of fasting (*aupavasatha*), the sacrificer’s cup is a cup made of *nyagrodha* fruit and not a cup of Soma.
Previously, they move about among the neighbors, performing acts of honor and the offering of food oblations (*naivedya*).
And this *phalacamas* is enjoined solely for the purpose of sacrifice; however, the consumption [of it] is established by another statement.

Regarding the point that "wherein they should draw up these *camasas* of Soma or of the remnant," this sūtra is stated as a reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) to explain that one should draw up this *yajamāna-camasa*, and that [remnant] therein.

"When they offer other cups (*camasa*), two young *darbha* blades (two firm *darbha* stalks) are obtained; then, having offered [the soma] from this [cup] using a young *darbha* blade, he performs the oblation. Since it is stated that these two [blades] are used for the oblation (in the manner of first throwing one and then the second), the *phalacamasa* is indeed a modification of the sacrifice (*yāga-vikāra*).
[In the middle,] when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, [he offers] the previously [thrown] blade within the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), because it occurs at the same time as the cup-offerings.
This sūtra is intended to state another reason for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the verse, "I have performed [the praise] of Dadhikrāvan" (*prāsvet dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam*).

According to the statement, "When [the cups] have been consecrated with *svāhā*, after the second *vaṣaṭ*-call, they draw up the other cups [from the *camasa* which was placed behind]; then he draws up this *camasa*," [it is shown that] in the case of the *darbha* [cup], the phrase "With the strength of Dadhikrāvan, [he has surpassed] the five peoples" establishes the simultaneity of the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) with the Soma cups.

When, at that point where the drawing of these cups—the *somacamasas* for the purpose of consuming the Soma—is performed, they should likewise bring the *phalacamasa*. They should bring this cup of the sacrificer (*yajamānacamasa*) at the same time as the drawing of those [other cups] has been prescribed. "Drawing" (*unnayana*) means taking [the Soma] from what is situated in another vessel; one should take this [cup] from that [source].

Thus, when the Hotṛ is invited to the cup (*camasa*) containing *iḷā*—the flour of ripe *nyagrodha* fruits mixed with curd—and when he should consume the cup (the Soma-cup), then the drawing [of the liquid] is for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*).
Consequently, the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) is intended solely for the sacrifice (*yāga*).
Therefore, the sacrificer should consume this [fruit-cup] at the same time as that [Soma-cup]; "that which has the same time as another is *tulyakāla*," namely, the fruit-cup.
The state of that [is] the remainder; the *rasa* of the son is that pure drink which Indra drank. Therefore, with a gracious mind, I partake here of this King Soma as his. Thus [he says].
Because of the observation of indicative marks.
This sūtra is stated to provide another reason for the Siddhānta [conclusion]. "May it be auspicious for our heart when drunk; may it extend our life;
may it come to you as food for living"—this is the reference to what has been offered.

In the statement "one should not give the Soma," regarding that Soma intended for the sacrifice, he causes the cup to swell with the two [verses] beginning with "āpyāyasva" and "sametu te," and "saṃ te payāṃsi" and "samyantu vājāḥ," by virtue of their suitability (*ābhirūpya*).

"In that case, they should set down these cups; he should set down this cup belonging to the sacrificer (*yajamāna-camasa*). Wherever they arrange those [other cups], he should arrange this one accordingly. Then he should consume it with the formula: 'O divine Soma, knower of the mind, of thee who art the essence of Narāśaṃsa and who hast been consumed by the Pitṛs, I consume. At the morning pressing, the consumption is for Narāśaṃsa; at the midday pressing, one should substitute 'by the Urvas'; at the third pressing, 'by the Kāṇvas' (the modification must be made). The self-touching is the same; the recitation regarding the cup is the same."
Then Satyāṣāḍha said: "For the two King Physicians (Vaidyarāja), there is no consumption of Soma (8.17.2).

If one who has missed his turn [for the Soma] should desire to drink Soma, he should take the shoots of a Nyagrodha tree that have fallen into a pit, grind them in curd, and having strained them, pour them as an offering into another *am̐sa* vessel. Then, by means of the *Dharmatapana* [offering], he should offer it within the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the formula: 'I am indeed you,' or having set it aside, he offers it with the formula: 'I am indeed you. This concerns the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) as the substitute for the *am̐sa*."

Therefore, the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*), while being set aside from its status as a mere purificatory consumption (*saṃskāra-bhakṣa*), can indeed be enjoined [as follows]: "If it serves some purpose, then you are purified by the act of consuming it, and not otherwise.
And that cup, seeking to be put to use, attains utility for the sacrifice (*yāga*) by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

In that case as well, until it is understood—through the principle of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*)—that being not otherwise employed, it serves the purpose of the ritual preparation for the sacrificer's consumption, it is restricted to being connected with only one repetition of the *yajamāna-camasa* (the sacrificer’s cup).
For its status as the sacrificer’s portion is not untenable even when it is not used in other *camasa*s.
Therefore, the Soma also will be preserved.
Alternatively, this word "eating" (bhakṣaṇa), being recited within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, refers specifically to the consumption of the Soma under discussion.
And since that [act of eating] is praised as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the remnants of the substance used in the sacrifice, it can only serve to consecrate the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) itself.
It cannot now be assumed to have any other purpose.
Furthermore, there is no entitlement for him to any other ritual action beyond what is indicated by the specific word;
moreover, the connection is understood with the consumption of Soma itself, which is introduced within its own sentence by the words "if he should consume the Soma.
Otherwise, the mention of that [consumption] would indeed be purposeless.
Nor is this [interpretation] tenable because of the restatement "not Soma.
If another consumption were enjoined as a remote auxiliary in this very manner, then, due to the absence of a common function, it would not exclude the Soma.
And if that [Soma] were not excluded, there could be no restatement by means of a prohibition.

Furthermore, a mandatory injunction (vidhi) is not tenable, because it would entail the fault of splitting the sentence (vākyabheda) and the postulation of multiple unseen effects (adṛṣṭa). Moreover, the sentence would become incoherent:

if one intended for the Soma to be consecrated through consumption, then one would have to perform the consumption of the fruit-cup as a remote auxiliary (ārādupakāraka), or else one would have to consecrate the fruit-cup itself.

But when this meaning is grasped—namely, "By whatever consumption one would wish to prepare the Soma as it truly is, by that same [consumption] one should prepare the fruit-cup (phalacamasa) in that very manner"—then, by implication (arthāpatti), how could there be a lack of connection with the repeated performance of the sacrificer's cup?
Therefore, it is established that this sentence concerning the sacrifice is a modification of the Soma sacrifice.
"This is the conceptualization of an exclusion" (Bhāṣya).

Just as in the Adhrigu-pratigraha-iṣṭi, where based on the Vedic text "as many horses as one might receive," it was determined and established that "one should cause [another] to receive them," so too, based on the text "he should offer for consumption" (bhakṣaṃ yacchet), it is inferred that "he should offer the means of sacrifice.
By this, passages such as "he should press the pūtika plants" are explained.
This is because of the oblation (homa).

The Commentary states: There is a specific statement regarding the oblation: "When they offer the other cups, then he offers this [fruit-cup] after having struck it with a *dharmataruṇa* [a darbha blade that is somewhat thick, forceful, and a span in length].
Since there is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyāvikāra*), the statement regarding the quality "with a *dharmataruṇa*" is appropriate for the act of offering.
Therefore, for this reason as well, there is a modification of the sacrifice.

Or rather—the injunction regarding the young *darbha* grass is appropriate as a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyāvikāra*) by way of restating the *homa*, because it occurs at the same time as the *camasa* cups. As the Bhāṣya states: "When they follow after the other *camasa* cups, then they draw out this *camasa*."
When there is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyā*), the observation of the pouring out (*unnayana*) is logical, but not when there is a modification of the consumption (*bhakṣa*).
For this reason also, it is a modification of the sacrifice.
Or rather—this syntactic unity (*aikavākyatā*) regarding the means of accomplishing the sacrifice, which was previously in doubt, is possible only if they are equal [in status], and not otherwise.
"And because of the observation of an indicative mark.
The Commentary: For this reason also we see that it is a modification of the sacrifice.
Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark.
What is the indicative mark? It is the restatement of the prohibition of Soma:
"One should offer him the portion, not the Soma.
When there is a modification of the sacrifice, the Soma is not consumed.
Therefore, we see that it is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyā-vikāra*).
Or rather—the indication (*liṅga*) consisting of the restatement of the prohibition of Soma has already been explained.
Śā—[The eating] is connected with the form of the consecration of the substance intended for the sacrifice.
It is established that the *stomaniya* cup is the substance [offered] in the sacrifice.

(Nyagrodhastimīḥ refers to the fruits of the *nyagrodha* tree; the cup [camasa] is prepared with those. Soma: Since in the previous case there was the hearing of the complete sacrificer [yajamāna], even though the term *vaṣaṭkartṛ* (the one who utters *vaṣaṭ*) applies to the sacrificer, here the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) has no connection to the sacrifice because it is not so heard. This is the connection [of the topic] due to consumption (*pratyavasānāt*). In the Sūtra, "due to the connection with direct statement" (*śrutisaṃyogāt*) means that the direct statement is understood from the connection of the fruit-cup with consumption. Vi: "The ball of *nyagrodha* [fruit] is in place of Soma for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya."
One may perform that transformation upon mere food, or likewise even during a Soma sacrifice.
The statement "he shall eat" (bhakṣayet), which begins with "he shall consume" (vibhakṣayiṣyā) and concludes with it,
indicates that the modification refers merely to the act of eating.

Because it is heard in scripture that "one should sacrifice with the cup of fruit," and because there is a modification in the sacrifice consisting of the preparation of the portion for consumption for the sake of the rite.

The section concerning the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) according to the Bhāṭṭa school: In that very context, it is heard in scripture: "If one should cause a Rājanya or a Vaiśya to sacrifice, and if he should desire to consume Soma, one should fetch Nyagrodha-stimbinī fruits, grind them, mix them with curds, and offer that as his consumption, not the Soma.
In this passage, the second occurrence of the word *yadi* has an unambiguous tone.
The word *āya*, however, refers exclusively to being the occasion (*nimittatva*).

Regarding the shoots and fruits [of the *stimi* plant], there arises a deliberation as to whether the term "fruit-cup" (*phalacamasa*) denotes merely the act of eating or whether it also denotes the sacrifice itself. In this regard, since it is logically impossible for the sacrifice—which is required as the occasion—to be connected with the fruit-cup, [the term must denote the eating].

Furthermore, since that [substance] referred to by the word "that" (tat) is heard as being connected with eating (*bhakṣa*), and because there would result a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) if one were to enjoin multiple subordinate qualities such as grinding and so forth by way of restating an already established sacrifice, a distinct act of eating itself—characterized by multiple qualities and having the *phalacamasa* as its instrument—is what is enjoined.

This is because, in the absence of a specific application (*viniyoga*) for the *phalacamasa*, it is impossible for it to undergo purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*); thus, by the principle of "satkṛtāya," a modification of the application is necessary.

Even that [prohibition], though it is a remote auxiliary (ārādupakāraka), applies to the person who consumes the Soma of the sacrificer, by virtue of the restatement (anuvāda) "not Soma"; for, as in the case of "one should not say 'gira-giri'," even in the absence of performing the same function, the principle of substitution (sthānāpatti) is understood as being of the nature of a prohibition. Or, let this prohibition stand as independent. This being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): although this is a different consumption, nevertheless it does not have the status of a remote auxiliary, because the accusative case-ending in the word "tam" indicates that it is for the purpose of consecrating (saṃskāra) the fruit-cup (phalacamas).

Even though there is no formal consecration (*saṃskāra*) for that which has not been employed, a functional application (*viniyoga*) may be postulated, as in the case of the injunction "he chooses the *adhvaryu* priest. Furthermore, since passages such as "if he should consume the *soma*" are merely restatements (*anuvāda*), and because the consumption of *soma* by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is already established by that much alone, there is no evidence to justify assuming that the fruit-cup (*phalacamas*) serves all purposes through the act of consuming *soma* in every instance. Therefore, it is simply postulated that the fruit-cup is the means for the preparation of the sacrificer’s cup; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
In reality, however, since there is no evidence for it being a separate act of consumption, the consumption of Soma itself is performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
It is enjoined as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *phalacamasa* cup, characterized by two subsequent stages: the grinding [of grains] and the wiping with curd.
There is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) here, because the injunction "The King [should sacrifice] with the Rājasūya" prescribes the performance of the ritual as a whole.

And since that [fruit-cup] serves the purpose of purifying the substance used in the repetition of the sacrificer’s cup and purifying it for consumption, the status of the fruit-cup as the means for the repetition of the sacrifice mentioned [in the text] is established by the previously cited inferred statement regarding its connection with the sacrificer.
Furthermore, because it is contingent (*naimittika*), it sublates the permanent *ūm* [syllable] in that context.

Thus, by the very principle of *sthānāpatti* (substitution based on position), since the consumption by the sacrificer (*yajamāna-bhakṣa*) can be obtained for the *phalacamasa* just like the other Soma-consecrations (*saṃskāra*), it should be understood that the injunction of the *phalacamasa* serves two purposes: first, to establish its status as the means of the sacrifice (*yāga-sādhanatva*) through the force of the prior application (*pūrvapravṛtti*), and second, to enjoin two specific qualities.

By this, the fact that even the *pūtīka* plants—associated with the pressing (*abhiṣava*) in the rule "If one does not find Soma, one should press *pūtīkas*"—serve as the means of the sacrifice is also explained.
Maṇḍana [says]: "There should be eating and so forth of the fruit."
Śaṅkara: "In the sacrifice, the *stoma* is the *camasa*.
In the section concerning the *phalacamasa*, there is an extension by way of position (*sthānāpatti*).
It has been explained [in the *Bālakrīḍā*, p.
118]: "In cases where there is the possibility of enjoining a different sacrifice, such as the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*), another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is also required."

In that case, even in the absence of the removal of a permanent [rule], there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the permanent by the occasional (*naimittika*) rule, because the latter has no other scope (*niravakāśa*).
*Bhāṭṭadīpikā* 6.1.1, p.

287. The *phalacamasanyāya*: (3.6.19.47–59). Regarding the *āgneya* oblation, since the status of being "cooked" (*śrapaṇa*) and so forth is occasioned by the cooking associated with the occasional [element], it is equal to the occasional; thus, by the principle of the *phalacamasa*, the curd (*dadhi*) and the *śruti* [milk] [are substituted] precisely through the principle of taking the place (*sthānāpatti*).
It is the attainment of the sublime Dharma,
and not according to the analogy of rice and barley.
The injunction regarding the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*).
This is a specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhi*) with a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).
Bāla., p. 21.

As a result: an explicit restricted option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) is, for example, in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice regarding the *Saubhara* chant: "One desiring rain should perform it with the syllable *hīṃ*; one desiring food with *ūrg*; one desiring heaven with *ū*. (Bāla. p. 160). As a result: an explicit restriction (*vyavasthā*) is, for example, "One desiring stability should lead [the water] with a vessel made of *muṇḍa* wood; one desiring Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) with a vessel of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*). However, in the Smṛti tradition, the injunction to study the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas is for the sake of a specific result, namely Vedic splendor itself.

Page 19, as a result: An established prohibition is, for example, as follows: "Whoever should threaten a Brāhmaṇa, him one should punish with a hundred [fines]; whoever should strike him, with a thousand; whoever should shed his blood, for as many years as he might gather grains of dust, for that many years he shall not know the world of heaven. Therefore, one should not threaten a Brāhmaṇa, nor strike him, nor shed his blood."

Page 35: An example of a *vyavasthita-vikalpa* (restricted option) by way of its result (*phalataḥ*) is as follows: In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the *saubhara* chant is prescribed as a permanent (*nitya*) means for the *stotra* of the *ukthya* [sacrifice], according to the rule: "The *saubhara* becomes the *brahmasāman* of the *ukthya*-associated chants. However, in the *atirātra* form of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there is the rule: "If the *atirātra* has the *Bṛhat-sāman*, then the *saubhara* should be made the *brahmasāman* of the *ukthya*-associated chants. Thus, by way of the result, the status of being the *brahmasāman* is merely occasional (*naimittika*).
[This concludes] the section on the fruit and the deity (*phaladevatādhikaraṇa*).

Although it was stated that "if one who has the Rathantara-sāman as his chant should perform the Saubhara," this prescribes an occasional (naimittika) rite; subsequently, both the obligatory (nitya) and the occasional Saubhara are prescribed again as means for attaining three results: "He who desires rain, he who desires food, and he who desires heaven—let him praise with the Saubhara."

Regarding the *saubhara* chant belonging to various Vedic branches, when an indefinite option (*avyavasthitavikalpa*) regarding its *nidhana* (concluding syllable) would otherwise arise, it is stated: "One should employ 'hīp' as the *nidhana* for one desiring rain; 'ūrji' for one desiring food; and 'ū' for one desiring heaven. Because these specific *nidhanas* of the *saubhara* are thus enjoined according to the respective occasion, there is a "regulated option" (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) in terms of the results. (Page 160). This is the section concerning the fruit and the deity (*phaladevatādhikaraṇa*).

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the ritual duties (*dharmas*) are prompted by the fruit [of the sacrifice]. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that those [duties] which are connected with the fruit and the deity—as stated in *‘phaladevatāyojya’* (9.1.3.4)—do not apply to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result). (Duṣ. 9.1.2.4)

"The deities associated with the fruit" (*phaladevatāyojya*) must be performed; thus, that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is the primary object (*upapūrva*). Alternatively, it is the very state of being (*bhāva*), by virtue of its being both that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) and that which is to be executed (*anuṣṭheya*), that is expressed by the suffix. (An objection is raised: If it is argued that because it falls within the category of the "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*), the fruit such as heaven (*svarga*) must be what is to be performed (*kartavya*). [The response: No, because since that fruit occurs at a later time, it cannot be co-present with the performance (*prayoga*); rather, it is precisely the means for achieving that fruit which is determined to be what is to be performed.
"Therefore, having performed [the rite] for the first time, it is not otherwise.

And likewise, after introducing the point that "the fruit and the deity are to be joined," it will be refuted (the construction being: "after introducing [the view] that 'the fruit and the deity are to be joined,' it will be refuted";
see *Sudhā*, p. 1256).
[The fruit and the deity are to be connected].

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the scriptural injunction regarding the connection with the fruit is: “O Agni, lead us to heaven; become light. This is the *dharma* [injunction] concerning the fruit.
Likewise, there is a connection with a deity in such [mantras] as: "I shall follow the winning of Agni; I shall follow the winning of Soma.

In this regard, when considering whether these mantras are prompted by the fruit (the result) and the deity—namely, by the fruit such as heaven and by the deity such as Agni and others—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated: the fruit and the deity would be the motivators for the employment of the mantra.

And likewise, in the *Saurya* sacrifice and others, because of the absence of both the fruit of heaven and the deity in the form of Agni, there is an absence of a motivating factor; thus, when the mantra is excluded, modification (*ūha*) is not possible.
"For such a quality [is established] from the injunction" (*codanāto hi tādṛgguṇyam*).
This is the sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, let the mantra "May we attain the light of heaven through Agni" (agnisvāhā saṃ jyotirbhūma), which is prompted by the fruit of heaven, and the mantra "May I attain the victory of Agni," etc., be set aside by the context of Agni and the other deities.
However, *liṅga* (indicative power) is stronger than that; therefore, it is not proper for it to be set aside by them.
Therefore, just as the restriction of speech is for the sake of the *jyotiṣṭoma* initiation (*dīkṣaṇīyā*), so too is the mantra.

Alternatively, this mantra reveals the fires by its own inherent capacity (the reading "by its own capacity" [*svāsāmarthyena*] is found in the *Tantraratna*, whereas there the reading is indeed in the ablative case).
In that regard, whichever fire it may be, each one is to be revealed through that specific capacity.

Thus, considering the sublation of the context (*prakaraṇabādha*) by means of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), he formulates the prima facie view (the reading is *ārabhate*, though in the *Tantraratna* the reading is simply *karoti*): "But the reply is like that of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*);
for such a quality does not arise from the injunction (*codanā*)."
Commentary: This [action] is prompted by the desire for heaven and so forth. From the injunction (*codanā*), there would be such a quality [of being effective].
That which is an injunction possessing a fruit is connected with the "how-to" (*itikartavyatā*).
And the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) possesses a fruit, whereas heaven, fire, and so forth do not.

Otherwise, even though such a statement exists, one would have to assume an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Furthermore, if the statement regarding the *apūrva*, the fruit, and the deity were taken literally, it would result in a violation of the metrical requirements (*chandaḥ*).
When this alternative view is observed, it is not logical to postulate an *apūrva* (unseen potency) for the mention of heaven, fire, and so forth;
for since the word-meaning itself is accepted as being the fruit and the deity, there is no need for indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of an unseen result.
Therefore, a duty (*dharma*) of this kind is indeed prompted by the *apūrva*.
What is the purpose of this deliberation? According to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the mantra should be employed without modification in the *saurya* rite.

However, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it should be used with modification (*ūha*), as in: "May the splendor of sacred knowledge [be mine] at the front; may Sūrya win the victory" (*sūryo 'jjiṃ srāham ujjitim*).
This is the final result.
In this regard, the consideration concerning the deity must be carried out.

Śabara says: "In that case, the two mantras would have heaven and so forth as their purpose on account of the indicative mark (liṅga), because the fruit is of an unseen nature and because [the deity] is in every respect subordinate."

Since it is possible for the Agni and other [deities] being mentioned to be the bestowers of the fruit, it is logical that the mantra subserves them alone, and not that it is a subsidiary to the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). (He states the final conclusion:
It is true that the fruit is primary over everything, but not for that reason alone.
The mantra should be subsidiary to that [form], because otherwise there would be the consequence of meaninglessness.

Soma: Just as in the previous case, the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyama*) serves the purpose of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* apūrva for the sake of the supreme apūrva (*paramāpūrva*), and not the supreme apūrva itself; likewise, the objection arises that the mantra also serves the purpose of Agni and others, and not the purpose of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices by way of them. Vi: "Is Agni and the rest the cause of heaven and the gods, or is it that which is enjoined here?"
"But [it is determined] by indicative mark (*liṅga*); do not say so, because it is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the *apūrva*.

Bhaṭṭa: This section (*adhikaraṇa*) is for the purpose of raising an objection to and then resolving the issue of the "objecthood" (*uddeśyatā*)—previously mentioned as being by virtue of connection with the *apūrva*—in certain cases.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is a mantra that expresses heaven (*svarga*): "O Agni, through this [sacrifice], may we go from this world to the heavenly world (*suvar*)."
Furthermore, mantras such as “*agnerahamujjitimanujjeṣam*” (‘May I win the victory of Agni... are heard which reveal Agni and other deities.

And since these two [mantras] are connected to heaven and so forth, when there is a scriptural statement (*liṅga*) regarding their application, they are to be understood as the objects of reference (*uddeśya*) because of their immediate presence; for it has been established that the rule of application (*viniyoga*) is generally directed toward the primary meaning itself, and not toward a connection with the *apūrva*, since the words ‘heaven’ and so on do not denote [the sacrifice] in that form [as the *apūrva*].

Nor is there futility regarding [the fruit] in the form of heaven and so forth; for since that [fruit] is the direct result itself, there is no pointlessness in its being for that purpose, as there is no distinction in its being an uncertain means. Since the production [of the apūrva] is established by the primary act alone when conjoined with other subsidiaries—apart from the manifestation through the recitation of mantras—the charge of futility applies equally even to the *apūrva*. This is because the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*) brings about the necessity of the concomitance of all subsidiaries, and thus the *apūrva* is not produced apart from the recitation of mantras and the like.

This point, however, applies equally even in the case of heaven (*svarga*). Likewise, regarding the deity as well, although there is an *apūrva* (unseen potency), the production of the fruit results solely from the grace of the deity generated by that *apūrva*, because there is no evidence for the production of such grace apart from the recitation and manifestation of the mantra. Therefore, it serves that purpose. For this very reason, since the application injunctions based on indicative power (*liṅga*) and direct statement (*śruti*) have [the deity] present, the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatā*) belongs to those very entities which are the substrata of the grace, and not to the deity as something characterized by the *apūrva*. Consequently, there is no fault—such as the lack of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)—in rites like the *saurya* sacrifice.

This being the position reached, it cannot first be suspected that threshing and other such acts—which are [ordinarily] for the sake of the *apūrva*—abandon their status as means to the *apūrva* and instead serve the purpose of attaining heaven (*svarga*). This is because, through the word "rice-grains" (*vrīhi*) and so forth, by virtue of their immediate proximity, these acts are indicated (by implication) as being the means for producing the *utpatty-apūrva* of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices, according to the principle of the "locus" (*adhikaraṇa-nyāya*). Likewise, one must reject the view that threshing and other acts are for the purpose of propitiating a deity by accepting the *apūrva*;
for the grace of a deity is not the primary goal, since it is produced by the *apūrva*.
Even in the case of the mantra cited, there is a connection between the mantra for heaven and its purpose of attaining heaven.

For, does the illumination produced by the mantra serve only for the specific instance of heaven generated by the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, or for another instance of heaven? It cannot be the former; otherwise, because it would not be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Darśapūrṇamāsa for that specific purpose, and because there is no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish a general relationship, the indicative power (*liṅga*) could not even lead to the assumption of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Thus, there would be no proof for its being for the sake of heaven.

Furthermore, the qualification for heaven (*svarga*) alone is not the authority that establishes the general connection, because since heaven has its requirement satisfied by being the object of the sacrifice as its instrument, it cannot bring about the qualification [for the mantra].

Nor can the *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) be inferred through the indicative power (*liṅga*) based solely on the mantra’s requirement for a purpose, because the mantra’s requirement is already satisfied by its application (*viniyoga*) within the *vācastoma*.
For this very reason, there is no assumption of a scriptural text (*śruti*) even on the basis of a mere indicative mark (*liṅga*).
This is because, even though Devadatta is capable of cooking, we do not observe his application [to that task] in the absence of a requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*).
Not the first [alternative].

For if that were the case, individual instances of heaven produced by the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices would not have "heavenness" (*svargatva*) as their objective (*uddeśyatā*), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor could they be so designated by way of being "heaven produced by the Darśapūrṇamāsa," because that is unnecessarily cumbersome (*gurubhūta*) due to its being mediated by the unseen potency (*apūrva*).
Rather, they are designated solely by virtue of their connection with a specific type of *apūrva*.

For this very reason, even though it is an auxiliary that assists through direct contact (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), because it is not produced by heaven, it is indeed the *apūrva* (transcendental result), and not an intermediate *apūrva* included within the scope of the defining characteristic of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). However, the property of "heaven-ness" (*svargatva*) enters [into the definition] just like "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*) and so forth.

Consequently, based on the indicative power of the mantra (*mantraliṅga*), the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is: "By means of this mantra, one should effect the connection with that which is to be accomplished by the supreme *apūrva*, through the mediation of the cognition produced by its expressive power."

Furthermore, the cognition produced by the expressive power (*śakti*) is, in reality, characterized by having "heaven" (*svarga*) as its qualifier and "heaven" as its qualificand; it enters [the definition] precisely as a cognition produced by the expressive power, and not as one characterized by a relation to the *apūrva*. For if it were so, the status of being produced by the expressive power would be untenable.

Precisely for this reason, in cases such as [the attainment of] "Vedic splendor" (*brahmavarcasa*), since there is no intermediate result (*dvāra*), the term "heaven" is omitted; thus, the substitution (*ūha*) of the word "Vedic splendor" is made in order to establish a cognition produced by the expressive power that has "Vedic splendor" as its object.

In this context, since the word *svarga* (heaven) functions through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its being the subject under discussion, it generates a cognition characterized by the relation to the *apūrva* (unseen potency). Consequently, it is logically consistent for *brahmavarcasa* (Vedic luster) to be understood through that very same form; thus, there is no logical inconsistency in the modification (*ūha*).

For this very reason, even when the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are performed for the sake of a son or other such goals, there is an omission of the mantra, because in those cases it is logically consistent [to use the word *svarga*] since the fruit to be accomplished by the *apūrva* is understood as being "heaven."

For this very reason, it is established that "the application of mantras is indeed to their primary meaning. Furthermore, because the *apūrva* (transcendental result) to be accomplished is known through the cognition produced by the mantra's power (*śakti*), its status as the object of refinement (*saṃskāryatva*)—which is synonymous with being the objective referent (*uddeśyatva*)—is not untenable. And such a cognition, by way of generating faith produced by itself, serves the purpose of the final fruit (*phala*) by producing a fitness conducive to the arising of that fruit within the supreme *apūrva*; however, it does not directly produce the fruit itself. For if it were so, there would be a loss of the distinction between principal and subordinate, resulting in the subversion of the ritual context (*prakaraṇa*).

Such is the detailed explanation for other [mantras] as well. Even though they manifest other [deities] and so forth, since it is useless for them to manifest an independent intention, and because there is no evidence to establish a general connection, it is—as in the previous case—impossible to assume such an intention. Therefore, one must necessarily assume that their purpose is solely to manifest the connection with Āgneya. Furthermore, since there would be a lack of purpose regarding the essential nature of Āgneya itself, and because of its proximity, it is assumed that the other deities (anyādi) are intended specifically as deities belonging to the sacrifice immediately following that [Āgneya].

But it is not by virtue of being the locus of *prasāda* (divine grace), because since *prasāda* is produced by a supreme *apūrva* (unseen merit), it is remote; therefore, it cannot logically function as the motivator (*prayojaka*).
For this very reason, that which is merely the locus (*āśrita*) does not enter into the scope of the defining condition (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*).

And thus, even if one assumes that being the locus of *prasāda* (divine grace) is the delimiting factor (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) for the object of the injunction, the modification (*ūha*) is established—specifically, of the *apūrva* alone. However, being the locus of *prasāda* in general cannot be the delimiting factor for the object of the injunction, because this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of the *Āgneya* sacrifice and others; for the nature of its deity (*devatātva*) is simpler than being the locus of the *prasāda* produced by the *Āgneya-apūrva*.

Therefore, here too, one should effect the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the deity associated with the *utpattyapūrva* (the transcendental result of origination) of the Āgneya sacrifice by means of the cognition produced by this mantra; having thus postulated a scriptural injunction (*śruti*) based on the indicative power (*liṅga*), the establishment of the *ūha* (modification) as previously stated should be justified.

Furthermore, the utility [of the mantras] in the *nirvāpa* and other mantras lies solely in producing the fitness for the sacrifice conducive to the *utpattyapūrva*, by way of quickly recalling the deity at the time of renunciation (*tyāga*) through the awakening of memory; the details of this are elsewhere.
Maṇḍana says: "For the performer does not indeed mix heaven with the deity."
(Dharmasva) 4. Śaṅkara states: "The apūrva has been declared to be the cause.
This is understood from the section concerning sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites being prompted by the *apūrva*, as established in the *Phaladevatādhikaraṇa* (Soma. 9.1.5).

Even mantras such as "Agnim īḷe" (I praise Agni), which are named for the purpose of encouragement (*protsāhanārtha*), serve to generate faith; since even that which is to be performed requires a clear manifestation of the fruit inherent in the ritual action, their function is established through a visible means (*dṛṣṭavidhayā*) for that very purpose. This was demonstrated in the *Bhāṣya* on the ninth book, in the section concerning the fruit and the deity (*phaladevatādhikaraṇa*). (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 1.2.42). Regarding the two types of mantras that reveal the fruit and the deity, they are prompted by the *apūrva*. Examples include the collection of fruits, the deities, and the performers.

The fruit is heaven; the rule is lifelong sitting [in austerity]; the agent is one who desires heaven; the composite whole is the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices. These do not apply to the Saurya and other such rites. (8.1.13.20–22). See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 250, under the entry "atideśo na phalanīyam... (transference does not apply to the fruit, etc.).

The maxim that "when it is possible for [a statement] to have a fruit as its purpose, it cannot have praise as its purpose" would, if applied here, lead to the consequence that even in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, the statement regarding their being the means of performing the ritual (*dharmakaraṇa*) would have to be taken as having a fruit as its purpose.
(In the prima facie view.
[This is the] Ornament.

Substances, purificatory acts, and preparatory rites do not possess a connection to a fruit; in that regard, the mention of a fruit is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). [PMS 4.3.11] The time for the production of the fruit is not non-existent.
[Vārttika 2.2.13, p. 483; Su. p. 733] The maxim: "Only those who partake of the fruit possess the status of being the primary agent."
*Parimala* on *Brahmasūtra* 3.1.13.44: The Section on the Abundance of Fruit. The subsidiary rites (*aṅga*), such as the *prayāja* offerings, are to be performed only once in a single performance.
"Or rather, by means of inference based on analogy with the seasons, there would be an abundance of results through repetition.
Commentary: Taking the *prayāja* offerings and others as examples, this is considered:
should these be performed only once, or should they also be performed repeatedly even though such repetition is not explicitly stated?

In this regard, although a single performance would seem to follow from the principle stated as, "In the case of a mere ritual act, there may be another [performance] for the sake of one's own desire for the view" (1.1.16.28), it is said: "Or rather, like a seasonal sacrifice, through inference there would be an abundance of fruit in repetition.
Repetition should be performed.
Why? Because there would be an abundance of fruit in repetition.

How is this known? By means of inference. What is that inference? Prior to the application of the subsidiary (*aṅga*), there was no assistance to the primary (*pradhāna*); subsequently, it arises. From this, it is understood that it is certainly produced by the subsidiary. If it is produced, then it will be produced again and again.

It is like the seasonal sacrifices; for example, in rites such as the *saurya* and others, the fruit is produced by the ritual act, so that through the repetition of the act there is an abundance of fruit. It is the same here as well.
Or rather, it should be performed only once, because the cause is one.
The Commentary states: "Or rather, the auxiliary (*aṅga*) should be employed only once, not through repetition."
Why? Because of the unity of the cause.
The single cause of the subsidiaries is their assistance to the principal act.
What, then, is this? It is that by which the principal acts yield their fruit.

If one knows that the auxiliary (aṅga) has been performed once and thus the primary acts (pradhāna) will be fruitful, then there is no need for repeated performance. But if it is not known [to have been performed], then performance is all the more necessary. For what hope is there that what did not benefit when performed once will benefit when performed again?
And there would be no restriction on the quantity.

The Commentary states: If there were no restriction such that the performance could be done once or repeatedly, then this statement regarding the fixed number of oblations as if it were permanent—namely, "Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day, thirteen on the new moon day"—would not exist.
That [number] would have to be assumed by you to be merely occasional (*pādhika*), and in doing so, its essential nature (*rūpa*) would be sublated.
Therefore, there is no repetition.

Because the fruit arises from the completion [of the action], there would be a difference in the fruits in the case of sacrifices (ṛtus). Commentary: As for the argument that it is "like the sacrifices," it is indeed appropriate that there should be repetition in the case of sacrifices.
Because of the commencement and completion of the fruit. Through the undertaking of an action, the fruit is produced therein;
through another undertaking, another [fruit] is produced.

Furthermore, the result of the auxiliary acts (*aṅga*), whose measure has already been stated, is the accomplishment of the primary acts' possession of fruit. If that [accomplishment] is achieved by performing [the auxiliaries] once, there is no further performance required.
Thus is the reason refuted.
Therefore, there is the introduction [of the example] (in the case of repetition).

However, repetition would be purposeless because the object is unitary; just as eating is not repeated because the object [of satiety] is unlimited, so too, since the primary act is for the sake of the ritual action, there would be no fixed rule [for repetition].

Commentary: Regarding what was stated—that because the purpose is accomplished by the limb being performed once, repetition is useless—here we reply: the repetition of the limb is indeed for the sake of the purpose; repetition is not purposeless. How so? Repetition would be purposeless only if there were oneness [of the act].
If one were to perform even a single object of action repeatedly, then that repetition would be purposeless;
just as eating at a single time, though repeated, produces only the single result of satiety and is not further practiced.
However, in this case, the objects [of meditation] are infinite in number.
It is not known that "this [pradhāna] performs such a benefit";
for surely, it is understood that it acts only to the extent that the pradhāna becomes possessed of a fruit.
This is true.
But because the subsidiary is for the sake of the primary action, there would be no fixed rule;
the subsidiary exists for the sake of the performance of the result of the primary,
whereas the primary is directed toward the ultimate fruit.
When the auxiliary assistance to that [primary factor] is greater, the result will be greater;
when it is lesser, it will be lesser.
Furthermore, through repeated practice, the assistance becomes immeasurable and increasingly great, because it is something produced as an effect.

Therefore, there would be no fixed rule as to whether the performance occurs once or through repetition. Because of the distinctness [of the acts], the measure [of the result] would be established. Commentary: As for the objection that it contradicts the number of oblations (*āhuti*), since the benefit is distinct, repetition is logically established; thus, this reference to the number of oblations would be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already prescribed. With respect to the injunctions regarding oblations, it is said: "There are fourteen oblation-injunctions on the full moon day; thirteen on the new moon day."
Regarding the phrase "in the axe," the number [five] would not be applicable to the oblations themselves;
rather, it is only through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) that the number qualified by the oblations becomes appropriate.

Or rather, there should be no repetition because the injunction for performance is a single unit, and because the fruit of the ritual action belongs to the whole [branch] simultaneously, since it exists for the sake of the action.
Commentary: Or rather, there is no repetition of the mantras.
Why? Because the injunction for performance is a single unit.
There is a single injunction for performance (*prayogavacana*) that applies to both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary rites (*pradhāna*).
Because it is singular, it prescribes everything simultaneously: "One should sacrifice with this rite together with its subsidiaries.
Since the rite becomes complete with its subsidiaries once they have been performed a single time, there is no reason for their performance again.
But surely there will be an abundance of assistance?

If the subsidiaries were to produce an unseen assistance (*adṛṣṭa-upakāra*), then by their repetition an abundance of that assistance would be inferred. However, the subsidiaries perform only a visible purpose for the principal, because they are its subsidiaries.
And even in the case of repetition, the possession of subsidiaries remains exactly as it was;
if that [principal action] is connected with the fruit by the injunction "one should sacrifice with the subsidiaries," then the subsidiaries themselves are not [directly connected].
The subsidiaries possess purpose through being the means for accomplishing that [principal action].
Is this not indeed improper?
For when the *prayāja* offerings take place, there is neither the principal sacrifice nor the *apūrva*;
and when the sacrifice and the *apūrva* exist, the *prayāja* offerings do not yet exist.
Thus, when there is merely the fuel-sticks (*samid*) and so forth, devoid of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), there is no status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*); how then could there be any benefit?

Moreover, if the sacrifice itself were the only thing present in the auxiliaries and no *apūrva* (transcendental result) existed, then there would be no extended application (*codaka*) at all for those sacrifices that are auxiliaries to the Soma-sacrifice, such as the *iṣṭi* and the *putreṣṭi*.
For in the absence of the *apūrva*, there is no expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Since the *yajati* (sacrifice) has its procedure (*itikartavyatā*) already known, the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) would not prescribe that procedure.
In that case, the following observations would not be possible:

"It has one hundred and one *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings; he does not offer the *samidh* oblations with clarified butter; having cast away the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he offers the *hāriyojana*."
There is another explanation for its beginning:

"Or there is no repetition because the injunction of performance is one for the subsidiaries (aṅgas) and the primaries (pradhānas). There is a single injunction of performance for both the subsidiaries and the primaries.
Because that entire collection of subsidiaries and principal acts is one, there is an instruction for them to be performed simultaneously.
In that regard, there is the placement (nyāsa) of the principal acts [only once].

For what reason? Because the purpose of the Vedic injunction is accomplished by the principal acts being performed just once; as it is said: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa."

When the purpose of the Veda has been accomplished, that fruit which is ordained by the scripture is obtained; there is no further cause for ritual action. Likewise, even in the case of those who practice repeatedly, that which is to be accomplished by the scripture—which leads ignorant persons [to the goal]—has been performed. When that is done, one should understand that this fruit of the auxiliary (aṅga) elements, as apprehended from the scripture, is obtained.
And that being the case, practice would be useless;
for it is untenable that there should be an increase in the fruit.

The fruit that belongs to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is utilized for the assistance of the subsidiaries within the process of *bhāvanā*, not for the production of a separate, unprecedented (*apūrva*) fruit.

If the fruit were produced by the subsidiaries in relation to an *apūrva*, then that would be merely the fruit of the subsidiaries themselves. Furthermore, the subsidiaries do not produce such [an *apūrva*].

And since it is accomplished by being performed only once, there is no increase in the fruit through the repetition of the auxiliary rites. (From the *Ṭup-ṭīkā* on the *Bhāṣya*): Heaven is the result; the sacrifice is that which brings it about.
The *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) provides assistance to the sacrifice; it is not itself the means of accomplishing the fruit.
Its own fruit is not heard in scripture, for the fruit arises from the instrument (*karaṇa*).
True, the fruit is accomplished by the instrument; however, the *itikartavyatā*, when being repeated, renders a great service to it.
And that [action], when assisted by a great preparatory rite (*upakāra*), produces a great result.
Here it is asked: Is the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) performed only once?
Why? Because both the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure are required by the productive activity (*bhāvanā*).

In that context, the instrument (karaṇa) operates toward the fruit; the procedure (itikartavyatā), by favoring the instrument, is required. And once the productive activity (bhāvanā) has been satisfied by being performed once, by what would a second or subsequent performance be required?

Therefore, the passage in this text—"When there are the *prayāja*s, then there is not the principal sacrifice (*pradhānayajña*); or rather, in the *apūrva*; and when there is the sacrifice (*yaji*) and the *apūrva*, then there are not the *prayāja*s"—is incorrect.

Why? Because at the very moment that the agent (*kartṛ*) assumes the status of being the doer with respect to the production of heaven (*svarga*), at that same moment the instrument (*karaṇa*) also operates as the producer (*bhāvaka*). The procedure (*itikartavyatā*) likewise assists the instrument at that very same moment.

If the agency were to be established in one moment for the production of heaven, and the instrumentality likewise in another moment for the producer, then in that case, there would be no relationship at all between the produced and the producer.
Therefore, there must be simultaneity between heaven and the sacrifice;
and in the same way, there must be simultaneity between the instrument and the procedure.
Therefore, these [actions] are simultaneous;
nor are intermediate actions intended by the opponent.
Rather, it is the very actions such as the *prayāja* offerings, though occurring at different times, that are intended.
And that is incorrect, because their own natures are distinct.
Or rather, there is repetition, because of the scriptural statement regarding the "once-ness" in the giving of the path of cutting and so forth.
The Commentary states: "Or there is repetition for those who lack knowledge."
Why? Because it is heard in the Pitṛyajña: "The sacrificial grass (barhis) is cut once";
likewise, in the Anuyāja: "He wipes the enclosing sticks (paridhi) once"; and [so too] in the Sviṣṭakṛt.

Section on the Fruit and the Ground (Phalabhūmādhikaraṇa): "And like the fruit, one cuts off [the portion] once from the upper part. Thus, there is the performance of the offerings for those who do not know [this], and consequently these scriptural statements become logical.
Therefore, there is practice;
however, there is non-practice for those who are ignorant, because [the truth] must be expressed.
The Commentary states: "However, there is non-practice for the ignorant according to the reasoning already stated."
Since the word "once" (*sakṛt*) is used in the case of *chenā* and so forth, it is understood that there is repetition (*abhyāsa*) elsewhere. To this we reply:
even though there is no repetition, nevertheless, the state of being "once" must be expressed in the case of *chenā* and so forth.

In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), because of the scriptural injunction, "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is to be cut more than once," it follows that by virtue of that rule, it would also apply more than once in the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*). When this [undesired consequence] has arisen, the rule of "once" must be stated.
Thus, the threefold wiping has been prescribed for the *prayāja* offerings;
it recurs again in the *anuyāja* offerings.
Since the state of being threefold would also apply there, the state of being single must be enjoined.

Likewise, in the case of the rule "he cuts off twice from the oblation," although a duality [of cutting] applies generally even to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, a single performance (*sakṛttva*) is prescribed therein.
