Therefore, since there is a single mention in the case of the *śyenādi* sacrifices and so forth, it is not logical to understand that repetition (*abhyāsa*) applies elsewhere.

Śābarabhāṣya: Once it has been established that rituals should be performed again and again because of the abundance of results (*phalabhūmā*), the following is considered: Does the abundance of results accrue to one who performs the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) repeatedly within a single performance, or not?

The reply to one who thinks that the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) being practiced therein produce great assistance, and that the principal act (*pradhāna*), when endowed with such great assistance, results in an abundance of fruit, is as follows: An effect repeats itself only when there is a deficiency in the totality of its causes. Now, the principal act together with its auxiliaries constitutes the causal complex for the fruit, not the auxiliary alone; therefore, by repeating only that [auxiliary] alone, there is no attainment of an abundant fruit.
Furthermore, an abundance of fruit does not follow from an abundance of assistance, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for this.
And in this case, there is no scripturally sanctioned repetition of the constituent parts (*aṅga*).
Nor can an abundance of results be postulated on the basis of the great effort involved in what is scripturally prescribed.
Therefore, one who desires an abundance of results must repeat the principal rite (*pradhāna*) together with its constituent parts, neither the parts alone nor the principal rite alone.

Soma: The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: "The subsidiary (aṅga) deserves repetition for the sake of an abundance of results, because it possesses fruit, like the Saurya and other such rites. By this inference, there would be an abundance of results through the repetition of the subsidiary. Viśvarūpa: "Is there repetition of the subsidiary or not? Repetition leads to abundance; there is no separate result for the subsidiary. Abundance arises precisely through the recurrence of the primary act; therefore, the subsidiary should be performed only once in the performance."

Bhaṭṭa: This is the reply of one who considers that there is an increase in the fruit due to the excessive effort involved in performing the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) repeatedly within a single performance.

It is not, first of all, the production of a different fruit, because of the rule that from a single primary act (*pradhāna*) only one fruit arises; thus, in the absence of the primary act, there is no basis for the production of another fruit due to the absence of the causal totality (*sāmagrī*).
Nor is it merely an excellence (*atiśaya*) within that very same individual instance of the fruit.

As in the case of "He takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice," there is an abundance of fruit (*phalabhūmā*). For that [abundance] is postulated only where the accomplishment of the ritual's assistance (*ṛtūpakāra*) is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being distinct from that [primary act], such as in the case of taking the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, or as in "One goddess," "Six goddesses," and so forth.

In the present case, however, since the injunctions for the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) have fulfilled their purpose through a single performance, and since the ritual requires only a single performance of the action, it does not necessitate a repeated undertaking; thus, there is no evidence for an increase in fruit resulting from repetition based on mere human desire.

For it has been stated in the Bhāṣya (on 11.1.14, regarding the difference in syllables) that whether a large animal is sacrificed in such cases as "one should sacrifice an animal" (*paśumālabheta*), or a small one, there is no difference in degree in the fruit.

In that context, what possibility is there for performing the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries again? However, it should be understood that in cases such as "one should give a cow," there is indeed an increase in the fruit when a proper cow is given.
Maṇḍana [says]: "One should perform the subsidiary parts, such as the *prayāja*, only once."
Śaṅkara says: "There is no great fruit from repetition of the limbs.
One who desires an abundance of results engages in the performance many times; one who is satisfied [with the minimum] performs it once. Bhāṣya 11.1.144.
The diversity of fruits is caused by the diversity of actions. (Su. p.
The principle is that the abundance of results does not carry any fault.
This [principle] operates wherever there is a perfection of result in the case of respect.

Just as this principle was established in the *Muktāvalī* during the discussion on the definition of compound [words], so too, in the case of the statement "one should cause the *Niṣāda-sthapati* to sacrifice," it is not a *tatpuruṣa* compound because that would entail *lakṣaṇā* (indication); rather, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound because there is no *lakṣaṇā*.

Nor should it be argued that because the Niṣāda—a specific mixed caste—is ineligible for the Vedas, the performance of the sacrifice is impossible; for since the Niṣāda is indeed enjoined to the study [of the relevant portion], such [performance] is possible through that very [study]. This is because, when a primary meaning can be consistently applied with parsimony, there is no justification for postulating a result-based burden (phalamūlagaurava), as the postulation would be more cumbersome. This is the general direction. Nor should it be argued that the very same action, as understood from the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), will be enjoined with respect to the fruit once it has been connected with curd by the quality-injunction (*guṇavākya*).

Thus (Vārttika, p. 541).

Nor should it be argued that there is an injunction of curd (*dadhi*)—which is already dependent on the primary oblation (*prakṛtahoma*)—for the sake of the fruit [of the rite], rather than resorting to the "redundancy of injunction" (*vidhigaurava*) and the assumption of a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
For if one were to enjoin both the connection of the curd with the fruit and its connection with the substratum (*āśraya*), there would result the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Nor should it be said that the substratum is obtained through context (*prakaraṇa*);
for, according to the maxim "context applies to what is not otherwise connected," it is impossible for curd—which is intended for a specific result—to be grasped by the context.
Nor should it be said that the substratum is obtained from a context characterized by an injunction (*vidhi*).
For a word indeed serves as the authority for being a qualifier by virtue of proximity;
however, there is no such thing as "proximity" that serves as an authority for the sacrifice.

Nor is there any word here that establishes a connection with a contextual substrate (*prakṛta*), because it has already been stated that a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) occurs if the sentence concerning the desire for sense-faculties (*indriyakāma*) were to effect a connection with both [the substrate and the result]. Furthermore, since the connection with a substrate would have to be assumed, such assumption itself constitutes a flaw. Therefore, it is proper that the very heard sentence should enjoin a qualified action.
Therefore, since a fruit is heard in the sentence concerning the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*), it would follow that a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) alone is what must be enjoined.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"And because of the inequality of the two sentences, [the result] is understood as belonging to the accessory (*guṇa*)."

This is the intended meaning: this would indeed be so if the injunction were directed toward the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) precisely because it is the substratum for the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

However, in all cases, it is the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) alone that is established by the injunction, and it is differentiated here and there according to the distinctions among the various purposes.

Where the productive operation possesses a fruit, the injunction is directed toward the verbal root-meaning; in such a case, it makes the verbal root-meaning itself the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the fruit.

However, where there is the inclusion of another quality (*guṇa*) to be enjoined mentioned within its own sentence, in that case—out of fear of the complexity of enjoining a qualified whole (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) and being intent on enjoining only the quality—if it perceives that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is already established, then it enjoins only the quality for the sake of the result.

But if it does not perceive such establishment, then it accepts both the injunction of the injunction and the indication by possessive implication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). For as long as the capacity of the injunction has not been extracted from the verbal root...

To that extent, the connection with the result is understood as belonging to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). However, when there is a scriptural mention of a result in an injunction concerning a subordinate element (*guṇa*), that [mention] is touched by an injunction of that which possesses [the subordinate element]; therefore, it attains syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with it.
(Vārttika, p. 546).

Therefore, here too, because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) under discussion, the injunction (*vidhi*), disregarding that [root-meaning], is transferred to the accessory (*guṇa*) and enjoins the accessory itself for the sake of the result.
The meaning of the root, however, is employed merely as the basis for the connection with the suffix.
And that [root-meaning], which has been introduced by the context through this verbal root, is here restated.
This being so, there will be no fault of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indication of possession) nor the burden of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
Now, let it be granted that the root-meaning—the oblation—is a restatement because it is already established; however, what about the connection between the curd and the oblation here?
It is understood; and it must necessarily be so understood,
for it is not possible for that which lacks an action as its substratum to be a means of accomplishing a result.

In this regard, the connection between the curd and the oblation (*dadhi-homa-sambandha*) as it appears in the sentence "One desiring sense-faculties should sacrifice with curd" is not merely restated (*anūdyate*), because it has not been previously established.
If it were being enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to enjoining both the connection of the single substance, curd, with the fruit and its connection with the oblation.
It is replied: even here, the connection between the curd and the oblation is indeed already established and is therefore restated.
For instance, by the word "dadhnā" (with curd), the curd is enjoined as being presented through the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) as an instrument (*karaṇa*).
And the state of being a factor of action (*kārakatva*) consists in bringing about a specific action that takes the form of the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
In that regard, what is this specific action that takes the form of the meaning of a verbal root?

When this [substance], having become a *kāraka* (instrumental factor), requires a basis for its status as a means to achieve a result, it is the very act of *homa* (oblation)—brought forward by proximity (*saṃnidhi*) and context (*prakaraṇa*)—that is connected as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Therefore, because the substance *dadhi* (curd) has itself become a *kāraka*, the connection with the previously mentioned *homa* is merely restated (*anūdyate*) through the reference to that *dhātvartha* which has become a *kāraka*; only the connection with the result is enjoined. Thus, how can there be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)? As it has been said: "The connection with *dadhi* is also merely restated, as its status as the substratum (*āśrayatva*) is already obtained from the context itself" (Vārttika, p. 548).
Nor should it be asked: "What is this dependence on a specific relation to a substratum here—is it by way of being a cause (*kāraṇatva*) or by way of being a procedure (*itikartavyatātva*)?

For, when that which has already acquired the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) possesses a desire for its own assistance, that [desire] is here perceived as the very state of being an instrument—even without determining a specific action—without the inclusion of another specific action; thus, it is established that it proceeds precisely through the expectation of an instrument (*karaṇākāṅkṣā*).

However, this must be addressed here: is that very same [action] modified by the curd, which is the meaning of the verbal root, or is a different [action] enjoined? First of all, it is not that very same one being modified, because its recognition is impossible due to the difference in the fruit and the difference in the means. Nor is a different [action] enjoined, because that would entail a difference in the ritual action (*karma*). It is said in reply: The text provided is already in English. Here is a faithful translation of the Sanskrit passage: But this must be stated here: is that very same [action], which has the meaning of the verbal root as its object, modified by the curd, or is another [action] enjoined? First, it is not that very same [action] being modified, because its recognition is impossible due to the difference in the result and the difference in the means.
Nor is another [action] enjoined, because that would entail a difference in the ritual action (*karma*). It is said in reply:
Indeed, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is not differentiated by a difference in result or a difference in the means (*sādhana*).
What then? It is differentiated by the difference in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which serves as its subordinate element (*anubandha*).

In each instance—whether in the sentence concerning the one desiring heaven, in the sentence concerning lifelong performance, or in the sentence concerning the one desiring sensory power—the same efficient force is recognized, because it is delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (such as *homa*, "offering") which functions as its subordinate element within the respective sentences, such as "Agnihotra. Thus, it is that very same efficient force.

However, the distinction based on differences such as the result (*phala*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) merely serves to qualify that [bhāvanā]. Nor should it be argued: "How can the connection with the sense organ (*indriya-sambandha*) be enjoined for the *bhāvanā* once it has already been established, as in the case of curd (*dadhi*) and the *viśvadhā* [rite]?
For nowhere is the connection of the *bhāvanā* with a result ever enjoined.

According to the principle of the *lipsādhikaraṇa* (4.1.1), there is an injunction regarding the means alone, by way of restating the connection with a result already established through natural inclination (*rāga*). As it is stated in the *Kārikā*: "When a fruit is heard [in scripture], the suffix denoting the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is not injunctive;
Jaimini will state here that its [injunctive force] is characterized by the desire for that [fruit]. (*mī. ko.* 364)

Thus, it is established that there is no injunction here for the curd—which serves as the substrate for the previously mentioned oblation—with respect to the result; therefore, it constitutes a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*).

The practical application (*prayojana*) is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because it is a novel rite (*apūrva*) by virtue of being a curd-oblation, it consists of a single oblation performed solely with curd as its material.

In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, because there is a distinction between the two oblations (*homa*), there is one in the evening and one in the morning; therefore, the oblation has curd as its means of accomplishment.

In the Sūtra, however: "Because the statement regarding the connection between the rite and its fruit is not equal to the statement regarding the connection between the quality and its fruit, the connection of that fruit of the sense organ is perceived in the quality.
The meaning is that the fruit arises from the quality alone.
Tautā: The connection with the fruit is the reason for the prior cognition [of the injunction].

Those [rites] perceived as connected with a fruit are primary; the others, being fruitless, are subsidiary. (Vi. 4.4.11).

Regarding the connection with a fruit, in the case of the *aveṣṭi*, there is the injunction: "One desiring food should cause [himself] to sacrifice with this"; it does not refer to a different ritual action.

Having prescribed the rule, "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born," it is further recorded: "He at whose birth one performs this sacrifice becomes indeed purified, radiant, an eater of food, possessed of sensory power, and rich in cattle.
In this regard, a doubt arises: does this sacrifice result in a fruit for the performer, or for the sake of the fruit belonging to the son?

When the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is reached—that it is for the sake of the father's fruit because of the connection between the agent of the action and the fruit of the action—the author states the final conclusion (siddhānta), which deviates from the initial sūtra.
If the remainder of the sentence were not heard—that is, if the father were not mentioned—the connection with the statement regarding purification and so forth would not occur;
for since the father is not a subordinate element (śeṣa) in the declaration of the fruit, he would lack that status.
Furthermore, the phrase "he becomes purified upon whose birth" clearly states that the fruit belongs to the son who has been born.
The general rule is that the fruit belongs to the agent;
however, by this specific statement, the fruit accrues even to one who is not the agent.
For those who are ignorant, the connection with the prescribed act serves merely as a causal occasion.
Now, one might raise the following objection as a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "In the case where a single potsherd (*kapāla*) should be lost, one month of the year would have passed away;

if then the sacrificer should die, he should offer a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) dedicated to Cyavana. Thus, just as this rite is an action whose fruit is the welfare of the self when the loss of a potsherd is the occasioning cause, so too is the *jāteṣṭi*. To refute this, [the author] states:
"The mention of 'destruction' refers to the connection with the impairment of the potsherds and other such implements which are not conscious beings."
The section on the connection with the fruit (phalasaṃyogādhikaraṇa):
[The statement] "for the sake of a cause" (nimittārtha) is appropriate only as being for the sake of a cause, not otherwise.
For the sacrifice is not performed for the sake of the potsherds themselves.

Since the birth [of a son] can be established in other ways as well, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the fruit—such as purification and so forth—accrues only to the son, and not to the performer [of the rite].

Alternatively, with this single *sūtra*, there is a second section (*varṇaka*). Regarding the sacrifice heard in the scripture, "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born," there arises a doubt: should the sacrifice be performed immediately upon the son's birth, or after the *jātakarman* (birth-rite)? When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that the sacrifice should be performed immediately upon birth, the author establishes the established conclusion.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the prima facie view.

For those who lack knowledge, the "affliction" (*upaghāta*) of this [wind] in the form of time consists in the digestive fire of the stomach being disturbed and the birth of a son; that is to say, it refers to the onset of such afflictions.
The "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) with the affliction serves merely as a causal condition (*nimitta*); its purpose is to enjoin [the rite] when the causal condition has arisen.
Therefore, the *jāteṣṭi* (the sacrifice performed upon birth) should be performed after the execution of the *jātakarman* (birth-rite).
Now, by means of this very sūtra, there is a third interpretation (*varṇaka*).

In the inquiry as to whether this *jāteṣṭi* should be performed within the ten-day period (*antardaśāha*) or after the conclusion of the birth-impurity (*jananāśauca*), on either the full moon or the new moon day—since there is no restrictive rule [to the contrary]—it should be performed within the ten-day period.

Section 2908: On the Connection with the Result; Section 2909: On the Result as a Purpose. In consideration of the destruction of sin, since the *punnāman* rite is lighter than the *ādhāna*, there arises a deliberation: is this [destruction of sin] prompted by a result residing in the son (*putragata*), or is it prompted by a result residing in the agent (*kartṛgata*)? Upon such reflection, because the injunction implies only that which is desired by the agent, and because it is understood from the word *eva* (only) that the result intended by the act of establishing the fires (*ādhāna*) accrues to oneself, the result is indeed one that must be accomplished by the agent himself.

Nor can there be a conclusion that purity (*pūtatva*) and so forth reside in the son by means of the *dharmigrāhakapramāṇa* (the proof grasping the subject) expressed in the passage beginning "when he is born," because even that [proof] is not in conflict; for the pronoun "he" (*sa*) in the phrase "he shall be radiant" (*sa tejasvī*) refers back to the very same thing indicated by the coreferential case-ending. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: since the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the meaning of the word "which" (*yat*) due to their syntactic connection, and since the result must reside in the son precisely because of that [connection], and since even that [result] is desired by the agent, there is no conflict with the injunctive suffix or the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); thus, the result indeed resides in the son.
In the case of a non-performance [of a rite], the causal condition (pratyaya) resides solely in the agent.

Regarding the purpose [of the rite]: even when the son dies, the *jāti-iti* (the ritual for birth) is performed; according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is for the sake of the refinement of the fruit in the father, whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is not so.

The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) states: Without reference to any specific context, it is heard: "One desiring splendor should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni"; "One desiring Vedic luster should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma"; "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra-Agni. Here a doubt arises: is the fruit enjoined for the archetypal *āgneya* and other offerings, or are these distinct rituals from those archetypal ones?
What is established? That there is an injunction of results regarding the archetypal rites.
Why? Because the Āgneya and other sacrifices, being already known, are recognized [here].
Therefore, they are restated for the purpose of connecting them with the results.
This being the case, we reply:
And the fruit [of an action] is a differentiator when it is heard in the absence of proximity to another ritual act.
How so? Because if it were a restatement (anuvāda), it would be impossible to enjoin the fruit, as it would lack injunctive force.
For it is understood that what is not being enjoined cannot function as a means (*upāya*).

Furthermore, if "desire for cattle" (*rukkāma*) were enjoined here, then because that desire is non-obligatory (*anitya*), while the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices are obligatory (*nitya*), their connection would not be possible.
This applies everywhere.

This being the case, we reply:
since the word is perceived even in external objects and the like, which are unrefined (*asaṃskṛta*), these are not words characterized by refinement (*saṃskāra*).
But was it not said that they will exist in a single part [of the object] due to similarity?

How so? By means of words such as "external" (bahir), refinements (saṃskāra) are enjoined for the learned.
Thus, there must be refinements when the words exist, and the acquisition of the words occurs when the refinement exists;

Furthermore, grammatical refinements (*saṃskāra*) are not unestablished; people employ words designated as "classes" (*jāti*) in common usage.

Therefore, people employ terms such as *bahir* with respect to refined forms. Consequently, since these are seen to be based on a class even in a single instance, they ought to be based on a class everywhere.

Furthermore, for those words that are not known from common worldly usage, it is not possible to determine their meaning through the Veda alone by means of the connection between preceding and succeeding words;
for such a connection would only be postulated so that the preceding and succeeding words might not be rendered meaningless.
However, that which is not apprehended at all cannot be postulated.
Furthermore, your preceding and following words will be meaningful through their worldly application as unrefined usage;

The purpose [of the discussion] is as follows: regarding the injunction "he strews the sacrificial grass around the base of the sacrificial post" (*barhiṣā yūpavaṭam avastṛṇāti*), if the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) holds, then the strewing must be performed with consecrated grass alone; in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is the opposite.
Or rather—by way of introducing the topic of names, three sections are commenced concerning the grounds for the names of substances.

Because the reason is the same, the *puroḍāśa* is also cited as an example. Why? "Even when a word is observed in only one part [of its referent], it is based upon a universal;

Since it is established that "those very words which are worldly are the same as those which are Vedic, and their meanings are the same" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.9, first section), when a word in the Veda— preserving its worldly status— is found even in a single instance to have a genus (*jāti*) as its basis for denotation, it is impossible to postulate a further power based on a different basis there. Furthermore,
because the genus does not depart even in the case of *saṃskṛta* (refined) forms, one cannot claim a departure from that [genus] as the basis for denotation.

Therefore, these do not deviate from the genus (*jāti*);

If this is so, then all [meanings] are primary;
for everything is understood from the word.
For just as when it is said, "fire carries," there is a cognition of the burning [element].
In the same way, when the word "fire-boy" (agnimāṇavaka) is uttered, there is a cognition of the boy.
Now, it might be argued: that which is cognized from a word without an accompanying term is primary (mukhya); that which is cognized from a word with an accompanying term is secondary (gauṇa).
This is not correct.
For when the form of a word is the cause for some particular meaning, that same form remains identical whether it is accompanied by an upapada or without an upapada.
And it is not possible for the effect (the signified meaning) not to exist when the cause (the word-form) is present.
What follows from this? If it were so, one could not say that "without the secondary word (upapada), that meaning does not exist, but when the secondary word has arisen, that meaning will arise.
Nor can that collective meaning be understood.

For the distinction [between word-meanings and sentence-meaning] is understood through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). If it is then argued that "this is the meaning of the sentence," such a claim cannot be maintained.
For the meaning of a word, when combined [with others], does not become the meaning of the sentence.
Let this be seen as follows:
this very word "fire" (agni) is a denotation of the burning flame.
The word "fire" itself is denoted as referring to the boy;
therefore, there is no distinction whatsoever between the secondary (gauṇa) and the primary (mukhya).
Now, it might be argued that that which is well-established [in its primary sense] is the primary, while that which is only slightly so is the secondary.
This also is not tenable.
For "notoriety" (prasiddhi) means cognition (prajñāna),
and there is no distinction whatsoever in the case of a question.
Now it might be argued: "That which has frequent usage is primary (mukhya), while that which is used rarely is secondary (gauṇa).
This is not so.
Even when employed in a minimal degree, it would not convey its capacity;
therefore, since that too is understood from the word, it is indeed primary.
To this, it is replied:
There is a distinction here:
the boy is understood from the word "nāma" (by name).
How is this known? It has been stated: "In the case of an unestablished [usage], it must be a matter of convention."
How is it that there is no misconception? It is said:
Indeed, by means of non-perception alone, one is seen to understand the cognition of "fire" from the word "boy," but one does not thereby understand the cognition of "sun" from the word "boy."

Whence is this [known]? Because whichever word "fire" (agni) is employed, in each instance that word "fire" is restricted [to its specific object]. For this very reason, it is observed that [the word] is devoid of similarity (*vigatasādṛśya*).
Therefore, this is the cause for the application of this word "fire."
Furthermore, as long as the flame is not cognized, its similarity [to the boy] cannot be cognized.
Therefore, the word "fire" has the flame as its primary cause (nimitta), not the boy.
Consequently, it is primary with respect to the flame, not the boy.
In the same way, the external word is the cause for the dissolution of the grass, but not for the cognition of something resembling grass.
Thus, since duality exists, it is appropriate to investigate whether the word has a primary sense or also a secondary sense.
What, then, is the prima facie conclusion? That there is an application to both the primary and the secondary senses.
Why? Because both are possible; both the actual grass and that which resembles grass can be conveyed by the word "grass.
The actual grass is conveyed directly, while that which resembles grass is conveyed through the cognition of grass.
And whatever can indeed be conveyed by the word "grass" as a means for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, all of that must be conveyed, since there is no reason for a restrictive selection.

Moreover, if it were studied in this manner, the mantras addressed to Pūṣan and others would not be set aside from the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; they would simply denote the deities of the archetype (prakṛti) by means of figurative designation (gauṇa-abhidhāna). This being the case, we reply:
The application of the mantra is to the primary [meaning] alone, not to the secondary;
why? Because it is connected with both.
For, due to its recitation within the context (*prakaraṇa*), it enters into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the principal act.
In this regard, the following point arises: one should accomplish that which can be accomplished by means of this mantra;
and since this mantra is capable of being helpful through its connection with the expression of the primary meaning, it is not capable of expressing a secondary (gauṇa) meaning.
Therefore, there is no application [of the mantra] to a secondary sense.
But surely, a secondary meaning can be conveyed through the cognition of the primary meaning.
True, this is so;
however, since its purposeful application is already fulfilled by the cognition of the primary meaning alone, there is no evidence whatsoever for its application to a secondary sense.
However, by application to the primary sense, the charge of meaninglessness is avoided;
and once meaninglessness has been avoided, there is no occasion for a secondary denotation.
For a word does not denote a secondary sense without first denoting the primary one.
Therefore, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition [for the primary sense], it is employed in a secondary (gauṇa) sense.

Moreover, many means for conveying a secondary sense are available; and it has been stated that "capacity is a part of the word," according to the principle: "Or rather, it is postulated from the meaning, because it is a part [of the whole]."
In that case, if the mantra were necessarily enjoined as a subordinate factor (guṇa), it would be sublated by another means of knowledge (pramāṇa) in the absence of any other alternative method.
If it is argued that the ignorance of the mantra is the means of knowledge, we say no; for that [ignorance] lacks the capacity to exclude other alternative methods.
But surely, even in the case of the primary [rite], the same fault applies to that which is being applied?
No, it is said:
if it were applied even to the primary, it would not at all be a benefactor to the principal.
And in that case, there would be identity of the intended meaning for it. Therefore, there is a distinction between the secondary and the primary senses.
Moreover:
He who applies a mantra to a secondary sense should be asked: "For what purpose do you cause the primary sense to be understood?
If he should reply, "Otherwise, there is no cognition of the secondary sense," one should answer him: "There are other means for the cognition of the secondary sense as well."
Now, if he, being thus challenged, should reply that "the primary cognition is also a contingent means," one should say to him:
"In that case, it cannot be applied to the secondary sense as a matter of necessity.
When the primary is employed for the sake of the secondary cognition, then this consequence follows: the application must be to the primary alone."

Thus, the purpose is understood through the meaning, not through the mantra which is the means of communication; therefore, when there is a different way of attaining it, the secondary [meaning] must be communicated.
That very mantra is not to be employed.

Even if there were a need for a mantra as a means of communication, since that purpose is already fulfilled by the primary meaning alone, it is all the more unlikely to be applied to a secondary sense.
Therefore, when a function is possible through both the primary and the secondary meanings, it should be performed through the primary.
Thus it is established.
Or rather—now the application by means of indicative power (*liṅga*) is introduced.
Indicative power (*liṅga*) is the capacity of mantras to convey their respective meanings.
And that [denotation] exists in both the primary (*mukhya*) and the secondary (*gauṇa*) senses in some manner.

Regarding the application (*viniyoga*) therein, when there is a doubt as to whether it occurs only in the primary sense or also in the secondary one, [the author], thinking that "there is no such thing as a secondary sense at all," asks: "What, then, is the primary, and what is the secondary? However, once the secondary sense is established, its distinction from the cause [of the primary] and its function of abandoning its own [literal] meaning have already been explained; thus, this inquiry should be understood as having occurred previously by implication.
And in that regard: "The primacy belongs to the word-meaning alone; primacy is that which is first expressed.
That which is understood through the meaning is secondary (*gauṇa*), because it comes about through qualities (*guṇa*).
[In the rule] *śāstrādibhyo ya* (Pāṇini 5.3.103), this term *mukhya* is used in the sense of 'primary' (*iva*)."

Since sound is denotable by sound, it follows that everything [is primary]. Because the characteristic of being secondary (*gauṇatva*) is defined as "the decline of another's qualities due to the absence of those qualities," therefore, when any word is uttered, since everything is being denoted, one who postulates a distinct power of the word for another meaning—because it is not separated from the other meaning—regards it as primary (*mukhya*) precisely because it is first. Thus, everything is primary.

In this regard, first, the reasons for [the term] being secondary (*gauṇatva*) as imagined by others are presented: "Now it might be argued: 'That in which [a word like] *niprapada* occurs,' and so forth.
'In every case, that which is a cause of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is called a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). And that which functions in dependence on another is always understood as secondary (*gauṇa*')."
(The application of words is indeed accepted as dependent on something else).
For, just as the cognition of fire arises from the word "fire" alone, the cognition of a young boy does not arise [from that same word] in the same way, because it is dependent upon another word.
Even where another word is not heard, it is precisely that [other factor]—obtained through context, purpose, and so forth—that functions; thus there is no deviation.
And that very thing called the universal (sāmānya) is the quality that serves as the cause for the application [of a word].
This is not so.
Why? Because this manifestation is produced solely through the coexistence of the word and its object.
Because it serves as an indicator (*dyotaka*) for another, it does not lose its primary characteristic (*mukhyalakṣaṇa*).

Just as color remains the object of the eye even though it requires the assistance of light, or just as a primary [word] whose doubt has been resolved requires the sequence of phonemes, the measure (*mātrā*), grasping, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), memory, connection, and experience, so too here, even with a prefix (*upapada*), the name cannot be expected to function without its own inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).
And even while requiring these, it does not obstruct [the operation of the name], since it occupies the position of a procedural requirement (*itikartavyatā*) by virtue of being an indicator.

Even without the secondary member (*upapada*), that meaning certainly exists for it; it is simply not manifested in some way, just as the earth and so forth are [meanings] of words such as *go* (cow). Now, setting aside the illuminative function (*dyotakatva*) of the secondary member, if it is argued that they have equal status—because the cognition of this meaning arises from the eternal combination of the words *māṇavaka* and *agni*, and therefore, given that the whole is the denoter like *aśvakarṇa* and other compounds, the individual parts possess a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*)—[then the following applies].
This is said in reply:
"And you cannot here maintain that this [word] has the collective whole as its meaning;
for a distinction in meaning is observed through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)."
In that case, there is conventional usage based on the whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*), where the meaning of the parts is obscured and the whole alone is perceived as distinct.

However, here, the specific denotation of the word *agni* (fire) is its reddish-brown color (*paiṅgalya*), and the specific denotation of the word *māṇavaka* (young boy) is the physical form of the individual;
therefore, both are primary (*mukhya*) because they denote their respective objects through their own expressive power.

Now, supporting the view that the meaning of the whole is derived according to its parts, he says: "Because it is understood through two words whose own meanings are mutually connected, the sentence-meaning is like [the case of] 'blue lotus';
and since it arises from the cognition of word-meanings, it is secondary with respect to the word, just as before.
He refutes this.
Just as in the expression "the fire-brāhmaṇa boy" (*agnimāṇavaka*), a single object is qualified [by two terms],

yet here [in the case of *agni* denoting a boy] its primary meaning is not present. Nor is its ruddiness (*paiṅgalya*) the denoted meaning, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of the non-difference between the unreal and the real.
Therefore, it is the sentence-meaning [that is primary].
Consequently, since the word functions equally with respect to both the fire's flaming and the boy's tawny color, it possesses primacy.
As for the genitive case in the Bhāṣya’s phrase "of the boy" (*māṇavakasya*), it is produced by the distinction from "tawniness," not by the distinction from the denotative function (*abhidhā*).
For the actual nature of the boy is not understood from the word "fire.
Indeed, if they were synonyms, the word "boy" would not be employed.

Now, it might be argued that by setting aside that which is well-established [as the primary meaning], and considering the operation of the accompanying word (*upapada*), both the act of employing and the act of relying upon what has been done [by that word] demonstrate the distinction between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*) meanings for those who are dull-witted and those who are well-established in their understanding.
To this, the reply is: "Familiarity is a form of cognition, and it does not exceed [the scope of] this [definition].
Therefore, a distinction based upon it cannot be properly stated.
Now, having explained the difference regarding familiarity as it pertains to the hearer, he shows the distinction between the speaker's frequent or rare usage for the sake of classification.
And as for the statement beginning with "for that which has been frequently applied," and so forth— that is refuted [by the following]:
"Even if it is applied only a few times, its meaning is determined once it has been heard."
"Thus, there is again an equality between the two cases in that [the word] does not turn back.
Furthermore, here too, the weak and strong usage of the word *go* with respect to the earth and so forth must be demonstrated.
And so they say: 'The praise is manifold by means of the *maṇḍakas*.'"
Sometimes with pieces of sweetmeats (*khaṇḍamodaka*).
And in this case, the *maṇḍakas* are neither primary nor secondary to the *khaṇḍamodakas*.
Now he states the distinction.

Even though there is co-referentiality with the boy (*māṇavaka*), since the word *aruṇā* denotes similarity when it exists and does not denote it when it is absent, and because its application is observed elsewhere where similarity exists and not observed where it does not, and because it functions as a qualifier, similarity must necessarily be understood first if the intended meaning is to be conveyed.
And since that [intended meaning] is not understood when the referent is not known, the referent is denoted first.
And therefore, since the remaining [elements] are understood solely through their connection with that [genus], the individual (vyakti) is not denoted.
Furthermore, it has been stated that in such cases there exist certain commonalities of form and so forth.
Consequently, the distinction between the primary and the secondary exists; thus concludes the section on "Commencement" (ārambhādhikaraṇa).
These, together with the nine secondary (gauṇa) views stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-sūtra*,
are to be understood as follows: "The denotation of its own meaning [by the whole], the collective [meaning], the conceptual construction,
likewise the function with an accompanying word (*sopapada-vṛtti*), and the conventional usage of the aggregate."

"The meaning of the sentence [is that] it has little common renown and thus involves the application of a secondary sense (*alapa*); having set aside these eight [objections], the definition of the quality (*guṇa*) is established. (1) That which abandons its own primary meaning is *jahatsvārtha*; that which denotes another meaning is likewise so called. The state of being such—namely, *jahatsvārthābhidhāyitva*—is the cause of figurative usage (*gauṇatva*), wherein there is a function (*vṛtti*) toward a secondary form such as *paiṅgya*, by abandoning its own primary meaning through the indication of a quality (*guṇa*).

2. A collection of qualities such as "tawny" (*piṅga*) and so forth, which belongs to a genus such as "fire" (*agni*) and is denoted by words like "fire," is a cause for figurative usage (*gauṇatva*) because it serves as the basis for the application of the word to a mere quality that is devoid of that genus.

3. The cause for figurative usage is the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) [of fire] in a boy (*māṇavaka*) and the like, based on the perception of qualities such as "tawny" belonging to fire and other things in the boy and others, even though he is denoted by words like "fire.
4. The function of words like "fire" in relation to a boy and others occurs when they are accompanied by the qualifying adjuncts (*upapada*) such as "boy" (*māṇavaka*).

5. The cause of figurative usage (*gauṇatva*) is dependence on a subordinate word that does not possess the quality [expressed by the primary term]. 6. The state of being a collection of phonemes (*varṇasamudāya*) that disregards the meaning of its constituent parts—such as the well-known usage of words like *agnimāṇavaka* in the *Paingya* and other texts—is a cause of figurative usage because the word "fire" (*agni*), which constitutes a part of that collection, serves as the basis for its application in the *Paingya* and other such contexts. 7. The status of the *Paingya* and other texts as the meaning of sentences such as *agnimāṇavaka*, wherein the word "fire" (*agni*) functions as a component of the sentence in the *Paingya* and elsewhere, is a cause of figurative usage due to its possession of the quality of abandoning its own [primary] meaning.

7. In the case of words such as *anyā* in the *Paiṅgi* and other texts, the cause for their being used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatva*) is their being well-known among those of little learning (*alpaśruta*), which is due to their dependence on a qualifying word (*upapada*) that possesses unknown qualities.

8. That text, such as the *Paiṅgi*, in which words like *anyā* are used by few speakers is "rarely used" (*alpaprayogin*); the state of being so (*alpaprayogitā*) is a cause for secondary usage, just like being little known (*alpasiddhatva*).

Having set aside these reasons for figurative usage (*gauṇatva*), it was established that the reason for the figurative application of words such as "fire" (*agni*)—namely, being denoted by a word like "fire" while possessing qualities such as fierceness (*ābhilāditva*) belonging to others—is the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of qualities like fierceness in others, such as a boy (*māṇavaka*), because this serves as the cause for the application of the word "fire" to one who possesses the qualities of fire.
(Sudhā, p. 1083). [The author] explains the *pūrvapakṣa* commentary: "In that case, because it is eternally for the sake of another, there is application in both ways;
there is no result superior to the direct denotation itself."
This being the case, since the words *pūṣan* and so forth would denote *anya* and so forth through a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*), there will be no displacement [of the mantras].
Otherwise, they would have to be transferred to wherever *pūṣan* and so forth occur.

Likewise, if the words *anya* and so forth were to denote the sun and so forth through a primary application (*mukhyā vṛtti*), then the Vedic text (*ārṣa*) and the water-offering (*udaka*) would be respected [as they stand].
This being the position reached, we reply:
"Because of the connection with the expression of meaning, the mantras are subsidiary to the sacrifice;
and since they have fulfilled their purpose through the primary sense, there is no assumption of Vedic authority for a secondary sense."

By the principle stated in [Jaimini Sūtra] 2.1.6.31, "Or rather, by virtue of the capacity for performance," mantras indeed postulate a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) for their application to the expressed meaning.
In that case, if there were a secondary (*gauṇa*) function that abandons its own primary sense (*jahatsvārthā*), then even a true [secondary] sense would lead to the postulation of a *śruti*.

If, however, even one who speaks of the secondary sense must first express its own primary meaning, then—since there is no reason to bypass that [primary sense]—once the scriptural injunction for application (*viniyoga-śruti*) has been postulated, the injunctions for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), along with the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the mantras, would already be satisfied and free from expectancy. Consequently, there would be no further cause for postulating a scriptural injunction, and thus no application [of the secondary sense]. Furthermore: "When the recitation of the mantra has already fulfilled its purpose, why should another means of recollection for the secondary meanings—which have attained their capacity unimpeded—not be accepted?"
Furthermore: "Why is the primary meaning conveyed even when a secondary meaning is intended?
If you say it is because [the primary] cannot otherwise be established, no; for it is established through meditation and so forth.
Even if it were merely optional, because it would be non-permanent, there would be a state of meaninglessness in the case where it does not apply."
One should always abandon the primary sense and resort to the side of the mantra;
for once the comprehension of the meaning is established, there is no need for a mantra to function as a denotative word.
Furthermore, the meaningfulness of the meanings of mantras will be accomplished through their primary sense.

The meaning of that very Sūtra is as follows: since the status of being subsidiary (*śeṣabhāva*) exists in the mantras due to their connection with the expression of meaning, therefore the connection with the meaning should occur through the very meaning that is innate (*autpattika*).
Why? Because its non-deviation [from the meaning] is established by that very [innate meaning] through eternal connection (*nityasaṃyoga*).
[Furthermore,] because they serve as sanctificatory acts (*saṃskāraka*), [the mantra] would not apply to what is not enjoined.
Commentary: Now, as for what was said— that there will be no displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the mantras beginning with "pūṣan"—
that displacement of them is indeed appropriate,
for a mantra is a purificatory agent (*saṃskāraka*).

Thus, since there would be no object to be modified (*saṃskārya*), [the mantra] would be purposeless; therefore, it will be applied to that purpose for which it was brought forth, and no fault whatsoever will arise.
This is the principle of the *barhis* (grass), ending with the disposal of the grass (*barhiḥ-praharaṇānta*). 2917. Barhiḥ-praharaṇāntam.

Or rather—since deities such as Pūṣan and others have not been mentioned, it is indeed appropriate that they are not employed through mantras in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), because a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is subordinate to that which is to be purified (*saṃskārya*), and because direct indicative power (*liṅga*) overrides the general context (*prakaraṇa*). But how can these [deities] be connected with Vedic rituals when they have not been so stated? Or, in the absence of an application to a general category of ritual parts (*aṅgasāmānya*), how can indicative power (*liṅga*) effect an application solely to the deity?
That is stated as follows:
"The designation [of the mantra] is applied by means of its completion through the recitation accompanying the sacrifice;
therefore, in accordance with its capacity, it belongs to that very deity in the rite."

For this designation (*samākhyā*)—namely, "the consecratory formulas for the sacrifice" (*yāgānumantraṇa*)—is untenable because of their connection with a specific sacrifice; therefore, it indicates [the application] by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the general nature of sacrifice.

Thus, since it is impossible to apply them through the specific [sacrifice], there arises the possibility of the force of the indicative power (*liṅga*) operating for the sake of applying them to a meaning that is possible.

Śabara: "Since mantras serve the purpose of reminding one of the ritual objects (*arthānām*), and since the power of the mantras is such that the subordinate elements (*guṇānām*) are repeated for each primary element (*pratipradhānam*), they serve both purposes. Therefore, there is an application (*viniyoga*) in both cases (the primary and the secondary)."
This being the position reached, it is replied:
Even in the case of a secondary (gauṇa) meaning, the capacity [of the word] does not manifest without another means of knowledge;
however, in the case of the primary (mukhya) meaning, that capacity is manifested from the word itself.

The primary intention (*tātparya*) resides in the literal sense, whereas the dependence on a secondary meaning is to be known through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); its existence is not established here [by the word itself].

[Soma]: The purpose is that even when there is an application (*viniyoga*) of mantras in a secondary sense, since it is possible for archetypal (*prākṛta*) mantras to manifest the modified (*vaikṛta*) substances, deities, and so forth through a secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*), the modification (*ūha*) is established; however, according to the final position (*siddhānta*), because the mantras must have a primary meaning, the modification is established.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: because of the connection with the expression of meaning—that is, due to the connection with the manifestation of the characteristics of the expression of meaning—the mantras would possess subsidiarity to the sacrifice (*kratuśeṣatva*). Therefore, there must be an "intrinsic connection" (*autpattika-saṃyoga*), meaning a connection precisely with the primary meaning that is innate; for there is an eternal connection with that meaning. [As stated in the Vṛtti: "In the case of *deya*, *upasādana*, *arhat*, *it*, *amī*, *gimul*, *gai*, and *yoṇi*..."
One applies a mantra to either the primary [meaning] or to both the secondary and primary meanings according to its indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Since both are the referents of the word, application to both is appropriate there;
however, because it occurs first, that application is restricted to the primary meaning.
Bhaṭṭa: Thus, the investigation into the application of *śruti* having been completed, the investigation into the application of *liṅga* is now introduced.

In this context, *liṅga* (syntactic indication) consists of the capacity to conform to the postulation of words expressive of the causal factors (*kāraka*) of the agent’s activity—which is characterized by being dependent on another (*parodeyatva*)—and to conform to the postulation of two words for the two substances, based on the established nature of the word as a noun-base (*suvinītva*).

Likewise, in the case of mantras, *liṅga* is the capacity to conform to the postulation of words expressing the status of being the intended object (*uddeśyatā*) regarding their own meaning, and to conform to the postulation of words expressing the status of being a causal factor (*kārakatva*) residing in themselves.
And since that [word] brings about the conceptualization of the form of the word, it is the authority for the application of its meaning through that medium.

In this regard, because it is impossible to investigate the specific details of *liṅga*—which consists in the inherent capacity of a thing—it must be considered whether the *liṅga* consisting in the capacity of a mantra applies the mantra only to a meaning that is directly denotable (*śakya*), or even to what is conveyed by a secondary (*jaghanya*) function. Since there is doubt regarding this, and because a mantra that serves as an auxiliary to the sacrifice possesses a specific capacity in the form of a requirement for recollection (such as the need to remember the act) even in a secondary sense—just as in the primary sense of "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*) and so forth—the application occurs by virtue of that capacity being common to both.

Just as in the case of [the command] "Bring [the cow]," and so forth, when there exists a cognizer who possesses expectancy and other such factors, the non-sublation of the primary meaning is of no consequence.

This being the position reached, because the cognition of a secondary meaning depends upon the apprehension of a relationship between the possible meanings, that cognition of the secondary meaning is delayed. Therefore, since the mantra and the like have already fulfilled their purpose through the application of the primary meaning, it is illogical for them to be applied to a secondary meaning. For this very reason, the requirement for its reminder is satisfied by other means such as meditation (*dhyāna*) alone.
For this very reason, in a context where the application of the primary meaning is not established, its assumption occurs solely by the force of the Vedic tradition (*mantrāmnāya*).

However, where there is a conflict with other qualities within the context, and where there exists a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) indicating a general connection, there is "transference" (*utkarṣa*), as in the case of the mantra for the *māruta-pūpa* [offering] in the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*; for it is the designation (*ākhyā*) itself—namely, "sacrificial consecration" (*yāgānumantraṇa*)—that indicates the general connection.
Even when transference is impossible, there is the application of the mantra to a secondary meaning within the context itself, as in the case of the *Manotā* hymn and others.

If that [primary meaning] is also impossible due to its being unapplied according to the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth, then the expression of that meaning serves only as a purposeless act (*aṣṭārthatva*), as in the case of muttering prayers (*japa*) and the like.
Maṇḍana states: "A mantra is not to be applied in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*). Śaṃkara says: "Because of its holding [the primary meaning], it has no secondary application."

The *barhirnyāya* refers to the principle stated in the sūtra: "The preparation of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) pertains to all rites because of its specific context" (3.8.15.13), which establishes that ritual properties (*dharma*s) are common to both the subsidiary and the principal acts. (Su. 3.8.15.136). This is the *barhirnyāya*.
The principle of the sacrificial post-hole, the grass-bundle, and the *barhis* is that which is not performed repeatedly; this is the worldly [application].
This principle of the sacrificial post-hole, the grass-bundle, and the *barhis* is to be observed here.

The ritual beginning with the *hāriyojana* cup and ending with the disposal of the *barhis* (*barhiḥ-praharaṇa*) is not to be performed on the first through ninth days of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), nor on the eleventh day; rather, a cessation must be made at the end of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

And on the twelfth day, the remainder of the rite must be performed, ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. (Vi. 9.1.9) [This concludes] the section concerning the strength [of the rule] starting from the sprinkling of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). 2918.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the requirements for the Upasad and Agnīṣomīya rites are fulfilled by extension (prasaṅga) through the sprinkling of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and other acts performed during the *ātithyā* rite. However,
regarding the cutting of the *barhis*, there is a repetition of the mantra for each individual cutting.
In the *Bhāṣya*,
it is stated that even in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and so forth is not for all purposes;
this should be consulted under the section titled "The Section on the Strainer and the Lightning" (3.8.17).
The word *barhis* is the cause for the cognition of grass, not for the cognition of something resembling grass.
Bhāṣya 3.1.15, p. 749. The word *barhis* does not invariably denote a consecrated object, as in the expression "the cows have gone away after taking the *barhis*";
rather, in all instances, this word denotes the genus (jāti).

For this very reason, in the case of the statement "the sacrificial grass (barhis) [is used] like the sacrificial post," the spreading [of the grass] is accomplished even without a formal consecration (*saṃskāra*). Regarding the doubt as to whether the word *barhis* is a term for a consecration or a term for a genus (*jāti*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that this is a term for a genus, not a term for a consecration.

According to the Bhāṣya (1.4.170), the word *barhis* can convey both: the actual grass and what resembles grass; the actual grass directly, and what resembles grass by means of the cognition of grass.

Regarding the mantra for binding the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), "The binding for Indrāṇī" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.1.2.2), and the mantra for carrying it, "I carry the head of Bṛhaspati," these two mantras are not to be employed when the *barhis*, having been prepared during the *ātithyā* rite, is being bound and carried to the location of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice. For those two mantras are to be employed when bringing [the grass] from the place of cutting, not when bringing it from the *gārhapatya* fire-place to the *āhavanīya* fire-place.
The *ātithyā* offering is performed at the site of the *gārhapatya* fire, and the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice at the site of the *āhavanīya* fire. (Vi.

1.1.2.1). In the mantra for spreading the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), in the case of the *maitra* oblation of cooked rice, there is a modification (*ūha*) of the word "green" (*harita*) by the word "red" (*rakta*).
This should be seen under the entry "Modification of the word 'red'" on page 1226 of the Mīmāṃsākośa.

In the section concerning strength and weakness (*balābalādhikaraṇa*, 3.3.14), it will be stated that although the status of the *videvana* and other rites as belonging to the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice appears to follow from their position in the text, this is set aside by their status as belonging to the *rājasūya* sacrifice because of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 1059). Regarding strength and weakness: in the absence of contradiction, even that which is weak is to be accepted.
That which is absolutely a semblance of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*), such as the cognition of a mirage, must be rejected at all times.

On the other hand, that which becomes non-valid (*apramāṇa*) due to dependence on a conflict of strength should be determined to be indeed valid when there is no such conflict. (Vārttika 1.1.5.10, p. 227: *balābala*).
"One has a single staircase and the other has a single pillar;
the speed of both is equal and there is no obstacle between them.
Yet, because they are adversaries, only one of the two shall obtain the fruit thereof."
"When this [subject] has been grasped by the first [means], the fifth descends in five ways" (1.3.1.14, p.
834). Regarding strength and weakness: "That which is established through conceptual construction is stronger than that which is established through conventional renown."
Page 227, 1|3|1|10: The relative strength (*balābala*) regarding the order [of ritual performance] as determined by direct assertion (*śruti*) and other means will be discussed in the fifth chapter.
Bhāṣya 5|1|12:
Furthermore, that which constitutes the relative strength when there is a conflict (*samavāya*) among direct assertion and the other criteria will be explained [there].

"Because it is not in conflict with that which remains [to be established], for us, it has as its scope only what remains. (*Vārttika* 3.1.11, p. 652). The relative strength characterized by the relationship of sublation and non-sublation is examined based on the scriptural text, the sense, and the position—such as in the passage "The *ṛc* is recited loudly," and so forth. And since that [relative strength] is caused by contradiction, it depends upon the primary scriptural text; it does not become the opposite through an examination of the words of the injunction or the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
(*Sūtra-bhāṣya*, p. 1171).

The Topic on Strength and Weakness: "In the case of a conflict between direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyāna*), each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding because of its remoteness from the purpose.
Commentary: The means of application have been stated—namely, direct assertion, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name.
When these come into conflict, it is considered which among them is more powerful.

Because words function toward a single purpose and cannot be combined simultaneously, there is a deliberation between each pair [of means of proof]. This is the investigation into the relative strength and weakness of direct statement (*śruti*). In this regard, which is stronger: direct statement or indicative mark (*liṅga*)?
What, then, is the illustrative example here? "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse."

In this regard, it is considered: is there a restrictive rule that the worship (upasthāna) must be performed either for Indra or for the Gārhapatya fire, or is it that it must be performed for the Gārhapatya alone?
If these two reasons possess equal force, then there is an option (vikalpa).

Now, if direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful, then the Gārhapatya fire alone is to be worshipped. But what here is the direct statement? And what is the indicative mark (*liṅga*)? Direct statement is the hearing of the word "Gārhapatya.
The indicative mark, however, is the capacity of the word "Indra" in the verse, "Never art thou barren, O Indra; thou never failest the donor," which denotes a specific deity.

Now, what is called a sentence (*vākya*)? A sentence is a collection of words that expresses a unified meaning. For example, this is a sentence: "He worships the Gārhapatya fire with the *aindrī* verse," and this too is a sentence: "Never art thou barren. In both cases, [the words] express [the meaning] by being combined.
Words denote meaning;
therefore, this deliberation concerns the sentence as a whole, not the relationship between direct assertion (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Or rather, direct assertion, indicative mark, and sentence must be distinguished: "this is the difference between direct assertion and sentence," and "this is the difference between indicative mark and sentence."
That is now explained: first, that which is the capacity of a word to denote its meaning is the *liṅga* (indicative mark).
That which is the denotation of the meaning, understood from the mere hearing of the word itself, is understood through *śruti* (direct statement).
Hearing is *śruti*.
It has already been stated that a single word or a sentence has a single meaning.
This [single meaning] is seen to be present in all sentences alike, yet it appears distinct in each case.
For instance, in this case, the fact that Indra is to be worshipped by means of the mantra "kadā cana starīrasi" is not understood merely from the hearing of any particular word therein.
Nor does a different word uttered in proximity possess the capacity by which this could be understood;
for in this very *ṛc*, the word "Indra" exists, which is able to make known a specific deity,
and having made it known through that, there is a purpose.
Therefore, the word "Indra" is employed in the *upasthāna* (ritual attendance) to Indra;
and because it forms a single syntactical unit with that [word], the other words are not distinguished [in their application].
However, for us, there is no such attendance performed for the sake of honoring the capacity of any particular word.
However, we understand this from the direct mention (*śruti*) of the word "Gārhapatya" itself, not from the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
If the indicative mark were stronger, Indra would be the one to be worshipped;
if it is the word "Gārhapatya," then the Gārhapatya fire is the one to be worshipped.

In that case, it is the conflict between *liṅga* (indicative power) and *vākya* (syntactical connection) that must be deliberated here, not the conflict between *śruti* (direct statement) and *liṅga*.
If *liṅga* is stronger, then Indra is to be approached because of the word "Indra's" capacity to denote that specific deity; but if it is *vākya*, then the *gārhapatya* fire is to be approached.
For this is indeed a syntactical connection: "One approaches the *gārhapatya* with the *aindrī* [verse]."

This is not so. Although this is a syntactical connection (*vākya*), there is also a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) intervening here; and that which is the *śruti* in this case is contradicted by the indicative mark (*liṅga*), not the syntactical connection.

How so? For even though the indicative mark is stronger, the phrase "he stands worshipping with the Aindrī [verse]" necessarily attains syntactical unity with the presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*).
For if it were not brought near, it would contradict the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
However, that meaning which is understood from the direct scriptural mention (*śravaṇa*) of the *gārhapatya* fire is set aside by the stronger indicative mark;
it is not connected with the act of worship (*upasthāna*).
For instance, the word *indra-gārhapatya* might denote proximity.
Now, if the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is the authoritative means of knowledge, then the worship of Indra, which has been suggested by the indicative mark (*liṅga*), is set aside.
Therefore, the conflict is indeed between the direct statement and the indicative mark, not between the indicative mark and the syntactical connection (*vākya*).
Alternatively, there is no single unified statement here regarding the worship of Indra or the worship of the Gārhapatya fire.
Why is that? Because of the presence of the word "Indra" in the mantra, Indra is primary; because of the hearing of the accusative case-ending, the Gārhapatya is primary.
Therefore, there is a conflict between direct Vedic statement (śruti) and indicative mark (liṅga).
Or—(in this section, this [discussion] is merely slightly modified according to the Bhāṣya and other sources prior to the Vārttika).
Now, the relative strength and weakness of all six means of proof, beginning with direct audition (śruti), is being investigated.
Since that [investigation] is not possible when they have different objects, "convergence upon a single object" (samavāya) has been cited as the subject matter.

Regarding this, some say that the inclusion of the term "non-contradiction" (avirodha) must be made. Why? Because, as it is said: "In the case of 'He buys with a red [cow],' even though there is a coexistence [of qualities], since there is no contradiction, they do not at all deliberate upon relative strength and weakness."

The single accessory (*śeṣa*), such as the act of purchasing (*haraṇa*) and so forth, is connected to the *prakriyā* (contextual procedure) through direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest; it belongs to the specific act of purchase by virtue of syntactical connection (*vākya*), and to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice by virtue of context (*prakaraṇa*).

Even though there is a coexistence of direct statement and context, there is no conflict because they serve as mutual supports; thus, an investigation into their relative strength (*balābala*) does not arise, since a general rule without a specific application is untenable.

Furthermore, if [the accessory] were connected merely to the essential form of the purchase, it would be purposeless; therefore, syntactical connection and context are required by direct statement and syntactical connection.
Therefore, the apprehension of contradiction must be performed;
or rather, it need not be performed.
Why? Because "having the same object" is stated [as the condition] for coexistence (*samavāya*).
Furthermore, when there is a single purpose, no coexistence of the remaining means of knowledge is perceived.
First of all, in the case of the "red" [calf] and so forth, there is no coexistence of means of knowledge;
for mere possibility in one place does not constitute coexistence.
What then? It is the unity of the object (*viṣayaikatva*).
Here, the connection of the redness (*aruṇya*) with the purchase (*kraya*) is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

However, that [redness], whose connection with the action and its factors is already established by the scripture, subsequently becomes the object of the purchase by virtue of further requirement (*apekṣā*).

Since the purpose is not accomplished by that much alone, when there is another requirement, the purchase—which possesses a connection to the *apūrva*—serves the purpose of the Jyotiṣṭoma; thus, there is no identity of subject matter. Consequently, it is not contradictory for all [the requirements] to be the cause of application (*viniyoga*).
Nor is the sublation of the proximate seen here upon the inclusion of the remote.

For one who accepts the purchase does not sublate the connection of the *aruṇā* (the red cow) with the action, nor does one performing it in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice sublate the connection with the purchase.

However, where there is a single subordinate element (*śeṣa*), and that very element is understood as being subordinate to one [action] by a single means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—without any obstruction from another connection—and where a subsequent [means of knowledge] is impossible without sublating that [first], it serves the purpose of another subordinate element; and since a thing that has already fulfilled its purpose through one connection lacks expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), a further application (*viniyoga*) is untenable. In such a case, there is a conflict (*samavāya*) between the two means of knowledge, characterized by their mutual exclusion and their having the same object.

Likewise, where even though there is a plurality of subsidiaries (*śeṣa*), they are based on an equal benefit toward a single principal (*śeṣin*)— such that by one means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) one subsidiary is perceived as a means of accomplishment, and by another means a different one— and wherein the principal, its benefit having been accomplished by one, does not require another subsidiary, there too there is a coexistence (*samavāya*) because they do not exclude each other's object.
And that [coexistence] constitutes a case of relative strength and weakness (*balābala-adhikaraṇa*) only when a contradiction exists.
Thinking, "I shall remove his remaining lingering doubt regarding the status of being a single sentence," he says: "Or rather, it is not because of a single sentence here.

Alternatively, intending to discuss the topic of "being a single sentence" as it pertains specifically to the Brāhmaṇa, he may extend [the discussion] by implication to the Mantra as well, since it is present there too. In that context, the sentence to be analyzed is: "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse. The intention of this is as follows: through the direct statement (śruti) of the instrumental case in "with the Aindrī," its status as a subordinate element (śeṣatva) is understood, though the specific object to which it is subordinate (śeṣin) has not yet been identified.

As for the fact that the accusative case in the word *gārhapatyam* expresses merely a state of being subordinate (*śeṣitva*) toward something, there is no contradiction between this and the indicative power (*liṅga*).
For, in connection with another word, the *aindrī* verse would indeed function as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) according to its actual meaning,
or the *gārhapatya* fire would be subordinate toward whichever Āgneyī verse it might be connected with.
"The mutual proximity of those two [words] sublates the indication of Indra, and that [proximity] constitutes the sentence.
To this, [the author] replies: "Not so," and first presents the scriptural mention (*śruti*) of the *gārhapatya* fire.
For even mutual proximity can be interpreted without contradiction by overriding the scriptural mention.
But if it is indeed [the case] regarding the Gārhapatya fire, this is because it is produced by a distraction;
for its validity is not intrinsic— this is the intended meaning.
Another opponent, however, taking the apprehension of a cognition to be absolute and considering it to be one of doubt, uncertainty, error, or indecision, says: "This is not correct;

because there is doubt regarding the cognition from the inferential mark (*liṅga*), and there is no such retention [of certainty] regarding that [cognition] or the sacred scripture (*śruti*). Thus, it remains undetermined whether this [mantra] belongs to Indra or not."
Since it lacks authority when there is a conflict with direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), there is no consideration of relative strength or weakness between the two.

However, since there is an unhesitating and absolute conviction that "this mantra is intended for this very purpose," that conviction deserves to be weighed as being equal in strength to the direct Vedic statement.
But surely, it is not so at all?
The proponent of the first position thinks that at times [the mark] may be indistinguishable from what is not a valid mark.
But the other [proponent], grasping this very state of doubt as his own intended point, says: "If this were so, there would be no such thing as a valid mark at all.

The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin), however, says: "If the mark, provoked merely by the apprehension of a qualified cognition, abandons its validity altogether—well, let it not be a valid means of knowledge; yet, a doubt certainly arises regarding those very things known through the mark."
But how is it that, having abandoned the state of being "with distinction" (*saviśeṣatva*), doubt itself is cited as being "with perplexity" (*savicikitsatva*)?
Or how is the thorough knowledge of the mark (*liṅga*) stated as if it were an established fact?
This is not a fault.
The state of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) being fully known refers to the time when there is no contradiction, while its state of being doubtful refers to the time of contradiction.
This is what is meant:
the power of application (*viniyojakatva*) of the indicative mark that was understood at a time of non-contradiction remains exactly so in all cases.
What then? A doubt arises.
Since application has been accepted elsewhere because of the absence of contradiction, does it remain exactly so here, or is it set aside by something?
Or rather, is its lack of authority quite evident?
As long as doubt persists, direct Vedic revelation (śruti) is not perceived;
and such being the case, since the assumption of anything else is untenable, [the inference] lacks authority.
For in the case of an indicative mark (liṅga), only its capacity is directly perceived.
And by that much alone, the application (viniyoga) has not been stated;
