nor does that which is unstated possess authority regarding the ritual action.
Just as, even though [the rule "one should sacrifice with the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya" exists], the Vaiśya does not perform that [sacrifice].

Its indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not the factor that determines its application. However, the opponent—fearing that the statement regarding non-authoritativeness refers only to cases of contradiction and is not universal—shows its authoritativeness by stating: "In the proximity of this [mantra], which possesses a context (*prakaraṇa*), they recite these words.
This very point has been explained under the sūtras *api vā prayogasāmarthyān mantro ’bhidhānavācī syāt* and *aviśiṣṭās tu vākyārthaḥ*.

Alternatively, the proponent of the final doctrine (siddhāntavādin), thinking, "I shall demonstrate that the proof for contradiction is even more easily available," first demonstrated the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) independently.
When this has been done, it follows that the opponent himself must conceive of its lack of authority by means of scripture (*śruti*) and inference (*anumāna*).
Consequently, my position will be easily won.
In this regard, the other [author]—without considering the subject matter of the contradiction—has established that there is validity for the time being and has asserted an equality of strength.
Even granting the relative strength and weakness, there is still no contradiction.

For example, there is no contradiction because, according to the *upadeśa* (direct instruction) and other criteria, the assistance provided by the *prayāja* offerings serves both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*).
This is because even when an auxiliary (*guṇa*) is enjoined only once, it follows the primary (*pradhāna*) as many times as necessary, since it must be performed by all [the subsidiaries].

If it is argued that there is a contradiction because the word "Indra" is secondary (*gauṇa*) due to its etymological derivation (*avayava-prasiddhi*), whereas it is primary (*mukhya*) with respect to the deity Indra due to its conventional usage (*samudāya-prasiddhi*):
No;
for the objection is answered by the difference in application (*prayoga-bheda*).
For when [the duties] are taught simultaneously, the possibility of [multiple] *hotṛ*s being present is heard from the scriptural texts concerning possibility and so forth.

But when there is a difference in application, at the time of designating the *gārhapatya* fire, one will proceed by accepting either the quality of being a means for sacrifice or the connection with Indra’s power and sovereignty;
however, at the time of designating *indra*, he is the primary [deity], so there is no contradiction. Therefore, there is no sublation (*bādha*). Thus [it is concluded].
This being the case, we reply:
Direct Assertion (śruti) is stronger than Indicative Power (liṅga).
Why? Because this mantra denotes the Gārhapatya fire by its very word.
The fact that Indra is the one who gives the command (*indrājñātva*) is inferred from its capacity (*sāmarthya*), even though it is not explicitly stated by words (*aśabda*).

As for the claim that inference of what is heard (*śrutānumāna*) occurs through context (*prakaraṇa*) and capacity—that was said to be invalid in such cases only when [the meaning] is already connected with the word itself.
However, the opponent, thinking that the non-verbal nature of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been stated as being universal, argues: "In that case, there is no contradiction."
What then? Intending to say that it is precisely because [the mark] lacks authority (*apramāṇatva*), he says "if it were so.

The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntavādin*), however, now demonstrates his own position just as the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) had previously stated the authority of the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
For such is the meaning of the context: that the sacrifice might be assisted by this [mark] through its capacity.

And since it is not possible for this [word] to assist [the ritual] otherwise than by expressing its own meaning, its application (*viniyoga*) therein is enjoined. But another [person] says: "This person has come to the path previously mentioned for my sake; he will now depart. To this he replies: "If it is rooted in *śruti*, it cannot be sublated by another *śruti*."
Therefore, if this object is non-verbal, then it is not an authoritative means of knowledge at all;
if, however, it is verbal, then it is of equal strength [to other means].
But the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) refutes both possibilities with the words "nor even."
Because an inferential scripture (*ānumānikī śruti*) comes into being when there is no contradiction, and fails to arise when there is a contradiction;

for in a case where a mantra has not been rendered free of expectancy by a direct scriptural injunction (*pratyakṣā śruti*) regarding its application, everything that is postulated for the sake of establishing that application becomes Vedic, since it is sealed by the principle that it could not otherwise be accounted for (*anyathānupapatti*).

Where it is clearly understood that "one should worship the Gārhapatya fire," and where the benefit to the performance—namely the purpose of the scriptural injunction—is already established, the Veda does not tolerate the assumption that "one must perform the worship of Indra.
Therefore, the indicative power (*liṅga*) is weak.
Furthermore, "in all cases, the occurrence of alternatives (*vikalpa*) is considered improper."
For the existence and non-existence of both [options] in a single object are difficult to maintain.
By an independent direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), the worship of the Gārhapatya fire is enjoined eternally; by an independent indicative mark (*liṅga*), the worship of Indra is enjoined.
When one of the two must be adopted, the other—though enjoined—is set aside; and according to that [adopted] alternative, the other—though enjoined—is performed.
Furthermore, the non-performance of that [act] is not enjoined;
moreover, the fault of assuming something else not heard in the Veda is equal [to the other],
because it contradicts what is well-known.

The performance of what is enjoined is established as "to be done," while the other is established as "not to be done"; thus, both are transcended by action. Therefore, there is no optionality (vikalpa) at all.
As for the claim that there is a combination (samuccaya) mentioned for the sake of resolving the contradiction, that is an error; the contradiction indeed exists.

How so? "For when the context of the mantra has been established here as one that leaves no further expectation, the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—which requires a goal to be accomplished—is understood as being restricted solely to that [context]. This mantra is one, and the context is one.
And that which has been enjoined once must possess a single uniform character.
In that regard, at the time of the application by the Śruti, there may or may not be a state of being free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) regarding the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the mantra.
If, first of all, that [expectancy] does not exist, then the very application (*viniyoga*) remains unestablished.
For it is not logical that there be an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for that which has already been applied.
If, however, such an expectancy exists, then—since the establishment of application depends upon expectancy—the application based on indicative power (*liṅga*) would be untenable.
Indeed, if both were to be resorted to simultaneously, there would be a contradiction as to whether this [mantra] possesses expectancy or does not possess it.

Even this being so, if the operation [of the cognition] were to occur solely by means of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it would be known by whom it is first rendered free from expectancy;
in that case, being rendered free from expectancy simultaneously by both, it would belong to both.
However, there is indeed a distinction between the two means of valid cognition.
Because verbal testimony (*śruti*) functions most rapidly;

therefore, once a mantra has been assigned by it, there is no further requirement for indicative power (*liṅga*). Thus, the superior strength of verbal testimony is established. When the weakness of the latter [indicative power] has been set forth in the Sūtra, the Commentator [states]:
Here, [the author] explains the superiority of the former due to disregard for the latter:

"(pp. 849–847). (Consideration of the Superiority of Śruti: What, then, is the prima facie view? It should be understood that all means of knowledge possess equal authority. Why? Because "in some cases, the authoritative status of a particular [means] is determined by its own inherent capacity."
For that capacity of his does not arise in dependence on anything else.

In all cases, including perception and so forth, the movement [of cognition] through a substance constitutes both the nature of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and a semblance of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*).

That which is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) therein never becomes a semblance of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*). Even that which is a semblance thereof does not at all become a valid means of knowledge.
Furthermore, the semblance of validity belongs eternally to the semblance itself, and not to the valid means of knowledge.
Nor is the validity of sublation (bādha) untenable therein, because a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is incapable of being sublated. Furthermore,
the validity of everything established by scripture and so forth has been firmly established within its own respective domain.
Nor is this [knowledge] subject to movement toward another object where weakness might be suspected; nor is it possible for the knowledge thus established to be known as unarisen;
nor is there destruction of what has arisen through a subsequent [state], because of its inherent fragility;
nor is there the removal of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Because the formative impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the cause of memory is not entirely destroyed in every case;
nor can there be an application [of the rule] based on the result of performance, because the cognition of performance is firm.
Therefore, in all cases, there is an option (*vikalpa*) due to equality of strength.
"If sublation were to be postulated, the opposite would follow;
for the subsequent cannot arise without first not being sublated by the preceding.
Indeed, among the means of knowledge such as scripture (*śruti*) and the rest, each preceding one operates more swiftly than the succeeding."
Therefore, he must subsequently attain self-mastery through that very restraint;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a contradictory sublation.
Furthermore, the application of that which is capable [of its function] is also established by means of direct revelation (*śruti*) and so forth.
"Capacity and so forth would not exist without syntactic unity and the like.
(Even though application is perceived through direct statement (*śruti*), nevertheless, it is not possible for that which lacks capacity; this is the meaning of "also" (*api*).

However, for capacity, there is no such uniformity as there is for sentence and context—namely, the fulfillment of expectancy in the form of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) and the removal of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣānirlepa*)—among the indicators (*liṅga*), sentence (*vākya*), and context (*prakaraṇa*); this is the meaning.)
*Sudhā*, p. 2918.
Although the reading here is "yogo 'vakalpate" in the *Ānandamaya* [section], nevertheless, the reading should be accepted according to the *Sudhā*.
(Ke.)
When the capacity of something for a particular syntactic connection is understood at the time of its origin, it cannot be overturned at the time of its application;
rather, the application is rightly determined by following that capacity.
Likewise, when no relationship with another exists through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), no power for such a connection is to be postulated.
When a relationship exists, the capacity [of words] is established because it would otherwise be impossible;
thus, the sentence possesses superior force.
Likewise, in all cases, the nature of being a sentence is rooted in expectancy (ākāṅkṣā).
Therefore, even in that case, for those who possess sufficient intelligence, it is understood with absolute certainty that this [conclusion] exists;
whereas in its absence, since this [conclusion] does not exist, the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself—consisting of the desire for the initial statement and so forth—is superior.
However, that which contradicts it...
The section on *balādalā* (the "forceful" and the "weak"): the perception of syntactic unity with another [word] is an error.
Likewise, all expectations (ākāṅkṣās) have as their objects those things that are proximate.

For it is not possible for that [expectation] to establish a connection with something expected that is not proximate; therefore, where there is proximity, everything [is understood], and thus proximity possesses greater force.
Furthermore, direct perception itself declares the connection in the case of generality (sāmānya).
Therefore, the relative strength and weakness is the reverse. Alternatively, this is considered only when there is a conflict;
and here, there is no conflict.
Since the application [of authority] is possible in both cases,
therefore, even when there is coexistence, all [means of knowledge] possess validity. This being established regarding the Śruti, it is now stated:
"Because of the remoteness of the meaning from the direct Vedic statement (śruti), the subsequent ones among these are sublated.
Why? Because regarding the declaration of application, direct Vedic statement (śruti) is accepted as the basis for all of these;
the cognition [of application] stands through proximity to it and through remoteness from it."

If even *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth were to possess independent authority, then this [objection] would be tenable; however, their authority, like that of *smṛti*, is mediated through the inference of *śruti*. For in this matter, *śruti* alone is the sole means of valid cognition.
That [perception], however, exists in six ways in accordance with the eight means of apprehension.
But how is it that these [means] do not possess independent validity?
It is said:
It has been established that "Dharma is a purposeful matter characterized by an injunction" (1.1.2).
And likewise it was stated: "It would be independent of the word" (1.2.11).
In this context, those syllables which are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and are employed [in the ritual] are called *śruti*, because they function through the sense of hearing.

But where syllables that cannot be applied are perceived directly, and those which do apply them are postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), there the [other] means of proof such as indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth come into play.
Consequently, in this way, there occurs a remoteness of the object (*arthaviprakarṣa*).

Regarding the application (*viniyoga*) of the *aindrī* verse, when both direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*) set out together, if the syllables of the direct statement that effect the application are perceived to be capable of bringing the mantra to mind through its indicative power (*liṅga*), then, before one begins to postulate the application of those [syllables] by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other such means through a process of inference, the application has already been communicated by those directly perceived [syllables]. And once that [application] is understood, the mantra becomes free of expectancy toward the contexts, and the context likewise becomes free of expectancy toward the mantra.

This being the case, since the fallacious context (*prakaraṇābhāsa*) can be accounted for otherwise, there is no force in the assumption of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) denoting Indra. Furthermore, application (*viniyoga*) is not established without a direct scriptural statement.

This has been explained in many ways previously: that whatever is assumed regarding the meaning of the Veda when it is still expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) is based on sense-perception (*aindrika*), and nothing else.
Therefore, direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful;
for there is nothing else to be directly depended upon in its case, as there is for indicative mark (*liṅga*) in relation to direct statement.
And it has been said:
"He who has no dependence upon anything whatsoever shall be stronger than it;
how indeed could one whose conduct is dependent on another act [otherwise]?

For among the means of knowledge beginning with direct revelation (*śruti*), each preceding one operates independently of each succeeding one and is therefore stronger; however, each subsequent one, whose authority is dependent upon the preceding, is unable to subvert that very [preceding authority].
It has already been stated that the authority of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is not determined by inferring a scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Now, it might be argued: "But was it not also said that what is incapable [of performing an action] cannot be enjoined"?
True, this was said.
This is improper; it is proper.
Why? "The application [of a mantra] by means of the Vedic text is not understood as being dependent upon the indicative power (*liṅga*).
Rather, once the application is known, the determination of its expressive capacity follows from that."
For once the application (*viniyoga*) has occurred, when the question arises, "How will this accomplish [the purpose]?", there arises the determination of how it is capable [of doing so].
In that case, although its capacity regarding that object is not perceived by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*), it is nevertheless inferred precisely from the observation of the application.

As it was said in the context of [Jaimini Sūtra] 3.2.13: "But on account of the scriptural statement, the *aindrī* mantra would be used [for Agni], even though it does not correspond to the actual fact."
But surely, since the application of that which previously lacked capacity is not possible, its capacity must be inferred as before;
and consequently, there would be the consequence of it being weaker than direct indicative power (*pratyakṣaliṅga*).
True.
It is postulated as existing prior [to the application], but it is not understood as being already present beforehand.
For there is no means of apprehending the capacity for denoting the *gārhapatya* fire in those verses dedicated to Indra (*aindra*) unless they have been applied.
Since they exist even before the application is accomplished, they are inferred only later on the basis of the impossibility [of their meaning] otherwise.

But even so, the remoteness of the meaning is equal. For it is said: "To whatever extent there may be a distraction in the case of the indicative mark (liṅga) when it leads to the inference of a direct statement (śruti), to that same extent there is also [a distraction] in the case of the direct statement itself, which has become the object of inference from the indicative mark."
"For in every case, when something is not perceived, its remoteness from perception is established through inference;
and that [inference] is the same in both instances.
It is true that this is the same, but it is not applicable with respect to their relative strength or weakness."
Why? "Because the designation of application is remote, it is understood to be weak;

and that [weakness] may exist in the former inference, but in some way not in the latter. For in the case of *liṅga* (indicative power), since the designation of application was previously non-existent, its remoteness arises from the necessity of inferring a *śruti* (direct scriptural statement).

Furthermore, when the expression of application (*viniyoga*) has ceased in the *Śruti*, because this is the case, the subsequent inference—which functions on the grounds that "surely there must be some capacity"—does not produce a specific cognition of application.
For when two means of knowledge proceed together, that which arrives by relying on the locus of application causes a displacement that results in weakness.
However, once the application has been determined, even if it subsequently withstands inference, there is nevertheless no such displacement.
By this, the [inferior] means of proof such as indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), and so forth, are explained.

For in every case, it is impossible to apply a subsequent [means of proof] after one has already inferred the application through a preceding one; however, once the application has been established by the preceding [means], the subsequent one follows as a necessary consequence.
The section concerning *balādalā* is the conclusion that it is a conceptualization based merely on its existence.
He said:
It is indeed logical that, for the time being, direct statement (śruti) possesses greater force than indicative mark (liṅga) due to its status as a substance (dravyatva).
(Page 828)

(Regarding contradiction with Śruti: Just as the relative strength and weakness among these [means of proof] arises from factors such as remoteness of meaning, so too must it be demonstrated among those of the same class due to the commonality of their logical grounds (*hetu*).
For example, first, regarding Śruti itself, there is a connection concerning subsidiary elements (*śeṣa*) through the relationship of general rule and specific exception.

Because of the hearing of a non-specific injunction, "One divides the *puroḍāśa* into four parts," which would apply even to the *āgnīṣomīya* sacrifice and others, the division into four parts is restricted to the specific case by the hearing of a specific injunction: "One divides the *āgneya* into four parts."

Likewise, in the case of the remaining conflict of co-occurrence (*samavāya*), when the *āhavanīya* fire is obtained even for the *avabhṛtha* rite through the general syntactic coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the injunction "one offers in the *āhavanīya*," that [application] is set aside by the specific connection expressed in the text, "one performs the *avabhṛtha* in the waters.
Furthermore, the distinction between strength and weakness will arise based on whether the application is doubtful or certain.

In this same manner, two scriptural texts (*śruti*) should be cited as examples for conflicts involving priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*), conflicts involving subordinate qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth.
Similarly, the fact that the animal is the object [of the sacrifice] is understood through word-hearing (*padaśruti*),
which is overridden by the stronger syntactic hearing (*samānapratyayaśruti*) established by the action;
likewise, when the status of the root-meaning as the object has been established by word-hearing.
"By the scriptural injunction regarding meditation (*bhāvanā*), the human goal is that which is to be accomplished" (p.
Furthermore, the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*) should be illustrated by analyzing each case individually.
Thus, first, the matter has been examined regarding the direct means of knowledge, such as verbal testimony (*śruti*) and the rest.
Following this very same method, it should also be investigated in the case of inference (*anumāna*) and the others, specifically regarding the coexistence of similar and dissimilar factors.

In that regard, the relative strength of the similar and the dissimilar—whether they are inferential means based on perception, or inferential means based on other inferences—should be explained by the same path previously described.

For example, the *śruti* and other means of knowledge obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) will be sublated by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the case of modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*). Furthermore, in this context, sublation may also occur in the reverse order; for even that which is inferential (*ānumānika*) in a preceding stage may be superseded by a subsequent direct perception.
Just as [the capacity] is obtained by implication (*sāmarthyena*) in the case of black peppercorns,

and this capacity has all things as its object, so too should it be understood that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) exists solely within the mantra. Furthermore, it will be explained that even those other word-meanings which have no other recourse also possess the status of being indicative marks.

What, then, is the "attainment" (prāpti) of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in this context? It is its impossibility of occurring otherwise, and so forth. But how is it when there is a scriptural statement (*śruti*) that is inferential while the indicative mark is perceptible, as in the case of a conflict between a Smṛti rule and a Vedic indicative mark?
In that case, while another basis for the Smṛti may be possible, such is not the case for the Indicative Mark (liṅga); therefore, it must be understood that the Smṛti alone is stronger.
Whenever even a weaker means of knowledge (pramāṇa) sublates [another], if some purposeful result ensues, then the sublation should be applied in the reverse manner.

As it has been said: "In the case of the injunction 'he sprinkles the rice-grains' (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), one sets aside the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and adopts [the meaning] as being the means to the *apūrva*. Likewise: "When a weak means of knowledge has a powerful support, even then there is a reversal [of the expected strength], as was stated in the case of the non-contradiction of the learned (*śiṣṭākopah*)."
For all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), mutual contradiction occurs through the medium of their objects, not by virtue of their own intrinsic nature.

In that regard, when two means of valid cognition conflict concerning an object and its properties, although there may be a different degree of relative strength (*balābala*) from the perspective of the means themselves, nevertheless, because they must rely upon the object to be known (*prameya*), even that which is weak by its own nature becomes stronger when it is sublated [by the stronger], thereby attaining conformity with that object.
As it has been said: "The ritual acts such as sipping water (*ācamana*) are the primary elements (*padārtha*); their sequence (*krama*) is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*)."
And thus it is said in the world: "Even the people of the city and the countryside, though they possess great power, are oppressed by even weak men who have taken refuge with the king.
In this way, the Sūtra has been explained, as well as the Bhāṣya up to the point where the contradiction between direct statement (śruti) and indicative mark (liṅga) is established.

(841) When there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*), how can it be determined that the quality of being one-year-old (*ekahāyanī*)—which, by the force of the sentence concerning the red cow (*aruṇā*) and so forth, would attain the status of a qualifier through non-difference and grammatical coreferentiality—is instead understood as a subordinate factor (*arthanirūpaṇa*) by virtue of the direct statement in the instrumental case? For while a sentence postulates the force (*sāmarthya*) of the verbal root’s meaning—just as one who ascends a staircase takes the second step—by that time, the application (*viniyoga*) has already been established by the direct statement; thus, there is a great difference [between the two].

When there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), since the recitations (*anuvacana*) such as the *viṃśati* are obtained for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and the like through context, whereas they are determined to serve the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*)—such as the desire for stability—by direct statement alone, there is an apprehension of context [in the case of the former].
And because these recitations consist of action and take the form of an agent's activity, they are subject to apprehension by context; thus, they serve as an illustration of such a conflict.

Regarding the statement, "The *tila* [sesame] itself is the *upasads* with the *sāhuti* for the twelve-day *ahīna* sacrifice," some maintain that since the number twelve is not an action (*akriyātva*), and thus lacks the nature of being something to be performed (*anitikartavyatātmakatva*), it is impossible for it to be grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*) as a non-existent entity. Consequently, because there is no actual relationship established except through mere proximity (*saṃnidhi*), which requires the prior assumption of a context, it is proper to cite this as an example of a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and position (*sthāna*). However, that view has not been accepted here. Why? Because: "If this number were either inherent in the substance or independent..."

"It is apprehended as a state of negation (*netthabhāva*) because it excludes the form of action. Thus, by means of that which establishes non-performance— namely, the performance [of the negative injunction] directed toward the object to be enjoined—
how can it be apprehended as a negation qualified by the number twelve?
And here too, how can there be a subordinate application for that which is assigned to non-existence? For as long as one imagines the capacity for a single syntactical unity with the truth,
so long has the state of being primary been attained by the directly perceived genitive case-ending.
For indeed, nothing other than a group of letters (varṇa) is called "ahīna."

"What is the example for a conflict between the order of the text (*śrutikrama*)? It is said: by virtue of the sequence, the properties of the cord, such as being made of the middle part of *darbha* grass and so on, would belong to the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice; however, by virtue of direct statement (*śruti*), they are assigned to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)."
Indeed, in this sequence of sacrificial posts, the entire girdle is heard [in the scriptures];
together with its ritual function (dharma), it gradually attains the state of being a remnant of the animal sacrifice.
To whatever extent one imagines its sequence— beginning with context and so forth—
it is superseded by direct Vedic statement (śruti), because it is devoid of those four [criteria].
To the extent that sequential order imagines even a mere desire as its sole basis,
the Vedic revelation (Śruti) removes the girdle of kings from afar.
"What is an example of a conflict between two [means of proof] that are equal in authority?

A mantra recited in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* section, which is designated by the name *pauroḍāśika*, exists within a general context (*prakaraṇa*). While it is not yet applied through the sequence (*krama*) and the inferred indicative power (*liṅga*), it would—due to the priority of the *puroḍāśa*—be understood as belonging to that alone; however, by direct statement (*śruti*), it is enjoined for the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice: 'With "iṣe tvā," he cuts the branch.'"

In that case as well, as long as even a slight commonality is postulated based on the name (*samākhyā*), there is sublation because [the item] has already been assigned by direct statement (*śruti*); thus, in the cases of context (*prakaraṇa*), syntactic connection (*vākya*), and semantic capability (*sāmarthya*), there is indeed sublation even before they have been postulated.
(pp.
835–836) Thus far, the conflict regarding a single subsidiary (*śeṣa*) being led toward multiple principals (*śeṣin*) has been illustrated.
Following this very same direction, the contradiction of multiple remainders being brought toward a single remainder must now be illustrated.

For example, in the case of a contradiction between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), when the injunction for the performance of a mantra—namely, "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindra [mantra]"—is established, a certain mantra belonging to Agni would, by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*), be obtained as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*). However, it is the Aindra mantra that is applied by the direct statement (*śruti*). And once the worship is occupied by that [Aindra mantra], there is no further expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for the other.

When there is a conflict between direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*), the example is the injunction of the word *irā* in place of the word *āpyāyadhvam*, which would otherwise be obtained through the context of the single-sentence passage beginning with *āgneyī*.

Similarly, by direct statement, the *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas, whereas by syntactical connection, the *vājina* is their remnant; because that [syntactical connection] is a weaker means of proof, it is set aside by the direct statement.

When there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and order (*krama*), in the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices by one desiring stability, although the recitation of fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses is established as an auxiliary through context, the number twenty-one is understood from the direct statement; thus, the constant recitation belonging to the context is set aside. In a conflict between direct statement and order, in the performance by one desiring cattle, the cup (*camasa*) is an auxiliary according to the sequence [of the text], and the *godohana* vessel is excluded by the direct statement.
"In the case of a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and name (*samākhyā*): by virtue of the name, the *vājapeya* would be performed by the Adhvaryu;
however, by the direct statement, the Adhvaryu is excluded for one who desires sovereignty."
Similarly, "the *yājyā* of the sacrificer" (*yajamānasya yājyā*) is an example.

For, while the *yājyā* is obtained for the *iṣṭis* by the general rule of the Hotṛ-priest through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), it is established here by the genitive *śruti* expressing a relationship with the agent—that the *yājyā* has the sacrificer as its performer.
(Page 838)
[Objection: But surely the conflict here is between the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the syntactical connection (*vākya*), not between the direct statement (*śruti*) and the indicative mark.
To this it is replied: "It is true that there is a conflict with the syntactical connection, but the direct statement is also contradicted;
for it is when they are combined that they are contradicted, but not by the indicative mark alone."
"Thus, there is indeed a conflict between direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*).
In that regard, it is held that the indicative mark and so forth possess intrinsic validity just like direct scriptural statement;
for its subservience to that [purpose] is understood simply from the observation of its capacity."
But since the purpose of the *gārhapatya* fire is not established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the two are of equal status;
therefore, because both are presented, there will be an option (*vikalpa*) between them.
The mantra should indeed be employed as a combination for both;
repetition with respect to each primary element is not contradicted even by the subordinate factor.
Even if the Śruti were stronger than the Liṅga, nevertheless, there would be no sublation because of the absence of conflict; for a combination is indeed possible.
Alternatively, because it consists of functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), the indicative mark (*liṅga*) would be stronger than direct assertion (*śruti*);
for every word operates in accordance with the actual power of things.
To this it is replied: True, if there were absolute equality;
however, the capacity of the mantra with respect to the *gārhapatya* fire is only secondary (*gauṇa*).

Or rather, there may be denotation based on a quality; this has indeed been established in that [context]. Therefore, the indicative mark (liṅga) possesses neither superior force nor equality [with other means of proof].
The application (*viniyoga*) [of a mantra] is near to *śruti*, whereas that of *liṅga* stands at a distance;
for as long as the meaning of a mantra is conveyed by the mantra itself, [it remains within the sphere of *śruti*].
One should first bring the heard mantra to the purpose of the *gārhapatya* fire;
having understood the meaning of the mantra through the mantra itself, one should subsequently determine one's own capacity.
If Indra were subordinate [to the mantra] by virtue of the requirement for a mantra, then a direct Vedic statement (śruti) would have to be inferred;
however, a direct statement regarding the Gārhapatya fire has already been established previously.
When the mantra has been rendered free of expectancy, the postulation of a Vedic text (śruti) becomes rootless;
therefore, by its rapid operation, the direct Vedic statement (śruti) sublates the indicative power (liṅga).

Just as in the world there is a relative strength between perception and inference due to the speed of their operation, so it is here between direct Vedic statement (śruti) and indicative mark (liṅga).
The sublation that was described on the grounds of non-contradiction is not tenable;
for the validity of the indicative mark (liṅga) is based upon the requirement of the mantra.
And that [indicative power], cutting through the direct statement, does not proceed without contradiction;
and in the case of contradiction, the indicative power sublates the direct statement by virtue of its superior strength.

*Soma*: Since the modes of application (*viniyoga*) have been thus described through the *Śruti* and other means, the investigation into relative strength (*balābala*), which was introduced at the beginning of this chapter, has now reached its proper occasion—this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*). [The doubt is as follows: "In the case of the *Aindrī* verse, should Agni or Indra be invoked? Is there an option (*vikalpa*) between them, or a combination (*samuccaya*), or is it possible that the verse refers to Indra alone?"
There is an option based on direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), while there is a combination (*samuccaya*) when [the requirements] such as qualities are met;
for "direct statement" follows the capacity [of the word], and by virtue of the indicative mark, there is only one that is capable.
The *śakti* is red, the *śruti* is swift, and the *liṅga* is that which follows from the *śruti*.
In the cognition characterized by the absence of expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*), this [cognition] abides solely in the *śruti*.
Bhaṭṭa: Thus, the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) having been examined, the relative strength and weakness (*balābala*) in cases of conflict (*virodha*) is now determined.

Conflict occurs when two means of valid cognition exist for two different subordinate elements (*śeṣa*) regarding a single primary element (*śeṣin*), such as when the *aindrī* mantra is a subordinate of the *gārhapatya* fire by direct statement (*śruti*), while it is a subordinate of Indra by indicative power (*liṅga*). Or, it occurs when there are two means of valid cognition enjoining two different subordinate elements for a single primary element, such as when the *aindrī* mantra is enjoined for the *gārhapatya* fire by direct statement, while the *āgneya* [mantra] is [enjoined] for it by indicative power.

And this application of the remaining two [means of proof] is a powerful motivator only when there is identity [of the means], but not even when there is a difference between them; for instance, although the *vākya* (syntactical connection) and *prakaraṇa* (contextual connection) establish that the *āghāra*, *prayāja*, and so forth share the same status as "remnants" (*śeṣa*), they lack that [powerful motivation] in such cases.

However, where there are two means of proof for one "remainder" (*śeṣa*) with respect to a single "residue" (*śeṣin*), then in the case of a disparity, only the stronger one possesses the power to apply [the rule] for the sake of its purpose.
But when there is equality, one serves as the applicator, while the other, being a mere repetition (*punarśruti*), is assumed to have a different purpose.
In the absence of a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*), one must either assume that both [the qualities] culminate in the same result or that they serve as auxiliaries to another ritual action.

Thus, in cases such as "He buys [the Soma] with red [cows]," where there are three means of proof for the fact that redness serves the purpose of the purchase which is itself a means to the *apūrva*, even there the application is determined by *śruti* alone, and not by any other [means of proof], because the latter merely provides the content for the syntactical connection (*vākya*).
For this very reason, there is no conflict between *liṅga* (indicative power) and *vākya* (syntactical connection) in the case of "With the *aindrī* [verse]."

Although syntactical connection (*vākya*) assists *śruti* by merely providing the presentation of the subject matter, it lacks the capacity to convey the status of being a factor in the performance (*kṛtikārakatva*) or to function as an applicator (*viniyojaka*).
Context (*prakaraṇa*), however, is merely that which grasps the intended meaning (*tātparya*) characterized by being a means to the *apūrva*;
even that is not an applicator, due to its complexity (*gaurava*).
For this very reason, the strength of the means of proof (pramāṇa) that effect application must also be examined.

Thus, in this case, when there is a conflict with direct statement (śruti), the *aindrī* mantra’s status as an auxiliary to the Gārhapatya fire is established by the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), and not its status as an auxiliary to Indra by a direct statement of purpose (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa-śruti*).
[Mīmāṃsākośa 367]
Because it is a *sūkta* (hymn), it lacks the status of being a primary agent (*kāraka*), and thus,
due to its lack of primary scriptural authority (*mukhya-śrutitva*), it is weak. Consequently,
by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*), that very mantra is subordinate to Indra.
Even in the case of a conflict of indicators (*liṅga*), this very same example applies.

For here, at the time of determining the truth, it has been established everywhere that the authority of each subsequent [means of knowledge] is based on its being produced by each preceding one; thus, when the subsequent [means] have been understood up to the level of the *Śruti-kalpa*, there occurs a sublation (*bādha*) because the preceding [means] render the relationship between the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*) free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*).

Furthermore, it cannot be argued that even though the *ajñāna* mantras do not have an expectancy for the archetype (*prakṛti*), they do have an expectancy for the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) due to the assumption of an extended application (*atideśa*), and thus the indicative power (*liṅga*) can be established as a substitute for direct statement (*śruti*) through its very expectancy for Indra; for since their recollection is established by other means such as meditation (*dhyāna*), they lack that expectancy toward the modified sacrifice.
Therefore, by direct statement (*śruti*), the status of being the *gārhapatya* fire is indeed established.

Nor should it be said that there is no conflict between *śruti* and *liṅga*, because while *śruti* merely denotes instrumentality, the fact that it is qualified by the *gārhapatya* fire depends upon syntactical connection (*vākya*).

Nevertheless, because it is a statement by a Brahmin, it is established as more powerful than the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra—just like [the rule] "even if they see something else"—and thus its strength is justified.

In reality, however, there is no contradiction with the *śruti* alone, nor is there a contradiction with the *vākya* (syntactical connection), since it can be explained as meaning "in the vicinity of the Gārhapatya fire.

Therefore, even though there is a contradiction between both, this is cited as an example of a contradiction between *śruti* and *liṅga*, according to the maxim: "Designations are made according to the principal factor."

Maṇḍana: "Direct assertion (śruti) is stronger than indicative mark (liṅga). Śaṅkara: "There would be a sublation of the indicative mark by direct assertion. (Consideration of the relative strength of indicative mark and sentence)—The Commentary: What is the example when there is a conflict between indicative mark (liṅga) and syntactical connection (vākya)? "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee; I fashion it well-soaked with a stream of clarified butter."
Sit upon that immortal foundation, O essence of rice, being well-disposed.
Thus [it is stated].

Here there is a doubt: should the entire mantra be employed for both the spreading of the underlayer (*upastaraṇa*) and the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśāsādana*), or should the portion beginning with "I spread thee" (*kalpyāmi*) be used for the spreading, and the portion beginning with "sit upon this" (*tasmin sīda*) for the placing of the cake?
If the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is more powerful, then the entire mantra applies to both.

How so? If one considers the phrase "I prepare a seat with clarified butter" (*ghṛtaidhaṃ kalpayāmi*), then the subsequent portion beginning with "sit upon that" (*tasmin sīda*) must be construed as syntactically connected with the preceding, forming a single sentence: "I prepare a seat with clarified butter; sit upon that. On the other hand, if the indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger, then the phrase ending in "kalpayāmi" is to be applied to the act of preparing the seat.
How so? Because the phrase "I make a pleasant seat for thee" (*syonaṃ te sadanaṃ kṛṇomi*) is capable of expressing the preparation of the seat.
The injunction "sit upon this" is also enjoined for the purpose of placing the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa); what, then, is the prima facie view?
"These two causes are of equal strength.

Just as it was stated that the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is stronger than the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is not likewise stated here that the indicative mark is stronger than the syntactical connection (*vākya*).
Or rather, the syntactical connection itself is stronger than the indicative mark.
Why? Because that [notion] is sublated even by scripture (śruti).
And a stronger cause cannot be sublated. Therefore, this [notion] possesses fragility and instability.
"Whatever is obstructed by one [means] can also be obstructed by another.
This being the position reached, we reply:
between indicative mark (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*), the indicative mark is stronger.
Why? Because of the remoteness of the purpose (*arthaviprakarṣāt*).

What is this remoteness of purpose here? Since the mantra is recited in proximity to that which possesses the context (*prakaraṇavat*), it is understood to belong to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

When the mantra "sit upon this" (*tasmin sīda*) is employed for the act of placing [the cake] because of its capacity to denote the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśāsādana*), the recitation of the mantra has already fulfilled its purpose; thus, there is no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by which it could also be employed for the act of spreading [the butter] (*upastaraṇa*).

Likewise, even in the case of the mantra "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee," its connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices occurs solely through the power of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Since its application to the act of spreading [the grass] occurs through the power of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), one who has already performed the effort [of establishing the connection] should demonstrate the absence of other [applications] and, having brought forward the specific property of the former, should exclude the property of the latter; thus, another [point] must not be confused. The distinction is as follows: the first discussion is by way of the two [criteria] resembling valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); the middle one is by way of the two called "capacity" (*śakti*); and the other is by way of the two, namely "having a visible purpose" (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) and "having an invisible purpose" (*adṛṣṭārthatva*).
Therefore, it is established that indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*). (pp.

847–851) Now, since indicative power, syntactical connection, and the others are all equally inferable from a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), and thus appear to be without distinction, by what is their relative strength determined? To this, it is replied:
"Produced by one, two, three, four, five, or seven intervening factors"—
thus is the disparity among the means of proof, such as *liṅga* and the rest, with respect to the meaning of *śruti*.
For the meaning of *śruti* consists in its being the immediate inference from *śruti* alone.
Furthermore, for a sentence, [the assumption of] direct assertion (*śruti*) is mediated by indicative mark (*liṅga*) and syntactic expectancy (*śruti*).

How so? "Because of the unity of the sentence with speech, even though there are [words] here that are directly perceived, one first assumes an expressive power (*abhidhāśakti*) and only afterwards is direct assertion (*śruti*) postulated."
For in every mantra, only a certain word expresses a meaning connected with the ritual action.

For example, in the mantra "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*), the word *nirvapāmi* [expresses the action]. The remaining words, however—such as *akṣamaveta*, *abhidhāna*, *prayoga*, and so forth—are seen to form a single syntactical unit; because their presence would otherwise be inexplicable, they are understood through inferred capacity to express meanings connected with that [action]. By subordinating their own literal meanings, they serve the purpose of the ritual application by manifesting the specific meaning connected [with the action].

Consequently, they are applied by inferring the Vedic revelation (śruti). And since there is no distinction [in the general requirement], all [mantras] are permitted [for application]. When two mantras observed to form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) are seen to each have a distinct meaning connected with the ritual act, then—since both require a separate illuminator and the illuminators require what is to be illuminated—they proceed toward their respective applications. In that case, whichever mantra possesses an established capacity for a particular purpose reaches it more swiftly; it cannot then be led elsewhere on the basis of syntactical unity alone.
Nor does it come from another fire; rather, it provides space [for the application].

How so? "By means of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the capacity (*sāmarthya*) is inferred as far as possible. By that capacity, the direct statement (*śruti*) which effects the application (*viniyojikā*) is then postulated."
For when something is enjoined with respect to a whole, it cannot be enjoined without enjoining its constituent parts.

In that case, the fact that the preceding and succeeding portions form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) is directly perceived; however, the capacity to express a single function is not [perceived]. Rather, the capacity to express distinct meanings is established by the observation of different suffixes at the beginning [of each part].

In that context, when the syntactical whole (*vākya*) and the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) set out together for the purpose of assigning the parts to the whole, since an assignment of what lacks capacity is impossible, as soon as it is inferred by means of the sentence that "the prior part is capable of expressing the meaning of the subsequent part," or "the subsequent part is capable of [expressing] the prior," the direct audition (*śruti*) is already satisfied by the capacity residing in each individual part, both for the prior part’s own meaning and for the subsequent part’s own meaning.

Consequently, by the time one relies upon the inference of a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) as an applicator for the other [mantra], the application of the present [mantra] has already been established; since it is then free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*), there is no basis whatsoever for inferring a direct statement. Thus, the application is sublated before its root has even sprouted. For regarding a mantra, the application of the preceding one to its preceding meaning occurs quickly, while that of the subsequent one occurs slowly.
Furthermore, between those two, the application of the subsequent one to its subsequent meaning occurs quickly, while that of the preceding one occurs slowly.
A mantra that has been quickly employed does not depend upon a long-term employment;
likewise, at the outset as well, once the delimitation of the mantra has been understood through its first occurrence, one does not apprehend others.
And when its own primary status is possible, it does not assume the state of being subordinate to another.
Therefore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is more powerful; having thus concluded that syntactical connection (*vākya*) is the means of application (*viniyoga*), [an objection is raised]:

"If this were so, then since the application to the purpose of delimitation would be quickly attained through the established capacity of the words beginning with *nirvapāmi*, there would follow a non-application of the words beginning with *devasya tvā*, which are reached only through a remote means (*viprakṛṣṭa*), because they are set aside by [the former].
Nor can there be a combination (*samuccaya*) of these because they have different purposes, for if that were the case, there would be a lack of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*).

Furthermore, this [meaning] must necessarily be revealed by the syntactical connections (*vākyaśeṣa*) alone, and not by another means of revelation, because otherwise it would follow that it is not an integral part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*).
Therefore, since they share the same object, when there is a conflict (*samavāya*), there must be a sublation of the other words obtained through syntactical connection. To this, it is replied:
"If other words were to express the meaning of the ritual performance,
then for the others there would likewise be no syntactical connection due to the lack of comprehension.
For those words whose meanings are not integrated [with the ritual], if they were performed independently, they would become meaningless."

Even though a meaning has been rendered free of expectancy by that relationship already established, it again attains the status of being manifested by the others because they themselves possess expectancy.
This is just as those [elements] whose requirements have been fulfilled by the context (prakaraṇa) may subsequently be reached again through the order of sequence (krama);
or as the primary (prakṛta) ritual elements, having become free of expectancy, proceed to apply to the modified (vikṛti) rites.
And this has been explained in the section on *klṛpti*.
Therefore, even such [words] as these are connected.

However, those words whose expressed meaning is seen to be inherent (*samaveta*)—even if they are not denotative (*anabhidheya*) or are not being syntactically connected—they possess meaningfulness (*arthavattva*); thus, they do not incur the status of being meaningless (*ānarthakya*), which would otherwise necessitate their exclusion (*avakāra*).

Furthermore, it is accepted that even when all means of knowledge, such as direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest, are obstructed by being rendered purposeless, they may be sublated by a more difficult-to-overcome [means].

For example, although the *vrīhi* grains attain the status of being the primary object (*śeṣin*) toward the acts of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth by virtue of direct statement, this is set aside; rather, a connection based on their being means for the unseen potency (*apūrva*) will arise through the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Thus, it is established that the power of indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*).
And so it has been shown in the Bhakṣānuvāka (pp. 839–843).
In this manner, an example of the conflict between indicative power (liṅga) and context (prakaraṇa) should be cited.
In that regard, concerning conflict with the context (*prakaraṇa*), the *pūṣānumantraṇa* formulas should be cited as examples.
For as long as it is being assumed that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the context, so long does the direct indicative power (*liṅga*) establish a scriptural injunction (*śruti*).

Likewise, for as long as it is [being established] elsewhere that the mantra lacks the capacity to manifest the primary deities such as Agni, so long does the application (*viniyoga*) occur here; thus, there is sublation (*bādha*).

The conflict between the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the order of sequence (*krama*) was demonstrated in the section concerning *stotra* and *śastra*: "But by the purpose, it is drawn away" (2.1.15).

An established example is as follows: regarding the two mantras for granting permission (*abhyanujñāpana*) and receiving permission (*anujñā*), which have a fixed order—namely, the mantras recited as "upahūta" and "upahavyasa"—they would, due to the commonality of location, be applied according to that very order: "upahūta" for granting permission and "upahavyasa" for receiving permission.
But since there is no such capacity [in the order], the subordinate status is the reverse.

For while the syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) is being inferred by generating a context (*prakaraṇa*) through knowledge, the application (*viniyoga*) has already been established by the indicative power (*liṅga*) through the inference of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); thus, the order is sublated even before its indicative power and scriptural statement have been inferred. Similarly, regarding the two acts of measuring—namely, the measurement performed with a rope (*parimāṇa*) and the act of making (*kriyā*)—the verses "parivīrasi" and "yuvā suvāsāḥ" are prima facie established as subsidiaries to the measuring of the Agni-Soma animal sacrifice; however, by virtue of their indicative power (*liṅga*), they also serve as subsidiaries to the second measuring for the sake of the *savanīya* offering.
If it is argued that the *manotā* [verse] does not apply because of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) capable of setting aside the sequence of the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice], [the answer is]:
no.

For, as in the case of the rule "But by virtue of a direct statement (*vacana*), the Aindrī [verse] would be used otherwise than its literal meaning" (3.2.13), it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Agniṣomīya on the basis of the assumption of an application (*viniyoga*) established by a more powerful direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
For thus it is said: "If the animal sacrifice belongs to another deity, the Manotā hymn must nevertheless be performed for Agni.
By this scriptural statement (śruti), the displacement of the Manotā—suggested by the indicative mark (liṅga)—is prohibited.
Even in the case of a sacrifice to two deities, the meaning is that [the hymn] is not restricted solely to the performance of the Āgnīṣomīya rite on the grounds that it is dedicated to Agni alone.

If the particle *eva* is removed from its original position and joined with the word *kāryya* (to be performed) in its proper sequence, the restriction of being "that which is to be performed" (*kāryyatva*) is established. However, when there is a conflict between indicative power (*liṅga*) and name (*samākhyā*), it is settled as follows: in the section on eating (*bhakṣānuvāka*), the sentences concerning the taking [of the cup] (*grahaṇa*) and so forth—which are connected by the name—are initially intended for application as subordinate parts of the eating due to the general relationship of connection; yet, by virtue of indicative power, they are applied to the acts of taking, looking [at the cup], and proper digestion. Similarly, regarding the *manotā* verse, it has been stated that although it is recited in the context of the *yājyā*, it is applied by indicative power as a *sāmidhenī* verse in the *pṛthu-paśu-yajña*.

(Regarding the status of the remainder as a subordinate element of many: When there is a conflict between indicative mark (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*), even the verse beginning with *asyona* is subordinate to the act of preparing the seat (*sadana*) by virtue of syntactical connection; however, by virtue of the indicative mark, it is subordinate to the act of settling (*sīda*) alone. Therefore, this [indicative mark] subverts the former [syntactical connection].

Likewise, in the case of the *abhicāraṇa* rite, even the phrase "sit down" (*sīda*) is subordinate to [the mantra] beginning with "pleasant" (*syonā*), because of its indicative power (*liṅga*); therefore, it sets aside what follows it. This involves multiple subordinates (*anekaśeṣa*).
Because they are subsidiary elements (*śeṣa*), these two were previously cited; now,
due to their connection with multiple subsidiaries for each principal element (*śeṣin*),
[the mantra] beginning with "śeṣaṃ te" was previously [cited] in relation to the act of spreading (*sadana*) and the act of sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*).
That which is obtained through syntactical connection (*vākya*) as being primary is set aside by indicative power (*liṅga*) for the purpose of scattering;
thus, the remainder obtained through the sentence "sit upon this" is used for scattering,
whereas by indicative power it belongs only to the act of settling, and therefore it is employed in that very context.
However, the status of being a subordinate element (śeṣatva) for each individual [rite] was obtained from the syntactical connection (vākya) regarding each pair;
but now, by means of indicative power (liṅga), that [status] is understood to belong to each one individually.
Thus, within a single path, there is this set of four mixed together.
The Commentator stated that, like the *viveka*,

the indicative power (*liṅga*) prevails over the context (*prakaraṇa*) when there is a conflict with non-proximity (*asamākhyā*), as in the case of the *nirvāpa* and other rites where the restriction of mantras such as "O God, thee" (*devasya tvā*) is obtained through context. Furthermore, there is a sublation by indicative power of the pair of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses belonging to the first optional *aindrāgna* offering— which, having entered into the function of the *sāmidhenī* verses by virtue of its position— is superseded by the indicative power of the mantras themselves.

In the case of the *samākhyā* (name/designation) known as *manotā*, examples include the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses that, having been obtained for the Soma-drinking deities (*somapīthinaḥ*) by virtue of their status as *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*, are replaced by those *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses which possess the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the Soma-drinking deities; such as "O Agni, bring hither" (*agna āyāhi*), etc.
Śabara says: "For as many words as are employed, provided there is the possibility [of their application]..."
There must be syntactic unity for them; a split in the sentence is not appropriate.
And because it is understood that "he should sit upon it" depends on what was previously stated, there is unity of the sentence; therefore, everything is employed in both places.
Or rather, there may be an equality of strength between both the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the syntactical connection (*vākya*);
for while the indicative mark is set aside by the directly perceived direct statement (*śruti*),
the indicative mark [itself] is equal to the direct statement that must be inferred for both cases.
To the objection that, on these grounds, there would be an equality of strength between them, it is replied:
It is true that a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) must be inferred; however, in this case, it is inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
First, the indicative mark is inferred by means of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), and from that, the direct scriptural statement is inferred.
It is so conceived because the direct meaning of the Vedic text (*śruti*) is remote from that sentence;
however, it is proximate to the indicative power (*liṅga*), and therefore that [indicative power] is stronger than it.
As it is said: "The first part, 'syonaṃ te,' and the second part, 'tasmin sīda,'" [are connected by *liṅga*].
Whether this [syllable] occurs in every instance of the word *sādana* or is restricted to half [of them],
it would follow that the former applies because of the unity of the sentence based on the direct mention (*śruti*);
however, since the indicative power (*liṅga*) is more proximate, the sentence-meaning (*vākya*) is sublated, and thus the restriction is established.
This has been stated: when there is a contradiction between a verbal statement and a sense-perception, it is not the sense-perception that is sublated;
for if it were sublated, it would follow that it possesses validity, which contradicts its nature as an invalidation.
In the case of a conflict between two indicative marks (*liṅga*), the primary one sublates the secondary one by virtue of its superior capacity.

Regarding the *liṅga* (indicative power) and the *vākya* (syntactical connection), however: since the first half of the mantra, "syonaṃ te" (*pleasant for you*), which reveals the act of preparing the seat, has a syntactic expectancy toward the second half, "tasmin sīda" (*sit upon that*), which reveals the act of sitting down by means of the word "tasmin" (*upon that*), the entire mantra would—by virtue of the *vākya* consisting in the proximity of the word "tasmin"—be applied to either the preparation of the seat or the act of sitting down, or even to both acts of establishing [the offering]. But before such an application could be intended, the previously operative *liṅga*—which, by its very nature as the primary indicator of its own meaning, lacks any basis for assuming a subordinate status toward another—establishes a separate application for each part. Furthermore, the word "tasmin" finds its fulfillment simply by referring back to the object already presented in the preceding sentence, just as in the case of "sā vaiśvadevī" (*that [offering] belongs to the Viśvedevas*). Therefore, the application is indeed individual.

Maṇḍana [states]: "The indicative mark (liṅga) sublates the syntactical connection (vākya). Śaṅkara [states]: "And even the syntactical connection is [sublated] by the indicative mark. This is the Bhāṣya.
8. (An Investigation into the Relative Strength of Sentence and Context) Bhāṣya: Now, what happens when there is a conflict between sentence (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*)?
But what, indeed, is called "context"? Context is the statement that expresses the requirement for the "how" (*itikartavyatā*) of that which is to be performed (*kartavyatva*).
Even though subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) is inferred, it dissolves right there because it resides in the process of accomplishment (*niṣpatti*).
Therefore, the *ācārya* (the teacher/injunction) is more powerful.

(Page 833) When there is a conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and sequence (*krama*), among those items being enumerated, the mention of the source (*apādāna*)—excluding the words *parivīraḥ* and *parivītaḥ*—such as “The youth, well-dressed, has arrived; he is indeed superior,” and so forth, is applied to the secondary binding (*sanīyaparivyāṇa*) because of its syntactic unity with the word *parivīta*, which is already assigned by indicative mark (*liṅga*).

In the case of a conflict between syntactical unity (*vākya*) and direct statement (*śruti*), when [mantras] such as "I have attained" (*sadhyāsam*) and so forth are being applied to the act of taking up the cup and other rites within the *bhakṣānuvāka* itself, the remaining words contained within that same sentence must be brought forward.

Likewise, when [mantras] recited by the Adhvaryu and others are obtained through the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, and are applicable for that very purpose, their status as having meaning and so forth is understood due to their syntactical unity with the phrase "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*).
Nor would this [syntactical unity] be nothing other than direct statement (*śruti*).
In this case, it is not understood from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) that anyone is the agent of that [hearing and so forth], because the agenthood is not denoted by it.
What then? This is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) arising simply from the proximity of the two words.
Ta...

Having proclaimed the *dāja* sacrifice, a modified limb (*vaikṛtam aṅgam*) is prescribed either before or after it; in that case, how could this [modified limb] be understood from the recitation in the context (*prakaraṇa-pāṭha*) as having its limb already grasped, since it has been so transformed?
And since that [contextual grasp] does not exist here, it is the function of sequence (*krama*) alone.
The phrase "even by that which is recited in proximity and is complete" intends to convey the fulfillment of the sentence-meaning (*vākya-artha*).
"Order is merely the recitation of multiple [texts] in close proximity," with this someone demonstrates the invariable concomitance of proximity.

For when something is recited for the sake of many [other elements], since it is impossible for it to be assigned to all of them simultaneously due to the effort required, its connection with one or another through that effort is inevitable.
However, such invariable concomitance does not apply to recitation within a single context (*prakaraṇa*).
Therefore, between the simultaneous operation of *krama* (order of sequence) and *prakaraṇa* (context), the latter possesses greater strength because it attains its scriptural meaning more rapidly.
(Page 855) Likewise, between *krama* and *prakaraṇa*, there is a greater remoteness of meaning for *krama*.
How so? "From the very moment of expectancy, one proceeds toward the meaning of the Vedic text;

yet, having obtained that [meaning] from another source, the Vedic text is postulated for only one [part]. Sequence (*krama*) is merely the identity of position regarding the recitation or performance of those [elements] which are otherwise independent.
If, however, it were recited in proximity to that which has a requirement [for it], then it would indeed constitute a *prakaraṇa* (contextual application).
And in this case, the examples are generally the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) where the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) applies;
for in those cases, since the archetypal subsidiary (*prākṛtāṅga*) has not been produced by a path already traversed, its position—whether preceding or following—becomes one of sequential occurrence.

Because the context (*prakaraṇa*) has already been satisfied by the archetypal elements (*prākṛta*) which have established auxiliary functions, [the following applies]: when something is recited in proximity to a certain element that possesses an inherent expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and there is an expectancy for another, then that [element] being grasped by both—while satisfying the expectancy of the one possessing sequence (*krama*)—enters into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the possessor of the context, as long as such unity exists elsewhere. As long as there is unity with the other, there is the postulation of a capacity for assistance toward the context;
as long as it is otherwise, there is the inference of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

As long as a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is sought elsewhere, so long as the application (*viniyoga*) is already established here, everything that lacks the seed of inference (*anumāna-bīja*)—namely, all unestablished scriptural statements—is invalid. (Regarding the subsidiarity of multiple subsidiaries: When there is a conflict between context (*prakaraṇa*) and order (*krama*), the example is the substitution of the word *girā* for the word *pada* in the *stotra*.
In the sequence of the Agniṣṭoma, the word *girā* is mentioned [as a substitute]; however, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is the word *irā*.
And that [context] is stronger.
But since the former was cited with reference to the Sāman, there is no confusion regarding their respective domains.

When there is a conflict between *samākhyā* (name/designation) and *prakaraṇa* (context), the example with respect to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is precisely this: "Therefore, the Maitrāvaruṇa gives the directions and recites the responses.

For by *samākhyā*, the giving of directions and the reciting of responses would be understood as being performed by the Hotṛ priest; however, by virtue of *prakaraṇa*, it is determined that they are to be performed by the Maitrāvaruṇa.
Furthermore, the previously mentioned example depends upon the [general] category of giving directions and reciting responses, whereas this case is distinct.
(On pages 839–840):
