On page 446: In such cases as "citrāṇāṃ gavām ayam" ("this [person] belongs to the cows that are brindled"), the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound functions in this way.
It is understood that Devadatta or another person is qualified by cows characterized by a specific relation; thus, the meaning of the compound is apprehended.
Even in a *bahuvrīhi*, there is no predominance of the relation itself.

And that external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is understood—by virtue of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*)—as being either a genus (*jāti*), a substance (*dravya*), a quality (*guṇa*), or an action (*kriyā*).
Vākyapadīya 3.16.12, p. 677. This is the determination that the *bahuvrīhi* compound possesses denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the external referent.

In the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (3.1.12), it is stated that the *bahuvrīhi* has denotative power with respect to the external referent; "and therefore, by the word *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer), the relation is expressed, just as..."

Likewise, [this is established] from the introduction with the words "In the same way, by means of derivative (*yaugika*) terms, even in the case of words such as *piṅgalākṣī*," (Vākyapadīya, p. 677), and from the conclusion with the words "Therefore, it is logical that words such as *piṅgalākṣī* denote substances" (Vākyapadīya, p. 679). [This applies] to the referents of the terms *indrapīta* and *niṣadha*.
Regarding the *bahuvrīhi*:
the investigation of the *bahuvrīhi*—

through a consideration of two rules (*Pāṇini* 2.2.24 and 6.1.23)— appears to be technical (*lākṣaṇika*) and to have as its referent a meaning other than that of the constituent words (*anyapadārtha*).

For instance, regarding the word *indrāpīta*: if it were a *tatpuruṣa* compound qualifying *soma*, there would be the contingency of indicating (*lakṣaṇā*) only the meaning of the first member; thus, it cannot be a *bahuvrīhi* [qualifying *soma*], because in that case there would be the contingency of indicating the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) in both members.
To this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the reply must simply be stated: "In a *bahuvrīhi*, the meaning of another word is directly denotable (*śakya*).
Without stating that, [the opponent] speaks of [the word] as denoting a collection of what has been drunk and what has not been drunk.

The meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound: Section 2952, the *Bādaryadhikaraṇa*. In the inquiry as to whether the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound is directly denoted (*abhidheya*) or merely indicated (*lākṣaṇika*), if it is argued that it is indicated, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is directly denoted.
Vākyapadīya, pp. 678–79. An investigation into the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Regarding the entry for *aruṇāyāḥ* on page 608 of Mīko., it is stated in the Bhāṣya section that this refers to a substance.
Those who teach the *Bahu-vrīhi* [grammar] are students of the *Kalpasūtra* composed by Āśvalāyana which expounds the *Mahāvrata*; they refer to it as the "fifth Āraṇyaka."
And that [dispersion of the agent] is rooted in the spreading out [of the ritual action].
Vi. 9|2|1, Commentary 2. By means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the *Dharmasūtra* of Vasiṣṭha is accepted.

Vā. 13|1|9. In the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa* (or, according to the *Vārttika*, the *Adhvaryubrāhmaṇa*), the statement "one performs the *Agnihotra* as long as one lives" prescribes the obligatory performance of the *Agnihotra* by making living the occasion (*nimitta*), and not a temporal attribute (*dharma*) belonging to a desire-based (*kāmya*) rite.

2|4|1|1–7. The Maxim of the Arrow and the Boa Constrictor (*vāṇoṣṭrīnyāya*). Just as there is a popular verse stating that a certain man, protecting himself from being encircled by a high boa constrictor, killed the snake with arrows—so too, prohibitive statements protect the Self by serving as the limit of sublation and thereby sublate what is not the Self.
*Sāhasī*, p. 104. As for the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*): wherever there are so many [sticks], exactly that many must be produced according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The *Pālaśāstra* [is cited] as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Bhāṣya 2.1.4.12. Bādari: The teacher Bādari considered the scripture to have universal eligibility (*sarvādhikāra*, i.e., eligibility for all four social classes).
Bhāṣya 6.1.7.27. The Section on Bādari (*Bādaryadhikaraṇa*).
"Bādari [holds that the term 'remainder' (aśeṣa) applies] to substances, qualities, and purificatory acts.
Commentary: The teacher Bādari considered the word "remainder" here to apply to substances, qualities, and purificatory acts, and not to sacrifices, fruits, or persons.
A substance is for the sake of action.

If an action is purposeful, it must clearly be accomplished by means of a substance. Since that action is brought to completion, it does not exist thereafter; therefore, a substance must be sought for its accomplishment.
Consequently, the substance exists for the sake of the action.
A quality is capable of indicating a qualified substance when it is mentioned;
and there is a purpose for it being so indicated,
because only a qualified substance serves as the means for accomplishing an action.

Therefore, since that [substance] also assists the action by means of its substance, it is indeed for the sake of the action. That which is called a *saṃskāra* (consecration) is that which, when produced, renders an object fit for some purpose; since there is also a need for it when an action is to be performed, that too is for the sake of another (*parārtha*).
Therefore, substances, qualities, and preparatory acts are subsidiary because they exist for the sake of another; however, the sacrifice, the fruit, and the person are not so.
For the sacrifice must be performed by the person;
once it has been accomplished, there remains nothing further to be done.
For that indeed is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

Whatever else there is, such as substances and so forth, exists for the sake of that [goal] and is subordinate to it; however, that [goal] itself is not produced in order to bring about anything else.
Even the fruit is not produced by him;
rather, when that [action] has been performed, the fruit comes into being of its own accord. It is merely stated that "when this has been performed, the fruit accrues to him."
There is no scriptural statement that the fruit is produced by the sacrifice;
therefore, the sacrifice is not a subordinate element (śeṣa) of anything else,
nor is the fruit taught as being for the sake of the person.
It is taught by these words alone that "he who desires heaven should perform the sacrifice," without specifying whether it is for himself or for another.
One becomes "desirous of heaven" merely by having a desire for heaven.
Therefore, heaven is not heard of as being subordinate to the person.
Therefore, that [person] also is not a subordinate element (*śeṣa*).
If the two sacrifices for the fruit are not enjoined as having a subordinate status due to the absence of a quality (*guṇa*), then of what would the person be the primary element?
Moreover, because he is a substance (*dravya*), his subordinate status toward the action (*karman*) is directly perceived.
Therefore, Bādari considered the status of being a subordinate (śeṣabhāva) to apply only to substances, qualities, and purificatory acts (saṃskāra).
Now, he states the scope of this subordination.
In that regard, according to the opinion of Bādari, there are only three things that are subordinate.

For a substance is inherently subordinate (*śeṣabhūta*) by its very nature, as it is connected as a quality (*guṇatvena*) to other substances in connection with an action; only its restriction to a specific purpose is excluded. Likewise, a quality such as "red" (*aruṇādi*) is subordinate from the very moment of its arising, because of its capacity to delimit the substance that serves as the means for the action.

Likewise, a preparatory act (*saṃskāra*) such as threshing also comes into being at the very moment of its production; it brings about the fitness for the sacrifice of rice and other grains that have been enjoined for the purpose of producing the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the like, by removing their unsuitability through striking them so that they may become fit for the deity.
However, no inherent status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) is observed in the case of the sacrifice itself, nor is it enjoined by the verbal testimony of scripture.
The sacrifice is indeed performed by means of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*),
and it is not observed to be pervaded [by them] elsewhere.
If it is argued that [the sacrifice is pervaded] in the fruit, we say no.
For when a sacrifice has long since ceased, the desired result is still perceived.

Now, it may be argued that the status of the sacrifice as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) was stated in the section concerning the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*). True, it was stated, but it was not proven.

Since its establishment depends upon the *svargakāmādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning one who desires heaven), that [section] merely refutes the status of the name as an instrument; therefore, because it remains unestablished at present, he treats it specifically as an instrument. Furthermore, the fruit (*phala*) is primary with respect to the sacrifice because it is that which is to be accomplished, whereas its status as a subordinate element (*śeṣabhāva*) with respect to the person is not due to being a means, since it is even more primary by virtue of being desired.
However, the person may indeed be subordinate (*guṇatvena*) in the relinquishing of the substance;
therefore, the status of being a subsidiary (*śeṣabhāva*) applies only to substances, qualities, and purificatory acts.
Jaimini, moreover, maintains that actions [are subsidiaries] because they exist for the sake of the fruit.
Commentary: The teacher Jaimini, however, indeed considered ritual actions (*karmāṇi*) to be subsidiary (*śeṣabhūta*), whereas Bādari did not maintain this as a universal rule.
For he [Jaimini] held that it is not the sacrifice (*yāga*) itself that is enjoined as something to be performed;
rather, it is enjoined as a means for one who desires a result (*phalakāma*).
In this way, the meaning heard will be fully grasped, as will the instruction regarding that meaning. He will establish this very point through the sūtras themselves in the sixth chapter;
however, here he establishes the subordinate status of the sacrifice by means of its being for the sake of a result, which is already established there.

Therefore, there is no definitive restriction; substances, qualities, and preparatory acts are subsidiary elements, and even in the sacrifice, the fruit is a subsidiary element that brings about the result.
Or—this has already been explained.
And the fruit exists because it serves the purpose of the person.
Commentary: Even the fruit is taught with reference to the person.
For one who desires, "May heaven be mine," there is the sacrifice;
it is not that heaven itself attains itself.
Why? Because of the use of the middle voice (ātmanepada). This [suffix] occurs when the action is intended for the agent;
the sacrifice is employed with the thought, "How may the person obtain the fruit of the action?"
Therefore, it is heard that the fruit [arises] from the sacrifice for the sake of the person, not for the sake of the self's own fulfillment;
therefore, it is a subordinate element (śeṣa).
Or rather—by the very employment of the word "desire" (kāma), it is understood that the fruit has the person as its purpose.
For no one, even when instructed, desires to perform what is not their duty with the thought, "May heaven be attained by himself. What then? [They desire it] thinking, "May it be for my enjoyment.
Furthermore, from the use of the middle voice (ātmanepada), it is understood that it is to be enjoyed by the agent alone, and not by anyone else.
Therefore, even the fruit is subsidiary with respect to the enjoyer;
and the person [is subsidiary] because he exists for the sake of the ritual action.
The Commentary states: "The person is also heard of as being subsidiary in such acts as the rubbing of the Audumbarī post."
Because of this lack of restriction, Bādari held that subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) applies to substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*).
Now, the venerable Vṛttikāra establishes the following:
the status of being subsidiary to the sacrifice is fixed only for substances, qualities, and preparatory acts; for all others, it is relative.

The sacrifice has the status of a primary factor (*pradhāna*) with respect to its material substance, but the status of a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) with respect to the fruit. The fruit has primacy with respect to the sacrifice, but subordination with respect to the person. The person has primacy with respect to the fruit, but subordination with respect to such acts as the rubbing of the *audumbarī* post.
Therefore, there is an ascertainment of equality: substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*) are invariably subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) with respect to the sacrifice.
(Mīmāṃsākośa 370) — Furthermore, the person (*puruṣa*) is also implied as being subordinate by the verbal suffix in "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*);
the ellipsis is that [the person] is enjoined in such cases as the rubbing of the *audumbarī* post.
Thus, by means of this group of four sūtras, the entire subject matter concerning subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) has been established.
Here, an objection is raised:

regarding the statement in the sūtra "In substances, qualities, and preparatory acts" that "subsidiarity does not, however, exist in sacrifices, fruits, and persons," the final rejection of the person's status as a principal (*śeṣin*) is untenable.

As for the argument that "the status of being subordinate to the action is directly perceived because it is a substance," that too is contradictory and redundant, since it has already been stated previously.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to mention [substance] alongside [action], as they do not have an equal mode of operation, unlike the refutation of the subordinate status of sacrifice and its fruit.
Therefore, that is incorrect.

If it was stated based on the *adhikaraṇasamāsa* [compound] that "now, here, the venerable author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*), having reached a firm conclusion regarding this," even that appears to yield little fruit; for since the substances, qualities, and purificatory acts were first mentioned as being independent, and since it was already established that action, result, and person are primary with respect to substances and the rest, their mutual relationship as subordinate (*śeṣatva*) was demonstrated by the Sūtras themselves, thus rendering the point already explained.
Therefore, it should be resolved in this way:
now, two interpretations of the *adhikaraṇa* have been provided.

In this regard, first of all, having stated his own view according to the principle "the rest [is subordinate] because it exists for the sake of another," he introduces the view of Bādari with the intention that subordination is characterized by utility; he then establishes Jaimini’s view as the final conclusion (siddhānta) after setting forth the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) that subordination applies only to substances, qualities, and preparatory acts. Accordingly, in the preceding section, the commentary (bhāṣya) is seen to follow the sequence of visible utility. And in that case, since the person is a substance, their status as subordinate is indeed accepted, as they are directly perceived to be the cause for the accomplishment of the action.

Regarding the statement that "nothing perceptible is found to be the means for the fruit of sacrifice," this is the view of Aupamanyava. As for the mention of all three—sacrifice, fruit, and person—in the Bhāṣya, namely, "not in the sacrifice, the fruit, or the person," one should not assume that this implies they lack the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) simply because of the connection with the words of the relevant context.
What then? The connection is simply this: "that which is accepted by the proponent of the final conclusion (the Siddhāntin) exists therein."
For in every case, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) must refute the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntavādin*), not just anything at random.
He refutes only that which the latter intends by the term "subservience" (*śeṣatva*), and not its mere essential nature.

Regarding the final point of the *siddhāntavādin*—namely, that the sacrifice, the fruit, and the person possess a dual aspect, such that they are subservient in relation to one thing and subservient in relation to another—the author of the *Bhāṣya*, following the opinion of Bādari, refutes this; however, he does not refute the dual aspect of the sacrifice, the fruit, and the person as accepted by the *siddhāntavādin*.
Because the fruit of the sacrifice is exclusively subordinate [to the person], and because the person is absolutely subordinate [to that fruit], there is a joint mention [of both] since,
in every respect,
they possess the same nature by virtue of this much.

By such statements as "Jaimini [holds that] even with respect to action," subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) is established as having the very form of *dharma* internalized within it, because subsidiarity is accepted as being characterized by subservience to another (*pārārthya*).

Now, if this is so, since the person (*puruṣa*) is a substance (*dravya*), one might object: "Having already accepted subsidiarity from the perspective of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), when that subsidiarity is refuted by the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*), he should not state 'And the person [is subsidiary] because he exists for the sake of action' (JS 3.1.6), as that has already been established.
This is not a fault.
Therefore, because the sacrifice and its fruit are not subordinate (*aśeṣatva*), its status as the principal (*śeṣitva*) was refuted.

Consequently, as soon as the subordination of both the sacrifice and the fruit was established by the two preceding sūtras, it followed that—since the fruit is primary with respect to the sacrifice—the sacrifice would possess only the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) with respect to the person. Thus, in order to restore the dual nature [of the sacrifice], it is stated: “And the person [is subordinate], because he exists for the sake of the ritual action” (*puruṣaśca karmārthatvāt*).

Alternatively, having accepted that [the person] is subordinate by way of benefiting others, and considering that to be incorrect, he will state—after establishing that even the fruit and the sacrifice are subordinate solely because they exist for the sake of another—that "the person also exists for the sake of action, not because of being beneficial to it.
He says, "Or rather, the Blessed One," intending to explain the four sūtras differently according to the opinion of the Vṛttikāra;
thus, Bādari’s view is no longer the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
What then? Having stated the general definition that "the subsidiary (śeṣa) exists because it is for the sake of another," an elaboration is now made by way of demonstrating its specific scope.

In that regard, in the previous commentary, a restrictive determination was made in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that subsidiarity applies only to substances, qualities, and purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*).
Now, however, taking the view of Bādari—which denies [that restriction]—as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), subsidiarity will be described through both its definition and its elaboration.
It determines that subservience (*śeṣatva*) belongs exclusively to substances, qualities, and purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*).
Consequently, substances, qualities, and purificatory acts are restricted to being subservient;
they do not attain the status of being the principal (*śeṣitva*).

Furthermore, since subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) is not fixed, it belongs to the sacrifice, the fruit, and the person’s desire alike; therefore, it is postulated that the sūtra is intended for the exposition of that [subsidiarity]. Consequently, what is propounded by these sūtras is merely an illustration of relative subsidiarity.
And this has been shown in the Bhāṣya.
Consequently, this domain of the "subsidiary" (*śeṣa*) is of two kinds: it is both mandatory (*naiyamika*) and relative (*āpekṣika*).
Now, one might object that even substances, qualities, and purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*) possess only a relative status of subsidiary and principal with respect to their own respective cognitions;
for instance, the primacy of rice and other grains is established in relation to acts such as threshing.
In this way, with respect to the pestle and other such implements, the threshing is the primary factor.

For grains such as rice are the primary elements in relation to the acts of threshing and so forth, yet they are subordinate in relation to the preparation of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Likewise, qualities such as number are subsidiary because they serve to delimit that which is to be numbered.
However, with respect to those qualities which are to be accomplished by it, that [action] is subordinate to them;

likewise, a consecration such as sweeping or striking is subordinate to the sacrificer (ibhya) and others, while it is the principal (śeṣin) with respect to its own means, such as the fuel-bundle (idhma-sannahana), the mortar, and the pestle.
Therefore, the maintenance [of the fire] is established.
Thus it is said: "Where there is subsidiariness (*śeṣatva*) on the part of the substance and so forth, there is no primary status (*śeṣitā*) at all;
however, among the fruit, the sacrifice, and the agent, there is mutual expectancy (*vyākāṅkṣatva*)."
For substances, qualities, and preparatory acts (saṃskāra) are, by necessity, subordinate (śeṣa) with respect to the sacrifice that possesses the fruit.
Even though they possess the status of being principal (śeṣin) with respect to their own injunctions, it is stated that they do not have that status with respect to [the sacrifice].
For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya also says, "There is a state of subordination with respect to the sacrifice by necessity," and does not say, "The state of subordination is fixed."

In the phrase “relative to the others,” the suffix *yat* (forming the word *yājam*) also carries over. For in this way, one thing is seen to possess both the quality of being subordinate (*guṇatva*) and the quality of being primary (*prādhānya*) in relation to two different things.
First, the sacrifice possesses primacy with respect to the person who accomplishes it by means of the material substance, while it possesses subordination with respect to the fruit.
Furthermore, that which is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) with respect to the fruit can all the more be said to be a subordinate factor even with respect to the person who is the master of that fruit.

Likewise, for that which has primacy (*prādhānya*) with respect to the person, its being a subordinate factor (*upasarjana*) with respect to the fruit—as established by scriptural authority (*śruti*)—is also capable of being defined.

Thus, because the fruit has primacy with respect to the sacrifice, it also has primacy with respect to the person who is the means (*sādhana*) [of attaining it]; and because it is subordinate with respect to the person, it is also subordinate with respect to the sacrifice to be performed.

Likewise, because the person is primary with respect to the fruit, he is also primary with respect to the sacrifice, which is the means to that fruit; yet, because he is subordinate with respect to the sacrifice, he is also subordinate with respect to the fruit. However, this is not the case for substances, qualities, and purificatory acts—this is the distinction.

As for this subordinate status (*śeṣatva*) and predominance (*prādhānya*) that have been described even in terms of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*), this definition of "purpose" (*arthalakṣaṇa*) is to be understood as pertaining merely to the essential nature of things (*vastumātra*).
It is not for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

This is so that there may be no contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) regarding the extension (*atideśa*) of both the fruit and the person to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by means of the eighth [book].

Therefore, it is established that this brief summary concerning the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*)—which will be elaborated upon in detail later—is restricted solely to what is to be accomplished (*kārya*). As the Śābarabhāṣya states: "Bādari declared that subordination exists only in the case of substances, preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and qualities;
and because they are seen through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means, these are the benefactors of ritual actions (*karman*)."

Jaimini, however, because the previously mentioned definition of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) is flawed, maintains that subordination consists solely in being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*). With this in mind, he asserts that even ritual actions (*karman*) are subordinate because they are for the sake of another. As stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "Is only substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and refinement (*saṃskāra*) subordinate? Or is the fruit (*phala*), the person (*puruṣa*), the action (*karman*), and the animal (*paśu*) also subordinate? This is the difference of opinion regarding what is to be given (*deya*)."

Bādari states that being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) consists in being helpful to a substance and so forth; Jaimini, however, holds that subordination is the state of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*), and that this [quality] belongs to all [factors]. This is the Bādari-adhikaraṇa (2.1.3). Sublation (*bādha*).

Bhaṭṭa: Although being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) constitutes being a subordinate element (*aṅgatva*), nevertheless, sacrifice and the like do not possess this definition [of being a subordinate]. This is because, by virtue of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) within the same word, the sacrifice itself is established as the object of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*); thus, it lacks the status of being prescribed as a qualifier of its own fruit. Furthermore, since the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is the nature of the inclination (*pravṛtti*) itself, it merely implies that [the act] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).

Even if there is such implication, since the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end—common to both error and valid cognition—is the sole cause [of inclination], there is no evidence to establish that [the sacrifice] is actually a means to a desired end.

However, since the term *svargakāma* (desirer of heaven) can be interpreted as referring to the agent—as in the expression “one desiring to purchase another should perform an expiation”—there is no necessity for it to refer to the verbal root (*bhāṣya*).
Therefore, sacrifice and the like do not possess the status of being an object (*karmatva*).
In fact, however, subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) consists precisely in being a means of assistance (*upakārakatva*).
For even that which is beneficial to it [the primary] lacks the designation of being a *śeṣa* (subordinate) if it causes harm;

and that [status of being a subordinate] is understood solely through the three means of valid cognition consisting of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*).

Therefore, because rice and the like are seen to be beneficial to certain qualities such as redness (*āruṇya*) and to certain preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as threshing (*avaghāta*), they possess the status of being subordinates (*śeṣatva*).

As for the consecratory rites such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), although their status as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is possible through indicative mark (*liṅga*), they are nonetheless subsidiaries by virtue of direct statement (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*). Since their utility as assistance is established through their being subordinate (*śeṣatva*), it follows that these alone are what is indicated [by the term *śeṣa*].

This being the position reached, we reply: being a subsidiary is not merely being an assistant (*upakārakatva*), for if it were, then even the fetching of water in a milking vessel (*godohana*) or the carrying of the *ājya* would result in being a subsidiary to the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice.
Rather, it is simply being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*).

However, for one who causes harm, the intended object (*uddeśyatā*) is that very act of harming because it is desired [by the agent], and not the person themselves; thus, even in the case of such a harmful agent, there is no application of the term "subsidiary" (*śeṣatva*).
It will be explained later that this too is to be understood through the means of valid cognition consisting of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth.
Consequently, by virtue of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), the sacrifice is also a subsidiary to the fruit.

For instance, although the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others convey that an injunction is conducive to activity by its very nature as a formal capacity, nevertheless, since an injunction would result in futility if there were never any activity at all, it must necessarily be such [i.e., conducive to activity] at some time. And since that [activity] is impossible without the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), and since that [knowledge] cannot be erroneous in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), the status of being a means to a desired end is first understood through the force of the injunction itself. Furthermore, the status of being a means to a specific desired end is understood from the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*); thus, the fact that sacrifice is a means to heaven is established.
In this way, the fruit as well is possessed by the person who is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).

pp. 138–139: The scriptural varieties of non-attainment-based sublation (*aprāptabādhabheda*) occur in the case of the authoritative sequence [of injunctions] based on direct statement (*śruti*), meaning (*artha*), textual order (*pāṭha*), position (*sthāna*), primary [function] (*mukhya*), and application (*pravṛtti*).
There are five types of sublation, as [each subsequent one] sublates the preceding ones beginning with *śruti*.
There are four types of sublation, as [meaning] sublates the four beginning with textual order.

There are three types of sublation (*bādha*) due to the sublation of the three factors—textual order (*pāṭha*), position (*sthāna*), and so forth. There are two types of sublation due to the sublation of primary sense (*mukhya*) by position (*sthāna*). There is one type of sublation due to the sublation of application (*pravṛtti*) by primary sense (*mukhya*).
However, there are no examples for all of them.
On page 136, the scriptural distinctions of sublation by non-attainment (*aprāptabādha*) are given:
by direct statement (*śruti*), the five [means of proof] beginning with indicative mark (*liṅga*) are sublated.
By means of indicative mark (*liṅga*), the four beginning with syntactical connection (*vākya*) [are set aside];
by means of syntactical connection, the three beginning with context (*prakaraṇa*);
and by means of context, the two beginning with order (*krama*).
Regarding the phrase "successively designated":

likewise, among the means of proof such as direct assertion (*śruti*) and the rest, when a single subordinate element (*śeṣa*) is assigned to two principal elements (*śeṣin*), there is sublation (*bādha*) due to its weakness; these are five types.

Similarly, when two subordinate elements are assigned to a single principal element by two means of proof, there is sublation of the weak one due to its strength; these are five [types]. Altogether, there are seven scriptural varieties of sublation of what was not previously established (*aprāptabādha*).

1. An unambiguous direct statement (*śruti*) [sublates] a doubtful direct statement; 3. an indicative mark (*liṅga*) [sublates] another indicative mark; 4. a syntactical connection (*vākya*) [sublates] another syntactical connection; 5. a context (*prakaraṇa*) [sublates] another context; 6. a sequence (*krama*) [sublates] another sequence; 7. a name (*samākhyā*) [sublates] another name.
These seven [means of proof] become fourteen when doubled by the distinction between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*).
Page 135: The scriptural varieties of sublation of what has not yet been established [occur] through traditional law (*smṛti*).
A Smṛti that originates from Śruti is sublated by a Smṛti that originates from [other] means such as indicative mark (liṅga) due to their similarity.

Here, because there are fifteen varieties of sublation involving Śruti, indicative mark, and so forth, there are likewise fifteen varieties regarding the Smṛtis based upon each of those. Thus, there are thirty varieties.

Page 140: There are six scriptural types of sublation (*bādha*) related to tradition (*smṛti*) and custom (*ācāra*). And that [sublation] is of two kinds: sublation of what has been attained (*prāptabādha*) and sublation of what has not been attained (*aprāptabādha*).

Where, in a cognition produced by a general rule, a secondary rule, or the like—whether regarding a specific part or the entire object—there arises another cognition to the effect "this is false," that is sublation of what has been attained.

However, where the very arising of knowledge is obstructed due to the impediment to the postulation of a scriptural basis (*śruti*) regarding an inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, that is "sublation by what was not yet established" (*aprāptabādha*). Between these two, the former is mixed and is designated as "sublation characterized by the removal of the object of cognition" (*prameyāpahāralakṣaṇa*), and so on;
while the latter is also called "characterized by the cutting off of the root" (*mūlocchedalakṣaṇa*).
In that regard, sublation of what has been attained (*prāptabādha*) is also twofold: eternal (*nitya*) and optional (*vaikalpika*).
Among these, the eternal consists of twenty-one varieties, as follows:
[1] an appearance resembling direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) is sublated by direct perception.
[2] Its semblance by means of inference; [3] its semblance by means of verbal testimony; [4] its semblance by means of analogy.
[5] Through presumptive implication (arthāpatti), there is the appearance of that; [6] through non-existence (abhāva), there is the appearance of that. These are the six worldly subversions (bādhā).
Now, the scriptural [sublation].

[1] The permanent by the occasional, as in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, where it is prescribed that "one should recite fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses"; this is the examination of the sublation of the permanent by the occasional.

Regarding the sequence based on the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), that example was stated in the section (5.1.8.16) beginning with "But in the archetype, because of its own word" (*prakṛtau tu svaśabdatvāt*): the offering of the *āgneya* and *aindrāgna* cakes follows the offering of the *ājya*; however, by the order of the principal acts, the offering of the *āgneya* cake—which belongs to the class of vegetable offerings—should be performed before the offering of the *ājya*, as indicated by its position in the text. Regarding the sequence based on the order of performance (*pravṛttikrama*), it was stated in the section (5.1.2.4) beginning with "In the sequence of cutting, sprinkling, and placing, it should be according to the performance" (*avadānābhighāraṇāsādanānām ānupūrvye pravṛttyā syāt*).

For the ritual procedures (*dharma*) of the *sāṃnāyya* offering were established first, and subsequently those of the *āgneya* offering; however, the actual offering (*pradāna*) of the *āgneya* comes first, followed by that of the *sāṃnāyya*, and then the cutting of the portion for *sviṣṭakṛt*.

As for the sprinkling with the remains of the *prayāja* offerings and the placing on the altar (*vedyāmāsādana*), these would logically follow the order of commencement (*pravṛttikrama*) and thus belong first to the *sāṃnāyya*; yet, according to the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), they must be performed first for the *āgneya*.

Thus, among the fifteen types of sublation (*bādha*), four specific varieties—namely, sublation of the reading by the meaning (*arthena pāṭhabādhaḥ*), sublation of the position by the reading (*pāṭhena sthānabādhaḥ*), sublation of the primary by the reading (*pāṭhena mukhyabādhaḥ*), and sublation of the application by the primary (*mukhyena pravṛttibādhaḥ*)—have been specifically illustrated with four examples in four respective sections. Furthermore, the example for the first variety of sublation was set forth by Jaimini himself as a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*) in the aphorism: "By sequence and by the word *artha* [there is sublation]. (Jaimini Sūtra 5.1.13).
However, the examples for the other ten types of sublation (*bādhameda*) were not mentioned in the fifth book because they were not found; they have been set aside by me.

Furthermore, regarding *śruti* and the others, there is mutual sublation even among those of the same class—such as between two *śruti*s, two meanings, two positions (*sthāna*), two primary [meanings], or two applications (*pravṛtti*)—just as there is between *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth. Because such examples are possible, they were not considered in the fifth book.

It has been stated in the section *Mantrastu virodhe syāt* (5.1.9.16) that between the order of the injunction (*vidhi*) and the order of the mantra, the order of the mantra is stronger. For instance, the offering (*nirvāpaṇa*) for Agni-Soma is recited first, while the Brāhmaṇa passage for Agni follows later; however, in the Mantra Section (*mantrakāṇḍa*), the pair of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for Agni comes first, followed by those for Agni-Soma. In this case, because the order of the mantra-recitation overrides the order of the injunction-recitation, the offering for Agni comes first and the offering for Agni-Soma comes later.
These sixteen varieties of sublation, together with the previously mentioned sixty-two varieties of sublation, establish seventy-eight varieties of sublation regarding what has not been attained.
Likewise, a Smṛti rule is sublated by a Śruti rule;
for example, the Smṛti rule "The Audumbarī post must be entirely covered" is sublated by the Śruti rule "One should chant the Udgītha while touching the Audumbarī post."

Likewise, established practice is sublated by Śruti; for example, a practice in the form of an exception is sublated by a Śruti in the form of a prohibition, such as: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not speak like a barbarian. Similarly, practice is also sublated by Smṛti.
For instance, according to the Smṛti: "Having married the daughter of a maternal uncle, or likewise one of the same maternal lineage (mātṛgotra),
or even one with the same *pravara*, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance"—
this [text] establishes the custom among Southerners of marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle.
Likewise, Smṛti is sublated by a directly perceived Vedic indicative mark (liṅga).
An example of this has been stated by Someśvara:
the aforementioned Smṛti prohibiting marriage with the daughter of one's maternal uncle is sublated by the Vedic indicative mark previously mentioned.

And two scriptural indicators (*śrauta-liṅga*) are stated therein: one is the mantra-form, "Now our progenitor has brought us together as a husband and wife; may the god Savitṛ, possessing all forms, [unite] you"; another is the mantra-form, "Come, O Indra, by these paths praised [by us]"; and the third is the form of a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the injunction for spreading the two ladles (*srucau vyūhati*) in the Vājasaneyaka—"He spreads the *juhū* eastward and the *upabhṛt* westward"—which says: "Therefore, from the very same person, both the mother and the father are born; indeed, we meet in the third generation, we meet in the fourth."
The meaning of that and its refutation have been explained at length in the *Śābdīprabhākara*;
however, an example from that work is stated here:
"Behold the forms of Sūryā—blessing, slaughter, and excessive cutting; even the Brahmans listen to them."

Thus, by means of the Vedic mantra pertaining to the wearing of three garments— namely, the *āśāsana*, *viśasana*, and *vikartana*— in the case of Sūryā’s daughter-in-law (*vadhūvadhu*), there is a sublation of the Smṛti rule stating, "One should give the bride to the one who knows Sūryā," which prescribes the wearing of a single garment.
Likewise, through direct Vedic indicative marks (*liṅga*), established custom (*ācāra*) is sublated.

Just as in the *Yavavarāha-adhikaraṇa* (11.4.8–9), the practice consisting of the use of the word "barley" (*yava*) for *priyaṅgu* plants is set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the statement: "When other plants wither, then these stand up as if rejoicing. Thus, the eighty-two varieties of sublation (*bādha*)—comprising the five types of sublation involving the relationship between Śruti, Smṛti, and Ācāra, together with the seventy-eight previously mentioned varieties of sublation—are established as varieties of sublation regarding what has not been obtained (*aprāpta-bādha*).

Likewise, [1] a Smṛti that is not contradicted by the Veda (anāgamasmṛti) sublates one that is so contradicted (āgamasmṛti), just as the Smṛti of Manu and others stating "one should not kill oneself" sublates the Smṛti of heretics and others stating "one should throw one's body into a pit.

[2] Similarly, a Smṛti that is not censured (avigītasmṛti) sublates one that is censured (vigītasmṛti), as in the case of the rule "one should not be a thief," which sublates the rule: "Likewise, having fasted for six meals, at the time of the seventh meal, one may take food from a person of low conduct according to the rules for a horse-stealer."
[1] Thus, this Smṛti rule as well is intended merely to indicate the absence of punishment and refers to minor offenses.

[2] A Smṛti rule concerning an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha) sublates a Smṛti rule concerning a seen purpose (dṛṣṭārtha); for example, by the rule "One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa," the rule "One may strike back against one who seeks to kill" (which serves the seen purpose of self-protection) is set aside. [3] Likewise, a practice based on the Veda (āmnāta-ācāra) sublates a practice not based on the Veda (anāmnāta-ācāra).

It is sublated, as stated in the *Pīlvadhikaraṇa* (Śābarabhāṣya 1.3.15): that is, the practice consisting of the use of the word *pīlu* in the sense of a tree sublates the practice consisting of the use of the words *salla* and *iccha* in the sense of an elephant.

[5] Likewise, a contradicted practice (*vigītācāra*) is sublated by an uncontradicted practice (*avigītācāra*), as for example, the practice among Southerners (*dākṣiṇātya*) of abstaining from eating meat sublates the practice among Easterners (*prācya*) and others of eating meat.

In this regard, the inference from scripture (*śruti*) based on these two practices would apply only in a general sense, because the postulation of qualifying terms such as "southerner" or "easterner" has been rejected by the logic of the *Holākā* section (PMS 1.3.16–23).

Consequently, there arises the question: is there an option (*vikalpa*) between the two, or is there an absolute annulment (*atyantabādha*) by one of them? Even if there is annulment, upon inquiry as to which annuls which, the practice of eating—which is censured (*vigīta*) and rooted in greed and other such motives—is annulled by the practice of abstaining—which is uncensured (*avigīta*) and whose roots in greed and the like are impossible.

[6] Likewise, a practice (*ācāra*) with a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) is sublated by a practice with an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), as for example, by the practice of the spring festival (*vasantotsava*). In the commentary on *Śābarabhāṣya* 11.3.17, which states, "Or rather, when no specific cause is perceived, other [practices] are understood [as authoritative]," there is a sublation of any practice with a visible purpose that is contemporaneous with it, by means of one with an invisible purpose established through direct revelation (*śruti*).
Thus, these six types of relationship between *smṛti* and *ācāra*, together with the eighty-two previously mentioned varieties of sublation, establish eighty-nine distinct types of sublation.

Similarly, just as in the case of the expression "aindyā," that which originates from *smṛti*—starting from the third [source] and so forth—is sublated by that which originates from the [sources] beginning with *liṅga* and ending with *samākhyā*.

Just as the scriptural injunction regarding the adoption of a son—beginning with "One should adopt a son by performing oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* in the midst of the household" and so forth—is concerned with the adoption of a son accompanied by the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) such as the fire-oblation, and thus its primary force is that of an injunction; whereas the Smṛti text beginning with "There is no remainder for one born from another lineage" and so forth is a supplementary rule (*śeṣa*), serving as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the prohibition of the adopted son (*dattaka*) by the sense that "there is no [inheritance] beyond [the biological father], nor is there anything given by another," and thus it is subordinate to the former; likewise, the Smṛti text beginning with "Those sons who are born from whose seed belong to him, and not to the other" is also subordinate.

Thus, these fifteen varieties [of sublation] occur in the case of the sublation of the subordinate (śeṣa-samavāya), and another fifteen in the case of the sublation of the principal (śeṣi-samavāya), making thirty in total.

Consequently, when combined with the eighty-nine previously mentioned varieties of sublation, one hundred and nineteen varieties of sublation regarding that which has not yet been established (aprāpta-bādha) are established.

[1] Likewise, that which originates from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is sublated by that which originates from an injunction (*vidhi*), just as the explanatory passage "When the king of men arrives, they slaughter a bull or a barren cow" is sublated by the injunction "One should not kill a cow," which itself originates from an injunction such as "Do not come, do not go, lest you be slain. Similarly, the explanatory passage "One should provide a large ox or a large goat for a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*)" is sublated by the injunction "One should offer clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

[2] Likewise, that which is doubtful is sublated by that which is certain, just as the doubt regarding "With what [is the sprinkling]?"—namely, whether with water or something else—is resolved by the praise of clarified butter.

[3] Likewise, that which has a weak purpose is sublated by that which has a strong purpose; for example, the Vedic statement "Having prepared the grass-bundle (veda), one prepares the altar (vedi)," which rests on a weak sequence, is sublated by the Smṛti statement "One should recite the *ānām* [sūtra] upon sneezing," which rests on a strong ritual substance.

[4] Likewise, a concluding passage (*upasaṃhāra*) is sublated by an introductory passage (*upakrama*); for example, the words "Ṛg" and so forth in the conclusion of the passage "Loudly with the Ṛg [verses]" are sublated by the introduction to the Vedas.

[5] Likewise, that which has an entirely unseen purpose is sublated by that which has a restrictive unseen purpose; for example, the status of being for the sake of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the milk-offering (*sāṃnāyya*) in the act of threshing is sublated by its status as being for the sake of the medicinal herbs (*oṣadha*).
[6] Remoteness of assistance (*ārādupakārakatva*) is set aside by immediate conjunction (*saṃnipātitva*), as in the case of the *paśupuroḍāśa* and similar offerings.

[7] The injunction of multiple matters is sublated by the injunction of fewer matters, as in "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and so forth, where the qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is sublated by the injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
[8] Likewise, multiplicity of purpose is sublated by singleness of purpose, as in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.30–35, second exposition).

[9] Likewise, multiplicity of words is sublated by singularity of words, as in the section on Grammar (PMS 11.1.24–29). [10] A plurality of statements is sublated by a single statement, as follows: in the case of the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi*, if the sacrifice were intended for the recipient, then the dative case in "avadyanāya" would have to signify the ablative; the verb "anayat" would have to mean "received"; and in the phrase "sa svāṃ devatām," the pronoun "sa" (he), being non-primary, would have to refer back to the previously mentioned color (of the horse); furthermore, since Varuṇa would be the giver, he could not be joined with the word "devatā" (deity). Thus, there is a sublation of many [interpretations].
[11] Because, in the case of the donor and the recipient, it is the recipient alone who has a self-interest.

Likewise, that which arises in one Veda is sublated by what is prescribed in another Veda; for example, at the *āghāna* sacrifice, the *vāravantīya* and other chants originating in the Sāmaveda—which would otherwise be performed loudly—are sublated by the prescription of the Yajurveda, which requires them to be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).

[12] Similarly, that which is prescribed in another recensional branch (*śākhā*) is sublated by what is prescribed in one's own branch; for example, the offering after sunrise (*uditahoma*) and so forth are sublated by the offering before sunrise (*anuditahoma*) and so forth.

[13] That which is studied outside of the context (*anārambhādhīta*) is sublated by that which belongs to the context (*prākaraṇika*). For example, the *sāma* consisting of fifteen parts studied outside the context is sublated by the two feet [of the *jagatī*].

Now, one might object: here, because of the mixture [of elements], it is precisely through the principle of "conclusion" (*upasaṃhāra*) that the injunction for the *yacchabda*-sacrifice—which was not obtained in the archetype (*prakṛti*)—is established according to the Vārttika school; by that, the injunction for the fire-altars (*agni*) studied within the context of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* is sublated.

"The intermediate sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) are the measure; they become intermediate sacrificial posts"—these are *anāramyavāda* (unattached statements) which apply to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) even when devoid of the original injunctions (*codaka*).
This very point was stated in the section concerning other scriptures (*śāstrāntarādhikaraṇa*, 2.4.18).

[14] Likewise, the statement regarding performance (*prayogavacana*) is set aside by reliance on the *codaka*, just as in the *Śyena* sacrifice, the elevated status (*udātta*) of the archetypal subsidiaries is set aside by the *codaka*-obtained quality of being performed by non-sacrificers (*nāntvikakṛtva*).

[15] Likewise, that which rests upon the deity is set aside by that which rests upon the substance; for example, in the case of the *aindrapuroḍāśa* (the cake for Indra), the procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *sānnāyya* might apply due to the commonality of the deity, but it is set aside by the procedure of the *neya* (the cake for Agni) which applies due to the commonality of the substance.

[16] That which is subsequently established sets aside that which was previously established; for example, in the *adhvarakalpā*, because the twelve-pot-sherd offering to Agni-Viṣṇu is a subsidiary (*aikādaśinī*) of the offering to Indra-Agni, the full-moon ritual procedure (*paurṇamāsatantra*)—which had been reached for the butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) to Sarasvatī by means of the new-moon ritual procedure (*āmāvāsyatantra*)—is set aside.
[17] Direct denotation (*śruti*) sets aside metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for example...
Even a prescriptive rule (vidhi) is set aside when its application is impossible, as in the case of the *pūtīka* plants.
Likewise, by way of subsequent application (*anuprakṣeṇa*), an ellipsis (*abhyāhāra*) is set aside, as in "O Agni, that which is your rajasas... and so forth.
Similarly, by way of conventional usage (*klṛpti*), etymological derivation (*yoga*) is set aside, as in the word "charioteer" (*rathakāra*).
[50] Likewise, in another case, conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is sublated by etymological derivation (*yoga*), as in the word *prokṣaṇī*.
[51] Similarly, as in the cases of *barhis*, *ājya*, and *puroḍāśa*.
[52] Likewise, when an established etymological derivation exists, the basis for [conventional] respect is sublated, as in the very case of the word *prokṣaṇī*.

Likewise, in the case of [terms] distinguished as derivative (*yaugika*) or literal (*prasajya*), and in their respective cognitions and designations, the status of being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is sublated by the status of being a name (*nāmadheya*). However, in the case of established (*nirūḍha*) terms such as *soma* and others, the status of being a name is sublated by the status of being an injunction of a quality. These are the five types of sublation (*bādhameda*).
The fifty-seven varieties of non-obstruction (*aprāptabādha*) along with the directions [and sub-directions] are established.
Together with the previously mentioned one hundred and nineteen varieties of non-obstruction, there are one hundred and seventy-six varieties of non-obstruction established.

Likewise, the previously mentioned one hundred and sixty-six varieties of obstruction (*prāptabādha*), combined with these one hundred and seventy-six varieties of non-obstruction, result in two hundred and forty-two varieties of obstruction in total.

Furthermore, among all these various forms of sublation (*bādha*), when there is an obstruction by purposelessness (*ānarthakya-pratighāta*), a contrary sublation occurs; thus, all these [conflicts] being classified according to their respective types, four hundred and eighty-four possibilities are conceived.
For example, in the case of "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) which establishes the threshing of all rice is sublated by the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Likewise, in that very instance, even the primary mode of operation (*mukhya-vṛtti*) is sublated by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

And in cases such as *dyena*, because the original meaning (*upamāna*) would be purposeless, it is set aside by the secondary sense (*gauṇī*) through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).

Not only is the third means of proof (*tātīyapramāṇa*) set aside by the obstruction of purposelessness, but even the second means of proof (*dvitīyapramāṇa*) is so set aside; for example, in the *Abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice, in the two sentences "those which are *svaviṣṭhā*" and "those which are *agniṣṭhā*," since multiple objects are mentioned, there arises the contingency of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Consequently, the differentiation of rites (*karmabheda*) that would otherwise follow from the quality is set aside because the injunction "he cooks them together" (*saha śrapayati*) would otherwise be rendered purposeless.

Even when there is no total lack of purpose for the *śruti* and the other means of proof, the sublation (*bādha*) of each preceding one by each succeeding one occurs through the force of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) and so forth. We shall elaborate upon this with examples. To begin with, regarding the sublation of *śruti* by *liṅga*: in the case of the injunctions "he cuts with a ladle" (*suveṇāvadyati*) and "he cuts with a knife" (*svadhitināvadyati*), the *śruti* establishes that the sacrificial butter (*ājya*) and the flesh (*māṃsa*) are respectively the objects to be cut (*śeṣa*) in the act of cutting, whether it be the cutting of liquid or the cutting of something else. Thus, while the object to be cut (*śeṣin*) is initially understood to apply to multiple instances, it is restricted by *liṅga* (syntactic indication) to the cutting of liquid alone; consequently, [the application of] the sacrificial butter is sublated in the case of the cutting of solid meat.

Likewise, when there is a single *śeṣin* (the principal item), such as the *dravadravya* (liquid substance) for the offering, the use of the *sruva* ladle is established by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). However, since multiple *śeṣas* (subsidiary items) are also applicable, the *sruva* itself is restricted to that specific case by indicative power (*liṅga*), thereby setting aside even the direct Vedic statement regarding its use as a general instrument.

Furthermore, by syntactical connection (*vākya*) and indicative power (*liṅga*), the capacity of the mantra "devasya tvā" to reveal deities such as Savitṛ is applied by syntactical connection to the pouring of the oblation for those specific deities, thereby setting aside its application to the pouring for the primary deity and others.

And in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), it is established in the tenth book (*daśama*) [sūtras 10.3.12–17] that the mantra "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre" belongs to the first libation (*pūrvāghāra*) because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the *hiraṇyagarbha* mantra; whereas for the one performing the second libation (*uttarāghāra*), the indicative mark is set aside by the syntactical connection (*vākya*) consisting of its co-utterance with the mantra "Indra ūrdhvo'dhvare," since the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) arising from that mantra is already established for the second libation. Thus, the indicative mark is overridden by the sentence.

Alternatively, by means of the *prakaraṇa* (context), the *nivīta* prescribed in the sentence "The priests proceed without the *nivīta*"—which is established through the third [book]—becomes applicable to the primary rite alone due to the *barhis-tanmanya-nyāya* (3.7.11–15). Consequently, it serves as a subordinate element for the sake of the principal rite.

For this very reason, it will be stated in the tenth book (10.4.1.1–2, varṇaka 1) that since the *upavīta* obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) regarding those *aiṣṭika* rites belongs to a different domain, the discussion concerning sublation (*bādha*) or combination (*samuccaya*) with the *nārīṣṭa-homa* does not apply here.
[Objection: In that case, would the *nivīta* not also fail to apply to the other [subsidiary] rites? [Response: However, there is a disparity in the logic regarding the third type of oblation.
It is said in reply:

Just like the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) belonging to the Soma sacrifice, which exist solely for the sake of the primary rite, they provide assistance to the other [subsidiaries] through the agent or by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*) across the two performances; therefore, the scriptural statement need not be strained to apply to those [subsidiaries] as well.

However, since the principal oblation (*pradhāna-havis*) is already present on the altar and the sacrificial grass (*vedibarhis*), while the subsidiary oblations (*aṅga-havis*) have not yet been placed there, one would have to exert a separate effort for that purpose as well through the syntactical connection (*vākya*). Thus, the principle of the third [book] (*tātīyanyāya*) would be rendered void.

Furthermore, the *prakaraṇa* (context), which by its sequence applies the mantra "Thou art named Darvi" even to the Āgneya and other sacrifices, is sublated by the *yathāsaṃkhya* (order of enumeration) when it is restricted to the Upāṃśuyāja alone.
Moreover, a mantra, being non-active in itself, cannot issue commands regarding specific ritual procedures based merely on the meaning.
And since this [word] has an indistinct gender and expresses this meaning [of *prakaraṇa*], how can it be said that it is not the subject matter of the context (*prakaraṇa*) due to such ignorance?
For according to the opinion of Miśra, its apprehension is possible precisely through the force of its pronunciation (*uccāraṇavaśena*).
Other matters should be understood from the *Prakāśa*.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the sequence of recitation for the *varuṇapraghāsas* and so forth, since the name (*samākhyā*) is present, it establishes the restriction of agency; thus, when the name provides the restriction, the sequence does not apply.
In this same way, there are fifteen such sublations even in the case of those separated by one [step].
These too, due to the distinction between the principal (*śeṣin*) and the subordinate (*śeṣa*), become doubled, resulting in thirty, along with the previous ones.

**Examination of the Varieties of Sublation (Bādhabheda-nirūpaṇam)** The relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) consists of five hundred and fourteen varieties of sublation, occurring in conjunction with four hundred and eighty-four [other factors].

Among these, there is the sublation of inferential *śruti* and so forth by perceptual *śruti* and so forth. For example, in the case of the Śyena sacrifice and others, the perceptual *śruti*, "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is made of reeds (*śara*)," sublates the inferential *śruti*, "He places the oblations upon the sacrificial grass."
These are the fifteen types of sublation (*bādha*).

Likewise, there is the sublation of inferential [means of proof] by means of scriptural testimony (*śruti*) and so forth, which are themselves inferential; for example, in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the inferential *śruti* and other means that enjoin the animal cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) are sublated by the scriptural testimony and other means—such as direct statement—that enjoin the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and so forth, which are themselves to be inferred.
These too constitute fifteen types of sublation.

Likewise, there is the sublation of scriptural texts and the like—which are based on inference—by means of direct perception, indicative marks (*liṅga*), and so forth; for example, in the case of *kṛṣṇala* berries, by virtue of their inherent capacity, there is the sublation of the scriptural text inferred through extended application (*atideśa*) which states, "One threshes the rice grains.
These [sublations] also number fifteen.
Thus, there are forty-five varieties of sublation.
Together with the previously mentioned five hundred and fourteen varieties of sublation (*bādha*), there are five hundred and fifty-nine varieties of sublation.

Whenever it is stated that "this is sublated by that," [the process] is as follows: inference is sublated by perception, as for example, the inference of being without an objective basis (*nirālambana*) is sublated by the perception of external objects such as "this is existent" and so forth; likewise, a cognition of a mirage and the like [sublates] the inference.
Similarly, a fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) is sublated by all six valid means of knowledge.

Scripture (*śruti*) sublates tradition (*smṛti*); for example, the scripture stating "one should sing the *udgītha* after touching the *audumbarī* pillar" sublates the tradition stating "the entire *audumbarī* pillar is to be covered with cloth."

An unauthoritative Smṛti (anāpta-smṛti) is that which is contradicted by an authoritative Smṛti—for example, the Smṛti stating, "A wise man should not kill himself," because it is not opposed [to other sources], versus the Smṛti stating, "One should cast off the body in a field of Kedāra," which is refuted by the fact that its author is untrustworthy. An opposed Smṛti (vigīta-smṛti) is refuted by an unopposed Smṛti—for example, the Smṛti stating, "The wife of a Brāhmaṇa may be from the Śūdra caste," is refuted by the Smṛtis of Yājñavalkya and others, such as: "That the taking of a Śūdra woman as a wife for the twice-born is permitted—that is not my opinion."

(1.56) Contradicted: A Smṛti rule with a visible purpose, such as "one should strike back at one who seeks to kill," is contradicted by a Smṛti rule with an invisible purpose, such as "one must never kill a Brāhmaṇa," for the sake of self-protection.

It arises from the authority of Śruti, as well as from the indicative power (*liṅga*) and other means of proof, such as the injunction for the formal adoption of a son—which is accompanied by ritual procedures like the *homā* sacrifice—as stated in Vasiṣṭha Smṛti 1.56: "Having informed the kinsmen and the king, and having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* mantras in the midst of the settlement, one should accept [the son]"; and because it arises from the indicative power of prohibitions regarding the adopted son (*dattaka*), such as the text: "O Agni, there is no other offspring born of another."

Practice based on Smṛti: for example, the practice of giving the bride’s garment on the fourth day of the wedding, as established by Smṛti texts such as "One should give the bride’s garment to the sun and so forth. The doubtful is [resolved] by the non-doubtful—as in "the pebbles are smeared" (*aktāḥ śarkarāḥ*), where the doubtful is resolved by the non-doubtful statement regarding the essence of ghee (*ghṛtasattvena*). That which has a weak basis is [resolved] by that which has a strong basis—as in the Vedic sentence "having made the *veda*, he makes the *vedi*," where the sentence with a weak basis is resolved by the sentence concerning the sipping of water (*ācamana*) based on the stronger grounds of direct revelation (*śruti*) and so forth. That which stands in the conclusion is [resolved] by that which stands in the introduction—as in the word *ṛc* and so forth, which stands in the conclusion, being resolved by the word *veda* standing in the introduction.

An absolutely unseen purpose [is superseded] by a restricted unseen purpose—for example, the threshing and so forth for the *sāṃnāyya* offerings, which serve an absolutely unseen purpose, [is superseded] by the threshing and so forth for the vegetable offering (*auṣadha*), which serves a restricted unseen purpose. An indirect auxiliary function (*ārādupakārakatva*) [is superseded] by a direct auxiliary function (*sāmavāyikatva*)—for example, the indirect auxiliary function of the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) [is superseded] by its direct auxiliary function. The prescription of multiple purposes [is superseded] by the prescription of a single purpose—for example, in the view that "He offers with the *darśa*" is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there is the prescription of multiple purposes in the form of the qualifier and the qualified; however, in the view that it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), there is the prescription of a single purpose.
