The maxim of the seed and the sprout (*bījāṅkuranyāya*).
According to Amarasimha, "the sprout is the growth of the seed.
Without the seed, the sprout does not arise; and without the sprout, there is no production of the seed.
Thus, this principle applies wherever there is a mutual relationship of cause and effect.
Accordingly, a type of seed is not the cause of a type of sprout, nor is a type of sprout the cause of a type of seed.

Therefore, because the stream of seeds and sprouts is beginningless, the fact that a particular seed is the cause of a particular sprout does not mean that the same seed is the cause of that very sprout; thus, there is no circularity of dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
And thus it is accepted because it is authoritative; for where there is authoritativeness, there is no assumption of beginninglessness.
This is indicated by the established doctrine that the assumption of beginninglessness applies only to an authoritative tradition and not to anything else.

Accordingly, it is stated in the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*: "If it is argued that embodiment is caused by the merit and demerit produced by that [body], then, because of the mutual dependence between the connection with a body and the merit and demerit, as well as their being produced by that [body], this would result in an infinite regress."

He offers a rebuttal with the words "No," etc., [anticipating the objection]: "When the soul's connection with a body has arisen, there is the production of merit and demerit; and when that exists, there is the birth consisting of the form of that connection. Thus, due to mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), because one is unestablished, the second is also unestablished.
However, this mutual dependence would only occur if the action of merit and demerit produced by this body were the cause of the soul's connection with this very body.

The production of the connection with this body arises from the karma of a previous body; the production of the connection with that [previous] body arises from the karma of the body prior to that; and so on, ad infinitum like the seed and the sprout—thus there is no fault. To this he says: "anyā" (other).
The meaning is that such a [regressus ad infinitum] is not supported by valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇika*).

For just as a sprout from a seed and another seed [from that sprout] are perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the connection of the self with the body produced by prior karma is not perceived directly, nor is there any scripture (*āgama*) to that effect; on the contrary, the intention is that scriptural passages such as "for he is unattached" (*asaṅgo hi*) preclude its being the agent of all actions—so says Ānandagiri.
(Sāhasī 217). By the maxim, "In the absence of a seed, whence can there be fruit," he elucidates the non-duality (*advaitatva*) of the Self.

*Upadeśasāhasrī*, verse 1919, by Rāmatīrtha: "By the maxim that 'in the absence of the seed there is the absence of the fruit,' it is the firm conviction of those who know the Vedas that when ignorance—the cause of grief and delusion—is removed, birth and other states of the self will no longer occur.
[This concludes] the sowing of the seed;
[it belongs to] the fire-piling ritual (*agnicaya*).

In the *kuṣṭa* fire-piling (*agnicaya*), the sowing of various seeds is performed. In that context, fourteen mantras belonging to that section are to be taken up without following the [original] sequence, and not from the very beginning. This is to be seen under the section titled "The Adhikaraṇa on the Exception to the Elision of the Final [Syllable]" (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 455).
The sowing of seeds is performed upon a black antelope skin placed on the mortar;
that barley is the substance to be threshed.
(Vi.)
The maxim of the seed and the tree:
just as from a seed a tree arises, and from a tree a seed [arises]. Sāhasī, 216. Even when [the meaning] is already known (*buddhe*), a specific mode of pronunciation is still postulated.

Just as in the case of [the authority of] the Buddha and others, there is not even the slightest possibility of establishing the validity of those whose very foundation is impossible. *Bubhukṣitaḥ* (hungry).
Just as in the case of the Buddha and others, for those whose root is impossible, there is no possibility whatsoever of validating their authority.
Vaidyanātha:
212.2, p. 16. According to the Mīmāṃsaka, cognition (*buddhi*) is inferable.
*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 60: "Cognition is indeed formless; it is the external object that possesses form."
The Buddhists maintain that cognition possesses a form (*sākārā buddhiḥ*);
the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that it is formless (*nirākārā*).
The Buddhists maintain that cognition is directly perceived (*pratyakṣā*).
The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that [cognition] is not perceptible.
Bhāṣya 1.1.5 states: "Cognition is formless;
it is to be inferred through an inference based on the 'hundred-fold' mark once the object has been known."
The inference is as follows:
"The pot is qualified by cognition through the relation of objecthood (viṣayatā), because it possesses the property of being known (jñātatva) through the relation of self-nature (svarūpa).
What is called "being known" is a specific excellence (atiśaya) residing in the object of knowledge, produced by cognition.

And that [object] is the object of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). Vaidyanātha, page 33, 1.15.5: "Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Śūnyavāda* that cognition, which has the noble [object] as its cause, arises experiencing only the form of the self (*ātman*)."

Or [as stated in] Pāṇini 1.4.123, p. 358: "And without linguistic usage (vyavahāra), it is not possible to infer the cognition of another. Ṛjuvimalā, p. 16: "For no one perceives a cognition regarding an object that is unknown;
but when [the object] is known, one understands [the cognition] through inference."
Bhāṣya 1.1.5, p. 32: Sublation is possible for that which has been made an object by the intellect (buddhi). Vi. 3.2.12: This intellect (buddhi) is for the illumination of objects;
the illumination of the object is the result, the intellect is the instrument (karaṇa), and the operation here is nothing other than that which is produced by the intellect itself.

If it produces only another birth, then its operation therein is simply that birth itself. (Ratnaprabhā 6.1.13) And there is no perception of the form of cognition without the designation of an object.
And therefore, cognition is designatable [as such].
Bhāṣya 1.1.5, p. 34. Although the preceding cognition is momentary and perishes by its very nature, it is not lost through the medium of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 694. [This refers to] the momentariness of cognitions.
Vārttika 1.2.137: That which is present in the intellect is said to be the "mark" (liṅga) [of inference] (Bhāṣya 8.1.17.33).

Bhāṣya 8.1.17.34: Cognition and action are not perceptible; therefore, they are not recognized [by means of perception]. There is no recognition of cognition and action, which are respectively the cause and the effect.
*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 247: First of all, one who acts with prior deliberation (*buddhipūrvakārī*) does not even determine [the object] as the agent, nor does he exert effort.

However, by a person acting without prior deliberation (*abuddhipūrvakārī*)—that is, one who acts by chance regarding an unknown object—even when an activity called "effort" is performed, the accomplishment of the object does not necessarily follow. *Sūtrabhāṣya*, 3.7, p. 13: A person acting with prior deliberation does not perform an activity devoid of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), even if told so a hundred times.

Vārttika 2.1.12, p. 383: Regarding the statement "The offering to Agni (āgneya) should be made accompanied by *budhanvat*," the word *agni*, which denotes the deity and functions as a prefix within the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) term *āgneya*, cannot qualify the word *budhanvat*.
Thus, the sentence refers to the mantra:
the meaning is that the *ājyabhāga* offering to Agni should be performed with a mantra containing the verbal root *budh*.
In the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, the two Ājyabhāga deities do not possess their specific qualities; therefore, the qualification "Budhanvān" (awakening) for Agni is not possible.

The mantra "Agniṃ stomena bodhaya" (Awaken Agni with the hymn) is what constitutes "Budhanvān. (Note: While the Bhāṣya reads "agniṃ stomena vardhaya," the Taittirīya Saṃhitā and Ṛgveda Saṃhitā read "bodhaya" here.)
VI. 10|4|147. [The term] *budhanvān* [is used] like *pavamānavat*, because of the specific designation.
In the *pavamāneṣṭis*, regarding the two *ājyabhāgas*, it is heard in scripture: "The *āgneya* [portion] is to be made *budhanvān*; the *saumya* [portion] is *pāvakavān*.
In that context, during the acts of renunciation (*tyāga*) and so forth, *agni* as *budhanvān* and *soma* as *pāvakavān* are the designators (*abhidhātṛ*) endowed with their respective qualities.

"To Agni accompanied by the wise (Budhanvat), this [is offered], not mine"; "May Agni accompanied by the wise enjoy this oblation"—and likewise, "To Soma accompanied by the purifier (Pāvakavat), this [is offered], not mine"; "May Soma accompanied by the purifier enjoy this oblation. Because there is thus a specific designation in the injunction, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is just like the case of the Pavamāna offerings, where the word "Agni" is used as qualified by specific attributes such as "Pavamāna" and so forth.
Due to the specification of a particular mantra, there should be no modification of the deity.
When the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) has been established by the sūtra, he states the final conclusion (siddhānta):
"This should not be a modification of the deity."
Regarding the "specification of a particular mantra": this refers to the specification of a particular mantra, such as "The *budhanvat* [mantra] dedicated to Agni is to be performed," and so forth.
A mantra such as "Awaken Agni with the hymn, kindling him, the immortal" (*agniṃ stomena bodhaya samidhāno amartyam*) is called *budhanvat* because it contains the verbal root *budh*.
Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that this is a specification of a mantra, not a specification of a deity.
Some, desiring to eat, partook of the meal of Śrī Rājaka.
Bhāṣya 1.3.14, p. 186. "Why should one who is hungry eat with two hands?"—this is a maxim used to express an excess of longing.
"Just as the world awakens, the lamp burns, and life itself beholds my curiosity; O beloved, being hungry, exercise patience for just a moment— why should one who is hungry eat with only two hands?"

The reckless one. 641. There is a maxim: "What sin does a hungry man not commit? (And what does a poor man not do?). The reckless one. 643, 644. There is a maxim: "Nothing occurs to a hungry man. And it has been said: "The world is awake, the lamp is burning; let the living one behold your wonder!"
"I shall not maintain my composure for even a moment; to one who is hungry, nothing at all appears [clearly].
(Sāhasī. 642). "For one who is hungry, there is an agitation of the *pitta* humor due to lack of food. (Vi. 6|3|2). "For one desiring to eat, the *Sarvastoma-atirātra* [sacrifice is prescribed]."

The word *bṛhaspati* conveys the meaning of the word *bṛhat* (great), as in the passage: "May Sarasvatī drive away the revilers of the gods and the wisdom of every great (*bṛhat*) deceiver" (Bhāṣya 10.12.132).
[It is used] in the *Bṛhat-sāman*, in the *Ārbhava-pavamāna*, and in the *Viśvajit* sacrifice where all the *pṛṣṭha-stotras* are performed.
Bhā. 10|6|15|14; Bṛhadeva, pṛṣṭha in a specific *vikṛti* [rite], 10|17|16|15–57: The source (*yoni*) of the *bṛhat* [Sāman] is the *bṛhatī* [meter], namely "tvāmiddhi havāmahe";
the subsequent *paṅkti* [verse] is "sa tvaṃ naścitra".
9|2|6|25. The *pṛṣṭha* group [of chants] originates from Bṛhadratha.
Ratna. 10|5|25|85. In the Viśvajit sacrifice, there is no simultaneous placement (*naikatra-niveśa*) of all the [chants] beginning with the *bṛhat*.
Bhā. 10|6|8|24. The *bṛhat* chant is composed in the *pragātha* meter.
The interweaving (*pragrathana*) of the *bṛhatī* and *paṅkti* meters results in the *kakub* form.
Bhāṣya 9.2.6.26, Section 1: "One desiring heaven should perform the greatest, the unlimited [sacrifice].
Saṃkarṣa 2.1.30: The *bṛhat* chants, being composed of various meters and so forth, should be performed in the *bṛhatī* meter, not in the *rayantara*.
Bhāṣya 9.2.16.47: The *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] in the *ārbhava-pavamāna* of the *viśvajit*.
Bhāṣya 7.3.18: Regarding the *pratipad* of the *bṛhat-pṛṣṭha* in the *jyotiṣṭoma*:
"One should make the *upavatī* the *pratipad* of the *rathantara-pṛṣṭha*, and the *agravatī* the *pratipad* of the *bṛhat-pṛṣṭha*."
The opening verse (*pratipad*) is the *ṛc* beginning with "prayujo vāco agriyaḥ" (Vi.
10.5.16). It is characterized by the *bṛhat* sāman, not the *rathantara* sāman;
thus, in that case, neither the *bṛhat* nor the *rathantara* serves as the determining cause (*nimitta*).
Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 6.1.19: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the *pṛṣṭha* chant is accomplished by either the *Bṛhat* or the *Rathantara* [sāman].
Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 10.6.124: There is an option (*vikalpa*) between the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara* in a single ritual act, because they serve the same purpose.
Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 12.2.18–15: In the *gavāmayana* sacrifice, the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara* are to be performed individually, one at a time, during the *pṛṣṭha* extraction.
10.6.314–5. See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1550, under the entry "gavāmayane pṛṣṭhe ṣaṣṭhe.
In the case of the *saṃsava*, the *gosava*, and the *apaciti* sacrifices, the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] are to be employed together specifically in the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*.
10.6.8.24–26. See [the discussion] under "saṃsavādau ubhayasāmake kratau."
In the case of the *saṃsava* sacrifice involving the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans], their coexistence (*sāhitya*) is dependent upon the primary action.
In that context, even when they are performed separately, their coexistence is not precluded;
one Sāman will accomplish one stotra, and the second will accomplish another.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction in the conjunction of all [factors] because their cooperation depends upon assisting the primary [element],
then the following is stated in response:

Where there is a mutual connection of assistance, it is only logical that this [assistance] occurs through that which is joined with both actions—whether by the beginning, the mantra, or the conclusion—and not separately.
Just as it is understood that "by this one assistance must be rendered," so too it is understood that "[it is to be rendered] together with the other.
And those two, being joined with their respective capacities, assist the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] in its consecration.
Therefore, their combination alone is appropriate.
Bhāṣya 10.6.8.25. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the singing of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] is accomplished by means of their mutual non-suppression.
9.2.6.25–28. See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1822, under the entry "Bṛhat-Rathantare jyotiṣṭome."
For the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* are employed as means for the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *ṛc*.
Bhāṣya 10.6.8.25. Words such as *Bṛhat*, *Rathantara*, and so forth, denote specific *sāmans*;
however, the word *sāman* is a general term that refers to mere chanting (*gāna*), and not to a *ṛc* qualified by chanting.

VI. 9.2.1. In a sacrifice (*kratu*) that has both the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara* as its *sāman* chants, the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the *Rathantara* and so forth are to be established according to the model of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
And it is the same when there is a single purpose in both *sāmans*. Commentary: Sacrifices that have both *sāmans* are those [in which] both [the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara*] serve as the *sāmans*.
It is heard in scripture: "One should perform both [Sāmans] at the Saṃsava; one should perform both at the Gosava; at the Apavitra and the Ekāha, one should perform both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara.
However, the properties of the Bṛhat and the properties of the Rathantara exist in the archetype (prakṛti), and these are extended here by the force of the general rule (codaka).

In this regard, there arises a doubt: should both sets of characteristics be performed in the *ubhayasāman* sacrifice, or is it merely restated— as in the case of the sentences concerning *vrīhi* and *yava*— for the purpose of enjoining both, namely that the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* are both [to be used] as the *sāman*?
But the production of the sacrifice is not effected by those two [mantras],
whereby there would be a difference in the sacrifice and a difference in the *apūrva*.
Therefore, in that case, the distinction is established because of the distinctness of the *apūrva*.
Others say:
although the *sāman* provides a visible benefit, the *stomas* provide an invisible benefit;
therefore, properties such as loudness (*uccaiṣtva*) and so forth are prompted by the *stomas*.
Therefore, there is a fixed rule.
And so the Commentator will say: "Even by means of a *sāman*, both the seen and the unseen are accomplished.
That is incorrect.
The word *rathaṃtara* would have to serve as an indicator (*lakṣaṇā*) for the *stoma*.

Furthermore, the *stobhas* and the high pitch (*uccais-tva*) and so forth are subordinate elements (*guṇa*) within the *sāman*; as it has been stated: "And because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another, there is no [independent] connection" (3.1.12).
The principle of "no other means" (*aṇanā-nyāya*) also does not apply here, because the *stomas* and the loudness of the voice (*uccais-tva*) and so forth are mutually independent.

As for the statement, "By the *sāman*, both the seen and the unseen [results] are achieved": that which occurs through the manifestation of the syllables of the *ṛc* is the seen; whereas that by which it produces praise for the sake of an unseen result is the unseen.
The Śāstra says: "Because both have a single purpose, those [means] operate within the sphere of accomplishing the task."

When it is argued that "dharmas flash forth in both [the Sāman] pairs as well," and thus one may proceed exactly as desired, we reply: "Since a fixed restriction (*vyavasthā*) between the two Sāmans is indicated in cases such as the *mīlana* [chanting], therefore a confusion (*saṃkara*) is not appropriate; however, this is not the case with [rites such as] sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the like."

Soma: If dharmas are employed for the accomplishment of a specific effect (*kārya*), then because the *rathaṃtara* and the *bṛhat* serve a single purpose, there would be a confusion (*saṃkara*) of their respective dharmas; this is the connection (*saṅgati*) arising from such an objection. Furthermore, the traditional doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas is that the scriptural injunction (*vacana*) in this context takes the form: "Either the *rathaṃtara* or the *bṛhat* is to be used as the *pṛṣṭha* [chant]. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: because the *rathaṃtara* and the *bṛhat* have a single purpose, there would be no distinction among their dharmas, resulting in their confusion.
Vi—“When the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [sāmans] are mixed according to their respective duties, or when they are established separately, there is a mixture of duties from the *Pṛṣṭhya* [rite];
however, the specific arrangement is determined by the direct injunction.
Bhāṭṭa—In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, six *Pṛṣṭha-stotras* are prescribed by the rule: “They praise with the *Pṛṣṭhas*.”
In that context, regarding the *Bṛhat* and *Rathaṃtara* *sāmans*, there is an option based on the scriptural statement: "The *pṛṣṭha* [laud] is either the *Bṛhat* or the *Rathaṃtara*.
The same applies to the pair consisting of the *Naudhasa* and *Dyautavāda*.
Thus, it is clearly stated in the *Kaustubha* under the *Citrādhikaraṇa* section that there are four fixed [options], and so forth.
In that context, certain duties are prescribed with reference to the *rathaṃtara*:
"While the *rathaṃtara* is being chanted, one should close one's eyes; it should be sung in a low voice," and so forth.
And certain others are prescribed with reference to the *bṛhat*: "While the *bṛhat* is being chanted, one should meditate on the ocean in one's mind; it should be sung loudly," and so forth.

Therefore, in both cases, the *sāman* is indeed the subordinate element (*śeṣin*), and not the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), because it is read in the same context as "loudness" (*uccaiḥ*) and other such qualities.

When considering whether these [qualities] are mixed in both cases or restricted, even though there is a difference in the *stomas*, because they are produced by that [same *sāman*], one assumes a single type for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*). Thus, since they serve as means to a single primary result (*pūrva*), there is a mixing (*saṃkara*) of the ritual properties (*dharma*), just as in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*) and similar rites.
For there is no conjunction of these two, as there is between the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, which would result in the absence of non-knowledge regarding the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).
Therefore, it is equally easy to maintain that even the statement regarding their optionality has its purport solely in the unseen.
Consequently, since the *apūrva* is one, and because each respective *stotra* and *sāman* enters into its essential nature, a commingling of ritual properties (*dharmasaṃkara*) is appropriate.

For this very reason, although there is a difference in the manner of invocation and so forth because the *rathantara* is produced upon the verse "Abhi tvā śūra," there is no [substitution] of one for the other; furthermore, because this [verse] is a means (*sādhana*) for the [melodic] form, it lacks the status of being a means for the *sāman*. Indeed, even when there is a difference in the verses, the manifestation of the syllables of the *sāman* does not differ.
In the case of the *kaṇvarathantara*, since neither of the two forms exists, there is no requirement for the acquisition of ritual properties (*dharma*).

For this very reason, let it be granted that the allocation of ritual properties is determined by the specific designation of the *rathantara* in some instances and the *bṛhat* in others, based on their distinctness and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that even so, although the syllables of the *ṛc* in the *Rathantara* and other chants serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), the *stobha* syllables serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*); and since that invisible result differs according to the difference in melody, there would be no confusion of ritual properties (*dharma*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*) because they are defined as the means for their respective prior results—given that the *Kaṇvarathantara* occupies the place of the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*, and thus its connection to the ritual properties follows the logic of the *Hiraṇyagarbha-mantra* by assuming an invisible result produced by the melodic portions based on the *stobhas* belonging to those respective archetypal melodic parts. This is not to be said.

Even so, this is because the possibility of confusion (*saṃkārya*) regarding the properties of the person—such as being loud (*uccais*) and so forth—is avoided by means of the singing itself, which takes the form of the syllables of the *ṛc* and other elements.

Nor should it be argued that, despite this, there would still be no occurrence of confusion because the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restriction produced by the two types of *sāman* differs, and because the status of being a means for that restricted unseen merit serves as the delimiting factor (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) for the injunction of those properties; for in the case of the *kaṇvarathaṃtara*, there is an absence of such differentiation according to the logic of the *hiraṇyagarbha-mantra*, and thus confusion would indeed result.
This is not correct, because the unseen merit of the restriction is produced by the restriction itself, and therefore does not arise from the *sāman*.

Even if [the performance] were produced by that [injunction], since the manifestation of the syllables and so forth—which have a visible purpose—present themselves first, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*) does not serve as the motivator for the property of being a means (*sādhanatva*), because the visible purpose alone is the motivator.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of non-dharma arising from the threshing of *kṛṣṇala* grains in the *caru* offering.

This being the position reached, we reply: even though there is the state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) by what is produced by the hymn (*stotra*), the establishment of the settled rule (*vyavasthā*) is achieved due to the difference in intermediate effects (*antarakāryabheda*).

For instance, the status of being a *stotra* (hymn) consists of the properties of the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [sāmans]. In the case of the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, there is either a difference in genus (*vaijātya*) or not; however, it does not reside in the individual manifestation of the expression of each quality, because the status of having twelve *stotras* would otherwise be untenable. Rather, it resides distributively across the individual manifestations of the expression of the qualities of those respective *stotras*. And there is no simultaneity among them, because they are momentary and occur sequentially.

Therefore, it must necessarily be stated that from the denotation of each respective quality (*guṇa*), there arise *saṃskāras* (purificatory impressions) which are of the nature of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).

And by means of these, a single individual instance of denotation (*abhidhāna-vyakti*) arises, which consists of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of the entire group of qualities and is delimited by being a praise (*stotra*) belonging to each respective class. Furthermore, since this [denotation] produces praises of different classes, a distinction in kind (*vaijātya*) must necessarily exist even in the *saṃskāra*. Thus, according to the principle of the "restriction of speech in the Dīkṣaṇīyā" (*dīkṣaṇīyā-vāg-niyama-nyāya*), those specific properties (*dharmas*) are prompted solely by the respective collection of *saṃskāras*; consequently, there is no confusion (*sāṃkarya*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

And in the case of the *Kaṇvarathantara*, by the principle of the *Hiraṇyagarbha* mantra, since there is an injunction for the manifestation of the expression of qualities numbering ten each produced by the respective other *ṛc*s—precisely through the generation of the two groups of those respective sets of consecrations (*saṃskāra*)—there follows the attainment of the properties (*dharma*) prompted by those respective groups of consecrations; thus, everything is free from confusion.
Maṇḍana [states]: “The properties of the *sāman* are fixed. Śaṅkara [states]: “There is a distinction between the *pṛṣṭhya* and the *ṛca*.”
"Bṛhadyantarasāman" (referring to the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha in the Gavāmayana) is a multi-word *bahuvrīhi* compound;
it is not a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva*.
Thus, on some days the *rathaṃtara* is used, and on others the *bṛhat*.
It is not prescribed as belonging to both *sāmans* combined.
Bhāṣya 10.6.14–5: In the archetype (*prakṛti*), only the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* *sāmans* are prescribed as subsidiaries, but not both of them together.
Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*) [between them], and there is no extension (*atideśa*) of their respective sources.
There is no *bṛhat-sāman* consisting of a single metre;
its first [part] is a *kākubha-pragātha*.
The first is a *bṛhatī*, the second is a *paṅkti*.
By means of the first of these two, they become one *bṛhatī* and two *kakubhs*; in these, the *bṛhat-sāman* is to be sung.
(This is the point of reflection.)

Regarding this, it can indeed be stated in the *Sarvānukramaṇī* that the *kākubha-pragātha* consists of a *kakup*, a *satobṛhatī*, and a *sthita-paṅkti*; however, the *kakup* belongs to the *uṣṇih* class and not to the *bṛhatī* class (Ke.).
